Ache and Batak hunters are reported to receive no more than other band members. Small game was often eaten within the acquirer's own family among the Dobe !Kung and the G/wi.

Among the Ache and the Hiwi, women gave away about 55% of all the plant food they collected, and there was no sex difference in sharing once package size was controlled. Across societies, direct requests for food, when not excessive, were rarely refused, while unsolicited giving varied widely. Gurven also lists reported sanctions against people who did not share or produce (gossip, exclusion from shares, being forced out of the household or village) and cases where low producers were tolerated, and notes that punishment has not been studied systematically in any group.

197.content: Among Ache foragers, meat and honey were shared across the whole band, so a hunter's own family ate only a small share of what he brought in.

198.content: Much forager sharing happens because others ask for it, and refusing is hard, so sharing is driven as much by demand as by generosity.

In the abstract Peterson argues that demand sharing is testing, assertive or substantiating behaviour, and that it matters for building social relations in egalitarian societies. He says a behaviouristic model of demand sharing fits sociobiological expectations, and that his emphasis is on the social and symbolic meaning of the practice.

199.content: Forager adults produced more food than they ate and transferred the surplus to children and others, because children take many years to become net producers.

In Kaplan and colleagues' Table 1, women's mean age at first reproduction was 19.5 years among the Ache, 20.5 among the Hiwi and 19.2 among the !Kung (forager mean 19.7); the mean interval to the next birth after a surviving infant was 37.6, 45.1 and 41.3 months (mean 41.3, about 3.4 years); and mean age at last reproduction was 42.1, 37.8 and 37 years (mean 39.0). Female chimpanzees give birth for the first time about five years earlier, and their interbirth interval after a surviving infant is more than 1.5 times longer.

Using measured food acquisition and estimated consumption by age among the Ache of Paraguay, the Hiwi of Venezuela and the Hadza of Tanzania, the authors find that by age 15 forager children had consumed over 25% of their expected lifetime energy but had acquired less than 5% of their lifetime food. Chimpanzee juveniles, by contrast, feed themselves from weaning, and acquisition and consumption are almost the same from the juvenile period on.

In the same three forager societies, daily food acquisition rose steeply in the late juvenile years and kept rising until mid-adulthood; Ache and Hiwi men's daily returns from hunting did not peak until about age 35. The surplus of acquisition over consumption came in the later part of life, and the authors read the averaged data as showing that men provided most of the surplus that fed juveniles and women of reproductive age. Across ten foraging societies with quantitative data, men provided more food energy per day than women in all but one or two.

200.content: Some anthropologists argue that men hunt big game partly to gain status and allies, since the meat is shared widely and their own families get little extra.

201.content: A review of ethnographic reports found that women in many forager societies took part in hunting.

202.content: Across ten Agta camps whose non-foraging share of out-of-camp work ranged from 0% to 80%, a higher share of non-foraging (mostly farm) work went with less leisure (beta -0.185, 95% CI -0.35 to -0.02, P = 0.031) and more total out-of-camp work (beta 0.164, P = 0.041). The link held for women (beta -0.278, P = 0.003) and not for men (beta -0.090, P = 0.357), and a multilevel model controlling for age, sex and having a child under two gave the same result.

Among the Agta, small-scale hunter-gatherers of the northern Philippines (fieldwork 2013 and 2014, 359 people in ten camps, four observational scans a day in daylight, 10,706 person-observations), adults (N = 142) spent on average 29.2% of daylight time on out-of-camp work (foraging and non-foraging), 24.0% on domestic chores, 12.2% on direct childcare and 34.7% at leisure (socialising, resting, playing and sleeping). Men did more out-of-camp work (41.1% against 17.3%) and women more chores and childcare, but leisure did not differ by sex (33.8% against 35.5%), about one third of daylight hours.

Among Agta adults, 71.9% of leisure time (1,491 observations) was spent in close proximity to at least one other adult, on average 2.20 other adults, with no sex difference; 49% of these adult interactions were with people unrelated by genetic or marriage kinship.

203.content: Sahlins argued that foragers met their needs with a few hours of food-getting a day and had much free time, calling them the original affluent society.

204.content: Hadza participants averaged over two hours a day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, more than 14 times as much as participants in large US studies.

Continuous heart-rate monitoring of 46 Hadza adults from two camps in northern Tanzania found 134.9 minutes a day (plus or minus 8.6) of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, kept up across the lifespan and over 14 times the amount measured in large US epidemiological studies. Blood pressure (198 people) stayed low across ages, and blood markers of heart health (23 people: C-reactive protein, cholesterol, triglycerides) were at optimal levels.

205.content: A meta-ethnography of 58 publications on how forager children learn subsistence skills found that learning starts in infancy, when parents take children on foraging trips and give them toy versions of tools. In early and middle childhood children move into the multi-age playgroup, where they learn through play, observation and participation, and most are proficient food collectors by the end of middle childhood. Adults, not necessarily the parents, begin directly teaching complex skills such as hunting and complex tool making only in adolescence.

The same review reports that across cultures forager children keep taking part in foraging activities when no adults are present, and the authors describe forager learning as an ongoing, playful activity that children join by choice and that is not set apart from the rest of life. They contrast this with studies of small-scale farmers, which describe a compulsory chore curriculum.

206.content: Observers listening to relaxed conversations in public settings found they consisted mostly of social information, mostly personal relationships and experiences, and most exchanges were about the speaker or third parties; very few were criticism or the asking or giving of advice.

Observational studies of human conversations in relaxed social settings found that they consist mostly of exchanges of social information, mostly about personal relationships and experiences; most exchanges concerned the speaker or third parties, and very few were critical comments or the asking or giving of advice.

207.content: In five naturalistic studies (467 people wearing an audio recorder that sampled 5 to 12% of 2 to 5 days), gossip tended to be neutral rather than positive or negative, and was mostly about social information.

Across five naturalistic studies (467 people wearing an audio recorder that sampled 5 to 12% of 2 to 5 days), women engaged in more neutral gossip than men. The abstract does not report a sex difference in total or negative gossip.

208.content: In experiments, people passed on reputational information about selfish players even at a cost to themselves, and the threat of gossip made others behave more generously.

209.content: Among the Ju/'hoansi, daytime talk was mostly about economic matters, complaints and gossip, while firelight talk at night was mostly stories.

Among the Ju/'hoansi of /Kae/kae and Dobe, Botswana, in 1974, families ate the evening meal each at their own fire. After dinner and dark, people gathered around single fires to talk, make music or dance, in larger or smaller groups, and went back to their own hearths to sleep. Wiessner states that meat was shared in waves, each receiver giving on to kin, until every person present had a share.

In 122 daytime conversations among the Ju/'hoansi, 34% of talk was complaint or criticism, and the author judged about a third of that criticism to be moved by envy. Close to 95% of these disputes were between the people directly affected. Where talk did not settle a dispute, people moved away. Two disputes in the sample went as far as brandishing poison arrows, and both times others physically held the aggressor back. Complaint and criticism were rarer at night.

On 6 of the 36 evenings Wiessner observed among the Ju/'hoansi, a trance-healing dance was held: three smaller ones and three that lasted all night and drew people from three or more camps. She describes trance healing as the only activity in which whole bands worked together toward one result, with women clapping and singing for hours in support of the healers. On 8 of the 36 evenings women broke into festive song and dance.

Among the Ju/'hoansi of /Kae/kae and Dobe, northwest Botswana, Wiessner noted 174 conversations in July to August and November 1974 (122 by day, 52 at night). At night, 81% of lengthy conversations involving many people were stories, and she reports these were largely about known people. 41 of the 52 night stories (79%) were about the exploits of people who were direct or indirect xaro (gift-exchange) partners, against 9 of 122 day conversations (7%). Protagonists came from places across the region, some up to about 200 km away, and she writes that people went to sleep with absent kin in their thoughts and not infrequently left to visit them soon after.

210.content: In the US, India and Israel, how much shame people expected to feel in 29 imagined situations closely matched how much a separate group of local raters would think less of someone in that situation (mean r .72 across the three countries). Shame also tracked devaluation by raters from the other two countries (mean r .64).

211.content: Among 899 people in 15 small-scale communities (farmers, herders, fishers and horticulturalists on several continents; none of them mobile foragers), the shame people expected to feel over 12 imagined acts or traits tracked how much their own community would devalue someone for them (mean r 0.84). It tracked the devaluation of the other communities less closely (mean r 0.69).

212.content: In hunter-gatherer populations with minimal or no exposure to modern medicine, about 57 percent of children survived to age 15, and the most common age of adult death was about 70 (68 to 78 across populations).

Pooling 3,328 recorded deaths from hunter-gatherer and forager-horticulturalist populations (among them Hadza, !Kung, Ache, Hiwi, Agta, Yanomamo and Tsimane, some partly acculturated), Gurven and Kaplan find that illness accounted for about 70% of deaths, violence and accidents for about 20%, and degenerative disease for about 9%. Fewer than half of all deaths in the sample were from contact-related disease.

Violent death varied widely between the populations: the Agta, Ache, Yanomamo and Hiwi had high levels of homicide, falling mostly on adult men, while homicide was low among the Hadza, Tsimane and Northern Territory Aborigines. Accidental and violent deaths together ranged from 4% to 69% of all deaths across groups, averaging 19%. The authors judge that violent deaths fall with state intervention and missionary influence.

Among the Ache of Paraguay the share of violent death changed with contact: in the pre-contact forest sample violence made up a large share of deaths, which the authors put down to the small number of illness deaths in that sample, and much of the violence was infanticide, child homicide and skirmishes with rural Paraguayans, while the post-contact Ache sample shows 14% violent and accidental deaths and 68% illness.

213.content: Across 20 forager societies, about 49 percent of children died before age 15.

214.content: In a cross-cultural sample, foragers had famine less often than farmers, after controlling for habitat quality.

215.content: Ethnographic accounts show forager societies were no more food insecure than farming societies, against the assumption that foragers lived through constant feast and famine.

216.content: Most major crowd infections of today, such as measles and smallpox, arose after farming, when dense settled populations lived close to domestic animals.

217.content: Using the most recent ethnographic compilation of plant-to-animal subsistence patterns among hunter-gatherers, the authors report that 73% of worldwide hunter-gatherer societies got more than half of their subsistence from animal foods and 14% got more than half from gathered plant foods. From these ratios they estimate that hunter-gatherers took 45 to 65% of energy from animal food wherever the environment allowed, with protein at 19 to 35% of energy and carbohydrate at 22 to 40%.

218.content: Hadza men and women both rank honey as their favorite food, and it supplies a substantial share of Hadza calories, especially for men.

219.content: In a meta-analysis of 288 results from 46 studies in 33 non-industrial societies, higher-status men had greater reproductive success (overall r 0.19, against 0.80 in non-human primates). The effect in foragers (Zr 0.18, 64 results) was about the same as in horticulturalists, pastoralists and farmers.

In the same meta-analysis, status went with men's fertility and mating success more than with lower child mortality. Status was linked to fewer child deaths only in polygynous societies, and the link between status and number of surviving offspring was about a third smaller in monogamous societies.

220.content: A review of the evidence concluded that the desire for status, meaning respect and admiration from others, is a fundamental human motive.

221.content: A meta-analysis found that males are more physically aggressive than females at all ages and across cultures, while girls show more indirect aggression than boys only in later childhood and adolescence, depending on how it is measured.

222.content: Women compete with other women mainly through indirect aggression, such as gossip and social exclusion, which costs the aggressor little physical risk.

223.content: Roughly half or more of people who lose a close person keep a stable pattern of healthy functioning, while about 10 to 15 percent keep high scores on depression and distress measures.

In this narrative review Bonanno states that across bereavement studies chronic high scores on depression and distress measures tend to occur in 10 to 15% of bereaved people, that many more show disruptions lasting several months to one or two years, and that people with relatively low depression or distress scores have approached or exceeded 50% of the sample in studies reporting aggregate data. He reports that absent grief was treated by most bereavement experts surveyed as denial that would surface later, and that the studies he reviews found no delayed grief among people with low scores.

For violent and life-threatening events Bonanno reports that the large majority of exposed people in the studies he reviews did not go on to meet criteria for chronic PTSD. The shares he cites of people who met criteria for chronic PTSD run from 6.6% and 9.9% after the 1992 Los Angeles riots, 12.5% of Gulf War veterans and 16.5% of people hospitalised after motor vehicle accidents to 17.8% of physical assault victims. He cites a survey of Manhattan residents after the attacks of 11 September 2001 in which the share estimated to meet PTSD criteria fell from 7.5% at one month to 1.7% at four months and 0.6% at six months.

224.content: A meta-analysis estimated that about one in ten bereaved adults develops prolonged grief after a natural death.

225.content: Chimpanzees observed around a dying group member behaved in ways that resemble human responses to death, such as attending closely and staying near the body.

226.content: Music is found in every society studied, and songs used for the same purpose, such as lullabies, dance songs or healing songs, share acoustic features across cultures that let listeners and computer models identify their purpose better than chance.

227.content: A global sample of 304 recordings found statistical universals in music, and the authors suggested that many of them may help groups coordinate and hold together.

228.content: Dancing in synchrony raised people's pain thresholds and their feelings of closeness to the other dancers.

229.content: One account holds that music evolved with culture as a system for social bonding between people.

230.content: Among Agta foragers of Palanan, the Philippines, 291 adults in 18 camps named who they would most like to live with. People rated as skilled storytellers by their campmates had about twice the odds of being picked (odds ratio 1.95), more than for any other skill measured (good fishers came second, odds ratio 1.5), after controlling for kinship, reciprocal nominations, distance, age and sex. Skilled storytellers had 0.53 more living children than less skilled ones (n = 324, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.96, controlling for age, sex and camp).

231.content: The grandmother hypothesis holds that long human life after menopause evolved because older women fed their weaned grandchildren, which let their daughters have babies sooner.

232.content: Across hunting records from 40 sites in subsistence societies, hunting skill rose into adulthood and peaked on average around age 33, then declined only slowly, so skill stayed high through much of adulthood.

233.content: In three pre-industrial groups (Hadza, San and Tsimane), people slept about 6 to 7 hours a night, did not sleep longer than industrial adults, and fell asleep as the night got cooler.

Wrist-sensor recordings of Hadza (Tanzania), San (Namibia) and Tsimane (Bolivia) adults showed sleep periods of 6.9 to 8.5 hours with 5.7 to 7.1 hours asleep, near the low end of industrial societies. No group went to sleep near sunset: sleep began on average 3.3 hours after sunset, waking usually came before sunrise, and sleep fell in the night-time period of falling air temperature, ending near its daily low.

Naps were rare. Automated scoring found no afternoon naps in 210 winter days of San recordings and 10 naps in 364 summer days (3% of days). Visual scoring of low-movement spells of 15 minutes or more found them on 7% of San winter afternoons and 22% of summer days, averaging 32 minutes; the authors treat these as an upper limit, since some may be resting awake. The Hadza and Tsimane records showed a similar lack of naps.
Light exposure in all three groups peaked in the morning and dropped sharply at noon, which the authors read as people seeking shade at midday.

234.content: Two Toba/Qom communities in Formosa, Argentina, of the same ethnic background, were compared with wrist actimeters: one with electricity around the clock, one 50 km away with natural light only. The community with electricity went to bed and fell asleep later, with similar wake and rise times, so it slept less: about 43 minutes less near the summer solstice (6 and 6 participants; a trend, significant only on a one-tailed test) and 56 minutes less near the winter solstice (11 and 8 participants; significant). In winter evenings the community with electricity was exposed to brighter light.

235.content: Among Hadza hunter-gatherers in a bush camp near Lake Eyasi, Tanzania, 33 healthy adults (21 women, 12 men; up to 22 per night) wore wrist actigraphs over 20 nights. All of them were scored asleep at the same time for only 18 one-minute epochs in total (0.002% of 13,408 night epochs); a median of eight people were scored awake at any moment, and one or more people were awake or in light sleep during 99.8% of the time between the first person falling asleep and the last waking.

In the same Hadza camp, the midpoint of sleep differed significantly between individuals and shifted with age, while sex, nursing status, number of children sharing the bed and study day did not account for it. A simulation that gave individuals their observed sleep timing reproduced the number of people awake at night (mean 8.94 simulated against 8.65 observed), which a model of identical sleepers did not. Group sleep, from the first person asleep to the last awake, lasted 12 h, against about 6.25 h of sleep per individual, with on average 2.4 h awake after first falling asleep.

At the start of the Hadza sleep study, participants ranked five possible threats. Lack of food was ranked the most urgent threat by 48.6%, other people came second (29.7%), animals and disease tied (10.8% each), and 75.7% put weather in the least threatening category.

236.content: Historical records from the pre-industrial British Isles describe sleep in two segments, a 'first' and a 'second' sleep, with a waking period between them.

237.content: Forager infancy, as documented among the !Kung and other groups, involved near-constant carrying and body contact, frequent nursing and quick response to crying.

Konner restates his own 1970s spot observations of !Kung infants in Botswana: passive physical contact with the mother fell from about 70 percent of observations in the first months to about 30 percent in the middle of the second year, peaking at about 15 weeks, and contact with anyone peaked at about 90 percent between 10 and 20 weeks, falling to about 42 percent in the middle of the second year. Mothers accounted for 75 to 80 percent of all physical contact infants received.

Reviewing Tronick, Morelli and Winn's study of Efe foragers of the Ituri forest, Konner reports that people other than the mother accounted for 39 percent of an infant's physical contact at 3 weeks and 60 percent at 18 weeks, that infants were passed between carers 3.7, 5.6 and 8.3 times an hour at 3, 7 and 18 weeks, that each infant was cared for by 5 to 24 different people (mean 14.2), and that eight of ten infants were sometimes nursed by women other than the mother. Fussing or crying drew an attempt to comfort within ten seconds 85 percent of the time in the first seven weeks.

Konner quotes Tronick and colleagues' later report on the Efe: infants and toddlers spent almost all their time in social contact with others, and although contact declined with age, 3-year-olds still spent most of their time in physical and social contact; Efe infants and toddlers were almost never out of sight or hearing of other people.

238.content: Among the Hadza, people other than the mother spent time holding infants and toddlers, with closer kin holding them most and unrelated helpers of all ages also providing a substantial amount of care.

Among the Hadza of Tanzania (42,031 person scans of 470 people in ten camps over 17 months; 68 children aged four and under), 69% of the total time children were held was by their mother and 31% by allomothers, who ranged in age from 1.5 to 79 years. Unrelated people accounted for 12.4% of holding time and fathers for 7.1%.

Among Hadza holders, juveniles aged 1.5 to 17.9 years made up 62% of all allomothers; girls far outnumbered boys and spent a significantly greater share of their time holding children, with holding by girls highest between eight and twelve years of age.

239.content: Woodburn described some African forager societies in which disposal of the dead went little beyond practical need and the camp was generally abandoned after a death.

240.content: In 1974, Ju/'hoansi men and women at /Kae/kae (Botswana) each kept on average 15 hxaro gift-exchange partnerships with kin living 2 to 200 km away. The average person spent 4.4 months a year living with hxaro partners, and 69% of possessions had been received as hxaro gifts. About 70% of /Kae/kae residents' partners lived across the border in Namibia, in the same ethnic group.

Among the Ju/'hoansi, 44 years of possession and spending data (1974 /Kae/kae, Botswana; 2017 to 2018 Nyae Nyae, Namibia) show that cash income brought large differences in material wealth, even between neighbours, while hxaro gift partnerships shrank. Social, gender and political equality held: people did not hire other Ju/'hoansi as workers and fewer than 6.7% of debts were owed to other Ju/'hoansi, and money was rarely spent on status beyond clothes and a phone.

Wiessner and Huang describe hxaro, the Ju/'hoansi gift-exchange partnership, from Wiessner's fieldwork at /Kae/kae, Botswana, in the 1970s: partners stored help in each other and planned for returns that came years later. Partnerships began with close blood kin, and relatedness thinned as partnerships were passed down from parents to children across generations, so that trust rested on a history of mutual support. One Ju/'hoan explained why unproductive partnerships were kept up: useless people often have good children.

Comparing 1974 /Kae/kae (Botswana) with 2017 to 2018 Nyae Nyae (Namibia), the share of Ju/'hoansi gifts that came from distant kin or non-kin fell from 23% to 1%, and the share of gifts that came from within the person's own village rose from 35% (187 of 538 gifts) to 45% (608 of 1,337). Hxaro partnerships had already halved by 1997, and by 2018 few people knew hxaro except from stories.

241.content: Among Aka forager children aged 4 to 16, play gave way to work as they grew older, and Aka children did less rough-and-tumble play and fewer competitive games than neighbouring farmer children.

242.content: In Marlowe's cross-cultural sample of foragers, the median residential group size was 27 people (mean 41.4, range 13 to 250, across 263 societies).

243.content: In a cross-cultural study of bereavement, women cried more often than men during bereavement, and where final ceremonies for the dead were held, prolonged grief was less common.

244.content: Singh and Glowacki review ethnographic and archaeological findings from 34 world regions and conclude that non-agricultural peoples often live in groups that are more sedentary, unequal, large and politically stratified, and more capable of large-scale cooperation and resource management, than the nomadic-egalitarian model assumes. Archaeological findings from 27 Middle Stone Age sites suggest to them that such societies existed throughout the Late Pleistocene (to about 130,000 years ago). They propose a diverse histories model in its place.

245.content: A meta-analysis found that the sex differences people state in mate preferences for looks and earning prospects barely predict whom they actually like in face-to-face meetings or relationships.

246.content: A review argued that the sex difference in jealousy appears mainly in hypothetical forced-choice questions and weakens or disappears in reports of real infidelity and other measures.

247.content: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends room-sharing without bed-sharing, saying room-sharing on a separate surface can cut SIDS risk by up to half and avoids the suffocation risks of adult beds.

248.content: A reanalysis argued that women's hunting in forager societies was occasional and that a sexual division of labor in hunting was real.

249.content: Data from the Alyawara showed that once food processing is counted, foragers spent far more time on getting food than the original affluent society figures suggested.

250.content: A review found weak and inconsistent evidence that pretend play causes the developmental gains often credited to it.

251.content: Forager diets varied so widely with habitat and season that they fit no single standard pattern that modern people could copy for better health.

252.content: A meta-analysis of 148 studies of children and adolescents found that boys showed more direct aggression than girls, while the sex difference in indirect aggression was trivial.

253.content: A rival account holds that music evolved as a credible signal, of coalition strength in group song and of parental attention in infant song, and that it signals existing social bonds rather than creating them.

254.content: A simulation model found that grandmothering alone was not enough to select for the long human post-reproductive lifespan.

255.content: Among foragers in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, societies where men contributed more to subsistence were more monogamous.

256.content: Across societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, closer father-infant care and higher male contribution to subsistence go with less polygyny, and foragers tend to show closer father-infant relationships than pastoralists.

257.content: About 85 percent of societies in the anthropological record permitted a man to have more than one wife. Normative monogamy spread from classical Greece and Rome and, in recent centuries, worldwide, with laws against polygyny arriving in Japan in 1880, China in 1953, India in 1955 and Nepal in 1963.

Henrich and colleagues state that in relatively egalitarian societies, including most foragers, few men gain enough status to attract a second wife, usually no more than one extra, and very successful men rarely obtain three or at most four. Among tropical African foragers, rates of polygyny range from 3 to 20 percent.

258.content: In five societies with detailed data (Ache, Hadza, !Kung, Lamalera and Meriam), better hunters had higher age-corrected reproductive success than other men in their group.

259.content: Among Hadza men, upper-body strength predicted their reputation as hunters and their reproductive success.

260.content: Among 49 Hadza men from nine camps, those with lower-pitched voices had more living children and more children born, controlling for age; pitch did not predict child mortality. In 52 Hadza women, pitch did not predict any reproductive outcome.

261.content: Hadza participants preferred symmetric faces, as UK participants did, and the preference was stronger among the Hadza.

262.content: Hadza and British participants both preferred averaged faces, but the Hadza did not prefer averaged faces made from European faces.

263.content: Across 128 lowland South American societies, ethnographies report a belief that a child can have more than one biological father in 53 societies and single paternity in 23, with 52 unknown; the authors judge the true share somewhat below the 70 percent (53 of 76) this gives, because unusual beliefs are more likely to be recorded. Phylogenetic reconstruction places the belief deep in Amazonian prehistory.

264.content: Among Himba pastoralists in Namibia, a double-blind genetic paternity study estimated that 48 percent of children were fathered outside the marriage (95 percent credible interval 32 to 66 percent), and 70 percent of couples had at least one such child. The community's own estimate was 47 percent, and both men and women were accurate at telling which children were extramarital.

Scelza and colleagues note that genetic studies of contemporary and historical populations, almost all of European descent, have consistently found very low rates of children fathered outside the pair (about 1 to 2 percent), and the one earlier non-Western study, of the Dogon of Mali, found 1.8 percent. Ethnographic codes tell a different story: 57 percent of societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample are reported to have moderate to universal rates of female infidelity.

265.content: Across 11 populations, eight of them small-scale societies, men were more likely than women to choose sexual infidelity as the more upsetting kind, and both sexes rated infidelity more severely where paternal investment was higher.

266.content: A cross-cultural review of homicide records and adultery laws found male sexual jealousy to be a leading motive in homicide, and male violence or its threat used to control women's sexuality appeared in every culture reviewed.

267.content: Across 48 nations, men on average reported more interest in uncommitted sex than women, and the difference was smaller where women had more economic and political power.

268.content: Most primates share little food, mostly by tolerating scrounging, while human foragers share widely among adults through kin ties, reciprocity and signaling, and rely on sharing more than any other primate.

269.content: Among the Hadza, at least 90 percent of the meat from large game went to households other than the hunter's, and the hunter's household got no bigger share than other households except from the very largest kills (over 180 kg), where it took about 10 percent against about 5 percent.

Among the Hadza of Tli'ika, Tanzania (camps of about 35 to 50 people, 20 large animals and 113 household shares recorded in 1985 to 1988), at least 90% of the meat of large prey went outside the hunter's household. The successful hunter's household took about 5% of prey under 180 kg and about 10% of prey over 180 kg; other men's households took about 5% each. A household was left out of a distribution in fewer than 10% of cases, and men who supplied more meat did not get more back.

In the same Hadza record, large carcasses were butchered on the spot and much meat was eaten at the kill site, sometimes over several hours, by men, women and children who gathered there. Meat carried back was assigned to households before transport and was usually cooked and eaten by the household it was assigned to, with others often joining in. Most honey was eaten where it was collected. Claims at kill sites were insistent, and the authors call the style demand sharing.

Hawkes and colleagues state that among the Hadza everyone knows who acquired a large carcass, while the hunter does not control where the meat goes. They contrast credit for the kill with title to the meat, citing the !Kung rule that names the owner of the first arrow, who may be someone other than the hunter, as owner of the animal, and they propose that what a hunter earns is favourable attention that raises his standing among men. The knowing is their field observation; it was not measured.

270.content: In a settled Ache community of forager-horticulturists in Paraguay, adults who gave away more of the food they produced received more food from more people when they were sick or injured.

Among the Ache of Paraguay living at the Arroyo Bandera settlement (117 residents, studied January to May 1998), 50 adults were asked to recall the last time they were so hurt that they had to stay in bed; 39 described an episode (61 percent sickness, 26 percent injury, 13 percent recent childbirth; median length 3.5 days). On average a disabled adult received 3.3 food items, 0.7 of them meat, from 2.4 people, of whom 1.7 were outside the nuclear family. Men received food from more people than women did.

Among the same 39 Ache adults in Paraguay, those who gave away more than the median share of the food they produced (the median was 87 percent; n = 19) received food from more people, including more people outside the nuclear family, and received more food items when sick or injured than those who gave away less (n = 20; Wilcoxon rank sum tests significant at the 5 or 10 percent level). High production alone showed little association with help received: the 3 high producers who gave away a small share received less help than the 12 low producers who gave away a large share, although the 3 gave away more food in absolute terms. The authors conclude that the share a person gave, more than the amount, shaped who was helped, and state that they cannot rule out reverse causality or separate the result fully from the length of the episode.

271.content: In economic games played in 15 small-scale societies, including foragers, offers varied widely between societies and were higher where daily life involved more market exchange and cooperation.

272.content: Among Martu hunters of Australia, the authors find a significant association between how large a share of their own harvest a person gives away and how central that person is in the cooperative hunting network. People who consistently paid higher relative costs to share, not necessarily the better hunters, were the preferred partners for cooperative hunting. The authors read this as generosity that signals prosocial intent and builds trusting partnerships.

273.content: In the same study, 60.1% of children's social play observations were in mixed-gender groups (70.1% among the Hadza, 54.8% among the BaYaka), and children played in mixed-gender groups less often in camps with more available playmates; camps held on average 15.7 children aged 3 to 18. Pretend and object play were the most common types of play, and pretend play usually copied adult activities, such as building small huts, and children were more likely to take part in work-themed pretend play that matched their society's gender roles.

In focal follows of Hadza (Tanzania, 46 children from 3 camps, 2017) and BaYaka (Republic of Congo, 65 children from 7 camps, 2016 to 2018) children and adolescents aged 3 to 18, each child was observed in a morning and an afternoon 2-hour block (roughly 8 am to 3 pm). Children and adolescents spent 24.2% of observations in play (Hadza 17.6%, BaYaka 27.7%), 16.8% and 12.2% in foraging or gardening, 5.1% and 11.7% in domestic work, 23.6% and 17.6% in travel and 26.5% and 19.1% at rest. Adolescents played about 4.8 times less than children aged 3 to 6, and adolescent girls played less than younger girls while adolescent boys did not. Most play happened in or near camp (about 70%) and most of it was social (92.5% of Hadza play, 83.9% of BaYaka play).

274.content: A review of 77 publications on forager children found that adults actively teach sharing from infancy, that children learn cooperation from other children in playgroups, and that gender roles are learned mostly by imitating same-sex adults, with more direct teaching and chores among settled foragers.

A meta-ethnographic review of 77 publications with primary data on how hunter-gatherer children learn social and gender norms found that adults rarely use coercion or punishment to control children, with reports from the Batek, Paliyan, Baka and Wik among others. Misbehaviour is reported to be met with distraction, persuasion, ignoring, or threats. Actual violence against children appears uncommon in these accounts, while the threat of it, by gesture or by a bogeyman figure, is common; as an exception the review cites a 1941 report that the Crow and Blackfoot dunked or doused children with water. When small children fight, adults among the San, Mbuti, Anbarra and Batek separate and distract them, and older children in the playgroup often step into quarrels.

275.content: Hadza children, even very young ones, collected a considerable amount of their own food, and older children collected more.

276.content: In focal follows of Hadza and BaYaka children, teaching of foraging skills did occur, and much of it came from other children.

277.content: Konner's hunter-gatherer childhood model describes a gradual shift after infancy from close contact with the mother to a mixed-sex, multi-age play group.

278.content: A review found that physical activity play, including rough-and-tumble play, peaks in childhood, is more common in boys, and may serve physical training and social functions.

279.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalist women, what a woman reported about another woman's reputation predicted how attractive she ranked that woman, which the authors propose as one way women compete.

280.content: Among the Tsimane, women held less political influence than men, and the gap was linked to differences in physical size, education and social network size.

281.content: Campbell argued that women compete with each other mainly through low-risk tactics such as indirect aggression because a mother's survival mattered more for her children's survival than a father's.

282.content: Benenson argued that girls and women compete in ways that keep the risk of retaliation low, such as avoiding open interference, disguising competition, enforcing equality and socially excluding rivals, and that they rely on exclusive one-on-one friendships as allies.

283.content: In a study of 255 undergraduates, young women reported a stronger desire than young men to retaliate with indirect aggression such as gossip against a same-sex classmate who had spread false accusations about them.

284.content: In experiments, women passed on damaging social information about a romantic rival more often than about a non-rival.

285.content: Listeners in 60 countries rating short excerpts of unfamiliar songs from 86 mostly small-scale societies correctly inferred which were dance songs and lullabies, and to a lesser degree healing songs, but did not reliably recognise love songs.

286.content: Hagen and Bryant proposed that music and dance evolved as signals of a coalition's quality, and found that altering a performance's synchrony changed how good listeners judged the music, while listeners' music-quality ratings correlated with their coalition-quality ratings.

287.content: Seven new weekly adult education classes in the UK (four singing classes with 84 participants, two craft classes and one creative writing class with 51 participants; mostly women, aged 18 to 83) were followed over seven months. At months 1, 3 and 7, participants rated their closeness to their class as a whole (Inclusion of Other in Self scale) before and after class. Singers showed a significantly greater rise in closeness within the session at month 1; the non-singers' more gradual rise had caught up by month 3, when both groups felt equally connected.

288.content: A meta-analysis found that moving in synchrony with others increased prosocial behaviour and positive feelings toward them, with small to medium effects.

289.content: Four-year-olds who had made music together helped each other more afterwards than children who had played a similar game without music.

290.content: Forager stories carry practical information about animals, plants and landscapes, which suggests storytelling helped pass on subsistence knowledge.

291.content: Ethnographic accounts from forager, forager-horticulturalist and forager-pastoralist societies describe adults telling stories to teach children about the land, animals and proper behaviour, and describe stories that map places and warn of environmental hazards.

292.content: Genetic studies of historical and contemporary Western populations put the rate of children fathered by someone other than the presumed father at about 1 to 2 percent per generation.

293.content: A cross-cultural review argued that sex differences in behaviour come mainly from the division of labour and physical sex differences interacting with local economies, and so vary with social conditions.

294.content: A cross-cultural survey found reports of women's physical aggression, often against other women and often over men, in a large share of societies.

295.content: Pinker argued that music may be a by-product of faculties that evolved for other purposes, with no adaptive function of its own.

296.content: !Kung camps were highly crowded, and the !Kung showed no biological indicators of stress from it.

Among the !Kung of the Kalahari in Botswana and South-West Africa, living conditions in camps were highly crowded, the !Kung appeared to be crowded by choice, and biological indicators of stress were absent; the author concludes that residential crowding alone does not produce symptoms of pathological stress.

297.content: Among the Nyae Nyae !Kung observed between 1951 and 1961, the medicine dance drew in the whole community: the women sang and clapped while the men danced in a circle around them.

298.content: Hadza men in the 1980s hunted big game almost to the exclusion of other prey even though they rarely succeeded, and most of the meat went to people outside their own households.

Reanalysing Wood and Marlowe's published Hadza tables (2005 to 2009), Hawkes, O'Connell and Blurton Jones report that hunters' households received on average 42% of a large animal in the primary distribution in camp, but that Wood and Marlowe's own estimate of the big-game meat brought to camp that was eaten in the producer's household is 18%, so on average 82% was eaten in other households. Their own 1980s Hadza data put the hunter's household share at 10% or less of a big animal's live weight.

In the authors' own Hadza sample from the 1980s, hunters chose big game over small animals they encountered even though big-game captures were rare (one large carcass per 29 hunter-days on average) and their household's share of a big animal averaged 10% or less of its live weight; by their calculation men were often choosing a household income rate from big game more than ten times lower than they could have earned by taking small game on encounter.

299.content: In one study of Savanna Pume hunter-gatherers and one Yucatec Maya farming village sampled in 1992 and 2011 (27 mother-infant pairs), mothers gave on average 57 percent of an infant's direct care and other people 43 percent, with siblings the main helpers after mothers.

Using behavioural data from Savanna Pume foragers of Venezuela and Yucatec Maya farmers, Kramer and Veile found that across their hunter-gatherer and farming samples mothers gave on average 57 percent of the direct care an infant received and others 43 percent (plus or minus 20). In their models, each 10 percent rise in allocare lowered the probability that a mother was giving direct care by 25 percent, an estimated saving of about 165 kcal a day. Published data they assembled from nine traditional societies show the same pattern: mothers give the most care and others give close to half.

In the same analysis, allocare showed no detectable effect on longer-run fitness measures (birth interval and surviving fertility) or on infant weight status among the Pume and Maya mothers studied, although it changed how mothers spent their time.

300.content: Quebec's Allowance for Newborn Children, a cash payment for each birth, raised fertility among eligible families, with larger effects where the payment was larger.

301.content: In Hungary, the effect of new family-policy measures for parents of three or more children was hard to see in aggregate birth statistics; survey data showed the flat child-rearing payment raised third births among the least educated and the tax relief raised them among the university educated.

302.content: South Korea's fertility fell from 6.0 children per woman in 1960 to 1.3 in 2001 and stayed below 1.3 through the early 2010s, despite government programs to help families raise children.

303.content: Among the Kalahari Kung (Ju/'hoansi), the healing dance began at night, with the women sitting around the fire singing and rhythmically clapping while the men, sometimes joined by women, danced around them, at times until dawn.

304.content: Ache men and women spent on average about 10 percent of their foraging time on cooperative help that cost them time and energy and mainly raised others' foraging success.

Among Ache foragers of Paraguay, the most time-consuming kind of costly help during food acquisition, for both men and women, was helping others in the pursuit of game animals, which the author links to the wide sharing of game among the Ache.

305.content: In an individual-participant meta-analysis of 13 European cohort studies (1985 to 2006; 197,473 employed men and women free of coronary heart disease at baseline), 15% reported job strain (high demands with low control). Over a mean follow-up of 7.5 years there were 2,358 first coronary events. The age and sex adjusted hazard ratio for job strain was 1.23 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.37), 1.17 (1.05 to 1.31) after socioeconomic adjustment; excluding events in the first 3 and 5 years gave 1.31 and 1.30. Published studies gave 1.43 and unpublished ones 1.16. Adjustment for lifestyle factors or the Framingham score changed the estimate little. Population attributable risk was 3.4% if the association is causal.

306.content: A meta-analysis led by a Gallup researcher, covering 7,939 business units in 36 companies, found that unit-level employee satisfaction-engagement relates to customer satisfaction, productivity, profit, turnover and accidents.

307.content: US time-use data show time with friends fell sharply from 2003 to 2019 for Americans aged 15 to 24, and the pandemic deepened the national decline already under way.

In the American Time Use Survey (nationally representative one-day time diaries of US residents aged 15 and over, 2003 to 2020), average time spent with friends fell from 60 minutes a day in 2003 to 34 minutes in 2019 and 20 minutes in 2020. Time with friends fell most steeply among people aged 15 to 24.

In the American Time Use Survey (one-day time diaries of US residents aged 15 and over, 2003 to 2020), average time spent alone, meaning with no one else even if others were nearby, rose from 285 minutes a day in 2003 to 309 in 2019 and 333 in 2020: 146 more hours a year by 2019, and as many again in the single year to 2020. The rise was steeper for men (176 hours over the period) than for women (73 hours). The authors add that some time alone is chosen and can be good, so time alone should be read alongside free time and time with others.

308.content: In 68 girls aged 7 to 12 after a lab stressor, talking to their mother by phone kept cortisol low and raised oxytocin, while instant messaging her did not.

In 68 girls aged 7.5 to 12 who did a 15-minute laboratory social stress test (TSST-C) and were then randomly assigned, 17 per group, to be with their mother in person, talk to her by phone, send her instant messages on a lab computer, or rest alone, salivary cortisol change 30 minutes after the stressor was as high in the instant-message group as in the no-contact group, while girls who heard their mother's voice (in person or by phone) had comparably low cortisol change. Girls who instant messaged did not show the urinary oxytocin release seen with voice contact.

309.content: Agta children had on average 8.9 non-kin carers, and child playgroups stood in for mothers; the link to fertility is untested.

Among Agta foragers (78 children aged 0-6 observed in 2014), children aged 2-6 spent about 13 percent of observations in children-only playgroups, where most care partners were children aged 6-11, with sisters more common than brothers, and playgroups were linked to less maternal childcare.

310.content: In the Netherlands, frequent grandparental childcare went with a 66 percent predicted chance of another birth against 35 percent without, while occasional care showed no significant effect.

311.content: In Germany, a 10 percentage point rise in public childcare coverage for children under three raised the county birth rate by about 2.8 percent the following year.

312.content: Newson and colleagues' model predicts that pronatal norms weaken when kin make up a smaller share of people's social contacts, and their role-play studies supported the model's assumption that people judge reproductive choices partly by inclusive fitness.

313.content: In two lab studies with US students, people who briefly walked into a room wearing a T-shirt with a large face on it estimated that about half the people there could name the face (46% for an embarrassing shirt, 48% for a shirt they liked); 23% and 8% actually could (15 wearers and 64 observers per study).

314.content: Elkind described the adolescent 'imaginary audience', the belief that others are as concerned with one's appearance and behaviour as oneself.

315.content: In Study 1, 1,486 people from 62 countries took part in an online experiment, playing a virtual tossing game with two others who were in fact computer-controlled. The more they were left out of the tosses, the more they reported feeling bad, having less control and losing a sense of belonging.
In Study 2 of the same paper, participants who had been ostracized were more likely to conform to others on a later task.

316.content: With Hadza data from 2005 to 2009, hunters' own households were favoured when large game was shared.

With data collected among Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania from 2005 to 2009, Wood and Marlowe report that men foraged for fruit, honey, small animals and large game, and channelled food to their wives, children and kin in other households. Single men brought food to camp on 28% of days, married men without children at home on 31%, and married men with children at home on 42%. In their model the best hunters provided their families 3 to 4 times as much food as median or poor hunters.

317.content: Two meta-analyses found no evidence that artificial surveillance cues, such as images of watching eyes, increase generosity.

318.content: Out of camp, Hadza men and boys were usually far from other GPS-wearing campmates (median 63 m to the nearest one, against 3 m for women and girls).

Among the Hadza hunter-gatherers of northern Tanzania (179 people in 15 camps where 90 to 100% of calories came from wild foods; 2,078 days of GPS-recorded travel), adult women walked on average 7.6 km a day and took 10,888 steps, and adult men walked 12.9 km and took 18,476 steps. Hadza women took about twice and Hadza men about three times the daily steps of smartphone users aged 18 to 75 in a 111-nation sample from middle- and high-income countries (women 4,064, men 5,332). Urban adults in Pretoria, South Africa walked 2.9 km (women) and 3.9 km (men) a day in a GPS study the authors cite.

Among the Hadza, daily walking distance rose steeply with age in boys up to about 15 years and less steeply in girls; at 15, boys walked 12 km a day on average and girls 9 km. The gap was largest at ages 30 to 45 (men about 14 km, women about 8 km). Men's travel peaked near age 32 at about 15 km a day; women's peaked at ages 17 to 20 at about 9 km, fell until 40 and held at about 7 km through age 60. Between 60 and 68, men's daily distance fell by 3.2 km and women's by 0.72 km. Women caring for a child aged 2 or under did not walk clearly less than women without one (difference at age 30 about 0.84 km, credible interval crossing zero; 19 women with and 39 without).

319.content: Fifteen minutes alone calmed people in lab and diary studies, but in the lab it also tended to make them lonelier; in a two-week diary study, people who chose solitude for their own reasons got the calm without the loneliness.

320.content: Apart from the Great Recession's role in the first years, Kearney and colleagues could not identify any economic, policy or social factor responsible for much of the US birth-rate decline from 2007 to 2020.

321.content: A 2023 World Psychiatry narrative review of the most promising candidate biomarkers (neuroimaging, genetic, molecular and peripheral assays) for autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders and PTSD, major depression and bipolar disorder, and substance use disorders states that an enormous societal investment over the past 50 years has identified numerous candidate biomarkers, yet the overwhelming majority have not been proven sufficiently reliable, valid and useful to be adopted clinically. In the general discussion the authors write that most are in the very early stages of development and validation, so an assessment of their clinical utility is premature, and that the general consensus is that psychiatry does not yet have clinically actionable biomarkers. For schizophrenia, none of the reviewed candidate biomarkers has established clinical utility, the fourth and final stage of biomarker development required for incorporation into clinical practice. For autism, the authors write that only genetic testing is regularly used in the clinic, and the genetic syndromes it finds are not specific to autism. The authors name a few candidates for definitive testing: the N170 EEG signal for subgroups within autism, striatal resting-state fMRI indices for treatment response in schizophrenia, and error-related negativity for first onset of generalized anxiety disorder.

322.content: The US National Institute of Mental Health began the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) project in 2009 to develop a research classification system based on dimensions of neurobiology and observable behaviour. The rationale was that current diagnostic systems (DSM, ICD) rely on presenting signs and symptoms, and the validity of their categories has been questioned because they do not map well onto emerging findings from genetics, systems neuroscience and behavioural science. The authors, both at NIMH, write that the reliance on biologically heterogeneous categories as the gold standard for diagnosis has clearly precluded the identification or validation of biomarkers.

323.content: The authors note that patients given psychiatric diagnoses show many biological differences from healthy volunteers, but few of these have led to tests with clinical utility. The reasons the authors give include the lack of a biological gold-standard definition of psychiatric illnesses and a profusion of statistically significant but minimally differentiating findings. They propose that the field stop seeking tests that diagnose DSM-defined disorders and instead identify biologically homogeneous subtypes that cut across diagnoses.

Kapur, Phillips and Insel state that patients with mental disorders show many biological abnormalities that distinguish them from healthy volunteers, but few have become clinical tests. They attribute the delay to the lack of a biological gold-standard definition of illness, many significant but weakly differentiating findings, approximate replications, and comparisons of typical patients against healthy controls.

Kapur, Phillips and Insel state that patients diagnosed with psychiatric disorders show many biological differences from healthy volunteers, yet few of these have become tests with clinical use. They state four reasons: no biological gold-standard definition of psychiatric illnesses, many statistically significant but minimally differentiating findings, approximate replications that neither confirm nor refute, and comparisons of typical patients with healthy controls that do not carry over to the clinic. They propose seeking biologically defined subtypes that cut across the DSM categories.

324.content: In 100 patients with anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis (antibodies against NR1-NR2 NMDA receptors; median age 23, 91 women), 77 presented with prominent psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, agitation, bizarre behaviour, delusional or paranoid thoughts, visual or auditory hallucinations) and were first seen by psychiatrists. 58 of the 98 patients with oncological results had a tumour, most often an ovarian teratoma. Early tumour treatment, usually with immunotherapy, went with better outcome and fewer neurological relapses, and improvement went with falling serum antibody titres.

In 100 patients with antibodies against NR1-NR2 heteromers of the NMDA receptor (median age 23, range 5 to 76; 91 women), 77 presented with prominent psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, agitation, bizarre behaviour, delusional or paranoid thoughts, visual or auditory hallucinations) and were first seen by a psychiatrist, and 23 were first seen by neurologists. Within three weeks 76 had seizures; 88 lost responsiveness, 86 had dyskinesias, 69 had autonomic instability and 66 hypoventilated. Seven patients died of the neurological condition, and in all seven it was identified afterwards from archived cerebrospinal fluid, the authors report.

Fifty-eight of 98 patients assessed had a tumour, most often an ovarian teratoma; 75 of the 100 recovered or had mild deficits and 25 had severe deficits or died. Patients whose tumour was treated within 4 months of neurological onset had better outcomes than the rest, and improvement went with a fall in serum antibody titres. In cultures of rat hippocampal neurons the patients' antibodies lowered the number of cell-surface NMDA receptors and receptor clusters, and removing the antibodies reversed the change.

325.content: An international consensus group describes patients with isolated psychotic presentations, with no or minimal neurological features, who tested positive for neuronal autoantibodies (mainly NMDA-receptor antibodies) and responded to immunotherapy, and proposes criteria for possible, probable and definite autoimmune psychosis for use in psychiatric practice, with the investigations needed to identify such cases.

326.content: The social defeat hypothesis proposes that long-term experience of social defeat, defined as the negative experience of being excluded from the majority group, may sensitize the mesolimbic dopamine system and thereby increase schizophrenia risk, and that it is the common factor behind urban upbringing, migration, childhood trauma, low intelligence and drug abuse as risk factors. In the 2013 update the evidence for social defeat as the mechanism was strongest for migration and childhood trauma and suggestive but insufficient for urban upbringing, low intelligence and drug abuse; evidence that social defeat sensitizes the dopamine system was strong in animals and insufficient in humans for lack of studies.

The 2013 update of the social defeat hypothesis reports that in The Hague and London people from ethnic minorities who lived in neighbourhoods with a high share of their own group had a lower rate of schizophrenia diagnoses, and those in neighbourhoods with a low share a higher rate. It reports a Swedish study that found the same pattern at school level, including for children of Swedish parents in schools with many foreign-born children, and that the raised rate among migrants persists into the second generation.

The authors define social defeat as the negative experience of being excluded from the majority group and propose that long exposure sensitises the mesolimbic dopamine system. They state that this experience is no specific cause of schizophrenia, since many exposed people receive other psychiatric diagnoses, and that it is unlikely to be a necessary or sufficient cause. For the dopamine step they report strong and replicated evidence in rodents and insufficient evidence in humans, with no dopamine studies at all in migrants, people raised in cities, people with low IQ or traumatised people.

327.content: A meta-analysis of population-based incidence studies published 1977-2003 found a mean weighted relative risk of a schizophrenia diagnosis of 2.7 (95% CI 2.3-3.2) for first-generation migrants (40 effect sizes) and 4.5 (95% CI 1.5-13.1) for second-generation migrants (7 effect sizes). Risk was higher for migrants from developing countries (3.3) and from areas where most of the population is black (4.8). The authors read the pattern as suggesting a role for psychosocial adversity.

328.content: A meta-analysis found a linear association between the log odds of a schizophrenia diagnosis and the level of urbanicity: risk in the most urban environment was estimated at 2.37 times that in the most rural (pooled from the 4 studies meeting strict criteria, 95% CI 2.01 to 2.81, with high heterogeneity), and the same effect held when studies of nonaffective psychosis were included.

In the full text, the pooled odds ratio for a schizophrenia diagnosis in the most urban against the most rural setting was 2.37 (95% CI 2.01 to 2.81) across the 4 studies that met strict criteria (urban exposure measured at birth or before age 15; I2 82 percent), and 2.38 (95% CI 1.6 to 3.5; I2 99 percent) across 8 studies when residence-based measures and nonaffective psychosis outcomes were added. All studies came from developed countries and the pooled figure used unadjusted estimates. The authors write that the association does not necessarily imply causation and list selective migration, family-level factors, infections, pollutants, diet and the social environment as candidate explanations.

329.content: Among Aka foragers of the Central African Republic, the exploration range, the area a person explores over a lifetime searching for a mate, visiting kin, hunting and learning, is approximately 50 km and covers an area where they can meet and get to know about 700 people.

Aka adolescents described a death in camp as bringing men, women and children together to cry and talk about the person, followed by a funeral dance of two or three days. They said the ceremony is not for babies because babies return, though one young couple held a small ceremony and dance for their baby; grieving adolescents were consoled mainly by kin.

Among Aka foragers near Bokoka, Central African Republic (20 adolescents aged 10 to 20 interviewed; camps of 25 to 35 people), informants described a death in camp this way: men, women and children all cry, stay together in a group and talk about the person; the body is buried the same or the next day; the camp dances and sings for two or three days. A small ceremony is held a year later, and when prominent people die many camps gather for a memorial. Babies get no ceremony since they are held to return, though one young couple held a small ceremony and dance for theirs. The neighbouring Ngandu farmers laid the body out for several days and kept rituals for adults for years.

Asked who answered their grief, almost all 20 Aka adolescents named family: a mother, father, older sibling or other kin who held them, talked with them, gave them food and kept them company, and one girl said the people in camp listened to her and held her after the burial. None of the Aka said life became harder after a death. The 20 Ngandu farmer adolescents said their sadness eased when they were given the dead person's clothes, money or goods. Some Aka were told to stop crying or they would fall ill. A young mother whose first baby died was consoled by her husband and her parents.

Hewlett summarises Woodburn's 1982 model as holding that foragers, with immediate-return economies, have relatively temporary grief and do not stress social continuity, while farmers and pastoralists, with delayed-return economies, grieve longer for particular lineage kin. Comparing Aka forager and Ngandu farmer adolescents in the Central African Republic (20 interviewed in each group), she found general support for the distinction in ritual: Aka death rituals were shorter and burial quicker, and Ngandu adolescents remembered significantly more male, patrilateral dead. Against the model, the Aka remembered many dead family members and she found no sign that their felt loss was more temporary than the Ngandu's; adolescents in both groups could also say what each person had died of, where Woodburn suggested foragers are less concerned with this.

330.content: Aka forager fathers give more direct care and stay near their infants more than fathers in any other population studied; earlier work credited the net hunt, which takes women and children along with men. Yet fathers give at least four times as much care in camp as out of it, and the author notes that in most preindustrial populations men travel far from camp to hunt or trade.

Hewlett reports that Aka forager fathers give more direct care and are near their infants more than fathers in any other population studied: they are within arm's reach (holding or within 1 m) of their infant more than 50 percent of a 24-hour period and hold their very young infants during the day at least five times more than fathers elsewhere. Father care is at least four times higher in camp than when the father is out on the net hunt or in villagers' fields.

331.content: In four modern human foraging groups, women's average age at first birth was 18.8 to 20.5 years: Hadza 18.77, !Kung 19.2, Ache 19.5, Hiwi 20.5.

332.content: Among Agta foragers of the Philippines interviewed in 2013-14, the 130 women who had given birth reported a mean age at first birth of 20.2 years (SD 4.3), and births were spaced on average 2.7 years apart (SD 1.4, 258 intervals).

333.content: !Kung foraging mothers at Dobe observed by Howell had birth intervals of about four years, which Blurton Jones and Sibly's backload model explained as the interval that maximised surviving offspring given the weight mothers had to carry.

334.content: Among Mbendjele BaYaka forest foragers, men who hunt a lot are teased and mocked when people feel the group eats their meat too often, and one persistent hunter was in effect exiled; elderly women's mocking re-enactment of misconduct (moadjo) ends, if the target is present, only when they laugh too. Lewis says of immediate-return societies generally that braggarts are teased, avoided and, if they persist, exiled.

Among the Mbendjele BaYaka, people with recognised skill hold named specialist roles (spirit guardian, song composer, speaker, healer, elephant hunter). In elephant hunting, childbirth, severe illness or ritual, the most skilled person is consulted for advice in that area, but cannot oblige anyone to follow it and gets no standing or privilege outside that activity.

335.content: Among Mbendjele BaYaka foragers, camp members are called to the middle of camp for spirit plays where they sing interlocking parts together, some stand up to dance, no one directs participation, and people who sit apart or sing weakly are criticised; a minority of plays are gender-exclusive and initiates control secret parts.

336.content: Across 131 largely non-industrial societies coded from ethnography, reputational punishment (community-endorsed reputational damage, coded as more than gossip) was associated with egalitarianism and absence of food storage, while physical punishment was moderately associated with greater dependence on hunting.

Coding ethnographic documents for 131 largely non-industrial societies (Standard Cross-Cultural Sample), Garfield and colleagues found evidence of physical punishment in 38% of the documents, material punishment in 35%, execution in 34% and reputational punishment in 25%; 66% of the societies showed evidence of at least one punishment type.

Execution as a punishment was moderately associated with social stratification and with the absence of food storage; community size and external trade showed only weak links. The authors state that coercive punishments, execution included, were not concentrated in small 'simple' societies, and that the link with stratification points the other way.

337.content: In compiled fertility and mortality schedules for ten small-scale natural-fertility societies (five foragers: Ache, Agta, Hadza, Hiwi, Ju/'hoansi), mean total fertility was similar to wild chimpanzees, the human maximum was 9.2 births among the Tsimane, and about a third of hunter-gatherer women (33 percent) survived to complete their potential fertility, against 49 percent in non-foragers and 10 percent of chimpanzees.

338.content: Across 22 small-scale societies, African Pygmies, Philippine Negritos and the Hiwi had relatively early puberty, menarche and first reproduction for their adult body size, alongside low subadult survival.

339.content: Among Ariaal pastoralist men in northern Kenya, DRD4 7R allele frequency did not differ significantly between nomadic (n = 65) and recently settled (n = 87) men; 7R carriers had higher body mass index among the nomads and lower among the settled, and the study analysed only body composition, not attention or behaviour.

Among 152 Ariaal pastoralist men in northern Kenya (65 nomadic, 87 recently settled), the DRD4 7R allele occurred at 19.4% and the DRD2 A1 allele at 28.2%, with no difference between nomads and settled men. Men carrying one or two 7R alleles had higher body mass index among the nomads and lower among the settled, a difference the authors trace mainly to fat-free mass. Height was unrelated to either gene.

The authors suggest that the 7R allele may help nomadic men through behaviour, and speculate that the attention profile linked to it might suit learning in a moving, school-free life while hindering classroom learning in the settled community; they did not measure attention or behaviour.

340.content: A network meta-analysis of 522 double-blind randomised trials (116,477 adults with a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder by standard operationalised criteria such as DSM or ICD-10; mean baseline HAM-D17 score 25.7 where reported, which the authors describe as mostly moderate-to-severe) compared 21 antidepressants with placebo and with each other. In the efficacy analysis (432 trials, 102,443 patients), every drug produced more responders than placebo at about 8 weeks (milnacipran through indirect comparison only), where response means a drop of 50 percent or more in total score on an observer-rated depression scale; odds ratios ranged from 1.37 (reboxetine) to 2.13 (amitriptyline), and the authors describe the summary effect sizes as mostly modest. Of the 522 trials, 9 percent were rated high risk of bias, 73 percent moderate and 18 percent low; response was imputed in 17.7 percent of cases, the certainty of evidence was moderate to very low, and effect sizes were smaller in more recent and larger placebo-controlled trials, which the authors say might indicate bias.

The network meta-analysis took double-blind trials of adults with a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder by operational criteria (DSM or ICD) and excluded trials in which 20% or more of participants had bipolar disorder, psychotic depression or treatment-resistant depression, or patients with a serious medical illness. Across the 522 trials the median length of acute treatment was 8 weeks (IQR 6 to 8), and outcomes were taken as close to 8 weeks as possible. Rescue medication, typically benzodiazepines or other sedative hypnotics, was allowed in 36% of trials, 77% recruited outpatients only, and 78% were funded by pharmaceutical companies. The authors note that the trials were short and that some adverse effects of antidepressants appear only over longer periods.

341.content: An umbrella review of 17 studies (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, a large genetic association study and others, searched to December 2020) found no consistent evidence of an association between serotonin and depression and no support for the hypothesis that depression is caused by lowered serotonin activity or concentration; it also reported some evidence that long-term antidepressant use may lower serotonin concentration. This conclusion is disputed in print by 35 authors (Jauhar et al. 2023).

342.content: In UK primary care records (CPRD, 138 practices, 1,524,201 patients, 1995 to 2011), antidepressant prescriptions roughly doubled from 61.9 to 129.9 per 1000 person-years while the rate of people starting antidepressants stayed roughly flat (21.3 to 17.9 per 1000), and treatment courses got longer; the authors conclude the rise appears driven by long-term use. Only 67 percent of patients prescribed an antidepressant had a depression-related Read code (as coded by the authors), and only 39 percent of those starting one had such a code recorded in the year before the first prescription.

343.content: Pooling 30 studies of people classed as depressed by clinical criteria or a validated scale, about 27 percent had CRP above 3 mg/L (very high heterogeneity), and pooling 25 studies, 58 percent had CRP above 1 mg/L; against matched controls (17 studies) the odds of CRP above 3 mg/L were 1.46 times higher, with substantial heterogeneity (I2 72 percent).

344.content: In an internet survey of 669 people on antidepressant treatment for depression, 46 percent reported emotional blunting on the Oxford Questionnaire on the Emotional Side-Effects of Antidepressants (OQESA); blunting scores correlated with HAD depression scores (r = 0.521), and the authors conclude blunting is partly a feature of the low mood itself as well as a drug effect.

345.content: On the parent-report SDQ, read aloud in Swahili through an interpreter, 113 Hadza children aged about 5 to 16 had a lower mean hyperactivity score than children aged 5 to 16 in England's 2017 national survey (2.5 vs 3.1; a descriptive comparison with non-overlapping confidence intervals for boys, overlapping for girls). On the parent DAWBA interview, completed for 107 of the 140 children aged 3 to 17, two met ADHD criteria: a 6-year-old girl who also met criteria for autism and several other disorders, and a 4-year-old boy, outside the 5 to 16 comparison group, who also met autism criteria.

On the parent-report SDQ given through an interpreter, 113 Hadza children aged 5 to 16 in northern Tanzania scored lower on the emotional problems scale than children of the same age in England's 2017 national survey (mean 1.3 against 2.1, with confidence intervals that did not overlap). They scored higher on prosocial behaviour and also higher on peer problems (2.8 against 1.4). On the parent DAWBA interview (83 of the 113 children aged 5 to 16), the authors report that no Hadza child met the criteria for an emotional disorder, against 4.1% of English children aged 5 to 10 and 9.0% aged 11 to 16, and no child received a diagnosis of a current depressive disorder.

The authors report that no current depressive disorder was diagnosed among the Hadza children. One mother reported a brief episode of depressive features in two of her children, with sadness, loss of energy and interest, irritability, negative thoughts and poor sleep, which went with the mother leaving the camp to search for food and with hunger.

346.content: A 35-author reply argues that the Moncrieff 2022 umbrella review overstated its conclusion through methodological weaknesses, selective reporting and misinterpretation, citing tryptophan depletion and plasma tryptophan meta-analyses and molecular imaging, and proposes instead that this evidence indicates a role for serotonin in people vulnerable to or suffering from depression and that the system is perturbed.

347.content: Two severely obese children from one highly consanguineous pedigree had very low serum leptin despite markedly elevated fat mass, and both carried a homozygous frame-shift mutation in the leptin gene (deletion of a single guanine in codon 133). The authors report this as the first genetic evidence that leptin regulates energy balance in humans.

348.content: Sequencing the MC4R gene in 500 probands with severe childhood obesity found mutations in 29 (5.8 percent), 23 heterozygous and 6 homozygous. Carriers had severe obesity, increased lean mass, increased linear growth, hyperphagia and severe hyperinsulinemia, and homozygotes were more severely affected than heterozygotes.

349.content: Sequencing MC4R in 2,257 obese and 2,677 nonobese people of European origin, loss-of-function mutations were found in 1.72% of obese versus 0.15% of nonobese subjects. In 25 carrier pedigrees, penetrance of obesity was 40% in carriers older than 52, 60% in carriers aged 18 to 52 and 79% in children.

350.content: In rats and mice fed a high-fat diet, markers of hypothalamic inflammation rose within 24 hours, and reactive gliosis with markers of neuron injury appeared in the arcuate nucleus within the first week; after a temporary subsiding, inflammation and gliosis returned with continued feeding. In a retrospective set of MRI scans from 34 humans, T2 signal in the mediobasal hypothalamus, read as a sign of gliosis, was higher in 12 obese than in 11 normal-weight subjects and correlated with BMI across all 34 (r = 0.38).

351.content: Of 50 overweight or obese adults without diabetes enrolled in a 10-week very-low-energy diet program, participants lost a mean 13.5 kg.
