At 62 weeks, levels of leptin, peptide YY, cholecystokinin, insulin, ghrelin, gastric inhibitory polypeptide and pancreatic polypeptide, and hunger ratings, still differed significantly from baseline.

352.content: In an inpatient randomized crossover trial, 20 weight-stable adults ate as much or as little as they wanted from ultra-processed or unprocessed diets for 2 weeks each, with meals matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fiber. Energy intake was 508 kcal/d higher on the ultra-processed diet, and participants gained 0.9 kg on it and lost 0.9 kg on the unprocessed diet.

In the same inpatient crossover trial (20 adults, two weeks on each diet), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein was lower after the unprocessed diet than at baseline (1.5 against 2.7 mg/L, P = 0.014) and did not differ from baseline after the ultra-processed diet (2.5 mg/L, P = 0.48).

353.content: Review: GLP-1 is a 30-amino-acid peptide hormone made in intestinal L-cells and released in response to meal intake. It stimulates insulin and inhibits glucagon secretion, inhibits gastrointestinal motility as part of the ileal brake, appears to be a physiological regulator of appetite and food intake, and is extremely rapidly inactivated by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, even before it leaves the gut.

354.content: Review: GLP-1 released from gut enteroendocrine cells controls meal-related glucose excursions by augmenting insulin and inhibiting glucagon secretion, and also inhibits gastric emptying and food intake. The review covers the circuits engaged by endogenous versus pharmacological GLP-1 action and the GLP-1 receptor agonists developed for diabetes and obesity.

355.content: Novo Nordisk researchers designed semaglutide as a once-weekly GLP-1 analogue by raising albumin affinity through its fatty-acid side chain and linker and securing full stability against metabolic degradation, with two amino acid substitutions versus human GLP-1 (Aib8, Arg34). Its plasma half-life was 46.1 h in mini-pigs after intravenous dosing.

356.content: In 396 US adults from an online vendor panel (recruitment targeted national BMI, sex and race distributions, but the sample was 67% female and 72% non-Hispanic White), the five-item Food Noise Questionnaire, which the authors describe as, to their knowledge, the first validated measure of food noise, showed high internal consistency (Cronbach alpha 0.93) and, in a subsample of 137, test-retest reliability over about 7 days of r = 0.79. The study was funded by WW International, and four of its ten authors are WW employees and/or shareholders.

357.content: A meta-analysis of 125 epidemiological studies found that perceived food insecurity was associated with higher body weight, an association restricted to adult women in high-income countries, where the odds of high body weight were about 50% higher for food-insecure than food-secure women; it was weaker or absent in men, children and low- and middle-income countries. The authors interpret this through the insurance hypothesis, that fat storage rises when cues signal insecure access to food.

358.content: In the STEP 1 off-treatment extension (327 adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes), participants who lost a mean 17.3% of body weight over 68 weeks of weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg plus lifestyle intervention regained 11.6 percentage points within one year after both were stopped, leaving a net loss of 5.6% at week 120 versus 0.1% with placebo. Most cardiometabolic improvements reverted towards baseline.

359.content: In a 9-week phase 2 double-blind randomized trial of 48 non-treatment-seeking adults who reported past-year symptoms meeting DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder, low-dose weekly semaglutide reduced grams of alcohol consumed in a laboratory self-administration task, drinks per drinking day and weekly alcohol craving relative to placebo, but did not change average drinks per calendar day or the number of drinking days.

360.content: Reviewing hunter-gatherer and other small-scale societies and adding new Hadza data, Pontzer and colleagues report very few people with obesity (under 5%), modest mean body fat (women 24-28%, men 9-18%), more than 100 minutes a day of moderate and vigorous activity, and daily energy expenditure similar to industrialized populations. Diets tended to be less energy dense and richer in fibre and micronutrients than modern diets, and were not invariably low in carbohydrate.

361.content: In a review of human reproductive energetics, Ellison reports that female ovarian function is particularly sensitive to energy balance and energy flux, that gestation length and birthweight are very sensitive to maternal energy availability, and that the duration of lactational amenorrhea tracks the metabolic load of lactation, while male gamete production is very insensitive to energetic constraints.

362.content: Using factorial estimates built on calorimetry, doubly labelled water and body composition data from healthy women, Butte and King estimate the total energy cost of a pregnancy with 12.0 kg gestational weight gain at 321 or 325 MJ, rising across the three trimesters, and the cost of exclusive breastfeeding at 2.62 MJ per day, of which about 0.72 MJ per day may come from tissue stores in well-nourished women.

363.content: In NHANES 2015-2016, 39.8% of US adults (crude) and 18.5% of youth had obesity, measured as body mass index; the crude adult figures were 38.0% in men and 41.5% in women, with no significant difference between men and women overall or by age group.

364.content: In NHANES 2013-2016, 49.1% of US adults (age-adjusted) reported trying to lose weight in the past 12 months, with a higher age-adjusted percentage among women (56.4%) than men (41.7%); among those who tried, the most common methods were exercising and eating less food (62.9% each).

365.content: In NHANES August 2021-August 2023 (5,929 adults aged 20 and older), 40.3% had obesity measured as body mass index, 39.2% of men and 41.3% of women, with no significant difference between men and women overall or in any age group. Severe obesity was 9.4% overall and lower in men (6.7%) than women (12.1%).

366.content: A meta-analysis of the five twin studies of major depression that met the authors' inclusion criteria estimated the heritability of liability to the diagnosis at 37% (95% CI 31% to 42%), with near-zero effects of environment shared by siblings (0%, 95% CI 0% to 5%) and 63% (95% CI 58% to 67%) individual-specific environment and measurement error. Five family studies gave a pooled odds ratio of 2.84 (95% CI 2.31 to 3.49) for diagnosed major depression in first-degree relatives of probands against relatives of comparison subjects. Read from the abstract only.

367.content: In 42,161 Swedish twins (15,493 complete pairs) interviewed with modified DSM-IV criteria, the heritability of liability to lifetime major depression was 42% in women and 29% in men (a significant difference); the roles of genetic and environmental factors did not differ significantly across three birth cohorts spanning 1900 to 1958.

368.content: In 2.3 million people born in Sweden 1950 to 1970, patients with each of six psychiatric diagnoses had significantly fewer children than the general population, except women diagnosed with depression; siblings of patients diagnosed with depression or substance abuse had significantly more children (fertility ratio range 1.01 to 1.05 across these sibling groups), which for depression more than compensated for the affected patients' lower fecundity.

369.content: In 22,599 day-3 and 15,112 day-5 IVF embryos tested by SNP-based preimplantation screening, the median euploid proportion per cycle was steady at women aged 27 to 35 (about 35% day 3, 55% day 5) and fell rapidly after 35; women in their late 20s averaged four euploid embryos per cycle, falling linearly after 35.

370.content: In 10,904 UK 14-year-olds in the Millennium Cohort Study, social media use was associated with higher depressive symptom scores on the short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire, more strongly for girls than boys: compared with 1 to 3 hours a day, 5 or more hours went with 50% higher scores in girls and 35% in boys. The data were largely cross-sectional.

371.content: Specification curve analysis across three large-scale adolescent datasets (total n = 355,358) found the association between digital technology use and adolescent well-being negative but small, explaining at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being.

In the same specification curve analysis of three large adolescent datasets (Monitoring the Future and the Youth Risk and Behaviour Survey in the US, the Millennium Cohort Study in the UK; 355,358 adolescents), bullying and smoking marijuana had much larger negative associations with well-being than digital technology use (4.3 and 2.7 times as large in the Youth Risk and Behaviour Survey), and getting enough sleep and regularly eating breakfast had positive associations 1.7 to 44.2 times as large. Regularly eating potatoes had nearly as negative an association as technology use (0.9 times, Youth Risk and Behaviour Survey), and wearing glasses a more negative one (1.5 times, Millennium Cohort Study).

372.content: A review proposes differential susceptibility: some individuals, by temperament, endophenotype or specific genes, are more affected than others by both negative and positive environments, and it reviews evidence consistent with this proposal.

373.content: A theoretical review proposes that depressed states evolved to minimize social risk when a person perceives their social value to others as critically low relative to their social burden, through heightened sensitivity to social threat, signals that reduce social risk, and inhibited risk-seeking behavior.

374.content: The analytical rumination hypothesis proposes that depression is an adaptation that evolved in response to complex problems, functioning to sustain analysis of the triggering problem by giving it priority over other processing, reducing interest in distractions (anhedonia) and changing psychomotor activity.

375.content: Whole-genome sequencing of 78 Icelandic parent-offspring trios (65 of the offspring had been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder or schizophrenia) found an average of 63.2 de novo single-nucleotide mutations per child, rising by about 2 mutations for each year of the father's age at conception; after allowing for Poisson variation, father's age explained about 94% (90% CI 80% to 100%) of the remaining variation.

376.content: McDonald, Navarrete and van Vugt propose the male warrior hypothesis: that humans, particularly men, carry psychological mechanisms for forming coalitions that plan and carry out aggression against outgroups, and that women respond to outgroup men with fear and avoidance. The supporting evidence, which they call preliminary, is mostly laboratory social psychology with modern samples, such as three studies in which men gave more to their group when it competed with rival universities and women's giving was largely unchanged.

377.content: Across 20 small-scale societies with published war mortality rates (10 classed as hunter-gatherers, 10 as farmers), the number of kinds of rewards that ethnographies report for warriors was positively correlated with annual war death rate (Spearman rs = 0.626, p = 0.003). Fewer rewards were reported for foraging than for farming societies, and the most common reward was increased prestige.

378.content: Among 120 Nyangatom men (East African agro-pastoralists), the 91 younger men's raiding frequency showed no association with their number of wives or children. Of the 29 elders, the 11 whom peers named as prolific raiders in their youth had more wives and children than the other elders, which the authors attribute mainly to delayed receipt of raided livestock usable as bridewealth.

379.content: In an archival sample, 123 US Medal of Honor recipients who survived World War II had more children than 449 regular WWII veterans (estimated means 3.18 vs 2.72, controlling for birth year). In two vignette experiments with university students (n = 92 and 340), women rated a male soldier as more sexually attractive when he was decorated for bravery in combat, while men showed no such effect for a decorated female soldier.

380.content: Trivers defines parental investment as any investment in one offspring that raises its chance of surviving at a cost to the parent's ability to invest in other offspring, and argues that the sex investing less per offspring will compete among itself for access to the sex investing more. He also argues that males, the sex that usually invests less, tend to suffer higher mortality.

381.content: In 512 solved homicide cases from Detroit in 1972, victims and offenders were mostly young men with near-identical profiles: 43% of adult male victims and 41% of adult male offenders were unemployed, against 11.2% of adult men in the city, and most were unmarried. Wilson and Daly read many of these killings as status competition and argue that a taste for risk is concentrated in young men.

382.content: In an online berry-picking patch-foraging game played by 457 US adults recruited on Prolific, the 206 (45%) who screened positive on a 6-item ADHD self-report screen (ASRS, score 14 or more) left depleting patches sooner (mean median 19.3 vs 23.4 seconds in a patch) and earned higher reward rates (1.59 vs 1.36 points per second) than the 251 who screened negative. The screen is a self-report scale and gives no clinical diagnosis, the positive-versus-negative split was not preregistered, leaving a patch cost only a 1 or 5 second travel wait with minor metabolic cost, and berries paid a small cash bonus.

383.content: Among the Waorani of Ecuador, horticulturalist-foragers with very high homicide rates, raiding histories of 95 warriors showed that men who raided more often than average did not have more wives or children than milder men, and had fewer children who survived to age 15. This contrasts with Chagnon's earlier Yanomamo finding.

384.content: Nesse and Berridge argue that pure psychoactive drugs and direct routes of administration are new in human evolutionary history. In their account such drugs act directly on old brain systems for emotion and behaviour and skip the information processing those systems normally run on. Drugs that produce good feelings send a false signal of a fitness benefit that takes over the incentive systems for liking and wanting, so use can continue after the drug no longer gives pleasure. Drugs that block bad feelings can disable useful defences, though the authors add that such use is often safe.

385.content: Sullivan and Hagen collect archaeological and contact-era evidence that people chewed psychoactive plants long before modern drugs. They report betel nut chewing about 13,000 years ago in Timor and 10,700 years ago in Thailand, Aboriginal Australian use of nicotine plants (pituri and a native Nicotiana) at European contact, khat use in Ethiopia described as already ancient at contact, and coca domesticated in the western Andes by about 7000 years ago with use in Ecuador dated to at least 5000 years ago.

Sullivan and Hagen report that at European contact betel nut, khat, tobacco and coca were chewed in the cheek, and that for all of these except khat users added an alkali such as lime or wood ash, which frees the drug base for absorption through the cheek lining and skips first-pass breakdown in gut and liver. They cite nicotine contents of up to 8% for Nicotiana rustica used by indigenous Americans and 3.5% to 5% for Australian pituri, against up to about 1.5% for modern commercial tobacco. They report that about 15 million coca chewers take around 50 g of leaf a day, equivalent to about 0.4 g of cocaine.

Sullivan and Hagen argue that the mismatch account fits pathological use of refined euphoric drugs, a small share of all drug use, while the most widely used drugs in prehistory and today, nicotine and betel nut, are taken unrefined or at comparable strength and are unpleasant at first. They cite a study in which 88% of 386 adolescents reported an aversive response to their first cigarette. They give heavy cocaine use in the United States as under 650,000 people, below 0.3% of the population.

Sullivan and Hagen do not reject mismatch outright. They write that drugs with structurally enhanced potency, such as heroin made from morphine, were absent in the past, and that substance seeking that was adaptive for ancestral humans may not be adaptive now. Their stated conclusion is that the mismatch idea must be extended to a past rich in plant drugs.

386.content: Sullivan, Hagen and Hammerstein argue that most common drugs (nicotine, morphine, cocaine) are plant toxins that evolved to deter animals from eating the plant. They point to the liver cytochrome P450 enzymes that break these compounds down: function is conserved, and a cited sequencing study of 11 such genes in 93 people found a non-synonymous to synonymous variation ratio of 0.27, which they read as stabilizing selection and recent exposure to plant toxins. They conclude that humans were exposed to plant neurotoxins throughout their evolution and are unlikely to be inherently vulnerable to drugs.

From the 2004 United States national drug use survey the authors report that regular heroin users were 0.2% of the population and regular users of cocaine, crack and amphetamines 2.4%, 0.5% and 0.6%, against 34% for tobacco and 11% for cannabis use in the last year. They argue that use of euphoric drugs is the exception and a poor model for a general theory of human drug use, while granting that heroin might be a genuine evolutionary mismatch.

The authors propose treating each drug as its own case. They note that the opium poppy makes morphine, which acts in place of the body's own endorphins at mu-opioid receptors, and tobacco makes nicotine, which acts in place of acetylcholine, and that opiate self-administration is easier to induce in laboratory animals than nicotine self-administration. They suggest that separate drug-by-receptor models may fit the data better than a single reward-pathway model.

387.content: Hagen and Tushingham review the archaeological record of drug use. Coca use in northern Chile is confirmed over 2000 to 3000 years by a cocaine breakdown product (benzoylecgonine) in the hair of burials. Betel vine and areca remains in Timor date to as early as 13,000 years ago, with betel-stained teeth in burials across Southeast Asia after 5000 years ago. Cannabis has an 8000-year record across Eurasia, with markers of psychoactive use rising around 5000 to 4000 years ago. Tobacco was probably first domesticated in the Andes 6000 to 8000 years ago, and pipes in North America date to as early as 4000 to 5000 years ago. After the Neolithic, European and Asian artifacts are linked to opium and cannabis.

The chapter states that, alcohol aside, all globally popular recreational drugs (caffeine, nicotine, THC, arecoline, opioids, amphetamines, cocaine) are plant defensive neurotoxins or close chemical analogs, and that all common plant drugs taste bitter. It gives absorbed nicotine as about 1 mg per cigarette and about 4 mg per chewed wad, with nausea and vomiting at 4 to 8 mg. It cites evidence that smokers adjust how they smoke to keep blood nicotine roughly constant when the nicotine content of cigarettes changes, and reads this as regulated intake.

388.content: Dudley proposes that ripe and decaying fruit contains ethanol, so frugivorous primates, including the line leading to humans, probably located fruit by the smell of alcohol, ate fruit with real ethanol content, and used ethanol as an appetite stimulant. He reads modern human drinking as a possibly maladaptive carry-over of that old feeding strategy.

389.content: Carrigan and colleagues rebuilt ancestral versions of the digestive alcohol dehydrogenase ADH4 across primate evolution and measured them in the lab. The enzyme of the last common ancestor of humans, chimpanzees and gorillas, about 10 million years ago, oxidised ethanol about 40 times better than the enzyme of the earlier ancestor, and this form is the main ADH4 in humans and gorillas today. The timing roughly matches the move to life on the forest floor, where fallen fruit holds more ethanol. The authors contrast this with about 9000 years of fermentation technology that made drinks without food bulk and with more ethanol than wild fermenting fruit.

390.content: Among adult Aka foragers in the Lobaye district of the Central African Republic (n = 379), self and peer reports put cannabis use at 70.9% of men and 6.1% of women. In 62 men living near a logging road, 67.7% tested positive for a urinary cannabis marker at 50 ng/ml. Users were younger and had less material wealth. Higher marker levels went with lower worm burden and with less reinfection one year after deworming in 23 men, which the authors read as support for unconscious self-medication against worms.

391.content: In the Aka, a Congo Basin forager group noted for high gender equality, tobacco use checked by salivary cotinine showed a very large male bias. Women gave aversion to tobacco, worry about harm to the fetus, and husbands' preference for non-smoking wives as reasons for low use. Men linked their use to better hunting and to attracting or keeping wives, who preferred husbands who smoke. The authors read low female use as an evolved avoidance of plant toxins in pregnancy and nursing, and high male use as possibly sexually selected.

392.content: Allain and colleagues review human data on route of use. Smoking and injection are the fastest ways to get a drug into the blood: peak venous cocaine levels come 2 to 5 min after injection or smoking and 30 to 60 min after snorting, and the self-reported high peaks 1 to 5 min after injection against 15 to 20 min after snorting. Across the cited studies, people who smoke or inject cocaine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, nicotine or heroin are more often addicted than those using slower routes, use more often and for longer, report more loss of control, and are more likely to overdose. The authors also link cigarettes' pull to the fast, puff-by-puff spikes of nicotine they deliver.

In rats, the same intravenous cocaine dose given over 5 s produced psychomotor sensitization and more c-fos activity in corticolimbic regions than the dose given over 25 to 100 s. In self-administration, injection speed made no difference over the first 3 to 4 sessions; after that, rats given slower injections cut their intake over days while rats given 5 s injections kept intake stable.

393.content: Reviewing studies from 1976 to 1996 that compared routes and forms of cocaine, Hatsukami and Fischman report that the body and mind effects of cocaine are similar whether taken as powder (hydrochloride) or as crack (base). Smoked or injected cocaine shows greater abuse liability, a greater tendency toward dependence and more severe consequences than snorted powder. They name how fast, how long and how strongly the drug acts, and how often and how much is used, as the variables that matter, rather than the chemical form.

394.content: Chemical analysis of residues in pottery from the early Neolithic village of Jiahu in China points to a mixed fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit (hawthorn and/or grape) made about 7000 to 6600 BC. Alcohol itself was not detected, since it does not survive; fermentation is inferred from the ingredients. By the Shang dynasty (about 1200 to 1046 BC) texts name a filtered rice or millet drink, jiu, which the authors estimate at probably 10% to 15% alcohol by weight.

395.content: Ripe fruit eaten by wild chimpanzees at Ngogo (Uganda) and Tai (Ivory Coast), 20 species weighted by feeding time, held on average 0.31% to 0.32% ethanol by weight. At about 4.5 kg of fruit a day this comes to an estimated 14 g of ethanol a day, about 1.4 standard drinks; scaled to body mass, about 2.6 standard drinks a day for a 70 kg human. The authors note that fruit ethanol is low, typically under 1%, and taken in with a large mass of food over the day.

396.content: From 1995 to 2012, wild chimpanzees at Bossou, Guinea, repeatedly drank fermented raffia palm sap, often in large amounts, using leaves as sponges. The sap averaged 3.1% alcohol by volume (16 palms) and reached up to 6.9%. The sap collected in containers that local people set when tapping the palms. The authors conclude that ethanol did not deter feeding in this community.

397.content: Coca leaves dated to at least 8000 calibrated years before present were found on house floors in the Nanchoc Valley, Peru, together with pieces of calcite, which chewers use to release the alkaloids from the leaf. Neighbouring sites suggest that lime or calcite, and with it coca, was being supplied as a community activity at about the time systematic farming began in the region.

398.content: Hagen, Roulette and Sullivan argue that under the hijack account children should take drugs about as readily as adults, since children's reward systems work, yet children almost never do. In US national survey data (1999 to 2010) on 5932 children aged 3 to 10, 94.5% had cotinine at or below 3 ng/ml, the range of second-hand smoke exposure, and coffee drinking in US children is also very low despite few restrictions. They propose instead that the brain evolved to regulate intake of plant neurotoxins, with children and to a lesser degree women of childbearing age avoiding them; in their account many, nicotine included, disrupt development.

399.content: Rats housed alone in standard cages and rats living together in a large open box (8.8 square metres) were given morphine solution as their only fluid for 57 days. On later choice days between morphine solution and water, and during a period of abstinence, the isolated rats drank significantly more morphine solution than the social rats, and females drank more than males. During repeated 3-day cycles meant to raise intake, isolated rats increased their consumption while the socially housed rats decreased theirs.

400.content: Rats caged alone and rats living in a colony chose between water and progressively sweeter morphine-sucrose solutions. Isolated rats drank significantly more of the opiate solution. In the phase of highest intake, isolated females took five times and isolated males sixteen times as much morphine (mg/kg) as colony females and males.

401.content: Rats were raised from weaning either alone or in a large colony, and at 65 days half of each group was moved to the other housing. At testing, rats living in the colony drank less morphine-sucrose solution than isolated rats, and no less of sweet or bitter-sweet control solutions. Colony rats that had earlier been isolated tended to drink more morphine than colony rats raised there, significant only at the lowest morphine concentration. The authors relate this to the idea that colony rats avoid morphine because it interferes with complex species-typical behaviour.

402.content: Two studies in outbred Wistar rats tried to repeat the finding that rats in a quasi-natural colony drink less sucrose-morphine than rats isolated in standard cages. The difference did not appear, because the isolated rats drank less sucrose-morphine than in the earlier work. The author suggests the supplier may have changed the strain and points to a role for genetics in morphine consumption.

403.content: Group-housed and individually housed rats were tested on learning to press a lever for intravenous heroin or cocaine, and both groups learned quickly. Isolated rats learned to take heroin earlier, but by the fifth week both groups took similar amounts. For cocaine, both groups learned at the same speed and took similar amounts throughout. The authors conclude that isolation can affect heroin intake but is not needed for heroin or cocaine injections to be rewarding.

404.content: Rats trained to self-administer heroin or methamphetamine, and also to press a lever for access to another rat, were then given a series of mutually exclusive choices between the two. Drug abstinence was almost complete. This held across sex, drug class, dose, training conditions, length of abstinence, social housing between sessions, and in rats scored as addicted in a model built on DSM-IV criteria. Rats went back to the drug only when the social reward was delayed or the social lever was punished with footshock.

The authors note that in people, addiction develops and persists even when social contact is available, including contact with abstinent peers. They suspect two species differences explain why a companion protects rats more than people: people weigh delayed outcomes such as a stake in conventional life, and people value company within a cultural frame. They add that not every addicted person responds to social-reward treatments.

405.content: Rats given mutually exclusive choices between water sweetened with saccharin and intravenous cocaine mostly chose the sweet water: 94% preferred saccharin. The same preference held with sucrose. Raising the cocaine dose did not overcome it, and it held in rats that were intoxicated, sensitized, or had escalated their cocaine intake.

406.content: In standard self-administration set-ups animals have no option other than the drug. Reviewing intravenous cocaine studies in rats, the author reports that when a valuable alternative is offered, even an inessential one, most rats readily stop taking cocaine regardless of how much they took before, and only a small minority keep choosing the drug. He proposes that this minority may correspond to the minority of human cocaine users who are diagnosed with addiction.

407.content: Six experienced cocaine smokers in an inpatient study chose, trial by trial, between a dose of smoked cocaine (0 to 50 mg) and a 5 dollar voucher paid as money or as merchandise. Choosing cocaine rose with the dose, and less cocaine was chosen when the alternative was money than when it was merchandise.

408.content: PET imaging of 20 cynomolgus macaques showed no difference while they were housed alone. After they were housed in social groups, dopamine D2 receptor availability rose in monkeys that became dominant and did not change in subordinates. Cocaine then worked as a reinforcer in subordinate monkeys and not in dominant ones.

409.content: In 16 female cynomolgus monkeys, D2/D3 receptor availability rose in females that became dominant after social groups formed, and dopamine transporter availability fell in subordinates. Dominant females then learned to self-administer cocaine at lower doses than subordinates. The authors conclude that the link between D2/D3 availability and cocaine vulnerability runs the opposite way in females and males.

410.content: Group-housed rats were ranked by who drank first when competing for a palatable liquid. Dominant rats kept up higher rates of cocaine self-administration than subordinates, with no difference in learning, extinction or cue-triggered reinstatement. Dominant rats had higher D2/D3 binding in the nucleus accumbens shell and dorsal striatum.

411.content: Male Wistar rats housed alone drank 30% more alcohol than rats housed in groups of four, and moving rats into more deprived housing raised intake further. Dominant rats took less alcohol and diazepam than subordinates. After nine months of free alcohol access and nine months without, rats drank twice as much as naive rats and kept drinking when the alcohol was made bitter with quinine; at that stage social factors no longer changed intake.

412.content: The authors review the Rat Park finding that single-housed rats drink more oral morphine than rats in a large enriched colony and judge its interpretation problematic: oral morphine tastes bitter, is a weak reinforcer for rats and is rarely preferred over water, and later attempts to show the housing effect with intravenous opiates did not succeed.

Subordinate male rats and monkeys drink more alcohol than dominant ones, and subordinate rats drink more of a potent opiate. In rats, though, these rank differences lasted only the first few months of access: after many months, all rats drank large amounts whatever their rank.

Among people exposed to heroin, cocaine or alcohol, the authors state that moving on to addiction is the exception, at about 20% of those exposed, citing national survey data. They name genetic vulnerability and lack of access to non-drug alternatives as risk factors for that transition.

In rats and monkeys given unlimited round-the-clock access to stimulants and nothing else, most die of overdose within weeks. By contrast, more than 80% of rats with extended daily access to cocaine or methamphetamine stop or sharply cut self-administration when offered a mutually exclusive choice of a non-drug reward such as palatable food, or when taking the drug is sometimes punished with footshock.

The authors propose a testable hypothesis: endogenous opioids acting on mu-opioid receptors buffer the distress of social exclusion, so people with impaired opioid function or under social stress would get relief from drugs that act on these receptors, such as heroin, oxycodone or alcohol. On this view, social integration that restores normal opioid function would lower the need for alcohol or opioids and reduce use and relapse.

413.content: In Robins' random sample of US Army enlisted men leaving Vietnam in 1971, 43% had used an opiate in Vietnam and 34% heroin. About 20% (46% of the opiate users) had used heroin often and long enough to have withdrawal symptoms for two days or more. Heroin there was cheap and nearly pure, and was mostly smoked (67%) or sniffed (24%), rarely injected (9%).

After return to the US, only 10% of the random sample reported any heroin use in the first 8 to 12 months, 2% used more than weekly for over a month, and just under 1% became re-addicted, a rate matched by urine tests. Three years on, 2% were re-addicted at follow-up and 5% had been addicted at some point. Those who did become re-addicted had mostly used opiates and other drugs before Vietnam and had injected heroin there; the few who sought treatment relapsed at the same high rates as patients treated at Lexington, Kentucky.

The men did not stop for lack of opportunity: most said heroin was easy to get where they lived and a tenth tried it after return. Their main reasons for not using were fear of addiction, health effects, arrest, and strong disapproval from friends and family. Hall and Weier attribute the drop mainly to the change in price, purity, route and social acceptability: US street heroin was under 10% pure against 90% in Vietnam, cost far more, and usually had to be injected.
The men said they used heroin in Vietnam to get high and to cope with boredom, homesickness and poor sleep, and mostly used behind the lines or on leave rather than in the field.

Heavy drinking fell in Vietnam, where the men were under the drinking age and the army allowed enlisted men only beer, and heroin users tended to be light drinkers. After return, heavy drinking and alcohol problems rose as heroin use fell, especially among men who had used heroin in Vietnam: in the first year, 42 to 45% of men who kept using narcotics had alcohol problems. Cannabis use also stayed high after return.

414.content: From all US Army enlisted men leaving Vietnam in September 1971, the authors drew a general sample and a sample whose departure urine test had been positive for opiates, and tried to interview every man. Before Vietnam, hard drug use was mostly casual and under 1% had ever been addicted to narcotics. In Vietnam almost half of the general sample tried narcotics and 20% reported opiate addiction. After return, use and addiction fell to about pre-Vietnam levels.

415.content: Looking back on the 1972 to 1974 follow-up of army enlisted men who served in Vietnam in 1970-71, compared with a matched group, Robins reports surprisingly low re-addiction and finds that addiction to narcotics alone was rare compared with dependence on several substances. She argues these findings were still not fully absorbed into public and scientific views of heroin addiction.

416.content: Reviewing US national surveys of representative drug users, Heyman reports that remission from dependence is common and orderly, against the view of addiction as a chronic relapsing disease. The half-life of cocaine dependence was four years and of alcohol dependence 16 years; most people dependent on cocaine remitted before age 30, while about 5% stayed heavy users into their forties. Each year a roughly constant share of those still dependent remitted.

417.content: All-cause mortality of US white non-Hispanic men and women aged 45 to 54 rose between 1999 and 2013, unlike other rich countries and other US ethnic groups. The rise came mostly from drug and alcohol poisonings, suicide, and chronic liver disease and cirrhosis. Among those with a high school education or less, the poisoning death rate rose more than fourfold, from 13.7 to 58.0 per 100,000.

The authors note that opioid prescriptions for pain became far more available from the late 1990s and that tighter controls later moved some users to heroin, which became cheaper, purer and more widely available. Reports of pain rose at the same time, and the authors say their data cannot establish whether the rise in opioid use or the rise in pain came first. They raise economic insecurity as a possible tie and note that other rich countries with slow earnings growth did not see the same deaths.

420.content: Low doses of morphine and oxymorphone sharply reduced the distress crying and motor agitation of puppies briefly isolated from their social group. With morphine the reduction in crying came without gross behavioural disturbance, and the authors propose that brain opiates set the intensity of the emotion that separation produces.

421.content: A review of the endogenous opioid system in social behaviour across non-primate mammals, non-human primates and humans concludes that opioids play a fundamental role in sociality and may matter more for social bonds in primates, humans included, than in other mammals.

422.content: In an fMRI study of a virtual ball-tossing game, the anterior cingulate cortex was more active when participants were excluded than when they were included, and its activity tracked their reported distress, a pattern the authors read as paralleling physical pain studies.

In the same fMRI study of a virtual ball-tossing game, the right ventral prefrontal cortex was active during exclusion and its activity went with less reported distress; changes in the anterior cingulate cortex statistically mediated that link, which the authors read as the prefrontal region damping the distress of exclusion by disrupting anterior cingulate activity.

423.content: In two experiments, people who took acetaminophen daily for three weeks reported less social pain day to day than people on placebo, and in fMRI showed smaller responses to social rejection in the dorsal anterior cingulate and anterior insula.

424.content: In a 20-day trial with 42 young adults split across acetaminophen 1,000 mg daily, placebo and no-pill arms, acetaminophen lowered daily social pain only in participants reporting high forgiveness, an 18.5% reduction over the period.

425.content: In 72 students given 1,000 mg acetaminophen or placebo, acetaminophen left the heart-rate slowing after unexpected rejection and the P3 brain response to social feedback unchanged. In an unplanned finding, the placebo group lowered its expectation of being accepted over the task while the acetaminophen group kept its optimistic prediction.

426.content: A preregistered systematic review of 50 studies that changed pain processing with opioids, opioid antagonists, acetaminophen, cannabinoids, ketamine, alcohol, placebo or hypnosis found inconsistent, small effects on social emotions in both directions; the most consistent effect was placebo analgesia lowering empathy for pain.

427.content: In 60 people who felt painful heat and, on other trials, viewed photos of an ex-partner after an unwanted breakup, fMRI pattern classifiers told pain from its control with 92% accuracy and rejection from its control with 80%. Each classifier performed at chance on the other condition, and inside the dorsal anterior cingulate the pain and rejection patterns were uncorrelated, although gross activation overlapped.

428.content: In a double-blind crossover study, 31 volunteers took the opioid blocker naltrexone for four days and placebo for four days. On naltrexone they felt less connected when reading messages from close others in the lab, and on the 50 mg days they reported feeling less connected in daily life; general positive mood in the diary did not change.

429.content: In 36 healthy adults, a single low dose (0.2 mg) of the opioid buprenorphine, compared with placebo, made people judge they had been included more during a rigged exclusion game. The drop in negative mood after exclusion was a trend only (p = 0.1). The drug also reduced first glances at fearful faces.

430.content: In a PET study of 18 healthy adults, being rejected by people they had hoped to date released the body's own opioids at mu receptors in the ventral striatum, amygdala, midline thalamus and periaqueductal gray. More release in the pregenual anterior cingulate went with less negative feeling during rejection.

431.content: Khantzian argues from clinical observation that people find each drug class relieves or changes particular painful feeling states, and that such suffering drives using, becoming dependent and relapsing. He states that diagnostic studies both support and fail to support the hypothesis.

432.content: Lembke reviews the literature on Khantzian's self-medication hypothesis and reports a striking lack of robust evidence that people with psychiatric diagnoses pick the drug that matches their symptoms or that treating the psychiatric condition resolves the addiction. She argues the hypothesis has led to under-recognition and under-treatment of substance use disorders.

433.content: In 34,653 US adults interviewed twice three years apart (NESARC), people with a baseline anxiety disorder diagnosis who reported using alcohol or drugs to relieve their anxiety had 2.5 to 5 times the odds of a new substance use disorder diagnosis. In the other direction, self-medication among people diagnosed with an alcohol or drug use disorder at baseline was associated with later being diagnosed with social phobia.

434.content: In the same national US cohort, adults with a baseline mood disorder diagnosis who reported using drugs to feel better had about 7.7 times the odds of a new drug dependence diagnosis three years later (95% CI 3.7 to 15.8), and self-medication accounted for about a quarter of new drug dependence in that group. In absolute terms, 5.6% of those who self-medicated were diagnosed with a new drug use disorder.

435.content: Koob and Le Moal propose that repeated drug use pushes the brain reward system into an allostatic state: counter-adaptations that normally limit reward fail to return to baseline, the reward set point shifts, and brain and hormonal stress systems are recruited. On this model compulsive use is driven by that shifted state and vulnerability to relapse persists long after use stops.

436.content: In 89 social drinkers randomly given one of 12 alcohol doses (placebo up to a blood alcohol level of about 0.11%), higher blood alcohol went with a steadily smaller startle response and less self-reported anxiety while waiting for an electric shock. The dampening was larger when the strength of the coming shock was uncertain than when it was known.

437.content: In a crossover study of 16 healthy adults, 1 mg alprazolam reduced the sustained rise in startle while people waited for predictable or unpredictable shocks, and left the startle response to an explicit threat cue unchanged.

438.content: In 60 healthy men randomised to 1.5 mg alprazolam a day, etifoxine or placebo for five days, alprazolam did not change the startle response to unpredictable threat on day 1 or day 5, and neither drug changed self-reported anxiety. The authors note this conflicts with earlier benzodiazepine studies that used higher single doses.

439.content: Leshner, then director of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, argued that research of the previous 20 years showed drug addiction to be a chronic, relapsing brain disease that results from the prolonged effects of drugs on the brain. He held that behavioural and social-context aspects are part of the condition itself, so the most effective treatment combines biological, behavioural and social-context components.

440.content: The review states that all known addictive drugs activate brain reward regions through sharp rises in dopamine release. With repeated use, dopamine cells come to fire to the cues that signal the drug (places, people, the person's own prior mental state), and these conditioned dopamine surges trigger craving and drug seeking. The authors report that such cue responses can trigger strong craving long after use has stopped, for example after incarceration or treatment.

The authors state that repeated exposure to most drugs adapts the stress circuitry of the extended amygdala (corticotropin-releasing factor, dynorphin), so stress reactivity and negative mood rise when the drug wears off or is withdrawn. The person then takes the drug mainly to get transient relief from this dysphoria, and each binge deepens the dysphoria of the next withdrawal. The circuit-level evidence they cite comes mainly from animal studies.

The authors state that only a minority of people who use drugs become addicted, and estimate that the most severe features develop in about 10% of people exposed to addictive drugs, so long-term exposure is necessary but by no means sufficient. Factors they list as raising vulnerability are family history, exposure in adolescence, socially stressful surroundings with poor family and social support and few behavioural alternatives, easy access to drugs, and other mental health conditions.

441.content: Robinson and Berridge propose that addictive drugs share the ability to enhance mesotelencephalic dopamine transmission, which attributes incentive salience ('wanting') to drug-related stimuli. In some individuals repeated drug use makes this system increasingly, and perhaps permanently, hypersensitive. They propose that this sensitized 'wanting' can grow independently of drug 'liking' and of withdrawal, so compulsive seeking can continue when pleasure and withdrawal have faded and despite loss of reputation, job, home and family.

In the review's section on persistence, the authors report that in rats a single injection of amphetamine, cocaine or morphine produced behavioural sensitization lasting weeks to months, and rats given escalating amphetamine doses were as sensitized a year after the last dose as at 2 to 4 weeks. Sensitization was reported to last over 3 months after cocaine and over 8 months after morphine. They note it was not known whether sensitization of drug 'wanting' lasts as long as sensitization of movement responses.

442.content: Kreek and colleagues review evidence that genetic variation may partly underlie impulsivity, risk taking and stress responsivity, and a substantial proportion of vulnerability to addiction. They propose that these traits may act differently at each stage: starting drug use, regular use, addiction, and relapse.

443.content: A meta-analysis of 12 twin and 5 adoption studies estimated the heritability of being diagnosed with alcohol use disorder at 0.49 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.53), with shared environment accounting for 0.10 (0.03 to 0.16). Estimates did not differ by sex, by design (twin versus adoption) or by assessment method (personal interview versus hospital or population records). The authors read the modest shared-environment share as evidence that environment also contributes to family clustering.

444.content: Hall, Carter and Forlini argue that the brain disease model of addiction promoted by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse since 1997 is not supported by animal and neuroimaging evidence to the extent its advocates suggest, has not delivered more effective treatments, and has had a modest effect on drug policy. They argue its focus on a minority of severely addicted people undermines population-level policies that discourage smoking and heavy drinking.

445.content: Heilig and colleagues summarise animal choice studies: rats extensively trained to self-administer cocaine readily gave up the drug when a sweet solution was offered as an alternative, and the same was later found for heroin, methamphetamine and alcohol. They also cite contingency management, which pays people for abstinence, as evidence that drug use in people with addiction stays sensitive to rewards.
The review cites Spragg's 1940 finding that chimpanzees normally chose a banana over morphine, but when they were physically dependent and in withdrawal their preference reversed to morphine.

The authors report that, over the long term, people with opioid addiction die at about 15 times the rate of the general population, and that among those still alive stable abstinence after 10 to 30 years of observation is under 30%. They state that return to controlled use is rare with opioids, and that outcomes improve markedly when opioid addiction is treated as a chronic relapsing condition with retention in treatment.

The authors acknowledge that brain-centred accounts long gave too little attention to social inputs, and summarise animal findings: in rats, lack of social play early in life raises the motivation to take addictive drugs in adulthood, and the opportunity to interact with another rat reduces addiction-like behaviour. In monkeys, changes in social hierarchy altered dopamine D2 receptor availability and the motivation to obtain cocaine.

446.content: Schuckit reports that alcohol, like benzodiazepines and barbiturates, increases GABA effects and inhibits NMDA glutamate activity; with repeated exposure the brain adapts, and when blood alcohol falls the symptoms are roughly the opposite of the drug's effects (insomnia, anxiety, raised pulse, breathing rate, temperature and blood pressure, hand tremor). About half of people diagnosed with alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop, and in 3 to 5% of these grand mal convulsions, delirium or both develop. Symptoms usually begin within 8 hours of falling blood alcohol, peak at about 72 hours and are much reduced by days 5 to 7.

Schuckit reports that about 1 to 4% of hospitalised patients with alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens, diagnosed by DSM-5 criteria) die, and that timely diagnosis and adequate treatment could lower this rate. Death usually comes from hyperthermia, heart rhythm disturbances, complications of withdrawal seizures or accompanying medical illness. Delirium usually begins about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms start and lasts 1 to 8 days or more; benzodiazepines are the mainstay of treatment, best given in an intensive care unit.

447.content: Petursson describes the symptoms reported in the benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome: sleep disturbance, irritability, tension and anxiety, panic attacks, hand tremor, sweating, nausea, palpitations, headache, muscle pain and perceptual changes, with seizures and psychotic reactions reported mainly after high doses. After normal therapeutic doses three symptom patterns are reported: short rebound anxiety and insomnia within 1 to 4 days, a full withdrawal syndrome usually lasting 10 to 14 days, and a return of the original anxiety. Physical dependence can follow prolonged treatment at therapeutic doses; withdrawal is more severe after high doses or short-acting drugs.

448.content: Brett and Murnion state that anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3 to 4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly, and that abrupt cessation after 1 to 6 months of use can bring life-threatening seizures, so the dose should be reduced gradually. Their list of withdrawal features includes grand mal seizures 1 to 12 days after stopping. Gradual withdrawal over at least 10 weeks has been successful in most primary care studies.

449.content: Kosten and Baxter report that after abrupt cessation of short-acting opioids (heroin, hydrocodone, oxycodone) withdrawal usually begins within 12 hours of a missed dose, peaks at 36 to 72 hours and eases over the following 4 to 7 days; methadone withdrawal is milder but may last 2 weeks or more. They trace much of it to the locus coeruleus, whose noradrenaline neurons raise their activity to offset the opioid and overshoot when it is removed. With prolonged use, avoiding withdrawal often becomes the strongest force keeping use going.

The authors state that opioid withdrawal is generally not fatal; death can occur when rehydration is poorly managed, which has happened in criminal justice settings. They stress the high risk of untreated withdrawal from dehydration through vomiting and diarrhoea, and from overdose soon after people drop out of residential treatment, and note that lowered tolerance raises overdose risk when opioids are restarted.

The review reports, from cited studies of patients on long-term opioid analgesics for non-cancer pain, that one study found 45% showed aberrant drug-taking behaviours and another found a lifetime rate of opioid use disorder, as defined by DSM-5, of 35%, while most such patients do not meet the criteria.

450.content: A meta-analysis of six studies from six prison systems (69,093 person-years; 1,033 deaths in the first 12 weeks after release, 612 of them drug-related) found a three- to eightfold increased risk of drug-related death in the first 2 weeks after release compared with weeks 3 to 12, and a pooled relative risk of 1.7 for weeks 3 and 4 compared with weeks 5 to 12. The authors attribute the excess mainly to tolerance lost during imprisonment.

451.content: Ducci and Goldman report weighted mean heritabilities of addictions from large twin cohorts ranging from 0.39 for hallucinogens to 0.72 for cocaine, with alcohol, opioids, nicotine and cannabis in between (their Figure 1). Heritability is usually higher for addiction than for use, but starting use is heritable as well. Specific gene variants found so far account for only a small part of the genetic variance; one nicotinic receptor variant accounts for about 0.5% of the variance in cigarettes smoked per day.

452.content: A meta-analysis of twin studies (28 on starting cannabis use, 24 on problematic use) estimated that genes accounted for 48% of the variance in starting use in males and 40% in females, with shared environment 25% and 39%. For problematic cannabis use, genes accounted for 51% in males and 59% in females, and shared environment 20% and 15%.

453.content: A meta-analysis of six twin studies of starting smoking and ten of persistent smoking estimated heritability of starting at 0.37 in men and 0.55 in women, with shared environment 0.49 and 0.24. For persistence of smoking, heritability was 0.59 in men and 0.46 in women, with shared environment 0.08 and 0.28.

454.content: In 1,196 male twin pairs from the Virginia Twin Registry, interviewed about lifetime use and abuse or dependence (as the authors measured it) of cannabis, cocaine, hallucinogens, sedatives, stimulants and opiates, one common genetic factor strongly influenced use and abuse or dependence for all six classes. Substance-specific genetic factors had a modest influence on use and none was detected for abuse or dependence. The authors conclude that experiences unique to the person largely determine which class a predisposed person uses or misuses.

455.content: In 1951 a postal survey of all UK doctors whose addresses the BMA held gave smoking histories for 34,439 male doctors (two thirds responded); only 17% of them were lifelong non-smokers. In the discussion the authors add that 70% of all UK men born around 1920 were smoking manufactured cigarettes in 1950, at ages 25 to 34.

A high proportion of the doctors who smoked in 1951 stopped during the following decades, after the British medical profession accepted the evidence linking cigarettes to lung cancer. Men born 1900 to 1930 who kept smoking cigarettes died on average about 10 years younger than lifelong non-smokers; stopping at about age 60, 50, 40 or 30 gained about 3, 6, 9 or 10 years of life expectancy.

456.content: Using smoking histories rebuilt from National Health Interview Surveys of 1965 to 2009, the authors estimate that about 80 percent of US men born in 1920 had smoked at least 100 cigarettes by age 30, the highest of any male birth cohort. Male smoking began to decline before 1964, which they suggest may reflect awareness of the early 1950s research linking smoking to lung cancer.

457.content: In five forager populations with full life tables, total fertility rate (births per woman surviving the reproductive years) was 8.2 among the Ache, 6.9 Agta, 6.2 Hadza, 5.5 Hiwi and 4.3 Ju/'hoansi, a forager mean of 6.2. Across 75 small-scale natural-fertility societies the mean was 5.98 (SD 1.40), and only 7 (9 percent) were below 4; of the 11 hunter-gatherers in that sample, two were below 4 (Batak, and Efe at 2.6, which the authors attribute to infertility from sexually transmitted infection). The average interval between births among hunter-gatherers was 3.7 years.

458.content: Across 18 human populations with lifetime data on men's and women's numbers of children, variance in men's reproductive success was higher than women's on average, with the male to female variance ratio ranging from 0.79 (historical Finland) to 4.75 (Dogon, Mali). In the forager populations in the table the ratio was 1.66 among the Aka, 1.77 among the Dobe !Kung, 1.93 among the Hadza and 4.22 among the Ache.

Brown and colleagues found that the ratio of men's to women's variance in reproductive success depends on the marriage system: in the six monogamous populations it was not different from 1 (Pitcairn Islanders' distributions overlap completely), while polygynous populations had higher ratios, and serially monogamous ones (Dobe !Kung, Ache, Pimbwe) resembled polygynous ones. They argue this variation is inconsistent with universal sex roles of the kind Bateman described and that sex roles in humans are better treated as varying with ecology and culture.

459.content: Schacht and Kramer report that although polygynous marriage is permitted in nearly 85 percent of societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, most marriages within those societies are monogamous. Among Savanna Pume hunter-gatherers of Venezuela, 20 percent of women and 11 percent of men are married polygynously at some point in their lives, and most marriages are monogamous, as in other foraging groups.

Schacht and Kramer summarise genetic estimates of nonpaternity in humans as ranging from 0 to 11 percent across societies, with median values of 1.7 to 3.3 percent, against rates that regularly exceed 20 percent in socially monogamous birds.

The review sets out the dispute over when the human pair bond arose: some researchers read modest body size dimorphism in australopithecines about 4 million years ago as evidence of early monogamy and male provisioning, others read the same fossils as highly dimorphic and place monogamy later, and the fragmentary fossil record may be an unreliable guide to mating systems at all.

Schacht and Kramer review marriage across societies and report that, although most marriages are monogamous at any one time, people often re-enter the marriage market: among hunter-gatherers, industrialising societies and many Western populations, remarriage after a spouse's death or after divorce is common, so that men and women have several partners over their reproductive years. They judge that serial monogamy was probably the norm through human history.

460.content: In 22 natural-fertility societies, mostly tropical foragers, horticulturalists and pastoralists, mean age at menarche ranged from 12.6 to 18.4 years. Age at menarche correlated with age at first reproduction (r = 0.76), and first reproduction followed menarche by four years on average. Menarche age was not related to total fertility or reproductive fitness.

461.content: Among the Dogon of Mali, a natural-fertility farming population with a mean of 8.6 live births per woman, hormone profiles of 93 women and a census of menstrual-hut visits showed that fertile women aged 20 to 34 had a median of only two menses each over two years. The median number of menses per lifetime was about 100, roughly a third of the number for an American woman with three live births.

462.content: Gluckman and Hanson argue that as age at menarche has fallen with better child health, biological maturation now comes well before psychosocial maturation, which they describe as happening for the first time in human evolutionary history. They add that contemporary early puberty should not be medicalised.

463.content: In two studies (3,177 online participants in 10 nations, and a re-analysis of Buss's 1989 data from 8,953 people in 31 nations), the sex differences in mate preferences presumed to have evolutionary roots were smaller in nations with greater gender parity on the Global Gender Gap Index.

464.content: A survey of 67 studies reporting nonpaternity found that for men with high paternity confidence the rate is typically 1.9 percent (excluding studies of unknown method), well below the 10 percent or more often cited. Cross-culturally, men's confidence of paternity goes with more involvement with children and more investment from paternal kin.

465.content: In two nationally representative US surveys (How Couples Meet and Stay Together, 2009 and 2017; 5,421 heterosexual couples), the share of heterosexual couples who met online rose from 2% of couples who met in 1995 to 39% of couples who met in 2017, while meeting through friends fell from 33% to 20%, through family from 15% to 7%, and through coworkers, neighbours, school and church also fell. The authors date the point where meeting online overtook meeting through friends to about 2013.

Among US heterosexual couples who met online, 89% in the 2017 survey had no personal connection before meeting online, and the share brought together online by a friend or other third person fell from 11.2% in the 2009 survey to 3.7% in 2017.

466.content: On one large free US dating site (New York, Boston, Chicago, Seattle, January 2014), attention was very unequal: most users received a handful of first messages at most while a small fraction received far more; the most contacted user, a 30-year-old woman in New York, received 1504 messages in the month. Desirability, measured from who messages whom, formed a clear hierarchy that was consistent across the four cities.

Men and women on the same US dating site mostly wrote to people ranked about 25% more desirable than themselves. Reply rates fell as the gap grew: men were more than twice as likely to get a reply from women less desirable than themselves, and for messages to more desirable women the reply rate never rose above 21%.

467.content: In the US General Social Survey, the share of men aged 18 to 24 who said they had no sexual activity in the past year rose from 18.9% in 2000 to 2002 to 30.9% in 2016 to 2018; among women of that age the change (15.1% to 19.1%) was not significant. Sexual inactivity also rose among men aged 25 to 34 (7.0% to 14.1%) and women aged 25 to 34 (7.0% to 12.6%), and weekly sex fell among married men and women. Men with lower income and part-time or no work were more likely to be sexually inactive.

468.content: In the US National Survey of Family Growth (in-person interviews; 10,590 women aged 15 to 44 in 2013 to 2017), the median age at first menstrual period fell from 12.1 in 1995 to 11.9 in 2013 to 2017, and the share of girls who had reached menarche by each age from 8 to 12 was higher in the later period.

469.content: An expert panel weighed US puberty data from 1940 to 1994. Most panellists judged the data enough to suggest a trend toward earlier breast development and earlier menarche in girls; a minority judged the data on girls insufficient for any marker, and almost all judged the data on boys insufficient to assess a trend.

470.content: From US birth certificates (all births), the average age of first-time mothers rose 3.6 years, from 21.4 in 1970 to 25.0 in 2006. In 2006 the average age at first birth in the selected rich countries compared ranged from 25.0 in the United States to 29.4 in Switzerland; every country shown rose since 1970, by 2.9 years in Sweden up to 4.6 years in Denmark.

471.content: From all US birth records, the mean age of mothers at first birth rose from 26.6 in 2016 to 27.5 in 2023, and rose in every racial and ethnic group and at every level of urbanicity; in 2023 it was 28.5 in large metropolitan counties and 24.8 in the most rural (noncore) counties.

472.content: The GBD 2021 estimates put the global total fertility rate (births per woman) at 4.84 in 1950 and 2.23 in 2021. Fertility fell in every country and territory since 1950, and in 2021 it was above the replacement level of 2.1 in 94 of 204 countries and territories (46.1%), 44 of them in sub-Saharan Africa.

473.content: From census data on European women born 1916 to 1965 (13 countries), the share of women who never had a child fell steeply until about the 1940 birth cohort in both Western and state-socialist Europe, then rose again in the West: in the 1960 cohort it ranged from 10% in Greece and Spain to 20% in Germany. The authors report that women born around 1900 in Northern and Western Europe and Italy had childlessness of up to 25 to 30%, and that the rise in women's education explained only a small part of the later trends.

474.content: In an experiment, women who saw highly attractive women rated their own desirability as a marriage partner lower, while seeing socially dominant women had little effect; for men the pattern reversed, with dominant men lowering men's self-rated desirability as a marriage partner more than attractive men did. The authors read the effect as a change in the perceived pool of competitors.

475.content: A meta-analysis of 77 experimental and correlational studies (141 effect sizes) found small to moderate links between exposure to media images of thin-ideal bodies and women's body dissatisfaction (d = -0.28), internalisation of the thin ideal (d = -0.39) and eating behaviours and beliefs (d = -0.30).

476.content: In a nationally representative sample of US adult internet users (N = 2,075), 1,461 people (about 70%) had viewed pornography at some point and 1,056 (just over half) had used it in the past year. Roughly 11% of men and 3% of women agreed at least somewhat with the statement "I am addicted to pornography".

In the same US national sample, agreeing with "I am addicted to pornography" went with being male, younger, more religious, more morally opposed to one's own pornography use (moral incongruence) and using more pornography. The authors conclude that feeling addicted reflects both how much a person uses and how they judge that use morally.

477.content: Grubbs and colleagues propose a model in which many pornography-related problems, especially feeling addicted, are better understood as a clash between a person's beliefs about pornography and their own use (moral incongruence), and test it with a systematic review and meta-analysis. They note that researchers remain divided on whether internet pornography use is addictive.

478.content: A meta-analysis of 50 studies (more than 50,000 participants, 10 countries) found pornography use associated with lower sexual and relationship satisfaction, in cross-sectional surveys, longitudinal surveys and experiments, with significant results for men only. Pornography use was not related to body satisfaction or self satisfaction.

479.content: In two experiments with US students, viewing centerfold nudes lowered how sexually attractive a nude stranger was rated. In the second experiment the drop appeared only for men shown female nudes, and men who found the centerfolds more pleasant rated themselves as less in love with their wives.

480.content: Three preregistered, high-powered close replications of Kenrick, Gutierres and Goldberg 1989 Study 2 exposed men and women in committed relationships to opposite-sex erotica or abstract art. Pooled with the original in a meta-analysis, they found no support for the original finding that such exposure lowers men's ratings of their partner's sexual attractiveness (original d = 0.91) or their love for the partner (original d = 0.69).

481.content: In a US probability survey of adults aged 18 to 60, most respondents had used pornography at some point. Among women, 21.4% had been choked during sex, 32.3% had had a partner ejaculate on their face and 34.0% had received aggressive fellatio. After adjusting for age, age at first exposure and relationship status, pornography use was significantly associated with these rough sexual behaviours.

482.content: From 1,162 population surveys in 204 countries and territories, 51.9% of all women aged 15 to 49 were using some contraception in 2019 and 47.7% a modern method, up 20.1 percentage points since 1970. Modern method use ranged from 1.9% of women in South Sudan to 87.9% in Norway.

483.content: Using old US state laws that banned the sale of contraceptives (in force until the 1965 Griswold decision) as a natural experiment, Bailey finds that birth rates fell more slowly in states with sales bans after the pill arrived in 1957; by 1965 the gap was about 8 births per 1,000 women of childbearing age. Without the bans, marital fertility would have been 8% lower in those states and 4% lower in the US as a whole. A simple counterfactual attributes about 40% of the fall in US marital fertility from 1955 to 1965 to the pill.

484.content: In Ton'tumsi, a Tsimane village of 57 adult men, peers rated four forms of status: winning fights, getting one's way in group disputes, community-wide influence and respect. The four forms and most of their predictors were held by the same few men; there was little sign of different men holding standing in different domains.

In the same village, men rated as good hunters were rated as more respected (r .47), but skill in food production did not predict community-wide influence once other factors were controlled; influence came mainly from allies and kin support and from market skills such as Spanish and wage work.

In Ton'tumsi, a Tsimane village in Bolivia, men ranked their 57 adult male fellow villagers from photographs on four forms of status and on predictors. Number of allies alone explained 40% of the variance in winning a fight, 28% in getting one's way in group disputes, 78% in community-wide influence and 43% in respect; it mattered more than the number of close kin. Social support was the strongest predictor of influence in the study, ahead of body size, hunting skill and age.

485.content: Among the Tsimane, leading a task and holding political standing were different things. Organising a group barbasco fishing trip rotated across households (organisers as young as 8, many of them women, and only 7 of 31 regular households never organised one), and organisers took no more fish than others. The elected village post went to few men: five in one village since 1989, and never a woman.

486.content: Across 21 small-scale populations, wealth inequality depended on how people made a living. Weighted Gini coefficients were 0.25 for hunter-gatherers and 0.27 for horticulturalists, against 0.42 for pastoralists and 0.48 for farmers, where land and livestock can be owned and passed on. The authors compare the forager figure to income Gini in Denmark, Norway and Finland (0.24) and note that pastoral and farming populations were more unequal than the US (income Gini 0.37).

487.content: In hunter-gatherer populations (Ache, Hadza, Tsimane, Lamalera, Meriam, Ju/'hoansi), Gini coefficients for eleven kinds of wealth (hunting and foraging returns, grip strength, body weight, reproductive success, Lamalera boat shares and housing, exchange and sharing partners) mostly fell between 0.2 and 0.5 when body weight is left out; the weighted average was 0.25, and the two material measures (Lamalera boats and housing) averaged 0.36. The authors call this moderate: very low by current world standards, and far from complete equality.

488.content: Using house size as a stand-in for household wealth at 63 archaeological sites, hunter-gatherer sites had a median Gini of 0.17, horticultural sites 0.27 and agricultural sites 0.35. Old World societies later reached about 0.48 to 0.60. The authors set these beside modern wealth Ginis cited from other studies: 0.80 for the USA in 2000 and 0.73 for China.

Placing house-size Gini coefficients from archaeological sites by years since domesticated plants arrived locally, Kohler and colleagues found a similar course in the Old World and the New until about 2,500 years after: in both, Ginis rose from levels typical of hunter-gatherers to levels typical of small-scale farmers by about 1,800 years after domestication. After that Old World societies kept growing more unequal while those in North America and Mesoamerica stayed level or declined, which the authors attribute mainly to domesticated draft animals, absent in the New World, that let richer households farm more land and later supported mounted warrior elites.

489.content: In four studies of US participants (college groups such as sororities and ROTC units, a broader national sample, an experiment, and a longitudinal study across graduation), respect and admiration in one's face-to-face groups went with life satisfaction and positive feeling more strongly than income or education did. When a person's standing in their group rose or fell, their well-being rose or fell with it.

490.content: Asked to name a famous person they were fond of, 151 US early adolescents (mean age 14.8) mostly chose actors, singers and athletes, and 61.1% thought of that figure as a relationship partner: girls mostly as a friend, boys more often as a mentor or authority. Those who did reported more involvement and stronger feelings toward the figure.

491.content: In a quota sample of 2,028 Hungarian adults aged 18 to 64, matched to the population by sex, age and region, 800 (39%) said they had a favourite celebrity. On a 7-item admiration scale with a cut-off of 26, the authors estimate that 4.53% of adults and 8.51% of 18 to 34 year olds have a high level of admiration for a celebrity.

492.content: In a survey of 838 people and interviews with 103, age was a strong predictor of interest in celebrity gossip, and media exposure predicted it while social isolation did not. The authors read this as celebrities serving first as models to learn from and, later in life, as people misperceived as part of one's own social network.

493.content: In memory-confusion experiments with University of California, Santa Barbara undergraduates, participants watched a dispute between two teams of mixed race. When team membership was marked by a visible cue that cut across race (shirt colour), participants confused people by team more and by race much less. Categorisation by sex dropped only slightly (effect size 0.91 to 0.84) and stayed stronger than categorisation by team. Less than 4 minutes of exposure was enough.

Kurzban, Tooby and Cosmides argue that ancestral foragers travelled on foot, rarely moved home more than about 40 miles, and so almost never met people from populations genetically distant enough to look like a different race. On this reading the mind has no built-in race category; it tracks alliances, and race is used when it signals alliance.

494.content: In further memory-confusion studies with UC Santa Barbara undergraduates, two groups that cooperated peacefully (for example volunteers of two charities) were enough for participants to sort people into alliances, with no rival or enemy needed and no team colours. When race did not predict who was cooperating with whom, categorisation by race fell, sometimes to zero, while categorisation by sex was unaffected.

495.content: A preregistered replication of Kurzban et al 2001 with 463 US adults on Mechanical Turk, powered at 95%, found that encoding of race fell and encoding of team rose when a visual team cue was added. The drop in race encoding was smaller than in the original, and race was not erased.

496.content: Tajfel and colleagues divided schoolboys into groups on a trivial basis and had them allocate real money between anonymous others. Participants favoured their own group, and the strongest pattern was maximising the difference between ingroup and outgroup even when that cost both groups absolute reward.

497.content: Across experimental studies of cooperation, people cooperated more with ingroup than outgroup members (d = 0.32). The effect was small with bare categorisation and no mutual dependence (dictator games, d = 0.19) and larger when outcomes were interdependent (social dilemmas, d = 0.42), and larger when group membership was common knowledge. The gap came from favouring the ingroup rather than derogating the outgroup.

498.content: In third-party punishment experiments with indigenous groups in Papua New Guinea, observers who could pay to punish a person who broke a sharing norm protected victims from their own group much more than victims from other groups, whatever the violator's group. Violators expected leniency from punishers of their own group, and norm violations were more frequent when punisher and violator shared a group.

499.content: In a game-theoretic model and agent-based simulations, Choi and Bowles find that under conditions they take as typical of late Pleistocene and early Holocene humans, neither altruism toward one's own group nor hostility toward other groups could spread alone, while the two could spread together if hostility produced conflicts that groups with more altruists won.

500.content: In the American National Election Study, the gap between how US partisans rated their own party and the other party on a 0 to 100 feeling thermometer grew from 22.64 degrees in 1978 to 40.87 degrees in 2016. The rise came from colder feelings toward the other party, not warmer feelings toward one's own, and the gap fell slightly between 2012 and 2016.

In US surveys, about 4 to 5% said in 1960 that they would be upset if their child married someone from the other party; by 2010 about one third of Democrats and one half of Republicans said so. Klar and colleagues (2018) found that much of this opposition falls away when the potential spouse is described as rarely talking about politics.

501.content: In 563,312 tweets about gun control, same-sex marriage and climate change, each additional moral-emotional word was associated with about 20% more retweets. The association was stronger for retweets within liberal or conservative networks than between them.

502.content: Burton, Cruz and Hahn re-tested the moral contagion model on six Twitter corpora (for example COVID-19, #MeToo, #MuellerReport).
