622.content: Men aged 18 to 50 who reported compulsive pornography use (n = 15, scored on the Compulsive Internet Use Scale) and men who did not (n = 10) showed no difference in striatal dopamine D2/3 receptor availability on [11C]raclopride PET, no correlation between compulsive-use scores and receptor availability, and no difference in frontal blood flow. The authors conclude the study gives no imaging support for the changes reported in other addictions.

623.content: Faraone and Larsson's review reports a mean heritability of 74% across 37 twin studies of ADHD, most of which scored inattention and hyperactivity as symptom counts on parent or teacher rating scales; the few twin studies using a categorical ADHD diagnosis gave 77 to 88%. Heritability is similar in boys and girls and for the inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive components.

The same review reports that heritability depends on who rates the symptoms: same-parent and same-teacher ratings give about 70 to 80%, while self-ratings and different raters for each twin give about 30 to 40%. The authors attribute the gap to rater effects and low reliability of self-reports, and cite a heritability of 72% for clinically diagnosed adult ADHD.

624.content: A systematic review of 780 studies of candidate biomarkers (biochemical, imaging, neurophysiological, neuropsychological and GWAS) for the diagnosis of neurodevelopmental conditions in children found none with at least 80% sensitivity and specificity in two or more independent studies. For children diagnosed with ADHD (53 studies, 4,164 cases, 229 biomarkers), the authors report that no replicated biomarker reached 80% sensitivity and specificity with an area under the curve of 0.8.

625.content: A systematic review of 19 studies in 13 countries (over 15.4 million children) found that in 17 studies the youngest children in a school year were more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD or medicated for it than their older classmates; two Danish studies found a weak or no effect, which the authors link to delayed school entry for younger children. Reported excess risks ranged from 8% (Denmark) to 143% (a small Dutch GP study); the strength of the effect was unrelated to a country's overall diagnosis or prescribing rate.

The review opens by noting that ADHD diagnosis is based on third-party reports of behaviour, often from teachers and parents, and quotes DSM-5 that no biological marker is diagnostic for ADHD; it cites a 2003 US study in which teachers were most often the first to suggest the diagnosis.

626.content: A meta-analysis of 23 double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject studies (16 reports) in which children ate a known amount of sugar or an artificial sweetener found mean effect sizes from -0.14 (direct observation) to +0.30 (academic tests), with every 95% confidence interval across the 14 behaviour and cognition measures including zero. The authors note that a small effect, or effects in subsets of children, cannot be ruled out.

627.content: Among 407,846 US children born 2007 to 2009 in a commercial insurance database, in the 18 states with a September 1 school-entry cutoff, the rate of children diagnosed with ADHD (from insurance claims) was 85.1 per 10,000 children born in August (youngest in class) and 63.6 per 10,000 born in September (oldest), a 34% higher rate. No such gap appeared in states without that cutoff or between other adjacent birth months, and August-born children had no excess of asthma, diabetes or obesity.

628.content: A systematic review of 32 papers (31 on ADHD, 18 countries) pooled risk ratios for children who are youngest in their school year: they were 38% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD (RR 1.38) and 28% more likely to be prescribed ADHD medication (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.21 to 1.36). Every study of diagnosed ADHD found higher risk in the youngest except one Danish study (RR 0.91). Teacher ratings of ADHD symptoms were more affected by relative age than parent ratings.

629.content: In a two-sample Mendelian randomisation study using UK Biobank activity data and Psychiatric Genomics Consortium genetic data for diagnosed ADHD (about 55,000 people), genetically predicted accelerometer-measured sedentary behaviour showed no reported association with ADHD (its associations were with schizophrenia and anorexia). Genetically predicted self-reported moderate-to-vigorous activity went with a higher, not lower, liability to ADHD (OR 1.69), and genetic liability to ADHD went with more self-reported activity.

630.content: In 535 recorded casual conversations from a Polish spoken corpus (274,954 lines, two blind coders per line), about 85% of agreed lines (89% of words) were social content. The authors count talk about the speakers themselves as social: about 48% of lines were about the people in the conversation, 30% about absent people the speakers know, about 5% about strangers or celebrities, and 15 to 18% was non-social.

In the same Polish corpus, women's speech was 91% social content and men's 86% (share of word tokens). In the authors' mixed-effects model there was no significant difference between women and men in how much they spent on social content.

The re-test authors report that the 1997 two-thirds estimate came from 45 conversations overheard in public places, over three quarters of them held by students in two university cafeterias in Liverpool and London, with topics noted every 30 seconds by a single coder. A later study by Dahmardeh and Dunbar (2017) put the social share at 76%.

631.content: A systematic review by two endocrinologists screened 3,470 articles and kept 58 studies that tested the adrenal axis against fatigue or exhaustion (33 in healthy or burnout groups, 25 in patients). Cortisol tests gave conflicting results, no test reliably told fatigued from non-fatigued people apart, and the ten papers that used the term adrenal fatigue were descriptive and tested nothing. The authors conclude there is no proof that adrenal fatigue exists.
The same review found that studies of people in burnout groups gave greatly inconsistent cortisol results, and the authors advise that adrenal axis tests should not be used as markers of burnout.

632.content: In a cluster randomised trial at 160 worksites of a US warehouse retailer (32,974 employees), 20 sites got an 18-month wellness programme with 8 modules on nutrition, exercise and stress reduction. Workers at programme sites more often reported regular exercise (69.8% vs 61.9%) and managing their weight (69.2% vs 54.7%), but there were no significant differences in 27 other reported health outcomes, 10 clinical markers, 38 spending and use measures, or absenteeism, job tenure and job performance.

In the same trial the prespecified mental health and well-being index did not differ between programme and control sites (0.001 SD), and neither did the share of workers reporting stress at work (56.2% vs 55.7%) or unmanaged stress (39.1% vs 41.8%).

633.content: In a randomised trial at a US university, 3,300 of 4,834 enrolled employees were offered a two-year wellness programme (health screening, online risk assessment, weekly wellness activities, paid time off and rewards of 50 to 650 dollars) and 1,534 were controls. The programme raised health screening rates, but there were no significant changes in total medical spending, other health behaviours, productivity or reported health after more than two years.

634.content: In a UK workplace survey (2017 and 2018 waves, 46,336 workers in 233 organisations), workers who reported taking part in mindfulness, resilience or stress management training, relaxation classes, coaching, time management training, well-being apps or sleep programmes scored no better on mental well-being, distress, life or job satisfaction than matched non-participants. Volunteering was the only exception, with small positive estimates.

In the same survey, participants in resilience and stress management training were more likely to report unrealistic time pressures, while also more often reporting that their organisation supported them with stress at work.

635.content: A meta-analysis of 7 vacation studies found a small improvement in health and well-being during or right after a vacation (d = 0.43). In the 4 studies with two measures after return to work, the gain had partly or fully faded (mean d = -0.38) by the second measure, taken 2 to 4 weeks after the vacation.

636.content: 96 Dutch workers rated their health and well-being two weeks before a winter sports vacation, during it, and one, two and four weeks after. Health status, mood, tension, energy and satisfaction improved during the vacation (mean d = 0.54), and all five were back at pre-vacation levels within the first week back at work. Fatigue was lowest in the first week back and at baseline by the second.

637.content: 76 clerks rated burnout twice before a vacation, once during and twice after. Burnout fell during the vacation, had returned part way to its earlier level 3 days after return and fully by 3 weeks after.

638.content: The authors reanalysed the data set of the Cipriani 2018 network meta-analysis (522 trials, 116,477 participants). In the 109 trials (166 comparisons) that reported scores on the 17-item Hamilton depression rating scale, which the authors give a range of 0 to 52 points, antidepressants beat placebo by a mean of 1.97 points (95% CI 1.74 to 2.21). Across all symptom-scale outcomes the pooled standardised mean difference was 0.29 (253 studies), close to the 0.30 Cipriani reported. The authors judge both figures likely below a clinically relevant effect and rate the certainty of the placebo comparisons very low.

In the same reanalysis, the antidepressant-placebo effect size on investigator-rated depression symptom scales was higher in published than in unpublished trials (p<0.0001) and higher in trials with a placebo run-in design than in those without (p=0.05). For 12 of the 19 trials with clinical study reports, the outcome data Cipriani and colleagues used differed from those reports.

639.content: In an opinion paper, Hengartner and Ploderl convert the overall antidepressant-placebo effect size reported by Cipriani 2018 (d = 0.3) to approximately 2 points on the 17-item Hamilton depression scale, which they give a range of 0 to 52 points. They note that by convention a difference under 3 points, or d under 0.5, is considered clinically irrelevant, and cite research that clinicians need a difference of at least 7 points on that scale to detect a minimal improvement in a patient.

The same authors argue that with a mean drug-placebo difference of only about 2 points on the 17-item Hamilton scale, a small bias in symptom ratings, such as raters or patients guessing the allocation from side effects, could account for the whole difference.

640.content: This systematic review of 131 placebo-controlled trials (27,422 participants) of SSRIs in adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder rated every trial at high risk of bias. In the 49 trials with usable end-of-treatment scores, SSRIs lowered the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score by a mean of 1.94 points more than placebo (95% CI 1.37 to 2.50), below the authors predefined threshold for clinical significance of 3 points.

641.content: The authors meta-analysed all 35 trials submitted to the US FDA for licensing four newer antidepressants (fluoxetine, venlafaxine, nefazodone, paroxetine; 5,133 patients), published and unpublished. Mean improvement on the Hamilton Rating Scale of Depression was 9.60 points on drug and 7.80 on placebo, a difference of 1.80 points, below the 3-point criterion NICE used for clinical significance.

In the same FDA data set, improvement on placebo was more than 80 percent of the improvement on drug. The drug-placebo gap grew with baseline Hamilton scores, reaching the NICE criterion only in trials whose mean baseline score was at the upper end of the very severe range (about 28), and the authors attribute this to a smaller placebo response at high severity rather than a larger drug response.

642.content: In an essay, Lacasse and Leo report that US direct-to-consumer advertising campaigns for SSRIs largely revolved around the claim that the drugs correct a chemical imbalance from a lack of serotonin. They cite a Pfizer television advertisement for Zoloft stating that the drug works to correct this imbalance, and a Paxil advertisement stating that the drug can help restore the balance of serotonin.

The authors state that, to their knowledge, no peer-reviewed article directly supports a serotonin deficiency in any mental disorder, that the DSM does not list serotonin among the origins of any disorder, and that the paroxetine prescribing information calls the link between the drug and serotonin activity presumed.

643.content: In a survey of 262 US undergraduate psychology students at one Midwestern university, 240 (91.6 percent) reported having heard depression described as a chemical imbalance. Of those, 88.6 percent reported hearing it on television and 46.0 percent (109 of 237) reported hearing it from a physician or other medical professional. Asked directly, 54.2 percent agreed that depression is primarily from a chemical imbalance, a figure the authors suspect the item wording inflated.

644.content: In a discourse analysis of research interviews, the authors found that both long-term users of antidepressants and family physicians invoked the comparison of depression to diabetes, which the authors call common, and that these participants explicitly or implicitly challenged how well the analogy fits.

645.content: In a secondary analysis of three 8-week randomized controlled trials in adult outpatients diagnosed with major depressive disorder (venlafaxine, bupropion, escitalopram and placebo arms; about 1,660 participants), emotional blunting scored on the single inability-to-feel item of the MADRS rose from baseline in 6 percent or fewer of participants, with no significant difference between treatment groups, placebo included. Roughly 20 to 25 percent still reported an inability to feel normal emotions at the end, and the authors suggest that in acute treatment blunting may be better read as a residual symptom than as an adverse drug effect.

646.content: In 66 healthy volunteers given escitalopram 20 mg (n = 32) or placebo (n = 34) for at least 21 days, hierarchical Bayesian modelling of a probabilistic reversal learning task found lower reinforcement sensitivity in the escitalopram group (mean difference -2.77, 90% highest density interval -5.29 to -0.40), the parameter for how far choices follow past wins and losses, with no group difference in the learning rate for rewards, the learning rate for punishments, or stimulus stickiness.

647.content: In the ANTLER trial, 478 adults in 150 UK general practices who had taken citalopram, sertraline, fluoxetine or mirtazapine long term and felt well enough to stop were randomised double-blind to keep taking the drug or to taper to placebo over one to two months. By 52 weeks, relapse of depression as defined by the trial's modified CIS-R interview occurred in 39 percent (92 of 238) of the maintenance group and 56 percent (135 of 240) of the discontinuation group (hazard ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.56 to 2.70).

At 12 weeks the discontinuation group scored higher on the modified DESS withdrawal-symptom checklist (mean 3.1 versus 1.3, difference 1.9 points), on the PHQ-9 (6.3 versus 4.1) and on the GAD-7 (5.3 versus 3.1). The authors report that by the end of the trial 39 percent of the discontinuation group had gone back to an antidepressant prescribed by their clinician.

648.content: Aaron Beck, who formulated the cognitive model, states its core claim: in people labelled depressed, highly charged negative beliefs about the self skew how experience is processed, producing a negative bias in attention, interpretation and memory, and that bias in turn produces the symptoms (hopelessness, loss of motivation, self-criticism). He proposes that the bias and the symptoms then feed each other in a loop. He reports that his 1999 review with Clark of over 1,000 publications found substantial support for the model's facets.

Beck's developmental version of the model proposes that early adverse events form negative beliefs (schemas), and that later adverse events activate those beliefs and set off the negative bias. He reports that the original model treated severe life events such as a death or a job loss as the usual triggers, and that later work points to milder events in vulnerable people and progressively milder triggers across successive episodes of depression.

649.content: In a randomized controlled trial in rural Kenya, poor households (503 recipient and 505 within-village comparison households at baseline, 94% and 93% re-surveyed) received unconditional cash transfers of at least US$404 PPP from GiveDirectly. About nine months after transfers began, recipients scored 1.16 points lower on the CES-D depression scale than comparison households (comparison mean 26.48, SD 9.31, so about 0.12 SD), reported 0.16 SD more happiness and 0.17 SD more life satisfaction, and 0.26 SD less stress. The authors report no average effect on cortisol, and no effect on trust, locus of control or self-esteem.

650.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of cash transfer programs in low- and middle-income countries pooled 11 studies (eight programs, 22,488 participants) that scored depression and anxiety symptoms on scales such as the CES-D, PHQ-9 and GHQ-12. Measured during or right after the program, cash transfers produced a small improvement (pooled d = -0.10, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.05). The authors rate overall confidence as moderate and note some sign of publication bias.

In the same meta-analysis, effects on depression and anxiety symptom scores measured after the cash transfer program had ended were smaller and not statistically significant (pooled d = -0.05, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.04). The authors say this analysis was underpowered, and that a sensitivity model did find a very small significant effect. They conclude that continued support may be needed for lasting gains.

651.content: In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, 4,604 low-income US public-housing families were randomly offered (or not offered) vouchers to move to lower-poverty neighbourhoods. Ten to 15 years later, among 3,273 adults interviewed, the offer raised happiness, rated by the adults on a single 3-point question, by 0.098 SD (P = .013). A mental-health index moved in the same direction by 0.070 SD and fell short of significance (P = .084). Instrumental-variable estimates linked a 13 point lower neighbourhood poverty rate to 0.141 SD higher happiness; economic self-sufficiency did not change.

652.content: In the same Moving to Opportunity experiment, 2,872 children aged 0 to 8 at randomization were interviewed at ages 13 to 19 with a research diagnostic interview for DSM-IV disorders. Boys whose families were offered low-poverty vouchers had higher 12-month rates of major depression as diagnosed by the interview (7.1% vs 3.5% in controls, OR 2.2), and higher PTSD and conduct disorder rates. After a 2016 correction, the reported reduction in girls' depression diagnoses was no longer significant (P = .06); only their lower conduct disorder rate remained.

653.content: In a representative sample of 1,420 rural North Carolina children (aged 9 to 13 at intake, assessed yearly for 8 years), a casino opening on a reservation gave every American Indian family an income supplement, which moved 14% of study families out of poverty. Before the opening, poor children showed more psychiatric symptoms than never-poor children (4.38 and 4.28 vs 2.75). Afterwards, symptom levels in the children whose families left poverty fell to those of never-poor children, while persistently poor children stayed high. The authors report the effect was specific to conduct and oppositional symptoms; anxiety and depression symptoms were unaffected.

In a representative sample of 1,420 rural children aged 9 to 13 at intake, given yearly psychiatric assessments for 8 years (1993 to 2000), a casino opening on an Indian reservation halfway through the study gave every American Indian an income supplement that rose each year; it moved 14% of study families out of poverty. Before the opening, persistently poor and ex-poor children reported more DSM-IV psychiatric symptoms than never-poor children (mean counts 4.38 and 4.28 against 2.75). After the opening, symptom levels among the ex-poor children fell to those of the never-poor children, while those of persistently poor children stayed high. Similar results were found in non-Indian children whose families left poverty in the same period.

654.content: Across 237 cross-sectional and 87 longitudinal studies, unemployed people reported more distress than employed people (average d = 0.51); 34% of the unemployed had psychological problems against 16% of the employed, on measures including depression and anxiety scales. The authors report that longitudinal studies and natural experiments indicate that job loss causes distress and is not only correlated with it, and that selection of distressed people into unemployment is weak.

655.content: In 952 undergraduates, shyness (tension and inhibition with others) and sociability (preferring company to being alone) loaded on two separate factors, and shyness as rated by the students themselves had only a moderate negative correlation with sociability. When pairs matched on both traits talked for 5 minutes, the shy and sociable students talked less, averted their gaze more and touched themselves more than the other three groups.

656.content: In their introduction, the authors summarise Cheek and Buss (1981): some people are quiet because they are shy and have little wish to affiliate (shy and unsociable), while others are inhibited and anxious although they want company (shy and sociable). They report that the separation of shyness from sociability has since been replicated in children, adolescents and adults, in clinical samples, and in German, Portuguese and Asian samples, with one adult study disagreeing. They also note that the two traits are moderately negatively correlated.

657.content: In 99 German children followed from the start of preschool through Grade 1, parents' ratings of a child's inhibition toward strangers correlated with four observed measures of holding back (for example, delay before the first request, time spent not interacting) in play sessions with an unfamiliar peer (all eight correlations significant) and did not correlate with the same measures in play with a familiar classmate (none of eight significant; 12 of 16 direct comparisons significant). The author concludes that children shy with strangers interact normally with familiar peers.

658.content: In an experiment with 144 male Munich students, each talked for 5 minutes with a complete stranger, with a stranger they had just got to know in a 10-minute game, or with a good friend. Self-rated state shyness was highest with the stranger, lowest with the friend, and in between after the 10-minute acquaintance; a closed body posture followed the same pattern. Students high in trait shyness felt shyer overall, and the familiarity effect was the same for them as for the others (no trait by situation interaction).

Across this study and an earlier reanalysis, none of 26 tested interactions between the situation (stranger versus friend, evaluation versus none) and trait shyness was significant: shy and non-shy students became less shy with familiar partners to the same degree, while shy students stayed shyer overall.

659.content: In a longitudinal twin sample of 1,285 Wisconsin infants, parent-reported fear of strangers rose sharply between 6 and 12 months, held steady to 22 months and rose again to 36 months. Three in four infants (42.3% steep and 32.9% slow increase) started low at 6 months and grew more wary of strangers over time; 11.8% stayed high throughout and 12.1% started high and declined.

The authors report that the onset of stranger fear is believed to be adaptive, balancing infants' tendency to approach and explore and contributing to the emerging attachment system, citing Bretherton and Ainsworth (1974) and Ainsworth (1973). They also report that extreme stranger fear is a precursor of later social anxiety.

Twin concordance suggested that the trajectory of stranger fear is heritable: having a co-twin in the persistently high group raised an infant's chance of being in that group about tenfold for fraternal twins and about thirtyfold for identical twins. Persistently high stranger fear went with less heart-rate (RSA) suppression at 6 months, more maternal stress reactivity, and more observed inhibition at 36 months.

660.content: Neolithic Çatalhöyük in south-central Turkey is a 13-hectare mound with about 21 m of layered deposits from roughly 1,150 years of continuous occupation, dated about 7100 to 5950 cal BCE (about 9,000 years ago). The authors describe it as a single early farming settlement with the attributes of a protocity.
At its peak in the Middle Period, the Çatalhöyük community is estimated to have held about 3,500 to 8,000 people, the most crowded phase in its history, judged from house number, size and density.

661.content: The first cities appeared on the plains of Mesopotamia (modern Iraq and Syria) in the fourth millennium BC, about 6,000 to 5,000 years ago. Before that, settlements rarely exceeded a few hectares; in the fourth millennium places such as Uruk and Tell Brak passed 100 hectares of settled area.

By 3100 BC the city of Uruk covered about 250 hectares, and Tell Brak in northern Mesopotamia had grown into a 130-hectare settlement by the middle of the fourth millennium BC; the earlier Ubaid villages (ca. 5500 to 4000 BC) were rarely larger than one or two hectares.

662.content: Prussia extended compulsory primary schooling to rural areas by a royal decree of Frederick II in 1763, and France passed its first Primary Education Act in 1833. In the early twentieth century only a handful of countries gave universal access to primary education; today most countries have universal primary enrollment.

Across 109 countries, compulsory primary schooling laws were usually the last form of state intervention in primary education, introduced on average about 52 years before a country's first democratization; while in the early twentieth century only a handful of countries offered universal primary access, most do today.

663.content: In one-day contact diaries kept by 7,290 people in eight European countries (Belgium, Germany, Finland, Great Britain, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland; 2005 to 2006), participants recorded 97,904 contacts, a mean of 13.4 different people per day (country means from 7.95 in Germany to 19.77 in Italy). A contact meant touch or a face-to-face conversation of at least three words.

664.content: Using 'How many people named X do you know?' answers from 1,370 US adults reached by random-digit dialing (a nationally representative telephone sample whose data were published by McCarty et al. 2001), the authors estimate a mean personal network size of 611 people (median 472; men mean about 640, women about 590). 'Knowing' meant mutual recognition by sight or name, ability to contact them, and some contact in the past two years.

665.content: In the International Social Survey Programme work-orientation surveys (over 100,000 workers in 47 countries in 1989, 1997, 2005 and 2015), about 8 percent of workers disagreed that their job is useful to society and another 17 percent were unsure; in the 2015 wave (over 27,000 workers, 37 countries) close to 75 percent agreed.

In the International Social Survey Programme work-orientation waves (over 100,000 workers in 47 countries, 1989, 1997, 2005 and 2015), about 8 percent of workers saw their job as socially useless and another 17 percent were doubtful about its usefulness, with sizeable differences among countries, sectors, occupations and age groups and no trend over time.

In the 2015 wave, among workers who care about holding a socially useful job, seeing one's job as useless went with lower job satisfaction on a 7-point scale, after controlling for age, gender, education and country; the relation was much weaker for workers who did not care, and stayed significant after adding other job characteristics.

Within business, the share of workers who see their job as socially useless is highest in jobs with simple and routine tasks and in finance, sales, marketing and public relations; public-sector workers were more than 6 percentage points less likely than private-sector workers to call their job useless, and managers were not more likely than other workers.

666.content: The US General Social Survey asked nationally representative samples in 1985 and 2004 to name the people with whom they discuss important matters. The mean number named fell by about a third, from 2.94 in 1985 to 2.08 in 2004; the number of people naming no one nearly tripled, and the most common answer in 2004 was no confidant, against three in 1985. Non-kin ties fell more than kin ties. The authors themselves note that the data may overestimate the number of social isolates.

667.content: Re-analysing the 2004 and 2010 General Social Surveys and other representative US samples, the authors found significant interviewer effects on the number of confidants recorded, with a negative correlation between interviewer effects and mean network size; in 2004 some interviewers obtained highly improbable levels of social isolation. They conclude that the inference that networks have become smaller is an artefact of data collection.

668.content: In US national travel surveys, 40.7 percent of students walked or biked to school in 1969 and 12.9 percent in 2001; distance to school grew over the period and was the strongest correlate of walking or biking.

669.content: In an fMRI study of 12 heterosexual and 12 homosexual men in Germany watching explicit sex films of a man and a woman or of two men, every man rated the films matching his orientation as more arousing than the other films (0 to 10 scale, means: heterosexual men 6.0 vs 2.5, homosexual men 6.5 vs 1.6). Arousal ratings did not differ between the two groups (F = 0.10, p > 0.75), and there was no group by film-type interaction (F = 1.07, p > 0.30).

In the same study, films matching each man's orientation produced the activation pattern the authors take as typical of sexual arousal in both groups, including the hypothalamus, where activity tracked the man's arousal rating; films of the other kind did not activate the hypothalamus in either group. The authors read this as one shared brain correlate of sexual arousal across orientations. Homosexual men showed weaker hypothalamic activation and fewer active regions of interest than heterosexual men despite equal ratings; the authors say this may partly reflect the different films used.

670.content: An eye tracker recorded pupil dilation in 165 men and 160 women (recruited at a US university and on a web forum) while they watched 30-second videos of a naked man or woman masturbating. In men, the difference in dilation to male versus female videos tracked sexual orientation in a straight line (beta = .55, p < .0001): men at the exclusively heterosexual and exclusively homosexual ends of the 0 to 6 Kinsey scale dilated almost equally strongly to their preferred sex.

671.content: In an fMRI study of US men aged 25 to 50 (26 heterosexual, 28 bisexual and 25 homosexual recruited; 60 analysed for videos and 62 for pictures after exclusions), heterosexual men showed more ventral striatum activity to erotic pictures and videos of women and homosexual men more to those of men, in line with their own ratings of the same stimuli. In whole-brain picture contrasts, neither group had any region more active to the non-preferred sex; for videos, only homosexual men showed a significant ventral striatum difference.

672.content: A coordinate-based meta-analysis of 61 fMRI studies (1,850 participants; on average 72% male per study) of people viewing erotic pictures or videos found that sexual orientation was a weak classifier of the pooled activation patterns (15.1% predictive power), while stimulus type (picture or video) was the strongest. Visual sexual stimuli activated the left cingulate gyrus in all orientation groups, and the middle occipital, superior temporal, fusiform and several other regions in heterosexual, homosexual and bisexual participants alike.

In the same meta-analysis, homosexual participants viewing their preferred stimuli showed additional activity in the caudate body, cuneus, cerebellum, lingual and fusiform gyri and right parietal and occipital areas, while heterosexual participants showed left-lateralised activity that included the thalamus and hypothalamus. The authors conclude that the brain basis of sexual arousal is associated with sexual orientation and does not differ between women and men.

673.content: The authors measured genital and rated sexual arousal to male and female sexual films in women, men and postoperative male-to-female transsexual women. Their abstract states that men's arousal is category-specific: heterosexual men are more aroused by female than by male stimuli and homosexual men the reverse, while women showed little category specificity on either measure.

674.content: In an online sample of 1,036 Polish adults (2019) matched to census figures for sex, age group, education and place of residence, men watched pornography more often than women (beta = 0.42) and younger people more often than older people (men beta = -0.23, women beta = -0.21), with relationship status and religiosity in the same model. Frequency was rated on a 0 to 8 scale for the past year.

In the same sample and model, being in a relationship was not significantly linked to how often men watched pornography (beta = -0.08, p = .075) or women (beta = 0.05, p = .23), adjusting for sex, age and religiosity. Men in a relationship did masturbate less often while watching pornography (beta = -0.15). After sexual attitudes were added, women in a relationship watched slightly more often (beta = 0.09).

675.content: Web-tracking data from the Polish GemiusAudience panel (at least 10,000 members in each of seven October months from 2004 to 2016, 241,102 overall, weighted to Polish internet users) showed that 47% of male and 27% of female internet users visited pornographic or erotic websites in a given month. The share was highest at ages 18 to 22 (45%) and 23 to 27 (43%), stayed fairly level from 33 to 47 and dropped after that.

676.content: In a Swedish nationally representative survey (2017; 14,135 people aged 16 to 84), 68.7% of men and 27.0% of women used pornography. Among men aged 16 to 24, 17.2% used it daily or almost daily, 24.7% 3 to 5 days a week and 23.7% 1 to 2 days a week, against 1.2%, 3.1% and 8.6% of women that age. Frequency of use fell with age in both sexes.

677.content: One hour of 2019 access logs from one US data centre of a content delivery network serving a major adult video site (20.08 million requests, about 62,000 sessions) showed that viewers usually loaded only part of each video. Access times per video were far shorter than video lengths (mean video length 920 seconds), and 45.69% of video views started from the site homepage loaded under 25% of the video. The paper reports no count of videos or performers per session.

678.content: Reanalysing the US World Values Survey sample (N = 6,906) used by Nelson and colleagues in 2013, the authors replicated that parents reported more happiness, more life satisfaction and more frequent thoughts about meaning in life than nonparents. Controlling for marital status, age, gender and income removed the parent advantage in happiness and satisfaction, while the link with thoughts about meaning in life remained (b = 0.07, p = .02, against 0.08 without controls).

Across both data sets the authors conclude that the Nelson et al. article gives at best inconsistent evidence that parents have more meaning in life: the meaning link survived controls in the World Values Survey sample and was reduced to non-significance in the smaller experience-sampling sample (N = 339).

679.content: In 373 US adults aged 65 to 74 from the 1995 MIDUS survey, those who lacked more of three major roles (partner, employment, parent) reported less purpose in life, more negative affect and less positive affect. Among those lacking more roles, formal volunteers reported less of a drop in purpose than non-volunteers.

680.content: In a randomised trial in Baltimore, 702 adults aged 60 or older (85% women, 92% Black) were assigned to serve about 15 hours a week helping children in public elementary schools (Experience Corps) or to usual volunteer referrals. Those assigned to the school role scored higher on generative achievement (items such as 'I feel like I am making a difference in the lives of others') at 4, 12 and 24 months; in intention-to-treat analyses the effect sizes were small (d = 0.29, 0.19 and 0.16), and larger among those who served more hours.

681.content: In the US Health and Retirement Study (N = 8,113, waves 2006 to 2016), retirement went with lower purpose in life on the 7-item Ryff scale in a cross-sectional model (beta = -0.21 SD) and in a fixed-effects model (beta = -0.08 SD). Using Social Security eligibility ages as an instrument, the estimated effect of retirement on purpose was positive (beta = 0.32 SD; 0.29 SD with controls), concentrated in the first 4 years and among people with lower socioeconomic status who retired from jobs they were dissatisfied with.

682.content: A meta-analysis of 20 controlled comparisons from 19 studies (1,550 physicians, 18 of them randomised trials, nearly all scoring burnout on the Maslach Burnout Inventory) found interventions were associated with a small reduction in emotional exhaustion (SMD -0.29, 95% CI -0.42 to -0.16), about 3 points on the emotional exhaustion scale (15.1 against 17.9 in controls).

In the same meta-analysis, physician-directed interventions (mindfulness, stress reduction, communication and self-confidence training, exercise) were associated with a small reduction in burnout (SMD -0.18, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.03; emotional exhaustion 16.2 against 17.9), while organisation-directed interventions (workload and schedule changes, teamwork and leadership meetings, structural changes) were associated with a medium reduction (SMD -0.45, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.28; 13.9 against 17.9). The difference between the two was significant (Q = 4.15, P = 0.04).

683.content: A meta-analysis of 27 samples (1,894 mental health workers, studies from 1982 to 2014, mostly scored on the Maslach Burnout Inventory) found burnout interventions had a small effect on burnout: Hedges' g = 0.13 from pretest to first posttest, 0.20 in the 13 randomised trials, and 0.22 in the 5 studies with a second follow-up. Emotional exhaustion and depersonalisation fell slightly; personal accomplishment did not change.

In the same meta-analysis, person-directed interventions (such as stress management training) reduced emotional exhaustion more than organisation-directed interventions (Q = 6.70, p = .010), while the two did not differ for overall burnout or personal accomplishment. Among organisational approaches, job training and education did best for overall burnout.

684.content: A meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (716 physicians) and 37 cohort studies (2,914 physicians) found that, across interventions, overall burnout fell from 54% to 44%, emotional exhaustion scores fell by 2.65 points (from 23.82 to 21.17) and depersonalisation scores by 0.64 points. The authors conclude that both individual-focused and structural or organisational strategies can produce clinically meaningful reductions.

685.content: A meta-analysis of 50 randomised trials (17,828 participants) found that one week after stopping, people who stopped an antidepressant scored higher on the DESS withdrawal symptom checklist than those who stopped placebo or kept taking the drug (SMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.39; 11 trials, 3,915 people), about 1 extra symptom, below the 4-symptom cut-off the authors use for a clinically significant discontinuation syndrome. At two weeks the difference was smaller (SMD 0.13).

In placebo-controlled trials, stopping an antidepressant raised the reported odds of dizziness (OR 5.52), nausea (OR 3.16), vertigo (OR 6.40) and nervousness (OR 3.15) against stopping placebo; dizziness was the most common symptom, 6.24 percentage points above placebo. In 5 trials of people diagnosed with major depressive disorder, stopping was not associated with more depression symptoms. Among single drugs, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine and vortioxetine showed significant symptoms at week 1 (about 1.6, 1.4 and 0.6 extra symptoms).

The authors report that abrupt stopping of desvenlafaxine was not associated with clearly more symptoms (SMD 0.46) than tapered stopping (SMD 0.36), that most trials used a 1-week taper, and that evidence on longer tapers such as hyperbolic tapering is limited; they write that their findings cast some doubt on the need for routine long tapers.

686.content: A meta-analysis of 79 studies (44 randomised trials, 35 observational; 21,002 patients) found that at least one discontinuation symptom was reported by 31% after stopping an antidepressant and 17% after stopping placebo; in the randomised trials the difference was 8 percentage points. Severe symptoms were reported by 2.8% after stopping an antidepressant and 0.6% after placebo. The authors estimate symptoms attributable to the drug at about 15%, one in six to seven patients; desvenlafaxine, venlafaxine, imipramine and escitalopram had more frequent symptoms and imipramine, paroxetine and desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine more severe ones.

687.content: A Cochrane review of 33 randomised trials (4,995 participants, all at high risk of bias, nearly all in specialist care with recurrent episodes of diagnosed depression) found the evidence on withdrawal symptoms after abrupt or tapered stopping very uncertain (one study each). Most tapers lasted four weeks or less, and the authors note that rapid tapers may carry a withdrawal risk similar to abrupt stopping; relapse outcomes were confounded by withdrawal symptoms.

688.content: SAMHSA's 2016 report reproduces the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for social anxiety disorder (social phobia) beside the DSM-IV ones. The DSM-5 criteria require marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the person may be scrutinised by others (conversations, meeting unfamiliar people, being watched eating or drinking, performing or giving a speech); fear of acting in a way that will be negatively evaluated; the situations almost always provoking fear; avoidance or enduring them with intense fear; fear out of proportion to the actual threat and to the sociocultural context; persistence typically for 6 months or more; clinically significant distress or impairment; and exclusion of substances, other medical conditions and other mental disorders.

The report notes one change it expects to matter for estimates: DSM-IV required that the person recognise the fear as excessive or unreasonable, while the DSM-5 criteria instead require that the fear or anxiety be out of proportion to the actual threat and to the sociocultural context, judged by the clinician. Under DSM-5 the person does not need to see the fear as unreasonable. A cited study of 3,000 psychiatric outpatients and 1,800 bariatric surgery candidates in one Rhode Island hospital system found that dropping the insight criterion added under 1 percent to those who met the criteria for lifetime social phobia.

SAMHSA's 2016 report reproduces the DSM-5 criteria for a manic episode beside the DSM-IV ones. Criterion A of the DSM-5 criteria requires a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood together with abnormally and persistently goal-directed behavior or energy, lasting at least 1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day, or any duration if hospitalization is necessary.

Under criterion B of the same DSM-5 criteria, three or more of seven listed symptoms must be present (four if the mood is only irritable) and represent a noticeable change from usual behavior. The list includes inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep, with the example 'feels rested after only 3 hours of sleep'; more talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking; racing thoughts; distractibility; increased goal-directed activity; and excessive involvement in activities with a high potential for painful consequences, such as unrestrained buying sprees. Decreased need for sleep is one option on the list and is not required by the criteria.

689.content: The WHO's ICD-11 diagnostic manual (CDDR, 2024) lists the label social anxiety disorder as code 6B04. Its essential requirements for the diagnosis are marked and excessive fear or anxiety that occurs consistently in one or more social situations (conversation, doing something while observed, performing); concern about acting or showing anxiety in a way others will judge negatively; consistent avoidance or enduring with intense fear; symptoms persisting for an extended period, for example at least several months; no better explanation by another mental disorder; and significant distress or impairment. The manual adds that people may not see their own fear as excessive, so the clinician judges whether it is out of proportion, taking account of cultural norms and the person's circumstances, for example bullying.

The same manual draws a boundary with normal shyness: it says many people feel fear in social situations, such as speaking in public, or have the normal personality trait of shyness, and that social anxiety disorder should only be considered when the reported social fear, anxiety and avoidance clearly exceed what is normative for the person's cultural context and come with significant distress or impairment.

The manual lists QD85 Burnout in Chapter 24, among problems associated with employment or unemployment, and defines it as a syndrome conceptualised as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with three dimensions: energy depletion or exhaustion; increased mental distance from one's job, or negativism or cynicism about it; and a sense of ineffectiveness and lack of accomplishment. It limits the term to the occupational context. The chapter introduction says Chapter 24 codes such as QD85 record reasons for contact with health services, and that burnout as classified there is not considered a mental disorder.

The WHO's ICD-11 diagnostic manual (CDDR, 2024) codes the borderline pattern as 6D11.5, a specifier added to a diagnosis of personality disorder. Its criteria allow it when the person shows a pervasive pattern of instability of relationships, self-image and feelings, and marked impulsivity, shown by five or more of nine features: frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment; unstable and intense relationships; an unstable self-image; acting rashly in states of strong negative feeling; recurrent self-harm; marked reactivity of mood; chronic feelings of emptiness; intense anger; and brief dissociative or psychotic-like features under high arousal. The manual says the specifier was included for clinical utility, overlaps considerably with the trait domain specifiers, and may help identify people who may respond to certain psychotherapeutic treatments.

The same manual's general account of the personality disorder label states that it tends to arise when a person's life experiences give inadequate support for typical personality development, given their temperament, which it calls the innate part of personality reflecting genetic and neurobiological processes. It names early life adversity as a risk factor that is not determinative, and says that in a person with a history of early adversity, ongoing behavioural, emotional or interpersonal difficulties suggest the label should be considered.

The manual lists the label autism spectrum disorder as code 6A02 in its chapter on neurodevelopmental disorders. Its essential requirement is persistent deficits in starting and keeping up social communication and reciprocal social interaction that fall outside the expected range for the person's age and intellectual level, together with persistent restricted, repetitive and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, with onset in the developmental period and significant impairment. It adds that some people with the label function adequately in many contexts through exceptional effort, so that their deficits may not be apparent to others, and that the diagnosis is still appropriate in such cases.

The manual lists the label attention deficit hyperactivity disorder as code 6A05. It requires a persistent pattern, for example over at least 6 months, of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity outside the limits of normal variation for age and intellectual level, with a direct negative effect on functioning. Its description of inattention includes difficulty sustaining attention on tasks that do not give a high level of stimulation or reward, and it notes that inattention may not be evident when the person is doing something that gives intense stimulation and frequent rewards. It states that these symptoms are present in many children, adolescents and adults.

690.content: In a preregistered online experiment, 151 adults spent several minutes thinking and writing about a real-life friend, a favourite media figure (a one-way, parasocial bond) or a non-social topic, with state loneliness, negative mood and social self-esteem measured before and after. Thinking about the media figure lowered negative mood more than the control task (d = 0.41) and about as much as thinking about a friend. It did not lower state loneliness: the change was no different from the control task, and smaller than after thinking about a friend (d = 0.59).

In the same experiment, an exploratory analysis that was not preregistered found no association between how lonely participants were at the start and how much their well-being changed after thinking about a favourite media figure.

691.content: In a secondary analysis of a 4-wave US panel survey (166 adults recruited on social media) during COVID-19 social distancing, the intensity of people's one-way bonds with a liked celebrity or fictional character grew over the 6 weeks. Less face-to-face contact with friends predicted more growth in these bonds, which the author reads as support for parasocial compensation; more contact with friends through screens also predicted more growth, which the author says arguably cuts against it.

692.content: Across four studies the authors report that people turn to favourite television programmes when lonely and feel less lonely while watching, and that thinking about a favourite programme buffered drops in self-esteem and mood after a threat to close relationships. The authors call this preliminary evidence that favourite programmes give an experience of belonging.

693.content: In a UK research cohort of 3140 adults diagnosed with bipolar disorder (DSM-IV, 66% bipolar I, 68% women), a trained interviewer asked whether sleep loss had ever set off a mood episode. 20% (627 people) reported that sleep loss had set off a high (manic or hypomanic episode) and 11.4% reported that it had set off a low. Among the five triggers asked about, sleep loss was the one reported most often (alcohol 7.4%, non-prescribed drugs 5.6%, medication 3.6%, physical illness 2.6% for highs). People diagnosed with bipolar I reported it more often than people diagnosed with bipolar II (24.7% against 10.8%, odds ratio 2.81), and women more often than men (21.7% against 16.3%).

694.content: 29 outpatients diagnosed with bipolar I or II, in remission at the start, logged their sleep hour by hour and rated their mood on a visual analogue scale every day for a year (9433 completed days). In individual time-series analyses, 28% (8 people) showed a significant inverse link between sleep duration and mood the next day, 31% (9) between time awake in bed and next-day mood, and 41% (12) between total time in bed and next-day mood: less sleep or time in bed the night before a shift up in mood, more before a shift down. Between 59% and 72% showed no such link. The 2006 cohort with the same method (59 patients) found 34% for time in bed.

In the same one-year diary study, the authors conclude that a clear, predictable link between sleep and mood shifts held for a large minority of the 29 people diagnosed with bipolar disorder and did not hold for most of them: around two thirds showed no significant link between a night's sleep and the next day's mood.

695.content: 29 outpatients diagnosed with bipolar I or II, in remission at entry, logged sleep daily for a year and were interviewed by a psychologist every two weeks for new episodes (SCID, DSM-5 criteria; Young Mania Rating Scale). Average sleep duration in the two weeks before a hypomanic or manic episode, as rated at the clinician's interview, did not differ from the person's own well periods (coefficients near zero, p 0.50 and 0.79); mean sleep was lower only more than two weeks into an episode. What did differ before such episodes was the night-to-night spread: sleep timing was less variable in the week before. After correction for multiple tests, the authors found that changes in average sleep did not reliably come before episodes.

696.content: Reviewing the field in 2005, Johnson reports that naturalistic and experimental studies both point to sleep disruption setting off manic symptoms: in the experimental work, more than 10% of patients diagnosed with bipolar depression developed hypomanic or manic symptoms after induced sleep deprivation (Colombo and colleagues 1999, 206 patients). She summarises that sleep disruption appears to trigger manic symptoms.

The same review reports that the evidence for schedule-disrupting life events (events that shift a person's daily routine) before highs is weak: two retrospective studies found more such events before manic than before depressive onsets, but when compared with control participants, these events were not more common before manic periods than in the general population. Johnson adds that people forget schedule disruptions within about a month, so interview recall is unreliable.

697.content: A systematic review of 17 studies (1191 people diagnosed with a mood disorder) on the early signs people notice before an episode. Sleep disturbance was the most consistent early sign of a manic episode, reported by a median 77% of people across studies. The authors report that early signs before a manic episode lasted on average more than 20 days.

698.content: In 206 inpatients diagnosed with bipolar depression who were kept awake for three cycles of total sleep deprivation as a treatment (alone or with various medications), 4.85% switched into mania and 5.83% into hypomania, about 11% in all. The authors report these rates as comparable to those seen with antidepressant drugs.

699.content: Wehr and colleagues propose that the many different things that seem to set off mania (psychological, interpersonal, environmental, drug) may work through one shared step, sleep loss, which experiments in bipolar patients had shown can switch them into mania. Because mania also cuts sleep, they argue the process can feed itself and continue on its own once started.

700.content: 59 outpatients diagnosed with bipolar disorder recorded mood, sleep and time in bed daily for a mean of 169 days. Changes in sleep plus time in bed were inversely linked to the next mood change, most often with a one-day lag, in 24 of 59 patients (41%). Those 24 reported about two thirds of all large sleep changes (over 3 hours) and three quarters of all large mood changes.

701.content: Eleven outpatients diagnosed with rapid-cycling bipolar disorder kept daily mood ratings and sleep logs for 18 months. Across the group, shorter sleep was the best of three sleep measures at predicting a day the patients rated as manic or hypomanic (self-ratings classified by the study) the next day; four of the eleven showed no link between mood and any sleep measure.

702.content: In 54 people diagnosed with bipolar I followed after an episode, sleep deficit measured at month 6 predicted depressive symptoms over the following six months and did not predict manic symptoms. The authors suspect a short-lived effect on mania was missed because symptoms were rated per month.

703.content: A preregistered systematic review of 13 studies (17 papers, daily data for at least three weeks) on sleep changes and later mood in people diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Across sleep measures and study lengths, longer sleep, earlier sleep and later waking were mostly followed by low mood, and the reverse (shorter sleep) by manic mood, the authors report. Results were too varied for a meta-analysis; 14 papers were rated at fair risk of bias.

704.content: In interviews with the Life Events and Difficulties Schedule, more people diagnosed with purely manic onsets (21) than people with cycling bipolar onsets (24) or recurrent unipolar depression (44) had events that disrupted their daily routines in the 8 and 20 weeks before the episode began. The authors report that an earlier finding of more such events in the 8 weeks before a manic onset than in a control period was repeated.

705.content: A selective review of studies on what sets off highs in people diagnosed with bipolar disorder. The authors find evidence for goal attainment events, antidepressant medication, disrupted circadian rhythms and spring or summer conditions, and weaker evidence for stressful life events and high expressed emotion in the family.

706.content: 43 people diagnosed with bipolar I (SCID, recruited after a hospital admission in Rhode Island) were rated monthly for manic symptoms on the Bech-Rafaelsen Mania Scale and interviewed about life events with the Life Events and Difficulties Schedule, by raters blind to symptoms; events possibly caused by symptoms were excluded. The bigger a person's goal attainment (for example acceptance into graduate school, a new job, a poetry award), the higher their manic symptom scores in the two months after, controlling for scores before (partial r = 0.37, p = 0.01). Depressive symptoms did not change, and general positive events with no personal striving (a lottery win, a tax refund) did not raise manic symptoms.

In the same study, few participants reached full manic episodes, so the authors state that the findings concern rises in symptoms below the episode threshold rather than the start of full manic episodes. At the symptom rating before the event, 7% met the scale threshold for a full manic episode.

707.content: 125 people diagnosed with bipolar I (SCID for DSM-IV, Florida and Rhode Island) had monthly symptom interviews for a mean of 27 months (3418 interviews), with life events rated by interviewers blind to symptoms and events possibly caused by symptoms excluded. The larger a person's goal attainment, the higher their Bech-Rafaelsen manic symptom scores over the following 3 months, controlling for earlier scores and number of past manic episodes (standardised beta 0.18, t = 2.45, n = 120); a within-person multilevel model gave the same direction month to month (coefficient 0.22, p = 0.02). Goal attainment did not predict depressive symptoms. Goal-attainment events were uncommon: 14.7% of people had a major one in the whole follow-up, 23.8% a minor one, 61.5% none.

The same study reports that no participant developed a full manic or depressive episode in the months after a life event, so the authors limit their findings to shifts in symptoms below the episode threshold, and they describe the size of life-event effects as small. The authors also note that others have suggested life events matter less after repeated episodes, and their sample had many past episodes (mean 10.6 manic).

708.content: In 159 students and non-students (68 diagnosed with bipolar II or cyclothymia, 91 controls), preparing for and completing final exams was associated with more hypomanic episodes and symptoms, and no more depressive ones, in the students with these diagnoses. Self-reported reward sensitivity moderated some hypomanic symptoms during exams.

709.content: In a review of dominance motivation and perceived power across psychiatric labels, the authors report that people diagnosed with bipolar disorder, and people scoring at risk on the Hypomanic Personality Scale, report a strong wish for power and see themselves as powerful even when they are well. Diagnosed people asked about life goals while in remission endorsed very ambitious goals for wealth and fame, a pattern found across seven at-risk samples. The authors read bipolar disorder as a chronically raised desire for power with large swings in how powerful people feel as mood shifts.

The same review reports how thin the evidence is for raised feelings of power during a high itself: the only study of people in a manic episode rating their own power (Gardner 1982) had no comparison group of people with remitted bipolar disorder, and the authors state that no study has followed people diagnosed with bipolar disorder over time to see how their sense of power changes with symptoms.

710.content: Across four student samples (454, 780, and two further samples including 514), scores on the Hypomanic Personality Scale, a self-report of frequent mild highs, correlated with dominance motivation (r = 0.36), with seeing oneself as dominant (r = 0.35) and as admired (prestige, r = 0.33), with ambitions for fame (r = 0.42) and wealth, with hubristic pride and with socially dominant behaviour. The links held after controlling for current manic and depressive symptoms, and the scale correlated much less with the wish for close friendship.

Johnson and Carver report an earlier study (Gilbert and colleagues 2007) in which people diagnosed with bipolar disorder and healthy controls rated their own superiority and attractiveness on 11 items: within the bipolar group, even mild positive moods went with above-average ratings of their own social rank.

711.content: A systematic review of 51 papers (32 on hospital admission rates by season, 6 on diagnostic categories, 13 on symptom ratings) reports that admissions and episodes the studies labelled manic peak in spring and summer and, less so, in autumn, while those labelled depressive peak in early winter. The authors also report that people diagnosed with bipolar disorder show larger seasonal swings in mood and behaviour than people with unipolar depression or healthy controls.

712.content: In a nationwide Danish register of all adult psychiatric admissions labelled mania in the register from 1995 to 2012 (24,313 admissions), admission rates peaked in summer. Years and months with more sunshine, more ultraviolet radiation, higher temperature and less snow had more admissions; rainfall showed no link. The seasonal pattern did not change over the 18 years and was the same for men and women.

713.content: In New South Wales, Australia (southern hemisphere), 27,255 people admitted to psychiatric hospitals from 2000 to 2014 with an ICD-10 diagnosis of mania or hypomania were admitted least in autumn and most in spring. Monthly rates were lower from January to June, jumped in July and rose further until December, so the peak follows the local spring (September to November), six months away from the northern spring.

714.content: An umbrella review of 9 systematic reviews on seasonality reports that hospital admissions coded as mania are 7.4% to 16% higher in spring and summer, while admissions for bipolar depression are 1.5 times higher in winter. The synthesis was qualitative because the reviews differed too much to pool.

715.content: In the NIMH Collaborative Depression Study, 314 people diagnosed with bipolar I or II disorder were followed for at least 10 years with weekly symptom ratings (from semi-annual then annual interviews, US sites at about 39 to 42 degrees N). Weeks with clinically significant manic or hypomanic symptoms peaked in August, September and October, around the autumn equinox, and were lowest in winter. The authors note this is contrary to the admission studies that report a spring or summer peak.

In the same cohort, new episodes labelled manic, hypomanic or mixed by interview criteria after recovery (502 in bipolar I) were spread across the year: most common in March (10.0%), July (9.4%) and October (9.4%), least in May (6.6%) and June (6.8%), against an even-spread figure of about 8.3% a month.

716.content: In the COBY study, 413 young people diagnosed with bipolar spectrum disorder were followed for an average of 92 months (274,123 weekly mood ratings, three US sites). Weeks labelled manic or hypomanic on the interview scale were slightly more common in summer than in winter (1.3% against 1.2% of weeks, odds ratio 1.09, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.18). The month-by-month difference (August highest, February lowest) was not significant, no other season pair differed, and after adjustment neither site showed a seasonal difference on its own.

717.content: In the Prechter Longitudinal Study (Michigan), 583 people diagnosed with bipolar I, 164 with bipolar II and 283 healthy controls rated themselves every two months for years. Self-rated mania scores (Altman scale) were higher in spring and summer and lower in autumn and winter, and the seasonal effect did not differ by diagnostic group: healthy controls showed it too. The size was small (least squares means of about -0.05 against 0.08 points on person-mean-centred Altman scores, a 0 to 20 scale).

718.content: At one general hospital psychiatric unit in Pondicherry, South India (about 12 degrees N), 357 admissions labelled mania from 2010 to 2013 showed a seasonal pattern, but the peak was November to January (32.8% of admissions in those 3 months, against 25% expected), during the rainy season and before the hot summer. The peak was seen in men and in people over 25, not in women.

719.content: In a single-blinded randomised trial at five Norwegian hospitals, inpatients diagnosed with bipolar disorder in a manic state wore orange blue-blocking glasses or clear glasses from 6 p.m. to 8 a.m. for 7 days on top of usual treatment. Of 32 enrolled, 23 were analysed (12 blue-blocking, 11 clear). YMRS scores fell by 14.1 points with blue-blocking glasses against 1.7 with clear glasses; the between-group difference appeared by day 3 and the effect sizes over the last three days ranged from 1.05 to 1.86 (Cohen's d).

The same trial reports two weaknesses in its own text: it was not double-blinded because coloured glasses cannot be masked, and medication during the week was lighter in the blue-blocking group (3 of 12 received two or more antipsychotics against 8 of 11 with clear glasses; 6 of 12 received an anxiolytic, hypnotic or sedative against all 11).

720.content: In a randomised trial with blinded raters at two Ottawa inpatient units (2022 to 2024), 42 inpatients who met DSM-5 criteria for mania wore blue-blocking glasses (20) or lightly tinted glasses (22) from 6 p.m. to 8 a.m. for up to two weeks on top of usual treatment. YMRS scores did not improve more with blue-blocking glasses: at week 2 the estimated change favoured the control group by 2.1 points (group by time p = 0.93). As reported, antipsychotic and benzodiazepine doses and all other secondary outcomes did not differ.

The authors state that this rater-blinded trial failed to reproduce the earlier Norwegian trial of 23 inpatients whose raters were not blinded. They list other possible reasons besides chance: heavy medication (mean over 17 mg olanzapine a day), higher baseline severity (mean YMRS 33 against 25) and control lenses that cut some blue light. They suggest future trials in less severely ill or less medicated people, or trials testing prevention in high-risk people, which have not been done.

721.content: A correspondence by the authors of the earlier positive trials (Henriksen, Barbini, Benedetti and others) argues the null Ottawa trial was underpowered: its patients were more severely manic, more medicated and less adherent than in earlier studies; blinded raters lost access to nurse observations; and by their reading of the paper's Figure 4 only 30 of 42 patients were still assessed at one week and 7 at two weeks (83% lost by week 2), likely as improved patients were discharged.

722.content: In a pragmatic randomised trial in Trondheim, Norway, 476 adults admitted for acute psychiatric care were allocated to a ward with blue-depleted evening light or a ward with standard light. Length of stay did not differ (7.1 against 6.7 days). Clinicians rated more improvement (CGI-I difference 0.28, number needed to treat 12), lower severity at discharge (number needed to treat 7) and less aggressive behaviour (number needed to treat 9) on the blue-depleted ward. Only 31 patients were diagnosed with a manic episode, and the effect did not differ significantly between diagnostic groups.

723.content: In a pilot study in Milan, 16 inpatients diagnosed with bipolar disorder in a manic episode spent 14 hours in enforced darkness (6 p.m. to 8 a.m.) for three nights on top of usual treatment and were compared with 16 matched inpatients on usual treatment alone (not randomised). YMRS scores fell faster with darkness only when the episode had started less than 2 weeks before; in longer episodes darkness made no difference. Good responders needed lower doses of antimanic drugs and left hospital earlier.

724.content: A single man diagnosed with rapidly cycling bipolar illness at the NIMH was asked to stay in bed in the dark for 14 hours each night, later reduced to 10, and was followed for several years with self-ratings, observer ratings, wrist activity and sleep recordings. The authors report that on his usual routine he cycled rapidly between depression and mania with erratic sleep; when he kept to the long nightly dark rest, his sleep and mood stabilised. The authors started from the idea that artificial light extending waking into the night might set off or worsen bipolar illness.

725.content: In a double-blind randomised trial in Japan, 43 outpatients diagnosed with bipolar disorder and insomnia wore orange blue-blocking glasses (21) or clear glasses (22) from 8 p.m. to bedtime for 2 weeks. Self-rated sleep quality, actigraphy sleep measures and mood symptoms did not differ between groups; only the morningness-eveningness score shifted earlier with blue-blocking glasses and later with clear glasses.

726.content: A secondary analysis of the same Norwegian trial as Henriksen 2016 (10 patients per group with usable actigraphy) found higher sleep efficiency with blue-blocking glasses on night 5 (92.6% against 83.1%) and fewer nights of interrupted sleep (29.6% against 43.8%), even though the blue-blocking group received less sleep-promoting medication.

727.content: A systematic review found 29 experimental publications on evening blue-blocking glasses, including 16 randomised trials with 453 patients in total. Only one randomised trial and one case report involved people in an acute high; both reported large falls in manic symptoms, which the authors call preliminary evidence. The sleep trials more consistently showed shorter time to fall asleep.

728.content: In a randomised trial in Pittsburgh, 175 acutely ill people diagnosed with bipolar I disorder, all on medication, received interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (which trains regular times for waking, first contact, work, dinner and bed) or intensive clinical management, in an acute and then a 2-year maintenance phase. Time to stabilisation did not differ. Those who received the rhythm therapy in the acute phase went longer without a new mood episode (P = .01) whatever their maintenance treatment, and people who made their daily rhythms more regular during acute treatment were less likely to have a recurrence (P = .05).

729.content: In a randomised trial in New Zealand, 100 people aged 15 to 36 diagnosed with bipolar disorder (78% bipolar I) and on medication received interpersonal and social rhythm therapy (49) or specialist supportive care (51) over 26 to 78 weeks. Both groups improved in depressive and manic symptoms and social functioning, with no significant difference between the therapies.

730.content: Linking Swedish national registers for 9,009,202 people in more than 2 million nuclear families, the authors counted who had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder in public psychiatric inpatient care between 1973 and 2004 (at least two admissions with the diagnosis). Children of a parent diagnosed with bipolar disorder had a relative risk of 6.4 of the same diagnosis and full siblings 7.9; adopted-away children of a biological parent with the diagnosis had more than four times the risk. Model fitting put the heritability of being diagnosed at 59%, with small shared-environment effects.

In the same Swedish family data, relatives of people diagnosed with bipolar disorder were also more often diagnosed with schizophrenia (relative risk 2.4 for parent and child, 3.9 for full siblings). The authors attributed 63% of the overlap between the two diagnoses to additive genetic effects common to both, with a genetic correlation of 0.60; 31% of the genetic variance for the bipolar diagnosis was unique to it.

731.content: In 67 twin pairs from the Maudsley Twin Register (30 identical, 37 fraternal) where one twin had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder by DSM-IV criteria, the heritability of the diagnosis was estimated at 85% with narrow concordance and 89% with broad concordance, with no shared-environment effect detected. In a model treating mania and depression as correlated liabilities, about 71% of the genetic variance for mania as diagnosed by DSM-IV criteria was not shared with depression.

732.content: Screening all 19,124 Finnish same-sex twins born 1940 to 1957 found 38 pairs in which a twin was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder in registers or surveys (68% took part); lifetime diagnoses were made with the SCID for DSM-IV. When one identical twin was diagnosed, the co-twin was also diagnosed in 43% of cases (probandwise concordance 0.43), against 6% for fraternal twins; the heritability estimate was 0.93 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.00).

733.content: Among 8,141,033 Swedes in 4,149,748 nuclear families, 54,723 had a register diagnosis of bipolar disorder. First-degree relatives of a diagnosed person had a relative risk of 5.8 to 7.9 of the same diagnosis, falling with genetic distance, and heritability was estimated at 58%. The diagnosis also went with other diagnoses in families, most strongly depression (correlation 0.62) and schizophrenia (0.44), mostly through genetic effects, the authors report.

734.content: In Swedish twins linked to the National Patient Register (804 diagnosed with bipolar disorder, 91,604 not), heritability of the diagnosis was 60.4% (95% CI 50.3 to 70.5) after accounting for age, sex, follow-up time and censoring. More of those diagnosed were women (62.2%), with no sex difference in heritability.

735.content: The authors pooled twin studies that met modern standards to compare heritability across twelve diagnoses. Bipolar disorder, as diagnosed in three twin studies, came out highest at 85% (three twin studies: Sweden 79%, UK 85%, Finland 93%), ahead of schizophrenia 81%, Alzheimer's disease 75%, cocaine use disorder 72%, anorexia nervosa 60%, alcohol dependence 56%, panic disorder 43%, major depressive disorder 37% and generalized anxiety disorder 28%.

From the same comparison the authors conclude that how disease-like a psychiatric condition looks says nothing reliable about how heritable it is: several conditions read as chosen behaviour (cocaine use disorder 72%, anorexia nervosa 60%) were more heritable than major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders, and Parkinson's disease, with known brain pathology, is not very heritable. They add that heritability is not fixed and depends on the environment of a given population.

736.content: A review of nine psychiatric diagnoses reports their heritabilities (Table 1): schizophrenia 0.81, autism spectrum disorder 0.80, bipolar disorder 0.75, ADHD 0.75, nicotine dependence 0.67, Alzheimer's disease 0.58, alcohol dependence 0.57, anorexia nervosa 0.56 and major depressive disorder 0.37. Lifetime prevalence reported for bipolar disorder is 0.007.

737.content: A genome-wide study of 41,917 people diagnosed with bipolar disorder and 371,549 controls of European descent (57 cohorts) found 64 associated loci. Common variants together accounted for 18.6% of liability to being diagnosed (SNP heritability, assuming 2% prevalence), well under the 60 to 85% from twin and family studies. A polygenic score built from the results accounted for about 4.6% of liability and separated those diagnosed from controls with an area under the curve of 65%.

Using a mixture model on the genome-wide results, the authors estimated that about 8,600 variants influence the bipolar diagnosis, and that 97% of them also influence major depression and 96% also influence schizophrenia. Among the variants shared with the schizophrenia label, 80% pushed both in the same direction; among those shared with the major depression label, 69% did. Diagnosed bipolar I correlated genetically 0.66 with schizophrenia and 0.34 with major depression; diagnosed bipolar II correlated 0.66 with major depression.

738.content: Members of 85 families with a member diagnosed with bipolar disorder and 63 controls filled in two temperament questionnaires (TEMPS-A and TCI-125) and were interviewed with the SCID. On the dysthymic, cyclothymic, irritable and anxious TEMPS-A scales, average scores ran from those diagnosed with bipolar disorder, to those diagnosed with major depression, to unaffected relatives, to controls. The authors report that relatives sat between patients and controls only as a trend: none of these differences between relatives and controls was significant in post-hoc tests.

On the hyperthymic scale, which scores a lasting high-energy, upbeat, eager style, the controls scored higher than all three family groups (people diagnosed with bipolar disorder, with major depression, and unaffected relatives), the opposite of what the authors expected. The hyperthymic scale and an anxious/reactive factor were the only measures that separated unaffected relatives from controls.

739.content: A meta-analysis of 26 studies using the TEMPS temperament questionnaire (2,025 people diagnosed with bipolar disorder, 436 of their first-degree relatives, 1,757 healthy controls) found cyclothymic, irritable and anxious scores highest in those diagnosed with bipolar disorder, lower in their relatives, and lowest in healthy controls.

740.content: Household surveys of 61,392 adults in 11 countries (Brazil, Bulgaria, China, Colombia, India, Japan, Lebanon, Mexico, New Zealand, Romania, United States) used the same lay-administered interview (WMH-CIDI 3.0). Pooled lifetime prevalence reported was 0.6% for a bipolar I diagnosis, 0.4% for bipolar II and 1.4% for subthreshold bipolar, 2.4% in all.
