The United States had the highest lifetime rate of the whole spectrum (4.4%) and India the lowest (0.1%); Japan was low (0.7%) and Colombia high (2.6%).

Fewer than half of the people who met the survey criteria for a lifetime bipolar spectrum diagnosis reported ever receiving mental health treatment: 50.2% in high-income countries, 33.9% in middle-income and 25.2% in low-income countries reported lifetime service use.

741.content: A door-to-door screening of 68,378 adults aged 15 to 49 in Butajira district, Ethiopia (83.1% of cases rural, 70.2% illiterate), with CIDI and key informants followed by confirmatory SCAN interviews, found a lifetime prevalence of a bipolar I diagnosis of 0.6% in men and 0.3% in women. In 77.3% of cases the reported illness began with a manic episode. 55.9% had never sought help from the modern health sector and 7.1% were in treatment at the survey. The authors report the prevalence and age of onset as within the range of Western studies.

742.content: In the Butajira cohort in rural Ethiopia (bipolar I diagnoses confirmed by SCAN interview; 93% treatment-naive at recruitment), 100 of 240 people (41.7%) followed for an average of 2.5 years had at least two manic episodes and no depressive episode, which the authors classify as unipolar mania. The authors report diagnostic stability over follow-up of 76.4% (24 of 110 developed depressive symptoms). This group reported no suicidal ideation (0% against 26.4%) and fewer suicide attempts (2% against 11.6%). The authors cite averages of 11 to 23% for this pattern in high-income countries.

743.content: 312 people diagnosed with bipolar disorder in a rural Ethiopian community were followed with symptom rating scales for an average of 2.5 years: 65.9% had a relapse (47.8% manic, 44.3% depressive, 7.7% mixed episodes) and 31.1% had persistent symptoms. Being on psychotropic medication went with remission, the authors report.

744.content: Reviewing two centuries of follow-up literature plus a lifelong follow-up of 220 Zurich patients, Angst and Sellaro report that modern follow-up findings closely match those from before modern antidepressant and mood-stabilizing drugs. Hospitalized patients spent about 20% of their life after onset in episodes; half of episodes lasted 2 to 7 months (median 3); later episodes returned at about 0.4 per year with wide variation between people.

745.content: Comparing hospital records for North-West Wales, the authors report that admissions for bipolar disorders ran at 4 per 10 years per patient in the 1890s and 6.3 per 10 years in the 1990s, and that 16 bipolar patients per million population were in hospital on any day a century ago against 24 per million in acute beds now. They write that these data are incompatible with simple claims that mood stabilizers 'work'.

746.content: 73 patients hospitalized and diagnosed with mania and 66 diagnosed with unipolar depression in Chicago were followed up 1.7 years after discharge under routine care. Over 40% of the mania group had another manic syndrome in that time, and those taking lithium did not show better outcome than those not taking it, the authors report.

747.content: This meta-analysis pooled 48 randomised trials (6674 participants) of long-term lithium in people diagnosed with mood disorders. In the placebo comparison for suicide, 4 small trials with 485 participants contributed: 0 of 244 on lithium and 6 of 241 on placebo died by suicide (Fig 2), Peto odds ratio 0.13 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.66). For deliberate self harm the authors found no clear difference from placebo (odds ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.27 to 1.32).

The authors report that the main limitation of their review is the small primary evidence base: 29 of the 48 trials had fewer than 100 participants, with few suicide and self harm events, so the treatment estimates were unstable with wide confidence intervals.

748.content: In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial at 29 US Veterans Affairs centres, 519 veterans diagnosed with major depression or bipolar disorder who had survived a recent suicide-related event were randomised to lithium (255) or placebo (264) added to usual care. The trial was stopped for futility. Repeat suicide-related events (attempts, interrupted attempts, admissions to prevent suicide, deaths by suicide) occurred in 65 on lithium and 62 on placebo, hazard ratio 1.10 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.55). Four deaths were reported: 1 on lithium (suicide) and 3 on placebo (one suicide after a primary event, one opioid overdose, one suicide in month 13 found only after data collection closed).

Of the 519 randomised veterans, 439 (84.6%) were diagnosed with major depression and 80 (15.4%) with bipolar disorder. The authors report that most participants also had substance use disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder or both, and that the trial had too few participants with a bipolar diagnosis to test that group on its own.

Adherence in the veterans trial was low: only 1074 of 2154 lithium blood levels (49.9%) reached 0.5 mEq/L or more, and only 88 of 519 participants (17.0%) took at least 80% of their study pills. In that adherent subgroup the result did not favour lithium (12 events on lithium, 8 on placebo; hazard ratio 1.49, 95% CI 0.61 to 3.64). Blinding was imperfect: 68.1% of lithium-takers who guessed their assignment were right, against 49.1% on placebo.

749.content: This meta-analysis pooled 12 randomised trials published after 2000 that compared lithium with placebo or usual treatment in people diagnosed with mood disorders, including trials with zero suicides. Of 1278 people on lithium 2 died by suicide (0.2%) and of 1300 on placebo or usual treatment 5 did (0.4%), odds ratio 0.41 (95% CI 0.03 to 2.49), not statistically significant; the Exact method gave 0.42 (0.01 to 4.5). Adding 15 pre-2000 trials gave 2 of 1953 against 7 of 1784, also not significant (p = 0.10).

The authors read the modern trial evidence as highly inconclusive: compatible with lithium being linked to an unchanged, lower or higher risk of suicide. They attribute the gap from earlier meta-analyses to newer data, to keeping trials with zero events that the Peto method drops, and to 3 placebo-arm suicides in one trial (Lauterbach 2008) whose blind was broken for low lithium levels or suspected suicide risk.

For non-fatal suicidal behaviour, 81 of 1278 people on lithium (6.3%) and 85 of 1300 on placebo or usual treatment (6.5%) were reported with some form of it, odds ratio 0.97 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.34). In the 5 trials that reported suicide attempts specifically, 23 of 532 on lithium (4.3%) and 21 of 565 on placebo (3.7%) made an attempt, odds ratio 1.17 (0.61 to 2.25).

750.content: In a letter, 18 lithium researchers argue that Nabi and colleagues chose trials arbitrarily (excluding pre-2000 and active-comparator trials), wrongly assumed zero suicides where none were reported, and counted only 1 placebo suicide in the veterans trial (Katz 2022). They state that counting all 3 placebo-arm deaths in that trial as suicides turns the pooled result into a statistically significant effect for lithium (p = 0.034, Peto method).

751.content: In their reply, the Nabi authors state that of the 3 placebo-arm deaths in the veterans trial only one was a suicide during the trial: one was an opioid overdose the trial authors did not class as suicide, and one was a suicide a month after the trial ended, found much later and also left out of the trial's own analysis. They add that observational lithium data are biased by healthier people sticking to treatment, by doctors avoiding a toxic drug in people at high suicide risk, and by raised suicide risk in the year after lithium is stopped.

752.content: This review found 15 ecological studies (Japan, Austria, USA, England, Greece, Italy, Lithuania; 1286 regions) comparing natural lithium in public drinking water with regional suicide rates. In the random-effects meta-analysis, higher water lithium went with lower total suicide rates (pooled standardised beta -0.27, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.08, I squared 83.3%) and lower female rates; the male estimate was not significant. Mean water lithium in the studies ranged from 3.8 to 46.3 micrograms per litre. The authors call the evidence a population-level association subject to ecological bias.

The authors list the limits of their evidence: ecological studies are observational and only generate hypotheses, they are open to confounding where confounder data are missing, an association across regions need not hold for individuals, and the populations compared differ in ethnicity, religion, class, care for mental health and mobility. Some studies used water samples and suicide data from different periods.

The review reports that the only published study linking water lithium to suicide in individuals (Knudsen 2017, the whole Danish adult population of 3.7 million, 1991 to 2012, mean water lithium 11.6 micrograms per litre) found no statistically significant association, though all its rate ratios were at or below 1. The review authors call this negative individual-level result challenging for the hypothesis.

753.content: According to its abstract, this meta-analysis pooled 13 ecological studies (939 regions) and one cohort study (3,740,113 people) and found higher drinking-water lithium associated with lower suicide mortality (odds ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.67). The authors state the analysis used crude associations without considering confounders, and call for clinical trials.

754.content: In a 1994 editorial, Goodwin summarised the pooled analysis by Suppes et al (1991): across 14 studies of 257 patients (he describes them as having first-episode bipolar disorder), more than half of new episodes after stopping lithium came within three months, after an average of about 30 months of treatment, and the authors reported mania as much more common than depression in those first three months. He reports a crude 28-fold difference in new episodes per month at risk between patients on lithium and patients just off it.

Goodwin wrote that manic symptoms after lithium withdrawal appear comparable in severity to manic illness generally, often requiring hospital admission, and that whether these recurrences last a shorter time or are easier to treat had not been established.

Goodwin argued from a model (a 50% recurrence rate in the three months after stopping, set against the untreated recurrence curve of 50 first-admission patients from Mander 1986) that lithium taken for less than two years and then stopped is almost certainly of negligible benefit or harmful, because stopping brings the next episode forward; he recommended a minimum of two years of treatment and ideally three.

755.content: Moncrieff re-examined nine placebo-controlled lithium maintenance trials from the 1970s and reported that three (Baastrup 1970, Cundall 1972, Hullin 1972) were entirely discontinuation trials, in which patients already stable on lithium were switched to placebo, with a high rate of manic relapse in all the placebo groups as the author reports. In Cundall 1972 the reported ratio of manic to depressive episodes was 0.67 to 1 before lithium and 3.5 to 1 after discontinuation. Her conclusion, as reported, is that lithium-placebo differences in several trials were probably due to discontinuation raising manic relapse in the placebo groups.

756.content: In a Swedish mirror-image study of 194 patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder or schizoaffective disorder (LiSIE cohort, Norrbotten) who stopped lithium after at least 2 years of continuous use (mean 9.4 years), the mean number of psychiatric admissions per patient rose from 0.44 in the 2 years before stopping, while on lithium, to 0.95 in the 2 years after (P<0.001), and bed days from 11 to 22. The authors report that the rise came entirely from the 100 patients diagnosed with bipolar I or schizoaffective disorder (0.33 to 1.30 admissions), with more admissions for both manic and depressive episodes, while the 94 with bipolar II or other bipolar disorder showed no change (0.56 to 0.59). Mean time to first admission after stopping was 14 months in the bipolar I or schizoaffective group, as reported.

In the same cohort, 70% stopped lithium rapidly (within 0 to 14 days) and the rest tapered over more than 14 days; the authors found no significant difference by speed of stopping in the change in admissions or bed days after adjustment, nor in time to first admission (P = 0.079 for the whole sample; P = 0.240 for those diagnosed with bipolar I or schizoaffective disorder). Not having consulted a doctor before stopping was associated with more admissions, as reported.

757.content: Tondo and Baldessarini, whose group produced most of the rapid versus gradual lithium data, summarise prior research as showing that stopping long-term lithium abruptly or rapidly (over 1 to 14 days) is consistently followed by earlier recurrences than slower stopping, with a risk of early relapse that exceeds what the same patients' earlier course of illness would suggest. They report that the effect is concentrated in the first months, after which risk over time runs parallel to the course before treatment, and they recommend stopping as slowly as circumstances permit, over at least several weeks.

They note that maintenance trials now commonly remove an apparently effective treatment, often relatively rapidly, and switch patients to placebo, sometimes before full recovery, and argue that this makes the scientific interpretation of such trials uncertain, since discontinuation and carry-over effects of earlier treatment shape the outcomes observed.

758.content: In his reply to Moncrieff, Goodwin accepted that placebo-controlled lithium trials with a discontinuation design inflated lithium's advantage through what he labels withdrawal mania, while arguing that this effect itself points to a real pharmacological action of lithium on the course of illness.

759.content: A pooled analysis of 14 studies covering 257 patients diagnosed with bipolar I disorder who stopped stable lithium maintenance (mean 30 months) found that more than half of new episodes came within 10 weeks of stopping; by survival analysis of 124 cases, 50% had a new episode by 5.0 months, and 25% had a manic recurrence by 2.7 months against 14 months for depression, as reported. In 16 patients with a mean cycle length of 11.6 months before treatment, time to a new episode off lithium was 1.7 months, and the authors conclude early risk may exceed that of the untreated course.

760.content: In 64 outpatients with diagnoses of DSM-III-R bipolar disorder, stable on lithium alone for 18 to 120 months (mean 3.6 years) and followed up to 5 years after a clinically chosen stop (chosen during prolonged wellbeing in 67%), 75% had a recurrence within 5 years. The authors report a higher risk of mania after rapid (under 2 weeks) than gradual (2 to 4 weeks) stopping (5-year hazard ratio 2.8) and a larger difference for depression (hazard ratio 5.4), with the excess concentrated in the first months, after which the two groups' courses ran nearly parallel.

761.content: Pooling 161 patients with diagnoses of DSM-IV bipolar disorder maintained on lithium for a mean 4.2 years, the authors compared stopping over 1 to 14 days with stopping over 15 to 30 days: median time to recurrence was 4.0 months after rapid and 20.0 months after gradual stopping, and 37% against 1.8% stayed well for 3 years off lithium. After rapid stopping, median time in remission (6.3 months) was 2.3 times shorter than the mean cycle interval before lithium (14.6 months), as reported; monthly recurrence rates were higher in the first year after rapid stopping (6.5% against 2.3%) and similar thereafter. Ratios of median survival were similar for first recurrences of mania and depression (4.4 and 3.4 fold), as reported.

762.content: In 78 patients diagnosed with bipolar disorders whose lithium was stopped either over 1 to 14 days or over 15 to 30 days, median time to first recurrence was 2.5 months after rapid and 14.0 months after gradual stopping, a 5.6-fold difference, with similar ratios (4 to 6 to 1) in bipolar I and II and for mania and depression, as reported.

763.content: In a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial, 14 patients with a history of mania meeting DSM-III criteria, well on lithium for at least 18 months and on no other psychotropic drug, spent four weeks each on lithium and on placebo; 7 (50%) had a manic relapse and 2 more were withdrawn for signs of incipient relapse, all in the placebo phase, with relapses starting 13 to 19 days after abrupt substitution of placebo, as reported.

764.content: Patients meeting DSM-III criteria for mania, admitted once, who stopped lithium after a mean 29 months were compared with a similar group never on lithium; significantly more of those who stopped relapsed in the first three months than controls, and after that the relapse rate was identical, as reported. The author reads this as a lithium withdrawal phenomenon and as showing that a period of lithium does not improve long-term prognosis once it is stopped.

765.content: In a record review of 14 patients who stopped lithium acutely and 28 controls matched for age, gender and time on lithium, followed for about 7 years, cases had more depressive episodes and more total affective relapses (log-rank P < 0.0009), but the authors report that the excess was largely confined to the interval just after stopping and that outcome over 7 years was not worsened.

766.content: A retrospective case-note review found 53 discontinuations in 48 patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder who stopped a maintenance drug after at least 6 months of remission; recurrence within 3 months followed 74% of all discontinuations and 86% of the lithium ones, and also most discontinuations of anticonvulsants (89%), antipsychotics (64%) and antidepressants (58%), with manic and hypomanic episodes the most common recurrences, as reported. The authors conclude that early recurrence is not peculiar to lithium, noting small non-lithium groups and simultaneous withdrawal of other drugs as limits.

767.content: Among 227 patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder who stopped lithium after a mean 4.47 years, rapid stopping, stopping for medical reasons, a bipolar I diagnosis, more illness during treatment and less education were associated with a new episode within 12 months, as reported; median time to a new episode was 3.50 months after rapid and 10.6 months after gradual (2 weeks or more) stopping, still so with very early recurrences excluded, and length of prior treatment showed no association.

768.content: Schou reviewed the evidence and reported that early manic and depressive recurrences after stopping lithium may suggest rebound but that studies with appropriate methods had failed to confirm it; stopping prophylactic lithium, abrupt or gradual, carries a risk of relapse, and he judged a special lithium withdrawal syndrome unproven.

769.content: In patients labelled manic-depressive who stopped long-term lithium, most had recurrences, but the authors report these were spread over months, with no evidence of an immediate and inevitable rebound of psychotic episodes.

770.content: In a naturalistic study of 213 patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder, stable for 2 years on lithium alone after their last manic episode, 54 were slowly discontinued by patient preference and clinical judgement and 159 continued; first-year recurrence risk was 0.45 in the discontinued group against 0.15 in those continuing, median time to recurrence was 1.33 against 7.33 years, and the adjusted hazard ratio for discontinuation was 4.85, as reported.

771.content: Thirty-two patients with bipolar diagnoses and a definite good response to at least 5 years of lithium stopped it under a controlled discontinuation protocol and were followed up to 9 years; recurrence reached 7% by the first week, 32% by the first month, 62% by the first year and 81% by year 9, as reported, and only 6 (19%) had no recurrence.

772.content: The CANMAT and ISBD 2018 guideline states that almost all individuals given the bipolar disorder label require maintenance treatment to prevent further episodes, and that comprehensive treatment should start even after a first episode. It reports that with treatment 19% to 25% of patients have a recurrence every year, against 23% to 40% on placebo. The guideline sets no end date for maintenance; in its section on cohort studies it notes that for some patients maintenance therapy may extend across decades.

For patients presenting with manic symptoms, the guideline's assessment covers risk of aggression, violence and suicide, insight and ability to adhere to treatment, comorbidity including substance use, and availability of a psychosocial support network. It encourages regular monitoring of sleep, cognition, functioning and quality of life alongside mood, and its psychoeducation section lists regulating sleep and wake times among coping strategies.

The guideline summarises the DSM-5 criteria: a manic episode requires abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive or irritable mood and increased activity or energy most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 1 week (or less if hospitalization is necessary), plus at least three listed symptoms (four if only irritable), among them decreased need for sleep and pressure of speech. In its bipolar II section it states that the DSM-5 criteria for hypomania require symptoms lasting at least 4 consecutive days.

773.content: Healy, a psychiatrist, describes US direct-to-consumer marketing of the bipolar disorder label in the early 2000s, including a Lilly-sponsored website with a mood questionnaire launched after olanzapine was licensed for mania. He reports that patient materials for olanzapine (Zyprexa) stated that bipolar disorder is often a lifelong illness needing lifelong treatment and that almost everyone who stops the medication will get ill again.

774.content: In a 2006 letter, Lacasse and Leo report that a widely disseminated US advertising campaign for aripiprazole (Abilify) said the drug worked in the brain like a thermostat to restore balance, and that print adverts for its use in people labelled with bipolar disorder said it lowers the activity of key brain chemicals when it is too high and raises it when it is too low. They note that the FDA-approved product information listed the drug's mechanism of action as unknown.

775.content: An ISBD task force paper (Delphi consensus of 41 listed authors and an international expert panel) reports that a review of 25 clinical practice guidelines for the bipolar disorder label found fewer than half included even a basic discussion of circadian disturbances. It adds that the words circadian, chronobiology and chronotherapy do not appear in the 2018 CANMAT/ISBD guideline, which the authors note does discuss bright light therapy for bipolar depression.

The same paper cites a survey of 409 medical schools in 12 countries that reported under 3 hours of sleep education on average, with about a quarter of respondents reporting no sleep curriculum at all.

776.content: A review of 25 English-language clinical practice guidelines for the bipolar disorder label published from 2007 onward rated their overall quality as high (median checklist score 10 of 14 items), but only 11 (44%) included even basic information about circadian rhythm disturbances. The authors call circadian rhythms and chronobiology neglected domains in these guidelines.

777.content: In a 2019 Australian national online survey, 624 adults who reported ever being diagnosed with depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety, panic disorder or PTSD answered questions on sleep, and 296 (47.4%) met the authors' criteria for probable insomnia. Of these, 64.5% reported discussing sleep with one or more health professionals in the past 12 months, mostly general practitioners, and 35.4% had not discussed it with any health professional. Results are not reported separately for people diagnosed with bipolar disorder.

778.content: Analysing physician-reported US National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey data from 1985 and 1995, the authors found that visits in office-based psychiatry became shorter, less often included psychotherapy and more often included a medication prescription, and that the proportion of visits lasting 10 minutes or less increased.

779.content: In nationally representative samples of 14,108 visits to US office-based psychiatrists (National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey, 1996 to 2005), the share of visits with psychotherapy, counted in visits longer than 30 minutes, fell from 44.4% in 1996-1997 to 28.9% in 2004-2005. The share of psychiatrists who gave psychotherapy to all their patients fell from 19.1% to 10.8%.

780.content: In a single-blind randomised trial in four English NHS trusts, 69 adults diagnosed with bipolar disorder (88% to 94% bipolar I, all with a relapse in the previous year, most on mood stabilisers) received either 7 to 12 one-hour sessions with a research psychologist plus routine care, or routine care alone. The sessions taught each person to identify their own early warning symptoms of a high or a low, with a written plan to seek prompt treatment. Over 18 months a manic relapse on standardised interview occurred in 9 of 33 trained patients (27%) against 20 of 35 controls (57%), and the 25th centile time to a first manic relapse was 65 weeks against 17 weeks (log rank P = 0.008).

The same training had no effect on depressive relapses: by 18 months a depressive relapse on standardised interview occurred in 18 of 33 trained patients (55%) and 13 of 35 controls (37%), P = 0.15, and the trained group received more antidepressants. The paper describes sharing each written relapse plan with the patient's consultant psychiatrist, key worker and general practitioner; it describes no role for relatives or friends, and having a carer was used only as a stratification factor at randomisation.

781.content: A Cochrane review found 11 randomised trials that taught adults diagnosed with bipolar disorder to recognise early warning signs of recurrence, added to usual care; 6 trials (690 participants) reported time to recurrence. Pooled, time to any recurrence favoured the training (hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.82, I2 69%) and fewer people were hospitalised (RR 0.67, 0.47 to 0.95, 4 trials). The pooled hazard ratio for a manic or hypomanic episode as reported was 0.66 (0.40 to 1.06), short of significance, and for a depressive episode 0.57 (0.33 to 0.99).

Of the six trials with usable recurrence data, the early warning training was delivered to the patient alone in five; only one (Miklowitz 2003, family-focused therapy) also included a carer, so the planned subgroup comparison of patient-only against patient-plus-carer delivery could not be run. The authors note that the trials with benefit used about 12 one-hour sessions with experienced therapists, and the one trial with an inexperienced therapist (Perry 1999) helped only against manic recurrence.

782.content: In a single-site randomised trial in Barcelona with masked raters, 120 euthymic outpatients diagnosed with bipolar I or II disorder, all on medication, received either 21 weekly 90-minute sessions of group psychoeducation (illness awareness, adherence, early detection of prodromal symptoms, regular habits) or 21 unstructured group meetings with the same therapists. Over 5 years the authors report fewer recurrences in the psychoeducation group (mean 3.86 against 8.37) and fewer days acutely ill (mean 154 against 586), the gap being largest for days with depression. The groups were patients only.

783.content: A network meta-analysis of 39 randomised trials (3863 participants diagnosed with bipolar disorder, all also on medication) compared add-on psychotherapies with usual care. In 24 trials with usable recurrence data, family or conjoint therapy was associated with lower odds of recurrence (OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.53), as were CBT (0.52), standard psychoeducation (0.52) and brief psychoeducation (0.34); family or conjoint therapy ranked first.

In the component analysis of the same trials, the two components linked to lower recurrence were delivery in a family format (iOR 0.16, 95% CrI 0.02 to 1.22) and encouraging patients to monitor prodromal symptoms (iOR 0.22, 0.04 to 1.35); both intervals include 1. The model estimated that psychoeducation with guided skill practice and self-monitoring in a family or group format beats the same components delivered one to one (OR 0.12, 95% CrI 0.02 to 0.94).

784.content: A network meta-analysis of 41 randomised trials of add-on psychosocial therapy for adults diagnosed with bipolar disorder found that only interventions delivered to carers or family members alone, with the patient not attending, significantly lowered the patient's relapse rate against usual care: RR 0.61 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.86), from two trials with 70 participants in total. Family-focused therapy, psychoeducation and CBT pointed the same way without reaching significance.

785.content: In a randomised trial, 101 patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder, referred after a manic, mixed or depressed episode and all on medication, received either 21 sessions of family-focused therapy with relatives (psychoeducation, communication and problem-solving training) or crisis management with 2 family education sessions, both over 9 months. Over 2 years, 11 of 31 (35%) relapsed with family therapy against 38 of 70 (54%) with crisis management (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.75).

786.content: In a Barcelona randomised trial, the caregivers of 113 medicated euthymic outpatients diagnosed with bipolar disorder, all living with those caregivers, received twelve 90-minute group psychoeducation sessions (illness knowledge and coping skills) or no specific intervention; the patients themselves did not attend. Over the intervention and 12 months of follow-up, the authors report fewer patients with any mood recurrence in the caregiver group (chi2 6.53, P = 0.011), with the effect significant for hypomanic or manic recurrence and not significant for depressive or mixed episodes.

787.content: At a tertiary hospital in Jaipur, India, 40 consecutive drug-naive patients diagnosed by ICD-10 with a first manic episode (known thyroid disease, chronic illness and substance use excluded) had thyroid blood tests: 3 (7.5%) had hyperthyroidism and 2 (5%) subclinical hyperthyroidism. Among 40 age- and sex-matched healthy controls none had an overactive thyroid, while 5% were hypothyroid and 10% subclinically hypothyroid. Mean TSH was lower in the patients (1.51, P < 0.001); thyroid values did not track YMRS scores.

788.content: In Taiwan's national insurance claims, 21,574 people diagnosed with hyperthyroidism between 2000 and 2010 were later diagnosed with bipolar disorder (diagnosis code plus mood stabiliser use) 2.31 times as often as 21,574 matched people without it (IRR 2.31, 95% CI 1.80 to 2.99); the absolute rate after a hyperthyroidism diagnosis was 1.6 per 1000 person-years. The authors state they cannot exclude that some of these diagnoses were bipolar disorder due to hyperthyroidism, and that the order could run the other way.

789.content: In 21,012 adults diagnosed with unipolar depression at a large London mental health trust (2006 to 2013), a later diagnosis of mania or bipolar disorder was recorded at 10.9 per 1000 person-years overall and at 13.1 to 19.1 per 1000 person-years in those with prior antidepressant treatment. Adjusted for age and gender, the hazard ratio was 1.34 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.52) for SSRIs and 1.35 (1.07 to 1.70) for venlafaxine. The authors state that an observational design cannot show that the drugs caused the highs.

790.content: An ISBD task force (systematic literature review plus Delphi expert consensus) concluded that the risk of switching into mania, hypomania or mixed states during antidepressant treatment is judged higher and more severe in patients diagnosed with bipolar I than bipolar II, and somewhat higher with tricyclic and tetracyclic drugs and perhaps some SNRIs than with most modern antidepressants; they rate the evidence quality C. They add that switches are hard to attribute, because highs also come unpredictably in the natural course, which makes drug-induced and spontaneous switches difficult to tell apart.

791.content: In a prospective 11-month study at a psychiatric institute in Ranchi, India, 30 patients were classified as having an organic manic syndrome: 1.75% of all admissions and 4.67% of all patients with mania. Compared with 60 age- and sex-matched patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder, the authors report they more often had no family history of mood disorder, were more irritable and threatening, had more delusions and cognitive problems, and had improved less at 3 months.

792.content: Among elderly patients admitted with mania to McLean Hospital in Massachusetts, the authors report that 10 of 14 (71%) whose first manic episode came in late life (mean age 74.6) had a comorbid neurological disorder, against 10 of 36 (28%) elderly patients with earlier manic episodes.

793.content: Reviewing all 533 admissions to a university general-hospital psychiatric unit (Yale, New Haven) over 14 months, the authors judged that 43 (8.1%) were admitted because of mania or psychosis associated with antidepressant treatment.

794.content: A meta-analytic review of 73 reports (109 trials, 114,521 adults diagnosed with bipolar or major depressive disorder) found that the risk of mania or hypomania averaged 12.5% with antidepressants and 7.5% without; tricyclics carried more risk than serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the added risk was larger in those diagnosed with major depression, and mood stabilisers showed little protection.

795.content: In UK primary-care records (THIN, 1990 to 2008), 372,696 adults given 786,868 courses of oral glucocorticoids were compared with people with the same underlying disease who were not given them. The hazard ratio for a recorded diagnosis of mania was 4.35 (95% CI 3.67 to 5.16); the authors report higher risk in older men, at higher doses and in people with a past neuropsychiatric history.

796.content: Reviewing 14 new cases, 79 published cases and 29 clinical studies of steroid treatment, the authors estimate severe psychiatric reactions in about 5% of patients given corticosteroids, often with mood or psychotic symptoms, usually early in treatment and more likely with female sex, lupus and high prednisone doses; most recovered within weeks, with steroid taper among the effective treatments.

797.content: Over 20 years in Christchurch, New Zealand, 18 inpatients with newly diagnosed thyrotoxicosis and an acute psychosis needing psychiatric admission were found; seven were classified as mania and seven as depression. Nine had a first admission classified as affective psychosis alongside thyrotoxicosis, against 0.36 expected by chance, and the authors report that more than half stayed free of psychiatric problems over a median 11 years after thyroid treatment.

798.content: Reviewing published cases, the authors describe mania arising after drugs, infection, tumours, epilepsy and metabolic disturbance in people with no history of mood episodes, call these secondary manias, and argue that mania is a syndrome with many causes, which casts doubt on any single-cause account; they urge clinicians to screen for it.

799.content: Tooby and Cosmides argue that give-and-take reciprocity leaves a gap they call the Banker's Paradox: a hunter-gatherer who is ill, injured or unlucky in foraging needs help most at the moment she looks least able to repay it, so helpers choosing where to invest would be selected to desert her. They hold that the ability to attract help in such crises may have had larger selective consequences than gains from exchange when a person is healthy, safe and fed. This is an argument from selection logic with no data.

Tooby and Cosmides propose that friendship does not run on turn-by-turn repayment of favours. In their model each person has a limited number of friendship slots and should fill them with partners of high association value: people who value them highly and specifically, who are hard to replace, who want the same things, and whose company brings benefits as side effects. Helpers should be loyal to a partner to the extent that the partner is irreplaceable to them, people should want to be valued for what others cannot get elsewhere, and the mind should monitor all returns from a relationship, with repayment of specific favours neither necessary nor sufficient. They write that asking to repay a favour at once is taken as a sign of a lack of friendship, and that they know of no experimental studies of the traits the model expects.

Tooby and Cosmides offer two hypotheses about modern life. First, times of personal trouble show who is deeply engaged in one's welfare, and safer, more stable modern environments supply few such events, so a person may have many warm contacts and still feel lonely and unsure whether anyone would help. Second, people in market economies make explicit exchanges, often with strangers, at a rate with no precedent in human evolution, and the authors argue that the alienation many feel in commercial society comes from a mind that reads explicit exchange as a sign of shallow engagement. Neither hypothesis is tested in the chapter.

800.content: In three US samples (54 University of Pennsylvania students, 49 adults approached in a Philadelphia park, and 182 people recruited online), participants ranked their ten closest friends, excluding family and partners, and rated each one. In all three samples the strongest predictor of how high a friend was ranked was the participant's belief about how high that friend ranked the participant: mean within-person correlations were .71, .50 and .68, and the standardized coefficients in the ordinal models were 1.68, 0.77 and 1.21, the largest in each model. Perceived rank was rated by the participants themselves and was not manipulated.

In the same three US samples, rated benefits received from a friend and rated similarity to the friend were also significant in every sample (benefits: standardized coefficients 0.55, 0.60 and 0.48, mean correlations .45 in each sample), smaller than perceived rank. Participants gave unequal shares of 100 friendship points to their ten friends, and the shares were more equal when they imagined the friends would see them: the spread was smaller in public than in private for 61, 39 and 40 percent of participants and larger for 14, 18 and 10 percent. The authors read this as people ranking their friends and hiding the ranking, and argue that if friends function as allies, exchange of benefits will not explain friendship well.

801.content: In one laboratory experiment, participants could look at lights that would signal either that another person needed help, which the participant could not give, or that the other person had made a substantial contribution to a joint task; the lights never changed. Participants looked more often at the needs signal when the other person was a friend than when a stranger, and more often at the inputs signal when the other person was a stranger than when a friend.

802.content: Hall reports two studies of time and new friendships. Among 355 adults recruited on Mechanical Turk who had recently relocated, more estimated hours spent with a new acquaintance went with a closer friendship, and so did time spent in leisure activities together. Among 112 first-year students who reported the hours spent with two new acquaintances three times over 9 weeks, hours together were associated with changes in closeness between waves.

In two studies, 355 adults recruited on Mechanical Turk who had recently relocated estimated the time they had spent with a new acquaintance, and 112 first-year students reported hours spent with two new acquaintances three times over 9 weeks. In both, more hours together went with a closer friendship; among the students, hours together went with changes in closeness between waves.

803.content: Silk reviews how friends handle give and take and states it as an unsolved puzzle. In the laboratory experiments she reviews, strangers kept their contributions to a joint task separate and watched each other's inputs, while friends obscured their own contributions and watched each other's needs, and repaying in kind or straight away was read as a sign of a weak friendship. Yet people were dissatisfied when a close friendship was unbalanced in either direction. She concludes that no existing model of reciprocity explains a relationship in which balance matters and careful count is avoided, and suggests, saying evidence is lacking, that people may track only costly acts or audit a friendship from time to time.

Silk reports from the social science literature that people become resentful when a close friend does not grant their requests or asks too much of them, and that failing to help a friend when help is requested or needed produces a sense of betrayal and can end the friendship. She argues, against Tooby and Cosmides, that close friendship involves real costs and that people benefit only to the extent that friends return similar help. She notes that scholars disagree on whether friendship as a private, voluntary tie between non-relatives exists in all societies or arose with commercial societies in the eighteenth-century West.

804.content: Sugiyama recorded 678 injuries and illnesses in 40 Shiwiar forager-horticulturalists from physical evidence and informant reports; 17 of them gave the length of disability for 215 of the cases. The abstract states that most living individuals had come through a temporarily disabling health crisis that would probably have been lethal without others provisioning them.

805.content: Among the Shiwiar, forager-horticulturalists of the Ecuadorian Amazon, 17 people in one village (8 males, 9 females) gave the length of disability for 215 injuries and illnesses, cross-checked with other informants; disability meant being unable to leave the house to forage or garden. 86 cases (40 percent) disabled the person for a day or more and 28 (13 percent) for about a month or more. 16 of the 17 had been disabled for a week or more at least once and 11 of the 17 (64.7 percent) for about a month or more. Sugiyama assumes that a disability of about a month would be lethal without others supplying food, and on that assumption reads the survival of these 11 as evidence of provisioning; the report gives no record of who supplied food or care.

In the Shiwiar study villages of the Ecuadorian Amazon, Sugiyama describes small kin-based communities in which some foods are shared. Residents were closely related to most of the people they interacted with daily and came into repeated contact with few others.

806.content: In resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) of British Columbia and Washington State, a photo-identification study that followed every known individual from 1973 to 1987 (two communities, 261 animals alive in 1987) saw no animal of either sex leave its natal group and none join another group. Membership at every level changed only through births and deaths. The smallest stable unit was a matrilineal group of 2 to 9 animals (mean 3.6) spanning 1 to 4 generations, typically a grandmother, her adult son, her adult daughter and the daughter's offspring. The authors call this absence of dispersal by both sexes apparently unique among mammals.

The same study reports that the transient (mammal-eating) form of killer whale (orca, Orcinus orca) in the same waters is organised differently. Offspring keep long-term bonds with their mothers, yet matrilineal groups appear to disperse and some individuals appear to leave: at least one juvenile male left its pod and travelled alone, and a number of transient pods were solitary adult males. Transient pods held 1 to 7 animals (mean 2.7), resident pods 3 to 49 (mean 12.3). The authors say the transient system had not yet been examined in detail and that the absence of dispersal may not hold for all populations of the species.

807.content: From repeated underwater recordings of 16 pods of resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) off British Columbia, Ford reports that each pod produced 7 to 17 types of discrete calls (mean 10.7), that call repertoires differed significantly among pods, and that the 16 pods formed four acoustic clans. Pods within a clan shared several call types, often in versions specific to one pod, and no call types were shared between clans. The abstract adds that individuals appear to acquire their pod's repertoire by learning and that repertoires can persist with little change for over 25 years.

808.content: In recordings from 16 photo-identified resident pods of killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) off Vancouver Island, 1978 to 1983, with 43 days on three pods analysed by five activity states (foraging, travelling, group-resting, socializing, beach-rubbing), discrete calls dominated in most contexts, and variable and aberrant calls increased during socializing and beach-rubbing. Each pod had its own repertoire of 7 to 17 discrete call types (mean 10.7), consistent over a number of years. The relative use of calls varied with activity, but no call type went exclusively with one behaviour. Ford concludes that discrete calls probably act as contact signals that keep the pod together and coordinate its activities, that changes in call structure and call rate appear to carry information on the caller's emotional state, and that group-specific repertoires may make the contact system more reliable and mark pod membership.

809.content: In southern Alaska, an analysis of 112 single-pod recordings made from 1984 to 1999 (about 9000 calls) from seven pods of resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) found 26 distinct discrete call types, 9 of them produced by one pod only. The pods fell into two acoustically distinct groups. A genetic analysis done separately and blind to the acoustic results (full mitochondrial D-loop sequences from 40 of 82 biopsied whales) found that each acoustic group carried a single maternal haplotype, a different one in each group. The author reads the two call groups as maternal lineages (vocal clans) and argues that calls are learned from maternal relatives.

810.content: Recordings of two matrilineal groups (A12 and A30) of northern resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) over 12 to 13 years (1985 to 1998, 100 recording sessions) show that a family's calls are stable and still drift. The structure of one shared call type (N4) changed significantly in both groups over the period; another shared call type (N9) did not change detectably. The N4 calls of the two groups changed without growing apart: a neural network told the two groups' calls apart no better and no worse at the end than at the start. The authors read the parallel change as a sign that call changes pass between matrilines by learning, and say maturation of the animals could also explain it.

811.content: Two juvenile resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) that became separated from their natal pods between their first and second year, the only two such cases in three decades of observation of their populations, were recorded while alone. One (L98, alone in Nootka Sound from 2001, recorded in 2003 and 2004) produced barks like those of California sea lions: of 39 such barks, 16 were recorded in daylight when only L98 and no sea lions were seen in the area. Its use of call types also differed from its natal pod: its most used call made up 50.0 percent of its calls per session and 0.04 percent of its pod's, and its pod's most common call was never recorded from it. The other whale (A73), recorded for 106 minutes in a holding pen, stayed much closer to its natal pod's call usage.

The authors report from earlier work (Hoelzel and Osborne 1986) that a captive killer whale (orca, Orcinus orca), Skana of the Vancouver Aquarium, captured from K pod as a subadult, produced a reduced repertoire of eight calls, and that her most common call (49 percent of recordings) was a call of L pod that had never been recorded from K pod in the wild. They also cite reports (Bain 1988; Ford 1991) of adult killer whales learning their tank-mates' repertoires in captivity.

812.content: Call repertoires and social association were measured in six killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) held together under controlled conditions (three adult females, two juvenile males and one adult male; authors at the Hubbs-SeaWorld Research Institute) in 2001 to 2003 and 2005 to 2006, with 1691 calls attributed to individuals. Three distinct dialect repertoires were represented among the six whales. After a calf was born and two other whales were moved in 2004, the two juvenile males spent more time with the unrelated adult male, and by the end of the period both had begun producing novel calls and call features of his repertoire. He showed little or no change in return, and the adult females did not take up his calls.

813.content: Three captive killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) with a history of living with bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) were compared with seven killer whales held with other killer whales and with nine bottlenose dolphins. The three produced a higher proportion of click trains and whistles, and the timing features of their click trains lay between those of the other killer whales and those of the dolphins. One of the three took up artificial chirps that had been taught to the dolphins and produced whistles like one dolphin's stereotyped whistle. The authors read this as substantial vocal plasticity and a motivation to match the sounds of social companions.

814.content: In an experiment with one captive killer whale (orca, Orcinus orca), a 14-year-old female at Marineland Aquarium in Antibes, France, the whale was asked with a trained 'copy' signal to reproduce sounds made by another killer whale (her own 3-year-old calf) or by a person. She produced recognisable copies of every familiar and novel sound tested, human speech sounds such as 'hello' among them, most within the first 10 trials and three at the first attempt. The authors conclude that the group dialects recorded in wild killer whales can be acquired and kept up by imitation, and ask for tests with underwater sounds made by other killer whales.

815.content: An analysis by SeaWorld-affiliated authors compared 65 killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) held at SeaWorld parks and Loro Parque between 1965 and 2015 with known-age wild northern and southern resident killer whales followed from 1975. Annual survival at SeaWorld rose from 0.906 (1965 to 1985) to 0.941 (1985 to 2000) and 0.976 (2000 to 2015). Wild southern residents (0.966) and northern residents (0.977) survived better than the SeaWorld animals until 2000; after 2000 the populations no longer differed. Animals born at SeaWorld had higher annual survival (0.979) than wild-caught SeaWorld animals (0.944). The authors conclude that life-history parameters of free-ranging and captive killer whales are similar.

816.content: A survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier and Cox models) of 201 captive killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) worldwide gave an overall median survival in captivity of 6.1 years, with no difference between the sexes. Median survival was 12.0 years in U.S. facilities against 4.4 years in foreign facilities, 11.8 years for whales that entered captivity after 1 January 1985 against 3.9 years for those that entered before, and 14.1 years for captive-born against 5.5 years for wild-captured whales (the last two did not differ within the post-1985 cohort). The authors conclude that survival of captive cohorts has generally improved over time and that survival to age milestones is poor compared with wild killer whales.

817.content: A narrative review by authors from the Whale Sanctuary Project, the Animal Welfare Institute and the Orca Research Trust reports that 63 killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) were held in tanks worldwide in January 2019. Citing an unpublished advocacy-group analysis of the U.S. federal marine mammal inventory, it states that at least 15 of the 22 killer whales that died in US marine theme parks between 1990 and 2010 died of infectious and inflammatory conditions: eight of pneumonia, three of encephalitis, three of bacteremia and one of leptomeningitis. The review notes that fungal pneumonia is also among the most common causes of death in free-ranging killer whales and gives no rates for the wild to compare with.

The same review states that captive killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) have killed four people (three trainers and one member of the public) in the 55 years since captive display began and seriously injured many more, that there are no reliable reports of a free-ranging killer whale killing a person, and that the only recorded death of a killer whale from aggression by another killer whale involved two females in captivity. It also lists reports of oral stereotypies (biting and chewing tank surfaces and steel gates) and of self-injury such as banging the head against tank walls and gates, and says self-harm has not been described in free-ranging killer whales.

The review argues that the conditions of the tank (confinement, artificial social groups, lack of stimulation, noise) keep the stress response of captive killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) active for long periods, and that this chronic stress weakens immune defence and contributes to illness and early death. The authors present this as a likely mechanism. The review reports no measurement of stress hormones in captive killer whales; the cortisol findings it cites are from captive bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus).

818.content: A published critique of the Marino review, by five authors who say they disagree among themselves about keeping killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) in facilities, lists unsupported claims, misreported references and selective citation in it. On the chronic stress argument it states that the review cites no study showing a raised stress response (cortisol, ACTH or any other marker) in killer whales in facilities, and no evidence that the whales experience the listed features of their tanks as stressful. On survival it notes that the captive study the review relies on counted calves from birth, stillbirths included, while the wild studies start at about six months of age, after an early calf mortality that one wild study put at 37 to 50 percent.

819.content: Dental photographs of 29 captive killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) owned by one US-based theme park company and held at four facilities showed tooth damage in every whale, starting at a young age. About 24 percent of the whales had major to extreme wear of the lower-jaw tooth crowns, more than 60 percent of lower teeth 2 and 3 were fractured, and more than 61 percent of those teeth had been drilled (bore holes). Four of the five whales with the highest age-adjusted damage scores were captive-born. The authors attribute the damage largely to oral stereotypies, the whales biting and chewing concrete tank surfaces and steel gates; the study scored photographs and did not observe or count that behaviour.

820.content: A database of official reports, local media articles and private communications, compiled by authors who conclude that keeping killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) in oceanaria is ethically indefensible, counts 29 of the 65 killer whales owned by SeaWorld since 1964 (45 percent) as involved in one or more published aggressive incidents. A small number of whales account for most incidents and about 55 percent have none on record. The paper also describes the authors' own unstructured contact with juvenile killer whales at SeaWorld San Diego in 1979 and 1980. It gives no rate for wild killer whales to compare with.

821.content: In two populations of resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) off British Columbia and Washington State, yearly census records from 1973 to 2016 for 378 whales with a known maternal grandmother (4,578 whale-years, 123 deaths) show that a whale whose maternal grandmother had died within the previous two years had a mortality hazard 4.5 times that of a whale with a living grandmother, at average salmon abundance. Where the grandmother who died had stopped reproducing, the hazard rose by a further factor of 1.5, to 6.7 in total. The benefit of a living grandmother showed in years of low to moderate salmon abundance. The model also carried a term for a mother's death in the previous two years, which applied to sons only.

822.content: Using multigenerational records for two populations of killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca), the authors report that mothers who have stopped reproducing increase the survival of their offspring, most of all their older sons. The abstract gives no figures.

823.content: In the southern resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca), a closed population of 71 to 98 animals censused yearly from 1976 to 2010, a male's position in the social network was tied to his survival: males in the most central positions had about one third of the mortality risk of the least central males (hazard ratio 0.33 for community closeness, 41 male deaths), and the link held only in years of low salmon abundance. For females, social position was unrelated to survival (hazard ratio 1.06, 40 deaths). The authors suggest that well-connected males have better access to shared food and to information when salmon is scarce.

824.content: Using a towed hydrophone array and visual tracking of photo-identified animals, the authors assigned calls to single free-ranging resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) that were more than 35 m from the other members of their matrilineal group and out of sight of them. Focal whales gave 36 percent of their calls within 5 seconds of a call from another group member, four times more than expected by chance, and consecutive calls by different whales matched in call type more often than chance. The authors say the function of these matched exchanges remains to be explored.

825.content: A Cochrane review pooled 15 randomised trials of a single session of psychological debriefing given within one month of an event (road accidents, burns, assaults, miscarriage, childbirth, soldiers on a peacekeeping mission; most trials in the United Kingdom, Ireland and Australia). Compared with no intervention, people who were debriefed were no less often diagnosed with PTSD at up to 3 months (Peto odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.10 to 3.26, 1 trial, 40 people), at 3 to 6 months (1.17, 0.70 to 1.98, 3 trials, 278 people) or at 6 to 12 months (0.93, 0.35 to 2.46, 1 trial, 105 people). Self-reported symptom scores did not differ at 1 to 4 months (SMD 0.11, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.32, 5 trials, 356 people) and were slightly worse in the debriefed at 6 to 13 months (SMD 0.26, 0.01 to 0.50, 3 trials, 265 people). The authors found no benefit on scores for low mood, anxiety or general functioning either.

In the same review, the one trial that measured diagnosis at 12 months or more (133 burn patients, assessed at 13 months) found more debriefed people diagnosed with PTSD than controls (Peto odds ratio 2.51, 95% CI 1.24 to 5.09). The two trials with the longest follow-up, the burn trial at 13 months and a road accident trial at 3 years, both reported worse outcomes in the debriefed. The authors add that in the burn trial the debriefed group started with larger burns and more perceived threat to life, and that more people were lost to follow-up in one arm than the other, so they call the exact size of the adverse effect open to question.

The review authors conclude that compulsory debriefing should cease and that routine single-session debriefing after individual trauma cannot be recommended in military or civilian life. They offer explanations they did not test: one session makes the person go through the event again without time for the distress to subside, it may turn ordinary distress into a medical matter and raise the expectation of symptoms, and trying to forget or keep one's distance may be an adaptive response that the session interferes with. They also suggest that family and friends may already give people an informal version of the same thing, which would leave a formal session little to add.

826.content: Three-year follow-up of a randomised trial in Oxford: 106 people admitted to hospital after a road traffic accident were allocated to about one hour of psychological debriefing, mostly within 24 to 48 hours, or to no intervention, and 61 of them (30 debriefed, 31 controls) answered at 3 years. The debriefed group scored worse at 3 years on general psychiatric symptoms (Brief Symptom Inventory, difference 0.08, 95% CI 0.009 to 0.15), enjoyment of travel as a passenger, pain, physical recovery, everyday functioning and financial problems. Intrusion and avoidance scores on the Impact of Event Scale did not differ between the groups overall (F(1,58) = 2.03, P = 0.16).

In the same trial the result differed by how people scored at the start. Among those in the top quarter of initial Impact of Event Scale scores (24 or above, about 17 people), the debriefed still scored high at 3 years (mean 25.9) while the controls had dropped to 11.8, the level of people who started low (t(14) = 2.56, P = 0.023). The gap was already present at 4 months. The debriefed high scorers had more severe injuries, and the difference stayed at least marginally significant after adjusting for injury severity (all P below 0.07).

827.content: Abstract only. 133 adult burn patients were randomly allocated to one session of individual or couple psychological debriefing or to no intervention, and 110 (83%) were interviewed 3 and 13 months later by an assessor who did not know the allocation. At 13 months 16 of the debriefed (26%) and 4 of the controls (9%) were diagnosed with PTSD. The authors report that the debriefed group had higher questionnaire scores at the start and more severe burns, and both went with a worse outcome.

828.content: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 114 randomised trials with 8,171 adults, at least 70 percent of whom in each trial were diagnosed with PTSD lasting 3 months or more. Against waiting list or usual care, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy lowered post-treatment symptom scores by a pooled SMD of -1.32 (95% CI -1.57 to -1.08, 51 comparisons, evidence rated moderate quality), prolonged exposure by -1.59 (-2.05 to -1.13, 12 comparisons), cognitive therapy by -1.33 (4 comparisons), cognitive processing therapy by -1.03 (4 comparisons) and EMDR by -1.23 (-1.69 to -0.76, 11 comparisons). The authors call the evidence for trauma-focused CBT and EMDR robust and recommend them as first-line treatments.

In the same review, treatments without a trauma focus and a guided internet version also beat waiting list or usual care on post-treatment symptom scores: CBT without a trauma focus (SMD -1.06, 95% CI -1.39 to -0.73, 7 comparisons), present-centred therapy (-0.97, -1.33 to -0.62, 2 comparisons) and guided internet-based trauma-focused CBT (-1.08, -1.80 to -0.37, 3 comparisons, 145 people). Supportive counselling (-0.43, -0.90 to 0.04, 2 comparisons), psychodynamic therapy and relaxation training showed no clear benefit over waiting list, and trauma-focused CBT did better than supportive counselling head to head (-0.63, -1.04 to -0.21, 8 comparisons). The authors note that supportive counselling was often run as a control in which talking about the event was barred, that a funnel plot points to publication bias in the main comparison, and that most trials left out people with substance dependence, psychosis diagnoses or severe depression scores.

829.content: Network meta-analysis done for the NICE guideline on PTSD: 90 randomised trials, 6,560 adults with a PTSD diagnosis or clinically important symptoms, 22 interventions, evidence rated moderate to low quality by the authors. Against waiting list, the drop in symptom scores at the end of treatment was largest for EMDR (SMD -2.07, 95% credible interval -2.70 to -1.44), trauma-focused CBT (-1.46, -1.87 to -1.05) and self-help with support (-1.46, -2.33 to -0.59), followed by CBT without a trauma focus (-1.22, -1.95 to -0.49), self-help without support (-0.91, -1.67 to -0.15) and counselling (-0.73, -1.41 to -0.05). EMDR and trauma-focused CBT still showed lower symptom scores than waiting list at 1 to 4 months after treatment (-1.12 and -0.73).

The authors state that every treatment found effective was a structured therapy delivered by healthcare professionals with specialist training and regular supervision. All but one of the trials of self-help with support used computerised trauma-focused CBT, and only 4 of the 13 trials of self-help without support did. Counselling was among the least effective, and the authors add that in 10 of the 11 counselling trials it served as the control arm for another therapy, so its benefit may be underestimated through researcher allegiance.

830.content: Cochrane review of 70 randomised trials with 4,761 adults treated for chronic PTSD as diagnosed in the trials. On clinician-rated symptom scores, individual trauma-focused CBT (SMD -1.62, 95% CI -2.03 to -1.21, 28 trials, 1,256 people) and EMDR (-1.17, -2.04 to -0.30, 6 trials, 183 people) did better than waiting list or usual care. CBT without a trauma focus and group trauma-focused CBT also did better than waiting list or usual care. More people dropped out of the active treatments. The authors rated the evidence for every comparison as very low quality, citing small samples, unexplained heterogeneity, high or unclear risk of bias in many trials and little follow-up data on long-term effects.

831.content: Meta-analysis of the experiments on trigger warnings, content warnings and content notes (12 manuscripts in the 2022 preprint, all from 2018 or later, most of them single-session experiments that randomised people to a warning or none). The published abstract states that warnings had no effect on affective responses to negative material or on educational outcomes, that they reliably increased anticipatory affect, and that findings on avoidance were mixed. The preprint gives these pooled estimates: affect after the material d = 0.02 (95% CI -0.05 to 0.10, 86 effect sizes, 9 manuscripts), distress after the warning and before the material d = 0.43 (0.09 to 0.77, 5 manuscripts), avoidance d = 0.06 (-0.09 to 0.21, 5 manuscripts) and comprehension d = 0.06 (-0.02 to 0.14, 3 manuscripts).

832.content: Review of extinction research, mostly in rats (Rattus norvegicus) and mice (Mus musculus), with pigeons and humans for some effects. When a cue that predicted shock is presented again and again without shock, the fear response drops, and four findings show the original learning is kept: the response returns when the cue is met outside the place where extinction happened (renewal), when time passes (spontaneous recovery), after the shock is given again on its own (reinstatement), and it can be relearned fast. The authors conclude that extinction is mainly new inhibitory learning laid over the old memory and expressed mostly in the context where it was learned, while the first-learned fear carries over to new contexts more readily.

At the neural level the review reports that extinction of fear in rodents (rats, Rattus norvegicus, and mice, Mus musculus) needs three connected regions: plasticity in the amygdala is needed to learn extinction, inhibition of amygdala neurons by the medial prefrontal cortex is involved in retrieving it, and hippocampal-prefrontal circuits carry the return of fear when the context changes. The synaptic changes of extinction are added to those of the original fear learning and do not reverse them. In humans, imaging studies show activity in the homologous prefrontal area when extinction is retrieved.

833.content: Two experiments in healthy adults measured fear by skin conductance. In the first (34 people), a picture paired with a mild wrist shock was shown repeatedly without shock straight after learning until the response was gone; after unsignalled shocks the response to the picture came back, in the same room (t(15) = 5.42, P < 0.001) and in a different room (t(17) = 2.52, P < 0.05). In the second (14 people), a response extinguished on day 1 had returned 24 hours later with no further shock (t(13) = 2.31, P < 0.05), and only to the picture that had gone with shock. The authors conclude that extinction, even when done at once, leaves the original fear memory in place and that the timing gives no support for intervening very soon after a traumatic event.

In the same paper, male Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus) that had learned to freeze to a tone paired with footshock were given 20 tone-alone trials in a different box either about 12 minutes or 3 days after learning. Freezing to the tone came back after unsignalled shocks and, in a separate experiment, 21 days later without any shock. It came back as much after immediate extinction as after delayed extinction (group by time F(1,14) = 0.3, P = 0.63 for spontaneous recovery).

834.content: Fourteen pairs of identical male twins, one of whom had served in combat in Vietnam while the other had not (in 7 pairs the combat twin was diagnosed with PTSD), went through fear conditioning and extinction on day 1 and a recall test on day 2, with skin conductance as the measure. The groups did not differ in learning the fear or in extinguishing it on day 1. On day 2 the combat veterans diagnosed with PTSD responded more than their own twins and more than the veterans without the diagnosis (diagnosis by exposure interaction F(1,12.1) = 4.3, P = 0.03). The authors read the weaker recall of extinction as acquired with the combat and the diagnosis, since the identical twin who stayed home did not show it.

835.content: Sixteen people diagnosed with PTSD and 15 trauma-exposed people without the diagnosis did a two-day conditioning and extinction procedure in an fMRI scanner. Skin conductance did not differ between the groups while fear was learned and extinguished on day 1. On day 2 the exposed people without the diagnosis responded less to the extinguished cue than to an unextinguished one (0.12 against 0.30 microsiemens), and the group diagnosed with PTSD did not (0.40 against 0.37; group by stimulus F = 4.99, P = 0.03). During recall the diagnosed group showed less activation in hippocampus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex and more in dorsal anterior cingulate, and across all 31 people better extinction recall went with more hippocampal and ventromedial prefrontal activation.

836.content: 106 trauma-exposed adults from a primarily African American, low-income inner-city population in the United States (53 with no diagnosis, 14 who met criteria for PTSD only, 17 for major depression only, 22 for both) learned that one pair of shapes came with an airblast to the throat (danger) and another pair never did (safety). Startle to a noise probe was the measure. People with no diagnosis and people who met criteria for depression only startled less to the safety cue than to the danger cue, and less again when a safety shape was shown together with a danger shape. The two groups who met criteria for PTSD showed no such drop, and a higher startle on the combined cue went with higher scores on hyper-arousal symptoms only.

837.content: Twenty university students in Los Angeles (15 women) each named the person who gives them the most support day to day and supplied a photo. Neutral pictures were then paired with an electric shock while either that photo or a photo of a matched stranger was on screen, with skin conductance as the measure. Fear was acquired for pictures shown with the stranger (t(19) = 4.86, P < 0.001) and was not acquired for pictures shown with the support figure (t(19) = 0.63, P = 0.54), and the difference between the two conditions was significant (t(19) = -3.80, P = 0.001).

838.content: Thirty university students in Los Angeles (22 women) first learned to fear two pictures paired with shock. During extinction one picture was shown with a photo of the person who supports them most and the other with a photo of a stranger. With the photos on screen, a fear response remained for the stranger-paired picture (t(29) = 3.88, P = 0.001) and none for the support-paired one. With the photos taken away the same held (stranger-paired t(29) = 2.85, P = 0.01; support-paired t(29) = 0.84, P = 0.41; difference between the conditions t(29) = 2.21, P = 0.04). After reminder shocks 24 hours later, fear came back for the stranger-paired picture (t(29) = 2.40, P = 0.02) and did not come back for the support-paired one (t(29) = 0.30, P = 0.77), though the size of the return did not differ significantly between the two conditions (P = 0.06). At 2 weeks neither picture brought fear back, which the authors put down to conditioning that was too weak.

839.content: Peer-reviewed commentary by a psychiatrist at Tulane University who examined 122 claims in the book The Body Keeps the Score (42 on neurobiology, 51 on treatment, 29 on other topics; the full analysis is in his own self-published book). He reports that the brain differences seen in people diagnosed with PTSD come from cross-sectional studies, which cannot show cause and do not replicate consistently, and that three reviews of studies measuring the brain or body before the event all concluded that the differences likely came first. He reports that the book's ten body-based treatments have not been shown to beat trauma-focused talking therapies, with EMDR the one that matches CBT without beating it. He concludes that the claims of trauma-caused brain damage and of unique efficacy for body-based treatments are not supported by the weight of research.

840.content: Qualitative review of 25 prospective studies (5,675 people) that measured brain or body variables before a traumatic event and followed people afterwards; 21 of the studies were of young adults in the military, police or fire services, and the 15 largest were 86 to 100 percent male. In 19 of the 25, a difference linked to later posttraumatic stress symptoms was already there before the event. Of the 10 studies able to test whether the event changed the measure, 3 found that it did and 7 found that it did not. The author concludes that most of the differences found in people diagnosed with PTSD are better read as there beforehand than as damage done by the event.

841.content: Review of the claim that people can block out a traumatic event and later recover the memory intact, which the authors tie to what they call the body-keeps-the-score hypothesis (van der Kolk and Fisler 1995): trauma held on an implicit level with no story of what happened. They report that the central parts of traumatic events tend to be remembered well, that complete loss of memory is rare among groups such as concentration camp survivors, and that in suggestive interview studies about 30 percent of participants come to remember an event that never happened.

Pooling the published surveys, the authors report that on average 58 percent of those surveyed (4,745 people) indicated some degree of belief in repressed memories. Among surveys they cite, 69.6 percent of a sample of clinical psychologists strongly endorsed that the mind can unconsciously block out memories of traumatic events, and 93 percent of a sample of EMDR practitioners answered that access to traumatic memories can be blocked. In a survey of 2,326 United States adults, 9 percent reported that a therapist had raised the possibility that they had repressed memories of childhood abuse.

842.content: Short review of three disputes about memory for trauma. On the claim that such memories are fragmented, it reports a study of 60 trauma-exposed adults, half of them diagnosed with PTSD, whose recorded accounts were scored on 28 measures of coherence: memories of the event were about as coherent as very positive and very important memories, and those diagnosed with PTSD gave no less coherent accounts than those without the diagnosis. In a treatment study it reports, fragmentation did not change reliably over treatment and was unrelated to who improved. The authors note that one researcher has challenged the first study's conclusion and judge the rebuttal convincing.

843.content: Altman, who studied the Kuninjku of western Arnhem Land from 1979, reports that direct demanding is one of several ways food and goods move. Most everyday sharing happens at the time of production, where game is divided among everyone in the hunt whoever made the kill, and unsolicited gifts are also made. By rule, direct claims are limited to close kin and people who share everyday space. He states that most sharing occurs within the household. He gives no counts.

Altman reports that Peterson's 1993 article looks more at the ways people avoid demands than at instances of demanding, and that Peterson himself noted there is no measure of how frequent demand sharing is compared with unsolicited giving. Altman questions the article's words 'much' and 'often' on that ground, and adds that later writers turned 'much sharing is by demand' into 'all sharing is by demand'.

844.content: Among the Batek of Peninsular Malaysia, 25 men and 19 women observed for an average of 39.7 days in 1975 to 1976 were followed for reproductive outcomes up to 2016. Foraging return rate, the number of people a person gave food to or received it from, cooperative foraging and the presence of kin were all unrelated to lifetime fertility and to number of surviving children, in men and in women. Fertility ranged from 0 to 17 (mean 7.4) and surviving children from 0 to 12 (mean 6.2).

The same paper gives the authors' power analysis: with the average effect that von Rueden and Jaeggi's meta-analysis reports for foragers (0.18), about 200 people are needed for 80% power, against the 44 in this study. With the largest forager effect in that meta-analysis (0.46) the number needed is 34.

Batek camps on the Lebir River in 1975 to 1976 held 34.2 people on average (11.3 men, 8.6 women, 14.4 children under 14) and stayed 8.2 days in one place. Food was shared at once and never stored. Almost nothing was eaten during foraging trips. A hunter usually came into camp quietly and gave the carcass to someone else to butcher and hand out, and gatherers passed surplus tubers to other families without display. Bragging was frowned on. On an average day a Batek adult gave food to or received it from between one and two other people (mean total sharing degree 1.7 for men, 1.58 for women).

845.content: Among the Aka of Linganga-Makaou in northeastern Congo (one residential group of about 80 people followed for 92 days in 1991 to 1992 and one of 43 people for 11 days in 1995), women stewed meat and plants in front of or inside their huts and served it out in plain view of the camp. A cook and her children ate only about 20% of the stew she cooked, and about 75% of the stew a woman ate had been cooked by other women. Adult men usually ate together at the men's shelter, where plates were carried to them, and sometimes ate with wife and children.

In the same Aka study, camp size set how far a meal reached.
