In the same lever task with young male Wistar rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), the drugs methylphenidate and cocaine raised lever pressing for the partner while lowering pinning during the earned contact; the dopamine reuptake blocker GBR-12909 raised pressing without changing pinning; atomoxetine lowered both (5 to 11 rats per drug). The authors conclude that how hard a rat works for play and how much it plays once with the partner can be separated, and they note that under the two stimulants they cannot rule out that social exploration, and no longer play, was what the rats worked for.

1008.content: Male Wistar rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) were conditioned from 26 days of age for eight days, each day 30 minutes with a partner in one compartment and 30 minutes alone in another, and tested at 34 days (12 per group). Rats housed alone throughout spent significantly more time in the partner-paired compartment. Rats housed in threes and isolated for 3.5 hours before each session showed a tendency in the same direction. Rats housed with a 12-week-old rat showed no preference. Rats conditioned with a partner given methylphenidate, which suppresses play and leaves social exploration, developed no preference. With 15-minute sessions no housing group developed a significant preference.

In young male Wistar rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) housed alone (12 rats), the preference for the partner-paired compartment was present on the first test and on the next two daily tests without a partner, and was gone from the third extinction session on. One further day of conditioning brought it back for a single test.

Discussing young rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), the authors write that social play 'can be seen as a homeostatically controlled behavior', raised by social deprivation and lowered by social satiation, like feeding and drinking. To explain why 15-minute sessions gave no place preference in rats housed alone, they offer the possibility that the need for interaction was so high that a short session left the rats frustrated. The paper measured time spent in a compartment; it did not measure frustration.

1009.content: Juvenile male Long Evans rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), kept apart from their cage mate for the seven test days, were recorded alone for two minutes each day in the box where the partner was then let in for five minutes of play. The number of 50-kHz calls in the waiting period rose from a mean of 92.9 on day 1 to 182 on day 7. Over the same days the time spent moving fell from 56.7 to 28.4 seconds while runs rose from 0.64 to 7.27 and jumps from 2.00 to 9.18 per session. The authors take the rise in calls as consistent with calls that communicate 'positive mood' and as a sign that the calls may be meant for the partner that is about to arrive.

In the same recordings of juvenile male Long Evans rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) waiting for a play partner (2,946 scored behaviours and 4,272 calls), particular call types went with particular movements. Runs were accompanied by a call 96% of the time, jumps 93% and shakes 83%, while resting, rearing and exploring went with few calls. The authors conclude that the calls are no simple by-product of movement, and also that the tie between call type and action is hard to explain if the calls only convey an affective state; they propose that the calls help coordinate interaction from moment to moment. Two coders agreed on 36% of call types until four similar types were merged, then on 98%.

1010.content: Thirty juvenile male Lister Hooded rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), housed three or four to a cage, were tested in pairs after 2.5 hours alone, and 12 of them were also tickled by an experimenter. The rats called at 50 kHz in both situations and made no 22-kHz calls in either. Calling was higher during tickling (mean 97.0 calls per minute) than during play with another rat (34.3 per minute per pair). In play with another rat the number of calls was unrelated to the number of nape attacks, and a rat that was not engaged with the partner or the hand rarely called.

The authors test the reading of Panksepp and Burgdorf, in which the 50-kHz calls of young rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) express positive affect ('laughter'), against the reading that the calls mainly serve as signals between play partners. Call types were tied to different actions in the two situations: with another rat the strongest links were with approaching, following, chasing and nape contact; with the experimenter's hand the strongest links were with being pinned. They conclude that tickling is not a simulation of play with another rat, while still describing both as positive experiences for the rat. They also report that the positive correlation between playful contact and number of calls found in earlier studies did not appear in their data.

1011.content: Male Lister Hooded rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) lived with a littermate throughout. In the play-deprived group a transparent wall with small holes divided the home cage from day 21 to day 42, so that the two rats could see, smell and hear each other and touch a little, and could not play. From day 42 the pairs lived together without the wall. Tested as adults after at least four weeks together, the deprived rats had a lower frequency of inhibitory currents in layer 5 cells of the medial prefrontal cortex (about 30% lower for miniature currents; 6 rats per group) and fewer parvalbumin synapses around those cells. In a probabilistic reversal learning task they earned as many rewards as controls and made more correct choices, and their choices fitted a simpler strategy of staying with the last rewarded lever (12 rats per group, in two batches).

In the same study of male Lister Hooded rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), a third group had the divided cage and one hour together each day. In that hour a pair made about 200 pins and about 300 pounces, which the authors put at four to six times the hourly rate of socially housed rats of the same age (40 to 60 pins per hour, taken from earlier studies); about 75% of it fell in the first half hour (10 pairs). As adults these rats had the same reduction in inhibitory currents as the fully deprived group, and their behaviour in the reversal task lay between the deprived and the control group. Of the rats deprived without the daily hour, the paper says they showed enhanced and somewhat altered play when the wall came out and that this had passed within a week; it gives no counts for that.

1012.content: Female Wistar rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) were reared from day 21 to day 50 either in a group of four or five Wistar females, or as the one Wistar among three Fischer 344 females, a strain that responds little to play attacks. In a 15-minute stretch of peak play filmed in the home cage on day 30, the Wistar rats among Fischer partners launched about twice as many play attacks as controls (31.03 against 15.77), and about half of their attacks got a playful defensive response, against almost all in controls (8 and 9 animals). On day 35 the difference in attacks was a tendency (17.5 against 10.56). Pinning counts did not differ, and baseline corticosterone did not differ between the groups at any age tested. The authors call the arrangement a model of 'peer-rejection' and suggest that the missing response may be a major part of its aversiveness.

Regrouped with Wistar females from day 50 and tested as adults from day 70 (18 controls, 15 reared among Fischer 344 rats), the female Wistar rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) that had been reared with partners that did not play back showed less anogenital sniffing and less following and approach in a social interaction test, poorer recognition of a familiar juvenile, less preference for a food signalled by a cage mate, and a longer latency on a hot plate. Object recognition, open-field locomotion and most elevated plus-maze measures did not differ. The authors note that their earlier design, one Wistar reared with one Fischer partner, left adult social behaviour unchanged.

1013.content: Female Long Evans rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) were housed from about 24 days of age either with a female of the same age or with an adult female (6 pairs each) and filmed for 10 minutes at 34 and 36 days, each time after 24 hours alone. Juveniles living with an adult launched more play attacks than matched juveniles living with a peer (80.00 against 51.33 per 10 minutes). The adults launched few attacks (6.17 against 40.33 for matched juveniles) and evaded more than twice as often. Pins were fewer in adult-juvenile pairs (4.50 against 20.17 per 10 minutes), and attacker and defender swapped roles in 13.33% of play fights against 30.00% in juvenile pairs. No attack by an adult on a juvenile ended in a role swap.

The paper sums up rearing studies in which a young rat (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) has company and little play. Daily time with a drugged partner that does not play failed to prevent the later learning differences that daily time with an undrugged peer prevented (Einon and colleagues 1978). Long Evans females reared with an adult showed less pruning of dendrites in the medial prefrontal cortex than females reared with a peer (Bell and colleagues 2010; Himmler and colleagues 2013). Wistar females reared with Fischer 344 partners later showed changed pain threshold and poorer social cognition (Schneider and colleagues). The authors state that isolation rearing withholds more than play, and that for rats reared with an adult a link to poorer social skills has not been shown.

1014.content: The paper reports that a rearing result found repeatedly in Long Evans laboratory rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), more dendritic pruning in the medial prefrontal cortex after rearing with a peer than after rearing with an adult, did not appear in laboratory-reared wild rats of the Warsaw Wild Captive Pisula Stryjek stock: pruning was the same with a peer or an adult. The wild-rat result comes from a doctoral thesis (Himmler 2015) and a book chapter and is cited here second-hand. The authors raise the possibility that the link between play and prefrontal development in laboratory rats is an artifact of domestication, and then argue for another explanation: wild adults play more with juveniles.

In 10-minute tests of adult-juvenile female pairs (6 pairs per strain, juveniles 30 to 35 days old, each after 24 hours alone), pairs of wild-stock rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus, Warsaw Wild Captive Pisula Stryjek stock) launched fewer nape attacks than Long Evans pairs (40.50 against 87.93 per 10 minutes). Wild-stock adults launched 25.86% of the pair's attacks against 7.52% for Long Evans adults; more of the wild-stock play fights involved wrestling (55.92% against 24.58%) and role reversals (23.46% against 15.22%). In both strains the juvenile launched most attacks and the adult often evaded. The authors conclude that wild adults give juveniles more of the reciprocal play that laboratory adults withhold.

1015.content: A review of the social life of the Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) states that wild rats live in colonies that can hold more than 150 animals of both sexes and several generations and share a burrow system; that wild mothers nurse pups until about 40 days and the young stay close to her for up to two months, while breeders separate laboratory pups from the mother at three weeks; and that wild rats interact with up to 30 times more group members than rats in captivity. The author notes that knowledge of wild rats rests almost wholly on a few early studies and that behavioural data are mostly lacking.

On play, the review states that wild rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) have been reported to play with each other (Calhoun; Ewer 1971), that most evidence on social play comes from domesticated rats, that play fights occur only during adolescence, and that in the one comparison cited (Himmler and colleagues 2013) wild-derived rats played less than domesticated rats and with less body contact.

The review argues for housing laboratory rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) with other rats: it cites a study in which rats put more effort into joining familiar rats than into reaching objects or a larger cage (Patterson-Kane and colleagues 2002), and work in which rats housed alone differed from socially housed rats in behaviour, cognition, physiology and neurobiology. It adds that partners can also bring stress and injuries, so that suitable partners matter.

1016.content: Calhoun watched a colony of wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) in a quarter-acre outdoor pen in Maryland for 27 months from 1947. The colony was started with five pairs trapped on Parsons Island in Chesapeake Bay and grew to over 200 marked animals across four generations. He describes play between young siblings and other juveniles of similar age as one of their most common interactions: approach and nose touching, standing on the hind legs and sparring with the forefeet, rolling over while holding each other, then a short chase, without the biting and loud calls that end adult fights, after which the two may stay close together. He counted adult aggression and gives no counts of play.

In the same outdoor colony of wild Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus), Calhoun reports that young rats hardly left the burrow before about 25 days of age, and that at 25 to 30 days they stayed within 10 to 15 feet of the home burrow, where they played among themselves at the surface and followed the mother. Their range widened with weaning.

1017.content: The abstract reports that in juvenile rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) short-term social isolation increased both pinning, taken as the measure of play, and social grooming; the opioid antagonist naltrexone weakened the increase and morphine and beta-endorphin strengthened it. The abstract gives no isolation lengths and no counts.

1018.content: The abstract reports that rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) housed from 15 days of age with mother and peers, with peers, or alone, and all housed singly from 24 days, were then tested in like-raised pairs. The rats reared alone showed no deficit in the frequency of rough-and-tumble play, and their dorsal contacts were raised. In a T-maze, rats reared alone chose social interaction over food more often than family-reared rats. The authors call the results inconclusive and suggest that prolonged isolation increases the appetitive motivation for play. The abstract gives no numbers.

1019.content: The abstract reports that dominant juvenile rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) were conditioned twice daily for four days: on their preferred side with a partner given scopolamine, which left it unable to respond to play solicitation, and on their less preferred side with a submissive partner that played. After conditioning, the time spent on the originally less preferred side had risen by 198.6%. PubMed cuts the abstract off before the second experiment.

1020.content: The abstract reports that juvenile rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) emit short ultrasonic calls at about 55 kHz during rough-and-tumble play. Before any play experience, rats separated by a screen called less than playing rats; after one play session, separated rats called more than playing rats. Rats called more in a chamber associated with play than in a control chamber, play deprivation raised the calls, and a bright light lowered them. The authors' wording for the state is that the calls 'may index an appetitive motivation to play'; the words joy and laughter are not in the abstract. It gives no numbers.

1021.content: The abstract reports that rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) housed alone during weeks 4 and 5 of life showed less social activity as adults than rats never isolated, whatever the history of the later cage mate. Isolation in week 4 alone gave a similar reduction, which was absent when the rats were rehoused with non-isolated rats. Isolation in week 5 alone left adult social activity unchanged. The authors suggest that missing the chance to acquire play behaviour underlies the later differences; the treatment was housing alone. The abstract gives no numbers.

1022.content: The abstract reports that rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) deprived of social interaction during weeks 4 and 5 of life showed, as adults, less social activity and a changed sexual pattern, with locomotor activity and elevated plus-maze performance unchanged. Placed with an aggressive resident, they did not readily show a submissive posture and showed no immobility when returned to the resident's territory, and their plasma corticosterone and adrenaline were higher than in non-isolated controls. Responses in a shock prod test were unchanged. The title names play; the treatment was isolation. The abstract gives no numbers.

1023.content: The abstract reports that rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) housed alone made more object contacts in an open field and were slower to emerge into an unfamiliar place than socially housed rats. Isolation between 25 and 45 days of age left a lasting change in object contact; isolation between 16 and 25 days or after 45 days left none. The change in emergence followed isolation at any age and was reversed by later social housing. The abstract does not mention play and gives no numbers.

1024.content: The abstract reports that female Long Evans rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) were raised in conditions that differed in peer play, and that the shape of neurons was then examined with Golgi staining. Neurons of the orbitofrontal cortex followed the number of peers present, whether or not those peers played. Neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex followed the experience of play. The abstract gives no group sizes and no direction or size of the differences.

1025.content: The abstract reports a comparison of juvenile play in rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) from a colony of wild rats kept in captivity and in Long Evans laboratory rats. Both attacked and defended the nape of the neck in play. The wild rats played less: the laboratory rats started playful attacks more often and more often used tactics that led to body contact. The abstract gives no numbers.

1026.content: An online survey of pet rat owners in the United Kingdom (677 complete responses) reports, among the good findings, that many pet rats (Rattus norvegicus) were provided with a social companion. The abstract does not give the share of rats kept without one.

1027.content: Four male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) raised alone from birth to 6 months were then given contact with four normal female infants 3 months younger, which the authors call therapists: 2 hours a day, 3 days a week for a month in the home cage, then in pairs in a playroom, about 6 months in all. The isolates at first huddled in a corner and the younger monkeys approached and clung to them; within a week in the cage and a month in the playroom the isolates clung back, and then played back. By the fourth month their rocking and stereotyped movement were near normal levels, and by 1 year of age the isolates were, in the authors' words, scarcely distinguishable from the therapists in exploration, locomotion and play. The authors report essentially complete recovery of social contact and play in the cage, and in the playroom complete recovery of contact and very satisfactory recovery of play.

The same paper sets out three earlier attempts with rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) isolated from birth. Six-month isolates tested daily for 8 months with normal age-mates were often attacked by them and recovered a little, toward each other only; monkeys isolated for the whole first year showed no such recovery under similar conditions. Four 6-month isolates given a heated cloth surrogate touched it more and longer within days and their disturbance behaviour fell; housed in pairs they then played and explored clumsily, and after 6 months had shown no marked improvement. Females raised in isolation and later made pregnant mostly ignored or abused their first infants and several killed them; the authors write that the surviving infants struggled for contact with the mother day after day for months, and that from the fourth month the infants that had won contact were punished less than the infants of normal mothers.

1028.content: At a US National Institutes of Health facility, 231 rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) born 2002 to 2007 were assigned at random at birth to stay with the mother in a group of other monkeys (122), to be raised in a nursery and from day 37 with three same-age peers (57), or to be raised in a nursery and from day 37 spend 22 hours a day alone in a cage with a cloth-covered hot water bottle as surrogate mother and 2 hours a day with three peers (52). Between 6 months and 1 year all were put into one mixed social group. From the second year on, stereotypic behaviour (digit sucking was the most frequent form; the list also has pacing, self-grasping, rocking and circling) was noted in 5-minute observations twice a year. Among mother-reared monkeys 21.5 percent of males and 7.0 percent of females ever showed it; surrogate-reared males were 71.6 percentage points higher and females 75.6 points higher, and peer-reared males 44.1 and females 77.0 points higher (all p = 0.000). In males the surrogate-reared showed it more often than the peer-reared.

In the same randomised sample of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), veterinary examinations four times a year after the first year recorded illness in 15.4 percent of visits for mother-reared males and in a predicted 27.4 percent of visits for males raised alone with a cloth surrogate; among the kinds of illness only diarrhoea held up after correction for multiple tests. Surrogate-reared males also had higher cortisol levels before 1 year of age. Peer-reared males did not differ from mother-reared males in illness. The authors conclude that the health difference outlasted the rearing period and was not made up for by living in a normal social group afterwards.

1029.content: Records of 4,013 rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) housed in indoor cages at the California National Primate Research Center, scanned for abnormal behaviour in 5-minute observations between 2006 and 2011, were modelled by rearing history. Monkeys raised in a nursery (taken from the mother at birth, housed alone to 3 weeks, paired with another infant at 5 weeks) showed 11.02 times as much motor stereotypic behaviour, such as pacing, flipping and rocking, as monkeys raised with the mother in a half-acre outdoor enclosure holding 50 to 200 animals. In 3,286 monkeys, the nursery-raised were about 5 times as likely to bite themselves (4.95 and 5.42 in the two final models). Motor stereotypy was 20 percent lower, and self-biting 42 to 46 percent lower, for each year a monkey had spent in an outdoor group.

In the same records of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), monkeys raised indoors in a cage with their mother and no social group showed 9.68 times as much motor stereotypic behaviour as monkeys raised in the large outdoor groups, and did not differ from the nursery-raised monkeys. The authors write that the stimulation and support of a mother did not appear to decrease or prevent this behaviour and that cage size and complexity early in life may be what matters most for it. For self-biting, nursery rearing was the only rearing condition that differed from outdoor group rearing. The data are retrospective, and the authors say an experiment is needed to show cause.

1030.content: On Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico, a provisioned colony of about 1,000 free-ranging rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), 47 infants aged 5 to 12 months in two groups of about 250 and 115 animals were each watched for 30 minutes a week. Mothers stopped the infant from reaching the nipple a mean of 2.2 times an hour. Infants screamed or geckered a mean of 2.6 times an hour, and more in observations with refusals: 1.42 an hour with none, 4.31 with few and 5.97 with many. They followed the mother a mean of 4.59 times an hour, and more following went with more time on the nipple. Faecal glucocorticoid metabolite levels were higher in weeks with more refusals and were unrelated to the rate of distress calls. The authors conclude that infants find the mother's refusal distressing and respond by working harder to stay near her.

1031.content: On Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico, 23 free-ranging rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) infants and their mothers were filmed and watched from birth to 42 weeks of age. Observers rated each infant's use of the mother as a secure base with a 94-item sorting method adapted from human attachment research. The field record counted how often an infant went to its mother after a serious risk event. Infants rated higher at 13 to 42 weeks went to her after a larger share of such events (r = .53 for the most serious events, r = .44 for serious ones), gave distress calls in fewer observations (r = -.44) and followed her more when she left (r = .46). Higher-rated infants spent less time in contact with the mother after 3 months of age and no less before. The paper gives no figure for how often infants as a whole went to the mother after a risk event.

1032.content: A review of rearing studies in non-human primates states that in a normally living group most monkey infants spend virtually all of their first days or weeks clinging to the mother, belly to belly. At about 2 months they begin to explore and to play with peers, and from 6 months to puberty play with peers is the main social activity, while the mother stays the protector in stressful situations. The review's sentence speaks of monkey infants in general and gives no numbers; the sources it cites for it are studies of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta).

The same review states that total social isolation was once considered to leave a permanent defect in monkeys, and that studies pairing isolated monkeys with what the original authors called therapist monkeys found fewer self-directed and stereotypic behaviours and more social contact and exploration. It concludes that rehabilitation is possible at least in part and takes several methods together and considerable time and effort, and it notes that enrichment devices eased only the less severe abnormal behaviours.

1033.content: In 16 laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) of a commercial strain, access from a home pen with food, water and a perch to a pen with two littered, enclosed nest boxes was made harder by narrowing the gap between the pens (220, 140, 125, 110 and 95 mm; the hens' mean body width was 117 mm). Entries fell and failed attempts rose as the gap narrowed, yet all 16 hens kept entering the nest pen before laying and laid in the nest boxes. Between 120 and 30 minutes before laying hens made 27.6 entries through the 220 mm gap and none through the 95 mm gap; in the last half hour before laying they made few entries (1.3) and this did not fall as the gap narrowed (1.1 at 95 mm). After laying, hens passed gaps of 220 and 140 mm to go back to the nest pen but not gaps of 125 mm or less. The authors conclude hens were willing to pay a high cost to reach a nest box before laying, so prelaying behaviour may be frustrated in hens without a well-defined, littered nest site.

1034.content: Twelve Isa Brown laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) were trained to push open a locked door wired to a load cell, once a day, to reach a pen with an enclosed nest box at 80, 60, 40 or 20 minutes before laying, and to reach their home pen with food, water, litter and a perch after 1, 2, 3 or 4 hours shut in the nest pen. As laying came closer the hens worked at a higher rate for the nest pen, used the nest box sooner and spent more of the visit in it. Their work-rate for the nest pen 40 minutes before laying matched their work-rate for the home pen after 4 hours without food, and was highest 20 minutes before laying. The authors conclude hens value reaching a discrete nest site before laying more than reaching food after 4 hours without it.

1035.content: In a Wageningen experiment, 20 laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus; 10 ISA Brown Warren, 10 ISA White Leghorn), each in its own wire-fronted cage with a nest box and a dust area, were watched for 15 minutes after settling in the nest before laying; each was then pushed off the nest and the nest box was closed for 15 minutes, then reopened. While the nest was closed the hens gave significantly more gakel-calls, more alarm cackles (mean 0.0 before against 8.0) and more escape attempts (0.0 against 11.4, counted as pushing the head out through the cage wire), and spent more time in stereotyped pacing (mean 306 seconds of the 15 minutes against 0 seconds before) and displacement preening (29.8 against 1.8 seconds). The authors measured these behaviours as indicators of a state of frustration, which they define as an aversive motivational state that results from nonreward in a situation that previously was rewarding.

In the same experiment the hens gave significantly more gakel-calls when the nest was closed than when food, water or the dustbath was withheld, and the nest-context calls lasted longer and had more notes. The authors do not read this as stronger frustration, because the other behaviours they used as signs of frustration were not higher in the nest treatment; they say the gakel-calls with the nest closed are probably given both in response to the thwarting of nesting and as part of normal pre-laying behaviour, since the call is given before laying under natural conditions. They also offer Wiepkema's model, in which the call is an emotional expression of a detected mismatch between the actual state (no nest site found) and the desired state (find a suitable nest site).

Reviewing earlier work, Zimmerman reports that the gakel-call is heard before laying under natural conditions, and that a hen about to leave the group to find a nest site utters it; as a rule the dominant male answers by escorting her to a nest site (McBride et al. 1969 and Thornhill 1988, as cited). He also reports that hens in battery cages gave more gakel-calls before laying than hens on wire-netting floors or deep litter, and their calls were longer and had more notes (Huber and Folsch 1978, as cited, who put this down to the caged hens being unable to find a suitable nest site), and that in alternative systems calling in the hour before laying was high at first and then fell sharply towards laying, while in battery cages it stayed high (Meijsser and Hughes 1989, as cited, who found only a slight difference overall).

1036.content: In 120 White Leghorn hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) at the University of Guelph, hens with a nest box in their cage spent the least time pacing in the hour before laying; hens with no nest box and hens whose nest box access was periodically restricted paced for similar amounts of time. Against the authors' expectation, eggshells from the three treatments carried the same amount of extra-cuticular calcium and tibia strength did not differ. The authors open from the position that the inability of caged hens to nest results in frustration, which shows as stereotyped pacing.

1037.content: In battery cages, hens of one strain of domestic fowl (Gallus gallus domesticus) typically paced backwards and forwards in the 10 minutes before laying, while hens of another strain did not pace and tended to sit. Each hen was consistent in which she did, both traits varied genetically and responded to selection, and crosses showed additive genetic variation for sitting and non-additive variation for pacing.

1038.content: Reviewing studies of free-living domestic fowl (Gallus gallus domesticus), Rietveld-Piepers reports that in Duncan, Savory and Wood-Gush's (1978) study of feral hens, a hen's absence from the flock usually meant she had come into lay. The nests of domestic fowl released on an island were no more than shallow scrapes or natural hollows in the ground, but all were very well hidden and covered by vegetation, which the reviewer reads as concealment being an important element of nest-site choice (Wood-Gush and Duncan 1976; Duncan et al. 1978). In feral red jungle fowl (Gallus gallus) a nest was only a slight hollow lined with a few leaves and small feathers (Collias and Collias 1967). Feral hens gave the pre-laying call, but never very loud or persistent, entered a nest without obviously examining other sites as penned hens do, and were never heard to cackle right after leaving the nest.

The same review reports that a cock escorting a hen to possible nest sites, scratching a hollow and calling, was seen in captive domestic fowl from a feral population (McBride et al. 1969) and in penned White Leghorn hybrids and red jungle fowl (Wennrich 1978; Folsch 1981), but that in Duncan, Savory and Wood-Gush's (1978) study of feral domestic fowl the cock was never seen to escort a hen to a nesting site.

Rietveld-Piepers reports that Folsch (1981) compared hens kept in cages without nests with hens in wire- or litter-floored pens with nests: the caged hens spent nearly the same total time in nesting behaviour, but the later phases (entering the chosen nest, laying, sitting) were much shorter and the caged hens appeared to spend most of the time in restless movements like pacing up and down the cage. Wood-Gush and Gilbert (1969) found the same in caged White Leghorns, while caged Rhode Island Red by White Sussex hybrids tended to sit, 'nest' and preen more and made fewer escape attempts (Wood-Gush 1969), which Wood-Gush (1972) put down to strain differences in response to suboptimal stimuli.

1039.content: The European Food Safety Authority's 2023 scientific opinion on laying hen welfare (Gallus gallus domesticus) states that pre-laying and nesting behaviour are among the most highly motivated behaviours of laying hens and that both are regarded as behavioural needs, citing Weeks and Nicol 2006. It describes pre-laying behaviour as searching for a suitable nest site and nest building (moulding substrate with body and feet where substrate is available), followed by laying and then resting in the nest.

EFSA reports that in 2021 about 376 million laying hens were kept in the 27 EU member states, of which about 45% were in furnished cages, 36% in barns, 13% free-range and 7% organic. Furnished (enriched) cages under EU Directive 1999/74 must provide nest boxes, perches and a pecking and scratching area; conventional (battery) cages are prohibited for laying hens under that Directive. The opinion adds that the pecking and scratching area in furnished cages may not allow full dustbathing, as the cage floor is wire and keeping friable substrate available is a challenge.

EFSA describes the individual cages in which male and female pure-line selection candidates at breeding companies (the breeding stock behind commercial laying strains) are often housed, for individual records of feed intake, egg production and fertility: wire cages with sloped floors, only occasionally a perch, and no nest boxes; it says they resemble the conventional laying hen (battery) cages that are prohibited for laying hens under Directive 1999/74/EC. Birds are placed in them at about 16 to 18 weeks of age and stay for their whole reproductive life, to about 60 to 70 weeks.

1040.content: In the introduction to their meta-analysis, Schuck-Paim and colleagues state that about 7.5 billion egg-laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) are alive worldwide, close to the human population, and that the overwhelming majority are still kept in conventional (battery) cages, which they describe as preventing hens from moving freely, opening their wings and performing behaviours they are strongly motivated to perform, such as nesting, foraging, perching and dust bathing. They give the United States as an example of the slow change: nearly 24% of hens were in cage-free systems as of March 2020, up from 12% in 2016 and 4% in 2010.

1041.content: Olsson and Keeling's review of dustbathing in jungle fowl (Gallus gallus) and domestic fowl (Gallus gallus domesticus) reports that under unrestricted conditions hens dustbathe about every two days, and that birds deprived of litter show a rebound in dustbathing when litter is made available again, which the authors read as a rise in motivation after deprivation. It also states that motivational studies of whether hens are motivated to dustbathe give somewhat conflicting evidence.

The review sets out the evidence against a strong dustbathing need. Widowski and Duncan (2000), using a weighted push-door, found that most hens pushed more weight for peat moss after deprivation, but some pushed heavier doors when not deprived and hens also opened the door without then dustbathing; the review says the authors did not find conclusive evidence of hens' willingness to work to dustbathe. In Dawkins (1983), hens chose litter over food only when they were not food deprived, and when daylight was cut short their motivation to enter a litter cage was no greater than to enter another wire cage, which the review reads as hens finding food much more important than litter. Widowski and Duncan proposed an 'opportunity' model, in which hens dustbathe and feel pleasure when the chance arises but motivation stays low without outside stimuli.

Hens without litter go through the dustbathing sequence on the bare wire floor, most often near the feed trough, which the review calls sham dustbathing. Sham dustbathing appears only after long deprivation in birds that have known litter: hens moved from sand to wire did no dustbathing for the first 20 days, then short sham bouts, and no complete sequence in 48 days; in another study sham dustbathing rose over 21 weeks to levels like the dustbathing of hens on litter, and after 23 weeks without litter 5 of 20 hens kept sham dustbathing even when litter was offered. Two studies found no sign that sham dustbathing lowers the later motivation to dustbathe in litter.

1042.content: Laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) were trained to push a vertically swinging door, with weights added, to reach peat moss, once while living in a cage without dustbathing substrate and once while living in a littered pen with a dustbath. Of 10 hens that opened the door, six pushed more weight when deprived, three pushed more when not deprived and one pushed the same; overall the hens tended to push more when deprived (860 against 682.5 g, P<0.10), and significantly more trials ended in dustbathing after deprivation. The authors conclude the results are hard to explain with a needs model in which deprivation leads to suffering, and fit better an opportunity model in which dustbathing, when the chance arises, leads to pleasure.

1043.content: A comparison across 50 parrot species (order Psittaciformes) used an online survey of pet owners run for 15 months (1,378 pet parrots after quality checks) and phylogenetic regression. Feather-damaging behaviour (chewing, plucking or eating their own feathers) was reported for 20.8 percent of the birds. Species whose wild diet relies more on food that needs extensive handling (tree seeds, nuts and invertebrates) had a higher share of birds with feather damage, with a partial R squared of 0.16, and the result held when each species was left out in turn. Reliance on food that needs extensive search (patchy or scarce food) showed no significant relation with feather damage (partial R squared 0.01). The authors note that handling time was inferred from diet type, as cross-species data on wild handling time budgets were unavailable.

The authors give two readings of the link between a handling-heavy wild diet and feather damage in pet parrots. Their first reading is that parrots stay motivated to handle food when captive diets do not require it and redirect these movements to their own feathers. Their second is that captive diets may lack nutrients or the cellulose or chitin in nuts, tree seeds and invertebrates, and that birds then eat feathers to make up the lack. They write that more research is needed to identify the mechanism.

In the same 50-species comparison, wild group size and communal roosting did not go with more stereotypic behaviour or poorer hatch rates in captivity (for feather damage the table shows a negative relation with maximum feeding group size, partial R squared 0.10). Relative brain size went with more oral stereotypic behaviour such as biting the cage bars (partial R squared 0.26) and more whole-body stereotypic behaviour such as route-tracing (partial R squared 0.19); route-tracing was the most common, seen in 45 of the 50 species and in 23.2 percent of the birds. Brain size did not go with more feather damage (partial R squared 0.02).

1044.content: Twelve grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus erithacus) at Utrecht University, each housed alone in a standard parrot cage (80 by 60 by 155 cm) with visual barriers between cages and fed 60 g of extruded pellets a day from a bowl, were video-recorded. The 11 birds analysed spent 47 plus or minus 18 minutes a day on foraging-related activity from the bowl, in about 17 bouts of about 3.1 minutes. With eleven foraging enrichments (multiple bowls, pellets mixed with marbles, larger pellets, eight puzzle feeders) given in random order, nine raised foraging time significantly, the best about 2.5-fold (up to 123 plus or minus 52 minutes a day). None raised the time spent moving to and from food. The authors write that no enrichment brought foraging time to the level they give for wild birds.

The same paper reports wild foraging time only from other studies, and gives it inconsistently: 40 to 75 percent of the daytime, or 4 to 8 hours a day, citing Magrath and Lill, Snyder and colleagues 1987, Westcott and Cockburn, Renton and others in the introduction; 4 to 6 hours a day in the abstract; and 4 to 8 hours a day citing Snyder and colleagues 1987 alone in the discussion. The authors state that foraging enrichment in captive parrots had so far not produced more than 3 hours of foraging a day.

During the same study one grey parrot (Psittacus erithacus erithacus) started mild feather-damaging behaviour shortly after being placed in its own cage behind visual barriers. The authors suspected a lack of social contact, removed the barrier so the bird could see one neighbour, and report that the feather damage stopped almost at once. This is a single bird, reported as an incident.

1045.content: In a balanced cross-over study, 12 adult grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus) from a Utrecht University research flock, normally kept in groups of six in outdoor aviaries, were each housed alone in a 50 by 80 by 100 cm cage for 30 days per condition. With free food in a food trough they spent 121 plus or minus 16 minutes per 24 hours on foraging (10 birds analysed). A device that made them search for and carry marbles to get food raised this to 176 minutes, food sealed in capsules they had to open raised it to 194 minutes, and both together to 234 plus or minus 42 minutes, about 4 hours, with no fall over the 30 days. Welfare and abnormal behaviour were not measured; the birds showed no abnormal behaviour at the start.

The same paper sets its control result beside earlier studies: grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus) and orange-winged Amazons (Amazona amazonica) given food in a bowl or trough spent about 42 minutes (Rozek and colleagues 2010), 47 minutes (van Zeeland and colleagues 2013), 116 minutes (Lumeij and Hommers 2008) and 121 minutes (this study) per 24 hours on foraging. The authors explain the spread by the type of food and how it was presented (pellets against seed mix, trough size).

1046.content: In a field study of wild Goffin's cockatoos (Cacatua goffiniana) on Yamdena, Tanimbar Islands, Indonesia, from January to November 2017 (about 100 hours of observation), the authors recorded 67 potential food sources, 32 confirmed by direct observation, many only seasonally available. At least three confirmed foods need extraction: the birds dig out cassava roots by biting at the base of the plant and shovelling soil with the beak, and open young coconuts by tearing strips from the fibrous husk, which the authors write may take several hours or even days with repeated returns until a hole big enough for the bird's head is made. They did not measure a daily time budget.

1047.content: Eight kea (Nestor notabilis) in a naturalistic zoo enclosure, with food freely available all day, chose between cups with food under a lid and open cups. At the group level they reliably worked (popped a lid) for preferred food over a less-preferred free food, chose lidded and open cups at chance when the food was identical (39 to 50 percent lidded per bird), and did not work for less-preferred food. The authors report the same pattern in the earlier grey parrot (Psittacus erithacus) study by the same lead author (4 birds; one grey chose the lidded cup for identical food 87 percent of the time, the other three 26 to 36 percent). With walnuts, all kea took the shelled-out nut over the nut in its shell, while two of five grey parrots significantly preferred cracking the shell.

In the nut task, which the authors treat as the more ecologically relevant test, two of five grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus) significantly preferred to crack a walnut shell over taking an identical shelled walnut, while all eight kea (Nestor notabilis) preferred the walnut without a shell. The authors note that grey parrots crack nuts in the wild and that nut cracking is not common in the kea diet.

1048.content: Abstract only. In the first contrafreeloading study of grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus), four birds chose between free and lidded food: one significantly preferred to work for food identical to free food and for preferred food, three only for preferred food. In a nut task with five birds, two significantly preferred cracking the shell to get the nut, two did not and one chose at chance. The authors suggest that individual differences relate to which task each bird treats as play.

1049.content: In 82 captive-born African grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus) in Italy, at least 36 months old, corticosterone metabolites in droppings averaged 587 ng/g in 30 parent-reared breeding pairs (none ever showed feather damage), 494 ng/g in 11 hand-reared pet birds kept alone without feather damage, and 1,744 ng/g in 11 hand-reared pet birds kept alone with feather damage, in which a veterinarian had ruled out clinical problems. The feather-damaging group was significantly higher than both others (p below 0.001); season made no difference. The authors use 'stress' for what the hormone indicates.

The same paper reports, from the authors' own earlier survey, that feather damage was seen in 1.3 percent of a parent-raised breeding population of grey parrots (1,488 birds) and in 17.5 percent of a pet population (292 birds). It also states, citing Wedel 1999, that feather damage has rarely been observed in the wild, and lists early weaning, social isolation and poor stimulation as proposed sources, citing other authors.

1050.content: Abstract only. In a nested case-control study of pet parrots, 42 birds whose owners reported feather picking were compared with 126 unaffected birds. Feather picking was more likely in African grey parrots (adjusted odds ratio 8.4) and cockatoos (12.7), in birds out of the cage more than 8 hours a day (7.4) and in rescued birds (4.7), and about 90 percent less likely in birds that interacted with people at least 4 hours a day (0.1).

1051.content: Abstract only. From an earlier survey of pet owners, 538 companion parrots of 10 species (at least 17 birds per species) were analysed; 15.8 percent showed feather-damaging behaviour. Age and sex were the strongest factors linked with it (juveniles less often), while the species effect (p = 0.047) is called not robust until replicated.

1052.content: Abstract only. Young orange-winged Amazon parrots (Amazona amazonica) reared in barren cages developed significantly more stereotypy than parrots in cages with enrichments for foraging and for moving about; onset time and the rate and size of the rise also differed. When the barren-reared birds were later given enrichment, stereotypy was significantly reduced after a 4-week delay. The abstract gives no numbers.

1053.content: Abstract only. Parrots in enclosures were given a wooden log with 50 food-filled holes covered with starch paper. During the enrichment period they spent significantly more time allopreening. The authors report some evidence of contrafreeloading and no preference for a variable over a constant food distribution. The abstract gives no species, sample size or numbers.

1054.content: At the University of Colorado (Anschutz) colony, 17 breeding pairs of Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus), each in a standard ventilated cage (12 by 17.5 by 8 inches) on aspen chip bedding with an opaque nest box and shredded paper, were video recorded in the light phase. All 17 pairs performed stereotypic corner digging at baseline (defined as digging of more than 12 seconds or at least 7 forelimb strokes at the cage wall, corner or floor), and 16 of 17 also jumped repeatedly at the corners, a stereotypy the authors describe as new for gerbils. In the last 30 minutes before lights off the authors counted 272 digging bouts against 44 at noon and 26 in the morning, and 61.1 percent of 9,118 corner jumps happened during a digging bout. The two most active pairs dug at the corner for 192 and 221 minutes of 1,020 minutes of recorded evening observation.

Over 12 weeks, the same 17 breeding pairs of Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) were given a 6 inch opaque PVC tube (straight, L, T or three-way) placed at the entrance of their existing opaque nest box, as a tunnel-like entrance to a simulated burrow. Stereotypic digging bouts were on average 25 percent longer than at baseline (95% CI 9 to 44 percent, age adjusted, P = 0.002), and in week 12 the pairs started 1.8 times as many digging bouts (95% CI 1.2 to 2.7, P = 0.005); corner jumping did not change (P = 0.713) and neither did pups weaned. The tubes were not fixed: all but one pair pushed or pulled the tube away from the nest box, which the authors note makes their set-up different from the artificial burrow that earlier reduced stereotypy.

1055.content: Abstract only. In an experiment on young Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) raised in laboratory cages with different features, young that could dig in a sand area still developed stereotypic digging, while young that had no sand but had access to an artificial burrow dug less and did not develop stereotypic digging. When the burrow was reduced to its parts, a dark, narrow chamber at the end of a tube connected to the cage prevented stereotypic digging, and a chamber without the tube did not. The author reads this as digging motivation being lowered by the perception of a burrow, the consequence of digging, rather than by performing the digging movement.

1056.content: Abstract only. Young Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) raised inside an artificial burrow first left it at a mean age of 21 days, kept a strong tendency to retreat into it and spent 91.6 percent of the time in it, and their digging stayed in short bouts the author classes as non-stereotypic. Young raised in standard laboratory cages dug in bouts that grew longer, with long stereotypic bouts alongside short ones, and their development differed significantly from the burrow-raised young from day 24. The author interprets stereotypic digging as digging intensified by the lack of a place to retreat to, and calls it abnormal because it fails to regulate retreating.

1057.content: Abstract only. At the University of Zurich, Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) reared with an opaque artificial burrow (a nest box with an access tube) developed significantly less stereotypic digging than gerbils reared with a transparent artificial burrow, and subadults preferred the opaque burrow when given the choice. Faecal cortisol did not differ between gerbils housed with the integrated opaque burrow system and an equivalent transparent one, although their behaviour differed.

1058.content: In a three-page project report, Waiblinger and Konig (University of Zurich) state that wild Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) live in large underground burrow systems that give shelter from climate and predators, that standard laboratory cages lack any burrow-like structure to retreat into, and that the gerbils are then highly motivated to try to create a burrow by digging; the efforts fail and the digging motions become stereotypically repeated. They cite Wiedenmayer 1997 for this reading. They report that gerbils raised with their artificial burrow (a separation wall, a dark nest box and an access tunnel fitted into a standard Makrolon Type IV cage) showed significantly reduced stereotypic digging, and give no numbers for it in this report.

The same report states that the authors observed laboratory Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) weekly from birth to adulthood and measured cortisol in fresh faeces once a week (ELISA) as an indicator of chronic stress, and that they found no increase in cortisol linked to the housing conditions.

1059.content: At Ghent University, 24 Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) about 7 months old, kept in groups of 2 or 3 in Makrolon Type IV cages (55 by 33 by 20 cm) with wood shavings, paper tissue, hay and chew blocks, were filmed for 4 hours from the start of the dark period on 10 days. All 24 showed stereotypic digging, at the cage corners. Stereotypic behaviour took 23.1 percent of the time the gerbils were active; stereotypic digging alone made up 1,476 of 1,685 stereotypic bouts and 17.3 percent of active time, and 13 gerbils also alternated digging with gnawing the bars of the food hopper.

In a preliminary observation of 4 Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus) in a glass terrarium with 6 kg of peat mixed with sawdust (14 hours), the Ghent authors scored 296 digging bouts that progressively created burrows. Burrow digging was 4 to 7 foreleg scratches followed by 1 or 2 hindleg kicks that throw the loosened soil back; digging that did not build a burrow lacked the regular hindleg kicks, and the authors used that incomplete pattern to define stereotypic digging.

The Ghent authors read gerbil digging and bar-gnawing in the cage as appetitive behaviour that the environment triggers but cannot bring to completion: the cage gives the cue to dig or gnaw but no tunnel can be made and the bars cannot be chewed through.

1060.content: In a mark-recapture study on the Inner Mongolian steppe (April to October 2014), the authors identified 253 wild Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus; 137 females, 116 males) living in 24 burrow systems, 11.6 to 147 m apart. They describe a typical burrow system in the field as entrance holes, feeding chambers, nest chambers and tunnels, with about 10 to 20 entrance holes at its core, and state that all members of a social group share the burrow system and that the groups are basically family groups (citing Agren and colleagues 1989 and Scheibler and colleagues 2006 for the burrow description).

1061.content: In a suburban nest-box population of free-living great tits (Parus major) near Antwerp, Belgium, in February and March 2014 (before breeding), 18 birds (11 males, 7 females) slept one night in a dark nest box and the next night with a small white LED inside the box giving 1.6 lux at the box floor; 9 control birds slept dark on both nights. Filmed with infrared cameras, the lit birds woke 26.3 minutes earlier (plus or minus 4.5), left the box 18.3 minutes earlier and slept 39.4 minutes less, which the authors put at more than 5 percent of their sleep. They did not enter the box or fall asleep later, and sleep bout length and frequency did not change; females (not males) spent a greater share of the night in the box awake, about 4 percent.

In the same experiment 27 great tits (Parus major) in the light group had slept in a dark nest box on the first night; when the LED was switched on in their box the next evening, 9 of the 27 did not enter it and were dropped from the sleep analysis, against none of the 9 control birds whose box stayed dark (Fisher exact test, P = 0.026). The authors write that great tits were less likely to enter an artificially lit nest box.

The own-world baseline in the same study: on dark nights, free-living great tits (Parus major) roosting alone in nest boxes before the breeding season stayed in the box all night once they had entered it in the evening, and the authors report they slept around 94 percent of the time in the box, against 48 to 74 percent reported for the breeding season. Males entered the box later, fell asleep later and slept less than females.

1062.content: At Voorstonden, a previously dark forest edge in the Netherlands lit since 2012 by rows of 4 m street-lamp posts with white, green or red LED light (and a dark control row), male great tits (Parus major) breeding in nest boxes near the posts carried 0.95 g light loggers in the 2014 and 2015 breeding seasons. Data came back from 13 of 30 males. The light measured on the bird during the middle of the night did not rise with the light at the entrance of the pair's nest box (n = 13, rho = 0.15, p = 0.63). For the three males whose nest boxes stood within 10 m of a green or red lamp post, the nest box entrance averaged 6.79 lux and the birds averaged 0.062 lux, about 100 times less. The authors read this as these males choosing a darker roosting place, and say it rests on a limited sample.

The same authors argue that in rural and semi-natural areas, where lighting usually runs in a line along a road with dark places around it, great tits (Parus major) can escape direct light, while in urban areas light levels are higher and dark places are harder to find; they conclude that effects found in urban areas may not carry over to more natural areas, and that the raised corticosterone and earlier laying earlier reported at their lamp site may be indirect effects (for example through more food) rather than direct effects of light on the bird.

1063.content: Thirty-five wild-caught male great tits (Parus major), 17 from forest and 18 from a city, were held in individual indoor cages in the Netherlands in October with food and water always available. Each bird had two connected sub-cages and over five nights per pairing could roost in either: darkness or white light, darkness or green light, white or green light, with the lamps at 1.5 lux at perch level and their sides switched mid-way. Against the authors' own hypothesis, the birds generally chose to roost under light rather than darkness (dark against white p = 0.002, dark against green p < 0.001), and chose green over white (p = 0.014), with no difference between forest and city birds.

When the same captive great tits (Parus major), 33 left after two died between experiments, were made to roost for 11 nights each under white light, green light (both 1.5 lux) or darkness, light moved the start of their activity earlier by about two to two and a half hours (white light: 148 minutes for city birds and 158 minutes for forest birds; green: 123 and 117), raised activity at night and raised daily energy expenditure measured by doubly labelled water in a subsample of 11 birds (p = 0.002). White light, against darkness, also raised the share of night minutes with movement (0.11 against 0.04). Plasma oxalic acid, used as a marker of sleep debt, did not change, and learning and memory tests in 22 birds did not differ between treatments.

1064.content: At a network of Dutch field sites where previously dark natural habitat is lit at night with white, green or red street lamps or left dark, the authors tracked night-time activity of adult great tits (Parus major) and within-bird changes in oxalic acid (used as a marker of sleep restriction), acute phase proteins, malaria infection and telomere length. The abstract reports that birds roosting in the white light were much more active at night, that their oxalic acid fell over the course of the study, and that they had a higher probability of malaria infection. Sample sizes and effect sizes are not in the abstract.

1065.content: At eight Dutch sites where previously dark forest edge was lit from sunset to sunrise since 2012 by rows of LED street lamps (8.2 lux directly under the lamp at ground level) in white, green or red, beside a dark control row, the authors followed 288 nest boxes in 2013 and 2014 (great tit, Parus major: 96 and 151 broods; pied flycatcher, Ficedula hypoleuca: 47 and 66 broods). Light had no effect in either species on breeding density, clutch size, brood failure, number of fledglings or adult survival. In 2013 only, great tits in green and white transects laid earlier than in the dark, and great tit chick mass depended on light colour and distance to the lamp; neither effect appeared in 2014. The authors conclude that effects on breeding success are absent or small, and that only fairly strong effects could have been detected.

1066.content: Free-living European blackbirds (Turdus merula) in the city of Munich and in a rural forest 40 km away carried light loggers and radio tags in 2009 to 2011; data came from 32 birds (rural forest 9, urban parks 11, business district 12). Using the light level at which forest birds began and ended their day as a threshold, the authors found that birds in the city business district were exposed to a day on average 49 minutes longer than forest birds (62 minutes in March, 17 in April, 6 in May), which they equate to a seasonal shift of about 19 days in March. Urban park birds did not differ significantly from forest birds (14 minutes). The authors say they did not know where the birds were during the night.

The own-world side in the same study: radio-tracked rural forest blackbirds (Turdus merula) carrying light loggers began their activity in the morning and ended it in the evening at light levels (about 0.0031 and 0.0040 watts per square metre) very close to the brightest light they met naturally at night in the forest (0.004 watts per square metre). The authors suggest rural birds may use this light level to measure day length and time their day.

1067.content: Free-living female great tits (Parus major) rearing 10 day old chicks in nest boxes near Antwerp were filmed over three nights: dark, then a 1.6 lux LED inside the box, then dark again. The abstract reports that under the light they fell asleep 95 minutes later, woke 74 minutes earlier and slept 56 percent less, with large differences between females, and that chicks begged more at night. On the following dark night the females slept 25 percent more than on the first night, mainly through more sleep bouts. Sample size is not given in the abstract.

1068.content: Free-living great tits (Parus major) roosting in nest boxes in winter near Antwerp slept one night in the dark and the next night with a 1.6 lux white LED shining on the nest box entrance from outside, a level the authors say matches nest boxes near street lights; control birds slept dark on both nights. The abstract reports that this treatment did not affect sleep behaviour, and the authors conclude that in winter cavities shield birds from some effects of light at night. Sample size is not given in the abstract.

1069.content: In a free-living great tit (Parus major) population in Belgium, the authors measured the light and noise already present at nest boxes (light from 0.01 to 8.5 lux, noise from 44.2 to 79.4 dB) and filmed sleep with infrared cameras from November to early March, with no lamp added. As the season moved on, birds on the darkest territories woke and left the box about 35 minutes earlier relative to sunrise, while birds on the most lit territories did not shift, so the seasonal change in sleep length was damped where light pollution was high. Males woke and left about 20 minutes later in the noisiest places. Sample size is not given in the abstract.

1070.content: In a forest population of five common songbird species, males of four species near existing street lights began dawn song significantly earlier than males elsewhere in the forest. Over 7 years, blue tit (Cyanistes caeruleus) females on edge territories with street lights began laying 1.5 days earlier on average, and males holding those territories were twice as successful at gaining extra-pair mates as their close neighbours or males in the forest centre; the effect was stronger in yearling males.

1071.content: On a roadless ridge in the Boise Foothills, Idaho, during autumn migration in 2012 and 2013, the authors hung 15 pairs of speakers in trees along about 0.5 km and played recorded car pass-bys (720 per hour, about 55 dB(A) at 50 m) from 04:30 to 21:00, in 4-day blocks on and 4-day blocks off, against a quiet control site 0.95 km away; the nearest paved road was 4 km away. Across 9,924 free-living birds of 51 songbird species caught in mist nets, the capture rate at the playback site fell by 31 percent while the noise was on, and 69 percent of birds stayed. Among birds that stayed, body condition (mass over wing length) fell as noise rose, by a full standard deviation of the community mean; with the noise off the two sites did not differ.

In the laboratory part, 20 Gambel's white-crowned sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys gambelii) were mist-netted in the wild in spring 2013, kept for 5 to 7 days and then released. Each bird fed alone on millet scattered over sand in a 38 square metre foam-lined flight room, three 8-minute trials each, with the same traffic recording at 61 dB(A), at 55 dB(A), or a silent track (room at about 32 dB(A)). At 61 dB(A) the sparrows lifted their heads more often (0.79 against 0.65 head lifts per second, about 21 percent more), kept their heads down for shorter spells (0.41 against 0.50 seconds, about 8 percent less foraging) and fed for about 30 percent less time (159 against 228 seconds per trial). Head-up rate did not change with the number of trials a bird had had.

1072.content: In the first season of the same phantom-road experiment (Boise Foothills, Idaho, 19 August to 9 October 2012), observers made daily point counts of free-living migrant birds within 50 m of three survey points along the speaker array and three control points about 0.8 km away (8,078 detections of 59 species). With recorded traffic noise on (about 55 dB(A) hourly level at the road points, 11 dB(A) above noise-off), 28 percent fewer birds were present along the phantom road than in noise-off periods, while the control site had 3 percent more. 13 of 22 species analysed were negatively associated with noise, 8 showed no effect, and one (Cassin's finch, Haemorhous cassinii) was more abundant; cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) and yellow warbler (Setophaga petechia) almost completely avoided the road during noise-on periods.

1073.content: In state parks beside two busy highways in north-central Florida (May to July 2014), the authors lured free-living northern cardinals (Cardinalis cardinalis) to a speaker and then played a 30-second tufted titmouse (Baeolophus bicolor) alarm call for a flying predator, which cardinals answer by freezing, falling silent and scanning. In quiet spots (49.9 dBA or less) 15 of 19 cardinals responded; at spots with real highway noise (50 dBA or more, all over 200 m from the road edge) none of 15 responded. Background noise level was the only significant predictor, with responses dropping off at about 47 dBA.

In the same study, the authors describe the cardinal's ordinary answer to the titmouse 'high-seet' alarm call (a flying predator): it freezes in place for extended periods, stops calling and scans for predators. In their quiet field sites this answer came in 15 of 19 trials, after the alarm call was played for 30 seconds at 52.2 dBA at 1 m.

1074.content: At 17 feeders placed 2 to 20 m from roads with frequent but not constant traffic, wild great tits (Parus major) heard recorded great tit mobbing alarm calls (made with realistic amplitudes from calls given to a stuffed tawny owl), alone or mixed with recorded traffic noise. With the calls alone the tits stopped feeding at once, approached the speaker and gave their own alarm calls. With traffic noise mimicking a road 20 m from the bird, they failed to respond: their behaviour (closest approach, share of the trial spent feeding, alarm calls given, latency to approach) did not differ from noise-only playback (p > 0.45 for all variables). Quieter noise, like a road at 40 m, gave responses in between.

1075.content: Quinn, Whittingham, Butler and Cresswell tested foraging chaffinches (Fringilla coelebs) with and without background noise. In noise the birds shortened the interval between head-up scans (other vigilance measures did not change) and made significantly fewer pecks, so intake rate fell; the birds did not habituate within a trial or over 5 later trials. The abstract does not say how many birds, whether they were captive, or what the noise was.

1076.content: On St John, US Virgin Islands, in October 2009, free-living Caribbean hermit crabs (Coenobita clypeatus) on forest trails let an approaching person, and also a silent looming object, come closer before hiding in their shells when a recorded boat motor was played (about 98 dB at 1 m) than in silence. Because the silent object made no sound to mask, the authors found no support for masking; adding flashing lights to the noise let the person come closer still, which they read as support for distraction. They propose the 'distracted prey hypothesis'.

1077.content: A systematic review of studies published 1990 to 2013 on anthropogenic noise and wildlife found that most studies documented effects, including changed calling to get round masking, fewer animals in noisy habitats, and changes in vigilance and foraging; about two-thirds of the data set were songbirds and marine mammals, mostly European and North American. Terrestrial wildlife responses begin at about 40 dBA, and 20 percent of papers documented impacts below 50 dBA. The authors note that noise comes with other human effects that can confound the results.

1078.content: In mixed-grass prairie around Brooks, Alberta (May to July 2013 and 2014), the authors played Savannah sparrow (Passerculus sandwichensis) alarm calls, and western meadowlark songs as a control, to free-living parents carrying food to 5-day-old nestlings in ground nests, and timed how long the parent took to go to the nest. At 21 nests on quiet control sites, parents took on average five times longer to go to the nest after alarm calls than on visits with no playback, and three times longer after meadowlark song.

At 38 further nests near real oil and gas infrastructure (15 at natural gas compressor stations, about 69 dB(A) at 10 m; 23 at screw-pump oil wells), the compressor stations had the greatest effect: there, parents went to their nests sooner after both alarm calls and meadowlark songs, relative to no-playback visits, than on control sites, and on no-playback visits they went sooner the closer the nest was to the station. The authors read this as the birds being less vigilant near compressor stations and say distraction explains it better than masking; they also raise fewer nest predators near the stations as an alternative they did not measure.

1079.content: Captive zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), 20 birds housed in an outdoor aviary at the University of Exeter, were tested alone in an arena with a quiet side and a side with artificial broadband noise (200 to 800 Hz, overlapping their contact calls). Birds foraging in the noisy patches spent significantly more time vigilant (head up, looking around) and less time foraging; time spent vigilant did not fall in the second trial. Birds did not spend more time on the quiet side overall, though more chose a quiet patch first in their second trial.

1080.content: The EFSA animal welfare panel (2022) states that where weaned and growing domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) are housed with inadequate enrichment material, their appetitive foraging behaviour (nosing, rooting, chewing and biting) is directed at pen mates and especially at their tails; once a tail is damaged and bleeding it draws more biting, and tail biting can spread quickly through the group. The panel names lack of enrichment or foraging material as a hazard for three welfare consequences: inability to perform exploratory or foraging behaviour, soft tissue lesions, and group stress.

The EFSA panel (2022) reports that, in an experimental study, giving long straw on the solid floor (20 g per pig per day) after a tail biting outbreak lowered the percentage of domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) with fresh blood on their tails in the following days, but tail biting still persisted. The panel concludes that 20 g per day of straw or similar substrate reduces tail biting in undocked pigs and that larger amounts (up to 400 g per pig per day) work better.

The EFSA panel (2022) states that the health status of domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and tail biting affect each other, that they share risk factors, and that deficiencies in feed composition and in how feed is provided (such as feeding space) are major risk factors for tail biting. In the same opinion the panel treats weaning age, space allowance, floor type, enrichment, air quality, health status and diet as separate risk factors and calls tail biting multifactorial and difficult to predict and control.

Citing an online survey by De Briyne and colleagues (2018), the EFSA panel (2022) reports that only 67 percent of pigs across the 24 EU member states surveyed were said to be given suitable enrichment materials, and that this share averaged 89 percent in countries where few or no pigs (up to 5 percent) are tail docked against 63 percent in countries where 70 percent or more are docked.

In its table of animal-based measures, the EFSA panel (2022) states that inability to perform exploratory or foraging behaviour is strongly related to tail biting risk in rearing domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), but that damaging tail biting does not always occur in barren pens where enrichment is absent, and that pigs which can explore and forage may still get tail lesions from other causes of tail biting. For pigs in barren pens the panel lists oral behaviour at pen fittings (biting, nosing and licking bars, floor or trough) and nosing, chewing or biting of pen mates (flank, tail, ear), which it interprets as exploration redirected to satisfy a behavioural need.

The EFSA panel (2022), drawing on a 1997 EU Scientific Veterinary Committee report, states that wild boar and semi-wild or free-ranging domestic pigs (Sus scrofa) find much of their food by rooting, with grazing and browsing also prominent, that this behaviour is intrinsically motivated, and that domestic pigs in a semi-natural enclosure have been noted to spend 6 to 8 hours searching for food even when fed full rations of commercial feed. It also states that weaned pigs on farms show a high level of exploratory motivation even when feed is freely available.

1081.content: In an online survey by the Federation of Veterinarians of Europe, the European Association of Porcine Health Management and the European Commission (57 usable responses from 24 European countries), respondents estimated that on average 77 percent of pigs (median 95 percent) are routinely tail docked, under 5 percent in Finland, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland, and that 67 percent of pigs (median 76 percent) are given suitable enrichment materials. Routine tail docking has been banned in the EU since 1994.

1082.content: On a 130-sow commercial farm in the UK, 706 undocked domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus, Large White x Landrace x Pietrain) in groups of 21 to 39 on solid floors were given straw throughout life, from weaning, from finishing (12 weeks), or no straw (wood shavings early on). Of the 20 groups analysed, 14 had tail-biting outbreaks (no straw 3, straw in finishing 2, straw from weaning 4, straw throughout 5) and 8 were severe; straw provision had no significant effect on the distribution of outbreaks (p = 0.336).

Statham and colleagues describe the link between missing rooting material and tail biting in domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as a theory: tail biting can be considered redirected behaviour, in which manipulative behaviour is redirected to pen mates when rooting material is absent. They note that much earlier work compared straw on solid floors with no bedding on slatted floors, which confounds lack of bedding with floor type and less chance to root, and that some studies also changed stocking density.

1083.content: In an experiment at Wageningen with domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus, Tempo x Topigs 20; 30 litters, then 192 pigs in 32 pens of 6), pigs kept in barren pens (partly slatted, with two chain toys) spent 2.4 percent of observed time orally manipulating pen mates (nibbling, sucking, chewing or biting ears, tails or other body parts) at 3 weeks of age and 2.6 percent at about 7 weeks, against 0.7 and 0.6 percent in larger pens with straw, sawdust and peat on the floor and changing toys. All exploring and chewing in barren pens was directed at the pen itself; pigs in enriched pens chewed for 23.8 percent of observed time at 7 weeks against 7.6 percent in barren pens, and were inactive less (44.7 against 58.2 percent).

In the same experiment, domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) that lost their enrichment at 7 weeks of age showed more oral manipulation of pen mates than pigs kept barren throughout, especially pigs classed as reactive in an early restraint test, while pigs moved from barren to enriched pens explored and played more than pigs enriched throughout. The authors conclude that behaviour reflected both the current pen and a match or mismatch with the early-life pen.

1084.content: Stolba and Wood-Gush kept a small population of domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) from 1978 in an enclosure near Edinburgh with woodland and bog, studied 13 groups over 3.5 years (typically a boar, four sows, a sub-adult boar and a young gilt), let sows choose weaning time, fed only for maintenance and reproduction, and report that the pigs showed most of the behaviour of the European wild boar.

1085.content: Reviewing only studies in which tail injuries in domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) were quantified, D'Eath and colleagues found good evidence that manipulable substrates and feeder space affect damaging tail biting; only epidemiological evidence for temperature and season; an unclear effect of stocking density; little effect of group size; and nutrition, disease and breed needing more research. Tail docking reduces but does not eliminate tail biting.

1086.content: Taylor and colleagues review tail biting in domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) and propose three descriptive types, 'two-stage', 'sudden-forceful' and 'obsessive', each of which may have a different motivational basis and different environmental and husbandry risk factors. They note that studies use different definitions, that abattoir records under-record tail biting, and that farm and abattoir data count only bitten pigs, not biters.
