1087.content: Schroder-Petersen and Simonsen define tail biting in domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) as one pig's dental manipulation of another pig's tail, split into a pre-injury and an injury stage, and propose that the biters may also suffer because they are frustrated by living in a stressful environment, a frustration that may produce an excessive motivation to bite pen mates' tails.

1088.content: Iberian domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus) kept free-range on six farms in Extremadura, Spain (2012 to 2014, whole groups of roughly 80 to 200 pigs per farm and cycle, scan samples every ten minutes over 133 observation days, mostly between 07:30 and 15:00) spent 56.5 percent of observed time resting and about 28.5 percent exploring. Exploring (which in this study could include foraging, sniffing, licking and rooting) took 50 percent of observed time in the acorn season, when the same pigs found all their food themselves, against 17.8 percent when they were fed concentrate.

In the same free-range Iberian domestic pigs (Sus scrofa domesticus), the authors note that exploring was still 17.8 percent of observed daytime when the pigs were given concentrate feed, and they compare their overall budget with a Danish study of cross-bred free-range pigs that rested 54.4 percent of the time and rooted 19.3 percent while also eating allocated feed.

1089.content: In a conditioned place preference test with 21 female crossbred piglets (Large White x Landrace, domestic pig Sus scrofa domesticus) from 4 litters, piglets later spent more time in the compartment where chocolate raisins had been hidden in straw than in the compartment where they had straw and the same number of raisins free in a trough (95 percent confidence interval for time share 54.65 to 67.46 percent, against 50 percent for no preference). The authors call this contrafreeloading: preferring to work for food when the same food is free nearby.

The same authors read their data as giving little support to the idea that the rooting and foraging movements are rewarding in themselves: in experiment 3 the domestic piglets (Sus scrofa domesticus) could forage in straw in both compartments, and the only difference in the preferred one was that foraging turned up food. Piglets also did not prefer straw with hidden food over an empty compartment more strongly than over straw alone.

1090.content: In a closed-economy experiment on 16 farm-raised American mink (Mustela vison; 8 males, 8 females, each housed alone with a standard farm cage plus seven resource compartments for six weeks), the mink had to push one-way doors weighted 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 or 1.25 kg (each weight for seven days) to reach a water pool (about 1.5 by 0.5 m, 0.2 m deep), a raised platform, novel objects, an alternative nest site, toys, a tunnel or an empty compartment. The water pool came out as the most valued resource on every measure: lowest price elasticity of demand (0.26, against 0.77 for the empty compartment), highest total expenditure (81.4 kg against 9.2 kg), and a mean maximum price paid of 1.25 kg, the heaviest door used (0.84 kg for the empty compartment). Food was not one of the resources in this demand test.

In the same study 14 American mink (Mustela vison; 7 males, 7 females) had access blocked for 24 hours to each of four resources in turn: the water pool, the alternative nest site, the empty compartment and food. Urinary cortisol (corrected for creatinine) rose by 50.0 percent over baseline when food was blocked and by 33.8 percent when the pool was blocked; the authors report that these two rises did not differ significantly, and that blocking the nest site or the empty compartment did not raise cortisol. The cortisol rise went with a rise in physical activity (pool: R = 0.70), and the change in activity was significant only for food. The authors call the state "stress" and "frustration".

1091.content: A review by eight researchers from the Dutch, Danish, Finnish, British and Norwegian mink groups of all studies on swimming water for farmed American mink (Mustela vison) concludes: bath use is most likely tied to foraging; mink that never had a bath show no consistent change in stereotypic or anticipatory behaviour when it is absent; blocking or removing a bath the mink has used may produce short-term stress (scratching, scrabbling at the door, raised cortisol for up to about two weeks); mink work hard for a bath and for a running wheel in consumer-demand tests; individuals differ in how much they value water; and swimming is likely an incentive that induces its own motivation, which the authors contrast with an innate need.

Reviewing time budgets of farmed American mink (Mustela vison) with free access to a water bath, the authors report that some mink never enter the water: in one study 14 of 40 mink given water never entered the bath, and in another 1 of 11 did not swim during 24 hours of recording. Juvenile mink reared with a bath spent 1.4 percent of observations in or around it, the same share as adults in another study; swims per mink per 24 hours ranged from 0 to 177, bouts from 2 to 55 seconds. Mink went to the bath more around feeding time.

Discussing deprivation tests on American mink (Mustela vison), including Mason et al 2001, the review authors raise two other readings of the cortisol rise when a bath is blocked: blocking a door the mink used before may be stressful whatever lies behind it, and mink prefer to drink from the bath, so a blocked bath may mean less drinking. They propose removing the whole bath out of sight as a better test.

Reporting the consumer-demand studies of Hansen and Jensen (2006a,b) on farm American mink (Mustela vison), in which mink pressed a lever on fixed-ratio schedules from 5 to 60 presses for access to a water bath or a running wheel, the review authors state that the elasticity of demand for swimming water and for the wheel did not differ, that both were valued above an empty water box, that neither substituted for the other, that the wheel was used more, and that the bath was used mainly in the morning when it was refilled and the mink were fed.

1092.content: In a second cohort of 16 adult farm American mink (Mustela vison) tested in closed-economy arenas with door weights up to 3,000 g, food was moved out of the home cage into its own compartment as a yardstick. Mean maximum price paid: food 2,062 g (plus or minus 602), swimming bath 2,000 g (plus or minus 605), social contact 1,687 g, novel object 1,625 g, water bowl in a bath 1,594 g, tunnel 1,312 g, toys 1,281 g. The authors report no statistical difference between the price paid for the bath and for food; the highest single price was paid for food. In an earlier cohort with doors up to 1,250 g most mink paid the top weight for several resources, so those could not be told apart.

1093.content: Six adult female farm American mink (Mustela vison; eight tested, two dropped after illness) worked for food, a water bath (about 1.7 by 0.7 m, 0.6 m deep), a toy and unpredictable social contact behind doors raised by 500 g each week, in two set-ups: resources visible and close at the choice point, or 7.5 m away behind opaque screens. Food ranked first in both. With the resources in view (the usual design) the bath ranked last on visit rate, consumer surplus and expenditure, with no significant differences between resources; with the resources screened the bath ranked second after food. Maximum price paid did not differ between resources in either set-up.

1094.content: Six American mink (Mustela vison; 3 males, 3 females, about six months old), each housed alone in a closed-economy arena with a home cage and seven resource compartments, faced door weights rising from 0 to 1,000 g and were filmed 8 hours a day. As the price rose they made fewer visits but longer ones, and the total time spent swimming (and with novel objects and in the hay box) did not fall; time on the platform, with toys and the cylinder, and in the empty compartment did fall.

1095.content: Fifty-six female farm American mink (Mustela vison) were reared from 6 weeks of age with a water bath (28) or without one (28), each family in three connected cages with a nest box, platform and cylinder. Anticipatory behaviour before a food reward did not differ between the groups at 16 weeks, nor after the water was removed for 2.5 weeks. In winter, with half the water group still having water, half having had it removed for 2.5 months and the other group never having had it, stereotypic behaviour did not differ significantly; only 13 of the 56 mink stereotyped at all during the observations, and the group with water had the lowest level (2.78 percent).

1096.content: In three experiments on singly housed farm American mink (Mustela vison) with access from the home cage to an extra cage with a 20.5-litre water bath, individuals differed clearly and consistently in how much they swam, juveniles' bath use correlated with their mothers', and in a four-month experiment juveniles housed with baths showed less stereotyped behaviour than juveniles without. The authors read this as a sign that long-term access to baths may ease frustration in singly housed juvenile mink.

1097.content: Time-depth recorders on free-living American mink (Neovison vison) on lowland rivers in southern England (feral population; 24 mink fitted, data from 16, adults and subadults, females about 710 g, males about 1,410 g) logged 3,750 dives over 5 to 6 days per deployment. Dives per mink ranged from 5 to 789 per deployment; the overall mean was 35.7 dives and 7.6 minutes diving a day, with maxima of 189 dives and 38.4 minutes in a day. Dives reached 2.96 m and 57.9 seconds, twice as long as measured in captive mink, and happened mostly in daylight.

In the same field study of free-living American mink (Neovison vison) in southern England, the number of dives per day and time diving per day differed significantly between individuals: some mink dived many times a day and others did not dive at all; two of the tracked mink made fewer than 20 dives and were left out of the analysis. Some females dived more in winter than in summer.

1098.content: The EFSA animal welfare panel describes the current European farm system for American mink (Neogale or Neovison vison): standard wire cages 70, 80 or 90 cm long and 30 or 31 cm wide, 0.21 to 0.28 square metres per animal, about 45 cm high, a nest box, paste feed, and drinking water from nipples or cups with no open water. The panel states that in this cage the mink run back and forth, which may develop into stereotypic pacing, and concludes that the inability to perform exploratory or foraging behaviour cannot be prevented or substantially mitigated in the current system, with the lack of open water among the listed hazards. The WelFur scheme it cites assessed 2,014 mink farms between 2017 and 2019.

Reviewing the motivation studies on American mink (Neogale or Neovison vison), the EFSA panel concludes that mink pay a high cost for access to open water in demand tests from two independent groups (Mason et al 2001 in England; Hansen and Jensen 2006 in Denmark), that the motivation for open water differs from the motivation for a running wheel (neither substitutes for the other), and that swimming itself is limited: mink with water do not swim every day, and in aviaries juveniles swam on average 123 seconds (females) and 49 seconds (males) per 24 hours. The panel reads open water as serving exploration, foraging and cognitive stimulation more than swimming as such.

On stereotypic behaviour, the EFSA panel reports mixed results for American mink (Neogale or Neovison vison) kept with and without open water: no difference in two studies (Hansen and Jeppesen 2001a, where 3.9 percent of all observations were stereotypic; Vinke et al 2006), and less stereotypy with water in two others (Mononen et al 2008; Ahola et al 2011, where juveniles with a basin of 0.61 square metres and about 30 cm deep spent 10 percent of active time stereotyping against 29 percent without). The panel adds that a cage may stay inadequate even with water added.

1099.content: In a registered randomised experiment, 2,743 US Facebook users recruited through Facebook ads stated what they would need to be paid to deactivate their account; the 1,661 with a price under $102 were randomly paid to deactivate Facebook for the four weeks before the November 2018 US midterm election or kept using it. Deactivation freed about 60 minutes a day, lowered other online activity and raised offline activities such as watching television alone and time with friends and family. The authors' index of subjective well-being, whose items include self-reported happiness, life satisfaction, depression and anxiety, improved by 0.09 standard deviations, about 25 to 40 percent of the effect of psychological interventions in a meta-analysis they cite; effects on brief daily text-message mood reports were positive and not significant.

Several weeks after the four-week deactivation ended, the treatment group's reported use of the Facebook mobile app was about 11 minutes a day (22 percent) lower than the control group's; the treatment group was more likely to click on an email about tools to limit social media use, 5 percent still had their accounts deactivated nine weeks after the experiment, and the authors' index of post-experiment Facebook use was 0.61 standard deviations lower. Deactivation also lowered how much people said they would need to be paid to give up Facebook afterwards.

1100.content: In two randomised experiments before the 2020 US election, 19,857 Facebook users and 15,585 Instagram users who spent at least 15 minutes a day on the platform were paid to deactivate it either for six weeks (treatment) or for only the first of those weeks (control). People who deactivated Facebook for six weeks reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression and anxiety, and people who deactivated Instagram a 0.041 standard deviation improvement. In exploratory analysis the Facebook gain came from people over 35 and the Instagram gain from women under 25.

1101.content: A preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of experiments in adults found ten peer-reviewed studies (4,674 participants, 38 effect sizes) on stopping social media use for a period. Pooled, abstinence had no significant effect on positive affect, negative affect or life satisfaction, and the length of abstinence was not related to any of the three. Most breaks were short (1 to 28 days, most often 7), several studies had low compliance, and studies that only reduced use were excluded.

1102.content: In a preregistered within-person study, 40 healthy, socially connected adults aged 18 to 40 spent 10 hours (9:00 to 19:00) alone with no social contact and no social media, and on another day fasted for 10 hours. After isolation they reported more social craving and loneliness and less happiness, and 36 of the 40 felt lonelier. In a midbrain region picked out by its response to reward (substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area), pictures of their favourite social activities drew a larger response after isolation than after fasting, the size of the response tracked self-reported social craving, and its pattern resembled the response to food pictures after fasting.

Participants who scored higher on chronic loneliness at screening reported less craving for social contact when shown social cues after 10 hours alone, and their midbrain (SN/VTA) response to social cues after isolation was smaller (r = -0.33, P = 0.036); the size of their social network did not relate to either response.

1103.content: In a correlational study, the participants who used Facebook most often had lower trait self-esteem, and this link was mediated by greater exposure to upward social comparisons on social media.

In an experiment, participants' state self-esteem and their ratings of themselves relative to another person were lower after viewing a social media profile with upward comparison information (for example a highly active social network and healthy habits) than after viewing a profile with downward comparison information (a low-activity network and unhealthy habits).

1104.content: In two preregistered observational studies of 7,331 Twitter users and 12.7 million tweets (users who had tweeted about the 2018 Kavanaugh confirmation hearings or about a United Airlines passenger incident), the likes and retweets a user received for outrage on one day were associated with more outrage expression the next day, after adjusting for overall tweeting and feedback not tied to outrage: a doubling of outrage feedback went with about 2 to 3 percent more outrage the next day. The association was weaker for users with longer tweeting histories.

In two preregistered experiments in a simulated Twitter environment (120 participants each), participants chose on each of 30 trials between posting an outrage tweet and a neutral tweet; when outrage tweets earned more likes, participants chose outrage tweets more often over the trials (odds ratio 1.10 per trial), and participants first shown a feed in which 75 percent of tweets carried outrage were more likely to pick an outrage tweet on the first trial (odds ratio 4.94).

1105.content: In three field experiments in 37 neighbourhoods of 12 UK cities and 12 towns and villages (879 stamped letters dropped in the street or left on cars, 398 trials of dropping a handful of cards in front of a passer-by, 90 trials of starting to cross the road in front of a car), whether people helped a stranger did not vary with urbanicity or with population density. Help was offered less often in more deprived neighbourhoods, and neighbourhood deprivation explained most of the variation in helping.

1106.content: In a laboratory experiment, 84 undergraduates were randomly assigned to use Facebook passively (scrolling the news feed, looking at friends' pages and pictures) or actively (posting, commenting, messaging) for 10 minutes. Mood did not change in either group right after; by the end of the day the passive group felt worse than at both its baseline and its post-session level, while the active group did not (67 analysed after exclusions). Life satisfaction did not differ by condition.

In a six-day experience-sampling study of 89 young adults recruited in Ann Arbor, Michigan, texted five times a day, more passive Facebook use between prompts went with a drop in how good people felt at the next prompt, controlling for active use, other online social network use and direct social contact. Passive use predicted envy and envy predicted the drop in mood; with envy in the model the direct link was no longer significant, and the reverse path (envy leading to passive use) was not significant.

1107.content: A scoping review of survey-based studies published January 2017 to October 2021 found 40 studies that used 36 different ways of measuring active and passive social media use and yielded 172 associations with well-being or ill-being; most studies did not support the claim that active use goes with more well-being and passive use with less. The authors argue that time spent on either kind of use may be too coarse a measure.

1108.content: In a randomised experiment with about 2,000 US adults with Android phones, recruited through Facebook and Instagram ads in 2020, an app recorded use of Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, web browsers and YouTube. Paying people $2.50 an hour to cut use of these apps for three weeks reduced use by 56 minutes a day (39 percent of the control average); in the three weeks after the payments ended the paid group still used them 19 minutes a day less, and in the three weeks after that 12 minutes a day less, which the authors read as habit formation.

In the same experiment, giving people a tool to set daily time limits on each app reduced use of the six apps by 22 minutes a day (16 percent) over 12 weeks, and 78 percent of those offered it set binding limits with no incentive to do so. Fitting an economic model to these results, the authors estimate that without self-control problems use of the six apps would fall by 48 minutes a day, or 31 percent of baseline use; this figure is a model estimate that rests on assumptions such as linear demand and geometric decay of habit.

1109.content: In an fMRI study of 32 adolescents aged 13 to 18 (34 scanned, 2 excluded) shown a simulated Instagram feed that included 40 of their own photos, participants were more likely to like photos shown with many likes than photos with few, for neutral photos, photos of risky behaviour and their own photos. Viewing their own photos with many likes rather than few went with greater activity in the nucleus accumbens on both sides, a hub of reward circuitry, and in regions involved in social cognition and attention; for neutral photos the effect was in the left nucleus accumbens, and for risky photos likes made no difference there.

1110.content: In a representative national US sample (GfK KnowledgePanel; 4,165 people in the model) surveyed four times over three years, more daily hours of media about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings went with more posttraumatic stress symptoms six months later; those symptom scores went with more worry about future negative events two years after the bombings, and that worry went with more hours of media about the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting and more acute stress symptoms after it, controlling for age, gender, income, education, ethnicity and area.

1111.content: After a week of baseline monitoring, 143 undergraduates at the University of Pennsylvania were randomly assigned to limit Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes per platform per day, or to use social media as usual, for three weeks. The limited-use group showed significant reductions in loneliness and depression scores over the three weeks compared with the control group, and both groups reported less anxiety and fear of missing out than at baseline, which the authors attribute to self-monitoring.

1112.content: Across four datasets of posts on Instagram and on three topic forums (men's fashion, women's fashion, gardening), totalling 1,046,857 posts by 4,168 people, the time between a person's posts followed the reward-learning rules found in animal experiments: the history of likes predicted how soon people posted again, people spaced their posts to maximise the average rate of likes given the effort of posting, and a reward-learning model fitted better than a model without learning. In an online experiment (n = 176) that mimicked social media, the rate of likes changed how fast people posted.

1113.content: In a European mobile phone dataset covering all of 2007 (34.9 million users, almost 6 billion calls, counting only pairs with at least one call each way), the 26,680 users who called at least 100 others had on average 129.9 contacts. Clustering each person's contacts by call frequency most often gave four groups (27.1 percent of users), holding cumulatively about 4.1, 11.0, 29.8 and 128.9 people; forcing everyone into four groups gave 3.5, 10.6, 31.1 and 129.9, a ratio of about 3.3 between layers.

1114.content: In a formal model of a platform that observes only engagement, users have two sets of preferences: an impulsive one that reacts to each item and keeps them on the platform, and a forward-looking one that judges whether time there is worth it. The model produces users who have long sessions on a platform yet derive very little utility from it, and platform changes that steadily raise engagement before users abruptly quit; whether raising engagement raises user welfare depends on which features of the content change, and in some directions more engagement makes users less happy.

1115.content: A grounded theory analysis of 582 mental-health-relevant posts made in the r/Replika Reddit community between 2017 and 2021 found harms that came about through emotional dependence on the social chatbot Replika, a dependence the authors describe as resembling patterns in relationships between people. Unlike other forms of technology dependence, it was marked by role-taking: users felt that Replika had its own needs and emotions to which they had to attend.

1116.content: In a survey of 1,006 students aged 18 or over who had used the chatbot Replika for more than a month (about 75 percent based in the US, recruited by email from the app's user list), 90 percent scored as lonely on the De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale and 43 percent as severely or very severely lonely, against about 53 percent of US students reporting loneliness in earlier studies; 90 percent also perceived medium to high social support on the Interpersonal Support Evaluation List.

Asked in open questions how Replika affected their human relationships, 23 percent of most participants said it stimulated them and 8 percent said it displaced them (69 percent did not say); among the 30 participants (3 percent) who said without being asked that Replika had stopped them from attempting suicide, the figures were 37 and 13 percent.

1117.content: Using the staggered arrival of Facebook at 775 US colleges between February 2004 and September 2006 and more than 430,000 responses to the National College Health Assessment, the authors estimate in a difference-in-differences design that Facebook's arrival raised their index of poor mental health, built from all mental health items in the survey, by 0.085 standard deviations. They put this at about 22 percent of the effect of losing one's job in a meta-analysis they cite, and equivalent to a 2 percentage point rise, over a baseline of 25 percent, in the share of students scoring as depressed on the PHQ-9. Students also more often reported that poor mental health hurt their academic performance.

The effects were larger for students more likely to compare unfavourably with their peers, such as those living off campus, those of lower socioeconomic status and those outside fraternities and sororities, and Facebook's arrival changed students' beliefs about their peers' social lives and behaviour; the authors read this as Facebook fostering unfavourable social comparisons.

1118.content: In a reanalysis of an earlier study in which the smartphones of 1,252 North American adults were signalled five times a day for three days to sample moral experiences, participants were more likely to learn about immoral acts online than in person or through print, television and radio, and immoral acts encountered online evoked more outrage (rated anger times disgust) than those encountered in person or through traditional media.

Crockett argues that digital media may increase the expression of moral outrage by enlarging its triggers, lowering its costs and raising its personal benefits: expressing outrage online takes a few keystrokes, is not limited by location, time of day or chance encounters with wrongdoers, carries little risk of retaliation in like-minded audiences, and is rewarded with likes and shares at unpredictable times, a pattern known to promote habit formation.

1119.content: In six months of Twitter conversations (over 380 million tweets, 25 million reply conversations) forming a network of over 1.7 million users, the average strength of each outgoing relationship rose with the number of contacts until it reached a maximum between about 100 and 200 contacts; beyond that, more contacts could not be kept up with the same attention to each, and the number of reciprocated connections levelled off between 200 and 300.

1120.content: In 16 countries on four continents (1,348 usable participants in Study 1; 2,085 across both studies), one group of people rated how positively they would view someone in each of 25 situations (acts, traits, circumstances) and a separate group rated how much pride they would feel in the same situation. Within each country the pride ratings tracked the local valuation ratings closely (mean r 0.82, range 0.72 to 0.90). Pride also tracked the valuations given in the other 15 countries (mean r 0.75). In a second study in the US and India, pride tracked valuation more closely than amusement, excitement or happiness did.

1121.content: Among 567 adults in 10 small-scale communities (Bosawas Reserve in Nicaragua, Cotopaxi in Ecuador, Draa-Tafilalet in Morocco, Enugu in Nigeria, two villages in Mauritius, Tuva in Russia, Shaanxi and Henan in China, and farming and fishing communities in Japan), the pride people expected to feel in 10 situations tracked how positively a separate group from their own community would view someone in that situation (mean r 0.66, range 0.36 to 0.92). Agreement between communities was much weaker (mean r 0.29 between one community's pride and other communities' valuation).

1122.content: In a German online diary study of adults (the authors report 241 included participants, 93% women, mean age 30), participants rated each day, for up to 25 days, how much time they spent with and how close they felt to their partner, a friend and a family member, and rated their self-esteem. On days when contact felt closer, self-esteem was higher, most strongly for romantic partners; lagged analyses suggested that closeness on one day went with a rise in self-esteem the next. People whose relationships were closer overall also had higher trait self-esteem.

Across up to 29 industrialized OECD countries (national self-esteem averages on the Rosenberg scale, mostly from student samples; contact with friends from the World Values Survey), countries where people met friends more often had higher average self-esteem (r 0.64). Frequency of meeting friends remained the only unique predictor when national happiness, individualism, GDP and neuroticism were entered together.

1123.content: A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies found that social relationships at one time predicted self-esteem later (48 samples, 46,231 participants), and self-esteem predicted later relationships (35 samples, 21,995 participants), each controlling for the earlier level of the outcome. Both effects were small and of the same size (standardized beta 0.08 each way). The effect of relationships on self-esteem held across age, gender, ethnicity and time between measurements.

1124.content: Reanalysing the data of the Harris and Orth (2020) meta-analysis, the authors found that controlling for the earlier level of the outcome gave paradoxical results, with effects in both directions at once, and read the prospective links between self-esteem and quality of social relations as statistical artefacts of measurement error and regression to the mean. They state that this challenges the sociometer claim that relationship quality is the cause and self-esteem the effect.

1125.content: Pooling 61 published estimates of human group and network sizes (support cliques, sympathy groups, forager overnight camps, communities, mega-bands and tribes, from many countries and from hunter-gatherer ethnography), the authors found mean sizes of about 4.6, 14.3, 42.6, 132.5, 566.6 and 1,728. A spectral analysis of all 61 values found a preferred ratio of about 3.2 between successive sizes (confidence 0.99 against white noise), and Christmas-card networks of 42 people showed the same peak.

1126.content: Festinger proposes that people have a drive to evaluate their opinions and abilities, and that where performance can be ordered, a person evaluates an ability by comparing it with the performance of other people, for example their running time against the times of others.

1127.content: A meta-analysis of more than 60 years of social comparison experiments found that, when offered a choice of comparing up or down and not under threat, people strongly preferred to compare with someone better off. The dominant reaction to a comparison was contrast: self-ratings moved away from the comparison target, so that comparing with someone better lowered people's ratings of their own ability and their mood. When the comparison varied participants' own standing, effect estimates were about -0.65 to -0.75 for ability and -0.65 to -0.83 for affect, and in studies with control groups upward and downward comparisons had effects of similar size.

1128.content: Compiling published data on where 10 neurochemical genes (hormone and neurotransmitter receptors and ligands, among them dopamine, steroid and nonapeptide systems) are expressed in 12 brain regions involved in social decisions, across 88 species from five vertebrate lineages (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and teleost fish), the authors found that these regions and their expression profiles are largely conserved over about 450 million years. Receptors were more conserved than the ligands that act on them.

1129.content: In the British Household Panel Survey (86,679 adult responses, 1997 to 2004), the rank of a person's household income within a comparison group (the whole sample, or people of the same region, of the same gender and education, or of the same age) went with life satisfaction on a 1 to 7 scale, while absolute income and the group's average income added nothing once rank was included. Comparisons with people ranked above weighed more than comparisons with people below.

127.content: Leary states sociometer theory: the self-esteem system evolved to monitor social acceptance, so that cues that a person is not adequately valued and accepted by others lower self-esteem and push the person to act to raise how others value them. On this view people do not seek self-esteem for its own sake; they seek to avoid devaluation and rejection.

128.content: Leary describes self-esteem as part of a system, the sociometer, that watches the social environment for cues of low or falling relational value, such as lack of interest, disapproval or rejection, and warns the person when it detects them. He argues that people seek to raise their relational value and acceptance, using self-esteem as a gauge of how well they are doing.

1130.content: Comparing 305 naturally occurring uses of malu (shame) recorded by participant observation in a Malay fishing village in Bengkulu, Sumatra, with 281 written shame stories from Californians, Fessler found that 9% of Bengkulu events (and a few more in mixed categories) arose from dealing with someone acknowledged as higher in the social hierarchy, with no failure or wrongdoing on the person's part, and none were guilt-like, while in California 20% of stories were guilt-like, 15% mixed shame and guilt, and none were about subordinance.

1131.content: Gluckman, Hanson and Low define evolutionary mismatch as the state in which the environments contemporary humans meet are markedly different from those of most of human evolutionary history, either wholly new (scurvy at sea after a lost vitamin C gene) or beyond the range the lineage met before (energy-dense processed food, which they say largely explains obesity and type 2 diabetes).

They separate a second kind, developmental mismatch: a fetus or infant uses cues such as maternal nutrition to set its body for the environment it expects, and harm follows when the later environment differs. If a low-nutrition world is predicted and a nutritionally rich one is met, they write, the risk of type 2 diabetes and obesity rises; survivors of infant marasmus who later live with plentiful food are their example.

1132.content: Across seven primate species (common marmoset Callithrix jacchus, cotton-top tamarin Saguinus oedipus, squirrel monkey Saimiri sciureus, rhesus macaque Macaca mulatta, cynomolgus macaque Macaca fascicularis, talapoin Miopithecus talapoin and olive baboon Papio anubis; 10 sex-by-species groups), subordinates' basal cortisol relative to dominants' was higher where subordinates met stressors more often and where they had fewer sources of social support, including close kin. These two features explained most of the variation between species (R squared 0.88, phylogenetically independent contrasts).

1133.content: Male cichlid fish (Astatotilapia burtoni) that watched pairwise fights between rival males in surrounding tank units, without fighting themselves, could then infer the rank order implied by those fights, including between rivals they had never seen fight each other (transitive inference).

1134.content: In a nationally representative US sample (NHANES 2003 to 2004), 6,329 people aged 6 and over wore a hip accelerometer for up to 7 days during waking hours (13.9 hours a day on average). They spent 54.9% of that time, 7.7 hours a day, in sedentary behaviour (under 100 counts a minute). Children aged 6 to 11 were least sedentary (about 6 hours), adolescents aged 16 to 19 and adults aged 60 and over spent about 60% of waking time sedentary, and adults aged 70 to 85 the most (about 9.1 to 9.5 hours).

1135.content: In Study 1, 277 US adults recruited online imagined an innocent act that coworkers might wrongly read as stealing; the more likely the false belief, the more shame they expected (F(2,157) 8.83). In Study 2, 57 undergraduate women played a public goods game and were then told, at random, that the others had chosen to keep them in the group or to exclude them. Excluded women felt more devalued (r 0.53) and more shame (r 0.37) than included ones, regardless of how much they had actually contributed, and even top contributors tended to feel shame when excluded.

1136.content: Among Aka foragers of the Central African Republic, behavioural observations of 15 infants aged 8 to 12 months found significant variation in how often infants received care, and who gave it, depending on whether the mother lived with her own kin or with her husband's kin. When all categories of caregivers were counted together, infants received similar overall levels of care in both settings.

1137.content: Across three observation periods (1994-1996, 2000-2002 and 2009-2013) covering 94 Aka forager infants aged 2 weeks to 12 months in the Central African Republic, about 846 hours of daylight focal observation, infants under 6 months were held in 95.7 percent of observations in the first period and 82.7 percent in the last, and were in physical contact with a caregiver (holding or touching) 91.4 percent of the time in the last period. Infants aged 6 to 12 months were held or touched by caregivers about 80 percent of the day.

In the same Aka observations, infants under 6 months were alone (in 2009-2013: no caregiver interacting or near and the mother out of view; in 1994-1996: no caregiver in view or within 5 meters) less than 1 percent of the time in both periods measured, and were within a forearm's distance of a caregiver 97.3 percent of the time in 1994-1996 and 94.5 percent in 2009-2013. For infants aged 6 to 12 months, proximity ranged from 86.5 to 91.3 percent of the day across the three periods and someone was available to the infant about 99 percent of the day.

1138.content: Among Hadza foragers of northern Tanzania (time budgets for 90 people, with children weighed across seasons), the time non-nursing mothers spent foraging accounted for 46 percent of the variation in their weaned children's weight changes, against 13 percent for mothers who were nursing a new infant. Nursing mothers foraged least when the infant was youngest and increased foraging across the nursing period.

In the same Hadza sample, postmenopausal grandmothers foraged most when their newest grandchild was youngest, the time when nursing mothers foraged least. With the child's and the mother's foraging time controlled, weaned children's weight changes correlated with the grandmother's foraging time, most strongly for the youngest weaned children of nursing mothers; with season controlled directly, no grandmother effect was detectable. No nursing woman in the sample lacked a postmenopausal helper, and in only two of eight cases was the helper assisting her own childbearing daughter.

1139.content: Among Mbendjele BaYaka foragers of the Republic of Congo, 12-hour daylight focal follows of 18 children aged 0 to 4 years recorded 289 crying bouts. Of the 220 bouts not already being attended to and not self-resolving within 30 seconds, 98.6 percent drew a response; about half were answered within 10 seconds and 90 percent within 25 seconds, mostly by comforting or nursing. No caregiver scolded or restricted a crying child, and only one child was left to cry, for 13 minutes.

In the same 18 BaYaka children, the mean number of allomothers (caregivers other than the mother) was 14.4 in the proximity network, 7.2 in the physical-contact network, 7.9 for close care and 2.5 for responding to crying. Allomothers gave 40 to 50 percent of care in each domain, though most of a child's allocare came from a few people. Infants under 1.5 years were alone (no one within 3 m and in sight) for about 15 minutes of the 12 daylight hours, in physical contact with someone for 9.2 hours and held for over 5 hours.

1140.content: In US census microdata (IPUMS) from 1850 to 2000, the share of people aged 65 or older living with an adult child fell from almost 70 percent in the mid-nineteenth century to fewer than 15 percent by 2000. Among whites it fell from two-thirds in 1850 to a low of 13 percent in 1990; among blacks from 50 percent in 1870 to 22 percent a century later. Ruggles concludes the decline came mainly from rising opportunities for the young and declining parental control, more than from elders' rising income.

1141.content: Hahn-Holbrook and Haselton review cross-cultural, epidemiological and experimental studies and propose a mismatch hypothesis of postpartum depression: early weaning, diets low in essential fatty acids, low physical activity, little sun exposure and isolation from kin support, each associated with postpartum depression symptoms in the studies they cite, mark departures from how humans are believed to have lived. The authors label postpartum depression a candidate disease of modern civilization and say more research is needed to establish causal relationships.

On kin support, the authors write that forager families typically live in kin groups where grandparents, aunts and uncles and older siblings help mothers and fathers with young children, while Western nuclear families often live hundreds or thousands of miles from close kin. They cite a meta-analysis reporting weak or absent social support as one of the most consistent correlates of postpartum depression symptoms, and a longitudinal study of 210 women in which support from family, not from the baby's father, buffered a rise in placental corticotropin-releasing hormone in pregnancy.

1142.content: In a Shuar village in Ecuador, 21 of 45 mothers were interviewed retrospectively about their most recent pregnancy: 62 percent reported sadness during pregnancy and 33 percent reported sadness after the birth. Mothers who had not wanted the child reported pregnancy sadness more often (77 against 29 percent, p = .052, one-tailed), and almost all the reasons mothers gave could be read as lack of social support or resources, poor maternal or infant health, or opportunity costs.

The authors note that the Shuar rates are quite similar to those found for postpartum depression in Western urban populations: a third of mothers in this non-industrial village reported sadness after birth.

1143.content: Newman reviews evidence that the distress or separation calls of infant mammals work as crying: studies across several mammalian orders find a shared basic acoustic structure (one group treated kittens' cries as essentially the same sounds as human infant cries), and playback studies show caregivers respond, for example squirrel monkey (Saimiri sciureus) mothers recognise their own infant from its cries alone and Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata) mothers respond more to their own infant's calls. He proposes that crying and the caregiver's response form one mammalian cry circuit that evolved early.

Newman reports that in adult squirrel monkeys (Saimiri sciureus), removing the rostral midline cortex including the anterior cingulate (areas 24, 25 and 12) eliminated or sharply reduced separation-induced cries for a long time, while removing the overlying neocortex had only a passing effect, and calls in other contexts (feeding, restraint, alarm) appeared unaffected. He reads this, with stimulation studies, as evidence that the anterior cingulate takes part in crying, beyond the brainstem model.

1144.content: In the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, the first randomised trial of foster care against continued institutional care (136 institutionalised children in Bucharest, Romania, enrolled at 6 to 31 months), Strange Situation assessments at 42 months found 49.5 percent of the foster care group securely attached against 17.5 percent of the care-as-usual group, and 13.1 against 40 percent classified insecure-other. Children placed in foster care before 24 months were more likely to be securely attached, and the younger the placement the more likely an organised attachment.

1145.content: Behaviour diaries kept at 8 to 14 days, 5 to 6 weeks and 10 to 14 weeks compared London parents, Copenhagen parents and a proximal care group who planned to hold their infants at least 80 percent of the time between 8 am and 8 pm, breastfeed often and answer cries fast. Proximal care parents held infants 15 to 16 hours per 24 hours; London parents had 50 percent less physical contact. London infants cried 50 percent more overall than infants in both other groups at 2 and 5 weeks. Bouts of unsoothable crying and colicky crying at 5 weeks did not differ between groups, and proximal care infants woke and cried at night most often at 12 weeks.

1146.content: Hagen proposes that postpartum depression, as the studies he reviews measured it, may be an adaptation that tells a mother she is bearing or has borne a fitness cost, moving her to reduce or end investment in an infant when help is lacking or the infant's health is poor, and that may help her negotiate more investment from others. He argues it is also a good model for low mood in general.

Hagen's review tables studies reporting a correlation between postpartum depression and lack of spousal or wider social support, a correlation he reports holds whether the outcome was scored on self-report symptom scales or by clinical diagnosis, and notes two meta-analyses (Beck 1996; O'Hara and Swain 1996) reporting the same association.

1147.content: Hewlett describes Aka forager infancy in the Central African Republic as indulgent: infants are held almost constantly, have skin-to-skin contact most of the day, are nursed on demand and attended to at once when they fuss or cry. In camp, infants aged 1 to 4 months were held by their mothers less than 40 percent of the time, were passed to other caregivers 7.3 times an hour on average, and were held by seven different caregivers on average during the day; out of camp the mother held the infant almost 90 percent of the time and transfers fell to about two an hour.

1148.content: Among 28 Aka forager mothers with children under 35 months, behavioural observation with energy expenditure data found that caregivers, largely grandmothers, lowered mothers' work energy expenditure by as much as 216 kcal over a 9-hour observation period, while the presence of fathers and juveniles went with higher maternal energy expenditure. Grandmothers' direct childcare replaced mothers' direct care about one to one; fathers' direct care cut mothers' care by almost 4 to 1, lowering total direct care from all caregivers.

1149.content: A meta-analysis of 285 studies (20,720 infant-parent dyads) using the Strange Situation found a global distribution of 51.6 percent secure, 14.7 percent avoidant, 10.2 percent resistant and 23.5 percent disorganized attachment, with no difference between mothers and fathers. Avoidant and disorganized attachment were more common in samples with socio-demographic risk and in maltreatment samples. Secure rates were highest in African and Asian samples, though only 4 African and 5 Asian studies were included against 203 from North America.

1150.content: Sbarra and Hazan propose a coregulation model of adult attachment: within a pair bond, partners' physiology becomes interwoven through conditioning of reward systems and the growth of felt security. Losing that coregulation through separation or loss can bring dysregulation, from diffuse arousal and disorganization to a full and highly organized stress response, and recovery requires a self-regulatory strategy that dampens the disruption. The article reviews evidence across levels of analysis and sets out testable questions.

1151.content: Among Agta foragers of the Philippines (200 people in six camps) and Mbendjele BaYaka foragers of Congo (132 people in three camps), wearable sensors recorded who was within about 3 metres of whom every 2 minutes, 15 hours a day for about a week in 2014. In both populations each person had between one and four unrelated close friends whom they were near as often as close kin. Unrelated people often lived in other households, so these few strong friendships were the links between household clusters, and randomly reshuffling non-kin ties in network simulations, which evened out these strong friendships, cut the network's efficiency drastically, while shuffling kin ties did not change it.

In the same sensor study, children's contacts already reached beyond the family. Among Agta children aged 3 to 7, 27% of recorded interactions were with non-kin, 32% with siblings, 13% with mothers and under 1% with grandmothers; among BaYaka children aged 2 to 7, 30% were with non-kin, 30% with siblings, 17% with mothers and 5% with grandmothers. At ages 8 to 12 the non-kin share rose to 39% (Agta) and 35% (BaYaka), and children's non-kin ties went preferentially to children of similar age.

Among the BaYaka of Congo, the authors modelled how much plant knowledge pairs of people shared. Close friendship went with the highest odds of shared knowledge (odds ratio 1.82), above mother and offspring (1.48), spouses (1.46) and siblings (1.31).

1152.content: In a prospective study of 400 largely working-class women with children living at home, the authors measured self-esteem and support at a first interview and then followed the women for a year. Once a stressor occurred, women with low self-esteem or little support from a core tie (a husband, lover or someone named as very close) had a greatly increased risk of an onset of depression as assessed by the authors. Lack of support from that core tie at the time of the crisis went with the highest risk, and women who were let down, getting less support than the first interview led them to expect, were also at high risk.

1153.content: In a random sample of women living in south London, the authors found a large social-class difference in the rate of psychiatric disturbance as they rated it, largest among women with young children at home. Severe life events and major long-term difficulties in the year before onset played an important part. Working-class women met such events more often, but this explained only a small part of the class difference; they were much more likely to break down once one had occurred, and the authors link this greater vulnerability to certain social factors.

1154.content: A meta-analysis of cohort studies published from 1980 to February 2014 that gave data on mortality by loneliness, social isolation or living alone. Across studies that controlled for several possible confounds, the weighted average odds ratios were 1.29 for social isolation, 1.26 for loneliness and 1.32 for living alone, that is 29%, 26% and 32% higher likelihood of death. Objective isolation and subjective loneliness did not differ; results held across gender, length of follow-up and world region, depended on initial health status, and were larger in samples with an average age under 65.

1155.content: A PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis of 90 prospective cohort studies with 2,205,199 adults. In the general population, social isolation went with a pooled 1.32 times the risk of death from all causes (95% CI 1.26 to 1.39) and loneliness with 1.14 times (1.08 to 1.20). Social isolation also went with higher cancer mortality (1.24) and cardiovascular mortality (1.34); loneliness with higher cancer mortality (1.09).

1156.content: In a four-week randomised trial, 981 adults were asked to use OpenAI's GPT-4o for at least five minutes a day and were assigned to one of nine conditions: text, a neutral voice or an engaging voice, crossed with open-ended, non-personal or personal conversation prompts. Weekly surveys measured loneliness, socialising with real people, emotional dependence on the chatbot and problematic use. The assigned conditions had no significant effect on loneliness or socialising; personal conversations went with slightly lower emotional dependence and problematic use than open-ended ones.

In the same trial, the time each person chose to spend with the chatbot each day (centred within condition) went with all four outcomes after four weeks: higher loneliness (standardised beta 0.02), less socialising with real people (beta minus 0.05), more emotional dependence on the chatbot (0.06) and more problematic use (0.02). Loneliness and socialising at the start did not correlate with later daily use (Spearman rho 0.1 and minus 0.09). The authors say they cannot tell from this whether more use worsened the outcomes or worsening outcomes led to more use.

1157.content: The authors followed 25 students for 18 months as they moved from school to university. Compared with ties to relatives, the emotional intensity of friendships fell more when contact became less frequent and when the friends did fewer activities together. The authors conclude that friendships cost much more to maintain than kin relations.

1158.content: Thirty students in their last year of school in an English city rated their emotional closeness (1 to 10) to every relative and friend in their active network, and 25 completed all three waves over 18 months (1,291 network members in all). Emotional closeness to family rose over the study (b 0.27) while closeness to friends fell (b minus 0.62). Friends known for a long time and friends in the inner layer of the network were not spared the decline.

In the same study, about half the students stayed in their home city and half left for universities elsewhere. Going to university went with a larger drop in closeness to old friends than not going. Going away made no difference: students at a university in their home city lost as much closeness to old friends as those who moved. For friends, more contact (for women) and more shared activities (for men) went with keeping closeness.

1159.content: Using the way the mix of new mutations changes with parents' ages, trained on a large pedigree study, and dated variants from whole-genome data, the authors estimate the average human generation interval over the past 250,000 years at 26.9 years (standard error 3.4), with fathers older (30.7 years) than mothers (23.2 years). They report that generation times fell for over a thousand generations and rose sharply in the recent past, and that the African population's estimate stayed longer than those of Eurasian populations far back in time.

1160.content: Reanalysing the approach of Wang et al. 2023, Ragsdale and Thornton argue that its results, especially the long-lasting sex differences and the higher ancestral generation times of West African than Eurasian populations, mainly reflect noise and biases in the allele-age data and lack validation with independent methods. In their refit, the inferred generation-time histories fit the mutation data poorly.

1161.content: Twenty-five university students in Glasgow and Aberdeen (mean age 24) spent an hour each listing personally known faces and an hour listing famous faces, then did recognition tests with famous faces. Extrapolating the recall rates and correcting by the recall-to-recognition ratio, the authors estimate that people know about 5,000 faces on average, with every participant between about 1,000 and 10,000.

1162.content: In a narrative review of the empirical literature, Baumeister and Leary report that people form social attachments readily under most conditions and resist the ending of existing bonds, that belonging has strong effects on emotion and thinking, and that a lack of attachments is linked to a range of ill effects on health, adjustment and well-being.

From that evidence the authors conclude that the need to belong, a need for frequent, pleasant interactions within an ongoing bond, is a powerful, fundamental and extremely pervasive human motive, and that evidence on satiation and substitution fits this reading.

1163.content: Hawkley and Cacioppo review evidence and set out their model: feeling socially isolated is read by the organism as being unsafe, which raises implicit vigilance for social threat and the wish to reconnect. In their account lonely people come to see the social world as more threatening, expect more negative interactions and remember more negative social information, and this vigilance alters physiology, worsens sleep and, in longitudinal studies they review, goes with higher morbidity and mortality.

The authors report an early version of their meta-analysis of 50 loneliness intervention studies (1970 to 2009). In the 20 randomised studies the average effect was small (minus 0.20). Among them, interventions that targeted how lonely people read social situations had the largest effect (minus 0.60, 4 studies), larger than those that added social support (minus 0.16, 12 studies), trained social skills (0.02, 2 studies) or increased opportunities for social contact (minus 0.06, 2 studies).

1164.content: Using the US General Social Survey of 1993, and controlling for age, race, education, marital status and total hours of television, the author reports that women who watched more prime-time dramas and sitcoms were more satisfied with their friendships (P < .05), and men who watched more TV news (P < .06) and public television (P < .01) were more satisfied with theirs. In the 1986 survey, having more friends and socialising with them more went with more satisfaction with friendships. The author reads this as the brain failing to tell people seen on TV from real friends, and calls the evidence merely suggestive.

1165.content: In six laboratory experiments with undergraduates (18 to 56 per study), people led to feel excluded, by false feedback that they would end up alone, by recalling a rejection, or by being left out by a group or turned down by a partner, then showed more interest in making new friends, more wish to work with others, more positive impressions of new people and gave larger rewards to new partners than control participants.

In the same experiments, excluded people did not seek reconnection with the people who had excluded them, nor with new partners they did not expect to meet face to face, and people high in fear of negative evaluation did not respond to new partners in a friendly way.

1166.content: Fifty-eight women aged 18 to 21 at a Los Angeles university, recruited as 29 pairs of close friends, had four short conversations each: in person, by video chat, by audio chat and by instant messaging. Bonding, measured by the participants' own ratings and by coded affiliation cues such as laughter and smiling, differed across conditions: highest in person, then video chat, then audio, lowest in instant messaging. Participants felt connected in all four.

1167.content: From household listings and censuses of English and other European settlements, Snell finds that many pre-industrial settlements had no single-person households and the average was around 5 percent of households (Laslett's 100 early modern English communities: 5.6 percent of households, about 1 percent of people), steady until about 1911. The share then rose, above all from the 1960s: 31 percent of UK households in the 2011 census, 40 percent in Norway, over 47 percent in Sweden and over 60 percent in Stockholm.

1168.content: Using census and survey microdata for 113 countries covering over 95% of the world's population (IPUMS-International, Demographic and Health Surveys, EU Labour Force Survey; most recent data since 2000), the authors find that at ages 25 to 29 most countries have under 5% of people living alone, with women in several African and Asian countries at 0 to 1%, while in Germany and Switzerland close to one third of 25 to 29 year olds live alone. At ages 75 to 79 living alone is much more common than at 50 to 54, in many countries two to three times as common, from near zero in some countries to 30 to 50% of women in others; Asian countries are lowest. Living alone rises with the Human Development Index, most clearly among elderly women.

1169.content: Using Binford's data on 314 hunter-gatherer groups that move camp at least once a year and Kelly's 47 estimates, the authors find that the total distance foragers move per year in residential moves averages about 158 km (Binford data) and 174 km (Kelly data), close to the annual migration distance expected for a 60 kg mammal.
In the same data, the average distance per residential move depends on temperature and rainfall, and the eight groups that reported the most moves per year are all tropical foragers.

Using Binford's data on 314 forager groups that move camp at least once a year, Hamilton and colleagues found that the total distance a group moves camp over a year averages about 158 km (Kelly's separate data set: about 174 km), close to the yearly travel distance expected for a 60 kg mammal from the scaling of migration distance with body size in land mammals.

In the same Binford data, the average distance per residential move falls as the energy available in the local ecosystem (net primary production, tied to temperature and rainfall) rises: groups in poor environments move farthest per move, groups in rich ones move short distances.

1170.content: In the Historical Sample of the Netherlands (over 35,000 people living between 1850 and 1950, about 300,000 recorded moves), the median number of residential moves over a lifetime was 10 (range 0 to 130), with moves peaking at ages 20 to 30; the authors note that 10 moves is far below highly mobile hunter-gatherer populations.

129.content: Henrich and Gil-White distinguish two kinds of rank: dominance, which rests on force or the threat of force, and prestige, which is deference that others confer freely.

The authors propose an 'information goods' theory: selection favoured social learners who copy the most successful models, and learners pay for close and prolonged access to those models with deference, so prestige is respect given to the skilled in exchange for the chance to learn from them; they test its predictions against data from across the social sciences.

1171.content: A meta-analysis of 259 studies with 219,625 participants found that 14 work characteristics together accounted on average for 43% of the variance in 19 worker attitudes and behaviours; the set of motivational characteristics (autonomy, skill variety, task identity, task significance and feedback from the job, plus task and knowledge features such as task variety, job complexity and problem solving) accounted for 34% of the variance in job satisfaction.

1172.content: Among the Northern Ache of eastern Paraguay, who split their time between forest foraging trips and a farming settlement, men spent on average 6.5 hours a day acquiring and processing food in the forest and less than 3 hours a day at the settlement; women spent 3.75 hours a day (including carrying) in the forest and 2.71 hours at the settlement.

1173.content: On Ache foraging trips in eastern Paraguay, men hunted about 7 hours per day with mean returns of 1,340 calories per hour, although the authors calculate they could get about 2,630 calories per hour by collecting palm products instead.

In the 1981-82 sample of Ache foragers in eastern Paraguay, men's foraging returned a mean of 1,339 calories per hour and women's 1,221 before processing. Among the 25 adult men with more than 10 sample days, mean returns per man ranged from 446 to 2,124 calories per hour, individual men's rates correlated between 1980 and 1982, and adolescent and old men returned almost an order of magnitude less than adult men (daily, 1,545 calories for males 14 to 20 and 797 for males 60 to 75, against 9,240 for men 21 to 59). Women nursing infants had significantly lower returns.

Across the resources the Ache take, return rates on encounter vary so much within each class (fruits, honey, game) that package size and resource type do not predict them; in eastern Paraguay honey generally returns more per hour than other classes, game slightly more than the commonest plant foods, large game such as peccaries can give medium or low returns when pursuits are long, and small game such as armadillos can rank very high.

1174.content: In four simultaneous experiments with college students, pretreatment with inescapable aversive tone or with insoluble discrimination problems was followed by failure to escape noise in a shuttlebox and failure to solve anagrams, compared with escapable or soluble and control pretreatments, across tasks and across motivational systems.

108.content: In the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, a randomised controlled trial, young abandoned children living in Romanian institutions were assigned either to continued institutional care or to foster care, and followed to 54 months. Children who stayed in the institution had cognitive outcomes markedly below those of never-institutionalised children and of children placed in foster care, and the improvements at 42 and 54 months were most marked for the youngest children placed.

1175.content: The Bucharest team report that at 30, 42 and 54 months, children removed from institutions and placed in foster care had higher IQ scores than children randomised to stay in institutions, and those removed before 24 months did best of all.

At the 8-year follow-up, 103 of the original 136 children were tested with the WISC-IV. Mean full-scale IQ was 81.46 in the foster care group, 76.16 in the care-as-usual group and 107.00 in never-institutionalised children. The overall multivariate group difference only approached significance (p = .14), with a significant effect on the verbal subscale; gains were clearest for children who stayed with their foster family, and earlier placement now went with higher processing-speed scores and predicted a profile of stable, typical IQ scores over time.

1176.content: In the Whitehall II prospective cohort (10,308 London civil servants aged 35 to 55; 6,895 men and 3,413 women; mean follow-up 5.3 years), men and women with low job control, whether rated by the workers themselves or assessed independently by personnel managers, had a higher risk of newly reported coronary heart disease. Those with low control at both measurements, three years apart, had an odds ratio of 1.93 (95% CI 1.34 to 2.77) for any later coronary event compared with those with high control both times, and the association was not explained by employment grade, negative affectivity or classic coronary risk factors.
In the same cohort, job demands and social support at work were not related to the risk of coronary heart disease.

1177.content: In three field experiments, fundraising callers who received a task significance intervention raised their job performance relative to callers in two other conditions and to their own earlier performance; among lifeguards, task significance raised job dedication and helping, through higher perceived social impact and social worth; among new callers, conscientiousness and prosocial values moderated the effect.

1178.content: In a field experiment with 39 callers at a university fundraising organisation, callers who briefly met a student whose scholarship their calls funded, compared with callers who read his letter or had no exposure, increased their persistence and performance: one month later they spent 142% more time on the phone and raised 171% more money than before, while the two control groups did not change.

In two laboratory experiments, respectful contact with the beneficiary of an editing task increased persistence, through perceived impact; mere contact with a beneficiary raised persistence only when the task was high in significance, and did not raise it on its own.

1179.content: A meta-analysis of 208 laboratory studies of acute psychological stressors found that stressors raised cortisol on average, with wide variation across tasks. Performance tasks elicited cortisol responses when they were uncontrollable or carried social-evaluative threat (performance could be judged negatively by others), after controlling for methods and other task features; tasks with both elements went with the largest cortisol and ACTH changes and the longest recovery times.

1180.content: In an internet survey 2 to 4 weeks after the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings, with representative samples from metropolitan Boston (846), New York City (941) and the rest of the US (2,888), 4,675 adults in all, people who reported six or more hours a day of bombing-related media (television, radio, print, online and social media) in the week after the bombings scored higher on acute stress symptoms (Stanford Acute Stress Reaction Questionnaire) than people directly exposed to the bombings: regression coefficient 15.61 for heavy media exposure against 5.69 for direct exposure. The models adjusted for physician-diagnosed depression and anxiety reported before the bombings, demographics and earlier collective trauma, and pre-bombing television habits did not change the result.

In the same survey of 4,675 US adults, 4.46% met the authors' DSM-IV based criteria for high acute stress. Direct exposure to the Boston Marathon bombings went with higher continuous stress scores but not with high acute stress, while six or more hours a day of bombing media in the following week went with about nine times the odds of high acute stress compared with minimal media exposure.

1181.content: In humans recorded by microneurography during soft brush stroking, low-threshold unmyelinated C-tactile afferents, unlike myelinated afferents, fired most vigorously at intermediate brushing speeds of 1 to 10 cm per second, and these were the speeds the subjects rated as most pleasant. The authors read C-tactile afferents as a privileged peripheral pathway for pleasant touch that is likely to signal affiliative social body contact.

1182.content: Recording from single C-tactile axons in the forearm nerve of 20 healthy adults in Gothenburg, Sweden, with a computer-controlled probe stroking at five speeds (0.3 to 30 cm per second) and three temperatures (18, 32 and 42 degrees C), the authors found that C-tactile fibres fired most to slow stroking at the neutral 32 degrees typical of skin, while myelinated hair afferents fired more the faster the stroke and did not respond to temperature. In 30 other participants who rated the same strokes, C-tactile firing correlated with rated pleasantness only at the neutral temperature.

1183.content: A systematic review of 51 original research articles found strong convergent evidence that perceived defeat and entrapment go with reported depressive symptoms across clinical and nonclinical samples, and preliminary support for a link with reported suicidality that comorbid depression did not readily explain. The review reports strong evidence linking defeat with PTSD as the studies measured it (possibly partly accounted for by co-occurring depression scores) and less consistent findings for other anxiety diagnoses; the authors report effects often in the moderate to large range.

1184.content: A random-effects meta-analysis of 40 studies (10,072 adults, 84 effect sizes) found that perceived defeat and entrapment correlated strongly, around r = .60, with scores for depression, anxiety problems, PTSD and suicidality alike, and defeat correlated most strongly with depression scores (r = .73). There was no between-study heterogeneity and no sign of publication bias. The authors note the analyses were cross-sectional, so they cannot show which comes first.

1185.content: In laboratory experiments in 17 countries on six continents (Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Denmark, France, Ghana, India, Israel, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Russia, Senegal, Sweden, the UK and the US), 1,156 participants watched real video news stories while skin conductance and heart rate variability were recorded. Pooled across all countries, physiological arousal was higher for negative than for positive stories: 20 seconds into a story, the change in skin conductance from positive to negative content equalled 65% of its observed standard deviation, and the change in heart rate variability over whole stories equalled 10% of its standard deviation.

In the same 17-country study, the negativity bias in skin conductance was statistically significant in 9 of the 17 country samples, and the bias in heart rate variability in only 5 (Brazil, Canada, France, Italy and Sweden). In New Zealand and Sweden the average skin-conductance effect ran opposite to the expected direction, though not significantly, and within each country individuals differed widely; the authors found the variation was not easily explained by culture or country.

1186.content: In male Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus) given 100 tailshocks they could end by turning a wheel (escapable) or identical yoked shocks they could not end (inescapable), inescapable shock raised c-Fos activation in serotonin neurons of the caudal dorsal raphe nucleus to about 300% of the level after escapable shock and produced a sustained rise in serotonin release there. Tested 24 hours later, rats given inescapable shock froze more after two new footshocks and failed to learn shuttlebox escape, while rats given escapable shock behaved like unshocked controls.

When the ventral medial prefrontal cortex (infralimbic and prelimbic regions) of male Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus) was temporarily silenced with muscimol during escapable shock, the rats still learned the wheel-turn escape, yet their dorsal raphe serotonin activation, serotonin release and later fear and escape failure matched those of rats given inescapable shock. Silencing the same region had no effect on rats given inescapable shock, and injections 2 mm in front of or behind it did not reproduce the effect. The authors conclude that the prefrontal cortex detects control and then inhibits the brainstem, so that the default response to shock is the uncontrollable-stress pattern.

1187.content: Three groups were shown 14-minute TV news bulletins edited to carry positive, neutral or negative material. Those who watched the negative bulletin showed increases in both anxious and sad mood and a significant increase in the tendency to catastrophize a personal worry, a concern of their own unrelated to the bulletin's content.

1188.content: In a Dutch convenience sample of 63 adults aged 18 to 82 who reported their news exposure and mood on a phone app five times a day for 10 days in December 2016, negative affect was slightly higher at moments when news had been perceived (Cohen's d = 0.18), and news perceived as more negative went with more negative and less positive affect, more strongly when the news was personally relevant. Neuroticism and extraversion did not moderate the link.

1189.content: In 14 healthy volunteers scanned with fMRI while a virtual predator chased them through a maze and could deliver one or three electric shocks if it caught them, brain activity shifted from the ventromedial prefrontal cortex when the predator was distant to the periaqueductal gray when it was close, most strongly when three shocks were at stake. Across people, imminence-related periaqueductal gray activity correlated with higher post-scan ratings of dread of capture and lower confidence of escape.

1190.content: The authors pooled 30 randomised trials of cash transfers (all unconditional but two) and multi-faceted anti-poverty programs in low- and middle-income countries that measured depression, anxiety, stress or wellbeing scores. Using the longest follow-up from each program, the pooled effect was 0.094 standard deviations toward better mental health scores (95% CI 0.040 to 0.147), with no sign of publication bias (Egger test p = 0.96); multi-faceted programs averaged 0.138 SD and cash transfers 0.067 SD.

Reporting a natural experiment by Christian, Hensel and Roth (2019) in Indonesia, the review states that sub-districts that received a conditional cash transfer program in the first wave of its roll-out saw 18% fewer suicides than sub-districts that received it later, although both had similar suicide trends before the program started. The cash transfer's effect on suicides was largest in districts undergoing drought.

1191.content: Ugandan Game Department archives for 1923 to 1994 recorded 636 human casualties (injuries and deaths) from wild animals, about 11 a year in years with good records. Lions (Panthera leo) accounted for 275, leopards (Panthera pardus) 114 and spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta) 4, so large carnivores accounted for 61.1% of all casualties; 247 of their 393 casualties (62.8%) were deaths, 75.0% of lion attacks and 32.5% of leopard attacks.

Among identified rural victims of large carnivores in the Ugandan records, 73% were men, 11% women and 16% children; men were most often attacked during hunting-related activities, but attacks on women and children were more often fatal. Women and children were attacked more by leopards (67% of 24 cases) and men more by lions (66% of 114 cases).

1192.content: In 404 healthy adults aged 18 to 55 from Pittsburgh (USA), daily conflict and being hugged were counted by telephone interviews on 14 consecutive evenings; participants were then given a common cold virus and kept in quarantine. Hugs were reported on a median 68% of days. Being hugged on more days went with lower odds of infection (odds ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.96), and frequent hugs weakened the link between frequent conflict and infection risk; hugs accounted for 32% of the buffering attributed to perceived social support.

Among the 315 participants who became infected, those who were hugged more often and those reporting more social support showed less severe objective signs of illness (mucus weight and nasal clearance time). The authors found associations of conflict, support and hugs with infection and with illness signs, and none of them with developing a clinical cold (infection plus objective illness criteria).

1193.content: Among 657 women in four places ordered from traditional to modern (rural Yorubaland in Nigeria, Yoruba living in urban Nigeria, rural Canada and the urban United States), the share who met the authors' depression algorithm, based on generally acknowledged criteria, was lowest among rural Nigerian women and highest among urban US women. The association with the modernisation continuum was strongest among women under 45 who had living children (odds ratio 2.1, 95% CI 1.6 to 2.9).
