1307.content: In several studies of hypothetical decisions to help, participants facing life-or-death situations chose to aid close kin over distant kin, the young over the old, the healthy over the sick, the wealthy over the poor, and a premenopausal woman over a postmenopausal woman. When the help was an everyday favour, they gave less weight to kinship and chose to help the very young or the very old over those of middle age, the sick over the healthy, and the poor over the wealthy. The authors read this as a decision rule weighting cues to the helper's inclusive fitness, strongest when the help matters for survival.

1308.content: Compiling published DRD4 allele frequencies for 2,320 individuals from 39 populations together with data on each group's migration history, the authors found that migratory populations had a higher proportion of long DRD4 alleles than sedentary populations; the correlation between macro-migration (long-distance group migration) and the proportion of long alleles was .85. They discuss long DRD4 alleles, linked in some studies to novelty seeking and hyperactivity, as possibly adaptive in migratory societies, and raise the possibility of natural selection.

1309.content: The authors describe the gap between sleep timing on work days and free days, between social and biological time, as 'social jetlag': late chronotypes show the largest gap and build up a sleep debt on work days that they make up on free days. In 501 volunteers who filled in the Munich ChronoType Questionnaire and questionnaires on sleep quality, current and past-week psychological wellbeing and use of caffeine, nicotine and alcohol, links between chronotype, wellbeing and stimulant use were strongest in teenagers and young adults up to age 25. The strongest correlation was between late chronotype and smoking, at all ages except in retirement. The authors argue these correlations most probably reflect social jetlag rather than chronotype itself, and recommend fitting work and school schedules to chronotype.

1310.content: Recording from retinal ganglion cells that project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the circadian pacemaker, the authors found these cells intrinsically photosensitive: unlike other ganglion cells, they depolarised in response to light even when all synaptic input from rods and cones was blocked. Their sensitivity, spectral tuning and slow kinetics matched those of photic entrainment, and the authors suggest they may be the primary photoreceptors for setting the clock. The abstract notes that entrainment of the clock by light requires neither rods nor cones. The species is not named in the abstract; the Brown University release of the same week says the cells were found in rat (Rattus norvegicus) retinas.

1311.content: Reviewing three decades of use, the model's originators state that the two-process model of sleep regulation posits a homeostatic process (Process S) interacting with a process controlled by the circadian pacemaker (Process C), with time courses derived from physiological and behavioural variables. They report that the model simulates the timing and intensity of sleep in diverse experimental protocols, and that recordings from the suprachiasmatic nuclei suggest S and C interact continuously. The model has been applied widely to fatigue, performance and individual differences in sleep regulation.

1312.content: Parents of 452 US children aged 5 to 18 who had been diagnosed with ADHD by a professional, recruited online through newspaper advertisements and the CHADD website (a nonprobability sample), rated how their child's symptoms were in the hour after each of 49 after-school and weekend activities. Parents rated activities in green outdoor settings as followed by milder symptoms than activities indoors or in built outdoor settings, also when the same activity was compared across settings, and the green advantage was significant or marginal in 54 of 56 subgroup analyses (age, sex, income, region, community type and diagnosis). Of 339 reasons parents gave for why an activity helped, only 2 referred to green settings.

1313.content: An umbrella review of 102 meta-analyses (3,782 randomised trials, 650,514 patients) of psychotherapies and drugs for the main diagnosed mental disorders in adults, keeping comparisons with placebo or treatment as usual, head-to-head comparisons and combined against single treatment, found that most effect sizes on the target symptoms were small. Pooled across the diagnosed disorders, psychotherapies beat placebo or usual care by a standardised mean difference of 0.34 and drugs by 0.36; psychotherapy against drugs head to head gave 0.11 and combined against single treatment 0.31. The authors report that risk of bias was often high and read the results as a ceiling for treatment research as presently conducted.

For diagnosed depressive disorders, every drug against placebo effect size in the included meta-analyses was below 0.50 (0.19 to 0.41), apart from ketamine in the first days after a dose (0.83 to 0.88, falling to 0.31 after 7 days). The authors note that differences of 0.30 to 0.50 correspond to about 2 to 4 points on the Hamilton depression scale, below the 7-point change some authors claim is the minimal clinically relevant improvement.

1314.content: Using three of the largest brain-imaging samples (the ABCD Study of US children, the Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank, about 50,000 people in all), the authors found that correlations between individual differences in brain structure or resting brain function and cognitive ability or psychopathology scores are small. In 3,928 ABCD children the median correlation across all brain-wide associations was 0.01, the top 1% of about 11 million associations exceeded an absolute correlation of 0.06, and the largest that replicated out of sample was 0.16. At sample sizes typical of such studies (the median is about 25) effects were strongly inflated by chance, and below 500 people only about 5% of significant associations replicated.

Brain-behaviour associations were more robust for functional than for structural MRI, for cognitive tests than for mental-health questionnaires, and for multivariate than for single-feature methods; the authors conclude that reproducible brain-wide association studies need samples of thousands of people.

1315.content: In a double-blind trial, 40 patients with malignant melanoma about to start high-dose interferon alfa (a cytokine, an immune signalling protein) were randomised to paroxetine (an SSRI) or placebo, starting two weeks before interferon and continuing for its first 12 weeks. Symptoms consistent with a diagnosis of major depression developed in 9 of 20 patients on placebo (45%) and 2 of 18 on paroxetine (11%), relative risk 0.24. Seven of 20 on placebo (35%) and 1 of 20 on paroxetine (5%) had to stop interferon before 12 weeks because of severe depression symptoms, and adverse events were similar in both groups.

1316.content: Panksepp proposes that one reason for rising ADHD diagnoses may be that pre-school children have fewer chances for natural self-generated social play, that animal work shows play can build behavioural inhibition in young animals while stimulant drugs reduce playfulness, and that daily rough-and-tumble play might ease ADHD symptoms in many children. He states that the idea of intensive play interventions remains to be evaluated and suggests play sanctuaries for at-risk children as an alternative to play-reducing stimulants.

Panksepp reports that in young animals all stimulant drugs of the kind given for ADHD reduce playfulness at very low doses, and that in one animal model, rats (Rattus norvegicus) with ADHD-type arousal, play therapy reduced some impulse-control problems later in life.

1317.content: In laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus), right frontal lesions made shortly after birth produced hyperactivity, and chronic rough-and-tumble play therapy during early adolescence reduced both the hyperactivity and the excessive playfulness later in development. In normal rats, access to rough-and-tumble play increased later freezing to a startle stimulus, which the authors read as better behavioural inhibition.

1318.content: A meta-analysis of 20 population surveys published since 1985 found significantly higher pooled urban than rural odds for the total prevalence of diagnosed psychiatric disorders and for diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders, and no significant urban-rural difference for substance use disorders as the surveys classified them. The authors report that adjustment for various confounders had a limited impact on the urban-rural odds ratios.

1319.content: Price and colleagues propose, from an evolutionary adaptationist standpoint, that the depressive state evolved in relation to social competition as an unconscious, involuntary losing strategy, which lets the individual accept defeat in ritual agonistic encounters and accommodate to what would otherwise be unacceptably low social rank. The authors state that the proposal covers what they label depressive personality and depressive illness.

1320.content: In a qualitative study of 38 adults in Oxfordshire, UK, who had taken SSRIs (individual interviews, a group interview and 11 validation interviews), plus posts on patient websites, most participants reported a general reduction in the intensity of all emotions, almost all reported fewer or weaker positive emotions, and most reported feeling emotionally detached from other people, including partners and children. Almost all reported no longer caring about things that used to matter to them, Participants put these changes down to the SSRI, and most reported they could tell them apart from symptoms of their depression or other illness.

Participants reported weighing these emotional effects against the risk of relapse: some felt that the effects, though unhelpful, were better than the possibility of relapse, others reported them as a reason for wanting to stop or having already stopped their SSRI. The authors report that the emotional effects bore on how participants saw their own parenting and were occasionally linked to thoughts of self-harm or suicide.

1321.content: In a computer simulation of groups of foragers learning which of several changing foods are safe, a group made up mostly of predictable individuals with a small minority (5%) of highly unpredictable individuals survived best of all groups tested. A wholly unpredictable group learned the most about the foods but lost members fastest to poisoning, a wholly predictable group lost members to malnutrition, and a group with 25% unpredictable members survived about as well as the predictable group.

From the model the authors argue that the traits labelled ADHD, especially the hyperactive-impulsive type, may persist in a minority of 5 to 10% since exploration by a few, whose risks fall mainly on the individual while the information is shared, benefits the group. They state the main criticism themselves: they cannot show that such tasks occurred often enough to shape human evolution.

1322.content: In a case-control study of 1,809 adults in Marburg and Muenster, Germany (861 patients who met DSM-IV criteria for a current or past major depressive episode, 948 healthy controls), the authors took, for each scan type (structural MRI, diffusion imaging, task fMRI, resting-state fMRI), the single measure that differed most between the groups. Even these best measures explained less than 2% of the variance (partial eta squared 0.004 to 0.017), the two groups' distributions overlapped 87% to 95%, and they sorted individuals into patient or control with 54% to 56% accuracy, close to the 50% of chance. The pattern held for patients scored as acute or chronic.

In the same 1,809 adults, two measures of life circumstances separated people diagnosed with major depression from controls far better than any brain scan: childhood maltreatment (Childhood Trauma Questionnaire) and perceived social support (Social Support Questionnaire) overlapped only 55.6% and 56.8% between the groups and sorted individuals with about 71% accuracy. A polygenic risk score for major depression did about as poorly as the scans (85.7% overlap, 58.3% accuracy).

1323.content: Honkasilta and Koutsoklenis, quoting the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013, pp. 59-60), report that the diagnostic criteria for ADHD are 18 listed behaviours, nine under inattention and nine under hyperactivity and impulsivity, and that six must be met in a domain for the diagnosis. Items they quote include 'often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat', 'often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected', 'often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly' and 'is often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli'. They note that all 18 begin with 'often' and that the manual gives no frequency threshold for it.

The authors argue that the ADHD diagnostic criteria are essentially lists of behaviours that are the contraries of socially valued norms, prescribing when a child should remain seated, how quietly it should play and how much it should talk, and that the manual attributes the behaviours to the child while ignoring the situation they occur in.

1324.content: A meta-analysis of 46 papers (49 samples, 3,454 patients diagnosed with major depressive disorder who had remitted and were then randomised to placebo) found that patients who had remitted on placebo relapsed at 24.7% while followed on placebo, against 42.0% to 55.6% for patients switched from an antidepressant to placebo (SSRIs 48.7%, SNRIs 42.0%, tricyclics 55.6%, MAOIs 45.4%; 42.1% across all 49 samples including the placebo group). In regression the placebo group had a significantly lower relapse rate than the drug classes (beta 0.277, p = 0.0001), and the result held when the stringency of each trial's relapse criteria was added.

The authors read the pattern as oppositional tolerance: if mood-related monoamines are under working homeostatic control, prolonged antidepressant use builds up opposing forces that make monoamine levels overshoot when the drug stops, so relapse risk after stopping should rise with how strongly the drug raises them. Using rodent prefrontal microdialysis data to rate each drug's strength, they found relapse after stopping rose with the drug's effect on serotonin and noradrenaline, and they state that the results give no evidence that monoamine regulation is malfunctioning in patients meeting current criteria for major depressive disorder.

1325.content: In a cross-sectional study of 86,772 adults (mean age 62.4, 57% women) with measured light exposure, greater night-time light exposure was associated with higher covariate-adjusted risk of being diagnosed with major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, PTSD, psychosis and bipolar disorder, and of self-harm. Independently of night light, greater daytime light exposure was associated with lower risk of being diagnosed with major depressive disorder, PTSD or psychosis and of self-harm. The authors report that the associations held after adjustment for sociodemographics, photoperiod, physical activity, sleep quality and cardiometabolic health.

Independently of night-time light, people with greater daytime light exposure had lower covariate-adjusted risk of being diagnosed with major depressive disorder, PTSD or psychosis and of self-harm behaviour.

1326.content: Chouinard and Jones propose that, as tardive dyskinesia is thought to result from drug-induced dopamine receptor supersensitivity in the neostriatum, chronic treatment with neuroleptics (antipsychotics) also makes dopamine receptors in the mesolimbic region supersensitive, producing what they label a supersensitivity psychosis. They illustrate the syndrome's clinical and pharmacological features with data from 10 patients, and they state that the tendency toward psychotic relapse in such patients is then determined by more than the normal course of the illness.

1327.content: In 788 twin pairs aged 7 to 15 randomly drawn from the Missouri Twin Study, with one parent completing the Social Responsiveness Scale for each child, autistic traits as scored on the scale were continuously distributed and moderately to highly heritable. Scores at or above the published mean for patients diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified were found in 1.4% of boys and 0.3% of girls, and structural equation modelling found no sex-specific genetic influences. The authors conclude that, given the continuous distribution, where the cut-off between 'affected' and 'unaffected' is drawn may be arbitrary.

1328.content: A network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind randomised trials (14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults diagnosed with ADHD) compared amphetamines, atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate and modafinil with placebo and each other at about 12 weeks. On clinicians' ratings of core ADHD symptoms in children and adolescents, every drug beat placebo (standardised mean difference -1.02 for amphetamines, -0.78 for methylphenidate, -0.56 for atomoxetine). On teachers' ratings, where available, only methylphenidate (-0.82) and modafinil (-0.76) beat placebo. In adults, amphetamines, methylphenidate, bupropion and atomoxetine beat placebo on clinicians' ratings and modafinil did not.

Few trials reported outcomes near 26 or 52 weeks, all in adults, so the authors could not analyse those time points and state that their findings inform only the choice of short-term medication for ADHD; they call for funded research on the drugs' long-term effects. Amphetamines were less well tolerated than placebo (more drop-out for side-effects) in children (odds ratio 2.30) and adults (3.26).

1329.content: A genome-wide association meta-analysis of 20,183 people diagnosed with ADHD and 35,191 controls from 12 cohorts (Danish iPSYCH register cases diagnosed by psychiatrists under ICD-10, plus European, North American and Chinese cohorts) found common variants at 12 independent loci, with common-variant (SNP) heritability on the liability scale of 0.216. The genetic signal for the diagnosis was nearly identical to that of a meta-analysis of ADHD symptom scores in the general population (genetic correlation 0.97 with the EAGLE/QIMR measure), which the authors read as the clinical diagnosis being an extreme expression of continuous heritable traits.

Of 219 traits tested, 43 shared genetic overlap with being diagnosed with ADHD, including lower educational outcomes, major depressive disorder (genetic correlation 0.42), smoking, obesity-related traits and insomnia. The authors also report that the common-variant risk for ADHD was genetically correlated with having children younger and having more children.

1330.content: A meta-analysis of 24 studies measuring unstimulated blood cytokines in patients meeting DSM criteria for major depression and in controls found significantly higher TNF-alpha (weighted mean difference 3.97 pg/mL; 438 patients, 350 controls) and IL-6 (1.78 pg/mL; 492 patients, 400 controls) in the patients. There were no significant differences for IL-1beta, IL-4, IL-2, IL-8, IL-10 or interferon-gamma. The authors note that individual studies had reported both positive and negative results.

1331.content: Horton and Wohl, writing about radio, television and film in the 1950s, name the 'para-social relationship': the media give the audience the illusion of a face-to-face relationship with a performer, who talks to them as if personally, and the audience answers as if in a primary group. They state the crucial difference from ordinary relationships as the lack of effective reciprocity: the interaction is one-sided, controlled by the performer and cannot develop mutually, and the spectator's only option is to withdraw.

Horton and Wohl argue that 'personality' programmes are especially suited to compensatory attachments by the socially isolated, the socially inept, the aged and invalid, the timid and the rejected, and they call it reasonable and natural that isolated and lonely people seek sociability wherever they can find it. They describe a radio persona, the Lonesome Gal, who addressed lonely men with endearments and received thousands of letters proposing marriage.

1332.content: In an experience-sampling study of 82 young adults in Ann Arbor, Michigan (mean age 19.5), texted five times a day for 14 days, the more a person used Facebook between two texts, the worse they reported feeling at the next text (B = .08, p < .0001), and the more they used Facebook over the two weeks, the more their life satisfaction fell (beta = -.124, p = .02). Feeling worse did not go with more Facebook use afterwards.

In the same study, interacting with other people directly (face to face or by phone) did not go with a fall in life satisfaction and went with feeling better at the next text (B = -.15 on the negative-affect scale, p < .0001), the opposite of Facebook use. Loneliness at one text went with more Facebook use afterwards, and Facebook use still went with feeling worse when loneliness was controlled.

1333.content: Montag and colleagues analysed prominent smartphone apps (YouTube, Facebook, WhatsApp, Freemium games such as Candy Crush Saga and Hay Day) and list six design elements that prolong use: endless scrolling and autoplay, the endowment and mere-exposure effects, social pressure (read receipts), a feed tuned to what the user likes, social comparison and social reward (the 'Like'), and the Zeigarnik effect (an unfinished level that pulls the player back). They link each to an existing psychological or economic theory and tie the design to a business model of personal data in exchange for use.

On endless scrolling and autoplay, the authors write that the user scrolls on with no natural stop at which they might reconsider quitting, and that occasional rewarding finds (a funny or interesting video) add intermittent reinforcement of the kind studied in slot machines; autoplay starts the next video or episode as soon as one ends.

1334.content: In an fMRI study at Cambridge, 19 heterosexual men who met proposed diagnostic criteria for compulsive sexual behaviour (mainly compulsive use of online explicit material) and 19 age-matched healthy men rated explicit videos: the compulsive-use group reported more sexual desire for the explicit videos than the healthy men (p = .032) but no significant difference in how much they liked them (p = .079). The authors read this split between wanting and liking as in line with incentive-motivation accounts of drug addiction.

Explicit video, compared with exciting non-sexual video, activated the dorsal anterior cingulate, ventral striatum and amygdala more in the men labelled with compulsive sexual behaviour than in healthy men; these are regions that a meta-analysis of drug-cue studies had found active for alcohol, nicotine and cocaine cues. In the compulsive-use group, desire scores went with stronger coupling of this network; there were no neural findings for liking. The men in that group reported more arousal and erection difficulty with partners and not with explicit material.

1335.content: In preregistered, incentivised online experiments with more than 1,000 US college students in 2023, users asked about paying or being paid to deactivate their own TikTok or Instagram for four weeks while everyone else kept using it needed about $55 (TikTok) and $47 (Instagram) to give it up. Asked instead about a deactivation of all participating students at their university, themselves included, 60% of TikTok users and 46% of Instagram users valued the platform's existence below zero, and users on average would pay $24 (TikTok) and $6 (Instagram) to have everyone, themselves included, deactivate.

Asked hypothetically, 57% of all respondents would prefer to live in a world without TikTok and 58% in a world without Instagram; among users, 33% (TikTok) and 57% (Instagram) said the same. Only 5% preferred a world without Google Maps, the comparison product. The authors report that answers to this question track the incentivised measure (p < 0.01 for both platforms).

1336.content: In a balanced crossover laboratory study of 13 young men, five hours of evening work at a white LED-backlit computer screen, which emitted more than twice as much blue light (464 nm) as a non-LED screen, significantly suppressed the evening rise of melatonin and reduced subjective and objective sleepiness (fewer slow eye movements and less frontal low-frequency EEG activity) compared with the non-LED screen. Sustained attention, working memory and declarative memory scores were higher in the LED condition.

1337.content: In a preregistered online experiment (preprint Study 3, published Study 2) with US Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, 296 of 601 recruits remained after comprehension checks and were randomised to 15 minutes of chatting with a GPT-3 companion chatbot, chatting with another person, a chatbot they believed was a person, watching YouTube, or doing nothing. Self-rated loneliness fell after chatting with a person (38.4 to 31.3, d = 0.24), with the AI chatbot (33.5 to 26.8, d = 0.25) and with the chatbot posing as a person (42.7 to 32.8, d = 0.30); it did not change significantly after YouTube and rose after doing nothing. Participants expected the chatbot to help less than it did.

In a week-long follow-up study (preprint Study 4, published Study 3), participants who chatted with a GPT-4 companion with memory for 15 minutes a day reported less loneliness after each daily session than before it (mean 36.6 before against 30.7 after over all days, d = 0.20). Loneliness also fell across the week in the control group that only rated loneliness daily, and the authors attribute that part to the study's daily check-ins.

1338.content: On a major US online dating site, 3,004 men and 2,783 women in Boston and San Diego (drawn from 22,000 users, all activity over three and a half months in 2003) were observed. Whatever the browser's own rated looks, the chance of sending a first-contact message to a profile rose steadily with the attractiveness of that profile's photo, so less attractive users did not hold back from writing to the most attractive ones.

From the same users' choices the authors estimate mate preferences: men and women both prefer better-looking partners with weights that differ only slightly by sex, women place about twice as much weight on a partner's income as men do, men avoid tall women and women prefer tall men, both prefer a partner of their own ethnicity and religion, and matched users sort on looks (correlation 0.31), height, weight, income and education, in patterns the authors find qualitatively similar to married couples.

1339.content: Matching two waves (1987-88 and 1992-94) of the US National Survey of Families and Households, limited to married or cohabiting adults, to the predicted average earnings of their local area (areas of about 150,000 people), Luttmer finds that, holding a person's own income constant, higher neighbours' earnings go with lower self-reported happiness, in specifications with individual fixed effects. A rise in neighbours' earnings and a similar fall in one's own income lower happiness by about the same order of magnitude.

Luttmer finds the link between neighbours' earnings and lower happiness is stronger for people who socialise more with their neighbours and is not stronger for people who socialise more with friends outside the neighbourhood, and it does not differ between renters and owners, which he reads as pointing to comparison with the people one actually mixes with rather than to housing costs.

1340.content: A systematic review of 65 papers (panel surveys, nationally representative surveys, psychological autopsy studies and studies of students, debt-advice clients and older adults) found that more severe unsecured debt went with worse health in most studies. In the authors' meta-analysis, pooled odds ratios for people in debt were 3.24 for a mental disorder as measured in the included studies, 2.77 for depression as measured there, 7.9 for completed suicide, 5.76 for completed or attempted suicide, 2.68 for problem drinking, 8.57 for drug dependence, 3.21 for a neurotic disorder as classified there and 4.03 for a psychotic disorder as classified there; there was no significant link with smoking (OR 1.35).

1341.content: Sell, Tooby and Cosmides state the recalibrational theory of anger: anger is a program built by natural selection to resolve conflicts of interest in the angry person's favour, by conditionally inflicting costs or conditionally withholding benefits, so that the person it is aimed at places more weight on the angry person's welfare. On this account anger is triggered when another person places too little weight on one's welfare, and it is aimed at that specific person.

Testing eleven predictions in 62 men recruited at a University of California, Santa Barbara gym and 125 men and 156 women from the same campus, the authors found that stronger men reported more proneness to anger, more success in getting their way in conflicts, a greater sense of entitlement to good treatment, more history of fighting, and more belief in the usefulness of personal and military force; in women, self-perceived attractiveness showed the same pattern except for history of fighting. Strength did not go with how long men stayed angry.

1342.content: In semi-structured interviews in 2019 with 18 Replika users from 12 countries (7 women, 11 men) recruited from a Replika Facebook group and subreddit as people who had developed a friendship with the chatbot, the authors describe the relationship as starting superficial, out of curiosity, then deepening through affective exploration as trust and self-disclosure grew, and settling into a stable state with less frequent contact that users still valued. Users called the chatbot accepting, understanding and non-judgmental, and reported that the relationship was rewarding and helped their well-being.

Asked about their wider social lives, some of the 18 Replika users said they had lost some interest in meeting or spending time with other people since the relationship began, and gave as reasons that the chatbot was easier, more fun or a better friend than people, or took up so much of their time; others reported a boost in social interest. Most found it hard to tell people about the relationship and described a sense of stigma.

1343.content: In a 14-day contact diary kept by 41 Oxford postgraduate students (2,856 contact entries with up to five network members each, the ones they had interacted with most often in the two weeks before), longer interactions went with more happiness afterwards only when the contact was face to face (the duration term explained 3.7% of within-person variance); longer Skype, telephone, instant message, text and e-mail or social network contact did not. Laughter, real or symbolic (such as 'haha' or emoticons), went with more happiness in every mode except Skype.

1344.content: In a field experiment in a nursing home, one group of residents was told they were responsible for themselves, was given the freedom to make choices and was given a plant to care for; a comparison group was told the staff were responsible for them, and the staff made decisions and cared for the plant for them. On questionnaire ratings and behavioural measures the first group improved significantly more than the comparison group on alertness, active participation and a general sense of well-being.

1345.content: Elderly nursing home residents who had taken part in an intervention designed to increase their feelings of choice and personal responsibility over daily events were re-evaluated 18 months later. The authors report that nurses' ratings and health and mortality indicators suggest that the treatment, or the processes it set in motion, had sustained beneficial effects. The abstract gives no figures.

1346.content: Retirement home residents who had first benefited from a positive event they could predict or control, in a field experiment, were assessed 24, 30 and 42 months after the study ended. Health and psychological status showed no lasting benefit of the interventions: the groups that had benefited declined steeply once the study ended, while the groups that had not benefited stayed stable.

1347.content: In a laboratory experiment, 40 male Harvard undergraduates were paid a falling piece rate (from $2.00 down) to build Bionicle Lego figures and chose when to stop. In the Meaningful condition finished figures stayed on the desk; in the Sisyphus condition the experimenter took each finished figure apart in front of the builder and the pieces were reused. Builders made an average of 10.6 figures in the Meaningful condition and 7.2 in the Sisyphus condition, and the median builder in the Sisyphus condition stopped at a wage about 40 percent higher.

In the paper's first laboratory experiment, 104 MIT students were paid a falling rate to find letter pairs on sheets of paper and chose when to stop. Students whose sheets were signed and looked over by the experimenter completed an average of 9.03 sheets; students whose sheets were put on a pile unread completed 6.77, and students whose sheets were shredded unread completed 6.34. The Acknowledged group worked significantly more than the Ignored group; Ignored and Shredded did not differ significantly.

1348.content: In a field experiment, a random subset of employees at three University of California campuses was told about a newspaper website listing the pay of every University employee, and all employees were then surveyed (6,411 respondents matched to salary records). Workers paid below the median of their unit and occupation reported lower pay satisfaction and job satisfaction after the information (satisfaction index down 6.3 points, about a tenth of a standard deviation) and were 4.3 percentage points more likely to say they were very likely to look for a new job, a 20 percent rise over controls. Workers paid above the median reported no higher satisfaction.

In the same experiment, the response to learning coworkers' pay followed a worker's rank within the pay unit more closely than the size of the pay gap: in models with both, the rank interaction stayed significant for below-median workers and the pay-gap interaction did not.

1349.content: In a laboratory study, 216 participants (mean age 20.4) at a large public university each played three six-round public-goods games in rotating groups of four: a plain game, a game in which they could send a note about a past partner to that partner's next group, and the same with an anonymous vote to exclude one member from the next round. Total contributions out of 60 points averaged 17.54 in the plain game, 29.79 with gossip and 42.89 with gossip plus exclusion, even though people were excluded in 15 percent of rounds. Contributions fell across rounds in the first two games and rose across rounds in the game with exclusion. Participants used 82 to 85 percent of their chances to gossip, mostly about those who had given less than their group.

In the game with gossip and exclusion, participants who were excluded raised their contribution from the round before to the round after exclusion by an average of 2.86 points (of 10), against 0.26 points for those not excluded. Participants who had given less than half their points in the first round (mean 2.67) were giving an average of 7.84 by the sixth round.

1350.content: A survey of 17,409 parents (71 percent mothers, mean age 39) in 42 countries scored parental burnout on the 23-item Parental Burnout Assessment questionnaire (score range 0 to 138). The share of parents scoring above the authors' cutoff, and the mean score, varied greatly between countries, with 33 points between the lowest mean (Thailand) and the highest (Poland). Of six Hofstede cultural values, only individualism was significantly associated with both the mean score and the share above the cutoff (effect size d = 1.16), and the association held in multilevel models adjusting for age, sex, education, neighbourhood, work status, number and age of children, family type, number of daily caregivers, hours spent with the children, economic inequality between countries and the other cultural values.

1351.content: A systematic review with GRADE grading and meta-analysis of 59 prospective or equivalent studies (published 1990 to June 2013, Europe, North America, Australia and New Zealand, at least 100 participants, follow-up 1 to 5 years) found moderately strong evidence (grade 3 of 4) that job strain (high demands with low decision latitude), low decision latitude and bullying are followed by rising depressive symptoms, scored on standardised questionnaires or diagnosed by clinical interview. Decision latitude was studied in 158,251 people in 19 studies and job strain in 197,682 people in 14 studies; the weighted odds ratio was 1.74 (95% CI 1.54 to 1.96) for job strain, 0.73 (0.68 to 0.77) for high decision latitude and 2.82 (2.21 to 3.59) for bullying. Effects did not differ between men and women.

1352.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled six published cohort studies (27,461 people, 914 new cases diagnosed by interview) and individual data from 14 unpublished European cohorts of the IPD-Work consortium (120,221 people, 982 first episodes of hospital-treated depression diagnosed in registers). Job strain (high demands with low control) was associated with a relative risk of later diagnosed depression of 1.77 in the published studies and a hazard ratio of 1.27 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.55) in the unpublished data. The association was similar across sex, age and socioeconomic groups and after excluding people with somatic disease or depressive symptoms at baseline.

In the same individual-participant analysis, the association between job strain and later hospital-treated depression disappeared after adjusting for a continuous score of depressive symptoms at baseline (hazard ratio 1.03), and among people without job strain at baseline, higher depressive symptom scores predicted reporting job strain at follow-up. The authors read the link between job strain and depressive symptoms as running in both directions.

1353.content: In laboratory dogs (Canis lupus familiaris), animals that had first learned to end shock by pressing a panel in a harness later learned to escape shock in a shuttle box normally, while dogs given the same shocks yoked so that nothing they did ended them showed profound interference with later escape in the shuttle box. This interference was still present after a 7-day rest. Dogs that first had experience of escaping in the shuttle box pressed the panel more during inescapable shock and did not show the later interference. The authors read the result as learned helplessness: the dogs had learned that shock termination was independent of their responses.

1354.content: A systematic review with GRADE grading and meta-analysis of 25 prospective or equivalent studies (Europe, North America, Australia and New Zealand, 1990 to 2013, follow-up 1 to 5 years) found moderately strong evidence (grade 3 of 4) that more job control goes with less emotional exhaustion later and that low workplace support goes with more. Limited evidence (grade 2) linked workplace justice, demands, high workload, low reward, low supervisor and co-worker support and job insecurity with change in emotional exhaustion. All 25 studies measured both working conditions and burnout symptoms by self-report questionnaires.

1355.content: In a large random sample of working Swedish men followed for six years, a hectic and psychologically demanding job went with more coronary heart disease symptoms and signs (standardised odds ratio 1.29, not significant at p < 0.25) and with premature cardiovascular or cerebrovascular death in a nested case-control analysis (relative risk 4.0, p < .01). Low decision latitude also went with higher cardiovascular risk: low intellectual discretion with coronary symptoms and signs (standardised odds ratio 1.44, p < .01), and low personal schedule freedom, among men with only the minimum statutory education, with cardiovascular death (relative risk 6.6). The associations held after controlling for age, education, smoking and overweight.

1356.content: In the Whitehall II cohort of British civil servants (7,372 people seen at all three phases, mean follow-up 5.3 years), men in the lowest employment grade (clerical and office support) had an age-adjusted odds ratio of 1.50 for any newly reported coronary heart disease compared with administrators, and 2.27 for doctor-diagnosed ischaemia; women in the lowest grade had an odds ratio of 1.47. Outcomes were chest pain and angina reported on the Rose questionnaire and doctor-diagnosed ischaemia. Of the factors examined, low control at work made the largest contribution to the grade gradient; height and standard coronary risk factors made smaller contributions. Adjusting for all of them reduced the odds ratio for the lowest grade from 1.50 to 0.95 in men and from 1.47 to 1.07 in women.

1357.content: In six studies, four in the laboratory with US undergraduates and two online with adults recruited through Mechanical Turk, the authors activated unfinished goals (for example, two important errands not yet planned). Unfinished goals were followed by intrusive thoughts during an unrelated reading task, higher mental accessibility of goal-related words and poorer performance on an unrelated anagram task. Letting participants write specific plans for when, where and how they would complete the goals removed these effects. In Study 1 (73 undergraduates), 65.2 percent of the unfinished-tasks group reported mind wandering during reading against 33.3 percent of the plan group; the control group (50 percent) did not differ significantly from either.

1358.content: A random-effects meta-analysis of studies of workers found that unfinished work tasks were positively associated with work-related thoughts during off-job time, more strongly between people (17 samples, 2,473 people, corrected correlation .38) than within people from day to day (14 samples, N = 12,129, .25). Associations were strongest for affective rumination as the outcome.

1359.content: A meta-analysis of experiments since Zeigarnik (1927) and Ovsiankina (1928) found no memory advantage for interrupted over finished tasks, while interrupted tasks were reliably resumed, roughly 67 percent of the time, when resumption was left to the participant. The authors suggest the original memory effect depended on conditions such as experimenter authority and task involvement that were more common in the early studies.

1360.content: Fischer re-examined the 2004 General Social Survey finding that respondents named about a third fewer discussion partners than in 1985, with the share naming no one rising from about 10 percent to about 25 percent. He reports that the 2004 results contradict other relevant data and contain serious anomalies, suggests possible sources (a taxing preceding section of the interview, or a random technical error) and concludes that no inference should be drawn from the 2004 survey about whether Americans' networks changed, and that they probably did not change substantially.

1361.content: In a content analysis of ethnographic reports on many societies, anger and aggression by bereaved persons appeared to be lower in societies that used ritual specialists in the period up to and including disposal of the body. In societies with institutionalised patterns of anger and aggression by the bereaved, customary isolation or marking of the bereaved appeared to keep that anger channelled.

1362.content: In juvenile laboratory rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus), direct exposure to a collar previously worn by a cat abolished play, and play stayed suppressed for up to 6 days. Giving the rats a place to hide did not change the effect. Exposure to cat odour in the home cage also suppressed play shortly afterwards, and substantial risk assessment behaviour was still present up to 24 hours later. Trimethylthiazoline, a component of fox faeces, reduced play only during exposure.

1363.content: Hughes and Stevens reviewed Portugal's official drug indicators from 1998 to 2008, with Spain and Italy as comparisons, and interviewed 13 key informants, to judge the 2001 decriminalisation and the national strategy that expanded prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration. Between 2000 and 2008 new HIV cases among drug users fell from 907 to 267 and new AIDS cases from 506 to 108; the number of drug users in treatment rose from 23,654 in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008; the estimated number of people who inject drugs fell from 3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000 people aged 15 to 64 between 2000 and 2005. The paper gives no figure for the job or reintegration measures.

Hughes and Stevens attribute the fall in opiate-related deaths mainly to the large increase in treatment, above all low-threshold opiate substitution, and the fall in drug-related HIV mainly to the expansion of harm-reduction services. They write that many factors, expanded treatment services and an ageing population of heroin users among them, contributed to the results, and that it is impossible to state that any of the changes were the direct result of the decriminalisation. They do not credit the employment or reintegration measures with any of the outcomes.

1364.content: Hughes and Stevens set the two most divergent published accounts of the Portuguese reform (a 'resounding success' and a 'disastrous failure') against the available data and conclude that the reform warrants neither label: both accounts used the evidence selectively, and the evidence points to nuanced, largely positive results. They add that both accounts put too much weight on decriminalisation and too little on the concurrent strategy that expanded services for drug users.

1365.content: An economic study of the social cost of illicit drug use in Portugal, counting health and non-health costs, found that it fell by 12% in the five years after the 1999 national strategy was approved and by 18% over the eleven years after approval. Lower legal-system costs (which the authors link to the decriminalisation of use) and a substantial fall in health-related costs were the main contributors.

1366.content: The EMCDDA report describes Portugal's Programa Vida-Emprego, a national scheme for people in or after drug treatment (outpatient, therapeutic community or prison). It ran a nine-month work placement paid at the national minimum wage, an employment support measure paying employers 80% of salary and social security costs for up to two years, a grant of 12 times the minimum wage for each job an employer committed to keep for at least four years, and start-up support for self-employment, with state-funded mediators supporting both worker and employer. More than 1,000 people a year took part; in 2009, 1,115 took part against over 4,600 treatment clients with identified employment needs, and Portugal rated its coverage as limited. The report gives no drug-use outcome for the scheme.

1367.content: In Baltimore, 40 pregnant and postpartum women in drug treatment who kept using heroin and cocaine were randomised to usual care or the Therapeutic Workplace, where they were paid (in vouchers, up to $4,030 over 6 months) to work or train 3 hours each weekday, and had to give a drug-free urine sample to enter that day. On average 45% of the workplace group attended on a given day. Over 6 months, 59% of their thrice-weekly urine samples were negative for opiates and cocaine, against 33% in usual care.

1368.content: In the same 40 women, randomised to usual care or the Therapeutic Workplace and able to work there for 3 years if their urine was drug-free, monthly urine samples up to 3 years after intake were cocaine-negative in 54% of the workplace group against 28% of controls, and opiate-negative in 60% against 37%.

1369.content: Adults who injected drugs and kept using cocaine in methadone treatment were offered 4 hours of work each weekday at about $10 an hour in vouchers. After 4 weeks, 56 who kept giving cocaine-positive urine were randomised for 26 weeks: one group had to give cocaine-negative urine to work and keep full pay, the other (work-only) could work whatever their urine showed. Work-only participants attended on 71% of days, yet only 10% of their mandatory urine samples were cocaine-negative, against 29% in the abstinence-and-work group. Six months after the end, the groups did not differ.

1370.content: Unemployed welfare recipients in Baltimore who kept using cocaine in methadone treatment went through 6 months of paid job-skills training with an abstinence rule. The 51 who stopped using, attended and learned the skills were hired as data-entry operators in a non-profit business and randomised for a year: 24 could work regardless of drug use (employment only), 27 had to give drug-free urine under routine and then random testing to work and keep full pay. Over the year, 79.3% of monthly urine samples were cocaine-negative in the abstinence-contingent group against 50.7% in the employment-only group.

1371.content: The same 51 data-entry employees were followed for 30 months. During the employment year, 82.7% of six-monthly urine samples were cocaine-negative in the abstinence-contingent group against 54.2% in the employment-only group. In the year after the intervention ended, the groups were alike (44.2% and 50.0%). Of the 27 in the abstinence-contingent group, 20 (74%) gave cocaine-negative urine at both checks during the employment year, and 6 (22%) at both checks in the follow-up year.

DeFulio and Silverman state that continuing employment on its own will not be enough to keep many people off cocaine, pointing to the relatively high rate of cocaine use in the employment-only group during its year of employment.

1372.content: The 40 women of the first Therapeutic Workplace trial were followed to 8 years after intake. In year 4, while the data-entry business was open, the workplace group gave more cocaine- and opiate-negative urine than usual-care controls, reported more days employed, higher earnings and less money spent on drugs; about 8 of 20 worked full time for most of that year against none of the controls. In years 5 to 8, after the business closed, the groups no longer differed in drug-negative urine or full-time work; only total income stayed higher in the former workplace group.

1373.content: A replication of the Therapeutic Workplace in crack cocaine users from community methadone programmes randomised participants to the workplace (n = 22) or usual care for 9 months, with daily voucher pay contingent on opiate- and cocaine-free urine. The two groups did not differ on cocaine or opiate use. Only 7 of the 22 began consistent periods of abstinence and attendance; 9 tried to get into the workplace but never gave a drug-negative sample.

1374.content: Reviewing eight of their own Baltimore trials (1996 to 2010), Silverman and colleagues report that paid work gated by drug-free urine initiated cocaine abstinence in methadone patients in 3 of 4 studies and maintained it in 2, promoted alcohol abstinence in homeless adults in 1 study and kept people taking extended-release naltrexone in 2; relapse occurred even after long exposure (1 study). They conclude that the reinforcement may need to be kept up indefinitely.

1375.content: A systematic review of 11 randomised trials, mainly of high methodological quality, found strong evidence that the community reinforcement approach (which rearranges a person's job, family and social activities so that sober living is rewarding) beats usual care on the number of drinking days, with conflicting evidence on continuous abstinence from alcohol. With incentives added, there was strong evidence for more cocaine abstinence; evidence for opioid detoxification and methadone maintenance was limited.

1376.content: Reviewing the evidence, Meyers, Roozen and Smith report that Azrin's first two trials of the community reinforcement approach, in alcohol-dependent inpatients (16 and 18 people, both with control groups), found it more effective in reducing drinking than the hospital's Alcoholics Anonymous programme, with better outcomes in jobs and family relationships as well. The approach was built to change the person's surroundings so that family, work and friends rewarded sober behaviour.

1377.content: A review of more than 130 studies published 1990 to 2010 reports that unemployed people more often drink at risky levels, smoke and use illicit and prescription drugs; that problem substance use makes job loss more likely and finding and holding a job less likely; that unemployment is a significant risk factor for later substance use; and that unemployment increases the risk of relapse after alcohol and drug treatment. Henkel notes that the research says little about which individuals are affected.

1378.content: Platt reviewed 20 years of research on what affects employment among people using illicit drugs and on vocational programmes built for them. The abstract concludes only that a number of programmes have shown some success in vocational rehabilitation, and notes that employment is commonly used, with abstinence and criminal involvement, as a measure of treatment outcome.

1379.content: In Connecticut, 210 men and women recruited from the community and diagnosed as alcohol dependent were randomised to network support, network support plus contingency management, or case management (control). At 15 months (186 analysed), both network support arms had better drinking outcomes than case management. Support for drinking in people's networks stayed as high as in the control arm. Network support raised behavioural and attitudinal support for abstinence and AA involvement, and both were correlated with drinking outcomes.

1380.content: At two years after treatment in the same 210-person trial, the network support arm had up to 20% more days abstinent than the other arms, and at 15 months more social network support for abstinence, AA attendance and AA involvement. Growth modelling linked the network changes to rises in self-efficacy and coping that predicted long-term drinking. In the trial's first report, adding one abstinent person to a social network raised the probability of abstinence over the next year by 27%.

1381.content: In 1,726 adults in the Project MATCH treatment trial, assessed at intake and at 3, 9 and 15 months, more AA attendance went with large falls in ties to people who supported drinking, smaller rises in ties to people who supported abstinence, fewer drinking activities and more sober ones. Lagged mediation found that AA's link with abstinence ran mainly through fewer pro-drinking ties and, to a lesser degree, more pro-abstinent ties.

1382.content: Testing several proposed mechanisms together in the same 1,726 Project MATCH participants, Kelly and colleagues found that among outpatients AA's link with percent days abstinent and drinks per drinking day at 15 months was explained mainly by adaptive social network changes and more confidence in staying sober in social settings; among more impaired aftercare patients, spirituality and lower negative affect added to these. The mediators together explained between 43% and 67% of the link.

1383.content: Re-examining Winick's 1962 'maturing out' data and the follow-up studies since, Maddux and Desmond found that Winick overestimated: across follow-up studies a minority of chronic opioid users, 19 to 40%, reached three or more years of continuous abstinence, and in their own cohort of 248 heroin users from San Antonio (treated 1964 to 1967) 54 (22%) had done so by 1979. The onset of long abstinence was not concentrated in the thirties; it grew gradually more frequent with age. Three years of abstinence did not guarantee lifetime abstinence: a further 27 reached three years and later used heroin again.

Among the 54 San Antonio heroin users who reached three or more years of abstinence, the conditions the authors judged had probably helped were: substituting alcohol (23, 43%), probation or parole of a year or more (22, 42%), moving away from their usual drug source (19, 36%), evangelical religious participation (13, 25%) and a job with a drug treatment agency (10, 19%). In interviews some credited their children, a wife, peers at work or new responsibilities; others credited adverse events, prison or simply being too old to hustle.

1384.content: In the US national NESARC survey (2001 to 2002), 4,422 adults whose answers met DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence before the past year reported, looking back, when they finished school, started full-time work, married, separated and became parents. The chance of abstinent recovery more than doubled in the 3 years after first becoming a parent (hazard rate ratio 2.22). Entering and leaving a first marriage each raised the chance of recovery with low-risk drinking in the following 3 years (1.37 and 1.76). Starting full-time work did not raise either kind of recovery; among those still dependent 3 or more years after starting full-time work, abstinent recovery became less likely.

1385.content: A meta-analysis of 47 treatment-control comparisons published 1970 to 2002 found that contingency management (vouchers or prizes for drug-free samples) had a mean effect of d = 0.42 on abstinence, larger for opiates (0.65) and cocaine (0.66) than tobacco (0.31). The effect declined over time after treatment ended. Larger effects went with shorter treatment, earlier studies and more researcher involvement.

1386.content: A meta-analysis of 23 randomised trials of contingency management for stimulant, opioid or mixed drug use, each with urine-tested outcomes up to 1 year after the incentives ended, found that people who had received the incentives were still somewhat more likely to be abstinent than those given a comparison treatment (odds ratio 1.22, 95% interval 1.01 to 1.44); nearly half the comparisons were community or protocol-based therapies. Longer active treatment went with better long-term abstinence.

1387.content: In the WHO International Study of Schizophrenia (ISoS), Hopper and Wanderling re-analysed the combined incidence cohort of 809 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and related psychoses (the treated incidence cohorts of the earlier DOSMeD and RAPyD studies plus samples from Hong Kong and Madras/Chennai). Course and outcome favoured the centres the WHO classed as developing on a range of measures, and the authors tested six possible sources of bias (differences in follow-up, grouping of centres, diagnostic ambiguity, choice of outcome measures, gender and age): none of them explained the difference away, the authors report.

1388.content: The WHO International Study of Schizophrenia traced 18 treated incidence and prevalence cohorts (1633 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and other psychoses, in many countries) for 15 and 25 years; about 75 percent were traced. About half of the surviving cases had favourable global outcomes, with marked differences between geographic centres; early (2-year) course was the strongest predictor of 15-year outcome, recovery varied by location, and 16 percent of those whose early course was unremitting reached late recovery, the authors report.

In the same follow-up, nearly all people in the cohorts received antipsychotic medication in the first two years, the authors report, so the WHO centres did not compare treatment with no treatment. Counting only those with no episode of treatment in the past two years, 16.3 percent of those diagnosed with schizophrenia in the incidence cohort were rated recovered, and the authors judge that about one sixth reached complete recovery in the sense of needing no form of treatment.

1389.content: Cohen, Patel, Thara and Gureje tabulated 23 longitudinal studies of people diagnosed with schizophrenia in 11 low and middle income countries (Brazil, Bulgaria, China, Colombia, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Jamaica, Nigeria, South Africa, Trinidad). Outcomes varied widely: good clinical and social outcomes in most Indian and Indonesian studies, poorer ones in Brazil, China and Nigeria, and much poorer ones in an untreated cohort in Chennai. Mortality was raised wherever it was measured: in a Chinese cohort of 510 followed for 10 years the standardised mortality ratio was 4.0. The authors read the evidence as linking lack of care with poor outcomes and access to care with better ones, and call for the WHO conclusion to be re-examined.

The same review reports mortality in long-term studies of people diagnosed with schizophrenia in low and middle income countries: crude rates from 9.0 to 30.7 percent across the ISoS sites, and a standardised mortality ratio of 4.0 (men 4.9, women 3.3) in a Chinese cohort of 510 followed for 10 years with 7.8 percent attrition. The authors warn that outcome figures that leave out the dead overstate prognosis.

1390.content: A meta-analysis of 27 studies of people diagnosed with schizophrenia found that a high expressed-emotion rating of the family (criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement shown by a relative in an interview) predicted relapse, significantly and robustly. The link was strongest for people with a longer illness history, and mean effect sizes for families of people diagnosed with mood disorders and eating disorders were higher still, the authors report.

1391.content: A meta-analysis of 30 prospective cohort studies (33 in the review, 2284 patients diagnosed with schizophrenia) found that a high global expressed-emotion rating of the family went with relapse, more strongly within 12 months (odds ratio 4.87) than later (odds ratio 2.13). Taken apart, more critical comments went with relapse (odds ratio 2.22) and more warmth from the relative went with fewer relapses (odds ratio 0.35). Culture, measure, age, length of illness and study quality did not change the results, the authors report.

1392.content: A Cochrane review of 53 randomised trials compared community family interventions (sessions with the families of people diagnosed with schizophrenia, aimed at lowering criticism, hostility and over-involvement) with standard care. Family intervention went with fewer relapses (32 trials, 2981 people, relative risk 0.55, number needed to treat 7) and fewer hospital admissions (8 trials, 481 people, relative risk 0.78), and with better medication compliance and lower expressed emotion; it did not clearly change leaving care. The authors warn the effects may be overestimated because of poor trial quality and possibly missed small negative trials.

The same review states that these family interventions are meant to be added to antipsychotic drugs, and the trials it reports compared family work plus drug with drug plus standard care. The review is therefore no test of family work in the drug's place.

1393.content: A network meta-analysis of 90 randomised trials (10,340 participants, median age 31) compared 11 models of family intervention for people diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders. At 12 months every model except crisis-oriented work and family psychoeducation of two sessions or fewer cut relapse against treatment as usual, with odds ratios from 0.18 for family psychoeducation alone to 0.63 for community-based interventions involving family members. Family psychoeducation alone did better than the more complex models; confidence in the estimates ranged from moderate to very low, the authors report.

1394.content: The Chicago Follow-up Study assessed 139 young patients after a first or early psychotic episode (70 diagnosed with schizophrenia syndromes, 69 with mood disorders) and followed them six times over 20 years. At each follow-up 30 to 40 percent of those diagnosed with schizophrenia were no longer on antipsychotics. From the 4.5-year follow-up on, those off antipsychotics for long periods were significantly less often rated psychotic, had more periods of recovery and did not relapse more often, the authors report. The authors describe this group as self-selected, with better prognostic factors, better premorbid achievements, better neurocognitive skills and less vulnerability to psychosis.

1395.content: Correll, Rubio and Kane review the case that antipsychotics worsen long-term outcome, and they argue against it. They cite the Chicago cohort (8 percent of 15 unmedicated people diagnosed with schizophrenia with some psychotic symptoms against 68 percent of 25 treated continuously) and argue that in such non-randomised studies adherence is unknown and the risk of confounding by indication and reverse causation is high: a more severe course may keep people on the drug.

1396.content: An international panel convened to examine concerns that antipsychotics harm long-term outcome (brain volume loss, dopamine receptor sensitisation) reported little evidence of a negative long-term effect of starting or maintaining antipsychotics compared with withholding them. They state that randomised trials strongly support the drugs for acute psychosis and relapse prevention, and that stopping or non-drug approaches may help a subgroup but may carry added relapse risk and need further study.

1397.content: In a Finnish multicentre study of 106 consecutive patients with a first episode of functional non-affective psychosis, all treated by the need-specific Finnish model (team work, participation of the patient and family, basic psychotherapeutic attitudes), three sites used a minimal neuroleptic regime and three used neuroleptics as usual, the authors report. Over two years 42.9 percent of patients at the minimal-neuroleptic sites never received a neuroleptic, against 5.9 percent at the usual-practice sites. Outcome (time in hospital, psychotic symptoms in the last follow-up year, employment, GAS score, Grip on Life) was equal or somewhat better at the minimal-neuroleptic sites after controlling for age, gender and diagnosis, the authors report.

1398.content: Bola, Lehtinen, Cullberg and Ciompi reviewed studies that gave people diagnosed with early-episode psychosis initial psychosocial treatment with antipsychotics postponed for a limited time, compared with initial drug treatment, in a quasi-experimental or better design with at least one year of follow-up. Five studies (261 people) were included; each reported modestly better long-term outcomes than initial drug treatment, a composite effect size of r = 0.17, and 27 to 43 percent of those in the psychosocial groups were taking no antipsychotics at the two or three year follow-up, the authors report.

1399.content: A systematic review of prospective research found 12 analyses from 8 cohorts (6844 participants, mostly diagnosed with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders) that compared the course of illness over time by employment status. Being employed went with less outpatient psychiatric treatment (2 of 2 studies) and better self-esteem (2 of 2 studies), went inconsistently with better symptoms, fewer hospital stays, life satisfaction and well-being, and never went with a worse course, the authors report.

1400.content: The EQOLISE trial randomised 312 people diagnosed with severe mental illness in six European centres to Individual Placement and Support (help to find and keep an ordinary paid job, n = 156) or to usual vocational services (n = 156), followed for 18 months. 55 percent of the IPS group worked at least one day against 28 percent; the vocational-services group was more likely to drop out of the service (45 against 13 percent) and to be readmitted to hospital (31 against 20 percent), the authors report.

1401.content: A meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (plus 2 follow-ups) comparing Individual Placement and Support with traditional vocational rehabilitation for people diagnosed with severe mental illness found a pooled risk ratio of 2.40 for getting competitive (open-market) employment. Neither region nor local unemployment changed the effect, it held when national GDP growth was under 2 percent, and it lasted over 2 years, the authors report.

1402.content: A systematic review of 38 papers on social networks and support in samples diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis and in general-population samples reporting psychotic experiences or schizotypal traits found smaller networks (close friends in particular) and less support in both, against varying comparison groups; the differences may be larger for men and for minority ethnic groups. The authors conclude, tentatively, that thinner networks and support appear to come before the onset of a diagnosed psychotic disorder, and stress that the heterogeneity of the studies makes this uncertain.

1403.content: A meta-analysis of 13 studies (15,647 participants diagnosed with psychotic disorders) found a moderate correlation between loneliness and psychotic symptoms, r = 0.32, rated moderate-quality evidence; whether loneliness was measured with one item or a full scale did not change the estimate. The authors note that the causal direction is unknown.

1404.content: In the Dutch trial (7 mental health organisations and the University Medical Center Groningen, catchment 3.1 million), 131 patients aged 18 to 45 with a DSM-IV diagnosis of schizophrenia or a related psychotic disorder, remitted for 6 months after a first episode, were randomised openly to gradual symptom-guided tapering and discontinuation or to maintenance treatment, and followed for 18 months. Relapse was twice as common with the discontinuation strategy (43 against 21 percent, p = .011). About 20 percent of that group were successfully discontinued, about 30 percent restarted because symptoms came back, and for the rest discontinuation was not feasible; social and vocational functioning showed no advantage, the authors report.

1405.content: A systematic review of 37 prospective trials of antipsychotic dose reduction in people diagnosed with schizophrenia found that 20 of 24 studies evaluating relapse or symptoms met the authors' criteria for successful reduction, and that deterioration was mostly re-stabilised by returning to the baseline dose (7 of 8). A meta-analysis of the randomised trials found more relapse with reduction than with maintenance (risk ratio 1.96, 13 trials with data, 902 people) and better neurocognition (standardised mean difference 0.69, 2 trials); the extra relapse risk appeared only when the reduced dose fell to 200 mg chlorpromazine equivalents a day or below (risk ratio 2.79). Success went with study length under 1 year, age over 40 and illness over 10 years.

1406.content: Horowitz, Jauhar, Natesan, Murray and Taylor propose that stopping antipsychotics may itself bring on relapse through adaptations to the drug (including dopamine hypersensitivity) that can persist for months or years after stopping, citing animal studies, tardive dyskinesia and the clustering of relapses soon after stopping. From PET data showing a hyperbolic relation between dose and D2 blockade they propose tapering over months or years in shrinking steps (a quarter or a half of the most recent dose every 3 to 6 months), with final doses possibly as small as 1/40th of a therapeutic dose. They state the proposal still has to be tested in randomised trials.

1407.content: HAMLETT randomised 347 patients diagnosed with a first psychotic episode and in remission, in 26 Dutch psychosis units (2017 to 2023) to early dose reduction or discontinuation (168) or to 12 months of maintenance (179), followed for 4 years. Patient-rated functioning (WHODAS-2, the primary outcome) did not differ. In the first year the reduction group had more relapse (odds ratio 2.84) and lower quality of life; at 3 and 4 years researcher-rated functioning (GAF) was better in the reduction group, with a similar trend for symptom scores. Doses were similar in both groups from 12 months on, and 40 percent of the maintenance group tapered against protocol, so the authors read the later gain as a learning experience of the tapering attempt rather than an effect of the lower dose.

In the same trial the reduction group had 5 deaths and the maintenance group 1; 3 deaths in the reduction group were confirmed suicides against 1 in the maintenance group. Hospitalisations were 32 in the reduction group and 42 in the maintenance group, and self-harm, violence and police contacts were similar, the authors report.

1408.content: The HAMLETT protocol describes what the reduction arm received: a tapering schedule chosen by the treating physician (average about 3 months to full discontinuation), a diary with practical advice and a questionnaire on early warning signs, a booklet listing early warning signs (such as social withdrawal and poor sleep) that the patient, carers and relatives can note, and a signalling plan agreed with the physician; when warning signs appear, tapering pauses and stress reduction is advised. Psychosocial treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy and Individual Placement and Support enter only as part of usual care in both arms and as a hypothesis (better functioning in those who took part), with no psychosocial arm in the randomisation.

1409.content: The REDUCE trial at Orygen, Melbourne (registered ANZCTR 12617000870358, recruiting from July 2017) plans to randomise 180 young people diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis and in remission to antipsychotic dose reduction or maintenance, both combined with an evidence-based intensive recovery treatment: Individual Placement and Support for work, education or training, delivered by a youth vocational consultant, and cognitive behavioural therapy for relapse prevention, up to twice a week for 9 months, then every 4 to 6 weeks. The primary outcome is vocational and social functioning at 24 months; relapse is a safety outcome. The recovery treatment is the same in both arms.

1410.content: Chouinard and colleagues review what they label dopamine supersensitivity psychosis: long-term antipsychotic use can upregulate D2 receptors, shown as behavioural supersensitivity in animals and as movement disorders and supersensitivity psychosis in patients. Its four clinical features are rapid relapse after stopping, cutting or switching the drug, tolerance to earlier therapeutic effects, tardive dyskinesia, and worsening with life stressors. Three recent studies they review put its prevalence at about 30 percent among people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 70 percent among those labelled treatment-resistant. They also propose three antipsychotic withdrawal syndromes like those of other drugs acting on the brain.

1411.content: A literature review reported evidence of a rapid-onset psychosis after clozapine withdrawal and weaker evidence for some other antipsychotics, including some cases in people with no psychiatric history; the author reads this as a feature of drug withdrawal in at least some patients rather than the return of an underlying illness. Meta-analyses of withdrawal studies suggest stopping may raise relapse above the underlying rate, though not every individual study shows this, and data on mechanism are sparse.

1412.content: Murray and colleagues argue, as the authors of an analysis, that evidence for years of preventive antipsychotic use after recovery from a psychosis is thin, that concern is growing over effects on physical health and brain structure, and that loss of effect through D2 receptor supersensitivity is possible. They advise psychiatrists to reduce the dose slowly, with each patient, to the lowest level that keeps distressing symptoms away, and estimate that up to 40 percent of those who remit after a first episode can do well long term on no antipsychotic or a very low dose.

The same authors state that reducing the dose this way needs ready access to non-drug treatments, that many psychiatrists rely on antipsychotics because money limits access to treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy and vocational training, and that more of these treatments would let clinicians judge when stopping is the better course.

1413.content: In the Danish OPUS cohort of 496 patients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (ICD-10 F20, F22 to F29), 61 percent attended the 10-year follow-up, and 30 percent of those were in remission of psychotic symptoms with no current antipsychotic use. This outcome went with female gender, a high GAF-F functioning score, taking part in the labour market and no substance abuse, the authors report.

1414.content: At the 20-year follow-up of the Danish OPUS cohort (496 people with a first episode of schizophrenia), 143 took part (71 percent attrition) and 36 percent of them (51) were in remission of psychotic symptoms off medication. Register data on all 416 with data showed, the authors report, that about 70 percent had stopped antipsychotics and about 30 percent were still on them; those still on them had spent far more days in treatment and more had used clozapine, and those who had stopped had higher employment at 20 years (28.4 against 12.5 percent). The authors read the poorer outcomes of those still on the drug as implying greater illness severity.

1415.content: AESOP-10 followed 557 people diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis in south-east London and Nottingham for ten years. Of those with data, 77 percent had at least one period of sustained remission and 46 percent had been symptom-free for two or more years at follow-up. Social outcomes stayed poor: only 22 percent were in paid work at ten years (against 49 to 67 percent of the local populations), 72 percent had worked less than a quarter of the time, 68 percent were single, and of those out of work at baseline only 15 percent were employed at follow-up, the authors report.

1416.content: In Karachi, Pakistan, 851 men aged 16 to 35 who came to a hospital for a free oral check-up (convenience sample, 2009 to 2010) were asked the seven DSM-IV substance dependence questions in Urdu; three or more in the same 12 months counted as meeting the authors' criteria. Of 314 who chewed areca nut only, 67.2 percent met the criteria, against 78.1 percent of 242 who chewed areca with tobacco and 89.8 percent of 295 cigarette smokers. After adjustment for age, education, family history and years of use, smokers were 7.87 times as likely as areca-only chewers to meet the criteria. Users were classified against a list of 50 areca products sold in the market.

In the same Karachi sample, 55.7 percent of areca-only chewers reported giving up important social, work or recreational activities because of use, against 39.3 percent of areca-with-tobacco chewers and 22.0 percent of cigarette smokers; areca-only chewers also most often reported using more than intended (76.1 percent). Smokers most often reported withdrawal (69.2 percent), failed cutting down (73.9 percent) and use despite known health harm (86.8 percent).

1417.content: Researchers at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences in Bangalore, India, assessed 98 people who used areca nut preparations without tobacco and 44 who used them with tobacco, plus non-users, with a checklist for dependence. Of the areca-only group, 38.8 percent met the authors' DSM-IV criteria and 40.8 percent their ICD-10 criteria for current substance dependence; 79.5 percent of the areca-with-tobacco group met both. Both groups reported a withdrawal syndrome.
