1418.content: The Asian Betel-quid Consortium drew multistage random samples of 8,922 people aged 15 and over in Taiwan, Hunan (mainland China), Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Nepal (2009 to 2010) and asked chewers the DSM-IV and ICD-10 dependence questions. Among current chewers, the share who met the authors' criteria was 20.9 to 33.3 percent in mainland China and Sri Lanka, 41.3 to 52.8 percent in Taiwan and Malaysia, and 84.4 to 99.6 percent in Indonesia and Nepal; in Nepal nearly every chewer met them. In the whole population, 2.8 percent (Taiwan) to 39.2 percent (Nepal) met the criteria.

In the same six Asian survey areas the consortium found that every community had easy availability, low prices and ready-made packaging of betel quid; it saw misleading advertising in Hunan and aggressive marketing of betel quid products in Nepal, the area with the highest share of chewers meeting dependence criteria.

1419.content: Reanalysing the 8,922 people of the six Asian Betel-quid Consortium samples with the 11 DSM-5 symptoms (two or more in 12 months counts), the authors report that 18.0 percent of the whole sample and 86.0 percent of current chewers met their DSM-5 criteria for betel-quid use disorder, half of current chewers at the severe level (six or more symptoms). The share of current chewers meeting the criteria ran from 55.8 percent in Sri Lanka and 61.1 percent in mainland China to 98.5 percent in Indonesia and 99.3 percent in Nepal. The authors state that in these places betel quid is sold ready-made at low prices (0.05 to 0.30 US dollars a quid).

1420.content: Among 2,078 betel quid chewers from the six Asian Betel-quid Consortium random samples, the share meeting the authors' DSM-IV dependence criteria over 12 months was 12.5 to 92.6 percent for tobacco-free quid and 47.9 to 99.3 percent for quid with tobacco. Among chewers of tobacco-free quid, the share was 23.3 to 95.6 percent when slaked lime was added and 4.0 percent without lime.

1421.content: Residues scraped from 12 stone and later pipes from five sites in Nez Perce ancestral territory along the Snake and Columbia Rivers (southeastern Washington State, USA) were tested by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry; 8 held nicotine. Positive pipes span about 1,200 years before present to historic times, and one likely dates to 2500 to 500 BC. The authors conclude that hunter-gatherers there smoked wild tobacco well before domesticated trade tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) arrived with fur traders after the 1790s.

The authors write that by European contact tobacco was used across the Americas as a plant of power with ritual, medicinal and ceremonial weight, and that in traditional contexts it is typically used in limited quantities and by certain members of the community. They describe trade tobacco brought by Euro-American traders as much more potent than any native smoke plant and say its use spread very fast in the 1700s; the Haida and Tlingit, who grew and chewed a wild tobacco (Nicotiana quadrivalvis), gave up that practice after getting trade tobacco.

1422.content: Excavation of hearth-side deposits at the Wishbone site in North America's desert west found evidence of human tobacco use about 12,300 years ago, which the authors say is 9,000 years earlier than previously documented.

1423.content: From explorers' diaries and later ethnography since 1770, the review describes how Aboriginal people in Central Australia chew wild tobacco (pituri, Nicotiana species): broken leaves are mixed with wood ash into a quid held in the lip or cheek for long periods, passed between chewers, kept behind the ear or under an arm-band between uses, and a last quid is kept in the mouth overnight. The authors read this as nicotine taken in almost without pause, by mouth and through the skin, and note that ash, an alkali, would raise nicotine release and uptake.

The review reports that pituri was a prized trade good along Aboriginal trade routes, cited as equal in status to boomerangs, spears, shields and ochre, and the authors attribute its value partly to the psychological and physical addictive effects of its nicotine. They quote a Pintupi text on the plant: "Let us eat it together with the ash, we who are starving for pitcheri."

1424.content: Among 206 healthy Aka men, Central African foragers with high worm burdens and little access to commercial worm medicine, tobacco use (checked by salivary cotinine) was very common, and cotinine was negatively correlated with worm burden. Men given the worm drug albendazole had lower cotinine two weeks later than men given placebo, and among treated men higher cotinine in year 1 went with less reinfection by year 2. The authors read this as men adjusting their nicotine intake to infection.

1425.content: Summarising a series of studies in the southern Peruvian Andes, Hanna suggests that coca chewers limit how many leaves they take so as to avoid the unwanted effects of large cocaine doses, that the smaller doses help in parts of hard work at high altitude, and that coca's place in Andean life is not explained by simple addictive properties.

1426.content: Reviewing archaeological, ethnohistorical and botanical evidence, Bray and Dollery report that before the European conquest coca was chewed everywhere from Nicaragua to Chile and at all altitudes, a pattern going back to at least 2000 BC in coastal Peru and Ecuador. Today coca taking is linked mainly with the survival of traditional Indian culture, and coca is everywhere regarded as a stimulant that gives resistance to hunger, thirst and fatigue.

1427.content: In a public health assessment of coca leaf chewing, Negrete notes that the number of chewers seemed to be falling with economic progress and schooling, compares coca leaf with pure cocaine use, mentions benefits for life at high altitude, and concludes that a mild cognitive defect from long-term chewing is probably a major public health problem, since it may go with social stagnation.

1428.content: Volunteers took 5 to 10 g of coca leaves or powder by mouth in the way South American chewers do. Cocaine appeared in the blood at once, peaked at 10 to 150 ng per ml plasma between 0.38 and 1.95 hours, and stayed for more than 7 hours, with absorption half-lives of 0.2 to 0.6 hours; the curves matched the effects the subjects reported. The authors conclude that the stimulating effect of the leaf is due to cocaine.

1429.content: Among 204 khat chewers recruited at khat sale outlets in the UK (Yemeni migrants), about a third (31 percent) reported symptoms the authors count as meeting the DSM-IV dependence syndrome, 17 percent reported withdrawal symptoms (among them more appetite in 74 percent, what the authors list as depression in 61 percent and broken sleep in 58 percent), and 38 percent reported going on chewing despite effects on their health. Meeting the criteria went with higher scores on a khat Severity of Dependence Scale and with nicotine dependence.

1430.content: From fieldwork in Hargeisa, North-West Somalia, the authors report that khat chewing used to be socially regulated: adult men, more rarely women, chewed together at a khat session, usually on weekends and in the afternoon until evening prayer. They observed that use had since moved to adolescents, tea-shops open day and night, early morning chewing and binges lasting more than 24 hours, and some heavy users whose pattern resembled that of amphetamine users in Western countries.

In a random household survey of 4,854 people in Hargeisa, the 38 men who met the authors' criteria for marked positive psychotic symptoms (CIDI items and PANSS ratings) were compared with matched controls. All but one had chewed khat (against 25 of 38 controls), had started regular chewing earlier (16.6 against 20.7 years), and in the weeks before symptoms began chewed 2.5 bundles a day against 0.5. More than two bundles a day was reported for 78 percent of chewing cases (29 of 37) and 4 percent of chewing controls (1 of 25). The authors conclude that early and heavy chewing, rather than khat as such, goes with these symptoms, and that cause and direction stay unclear.

1431.content: Samaha and Robinson state that it is widely accepted that drugs reaching the brain faster carry more potential for addiction, which may be one reason smoked cocaine and nicotine are more addictive than other routes. They judge the evidence that fast drugs are simply more euphoric or more rewarding as not compelling, and propose instead that rapidly delivered cocaine or nicotine engage mesocorticolimbic circuits more and more readily induce sensitization, changes that would feed compulsive pursuit of the drug.

1432.content: Twelve healthy volunteers each received, in separate weekly sessions, placebo, 150 mg of the sedative pentobarbital in one oral dose, or 180 mg in six 30 mg doses every 30 minutes, chosen to give similar peak blood levels. Peak levels were similar, but the single dose reached its peak faster, and with it subjects reported higher peaks of feeling high, wanted more of the drug and liked it more at the end of the session. Sedation and psychomotor impairment did not differ.

1433.content: In 32 current cocaine users given cocaine intravenously, smoked or by nose and scanned by PET, cocaine blocked the dopamine transporter to a similar degree by every route. At equal plasma levels and equal blockade, smoked cocaine gave higher ratings of feeling high than snorted cocaine. Feeling high peaked after 1.4 minutes when smoked, 3.1 minutes when injected and 14.6 minutes when snorted. The authors conclude that the route matters through the speed at which cocaine reaches the brain, since the blockade itself did not differ.

1434.content: Reviewing brain imaging and clinical studies of the stimulant methylphenidate, Volkow and Swanson report that its rewarding effects go with rapid changes in blood levels and presumably fast dopamine rises, as by injection or snorting, while its clinical effects go with slowly rising blood levels by mouth. They conclude that low doses taken by mouth and adjusted for the clinical effect hold back misuse of the same drug.

1435.content: Henningfield and Keenan, at the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, write that the nicotine delivery system is itself an important determinant of how addictive and toxic nicotine use is. Tobacco use often escalates to compulsive use with tolerance and physical dependence, which is not usually seen with nicotine gum or patches; laboratory data show that gum and patches deliver nicotine more slowly and at lower doses than tobacco, and human data suggest their abuse liability is substantially lower.

1436.content: Pankow and colleagues note that ammonia-forming compounds are routinely added to cigarette tobacco, which the US Food and Drug Administration argued is done to raise the volatile free-base form of nicotine in smoke. In laboratory measurements, gaseous ammonia at about 100 ppmV cut the partitioning of nicotine into smoke particles by more than 100-fold, moving it into the gas phase. Because gas-phase nicotine deposits more readily in the airways and free-base nicotine is more lipid soluble, the authors conclude this increases nicotine's availability to the smoker; they estimate about 25 percent of nicotine in the gas phase at body temperature under the full ammonia effect.

1437.content: Gray argues that over the past half century in the United States and other developed nations children's free play with other children declined sharply, while young people's scores on scales of anxiety, depression, helplessness (external locus of control) and narcissism rose, and he proposes that the decline in play contributed to the rise. He takes the decline from a US time-diary study (6 to 8 year olds played 25% less in 1997 than in 1981) and from parent surveys, and the rise from Twenge's analyses of personality-test scores and from youth suicide rates. He writes that the two trends do not prove that the loss of play is the cause, and he makes his case from what play does for children: building interests and competence, decision making and self-control, emotion regulation, friendship among equals, and joy.

1438.content: Gray and Ogas sent written survey questions on childhood and play to anthropologists who had lived among hunter-gatherers; ten researchers answered, covering seven cultures (among them the Nharo, Batek, Efe, Ju/'hoansi and Agta). Together with the published ethnography, the answers told a consistent story: children were free to play on their own essentially all day, every day, adults rarely gave formal instruction or intervened, and little productive work was expected of children (for the Batek, until the late teens; for Efe boys, until 15 to 17).

In the same survey, only two of the ten anthropologists said they had seen any competitive play among the hunter-gatherer children they had studied, and both said they had seldom seen it. Gray adds that small bands and wide birth spacing put children in mixed-age play groups (for example half a dozen children aged four to eleven), and an earlier Human Relations Area Files comparison by Roberts and colleagues found hunter-gatherer cultures the only type with no competitive games.

1439.content: A meta-analysis of 44 articles (N = 23,144 workers) found that meaningful work correlated strongly (r 0.70 or more) with work engagement, commitment and job satisfaction; moderately to strongly (r 0.44 to -0.49) with life satisfaction, life meaning, general health and (negatively) withdrawal intentions; and weakly to moderately (r -0.19 to 0.33) with organisational citizenship behaviour, self-rated job performance and (negatively) negative affect. The best-fitting structural model ran from meaningful work through engagement, commitment and satisfaction to performance, citizenship and withdrawal intentions.

1440.content: Using US Bureau of Labor Statistics employment data for 1960 to 2008 with a median MET value assigned to each occupation, the share of US private-industry jobs requiring at least moderate-intensity physical activity fell from 48% in 1960 to 20% in 2008, and estimated work-related energy expenditure fell by about 140 kcal a day for men and 124 kcal a day for women (8-hour day, 1960-62 body weights).

The authors fed the fall in work-related energy expenditure into a validated energy balance model: for men aged 40 to 50 it gave a predicted mean weight of 89.7 kg for 2003-06, starting from 76.9 kg in 1960-62, against a measured NHANES mean of 91.8 kg; the result for women was similar. On this model the fall in work activity accounts for a significant portion of the rise in mean US body weight.

1441.content: In an individual-participant meta-analysis of 11 European prospective cohorts (IPD-Work consortium; 90,164 employed men and women without coronary heart disease at baseline; mean follow-up 9.8 years; 1,078 first nonfatal myocardial infarctions or coronary deaths), the 31.7% who reported effort-reward imbalance at work had a hazard ratio of 1.16 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.35) for coronary heart disease after adjustment for socioeconomic position, lifestyle factors and job strain. Against people with neither stressor, the age and sex adjusted hazard ratio was 1.16 (1.01 to 1.34) for one of effort-reward imbalance or job strain and 1.41 (1.12 to 1.76) for both.

1442.content: Mummert and colleagues report that in Paleopathology at the Origins of Agriculture (Cohen and Armelagos, eds, 1984), skeletal evidence of declining health was found for 19 of 21 societies that went through the shift from foraging to farming: more infectious and dental disease and more nutritional deficiency. They attribute the nutritional decline to seasonal hunger, reliance on single crops deficient in essential nutrients, crop blights, social inequality and trade.

Reviewing studies of stature published since 1984, Mummert and colleagues found that the majority report adult height declining as reliance on agriculture increased, together with a general reduction of overall health, in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, South America and North America, regardless of when agriculture was adopted.

1443.content: In a laboratory experiment with 122 adults from a UK university community, participants played a simulated three-reel slot machine (choosing on each trial to gamble or skip) on a random-ratio schedule that paid on 30% or 70% of gambles, with 3 s or 10 s between trials, until they had won 10 pounds; then 50 trials followed on which no gamble could win. Those trained on the 30% payout kept gambling much longer in these losing trials (main effect of payout rate F(1,115) = 82.9, partial eta squared 0.42), and the group with the 30% payout and 10 s gaps persisted longest.

1444.content: In two experiments with pigeons (Columba livia) trained on multiple variable-ratio (or random-ratio) and variable-interval (or random-interval) schedules, response rates were higher under the ratio schedules. When reinforcer rates were equated or similar, responding was more resistant to extinction, prefeeding and free food on the interval schedule than on the ratio schedule, and the birds preferred the interval schedule; the difference grew with how much faster they responded on the ratio schedule.

1445.content: In a southern US urban school district with a policy against recess, two Grade 4 classes were allowed recess once a week so that behaviour on recess and non-recess days could be compared. The 43 children, serving as their own controls, were more on task and less fidgety on recess days (repeated-measures MANOVA and ANOVAs). Sixty percent of the children, including all 5 that the authors report as having attention deficit disorder, and boys and girls about equally, benefited considerably: they worked more, fidgeted less, or both.

1446.content: Kidd and Hayden report that rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) choose to learn the outcome of a gamble early even though it does not change the payoff; in a titration task the value of this information was about 25% of the value of the juice reward itself, and rose with the stakes (Blanchard, Hayden and Bromberg-Martin 2015). Pigeons similarly chose an option paying 2 pellets on average over one paying 3 when the first carried a cue predicting the outcome (Stagner and Zentall 2010). Midbrain dopamine neurons respond both to the prospect of reward and to advance information about it (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka 2009).

Kidd and Hayden report that curiosity peaks at intermediate knowledge: in a trivia study adults were least curious when they had no idea of the answer or were very confident, and most curious when they had some idea but lacked confidence, to the point of paying for answers they could have had free after the session (Kang and colleagues 2009). Infants likewise fixate most on sounds moderately different from what they already know (Kinney and Kagan 1976), the pattern the authors call the Goldilocks effect.

1447.content: In a theoretical review, Lambert proposes that the physical effort once needed to obtain food, water and shelter (effort-based rewards) has diminished in industrialised, service-oriented societies. She proposes that the accumbens-striatal-cortical circuitry evolved to sustain such effort, so that its reduced use lowers activation of systems for reward, motivation, problem-solving and coping, the states the source groups as depressive symptoms, and lowers resilience to stress. She argues for behavioural prevention that engages effort in context over drug strategies aimed at single neurochemicals.

1448.content: A meta-analysis of 49 prospective cohort studies (266,939 people, 1,837,794 person-years) found that people with high physical activity at baseline had lower odds of later meeting the studies' criteria for depression than people with low activity (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.88, I2 = 0). The lower odds held for youths (0.90), adults (0.78) and older people (0.79), in Asia, Europe, North America and Oceania (0.65 to 0.84), and both for a positive screen on symptom scales (0.84) and for a diagnosis of major depression (0.86). Significant publication bias was found, but adjusting for it did not change the size of the associations.

1449.content: In a 1954 field experiment at a Boy Scouts camp inside Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma, 22 boys about eleven years old (screened as well adjusted, middle-class, Protestant, previously unacquainted) were formed into two groups that then competed in a series of contests with prizes only one group could win. Hostile acts, insulting names and derogatory stereotypes of the other group followed, and friendship choices went overwhelmingly to the own group.

In the same experiment, bringing the hostile groups together for pleasant activities (meals in the same room, a film, fireworks) did not reduce friction and was used for further insults. A series of staged problems that both groups wanted solved and neither could solve alone (superordinate goals) was followed by cooperation, tool sharing and friendlier ratings. Friendship choices for the other group rose from 6.4% to 36.4% among the Rattlers and from 7.5% to 23.2% among the Eagles, though most choices stayed within the own group.

1450.content: Across six laboratory studies, 146 US college students left alone for 6 to 15 minutes in a bare room, without phones or anything to write with, and asked to entertain themselves with their thoughts, mostly found it hard to concentrate (57.5% at or above the scale midpoint) and reported mind wandering (89.0%); 49.3% rated enjoyment at or below the midpoint. Doing it at home was no easier. In a randomised comparison (study 8, n = 30), people enjoyed solitary external activities such as reading or listening to music much more than just thinking. Community adults aged 18 to 77 gave similar results, unrelated to age, education, income or smartphone use.

In study 10, US college students first rated an electric shock as unpleasant; those included had said they would pay to avoid it again. Left alone for 15 minutes to entertain themselves with their thoughts, with a button that delivered the shock, 67% of the men (12 of 18) and 25% of the women (6 of 24) shocked themselves at least once (men 0 to 4 shocks, mean 1.47, excluding one man who gave himself 190; women 0 to 9, mean 1.00).

1451.content: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at UCLA, 39 healthy adults aged 18 to 36 (screened for health, medication and drug use) were randomised to an intravenous bolus of E. coli endotoxin (0.8 ng/kg, n=23) or saline (n=16). Endotoxin raised IL-6 and TNF-alpha, temperature and pulse, and raised self-reported social disconnection (a five-item scale with items such as 'I feel disconnected from others' and 'I feel like being alone') at two, three and four hours after injection compared with placebo. Controlling for each sickness symptom did not remove the effect on disconnection.

In the same trial, endotoxin raised self-reported depressed mood (five Profile of Mood States items: unhappy, blue, lonely, gloomy, worthless) from baseline to two hours after injection, with no sex difference. In a mediation analysis the rise in reported social disconnection carried the effect: with disconnection controlled, the link between endotoxin and the rise in reported low mood was no longer significant, while controlling for low mood left the effect on disconnection in place. Controlling for fatigue also removed the effect on reported low mood.

1452.content: A PRISMA systematic review (CINAHL, Cochrane Library, PubMed and Web of Science to July 2014) of withdrawal symptoms after stopping a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor found 15 randomised controlled studies, 4 open trials, 4 retrospective investigations and 38 case reports. The authors report that symptoms typically begin within a few days of stopping and last a few weeks, also with gradual tapering, with variants of late onset or longer persistence, and that they are easily misidentified as signs of impending relapse. The authors add that the prevalence varied and was hard to estimate, as many studies did not identify cases.

The authors conclude that clinicians should add SSRIs to the list of drugs that can induce withdrawal symptoms on stopping, beside benzodiazepines and barbiturates, and that the term 'discontinuation syndrome' minimises the vulnerabilities SSRIs induce and should be replaced by 'withdrawal syndrome'.

1453.content: In 3,703 US outpatients who met DSM-IV criteria for nonpsychotic major depressive disorder (HAM-D 14 or more) at the start of the STAR*D trial, the authors dichotomised 12 symptoms from the QIDS-16 scale and counted 1,030 different symptom profiles. 864 profiles (83.9 percent) were reported by five or fewer people, 501 (48.6 percent) by a single person, and the most common profile covered 1.8 percent of patients. Restricting the count to patients with the median number of symptoms did not reduce the variety.

The authors note that, as all DSM-5 depression symptoms except depressed mood are compounds and three can be met by opposite changes (more or less sleep, appetite, movement), two people who meet the diagnostic criteria may share no symptom. Counting only the nine criterion symptoms, 227 profiles qualify for the diagnosis; splitting the opposite changes gives 945, and counting sub-symptoms gives 16,400.

1454.content: In a position paper by an international team of 28 experts, the authors write that newly identified forms of autoimmune encephalitis, linked to antibodies against proteins on the surface of nerve cells or at synapses, can present with neurological and psychiatric symptoms without fever or the raised white-cell count in spinal fluid that marks infectious encephalitis. They propose criteria built on bedside assessment and common tests (MRI, EEG, spinal fluid) so that treatment need not wait for antibody results.

For anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis the panel reports that teenagers and adults usually present with abnormal behaviour (psychosis, delusions, hallucinations, agitation, aggression or catatonia) with irritability and insomnia, followed by speech problems, abnormal movements, memory deficits and a falling level of consciousness. The antibodies against the GluN1 subunit are described as highly specific. In a multicentre cohort of 577 patients, 95 percent were under 45 and women outnumbered men four to one; in a retrospective check, 425 of 532 patients (80 percent) met the proposed criteria for probable disease within the first month.

1455.content: In a theory paper, two Harvard Medical School authors (McLean Hospital) propose that the interpersonal pattern of people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder rests on a heritable hypersensitivity to interpersonal stressors (abandonment fears, rejection sensitivity, intolerance of aloneness, for which they cite a heritability of 0.48 from Jang et al. 1996) that interacts with adverse early caretaking and later stressors. They summarise studies reporting that the intense distress of patients so labelled is often set off by rejection, criticism or being alone, that remissions follow positive interpersonal events and that relapses follow negative relationship events.

The authors report that studies of adult samples diagnosed with borderline personality disorder found insecure attachment in more than 90 percent, mostly of the preoccupied type (60 to 100 percent of patients across studies, on the Adult Attachment Interview) or the unresolved type (50 to 88 percent), and they propose disorganised attachment in infancy, later turning into controlling-caregiving or controlling-punitive strategies, as one pathway toward the adult pattern.

1456.content: In a historical review, the authors (the first from a pharmacology department in Madrid) write that the first two antidepressants of the 1950s were iproniazid, a monoamine-oxidase inhibitor first used against tuberculosis, and imipramine, the first tricyclic, and that these drugs served as research tools that allowed the first hypotheses about the origins of what they label depressive disorders to be put forward. They state that all antidepressants available in 2009, fluoxetine and its successors included, share one mechanism, the modulation of monoamine transmission at the synapse.

1457.content: A review of antidepressant history states that serendipity played an important role in finding the first drug treatment for depression: iproniazid was made in 1953 as an anti-tuberculosis compound, and tuberculosis patients on it showed 'side effects' of euphoria, stimulation, better appetite and better sleep; a 1958 study then reported improvement in 70 percent of patients with depression given it. Imipramine was tested by Roland Kuhn as an antipsychotic, showed no antipsychotic effect in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia, and was seen to improve patients with severe depression.

The same review states that the monoamine hypothesis, articulated in 1965, proposes that patients with depression have depleted serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, and that it came from two lines of evidence: reserpine depleting monoamines and lowering mood, and the way the antidepressant drugs already in use act on monoamines. The authors add that later studies found monoamine depletion produces no depressive symptoms in healthy people, so the hypothesis needs revising.

1458.content: The authors compared shy with non-shy people. 18 percent of the shy group met the authors' diagnostic criteria for social phobia against 3 percent of the non-shy group, so 82 percent of shy people did not receive the label. Shyness severity correlated with having the label, and shy people with the label were shyer, more introverted and more neurotic, but none of these measures was sufficient to tell shy people with the label apart from shy people without it. The shy group also more often met criteria for other psychiatric diagnoses.

1459.content: The ENIGMA ADHD Working Group pooled MRI scans of 1,713 people diagnosed with ADHD and 1,529 controls from 23 sites (ages 4 to 63, 66 percent male) and analysed them with one protocol. The diagnosed group had smaller accumbens (Cohen's d -0.15), amygdala (-0.19), caudate (-0.11), hippocampus (-0.11) and putamen (-0.14) volumes and smaller intracranial volume (-0.10). Differences were largest in children and absent in adults. Volumes did not correlate with ADHD symptom scores, and stimulant use and other diagnoses did not change the results.

1460.content: In a review, Hyman (Massachusetts General Hospital) and Nestler propose an 'initiation and adaptation' paradigm: the long-term actions of psychotropic drugs come from neural plasticity that chronic dosing sets off. They write that the mechanisms by which drugs of abuse produce dependence are better understood than those by which antidepressants, antipsychotics and lithium produce their therapeutic effects, but that the basic mechanisms appear similar: chronic administration produces adaptations in post-receptor signalling, including changes in gene expression, and whether the result is harmful or therapeutic depends on the neural systems the drug targets. They present the paradigm as an account of the delay before therapeutic effects begin.

1461.content: In 268 people diagnosed with first-episode schizophrenia, the authors found 15 with an organic disease that appeared relevant to the mental state: three cases of syphilis, two of sarcoidosis, three of alcohol excess, two of drug abuse, and one each of lung carcinoma, autoimmune multisystem disease, cerebral cysticercosis, thyroid disease and previous head injury. They report that identified organic disease went with less than 6 percent of the cases.

1462.content: The EU-GEI incidence study identified 2,774 people (median age 30.5) who contacted services with a first episode of psychosis (ICD-10 F20 to F33, confirmed by the Operational Criteria Checklist) in 17 catchment areas in England, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Brazil, 2010 to 2015, over 12.9 million person-years. The authors report a crude incidence of 21.4 per 100,000 person-years. After standardising for age, sex and racial or ethnic minority status, rates still varied 8-fold, from 6.0 per 100,000 in Santiago, Spain to 46.1 in Paris; crude rates varied 10-fold (6.3 in Santiago to 61.4 in southeast London).

In the same study, the authors report diagnosed rates higher in racial or ethnic minority groups (incidence rate ratio 1.6) and highest in men aged 18 to 24, and areas with more owner-occupied homes had lower rates (incidence rate ratio 0.8). The authors write that owner-occupancy may stand for socioeconomic position, social stability and cohesion, and acknowledge possible reverse causality; setting-level variation remained after the measured area factors.

1463.content: In an online survey of 657 people (autistic people, relatives and friends of autistic people, and people with no stated relation to autism), the authors report that identifying as autistic and being aware of neurodiversity were associated with seeing autism as a positive identity that needs no cure. Respondents' reported recognition of the negative sides of autism, and support for parenting that celebrates and ameliorates autism without trying to eliminate it, did not differ by relation to autism or by awareness of neurodiversity.

1464.content: A preregistered (PROSPERO) systematic review and meta-analysis searched PubMed, Embase and PsycInfo to June 2019 for prospective studies in which a biological marker measured beforehand was tested as a predictor of a later clinical-interview diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Of 67,464 articles, 75 qualified: neuroimaging 24, hormones 39, immune markers 8, and one or two each for gut, neurotrophic, neurotransmitter and oxidative-stress markers. Meta-analyses of brain volumes and immune markers were not significant. Only cortisol predicted onset or recurrence (19 studies, OR 1.29, p 0.024), a small effect that lost significance when outliers or low-quality studies were removed, after correction for publication bias, and when studies including people already diagnosed at baseline were removed.

In their discussion the authors write that it is striking that none of the postulated biological theories found strong prospective support, that most leading hypotheses rest on cross-sectional, treatment, symptom or animal studies that cannot settle cause, and that whether the observed biological changes are a cause or a consequence of the diagnosed condition remains unclear.

1465.content: In 66 healthy adults (University of Trier) waiting 10 minutes to give a public speech before an audience, participants got no support, instrumental and emotional support from an opposite-sex stranger, or the same from their boyfriend or girlfriend. Men supported by their partner showed a significantly smaller cortisol response than unsupported or stranger-supported men. Women showed no drop with stranger support and a tendency toward a larger cortisol response when supported by their boyfriend. Reported stress and mood changes did not differ by sex or group and did not correlate with cortisol responses.

1466.content: A meta-analysis of 28 experiments, in four separate analyses (1,207 to 3,469 participants each), tested how giving biogenetic explanations of psychological problems changes stigma. Biogenetic explanations reduced blame of the affected person (Hedges g -0.324) but raised pessimism about their prognosis (g 0.263) and raised endorsement of the stereotype that people with psychological problems are dangerous (g 0.198, possibly reflecting publication bias). They did not usually change desired social distance.

1467.content: Parents of all Swedish twins aged 9 or 12 born 1992 to 2000 were interviewed about DSM-IV ADHD symptoms (response rate 80 percent). Using two validated cutoffs, the authors compared children above the research-diagnosis threshold (prevalence 1.78 percent) with children above a lower screening threshold (prevalence 9.75 percent). Group heritability was almost identical, around .60, for both, showing a strong genetic link between the extreme and the subthreshold range. The authors conclude that the label is best viewed as the quantitative extreme of genetic and environmental factors that act across the whole range of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.

1468.content: In a double-blind randomised trial by groups in Groningen and Nijmegen, the Netherlands, 94 children and adolescents aged 8 to 18 who had taken methylphenidate in regular care for more than 2 years either continued extended-release methylphenidate (36 or 54 mg a day) for 7 weeks or were tapered off over 3 weeks to 4 weeks of placebo. Investigator-rated ADHD Rating Scale scores went from 21.4 to 21.9 in the continuation group and from 19.6 to 24.7 in the discontinuation group, a between-group difference in change of 4.6 points (95% CI 0.56 to 8.7) favouring continuation; teacher-rated scores also worsened more after stopping. On the Clinical Global Impressions scale, 40.4 percent of the discontinuation group were rated worse against 15.9 percent of the continuation group. The authors note that some patients may be withdrawn without deterioration.

1469.content: The MTA trial randomly assigned 579 children aged 7 to 9.9 diagnosed with combined-type ADHD (436 of them in the analyses reported here) to 14 months of medication management, behaviour therapy, both combined, or community care. At follow-ups 6 and 8 years after enrolment, the originally randomised groups did not differ significantly in nearly every analysis of symptoms and functioning, including school grades, arrests and psychiatric hospitalisations. Medication use fell by 62 percent after the 14-month trial; adjusting for it did not change the results. The early advantage of the medication arms had already gone by the 36-month follow-up.

In the same follow-up, the children's own symptom course in the first 3 years, regardless of which treatment they got, predicted 55 percent of the 8-year outcomes. As a group the MTA children did worse than 261 non-diagnosed classmates on 91 percent of the measures, with medium to large differences; 30.2 percent of the MTA sample still met DSM-IV criteria for ADHD at 8 years against 2.2 percent of the classmates.

1470.content: Keller and Nesse asked 445 participants which depressive symptoms followed a recent adverse event. Participants reported guilt, rumination, fatigue and pessimism most after failed efforts, and crying, sadness and a wish for social support most after social losses. The difference was replicated in an experiment in which 113 students were randomly assigned to imagine a major failure or the death of a loved one.

1471.content: In population survey data followed over 2 years (5,055 people) and 4 years (4,087 people), the number of social groups a person belonged to predicted later depression scores, fewer groups going with more depression, after controlling for earlier group memberships, earlier depression, age, gender, socioeconomic status, self-rated health, relationship status and ethnicity. The gain from group memberships was larger among people who scored as depressed at the start. Respondents who scored as depressed and had no group memberships had a 24 percent lower risk of relapse, as the authors define it, if they joined one group, and 63 percent lower if they joined three.

1472.content: In the Changing Lives of Older Couples sample, older married adults who at the start reported giving practical help to friends, relatives and neighbours, or emotional support to their spouse, were less likely to have died five years later. Receiving support showed no link with mortality once giving was taken into account. The pattern held after controlling for demographic, personality, health, mental health and marital-relationship variables.

1473.content: In three studies, of 115 undergraduates, 120 young and older adults, and 45 parents (of children with cancer or of healthy children), the authors examined how far people could abandon goals out of reach and put their effort into other goals. Being able to let go and being able to take up new goals each went with higher subjective well-being, and the two also combined in their link with well-being.

1474.content: Kahneman, Wakker and Sarin separate decision utility (the weight an outcome gets in a choice) from experienced utility (how pleasant or painful it is, moment by moment). They report that memory of an episode follows the average of its worst moment and its end and neglects its length, and that because people choose by memory, they can prefer an option that is worse in every moment.

In the cold-water experiment the authors report (Kahneman et al. 1993), 32 participants held one hand in 14 degree water for 60 seconds, and the other hand for 60 seconds plus 30 more seconds while the water warmed slightly to 15 degrees. Asked which trial to repeat, 69 percent chose the longer one, which contained all the pain of the shorter one and more; a replication with 37 new participants gave 65 percent. Among those whose pain fell at the end, 17 of 21 chose the longer trial. In a randomised trial with 682 colonoscopy patients, leaving the instrument in place about a minute longer, less painfully, improved how patients rated the whole procedure.

1475.content: Using the US General Social Survey from 1974 to 1996, Guest and Wierzbicki find a linear trend toward less socialising with neighbours and more socialising with friends outside the neighbourhood, with people increasingly specialising in one or the other. They call the evidence for less neighbourhood socialising slight.

1476.content: Kenrick and colleagues revise Maslow's 1943 hierarchy by asking what each motive did for survival and reproduction. They keep physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation and esteem (status) as distinct motive systems, remove self-actualization as a separate need (folding it into status and mating motives), and put three reproductive goals at the top: mate acquisition, mate retention and parenting.

In the revised hierarchy later-developing goals overlap with earlier ones and do not replace them: once a motive system has developed, it is switched on whenever cues relevant to it are present, so a person's priority at a given moment depends on what the surroundings signal.

1477.content: Klinger proposes that from commitment to a goal until it is reached or given up, a person stays especially responsive to cues tied to it (a 'current concern'). He proposes that giving up follows frustration and runs through a cycle of invigoration, aggression, low mood and recovery, and that this low mood, labelled depression in the abstract, is a normal part of disengaging from a goal.

1478.content: In questionnaire studies of over 600 participants aged 16 to 54, the years a person lived with a sibling up to age 18 went with more help given to that sibling (favours in the last month, willingness to donate a kidney), more disgust at imagined sex with that sibling, and stronger moral opposition to sibling incest among others. This held when the person had not seen the sibling as a newborn in their mother's care (younger siblings rating older ones), with similar effect sizes across all four measures.

Among older siblings rating a younger one (128 pairs), having seen the sibling as a newborn in their own mother's care predicted altruism toward that sibling (r = 0.32), and still did after coresidence was controlled (partial r = 0.22). Once that newborn cue was controlled, years of coresidence no longer predicted altruism (partial r = 0.04). The same pattern held in a smaller sample (30) for moral opposition to sibling incest.

1479.content: In five change-detection experiments with photographs of natural scenes (each with a different set of subjects), changes to animals and people were detected 1 to 2 seconds faster and 21 to 25 percentage points more often than changes to plants and artifacts in the first experiment and its replication. Overall 89 percent of changes to animate targets were caught against 66 percent for inanimate ones; the effect held after controlling for how interesting the targets were rated, and vanished when the pictures were inverted or blurred, so it rests on the category and not on low-level visual features.

Subjects caught changes to non-human animals better than changes to vehicles, although they are trained from childhood to watch vehicles: in the fifth experiment 90.6 percent of changes to animals and people were detected against 63.5 percent for vehicles, and animate changes were detected more than a second faster. A lifetime of looking at people gave no speed advantage for humans over other animals. The authors read this as a monitoring system tuned to ancestral rather than modern priorities.

1480.content: Phone records and three surveys tracked 24 students in one large UK city over 18 months as they left school for university or work. Each person put a large share of calls on a few top contacts, and the shape of this distribution stayed the same for that person even though many contacts changed: of the top 20 contacts in the second six months, 41 percent were new (29 percent of the top 5). As new people were added, old ones were replaced or got fewer calls.

1481.content: Hensch reviews how neuronal circuits are shaped by experience during critical periods early after birth. In the primary visual cortex this experience-dependent development is set off by the maturing of local inhibitory connections and driven by a late-developing subset of inhibitory interneurons, and the competing inputs are fixed in place by a rebuilding of the extracellular matrix that occurs only during the critical period. He notes that reopening this process, with recovery of function in conditions such as amblyopia, can now be studied.

1482.content: Barrett and Kurzban review arguments against a modular mind drawn from cognitive architecture, development, genetics and evolution, and report that some of the positions attacked were abandoned or never held by proponents of modular views. They propose that modularity, cleanly defined, is a useful framework for research on individual cognitive systems and on evolved human cognition, and note that modularity is a basic property of living things at every level of organization.

1483.content: In a population-based sample of 2,164 women from female twin pairs (53,215 person-months, 492 onsets of a major depressive episode by the authors' criteria), four events went with onset in the same month at an odds ratio above 10: death of a close relative, assault, serious marital problems and divorce or breakup. Genetic liability, indexed by co-twin status, also raised risk, and the best-fitting model had genes setting sensitivity to such events. The predicted monthly probability of onset was 0.5 percent without and 6.2 percent with a severe event in women at lowest genetic risk (identical co-twin unaffected), and 1.1 and 14.6 percent in those at highest risk (identical co-twin affected).

1484.content: Berridge and Robinson review the human evidence for incentive sensitization a quarter century after proposing it. Many brain imaging reports over ten years found raised mesolimbic responses to drug cues (photos of paraphernalia, of others using) in people with addiction, and more years of cocaine use went with stronger ventral striatum responses to cocaine cues; PET studies of dopamine release point the same way. They state that 'liking' need not rise with sensitization and may fall, and that sensitized 'wanting' can last for years after withdrawal has passed, even when the person does not want the drug and does not expect it to be pleasant.

About 15 percent of patients with Parkinson's disease treated with drugs that directly stimulate dopamine receptors develop what clinicians label dopamine dysregulation syndrome, with intense compulsive pursuit of gambling, shopping, sex, internet use or hobbies, which the authors give as proof of principle that over-stimulating dopamine-related systems can produce compulsive motivation for things that are not drugs. For eating, gambling, pornography, internet and shopping habits without any drug, they report only emerging evidence of sensitization-like brain over-reaction to cues for each person's own habit.

1485.content: Borsboom states that for all but a few of the symptom clusters labelled mental disorders, common disease pathways have proved elusive. He proposes instead that the symptoms cause each other: a belief that others can read one's mind brings suspicion, suspicion brings avoidance of people, and avoidance removes the correction that would end the belief. In his proposal such feedback loops keep symptoms active, and the clusters in diagnostic manuals are groups of symptoms that set each other off most strongly.

Borsboom proposes that a strongly connected symptom network shows hysteresis: an outside event (such as losing a partner) switches symptoms on, and when the event is gone the network stays active because the symptoms keep each other going. A weakly connected network recovers once the stress lifts; he gives normal grief as an example, which can show a symptom pattern like the one scored as major depression and then fades. He proposes defining mental health as the stable state of a weakly connected network, and treatment as acting on a symptom, on the outside trigger, or on the links between symptoms.

1486.content: Bourke collected 12 field studies that measured relatedness, benefit and cost of a social act in wild populations, among them the egg-plant lace bug (Gargaphia solani), the paper wasp Polistes dominulus, larval tiger salamanders (Ambystoma tigrinum), wild turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo) and white-fronted bee-eaters. In 10 the helper paid a cost in its own offspring. Among those 10, the benefit to relatives outweighed the cost as Hamilton's rule requires in 5 cases, in some years or group sizes in 3 more, was neutral in 1 and failed in 1 (a halictid bee).

Across almost 20 comparative studies of family trees of species, cooperative breeding in birds and mammals and eusociality in insects arose more often where relatedness was high and mating was lifelong with one partner, as Hamilton's rule predicts, and potentially where family life and low costs of helping favoured it.

1487.content: In an experiment, 112 young women were randomly assigned to spend 10 minutes browsing their own Facebook account, a fashion magazine website or an appearance-neutral control website. Those who browsed Facebook reported a more negative mood than those on the control site. Women who scored high on a trait measure of appearance comparison reported more face, hair and skin related discrepancies after Facebook than after the control site. The abstract does not report a result for body dissatisfaction.

1488.content: In a 64-page review of online dating, the authors report that browsing larger sets of dating profiles shifts choices: across experiments, people shown 4 to 64 profiles were about equally satisfied with the process, but with larger sets they used quicker shortcut strategies and chose partners further from their own stated preferences (sets of 30, 60 and 90, or 40 and 80). At speed-dating events, women who met 9 to 14 men were over 40% more likely to agree to a follow-up with any given man than women who met 15 to 21. The authors argue that ready access to a large pool can bring out an evaluating, shopping mindset that objectifies partners and may weaken willingness to commit, and they note that no study had then tested satisfaction with the chosen partner itself.

The same review finds no compelling evidence that the matching algorithms of dating sites produce better romantic outcomes than other ways of pairing people. The authors argue that the algorithms rest on similarity and complementarity, which matter much less to relationship well-being than assumed, and that no algorithm using information gathered before two people meet can account for more than a very small share of later satisfaction and stability.

1489.content: In the HomeNet field trial in Pittsburgh, 169 people in 73 households were given computers and internet access and followed through their first 1 to 2 years online (1995 to 1998), with logged hours of use. Holding baseline measures constant, more hours online went with later declines in communication with family members in the household and in the size of the local social circle (people seen at least monthly), and with rises in self-rated loneliness and in scores on a 15-item depression scale (CES-D). The authors call the effects small but statistically significant; social support and the distant circle also moved in the negative direction without reaching significance. Baseline social involvement and well-being did not predict later internet use, apart from a marginal finding that people with larger local circles used it less.

1490.content: In a 3-year follow-up of 208 of the original HomeNet participants (Pittsburgh, first online 1995 to 1996), the negative links between internet use and social involvement and well-being reported in 1998 had faded. In a second longitudinal survey of 406 people who bought a new computer or television in 1998 to 1999, internet use went with better communication, social involvement and well-being on average, but with better outcomes for extraverts and people with more social support and worse outcomes for introverts and people with less support.

1491.content: In 11,065 US adults aged 50 and over in the Health and Retirement Study (2004 to 2010), how often people met children, other family and friends in person at baseline went with their chance of scoring 4 or more on the 8-item CES-D depression scale two years later, after adjusting for 12 baseline variables including baseline symptoms. People with in-person contact every few months or less had an 11.5% probability of scoring above that cut-off, against 8.1% with contact once or twice a month and 7.3% with contact once or twice a week (6.5% at three or more times a week). Frequency of telephone contact made no difference. For written or email contact, every few months or less went with 9.7% against 6.2% for monthly, but the authors judged the pattern across levels too uneven for a conclusion.

1492.content: An app logged every use of their own Android phone for 14 days in 23 staff and students of the University of Lincoln, UK, aged 18 to 33. They used their phones a mean of 84.68 times a day (SD 55.23) for a total of 5.05 hours a day, and 55% of all uses lasted under 30 seconds. Asked afterwards, they estimated 37.20 uses a day, less than half the logged number, and their estimates did not correlate with the logs (r = .11); estimates of total time (4.12 hours) were close to the logged time.

1493.content: A meta-analysis of 20 cross-sectional studies covering 125,198 children and adolescents found that using a portable media device such as a phone or tablet near bedtime went with about twice the odds of too little sleep (OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.42 to 3.32), higher odds of poor sleep quality (OR 1.46) and of excessive daytime sleepiness (OR 2.72). Children who had such a device in the bedroom at night without using it also had higher odds of too little sleep (OR 1.79), poor sleep quality (OR 1.53) and daytime sleepiness (OR 2.27).

1494.content: In an fMRI study of 31 German young adults (19 to 31 years), chosen to span a range of Facebook Intensity Scale scores, participants received positive words supposedly chosen by strangers who had watched their video interview, saw positive words given to another person, and won money in a card game. The stronger the left nucleus accumbens responded to praise for themselves relative to praise for the other person, the higher their Facebook use score (r = 0.400). The accumbens response to winning money was not related to Facebook use.

1495.content: In an experiment, 142 participants were put in random pairs to discuss a dilemma and agree a solution by online chat, under a 2 x 2 x 2 design: anonymous or identified, visible or invisible to each other, with or without eye contact. Flaming (hostile, insulting messages) was measured by participants' own reports, by expert judges rating the chat transcripts, and by text analysis. Of the three factors, lack of eye contact contributed most to the hostile effects; the authors conclude that earlier studies defined anonymity too broadly.

1496.content: In a Pew Research Center survey of 6,034 US adults (5 to 17 July 2022, mostly the address-sampled American Trends Panel), 30% had ever used a dating site or app. One in ten partnered adults (married, living with a partner or in a committed relationship) said they met their current partner through a dating site or app; among partnered adults under 30 it was one in five, and among partnered LGB adults 24%.

1497.content: Nass and Moon review a series of experiments showing that people apply social rules and expectations to computers without thinking: they apply gender stereotypes to computers, identify ethnically with computer agents, show politeness and reciprocity toward computers, and respond to a computer 'personality'. The authors state that anthropomorphism and intentional social responses cannot explain the results.

1498.content: A random-effects meta-analysis of 63 independent cross-sectional samples (N = 36,552) found a small, positive, significant correlation between social media use and body image disturbance (r = 0.169, 95% CI 0.131 to 0.206). The strength of the link differed by type of social media use, body image dimension, country grouping and age.

1499.content: Suler argues that online some people disclose more or act out more often or more intensely than they would in person, and names six interacting factors behind this online disinhibition effect: dissociative anonymity, invisibility, asynchronicity, solipsistic introjection, dissociative imagination and minimization of authority, with personality setting how far each person is affected.

1500.content: Reviewing studies to 2015, the authors report that Facebook use, especially passive scrolling, goes with more social comparison and envy, and that in several studies comparison or envy statistically carried a positive link between Facebook use and negative feelings such as scores on depression scales. They add that the evidence on Facebook use and depression scores as a whole is mixed, with positive, null and negative links reported, and that causal links had not been established.

1501.content: In an online survey of 1,247 participants, pornography use and scores on the UCLA Loneliness Scale were positively and significantly associated in a measurement model and in two structural equation models that regressed each on the other. The authors present this as a pilot and as grounds for future testing of a two-way, self-reinforcing relation.

1502.content: In an experiment, online daters chose a partner from either a large set (24) or a small set (6) of profiles, with or without the option to change their choice later. A week later, those who had chosen from 24 were less satisfied with their choice and more likely to change it than those who had chosen from 6. Reversibility alone did not change satisfaction. Those who chose from the large set and could reverse their choice were the least satisfied.

1503.content: Forty novices played a multi-line video slot machine while skin conductance and heart rate were recorded. Skin conductance responses were about the same after real wins and after 'losses disguised as wins', spins where the machine played its winning sights and sounds although the amount won was less than the bet, and both were significantly larger than after plain losses.

1504.content: In a between-subjects experiment, 144 girls aged 14 to 18 were randomly shown either original or manipulated (retouched and reshaped) Instagram selfies. Girls who saw the manipulated photos reported a lower body image, and the effect was strongest in girls with a higher tendency to compare themselves with others. The girls rated the manipulated photos more positively, noticed filters but hardly noticed the reshaped bodies, and in both conditions found the pictures realistic.

1505.content: A meta-analysis of 187 effect sizes from social-dilemma experiments found that rewards for cooperating and punishments for not cooperating both raised cooperation, by statistically equivalent amounts (d = 0.51 for rewards, d = 0.70 for punishment). Incentives worked better when they were costly to give than when they were free, and punishment worked better when people kept playing in the same group than when groups were reshuffled each round or the game was played once.

1506.content: In a review, Dunbar traces gossip, which he defines broadly as talk about social topics, to social grooming among primates as a way of bonding groups, restates that about two thirds of conversation time in freely forming conversations goes to social topics, and presents evidence that besides servicing social networks a key function of such talk may be controlling free riders.

1507.content: A meta-study of 129 published dictator-game papers (616 treatments; individual data on 20,813 dictators) found that dictators gave on average 28.3 percent of the pie (random-effects estimate over 445 treatments), and that 63.89 percent gave something. Being identified to the recipient made dictators more generous: identified dictators were less likely to give nothing and the most common choice moved from zero to the equal split. Giving fell when dictators could hide their decision (concealment option) and when the game was repeated; a face-like cue of three dots raised giving in the individual data. Keeping the decision hidden from the experimenter as well (double-blind) lowered giving only slightly, and only once repeated play was controlled for.

In the same meta-study, the degree of social distance to the recipient (from total stranger through member of the same subject pool to friend) had no stable effect: in meta-regression giving even fell as the recipient came closer, which Engel reads as a statistical artefact, since giving was practically flat once the recipient was any closer than a fellow member of the subject pool; only in the model that controls for unobserved heterogeneity did closer recipients receive more, and social proximity was the strongest predictor of giving everything. Dictators from small-scale ('primal') societies were the least likely to keep everything: there the equal split was the most common choice and giving little was rare, against close to 40 percent of Western student dictators who gave nothing.

1508.content: In an online experiment with 265 American adults recruited on MTurk (2 by 2 between-subjects design, four-round public goods game in groups of four), the option to send notes about group members to their future partners (gossip) went with higher contributions (mean 7.44 against 6.38 of 10 points per round, a marginal effect, p = 0.051) and higher total earnings (64.3 against 55.9 points, p = 0.002). The option to pay to deduct points from others (punishment, 1 point to fine 3) had no overall effect on contributions, a trend toward higher contributions in rounds 3 and 4, and lowered earnings (55.2 against 65.0 points, p < 0.001).

In the same experiment, when gossip and punishment were removed for a following two-round trust game with new partners, people who had earlier been able to gossip sent more to their partner (trust: mean 7.91 against 6.41 of 10 points, p = 0.025) and returned more, compared with people who never had the option; earlier punishment had no effect on trust.

1509.content: In an experiment, participants were led to believe that their fellow group members had a low or a high tendency to gossip, and that their contribution to the group could or could not be identified. The authors report that the results confirmed their hypotheses: when members were expected to gossip and contributions were identifiable, people were more concerned about the group's opinion and contributed more to the group.

1510.content: A world atlas of artificial night sky brightness, modelled from 2014 VIIRS satellite data and calibrated with more than 35,000 ground observations of sky brightness, found that about 83 percent of the world's population and more than 99 percent of the US and European populations live under light-polluted skies (artificial zenith brightness above 14 microcandela per square metre, about 8 percent above the natural night sky). The Milky Way is hidden from more than one third of humanity, including 60 percent of Europeans and nearly 80 percent of North Americans; in Singapore the whole population lives under skies so bright that the eye cannot fully dark-adapt.

1511.content: In recordings of dopamine neurons (the abstract names no species), cues signalled different probabilities of reward. The brief (phasic) burst after the cue rose steadily with the probability of reward, as a code of the difference between predicted and actual reward. A second, previously unseen response tracked uncertainty, which is greatest at a probability of 0.5: a gradual increase in activity until the time the reward might arrive. The authors suggest this uncertainty signal may play a role in attention-based learning and risk-taking.

1512.content: In a review joining recordings and learning theory, Schultz, Dayan and Montague report that physiological work had identified dopamine neurons in the primate whose changing output apparently signals changes or errors in the predictions of future rewarding events, and that these findings fit quantitative theories in which learning is driven by changes in expectation.

1513.content: In a review of his laboratory's and others' work, Schultz reports that most dopamine neurons in the midbrain of humans, monkeys and rodents signal a reward prediction error: they are activated by more reward than predicted, stay at baseline for a fully predicted reward, and drop below baseline when less reward than predicted arrives. He also reports that dopamine neurons show the same nonlinear response increases with unpredicted rewards and with risky gambles.

Schultz argues from the prediction-error code that a reward which arrives as expected no longer raises a dopamine response, so getting the same response needs a bigger or new reward every time; he reads this as a mechanism behind always wanting more (a newer car, more clothes, a bigger house). He also writes that cocaine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, nicotine and alcohol overstimulate dopamine mechanisms and seem to hijack systems that evolved for natural rewards, because the drugs act on the brain directly and mimic a positive prediction error that is not compared against a prediction.

1514.content: In a review of nomadic forager ethnographies and comparative studies, Fry and Souillac report that the typical response to conflict among mobile foragers is to walk away: lacking authoritative leaders, band societies handle much conflict through avoidance, discussion, group meetings, contests and other nonviolent or aggression-limiting means, and bands often split (fission) after serious conflict. Disputes tend to be personal, such as jealousy or an insult between two men. Among the Paliyan of India people typically separate even after minor conflict, and a band may call a mediation assembly (kuttam) if a dispute persists.

The same review quotes Fry's 2006 book (p. 239) on the recurring features of nomadic band societies, among them group fission or interpersonal avoidance as a response to conflict, a devaluation of physical aggression, and social control through gossip, ridicule and withdrawal of support, and in extreme cases ostracism and execution. Members of mobile forager societies ridicule, criticise, tease, withhold support from and reprimand people who are overly aggressive, pushy or egoistic.

1515.content: In the skeletal record of central California hunter-gatherers from 1,530 to 230 calibrated years before present (burials from 329 archaeological sites), sharp-force or projectile trauma was the most common sign of violence, found in 7.4 percent of 6,278 assessed burials, more often in males than females and most often in young adult men; blunt-force cranial trauma ran at about 5 percent in adult males for most of the period. Across the region's ethnolinguistic territories, the share of burials with sharp-force trauma fell as environmental productivity (net primary productivity from satellite data) rose, and the link held when political complexity was controlled; political complexity did not track either kind of trauma.

1516.content: In Lamalera, Indonesia, a village of fishers and sea hunters, rights to shares of a catch (uma) are set by a detailed system of norms based on the role of each share holder and the anatomy of the prey: shares from the large-boat (tena) hunts go to members of the boat-owning corporation, the crew who took part in the hunt, and the craftsmen who built and maintain the boat and gear. Nolin restates Alvard and Nolin 2002: at least for the large boats, each person's return per head is higher from the cooperative hunt than from more solitary small-boat fishing, which is given as the reason people cooperate, and producers hold property rights to their shares.

In all 317 households of Lamalera, Indonesia, a village of fishers and sea hunters, each household named the households it most often gave food to and received food from in one sea-hunting season. In network models, the odds that household A gave to B were 192 times higher when B also gave to A; the odds of giving to a sibling's household were 122 times those for an unrelated household and 37 times those for a first cousin's; and the odds of giving to a household 100 m away were 12 times those for a household 500 m away.

In the same Lamalera network, reciprocal giving between two households accounted for 44.9% of the variation the models could explain, against 18.2% for distance and 15.9% for kinship. Added on top of reciprocity, kinship accounted for only 2.3% more and distance 3.7% more. Kin were sparse: only 4.1% of household pairs were related as closely as first cousins. Nolin cautions that mutual ties alone do not prove reciprocal altruism, but in networks simulated from kinship and distance alone the apparent reciprocity was small and vanished once those two were accounted for, so he concludes that kinship and proximity cannot explain the size of the observed mutuality, which reflects deliberate reciprocity between households.

1517.content: In three experiments, small groups of strangers did a painful task together (hands in ice water and leg squats in Experiments 1 and 2; eating a hot chili pepper in Experiment 3) or a painless control task. Sharing the painful experience raised how bonded the strangers felt toward each other (Experiment 1) and raised cooperation in an economic game (Experiments 2 and 3), compared with the no-pain control.

1518.content: In a Dutch panel followed over seven years, the average number of confidants and practical helpers people named changed only slightly, but the people filling those roles changed considerably. A lack of opportunities to meet (in contexts such as work, family, sports clubs, voluntary associations and the neighbourhood) was an important reason why many relationships ended, and new relationships were more likely to start in a context where a person already met existing network members.

1519.content: In two waves of the Survey of the Social Networks of the Dutch (2007 and 2014; 441 respondents, non-kin ties), tie loss was concentrated in young relationships: most ties lost between the waves were ties the person had known for up to 10 years, the risk of loss fell steeply over that period, and ties of about 20 years hardly changed. Ties to people unlike oneself in gender, age or ethnicity were lost faster, most of all in the early years (for education the difference was no longer significant once control variables were added). Sharing more meeting contexts went with a smaller chance of losing a tie, and people living 10 to 19 km away were more likely to be lost than those living less than 1 km away.

1520.content: In a review for education researchers, Pellegrini and Bohn argue that recess serves a positive purpose in the primary school day, against the practice of cutting it in many schools in North America and the United Kingdom, and they cite experimental and longitudinal data showing that recess breaks help children's cognitive performance and adjustment to school.

1521.content: In three field experiments in one elementary school, children in kindergarten, grade 2 and grade 4 had their recess moved 30 minutes earlier or later. Their inattention in class before recess varied with how long they had been kept from it, inattention was higher before recess than after, and after the longer wait children, especially boys, were more socially active on the playground. A third experiment with indoor recess and two replication samples gave the same pattern.

1522.content: Between 2010 and 2012, 18,303 children aged 7 to 15 and a subset of their parents in 16 countries (Australia, Brazil, Denmark, England, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Norway, Portugal, South Africa, Sri Lanka and Sweden) were surveyed on whether children were allowed to cross main roads, go places, travel home from school, go out after dark, use buses and cycle on main roads alone. Restrictions were found across all ages and nearly all countries, greatest under age 11, and parents named traffic as the strongest reason for keeping children in.

Finland ranked far above the other 15 countries: a majority of Finnish children could go places within walking distance alone by age 7, cross main roads and travel home from school alone by age 8, and use local buses alone by age 10. In the other countries these permissions came later; only in Finland, Sweden, Japan and Denmark was a majority of children of any age allowed out alone after dark.

Across the ten countries that also had a Unicef 2013 child well-being score, countries that gave children more freedom to travel and play without adults ranked higher on child well-being (Spearman rho 0.809, p below 0.01). The authors note that other factors may account for the link.

1523.content: Photographs of judo athletes right after Olympic and Paralympic matches in 2004 (87 sighted athletes from 36 nations, 53 blind athletes from 20 nations) were coded by raters blind to the aims. Winners, sighted and blind, showed the pride display (head tilted back, arms raised, fists, chest expanded) far more than losers. Twelve congenitally blind athletes, who never saw anyone show these displays, showed the same pride display after winning and the shame display (slumped shoulders, narrowed chest) after losing, with large effects.

Among sighted athletes the shame display after losing was weaker in those from highly individualistic, self-expression-valuing countries, mainly in North America and West Eurasia, while congenitally blind athletes from a range of countries showed it more strongly than athletes who lost their sight later. The authors read this as sighted athletes in those cultures holding back a shame display they learned to suppress.

1524.content: Belsky, Steinberg and Draper propose an evolutionary theory of socialization with two developmental pathways. In one, a stressful rearing environment brings insecure attachment and behaviour problems in childhood, early puberty and early sexual activity in adolescence, and unstable pair bonds and less investment in children in adulthood; the other pathway runs the opposite way. Each is proposed to favour reproductive success in the setting where it arises.

1525.content: A random-effects meta-analysis of 33 independent effect sizes from studies spanning 1972 to 2012 (70,403 women) found that girls who grew up without their biological father had their first period earlier (weighted mean r = 0.14, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.19, about d = 0.28). Effects varied between studies; there was no sign of publication bias and no decline over the years.

1526.content: In a review of evolutionary explanations for the demographic transition (the fall in family size from the late 19th century, when resources were more plentiful), Borgerhoff Mulder weighs life history trade-offs, cultural evolution and maladaptation to new social conditions. She concludes that empirical analyses and new models point to a reproductive psychology shaped by natural selection to maximize material wealth, which under modern conditions would yield fertility well below the level that would maximize fitness.

1527.content: A systematic review of 18 studies (21 articles, about 50,000 children aged 3 to 12, eight countries) found overall positive effects of risky outdoor play on health. Play where children could go out of adults' sight was linked with more physical activity and better social health in seven of eight papers; in one observation study, children were less likely to play vigorously when an adult was supervising (odds ratios 0.55 and 0.69). Rough-and-tumble play did not increase aggression and went with higher social competence for boys and popular children. The evidence was graded very low to moderate quality, and studies were too varied for a meta-analysis.

In the review's one study of play at height, the height of playground equipment was not related to how often or how badly children broke bones, and no serious head or spine injuries were reported in the year 25,782 children were followed.

1528.content: In a simplified two-reel slot machine task with 40 undergraduate volunteers who did not gamble regularly, near-misses (the reel stopping one position from the winning icon) were rated less pleasant than full misses yet raised the rated wish to continue playing, though both paid nothing. The near-miss effect on wanting to play held only on trials where the player had chosen the icon; with the computer choosing, it was absent. Removing nine moderate gamblers did not change the result.

In a separate fMRI group of 15 volunteers, near-misses activated the ventral striatum and the right anterior insula, the same areas that responded to monetary wins, although near-misses paid nothing. Insula activity to near-misses correlated with each person's rated wish to keep playing and with their score on a questionnaire of gambling-related thinking.

1529.content: In five studies, people who embarrassed more easily reported more prosociality and behaved more generously (Study 1), and observers rated people who showed embarrassment as more prosocial and less antisocial than people who showed another emotion or none (Studies 2 to 5). Observers were also more willing to give resources to embarrassed people and to affiliate with them, and these effects ran through seeing them as prosocial.

1530.content: Forty adolescents were observed with their peers in McDonald's restaurants in Paris and Miami. The American adolescents spent less time leaning against, stroking, kissing and hugging their peers than the French adolescents did, and showed more self-touching and more verbal and physical aggression.
