1531.content: Comparing the lamprey, whose line split from the mammalian line about 560 million years ago, with mammals, Grillner and Robertson find the basal ganglia closely alike in inputs, internal organisation and output projections, including the direct pathway (dopamine D1 receptor neurons that release motor programs) and the indirect pathway (D2 receptor neurons that suppress movement). Transmitters, connections and membrane properties are virtually identical in lamprey and rodent basal ganglia.

The authors propose that the basal ganglia hold a series of modules, each controlling one pattern of behaviour such as locomotion, eye movements, posture or chewing, with a direct pathway that releases that motor program and an indirect pathway that inhibits competing behaviours; phasic dopamine serves value-based decisions and motor learning, and new modules of the same design were added as behaviour diversified.

1532.content: From behavioural observations and interviews among Aka and Bofi foragers of the Central African Republic, the authors conclude that children learn mainly from their parents up to about age 4 or 5, while parents hold them or stay within arm's reach much of the day. Between 5 and 12, learning from other children and from adults other than parents dominates: children spend most of the day in multi-aged child groups, playing or resting, and mostly watch and imitate other children and adults. Adolescents begin to spend more time with adults.

In Boyette's observations, forager children aged 4 to 12 spent 31.4% of the day playing and 37.9% lying around idle; the authors note that forager children are not expected to contribute much to subsistence, whereas children in farming communities are more often given childcare and other tasks.

1533.content: Kaplan and Lancaster, summarizing forager food production and consumption data, report that chimpanzees feed themselves from about age 5, while humans produce less than they consume for some 15 to 22 years depending on the group; human net production is most negative at about age 14, then climbs, and peaks at about 35 to 45 years at roughly five times the chimpanzee peak. They note the same pattern appears to hold among subsistence farmers.

Kaplan and Lancaster report that in societies after the demographic transition higher-earning adults have no more children than lower-earning adults, even in well-controlled studies, while the data available on preindustrial societies consistently show a positive relationship between resources or power and reproductive success. Studies of post-transition societies find either no relationship or a negative one. They add that among men in Albuquerque, New Mexico, the number of grandchildren was highest among the men who had the most children (more than 12), against an observed modal fertility of two.

1534.content: A pooled time-allocation dataset of 690 children and adolescents aged about 3 to 18 (52% girls; 85,597 observations) from twelve hunter-gatherer and mixed-subsistence forager societies found that play took a large share of early childhood (9 to 58% of observations, by society) and fell with age. Work in middle childhood varied widely between societies (childcare 1 to 10%, food production 1 to 26%, domestic work 3 to 20%), and adolescents spent more time than middle-childhood children on food production (21 vs 11%) and household work (19 vs 12%). Boys did less childcare than girls (1 vs 4%).

In the same dataset, children living where dangerous animals were denser or drinking water was scarcer did less childcare and domestic work, while food production and play did not differ by this risk; climate and plant productivity did not strongly predict children's work, and gender differences in children's activities were larger where men supplied more of the food.

1535.content: McCullough, Kurzban and Tabak propose that humans have an evolved revenge system that deters exploitation by imposing costs on an aggressor, and a second system that restores valuable relationships after harm by inhibiting revenge and motivating signals of goodwill toward the harmdoer. Both systems are proposed to run on two estimates: the risk that the harmdoer will exploit one again, and the expected future value of the relationship with the harmdoer.

1536.content: In two cross-sectional studies in the US (120 undergraduates; 384 adults recruited online), participants scored their addictive-like eating on the Yale Food Addiction Scale and then picked or rated which of 35 foods they had such problems with. Among the undergraduates the ten foods picked most often were all highly processed with added fat and refined carbohydrate or sugar (for example chocolate, pizza, cake), and thirteen unprocessed foods made up the bottom of the list. In the online sample, being highly processed was a large positive predictor of a food being rated problematic (average rating 2.89 against 2.24 on a 1 to 7 scale, d = 1.44), and fat content and glycemic load were each large positive predictors.

1537.content: In a randomized 2 x 2 crossover feeding trial in England, 55 adults (BMI 25 to 40, habitually eating at least half their calories as ultra-processed food) were given two 8-week ad libitum diets that both followed the UK Eatwell Guide, one minimally processed and one ultra-processed, delivered to their homes. Both diets produced weight loss, and weight loss was larger on the minimally processed diet: 2.06 percent against 1.05 percent of body weight, a difference of 1.01 percentage points (95% CI 0.14 to 1.87, P = 0.024; intention-to-treat n = 50). Weight, BMI and fat mass fell more on the minimally processed diet, as did triglycerides and the cravings participants rated; LDL cholesterol fell more on the ultra-processed diet.

1538.content: Food sharing between households was tracked in six Agta camps (Philippines, 319 people) and three Mbendjele BaYaka camps (Republic of Congo, 103 people). Each household did most of its sharing with a few others: 88.3 percent of Agta and 89.1 percent of Mbendjele household sharing went to just three other households. Network analysis found three nested levels: the household (mean about 6 people among the Agta, 5 among the Mbendjele), sharing clusters of 3 to 4 households (about 23 and 15 people), and the camp (about 63 and 41 people). Larger camps held more clusters, not larger ones.

In the same Agta and Mbendjele camps, genealogies covering 19,949 Agta and 4,934 Mbendjele pairs showed that people were most closely related to their own household (mean r 0.39 among the Agta, 0.33 among the Mbendjele), less to their sharing cluster (about 0.08 to 0.10) and least to the wider camp (about 0.04). Ties between children and grandparents, and between children and aunts and uncles, fell inside the household or cluster more often than chance.

1539.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of lowland Bolivia, production and consumption by age showed that people consume more calories than they produce until their late teens; surplus production then rises to a peak in the mid-40s. With dependent children to feed, nuclear families run a net calorie deficit until the parents are about 40. Of 195 families in the production sample, 53 percent produced less than their estimated needs, and at least 20 percent of families of any age and number of dependents would run a deficit without sharing.

In interviews with Tsimane adults, 75 percent (508 of 673) said they had been too sick to get out of bed at least once in the past three months, with episodes lasting on average 8.7 days. In most of these episodes the sick person received food, help with childcare and help feeding the family, and in 39 percent medicinal plants; spouses gave the most help, then children and parents, and kin gave the great majority of it.

1540.content: Abstract only. In a randomized open-label crossover study at the University of Tokyo Hospital, nine overweight or obese Japanese men ate ultra-processed or non-ultra-processed meals, designed to be matched for total energy and macronutrients and eaten as much as they wanted, for 1 week each with a 2-week washout. During the ultra-processed week they gained 1.1 kg more (95% CI 0.2 to 2.0) and ate 813.5 kcal more per day (95% CI 342.4 to 1284.7) than during the non-ultra-processed week, and the number of chews per calorie was lower.

1541.content: Abstract only. In a cross-sectional study of 168 Australian adults (mean age 53) from the 2004-2005 AusDiab study, accelerometers worn for seven days counted every interruption of sedentary time. Independent of total sedentary time and of moderate-to-vigorous activity, more breaks went with smaller waist circumference (standardized beta -0.16), lower BMI (-0.19), lower triglycerides (-0.18) and lower 2-hour plasma glucose (-0.18).

1542.content: Abstract only. In monkeys (species not named in the abstract), the authors report changes in the brain opioid system contingent on grooming, measured as beta-endorphin in cerebrospinal fluid. Giving an opioid receptor blocker increased the monkeys' motivation to be groomed, and giving morphine decreased it. The authors read this as brain opioids mediating social attachment.

1543.content: Abstract only. On Kitava, Trobriand Islands, Papua New Guinea, people kept a subsistence diet of tubers, fruit, fish and coconut with no Western foods. Of about 1,816 inhabitants older than 3 years, 125 were estimated to be 60 to 96 years old. In semi-structured interviews with 213 adults aged 20 to 96 about sudden death, exertion-related chest pain, one-sided paralysis, loss of speech and sudden imbalance, no case of stroke, sudden death or angina was described. Resting ECGs in 171 people showed Minnesota Code items in 14, unrelated to age, sex or smoking. The authors conclude that stroke and ischaemic heart disease appear to be absent.

1544.content: Abstract only. Among the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania the diet falls into five main categories: tubers, berries, meat, baobab and honey. Shown photographs, Hadza ranked honey highest and tubers lowest. Tubers were the most continuously available and least preferred food, and were taken more often when berries were least available. Controlling for region and season, women of reproductive age had higher percent body fat in camps where more meat arrived and lower percent body fat where more tubers were taken.

1545.content: Abstract only. Ten middle-aged, overweight Aboriginal Australians with diabetes from the Mowanjum Community (Derby, Western Australia) were tested before and after living for 7 weeks as hunter-gatherers in their traditional country. All lost weight steadily (average 8 kg) on a low energy intake (about 1,200 kcal per person per day), 64 percent of it from animal food but only 13 percent from fat. Fasting glucose fell from 11.6 to 6.6 mM, glucose clearance after an oral glucose load improved, fasting insulin fell from 23 to 12 mU/L, and fasting triglycerides fell from 4.0 to 1.2 mM.

1546.content: Abstract only. Human hairy skin has two touch systems: fast myelinated fibres and slow unmyelinated C-tactile fibres that respond to light touch. In a unique patient lacking large myelinated fibres, activating the C-tactile fibres produced a faint sensation of pleasant touch, and fMRI during this stimulation showed activation of the insular region and none in the somatosensory areas S1 and S2. The authors identify C-tactile fibres as a system for limbic touch that may underlie emotional, hormonal and affiliative responses to caress-like skin-to-skin contact.

1547.content: Abstract only. In Copenhagen, ten healthy, nonexercising young men cut their daily walking from a mean of 10,501 to 1,344 steps a day for 2 weeks. Measured before and after with hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps, muscle biopsies and fitness tests, the glucose infusion rate during the clamp fell by 17 percent, reflecting lower insulin sensitivity in muscle with no change in liver glucose output; maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) fell by 7 percent; and lean mass of the legs fell, while arms and trunk did not change.

1548.content: Abstract only. Nine healthy young men in Copenhagen (age 24, BMI 21.6) cut their walking from 10,000 to 1,500 steps a day and ate 50 percent more calories for 14 days. Body weight had risen by days 7 and 14, visceral fat had risen by day 14, the insulin response to an oral glucose load had risen by days 7 and 14, and insulin sensitivity had fallen by day 3. Leptin and adiponectin rose, while inflammatory markers did not change. At day 30, weight and body fat were still raised, while insulin sensitivity was back to baseline.

1549.content: Abstract only. Video recordings of naturally occurring interactions in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Scotland and Ireland were coded for interpersonal distance, body orientation and touch. More touch was observed among Italian and Greek pairs than among English, French and Dutch pairs, which partly fits the expected split between contact cultures of southern Europe and noncontact cultures of northern Europe. Mixed-sex pairs faced each other less directly with age, and male pairs more directly.

1550.content: Abstract only. A meta-analysis of randomized monoamine depletion studies (MEDLINE and EMBASE to October 2006) found 73 acute tryptophan depletion, 2 PCPA, 10 phenylalanine/tyrosine depletion and 8 AMPT studies, of which 45 and 8 could be pooled. Lowering serotonin, or noradrenaline and dopamine, did not lower mood in healthy controls. It lowered mood slightly in healthy people with a family history of major depressive disorder (MDD), the studies' diagnostic label, and moderately (tryptophan depletion only) in drug-free patients diagnosed with MDD now in remission. In patients in remission who were taking serotonergic antidepressants, tryptophan depletion brought back symptoms. The authors conclude that depletion studies fail to show a causal relation between these transmitters and the diagnosed condition.

1551.content: In a review of taste-aversion experiments in rats and people, Garcia and colleagues report that an animal acquires an aversion to the taste of a meal followed by illness in a single trial, and rarely needs more than three to five, even though the illness comes hours later; they contrast this with the learning that occurs when visual and auditory signals are followed by pain, and report that limbic lesions disrupt conditioning to a buzzer followed by shock while helping conditioning to a taste followed by illness.
Garcia and colleagues report that people develop aversions to a food eaten before an illness even when they know that the food was not the source of the illness.

1552.content: In a human conditioning experiment with shock, Hugdahl and Ohman conditioned skin conductance responses to fear-relevant and fear-irrelevant pictures; when half of the volunteers were then told that no more shocks would come, the instruction completely abolished responding to the fear-irrelevant pictures and left responses to the fear-relevant pictures unaffected. In a second experiment, an instruction that threatened shock raised responses to fear-relevant pictures significantly more than responses to fear-irrelevant ones.

1553.content: In a nationally representative online survey of 6,251 US adults (Pew Research Center's American Trends Panel, 26 February to 11 March 2018), about three in ten said they knew all or most of their neighbours: 40% of rural residents, 28% of suburban residents and 24% of urban residents. Among adults aged 18 to 29, 15% in cities and 18% in suburbs said so.

1554.content: The UN Population Division estimates that 55 per cent of the world's population lived in urban areas in 2018, against 30 per cent in 1950, and projects 68 per cent for 2050. Close to half of urban dwellers lived in settlements of fewer than 500,000 people, and about one in eight lived in the 33 megacities of more than 10 million; a further 48 large cities had 5 to 10 million inhabitants.

1555.content: In two experiments, observer rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) watched, for 12 sessions, videotapes of model monkeys behaving fearfully that had been spliced so the models appeared to react either to fear-relevant stimuli (toy snakes or a toy crocodile) or to fear-irrelevant stimuli (flowers or a toy rabbit). The observers acquired a fear of the toy snakes and the toy crocodile and did not acquire a fear of the flowers or the toy rabbit.

1556.content: In field experiments, commuters on trains and on buses were instructed to connect with a stranger near them, to stay disconnected, or to commute as normal; in both settings those who connected reported a more positive, and no less productive, commute than those who did not. Separate commuters asked to predict the outcome expected the opposite, a more positive commute in solitude, and the authors trace this partly to underestimating others' interest in talking.

1557.content: In a two-scan PET study (11C-raclopride) of 16 people with Parkinson's disease, the eight who used their dopamine drugs compulsively and met the authors' DSM-IV criteria for substance dependence (labelled dopamine dysregulation syndrome) showed greater ventral striatal dopamine release after an oral dose of levodopa than eight levodopa-treated controls. In these patients the size of the release correlated with self-reported 'wanting' of the drug and not with 'liking', and went with more punding (repetitive, purposeless activity).

1558.content: Fanselow's review describes the predatory imminence continuum, a term he and Lester coined, which runs from no threat to fatal contact with a predator and holds three defensive modes: pre-encounter defense when an animal leaves safety and no predator has been detected (changed foraging, vigilance; rats take fewer, larger meals), post-encounter defense once a predator is detected (freezing, with foraging suppressed), and circa-strike defense when contact is imminent. Field observations show that flight distance is not fixed: Thomson's gazelles let a hyena come nearer than a lion, and flee sooner from the faster cheetah.

Fanselow reports that house mice (Mus musculus) given 10 unsignalled, inescapable footshocks spread over an hour later showed more defense in all three modes (less open-field exploration, more freezing after one-trial context conditioning, a larger burst of activity to a sudden noise), and that rats (Rattus norvegicus) given a similar shock block still showed enhanced one-trial fear conditioning three months later. He reads this as a lasting distortion of the continuum, in which defensive responses intrude into periods when the level of threat does not warrant them.

1559.content: Adults were randomly assigned to an escapable shock task, a yoked inescapable shock task with identical shocks, or no stressor; a week later all underwent fear conditioning and extinction with skin conductance, and an extinction test the next day (59 analysed: 20, 20 and 19). The inescapable group showed impaired extinction learning and more fear expression the next day; the escapable group showed better extinction and no spontaneous return of fear.

1560.content: Haselton and Nettle argue from signal detection and error management theory that where judgments are made under uncertainty and the costs of false positive and false negative errors were asymmetric over evolutionary history, selection favours a bias toward the less costly error. For hazards, misses usually cost more than false alarms, and they list biases of this kind that guard against harm: approaching sounds judged to arrive too early, fear easily elicited by snakes and spiders, easy inferences that a person is dangerous, avoidance of any food linked to sickness, and avoidance of people with physical afflictions.

1561.content: In a review of studies since the 1970s, Hennessy, Kaiser and Sachser report many cases across species in which the presence of a social companion moderates the stress-hormone (HPA axis) response to stressors, and also many cases in which this social buffering is not seen. They conclude that the nature of the relationship between the individuals is crucial, with further roles for the social organisation of the species, previous experience, sex, integration into a social unit and developmental stage.

1562.content: Reviewing animal and human studies, Hostinar, Sullivan and Gunnar describe social buffering as a dampened stress-hormone (HPA axis) response to threat or challenge in the presence or with the help of a member of one's own species, seen across species. In human infants they find little evidence of buffering of the cortisol response early in the first year and reliable effects repeatedly documented by its end; in adults, support from a romantic partner before a public-speaking stress task lowered the cortisol response of men, a result since replicated, and did not do so for women in the first study.

1563.content: In a longitudinal study of 24 day-care and 28 home-reared infants, fretting or crying during two minutes alone in an unfamiliar room after the mother left was measured every two months from 3.5 to 13.5 months and at 20 months. Both groups showed the same age course, with sharp drops in the time to crying and marked rises in crying at 9.5 and 13.5 months.

1564.content: Among 185 infants in rural Bangladesh, assessed at their mothers' departure, separation protest peaked around the end of the first year despite poor health and nutrition, the same peak the authors say has been documented for healthier samples in several cultural contexts; healthier infants were more likely to protest, and in the first half year there was an extra rise and fall in distress at departure, in which poorer health went with more upset.

1565.content: In two online experiments (80 adults judging within-person, 200 adults between groups), listeners judged sounds approaching them as moving faster than equivalent sounds moving away, discriminated the speeds of approaching sounds and not of receding ones, and judged close sounds as faster than distant ones (Experiment 1: close 40.6 against distant 30.8 metres per second on average; close approaching 45.9 against close receding 35.2). Neuhoff summarises earlier work in which listeners asked to predict the arrival of an approaching sound judge it to have arrived while it is still some distance away.

1566.content: In the first of four experiments, both men and women underestimated the time to arrival of approaching sounds, more strongly among women; in the others women also judged approaching sounds that stopped short of them as closer than men did, while no sex difference appeared for sounds moving away.

1567.content: A meta-analysis of 293 independent studies (319 articles, 18,941 participants) of psychological stress and the human immune system found that acute laboratory stressors lasting minutes went with upregulation of some parameters of natural immunity and downregulation of some functions of specific immunity; brief real-life stressors such as exams went with suppressed cellular immunity and preserved humoral immunity; and chronic stressors (such as dementia caregiving, living with a handicap and unemployment) went with suppression of both cellular and humoral measures, with reliable decreases in almost all functional immune measures examined. People's own reports of stress generally did not go with immune change.

1568.content: Slavich and Irwin propose a social signal transduction theory: experiences of social threat and adversity up-regulate parts of the immune system involved in inflammation, and the proinflammatory cytokines can in turn bring on what the authors list as depressive symptoms (sad mood, anhedonia, fatigue, psychomotor retardation and social withdrawal). They argue that this conserved response is vital during actual physical threat or injury and is also set off by modern social, symbolic or imagined threats.

Slavich and Irwin report a laboratory study in which people who gave a speech and did mental arithmetic before socially rejecting raters (the Trier Social Stress Test) showed greater stimulated production of the inflammatory cytokine TNF-alpha and greater glucocorticoid resistance than people who did the same tasks without the raters, although both groups judged the tasks equally challenging and controllable; those who felt more evaluated showed larger TNF-alpha increases.

1569.content: Among Mbendjele BaYaka foragers in three camps in Congo (97 adults played a honey stick gift game), people who received more gift nominations from camp members (relational wealth) received food from more camp members in observed food transfers (beta 0.24, p 0.005, n 53) and had a higher body mass index, in men (beta 0.53, p 0.032, n 39) and in women (beta 0.90, p 0.003, n 34).

Among Mbendjele BaYaka women, relational wealth from the gift game went with higher age-specific fertility (beta 0.19, p 0.010, n 49). Relational wealth was not correlated with a woman's current number of dependent children (G 0.14, p 0.280, n 51), which the authors read as relational wealth affecting fertility rather than need attracting gifts; they call the result preliminary because the two measures cover different time spans.

Among the BaYaka, an adult's relational wealth correlated with the father's relational wealth (gamma 0.65, p 0.002, n 14) and not significantly with the mother's (gamma 0.17, p 0.294, n 26). The authors read this as partial heritability, through genes or through alliances passed from parents to children, in a society without inherited rank.

1570.content: In a web-based survey answered by over 40,000 people, photographs of objects that carry a potential disease threat were rated as significantly more disgusting than similar photographs with little or no disease relevance, and the pattern held in every region of the world.

In the same survey of over 40,000 people, women reported higher disgust sensitivity than men, disgust sensitivity declined steadily with age, and the bodily fluids of strangers were rated more disgusting than those of close relatives.

1571.content: Diamond proposes a model in which the evolved processes behind sexual desire and behind affectional bonding (falling in love) are functionally independent, bonding is not built to aim at one sex, and love and desire still influence each other in both directions, especially among women. The model explains why people sometimes fall in love with partners outside their sexual orientation, and she supports it with social-psychological, historical and cross-cultural research and with work on mammalian mating and bonding.

1573.content: Fletcher and colleagues review evidence from several disciplines and conclude that romantic love works as an evolved commitment device for pair-bonding: their review finds it universal, finds that it damps mate-search mechanisms, that it has specific behavioural, hormonal and brain signatures, and that it goes with better health and survival. They argue that pair-bonding helped provide the heavy investment human children need, and that romantic love, pair-bonding and alloparenting played critical roles in human evolution.

1574.content: A systematic review of human brain imaging studies of sexual behaviour finds that the brain networks for sex are comparable to those for other rewards and follow the same phases of wanting, liking and satiety; the studies map networks for sexual wanting (motivation, anticipation) and sexual liking (arousal, consummation), with very little data on satiety or the period after orgasm. The authors conclude that nothing in the brain mechanisms for sex looks special compared with other pleasures.

1575.content: In an fMRI incentive delay task, 28 heterosexual men in Poland who sought treatment for problematic pornography use (PPU), as the authors label it, and 24 heterosexual men without it saw cues that announced either an erotic picture or a money reward. The PPU group showed more ventral striatum activation to cues announcing erotic pictures (t 2.62, p 0.011) and no difference for cues announcing money (p 0.963), and reacted fastest on erotic trials. The two groups did not differ in striatal response to the erotic pictures themselves.

In the same study, the two groups did not differ in how pleasant they rated the rewards (F 0.187, p 0.667). Across men, a larger striatal response to erotic cues relative to money cues went with relatively faster responding on erotic trials (R 0.76) and with higher scores on the SAST-R scale (rho 0.31), more pornography use per week (rho 0.305) and more masturbation per week (rho 0.296), as reported by the men. The striatal response to the erotic pictures themselves (the authors' relative-liking index) showed none of these links.

1576.content: In a study of 167 couples, with partners' physical attractiveness rated by coders, couples were more alike in attractiveness when they had known each other for a short time before dating and had not been friends first. The longer partners had known each other before they started dating, the less matched they were on looks. The authors tie this to weaker agreement on who is desirable once people know each other better.

1577.content: In one experiment, 128 people aged 17 to 62 ranked how interesting they found 12 tabloid stories about celebrities of different ages and sexes; in a second, 83 college students ranked interest in, and their likelihood of spreading, 12 gossip scenarios about professors, relatives, friends, acquaintances and strangers. Both showed most interest in gossip about people of the same age and sex as the reader, and damaging news about non-allies and good news about allies was the most prized and the most likely to be passed on.

1578.content: Using three-wave General Social Survey panel data (2006 to 2014) on married Americans, with entropy balancing and logistic regression, the probability of divorce by the next wave roughly doubled for those who began pornography use between waves (2,120 people, odds ratio 2.19), for women and men alike. Stopping pornography use between waves went with a lower probability of divorce for women only. The link between starting pornography use and divorce was strongest among younger people, the less religious, and those who reported greater marital happiness at the start.

1579.content: In 40 online sessions, 785 people recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk played repeated cooperation games on networks under four randomly assigned conditions: links reshuffled at random every round, links fixed, links open to change for 10 percent of pairs a round (viscous), or for 30 percent of pairs a round (fluid). Cooperation declined over the rounds with random, fixed and viscous networks, and held steady only in the fluid condition, which had significantly more cooperation than the other conditions in rounds 7 to 11 (p 0.006).

In the fluid condition, players were more likely to form new links with people who had cooperated in the previous round and to break links with people who had defected (both p below 0.001), and they almost never broke links with cooperators. Defectors who had links broken were more likely to switch to cooperating, while cooperators' behaviour did not change when links were broken.

1580.content: In the nationally representative US General Social Survey (26,620 adults, 1989 to 2014), American adults reported having sex about nine fewer times a year in the early 2010s than in the late 1990s. Part of the drop came from a larger share of people without a partner; reported frequency also fell among the partnered (married or living together) while it stayed steady among the unpartnered. In age, period and cohort analyses the decline sat mainly with birth cohort: those born in the 1930s had sex most often and those born in the 1990s least.

In the same survey data, the drop in reported sexual frequency was similar across gender, race, region, education and work status, and was largest among people in their 50s, those with school-age children and those who did not watch pornography. The decline was not linked to longer working hours or to increased pornography use. Americans in their 20s reported sex about 80 times a year, those in their 60s about 20.

1581.content: A meta-analysis of 22 general-population studies from 7 countries found that pornography consumption was associated with committing actual acts of sexual aggression, in the United States and in other countries, among males and females, and in both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies. Associations were stronger for verbal than for physical sexual aggression, though both were significant, and the pattern suggested that violent content may add to the association.

1582.content: A meta-analysis of experimental, correlational and population studies of pornography and sexual aggression from the 1970s on found methodological weaknesses very common. Nonviolent pornography was not associated with sexual aggression, longitudinal evidence was particularly weak, and violent pornography was weakly correlated with sexual aggression in a way the evidence could not separate from selection. Studies using more best practices found less evidence of a link, and population studies suggested that greater availability of pornography goes with less sexual aggression at the population level.

1583.content: Using data from the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, Apostolou tested whether parental control of mate choice, already documented for foraging societies, also describes agricultural and pastoral societies. He reports support for two hypotheses: parents have more control over their offspring's choice of spouse in non-foraging societies than among foragers, and fathers hold greater decision-making power in agropastoral societies than in hunting and gathering ones.

1584.content: In 22 heterosexual men tested in Cambridge, England, diagnosed by a psychiatrist with compulsive sexual behaviour (CSB) and 40 age-matched male volunteers, a choice task first made some images familiar and then offered familiar versus new images: undressed women, dressed women and neutral objects. There was a group by image-type interaction (p 0.035) and no overall group difference; men with CSB preferred new over familiar images more for the sexual images than for the object images (p 0.039), while volunteers showed their novelty preference for dressed women over objects (p 0.024).

In 20 men with CSB and 20 volunteers scanned with fMRI while sexual images were repeated, activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate fell off faster across repeats of sexual images, relative to money images, in the CSB group; across all men, faster fall-off went with a stronger preference for new sexual images in the choice task.

1585.content: In a cooperation game with 54 Cornell University students (31 women, 23 men), each person played three conditions: giving to a partner when a future partner would not see the gift, when a future partner would see it but be assigned at random, and when a future partner would see it and could choose between two givers. People gave more when watched (p 0.001) and more still when they could be chosen (p 0.021), and the higher giver was chosen 17 times out of 18. After pairing, when giving could no longer win a partner, most gave nothing.

In the same experiment, once people had been paired with a chosen or assigned partner and their giving could no longer affect being chosen, the median gift was zero in all conditions. Those who gave in order to be chosen gave little afterwards, so much of the generosity shown to attract a partner was not kept up; even so, choosers almost always picked the higher giver.

1586.content: Seventeen people who were deeply in love were scanned with fMRI while viewing photos of their partner and, for comparison, of three friends matched for age, sex and length of friendship. Viewing the partner raised activity in the medial insula and anterior cingulate cortex and, below the cortex, in the caudate nucleus and putamen, on both sides, and lowered activity in the posterior cingulate gyrus, the amygdala and, on the right, prefrontal, parietal and middle temporal cortex. The authors read the combination as a network distinct from those found in earlier studies of emotion.

1587.content: In one Tsimane forager-horticulturalist village in lowland Bolivia, 12 villagers ranked all resident adults from photographs on political influence (whose voice carries most weight in community debates), project leadership and respect. Among 142 children of 47 mothers and 47 fathers, measured by project physicians 342 times between 2012 and 2016, maternal political influence went with better growth (weight-for-age B 0.33, height-for-age B 0.32, weight-for-height B 0.24, standardised) and lower odds of any common illness (adjusted odds ratio 0.48), adjusting for parents' age, height, weight, schooling, income, number of births and kin in the village. The model puts children of high-influence mothers (75th percentile) at 40 percent with any common illness against 64 percent for children of low-influence mothers (25th percentile); the associations were stronger under age 5.

In the same Tsimane sample, fathers' political influence was not associated with child growth once mothers' influence and the control variables were in the model, and its link with fewer child illnesses when tested alone shrank or disappeared when mothers' influence was added. Women's influence was unrelated to their number of births for their age, unlike the status and fertility link reported for men.

1588.content: In a randomised trial, low-SES inner-city mothers of newborns were given either a soft baby carrier (more physical contact, n = 23) or an infant seat (less contact, n = 26). At 3.5 months, mothers given carriers were more contingently responsive to their infants' vocalisations in a play session, and at 13 months significantly more infants in the carrier group were classified as securely attached in the Ainsworth Strange Situation.

1589.content: A meta-analysis of 84 studies published in the 1990s found 13 significant predictors of postpartum depression as measured in the pooled studies. Ten had moderate mean effect sizes against the scored outcome: prenatal depression (0.44 to 0.46), self-esteem (0.45 to 0.47), childcare stress (0.45 to 0.46), prenatal anxiety (0.41 to 0.45), life stress (0.38 to 0.40), social support (0.36 to 0.41), the marital relationship (0.38 to 0.39), history of previous depression (0.38 to 0.39), infant temperament (0.33 to 0.34) and maternity blues (0.25 to 0.31). Marital status, socioeconomic status and unplanned or unwanted pregnancy had small effects.

1590.content: Daly and Wilson use homicide as an assay of conflict, since it has little reporting bias. On evolutionary models, genetic relatedness should go with less conflict, and the authors report that various analyses of homicide data support this. Most family homicides are spousal homicides, which they attribute to male sexual proprietariness. For conflict between parents and offspring, the model's expectations about how the risk of violence varies with the ages, sexes and other traits of the people involved held in tests with data on infanticides, parricides and filicides.

1591.content: In domestic guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus), single injections of low morphine doses (0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 mg/kg) significantly reduced the separation distress vocalisations of infants in a dose-dependent way, and the opioid blocker naloxone (1 mg/kg) reliably increased separation distress vocalisations in juveniles and adults. The authors read separation distress as alleviated by morphine and made stronger by naloxone, much like opiate withdrawal.

In the same guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) study, morphine at higher doses (1.0, 2.5 and 5.0 mg/kg) significantly reduced the time offspring spent keeping close to their mother. The authors suggest opiates may take over a function that the body's own endorphins normally serve in reinforcing attachment.

1592.content: Reviewing his laboratory's experiments on infant rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) separated from their mothers, Hofer reports that discrete sensorimotor, thermal and nutrient-based events within the mother-infant interaction have long-term regulatory effects on specific parts of the infant's physiology and behaviour, and that release from all of these regulators at once during separation produces the patterned response to loss. He reports evidence for similar early regulatory processes in monkey and human mother-infant interactions, and long-term effects of loss, and of selective replacement of regulators, on later development and vulnerability to disease.

1593.content: In a nationally representative US cohort of 373,189 elderly married couples drawn from Medicare records and followed from 1993 to 2002, the death of a wife was associated with an 18 percent higher all-cause mortality for the surviving husband (hazard ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.19) and the death of a husband with a 16 percent higher mortality for the surviving wife (HR 1.16, 1.14 to 1.17), adjusting for covariates including physician-recorded baseline health of both spouses. The rise ran across almost all causes of death of the survivor, including cancers, infections and all four categories of cardiovascular disease.

In the same US cohort, the excess mortality after a spouse's death depended on how the spouse died. Men's risk rose more than 20 percent when their wives died of lung cancer, infections or sepsis, COPD, other heart or vascular disease, or diabetes; women's rose more than 20 percent only after a husband's death from COPD or from influenza or pneumonia. The only survivors with no statistically significant rise were those whose spouse died of Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease.

1594.content: Fieldwork in West Turkana, Kenya, found Lomekwi 3, a 3.3-million-year-old archaeological site where stone artefacts lie in place together with Pliocene hominin fossils in a wooded palaeoenvironment. The makers combined core reduction (knapping flakes off a core) with battering, showing a developing grasp of how stone fractures. The authors name the industry the Lomekwian and state that it predates the Oldowan by 700,000 years.

1595.content: Reviewing the Lomekwi 3 finds, Lewis and Harmand state that the 3.3-million-year-old tools push back the known archaeological record by 700,000 years and place stone knapping half a million years before the earliest known fossils of the genus Homo (2.8 million years). The only hominins known in the region at 3.3 million years are Australopithecus afarensis and Kenyanthropus platyops, and the authors judge most plausible that stone tool making was not limited to Homo and grew out of the stone handling and tool use of earlier primates.

1596.content: Lieberman and colleagues propose the active grandparent hypothesis: humans were selected to live several decades past reproduction while staying moderately physically active, gathering and hunting surplus food for children and grandchildren. They hypothesise that this selection favoured two energy allocation pathways, activity diverting energy away from excess fat storage and reproductive tissue and activity stimulating repair and maintenance, which together slow senescence and lower vulnerability to chronic disease, so that long healthy lifespans are both a cause and an effect of habitual activity.

Citing earlier studies, Lieberman and colleagues report that Hadza hunter-gatherer adults average 15,800 steps (about 9 to 15 km) and 135 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity a day, against 4,774 steps and under 30 minutes for the average American adult. Postreproductive Hadza women forage about 6 hours a day, 20 percent more than younger mothers. Daily steps of older Americans fall by about half between ages 40 and 70, while Hadza daily walking distance declines only modestly with age, and hunter-gatherer walking speed, grip strength and VO2max decline less with age than in Westerners.

1597.content: A meta-analysis of studies on organisational volunteering by adults aged 55 and over found that volunteers had on average a 47 percent lower mortality risk in unadjusted comparisons (95% CI 38 to 55 percent) and a 24 percent lower risk after adjusting for other variables such as health (95% CI 16 to 31 percent). Preliminary interaction results suggested the inverse link was stronger where public religiosity was higher.

1598.content: Fieldwork at Gona, Ethiopia, from 1992 to 1994 with radioisotopic dating and magnetic polarity stratigraphy dated Oldowan stone tools securely to between 2.6 and 2.5 million years ago, which made them the oldest known artefacts at the time of publication. The artefacts show controlled stone fracture equal to much younger Early Pleistocene Oldowan assemblages, which the authors read as a long period of technological stasis.

109.content: Comparing death certificates for Roseto, a homogeneous Italian-American town in Pennsylvania, with neighbouring Bangor from 1935 to 1985 (age-standardised rates per decade), the authors found that Rosetans had a lower death rate from myocardial infarction for the first 30 years; it then rose to Bangor's level after a period in which traditionally cohesive family and community relationships eroded, mainly among younger Rosetan men and elderly women. Earlier studies had placed the end of the difference in the 1960s, as Roseto became more Americanised.

1599.content: Using records from Roseto and neighbouring Bangor, Pennsylvania, reaching back in some cases to 1925 (marriages, population composition, organisational memberships, voting patterns and social class indicators), the authors report that community changes which sped up in the 1960s coincided with Roseto's loss of its lower death rate from coronary heart disease after 1965, and propose that these changes may help explain it.

1600.content: Aiello restates the expensive tissue hypothesis from Aiello and Wheeler 1995. Brain tissue uses over 22 times the energy of the same mass of muscle, yet across mammals relative brain size does not track basal metabolic rate. For a standard 65 kg human, the brain is about 850 g larger than expected for a primate of that size and the gastro-intestinal tract about 781 g smaller, only about 60 percent of the expected mass, so the combined mass of the expensive organs (4.40 kg) is close to the primate expectation (4.45 kg). Across 18 primate species relative brain size and relative gut size were negatively correlated (r = -0.69). She argues that a high-quality, easily digested diet allowed the smaller gut and so released the brain to grow, with the marked increase shortly after 2.0 million years ago in Homo ergaster.

1601.content: Testing the expensive tissue hypothesis with brain and organ mass data from 100 mammal species, including 23 primates, the authors found that, controlling for fat-free body mass, brain size was not negatively correlated with the mass of the digestive tract or of any other expensive organ, and state that this refutes the hypothesis. Brain size and the size of fat depots were negatively correlated, which they read as encephalisation and fat storage being alternative buffers against starvation, combinable where fat storage does not unduly hamper locomotion.

1602.content: In a habituated troop of wild chacma baboons (Papio hamadryas ursinus) in the Okavango Delta, Botswana, faecal glucocorticoid levels of 22 females who lost a close relative (mother, maternal sibling or offspring) to observed or suspected predation rose significantly in the month after the death compared with the month before, while matched control females showed no rise. By the second month the levels were back to baseline (n = 15 with samples).

In the same baboon (Papio hamadryas ursinus) troop, 14 females who lost a close adult female relative did not groom less afterwards: over the three months after the death they groomed more partners (on average 1.86 before against 3.79 after), spread their grooming more evenly and groomed at a higher rate, while 14 matched controls showed no such changes. The authors read this as the bereaved females broadening and strengthening their grooming networks, perhaps the reason their stress hormones soon returned to baseline.

1603.content: In captive female rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), researchers set dominance rank experimentally: 45 adult females were introduced one by one into nine new groups of five, earlier arrival predicting higher rank, and after a year the groups were rebuilt so that many females changed rank. Low rank brought more harassment and less grooming. In sorted immune cells, rank changed the expression of 1,676 genes in natural killer cells and 284 in helper T cells, with genes of the innate immune and cytokine response higher in low-ranking females, a pro-inflammatory profile. The rank effects in phase one and phase two pointed the same way even though the females' ranks had been scrambled, so the expression followed the current rank.

In the same rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), blood cells challenged with bacterial lipopolysaccharide showed a stronger overall response in low-ranking females, with twice as many rank-responsive genes after the challenge (3,494) as without it (1,799). Low-ranking females leaned toward the pro-inflammatory, antibacterial NF-kB pathway and high-ranking females toward the antiviral interferon pathway. Grooming received mediated the rank effect for 33.4% of rank-responsive genes in natural killer cells, more than harassment did, so the authors write that a lack of positive social contact may matter as much as subordination itself.

1604.content: Sugiyama and Sugiyama propose that the risk of illness and injury selected for a drive to become valued by others by providing them, generously and repeatedly, with goods or services that are hard to get elsewhere, because beneficiaries then give costly care to their benefactor when the benefactor is sick or injured. They call the pursuit of such a hard-to-replace role social niche specialization, name meat-sharing as one documented niche, and present cross-cultural evidence that people also cultivate information and tool production as niches that buffer health risk.

1605.content: Among Hadza foragers of Tanzania, food preferences were elicited with photographs of species from the five major food categories of their diet: honey, meat, berries, baobab and tubers. Men and women agreed on the rank of three categories; women ranked berries second and meat fourth, while men ranked meat second and berries fourth, and the authors set this against the fact that the sexes target different foods.

1606.content: A review published by the Association for Psychological Science, weighting objective outcome measures over what people said of themselves, found that the modest correlations between self-esteem and school performance do not show that self-esteem leads to good performance; high self-esteem is partly the result of good results. Efforts to boost pupils' self-esteem were not shown to improve academic performance and may sometimes backfire. The authors found no evidence that boosting self-esteem by therapeutic interventions or school programmes brings benefits, and they do not support continued widespread efforts to raise it in the hope that it will by itself improve outcomes.

The same review reports that people high in self-esteem claim to be more likeable and attractive, to have better relationships and to make better impressions than people low in self-esteem, but objective measures disconfirm most of these beliefs, and self-esteem has not been shown to predict the quality or duration of relationships. The two benefits the authors do find are greater initiative and pleasant feelings: self-esteem is strongly related to happiness, and high self-esteem helps people persist after failure.

1607.content: Klinenberg, citing the national figures compiled for his book Going Solo, writes that until the middle of the 20th century no society sustained large numbers of people living alone for long periods. Today one-person households account for more than 40% of all households in Sweden and Finland, more than one third in France, Germany and England, and more than one quarter in the United States, Russia, Canada, Spain and Japan.

Klinenberg separates three conditions that he says are often conflated: living alone, being socially isolated and feeling lonely. Living alone does not necessarily bring the other two: survey data show that Americans who live alone, on average, spend more time with friends and neighbours and volunteer in civic organisations more often than married people, and many of the more than 300 people he interviewed said nothing had made them lonelier than a bad marriage.

1608.content: In an online survey of 1,746 adults during COVID-19 restrictions in 2020 (recruited through social media and Prolific, mostly in the UK, France and Mexico; on average 46 days of distancing), the authors computed lack of touch as touch before the restrictions minus touch in the past week. Greater lack of intimate touch (from a partner or close family) went with more loneliness on a short loneliness questionnaire and higher scores on the short State-Trait Anxiety Inventory; lack of friendly or professional touch did not. The links were small (R squared 0.02 for the anxiety score and 0.03 for the loneliness score), and the link with the anxiety score was no longer significant once the loneliness score was in the model.

In the same survey, intimate touch was the type of touch people most wanted in the past week (mean rating about 74 of 100, against about 47 for friendly and 23 for professional touch), and the more days people had been practising social distancing, the more touch they wanted (b = 0.20 per day, p = 0.009), most of all for intimate touch. People who scored higher on anxious attachment wanted more touch, and people who scored higher on avoidant attachment wanted less.

1609.content: In a non-randomised controlled pilot by a University of Queensland team, young adults who came with social isolation and low mood took Groups 4 Health, a manualised five-module programme that helps people build and keep social group memberships. Scores for depression, general anxiety, social anxiety, stress, loneliness, life satisfaction, self-esteem and social functioning all improved at the end of the programme and six months later. Gains in the depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness and life-satisfaction scores tracked how much participants came to identify with their programme group and with several groups.

1610.content: In a randomised controlled trial, 120 adults with psychological distress were assigned by computer to Groups 4 Health, a programme that builds social group memberships, or to treatment as usual, and assessed at baseline and two months later. Loneliness, the primary outcome, fell more with the programme (d = -1.04) than with usual care (d = -0.33), and social anxiety scores fell with the programme (d = -0.46) and not with usual care (d = 0.03). The programme group also made fewer visits to a general practitioner and reported a stronger sense of belonging to several groups. Depression scores fell in both arms (d = -0.63 with the programme, -0.34 with usual care); the extra fall with the programme showed among those not taking psychiatric drugs and with milder symptoms.

1611.content: Axelrod ran two computer tournaments of the repeated prisoner's dilemma. In the first, 14 strategies submitted by game theorists and a random strategy played each other over 200 moves; in the second there were 62 entries from six countries. Both times the highest average score went to the simplest strategy, tit for tat: cooperate on the first move, then do whatever the other player did on the previous move. In a simulation in which strategies multiplied in proportion to their success, tit for tat displaced all others. Its success rested on never defecting first, retaliating after a defection and forgiving after one act of retaliation.

Axelrod and Hamilton show that once tit for tat is common it cannot be invaded by any mutant strategy, provided the probability that the same two individuals meet again is high enough. Total defection is also stable, but a small cluster of reciprocators who interact with each other can invade it. They conclude that cooperation based on reciprocity can start in a mostly uncooperative world, thrive among many strategies and defend itself once established, so repeated meetings between the same individuals are the condition for it.

1612.content: In the 1965 Human Population Laboratory survey, a random sample of 6,928 adults in Alameda County, California, was followed for deaths over nine years. People who lacked social and community ties were more likely to die than those with more extensive contacts: the age-adjusted relative risk for the most isolated against the most connected was 2.3 for men and 2.8 for women. The association held independently of physical health as people rated it in 1965, socioeconomic status, smoking, drinking, obesity, physical activity and use of preventive health services.

1613.content: Floyd defines affection deprivation as wanting more affectionate touch and other tactile affection than one receives. In a survey of 509 adults (all 50 US states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and 16 other countries), affection deprivation was not related to age or ethnicity, and men reported more of it than women. Higher affection deprivation went with more reported loneliness, stress, alexithymia, depression scores and preoccupied and fearful-avoidant attachment, and with more reported diagnoses of personality, mood and anxiety disorders and secondary immune disorders; it went with lower reported general health, happiness, social support, relationship satisfaction and attachment security.

1614.content: In an experiment with 40 adults in the UK (27 women, mean age 27), participants were randomly assigned either to have a few drops of oil rubbed into the back of their hand by a female researcher for about a minute, or to rub the oil on themselves. Afterwards the overall loneliness score did not differ significantly between the groups. On one item of the short loneliness scale, how often they feel neglected, the touched group scored lower (F(1,36) = 5.03, p = 0.031), and the difference was clearest among single participants. Heart rate fell faster and further in the touched group over the following 20 minutes.

1615.content: Using a new panel data set, Lim and Putnam find that religious people are more satisfied with their lives in association with attending religious services regularly and building social networks in their congregations. The association with friends inside the congregation depended on a strong religious identity. Other private or subjective sides of religiosity showed little link with life satisfaction once attendance and friends in the congregation were taken into account.

1616.content: Comparing human hunter-gatherers and subsistence farmers with other great apes, Kraft and colleagues found that the humans spent more energy but less time on subsistence, acquired substantially more energy per hour, and reached similar energy efficiencies. They conclude that humans pay for their large energy budgets mainly by raising the rate of energy acquisition, rather than through energy-saving traits such as economical walking or tool use.

Kraft and colleagues argue that the time humans save on subsistence, compared with other great apes, gave more leisure time for social interaction and social learning at a home base, and that this time was critical for cumulative culture.

1617.content: Using coded data on traditional societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, Quinlan and Quinlan found that where divorce was common, children were weaned 3.5 to 4.8 months earlier than where divorce was less common (about 5 months in the bivariate analysis of 74 societies, mean weaning age about 31 months). The gap was not explained by women's own contribution to subsistence or by living with the wife's kin. Where other carers (allomothers) did most childcare, weaning came about 5.5 to 6 months earlier.

Quinlan and Quinlan report Marlowe's (2003) finding among the Hadza foragers of Tanzania: women had significantly lower foraging return rates when they had nursing infants, while men increased their foraging return and provisioning of wives with nursing children. They also report that among the Ache and Hiwi, nursing women spent less time foraging than non-nursing women.

1618.content: Pisor and Surbeck review encounters between groups in gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans. They list benefits that can favour tolerance toward members of other groups (scouting a group before transferring, mating, and access to food) and argue that humans, who show the widest range of behaviour between groups, were selected to rely more on tolerant relationships between communities in an ecology where food and water varied widely over space and time. They argue these ties were upheld by status for well-connected people and by institutions such as ritual kinship (San hxaro) and hospitality norms.

Pisor and Surbeck report ethnographic cases of ties across communities: in southwestern Africa water supply can differ over tens of kilometres, so ties to other communities give water in a local drought; in a regional drought among Aboriginal Australians in the 1960s these relationships spanned hundreds of kilometres; Coast Salish men with more ties to other communities held more status at home. They add that field studies which map only within-community networks have under-recorded such ties, which has led researchers to conclude that humans tend toward parochialism.

1619.content: In 2006 the authors interviewed 421 Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of the Bolivian Amazon (51% male, aged 15 to 86, eight villages) about 77 skills in food production, childcare, crafts, household work, social life, music and storytelling, and asked who in the village was most expert at each. Most skills were acquired by about age 20, but self-rated peak proficiency came at about 45 to 60 and expertise recognised by others at about 45 to 70. Older adults past their physical peak, despite more frailty, reported further proficiency and were most often named as experts, especially in music and storytelling.

Among the Tsimane, recognised expertise in food production skills that need strength peaked earlier (ages 40 to 64 for women and 62 to 70 for men) than in low-strength food skills (57 to 77 for women, 64 to 75 for men). Peak recognised expertise in music and stories, which the authors treat as traditional teaching, began later than any other category, at 65 for women and 66 for men, and showed the largest gains with age.

1620.content: In 12 Hadza camps in Tanzania (3 to 12 adults each), 94 judges ranked their campmates from photographs on good heart, generosity, honesty, hard work and (for men) hunting ability. Agreement between judges was weak for good heart, generosity and honesty (median Kendall's W 0.19; modal agreement between two judges in a camp of eight about r 0.03 to 0.04), and higher for hunting ability (r 0.23) and hard work (r 0.08). Judges did agree that generosity and hard work go with good character.

Smith and Apicella read the low agreement as a sign that Hadza moral behaviour varies across time and situations, changing to fit local circumstances, rather than as a sign that the Hadza are immoral. They contrast it with Western studies, where observers agree on others' character.

1621.content: Among the Shiwiar, hunter-horticulturalists of the Ecuadorian Amazon, 21 nonliterate villagers did a Wason selection task adapted with photographs and spoken instructions. On rules framed as social exchange, 86% chose the 'benefit accepted' card on both problems and 81 to 86% chose the 'requirement not met' card, the two cards that catch a cheater; 75 to 92% of Harvard undergraduates chose them in a comparable study. 62% of Shiwiar gave exactly the correct pair on at least one social exchange problem (chance 12%), while on a descriptive rule with no exchange their answers resembled Western subjects' low performance.

1622.content: In a systematic review of epidemiological studies and randomised controlled trials, Clark and Landolt report that caffeine typically lengthened the time taken to fall asleep, reduced total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and worsened perceived sleep quality. Slow-wave sleep and EEG slow-wave activity were typically reduced, while stage 1 sleep, waking and arousals increased, with dose and timing relationships established. Older adults' sleep may be more sensitive to caffeine, and sensitivity varies between young people with gene variants in adenosine signalling and caffeine metabolism.

1623.content: Gurven and Lieberman had original research articles published in 2018 in the New England Journal of Medicine, the Lancet and JAMA coded for where participants lived: 534 articles covering about 99 million participants. 80.2% of study inclusion was from WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialised, rich, democratic) regions and 19.8% from the rest, while WEIRD countries held 11.1% of the world's people and 8.9% of its disability-adjusted life years. Relative to population, a person from a WEIRD country was 37 times more likely to appear in these journals.

Using WHO burden-of-disease data, Gurven and Lieberman report that infectious disease made up a six-fold greater share of disability-adjusted life years in non-WEIRD regions than in WEIRD regions, while non-communicable diseases made up a 1.5 times greater share in WEIRD regions. They argue that understanding mismatch diseases needs population history, evolutionary biology and evolved reaction norms, and they reject simple fixes such as the Paleo Diet.

1624.content: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo- and sham-controlled 8-week trial at academic outpatient psychiatry clinics, 122 adults aged 19 to 60 diagnosed with non-seasonal major depressive disorder of at least moderate severity got 30 minutes a day of a 10,000-lux white light box in the early morning plus a placebo pill (32), fluoxetine 20 mg a day plus an inactive device (31), both (29), or an inactive device plus placebo pill (30). Mean drops in MADRS score were 13.4 with light, 8.8 with fluoxetine, 16.9 with both and 6.5 with placebo. Light (d 0.80) and the combination (d 1.11) scored better than placebo; fluoxetine alone (d 0.24) did not. Response was reached by 50.0% with light, 29.0% with fluoxetine, 75.9% with both and 33.3% with placebo.

1625.content: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of light therapy against inactive placebo or control in adults diagnosed with non-seasonal depression (searches to September 2015), 20 parallel-group trials with 881 participants gave a pooled standardised mean difference in depression scores of -0.41 (95% CI -0.64 to -0.18) in favour of light. In the 13 trials reporting response (a 50% fall in symptom scores), 59.1% responded with light and 38.0% with placebo or control. Morning light gave an SMD of -0.50. The authors rated the overall quality of evidence low, because of high risk of bias and inconsistency (I2 60%).

1626.content: 26 healthy adults aged 21 to 39 spent 11 days in hospital: 3 days with 10-hour bedtimes, then 8 days of sleep restricted to 5 hours, either at fixed night-time bedtimes (13 people, aligned) or with bedtimes delayed by 8.5 hours on 4 of the 8 days (13 people, misaligned). Sleep obtained was nearly identical (4 h 48 min against 4 h 45 min a day). In both groups insulin sensitivity fell without a matching rise in insulin secretion, and inflammation rose. In men, the fall in insulin sensitivity and the rise in the inflammatory marker hsCRP were both about twice as large with misalignment; in women the differences between conditions were not significant.

1627.content: In a laboratory study of the human melatonin rhythm, 6.5 hours of monochromatic blue light at 460 nm gave a circadian phase delay twice as large as 6.5 hours of 555 nm light at equal photon density, and suppressed melatonin twice as much; suppression also depended on how long the light lasted. The authors conclude that the circadian pacemaker's peak sensitivity lies at shorter wavelengths than the visual system's peak near 555 nm, so photopic lux is the wrong unit for measuring light's effect on the clock.

1628.content: In the HEIJO-KYO study, bedroom light at night was measured each minute over two nights for 528 older people (mean age 72.8), with overnight urinary melatonin and metabolic measures. Compared with those whose bedrooms averaged under 3 lux (383), those at 3 lux or more (145) had higher adjusted body weight (58.8 against 56.6 kg), BMI (23.3 against 22.7), waist (84.9 against 82.8 cm), triglycerides and LDL cholesterol, and lower HDL cholesterol. Light at night went with higher odds of obesity by BMI (OR 1.89) and abdominal obesity (OR 1.62) and of dyslipidaemia (OR 1.72), independent of demographic and socioeconomic factors. Urinary melatonin and glucose measures did not differ between the groups.

1629.content: In the Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study (all births in Dunedin, New Zealand, April 1972 to March 1973), 815 non-shift workers at age 38 reported their sleep times on work days and free days (Munich ChronoType instrument) and had clinical measures taken. Greater social jetlag (the gap between mid-sleep on free days and work days) went with higher BMI (beta 0.10) and fat mass (beta 0.08), with obesity (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.0 to 1.5) and with meeting the authors' criteria for the metabolic syndrome (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.0 to 1.6), after allowing for chronotype and sleep duration. Social jetlag was higher in obese people who were metabolically unhealthy than in people who were not obese, and among the metabolically unhealthy obese it went with higher glycated haemoglobin and an inflammation marker.

1630.content: 55 healthy adults aged 18 to 30 completed a 6 to 7 week within-person protocol with weekly evening light exposures of 10 to 2,000 lux for 5 hours against a dim control below 1 lux (351 nights). Light that halved melatonin (ED50) averaged 24.6 lux at group level, within typical indoor evening light. Between individuals the ED50 ranged from about 6 lux to 350 lux, so the least sensitive person responded to 400 lux about as the most sensitive did to 10 lux. Melatonin onset was pushed later by 22, 77 and 109 minutes on average at 10, 30 and 50 lux. The differences were not explained by sex, age, chronotype, season or recent light history.

Phillips and colleagues state that before electric lighting, humans were exposed mainly to intense daylight above 300 lux or to dim light below 30 lux after sunset (moonlight, small fires), the two ends of the clock's dose-response curve. Today people spend hours, especially in the evening, at intermediate intensities of 30 to 300 lux, the steepest part of that curve, where differences in sensitivity between people matter most.

1631.content: On Tanna Island, Vanuatu, indigenous Ni-Vanuatu subsistence horticulturalists in coastal villages with grid electricity (39 adults) and inland villages without it (43 adults) wore actigraphs in April and May 2017. Those with electricity had more light after sunset, fell asleep 23 minutes later on average, and slept 28 minutes less a night (7.42 h against 7.88 h); bedtime and waking time did not differ. The gap was driven by breastfeeding mothers with electric light, who slept 65 minutes less than breastfeeding mothers without it; men and other women did not differ significantly between communities. Daytime light exposure was similar in both groups (median about 1,550 and 1,720 lux).

Sleep on Tanna was long and of low efficiency in both groups compared with averages from actigraphy studies of industrialised populations (nocturnal sleep about 7.4 to 7.9 h). The authors contrast this with short sleep (group means about 5 to 6.5 h) recorded by actigraphy among Hadza, San and Tsimane hunter-gatherers and forager-horticulturalists, and suggest that long sleep on Tanna may reflect reliable food, a benign climate, and absence of predators and significant social conflict.

1632.content: Between May and September 1972, 8 to 12 months after their return from Vietnam in September 1971, the authors sought 943 former US Army enlisted men for interview and urine tests: 470 from a general sample and 495 whose urine had been positive for opiates at departure. In the general sample almost half had tried heroin or opium in Vietnam and one fifth had become physically or psychologically dependent; since return about 10% had used opiates at all and under 1% had shown signs of opiate dependence. In the urine-positive sample three quarters felt they had been addicted in Vietnam; after return one third had used opiates and 7% showed signs of dependence, and many had moved from heroin to amphetamines or barbiturates. Almost none wanted treatment.

In the same follow-up, the authors report that use of drugs before military service and the extent of use in Vietnam were the strongest predictors of continued drug use after Vietnam. The predictors named in the abstract describe the men before and during service; the abstract names no measure of the home, marriage, work or neighbourhood the men returned to.

1633.content: Robins reports the three-year follow-up of 571 Vietnam returnees (Army enlisted men back in the US in September 1971, interviewed twice, the second time October to December 1974; a general sample plus an oversample of men whose urine was opiate positive at departure, weighted back to the population). Forty-five men met the study's interview criteria for heroin addiction at some time in the three years after return, under 3% of the population after weighting (1.5% in the first ten months, 1.3% more over the next two years). The analysis set out to find characteristics of the men before service that predicted addiction afterwards, using four preservice scales: demography (age, race, rearing in a core city), parent behaviour (broken home, parents' arrests, drug use and drinking problems), deviance (arrests, school dropout, truancy, fighting, early drunkenness) and drug use before service. Together the four scales explained 6% of the variance in post-Vietnam addiction. No measure of the home, marriage, work or neighbourhood the men returned to entered the analysis.

Splitting the path into stages, Robins reports that 35% of the men used heroin in Vietnam, 28% of those continued after return, and 28% of those who continued became addicted by the study's criteria. The preservice scales explained more than 25% of the variance in heroin use in Vietnam and in addiction among men who used after return, and 13% in whether Vietnam users went on using after return. The demography scale ran in opposite directions: being black, from an inner city and young went with heroin use in Vietnam and continued use, while among men who used heroin after return, being white, from outside the central city and older went with becoming addicted. Among post-Vietnam heroin users, 59% became addicted if their parents showed two or three of the three problem-behaviour indicators.

Robins reads the reversal as a matter of the setting the men lived in: where peers do not use narcotics and supply is scarce, a man who still uses violates local norms and works hard for his supply, so use there marks a greater need; she compares this with alcohol in teetotal regions, where few drink but drinkers more often have problems. She describes the US outside the urban ghetto as a heroin 'bible belt' where the norm is abstention, and Vietnam as a place where narcotics were available to all.

1634.content: In her 1993 Eddy lecture Robins reports that among the Vietnam returnees, heroin use after return went with more crime, unemployment, illegal employment, divorce or separation, violence, transiency and credit problems than amphetamine or barbiturate use, and that the difference disappeared once preservice behaviour problems and the number of other drugs used were held constant; the variety of drugs used predicted adverse outcomes better than which drug was used. In this analysis the post-return conditions (work, marriage, moving about) are outcomes compared across drugs, not predictors of re-addiction.

Robins lists the variables that failed to predict re-addiction among veterans who had been addicted in Vietnam and used narcotics again after return: preservice behaviour problems; parents' substance abuse, arrests and psychiatric care; type, duration and injection of drug use in Vietnam; IQ; draftee or volunteer; combat; military discipline problems; demographic characteristics. None of these describes the home the men came back to. She reports that 12% of men addicted in Vietnam were addicted at any time in the three years after return, that nearly half of them tried narcotics again but 6% became re-addicted, and that the few who entered VA treatment relapsed at about the two-thirds rate of treated civilians. She states that epidemiologists have found no social variables that predict the move from heavy use to addiction.

Robins rejects the reading that the men recovered because the US setting lacked the cues of their Vietnam use. She grants that it fits the men who were not re-addicted, and argues that it fails to account for the high rate of recovery while the men were still in Vietnam, and for the shortness of re-addiction episodes among the minority re-addicted, who stayed in the setting where re-addiction occurred. She also rejects war stress as the cause: addicted men had typically begun use early in their tour before combat, the link between combat and narcotic use vanished once preservice history was controlled, and the men gave getting high (40%) and making army life bearable as their reasons.

1635.content: Reanalysing the Vietnam study, the authors took 374 veterans who had used heroin in Vietnam (1970 to 1971) and had been interviewed twice in the first three years after return, and looked for predictors of heroin injection after return. Predictors came from interviews and military records describing the men before and during service (region of residence, race, antisocial behaviour, type and level of drug use, association with illicit drug users). The authors also examined possible post-Vietnam correlates of injection: having no job or school enrolment, alcohol problems, reported depression, an absent or transient marriage, and association with illicit drug users and with other Vietnam veterans. The abstract does not report what these post-Vietnam correlates showed.

The significant predictors of injection after return were living on the east or west coast, deviant behaviour before and in Vietnam, opiate use before Vietnam, serious heroin involvement in Vietnam, use of non-opiate drugs before and in Vietnam, and associating with drug users before service. Among men who went back to heroin after return, living on either coast and non-opiate illegal drug use before service raised the probability of injecting; black men who went back to heroin were less likely to inject than others. Most men who had used heroin in Vietnam used it very occasionally or not at all after return.
