In a lab experiment (Study 2b), 45 participants read a real story about an airline damaging a band's guitars, written to evoke more or less anger; those who read the higher-anger version rated themselves more likely to share it (mean 5.71 against 3.37 on a 7-point scale), and their self-rated arousal statistically carried the effect. In Study 2a (49 participants), a funnier version of an advert likewise raised sharing (3.97 against 2.92). The authors conclude that the activation an emotion produces, more than whether it is positive or negative, makes people pass content on.

1833.content: In 5,221 adult twins and relatives from 3,083 families in the Australian Twin Registry (questionnaires 1988 to 1992), the authors related a depression symptom score (12 items from two symptom checklists) to polygenic risk scores built from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium genome-wide study of major depressive disorder, to personal stressful life events in the past 12 months, and to perceived social support. Personal life events explained 12.9% of the variance in the symptom score, lack of social support 3%, network life events 0.3%, and the best polygenic score at most 0.46%.

In the same sample, the interaction between the polygenic score and personal life events explained 0.12% of the variance in the symptom score (p = 0.0076): people with a higher polygenic score had a somewhat larger rise in symptom score with more life events, mainly in women. The authors read this as support for the diathesis-stress model, but caution that interactions depend on the scale of measurement and that personal life events are themselves partly heritable (twin heritability of the measures 30 to 40%).

1834.content: A consortium ran one shared analysis script on 31 data sets with 38,802 people of European ancestry who were genotyped for the serotonin transporter promoter variant (5-HTTLPR) and assessed for depression (current or lifetime, by the source's diagnostic criteria or symptom scales) and for childhood maltreatment or other stressful life events, then meta-analysed the results. No subgroup or variable definition showed a significant interaction between stress and genotype; the genotype had no main effect, while stress was a strong and consistent risk factor across studies.

1835.content: Patient SM, a woman with focal damage to the amygdala on both sides, was taken to an exotic pet store, through a professionally run haunted house and shown 10 fear-inducing film clips. She held a snake for over three minutes, asked 15 times to touch larger dangerous snakes, tried to touch a tarantula, and rated her fear at no more than 2 out of 10; on eight fear surveys filled in over three years and in three months of experience sampling she reported little fear, while she showed and reported disgust, anger, sadness, happiness and surprise. She described her pull toward the animals as curiosity.

SM's life history held many threats to her life (held up at knife-point and gun-point, nearly killed in domestic violence, threatened with death), confirmed by police reports, yet she recalled no fear in them, only anger and upset. The authors report that she has great difficulty detecting looming threats and learning to avoid dangerous situations, which in all likelihood contributed to how often she met them.

1836.content: Grupe and Nitschke review human and animal work showing that the threat response grows with uncertainty about a threat's nature, probability or timing. Humans startle more to cues that precede shock on 20% or 60% of trials than to cues that always precede it, and more under unpredictable timing. Aversive events that are not fully predictable lower mood and raise physiological reactions more than fully predictable ones, and unpredictably timed neutral tones alone raise amygdala activity and anxious behaviour in mice and humans compared with predictably timed tones.

The review reports that sustained, unpredictable threat and brief, certain threat run through different parts of the extended amygdala: the central amygdala coordinates rapid fear to imminent and certain threats, while the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis is activated by sustained, unpredictable threat. Benzodiazepines reduced fear responses to sustained but not to brief, certain threat in rodents, and in humans reduced startle to unpredictable but not predictable threat.

1837.content: Abstract only. Hammen reviews research on stress and depression and states that improved assessment methods and research designs have established a robust and causal association between stressful life events and episodes the source labels major depressive episodes. She names gaps: the measurement of chronic stress, differences between first and recurrent episodes, sex differences, sensitisation over episodes, and how natural stress acts on the body, and notes a move toward models in which stress and the reported symptoms shape each other over time.

1838.content: Abstract only. Isbell proposes that snakes, likely the first predators of crown-group placental mammals, drove orbital convergence, visual specialisation and brain expansion in primates. Primate brain expansion varies with how long each group lived with venomous snakes: Malagasy prosimians never did, New World monkeys did with interruptions, and Old World monkeys and apes did continuously. She suggests that the koniocellular visual pathway (retina to lateral geniculate nucleus, superior colliculus and pulvinar) expanded for fast, pre-attentive detection of feared stimuli such as snakes.

1839.content: A systematic review found 20 clinical trials of anti-cytokine drugs in chronic inflammatory physical illnesses (such as psoriasis, Crohn's disease and rheumatoid arthritis) that also scored depressive symptoms as a secondary outcome. In a random-effects meta-analysis of seven placebo-controlled randomised trials with 2,370 participants, the drugs lowered depressive symptom scores more than placebo (standardised mean difference 0.40); anti-tumour necrosis factor drugs, tested in five trials, gave 0.33. Adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab and tocilizumab each showed significant improvement. The effect grew with baseline symptom severity and was not associated with improvement in the physical illness, sex, age or trial length.

1840.content: In the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (south-west England, births 1991 to 1992), interleukin 6 (IL-6) and C-reactive protein were measured in blood at age 9 in 4,585 children without a recent infection, and 2,447 were interviewed at 18 with the Clinical Interview Schedule-Revised (17.2% met its case definition for depression). Children in the top third of IL-6 had higher odds of meeting the case definition at 18 than those in the bottom third (adjusted odds ratio 1.55), after adjusting for sex, age, body mass index, ethnicity, social class, earlier psychological and behavioural problems and reported maternal postpartum depression score, with a dose-response pattern; results with the Mood and Feelings Questionnaire were similar. C-reactive protein showed no association, and after imputation of missing outcome data the odds ratios for the binary interview definition fell short of significance.

1841.content: Kikusui and colleagues report their own rat experiment (Kiyokawa et al. 2004): rats (Rattus norvegicus) fear-conditioned to a shock box froze less and showed lower stress-nucleus activity (c-Fos in the paraventricular nucleus) when put back in the box with a partner, and the drop was larger with a partner that had not been shocked than with one that had also been fear-conditioned. The two kinds of partner did not differ in friendly behaviour, so another cue carried the partner's state; in rats, chemical cues from a cage mate injected with oxytocin also lowered stress hormones.

The review reports that sheep (Ovis aries) moved into a new environment showed lower behavioural, hormonal and heart responses and lower stress-gene activity in the paraventricular nucleus when shown pictures of sheep faces (da Costa et al. 2004). In rats, a free-moving companion reduced fear of a new place while a companion in a cage did not (Latane 1969), and in juvenile rats more play bouts with a free-moving partner went with a smaller hormonal stress response, an effect that faded when the partner was caged.

1842.content: Kushlev, Dwyer and Dunn report their own experiment (Kushlev, Proulx and Dunn 2016): 221 students each spent one week with phone alerts on and the phone within reach and one week with alerts off and the phone out of reach; they reported more symptoms of inattentiveness in the alerts-on week (d = 0.44).

In a preregistered field experiment the authors report (Kushlev and Dunn 2019), 200 parents visiting a Vancouver science museum with their children were randomly told to use their phones as much or as little as possible. Parents told to use their phones as much as possible felt less socially connected (printed as d = -.73) and reported less meaning (d = .30); they also felt more distracted (printed as d = -.63), and distraction statistically carried the effects on connection and meaning.

1843.content: Abstract only. In three national probability samples of adults aged 25 to 75 (1,014, 1,195 and 3,485 people), those with lower income reported lower mastery, more perceived constraints and poorer health. At every income level, more mastery and fewer constraints went with better health, more life satisfaction and lower depressive symptom scores, and in the lowest income group people with a high sense of control showed health and well-being comparable with the higher income groups.

1844.content: In male Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus) made helpless by 120 inescapable, unpredictable foot shocks, and in a strain selectively bred for helplessness, excitatory synaptic input onto lateral habenula neurons that project to the ventral tegmental area (the midbrain dopamine area) was potentiated through more presynaptic release: the share of cells with high-frequency activity rose from 2% to 14 to 20%, and the strength of this input correlated with each animal's helpless behaviour. Both kinds of helpless rats also stayed immobile longer in the forced swim test.

In brain slices, high-frequency stimulation like that used in human deep brain stimulation weakened synaptic transmission onto these habenula neurons. Delivered to the lateral habenula of helpless rats for one hour, the same protocol markedly increased escape behaviour at the next test, with a stronger effect at 300 than at 150 microamps, and only with electrodes in the lateral habenula and not in the nearby thalamus; in the habenula it also prevented the rise in immobility in the forced swim test, which sham stimulation did not.

1845.content: Comparing four foraging populations (Ache of Paraguay, Hadza of Tanzania, !Kung of Botswana, Hiwi of Venezuela), Blurton Jones and colleagues ranked marriage stability from most to least divorce as Ache, Hadza, then !Kung and Hiwi. Among Hadza couples married in 1985 to 1990, 11 of 28 had divorced by 1995; among !Kung, marriages that had lasted 5 years ended at 0.02 to 0.07 a year; among Ache, at 19 percent a year. Divorce did not track the 'father effect' (how much a father's presence raised his children's survival) or the ratio of that effect to mating opportunity. It tracked 'fertility units per male' (women aged 15 to 40 times the fertility rate, divided by men aged 20 to 55): marriages were less stable where there were more fertility units per man.

Among the Hadza, census and interview data for 1985 to 1990 and 1990 to 1995 showed no significant effect of a father's death or divorce on the survival of children under 5, while an earlier analysis by the same team had found a striking effect of losing the mother. The authors add that Hadza children supply up to half their own daily food from age five.

1846.content: Excavated Middle Stone Age sites in the Olorgesailie basin, southern Kenya, dated by argon-argon and uranium-series methods to between about 295,000 and 320,000 years ago, show hominins making prepared cores and points, processing iron-rich rocks into red pigment, and getting stone tool material from 25 to 50 km away or more. The animal remains suggest they took both large and small prey. The authors write that these practices imply notable changes in how individuals and groups related to the landscape and to one another.

1847.content: A meta-analysis of 753 effect sizes from 259 independent samples found that people with a stronger materialistic orientation report lower personal well-being. The association was r = -0.19 for measures of materialist values and beliefs and r = -0.16 for the relative importance of materialist goals, and weaker (r = -0.08 to -0.11) for measures of emphasis on money alone. It was largest for risky health and consumer behaviour and for negative self-appraisals (r = -0.28 to -0.44) and smallest for life satisfaction and negative affect (r = -0.13 to -0.15). Mediation analyses suggested the link may be explained by poorer satisfaction of psychological needs.

In the same meta-analysis the size of the link depended on setting: it varied with gender and age, was stronger or weaker in study or work environments that support materialistic values and in cultures that emphasise affective autonomy, and varied with economic growth and wealth differences. Mediation analyses pointed to poor psychological need satisfaction as a possible explanation of the negative link.

1848.content: In 22 heterosexual couples (aged 23 to 32, in relationships of about 3.5 years; 20 couples analysed) the woman received heat pain on her forearm under several conditions while both partners wore EEG caps. Her pain ratings on a 0 to 100 scale averaged 52.4 when alone, 37.7 with her partner in the room without touch, and 25.0 while holding his hand; the drop with hand-holding was significant against both other conditions. During hand-holding under pain the partners' alpha-mu brain rhythms became more coupled, and in one network the degree of coupling correlated with how much her pain dropped (r = -0.56) and in another with how closely his rating of her pain matched hers (r = -0.66).

1849.content: Grubbs and Gola studied three samples of sexually active US men who used pornography: 147 undergraduates, 297 men from an online sample matched to US national norms, and a one-year, four-wave online sample (433 men at the start, 196 at the end). Erectile function was scored on the self-report IIEF-5. In all three samples, men who reported their own use as problematic also reported more erectile problems at the same time, but how much they used showed no consistent association with the scores. Over the year, latent growth curve analyses found no significant relationship between any pornography measure and the course of the erectile scores.

1850.content: Using a nationally representative US sample, McCarty and colleagues estimated personal network size two ways: from how many people respondents said they knew in specific subpopulations (such as diabetics or Native Americans), and from how many they knew in relation categories (such as immediate family or coworkers). Both methods gave an average of about 291 people known, and a separate national sample gave similar results. A sample of clergy, expected to have large networks, gave a larger average. Respondents' preference for round numbers changed the estimate by no more than about 6 percent.

1851.content: 430 men and women in heterosexual relationships in which at least one partner used pornography, recruited online and through newspapers and radio, answered open-ended questions about what pornography use did to each partner and to the relationship. The most common answer was that it had no negative effect. Among the other answers, positive effects (better sexual communication, more sexual experimentation, more sexual comfort) were reported frequently and negative effects (unrealistic expectations, less sexual interest in the partner, more insecurity) were reported considerably less often.

1852.content: 40 New York adults (21 women, mean age 20.8) who had an unwanted romantic break-up in the past 6 months and felt rejected were scanned with fMRI. Viewing the ex-partner's photo while thinking about the break-up, against a friend's photo, and painful heat on the forearm, against warm heat, were rated as equally distressing. Both contrasts activated overlapping regions: the dorsal anterior cingulate and anterior insula, which carry the unpleasant side of pain, and also the thalamus, secondary somatosensory cortex and dorsal posterior insula, which carry its bodily, sensory side. In a database of over 500 published studies, activation in the latter two regions was highly specific to physical pain (positive predictive values up to 88 percent).

1853.content: In 64 healthy male adults in Berlin who reported a wide range of weekly pornography hours, more hours went with less grey matter volume in the right caudate (measured by voxel-based morphometry on 3-T MRI), with weaker left putamen activity while viewing sexual cues, and with weaker resting-state connectivity between the right caudate and the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The authors give two readings: a change in the reward system after intense stimulation, or a precondition that makes pornography more rewarding.

1854.content: Landripet and Štulhofer analysed a 2011 online survey of 2,737 Croatian, Norwegian and Portuguese men and a 2014 online survey of 1,211 Croatian men, all younger and heterosexual. Erection, orgasm and desire difficulties were self-reported on survey indicators and, in the second study, scored on the IIEF-5. In the first study only Croatian men showed a significant association between pornography use and erectile difficulty, which the authors call small and inconsistent: moderate use, not high use, differed from infrequent use. In the second study neither how often men used pornography nor recent changes in their use were associated with any of the reported sexual difficulties.

1855.content: In a laboratory experiment with 40 male volunteers, erotic stimuli of medium or high intensity were presented repeatedly, either the same stimulus each time or a varied set, in a 2 by 2 design. Penile response and self-rated sexual arousal both fell with repeated presentation, and because the design controlled for physical fatigue the authors read the fall as habituation. The varied stimuli produced faster attenuation than constant stimuli on both measures, which the authors had predicted. Stimulus intensity partly affected the fall in felt arousal and did not affect penile response.

In the same experiment, a series of varied erotic stimuli produced a faster fall in penile response and in self-rated arousal than one constant stimulus repeated, which matched the authors' hypothesis. Medium-intensity stimuli produced a faster fall than high-intensity stimuli on felt arousal only in part, and not on penile response.

1856.content: A review of the authors' laboratory work in the laboratory rat (Rattus norvegicus): in male and female rats, early sexual experience with partners scented with a neutral or even noxious odour produced a later preference for partners carrying that scent. The same preference could be produced by injecting morphine or oxytocin when a male first met scented females, and blocked by the opioid blocker naloxone. A rodent jacket worn during rewarded sex came to drive sexual arousal: males trained with it copulated very poorly when the jacket was off.

1857.content: 122 people who either reported or denied problems controlling their viewing of sexual images were shown emotional pictures, including explicit sexual ones, while the late positive potential (LPP, an EEG measure of motivational attention) was recorded. The LPP depended on problem group together with desire for sex with a partner: those reporting problems who also reported higher desire had a lower LPP to sexual images. The authors note this differs from the heightened cue response that substance addiction models expect.

1858.content: A cross-cultural survey of contemporary hunter-gatherers in a representative sample of world cultures, using numerically coded measures of infant care, found one uniform pattern: mothers were the principal caregivers and gave extensive body contact day and night and prolonged breastfeeding, uncarried babies moved freely, and care was affectionate with immediate nurturant response to crying. In most groups children nonetheless reached early independence and by 2 to 4 years spent more than half their time away from the mother.

The same paper contrasts the forager pattern with infant care in the United States of the late 1970s: infants spent little time in body contact with caregivers, their movements were restricted by playpens, high chairs or cribs, only a minority were breastfed and half of those were weaned within a few weeks, and separate sleeping and delayed response to crying were regularly recommended. The authors call this a shift from carrying to a pattern resembling nesting or caching.

1859.content: A Cochrane review of 46 randomised trials (3,850 women and infants, 21 countries; 38 trials with 3,472 pairs gave data) compared skin-to-skin contact between mother and healthy newborn, begun within 24 hours of birth, with standard hospital care. Mothers given skin-to-skin contact were more likely to be breastfeeding at one to four months after birth (risk ratio 1.24, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.43; 14 trials, 887 pairs; moderate-quality evidence), breastfed about 64 days longer (6 trials, 264 pairs; low quality), and were more likely to breastfeed exclusively from discharge to one month (RR 1.30) and from six weeks to six months (RR 1.50).

In the same review, newborns given skin-to-skin contact had higher scores on a composite of cardio-respiratory stabilisation (SCRIP; standardised mean difference 1.24; 2 trials, 81 late-preterm infants; low quality) and higher blood glucose (mean difference 10.49 mg/dL; 3 trials, 144 infants; low quality), with axillary temperature about 0.3 degrees C higher, a difference the authors judged not clinically meaningful. Subgroups showed no difference between contact begun within 10 minutes and later, or between 60 minutes or less of contact and more.

1860.content: In a randomised trial in five hospitals in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria and Tanzania, 3,211 infants weighing 1.0 to under 1.8 kg at birth were assigned to kangaroo mother care started immediately after birth (1,609) or to conventional care until stable and kangaroo care afterwards (1,602). Median skin-to-skin contact in the neonatal unit was 16.9 hours a day against 1.5 hours. Deaths in the first 28 days were 191 (12.0%) against 249 (15.7%), relative risk 0.75 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.89), a 25% improvement in neonatal survival; 27 infants needed the intervention to prevent one death. The trial was stopped early on the monitoring board's advice because of the lower mortality.

In the same trial, infants given immediate kangaroo care had less suspected sepsis (22.9% against 27.8%, adjusted RR 0.82) and less hypothermia (5.6% against 8.3%, adjusted RR 0.65), and sepsis-associated mortality was 4.4% against 6.9% (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.86). Within the intervention group, infants who received more hours of skin-to-skin contact per day had a lower risk of death.

1861.content: Observing 20 Aka forager, 21 Ngandu farmer and 21 upper-middle-class Euro-American families in Washington, D.C., each with a 3- to 4-month-old infant, for 3 hours on four days (12 hours per infant), the authors found that Aka infants were almost always held and never alone; Ngandu infants were held about half as often as Aka infants but significantly more than Euro-American infants, who were also more often alone. All Euro-American infants had their own crib in their own room.

In the same three samples there were no group differences in how often caregivers showed affection, soothed or fed their infants in total, but Ngandu infants fussed or cried substantially longer than both Aka and Euro-American infants, and Aka and Euro-American infants did not differ. Aka mothers fed their infants more often (4.02 bouts per hour) than Ngandu (2.01) and Euro-American mothers (1.61). The authors add that the Euro-American parents held and responded to fussing far more than in US studies of the 1970s or earlier.

1862.content: A comparative analysis of 445 mammal species coded for help with the young by individuals other than the mother (provisioning, carrying, huddling, protecting, allonursing) found that brain size correlated positively with the amount of such help across mammalian clades as a whole and within most orders, most clearly in the carnivores (order Carnivora), with the notable exception of the primates (order Primates).

In primates (order Primates) the same analysis found that help from non-mothers went with higher fertility, up to twinning in the marmosets and tamarins (family Callitrichidae), and with more helpless (altricial) newborns. The authors conclude that humans combine the carnivore pattern (help with larger brains) with the primate pattern (help with higher fertility), and that cooperative breeding let early humans sidestep the trade-off between brain size and reproductive output.

1863.content: In looking-time experiments with infants aged 5 to 6 months from monolingual homes in Boston and Paris, infants looked longer at a silent adult who had earlier spoken their native language than at one who had spoken a foreign language (61.25% of looking; 19 of 24 infants), and longer at a speaker with a native accent than one with a foreign accent (56.5%; 18 of 24). Reversed speech paired with moving shapes produced no preference (24 infants), so the effect was tied to people. At 10 months, Paris infants took toys more often from a French speaker and Boston infants from an English speaker (16 infants each).

In friendship-choice experiments, 5-year-old children from monolingual English homes in Boston (8 per experiment) chose a child who had spoken English over one who had spoken French, and chose a child speaking American-accented English over one speaking French-accented English just as strongly. A separate group of 8 children understood both the native and the accented speech (100% and 87% comprehension), so the preference did not come from failing to understand.

1864.content: Konner reports that among !Kung (Zhun/twa) foragers of north-western Botswana infants who had played happily with anyone began, between 7 and 9 months, to show uneasiness with people they did not know, like Western infants. In a standard approach by a female stranger (who then touched or picked up the child), given to 36 infants and young children (20 girls, 16 boys), the first clearly fearful response came at 8 months and the strength of the response was greatest in the second half of the second year, with no decline in fear scores before the end of the second year. Fear was no greater toward a European stranger than toward a !Kung stranger.

Konner describes the !Kung infants' reaction to strangers as markedly more extreme than in Western infants (immediate loud screams, flight to the mother, clinging and nursing while the stranger stays close), harder to overcome (sometimes taking days of familiarity) and lasting later into childhood, with no approach at all until familiarity is established. His simplest explanation is experience: urban Western infants meet strangers many times a day and habituate, while !Kung infants see only a tiny fraction of that number as people move between camps.

1865.content: Healthy Caribbean spiny lobsters (Panulirus argus), a normally gregarious species, avoided members of their own species infected with a lethal virus. The authors report this as the first record of social animals avoiding diseased individuals of their own species in the wild, and say the healthy lobsters detected and avoided infected individuals early, before those were infectious.

1866.content: In the Florida Keys, a cyanobacteria bloom in 2007 killed the sponges that give juvenile Caribbean spiny lobsters (Panulirus argus) most of their shelter over about 2,500 km2, crowding lobsters into the few remaining dens. In a field experiment in 46 natural dens (177 lobsters), significantly more lobsters left a den within 24 hours when a lobster infected with the PaV1 virus was tethered in it than when a healthy lobster was (G = 6.79, P < 0.009), even though other shelter was scarce and searching for it raised the risk of being eaten.

Although the sponge die-off crowded lobsters into the remaining dens, the share of juvenile lobsters infected with PaV1 at 10 monitoring sites was unchanged eight months later and stayed stable in yearly surveys for five more years. A simulation model of the region matched this; when the avoidance of infected lobsters was switched off in the model, an epidemic followed within a few months, with the mean share infected rising about tenfold to nearly 20% and peaks up to 77%.

1867.content: Among Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania, 146 person-day follows of men (921 hours, 2001 to 2013, 12 camps) showed that men ate a mean of 2,405 kilocalories per foray while out of camp, about 90% of their estimated mean daily total energy expenditure, and 85% of those kilocalories came from honey.

The authors conclude that men who came back to camp empty-handed had often eaten well while out; what failed was producing a surplus to share, so describing men's foraging as risky in terms of calories may be exaggerated.

1868.content: A rapid mixed-methods review (805 records screened; 17 studies of variable quality, 11 observational with 50 to 552 participants each and 6 qualitative, 1983 to 2019, mostly in the US with white Christian samples) found the evidence on whether funeral participation affects bereaved relatives' grief and bereavement outcomes inconclusive: five observational studies found funerals associated with significant benefits and six found no measurable associations.

In the six qualitative studies of the same review, the bereaved valued funerals and after-death rituals as a chance to say goodbye and to be comforted by others; the benefit depended on whether they could shape the rituals in a way meaningful to them. Immigrants who could not travel to a funeral in their home country reported distress, and in interviews with 4 Hong Kong widowers low attendance at a funeral was read as a lack of social support that made the bereaved feel worse. In Turkey the custom of not leaving the bereaved alone was felt as supportive by some and as difficult by others with little control over it.

1869.content: Fifteen healthy volunteers scanned with arterial spin labelling and a separate 15 with BOLD fMRI received intravenous placebo and then psilocybin (2 mg) in the scanner. Psilocybin produced only decreases in cerebral blood flow and BOLD signal, largest in hub regions such as the thalamus and the anterior and posterior cingulate cortex; the size of the decrease in the anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex correlated with the intensity of the subjective effects, and psilocybin reduced the positive coupling between the medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex.

1870.content: In a placebo-controlled, balanced-order within-subject study, 20 healthy volunteers were scanned with arterial spin labelling, BOLD fMRI and magnetoencephalography after LSD and after placebo. Decreased connectivity between the parahippocampus and the retrosplenial cortex correlated with ratings of ego-dissolution (r = 0.73) and of altered meaning (r = 0.82), and decreased integrity of the default mode network correlated with ego-dissolution (r = 0.49, P = 0.03), while the integrity of the other 11 resting-state networks did not.

1871.content: The authors combine the free-energy principle and the entropic brain hypothesis into a model they call REBUS (relaxed beliefs under psychedelics): by raising the entropy of spontaneous cortical activity, psychedelics relax the precision, or confidence, of high-level priors or beliefs, freeing bottom-up information flow, particularly from intrinsic sources such as the limbic system. They propose that the sensitised priors can then be revised, including heavily weighted beliefs about self and world.

1872.content: Coall and Hertwig report Gibson and Mace's time-series analysis of Oromo agro-pastoralists in southern Ethiopia: the presence of a hard-working maternal grandmother who helped the mother with heavy domestic tasks such as grinding maize raised a grandchild's probability of surviving to age three by 25%, an effect comparable to installing a new water supply. They also report negative effects of paternal grandmothers in some populations, for example a 35% higher stillbirth risk in a historical German population.

Coall and Hertwig report that grandparents in industrialised countries give much care: 28% of employed US women relied on their parents or in-laws for childcare for young children; across ten European countries 58% of grandmothers and 49% of grandfathers cared for a grandchild at some point in a 12-month period; Germans aged 55 to 69 spent on average 12.8 hours a month supervising grandchildren. Longer lives also lengthen the overlap: by a model estimate from survival rates, 27% of Swiss 20-year-olds would have had a living grandparent in 1900 against 92% in 2000.

The authors' systematic search of seven databases (1970 to 2007) for studies of grandparental investment and grandchild outcomes in low-risk industrialised families yielded 196 publications, of which only four met their criteria. One of these, using 8,752 families of the Avon Longitudinal Study in England, found that children cared for by grandparents at 8, 15 and 24 months were 28% more likely to score high on the hyperactivity subscale of the parent-reported Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire at age four. The authors find converging evidence of benefit only under duress, such as teenage pregnancy.

1873.content: Excavations in 2008 at Hohle Fels Cave in the Swabian Jura of south-western Germany recovered a female figurine carved from mammoth ivory in the basal Aurignacian deposit. The figurine was made at least 35,000 calendar years ago, which makes it one of the oldest known examples of figurative art and at least 5,000 years older than the well-known Venus figurines of the Gravettian.

1874.content: Curtis proposes a classification of infection-avoidance behaviour by the epidemiology of infection risk: animals, humans included, must avoid other members of their own species, parasites and their vectors, parasite-rich environments, and infestation of their own niche. She further proposes that the disgust system, which coordinates this avoidance, may form a continuum with the immune system through shared signalling pathways, sites of action and evolutionary history.

1875.content: In two studies, 191 undergraduates rating themselves and 91 male varsity athletes on four university teams (baseball, soccer, volleyball, rugby) rated by their own teammates, people higher in hubristic pride were rated more dominant and people higher in authentic pride were rated more prestigious. Among the athletes, hubristic pride went with peer-rated dominance (b = .36) and not with prestige, and authentic pride went with peer-rated prestige (b = .33) and not with dominance; the two pride facets were unrelated to each other (r = -.01).

Among the 91 athletes, teammates who were rated prestigious were also rated as good advice-givers and as intellectually, athletically and socially skilled, and as altruistic, cooperative, helpful and moral (r = .26 to .73). Teammates rated dominant were rated athletic (r = .29) and as leaders (r = .40), but not as better advice-givers or more skilled, and were rated less altruistic, cooperative, helpful and moral (r = -.32 to -.54).

1876.content: In ratings by 2,751 people in 14 nations, from Brazil, China and Eritrea to Japan, Russia, the USA and Zimbabwe, of how 240 acts, traits and events would change a man's or a woman's status, the ratings agreed closely between nations (correlations of 0.79 to 0.98). A separate group of 222 Americans forecast how much pride or shame they would feel if they showed each trait, and these forecasts closely tracked the status ratings of every nation (absolute correlations 0.74 to 0.98).

The links were not straight lines and pride and shame were not mirror images: pride intensity followed status-raising traits much more closely than shame did, and shame followed status-lowering traits more closely than pride did.

1877.content: Status ratings of 240 acts, traits and events by 2,751 people in 14 nations were compared with ratings by 515 separate Americans of what each trait shows about a person's ability and willingness to bring benefits to others and to inflict costs on them. Benefit-generation ability and willingness each had strong unique positive associations with status (standardised betas 0.28 to 0.60). Cost-infliction ability had a small unique association with men's status (0.11) and none with women's, and cost-infliction willingness had none for either sex; together the four ratings accounted for 90% of the variance in status.
The authors conclude that inflicting costs on others without also bringing benefits does not reliably raise a person's status among established human groups in the 14 nations studied.

1878.content: A meta-analysis of 204 experimental, correlational and longitudinal studies of thin-ideal (and, for men, muscular-ideal) media found little evidence of effects on body dissatisfaction, restrictive eating or reported eating-disorder symptoms in men, and minimal effects for most women. Some evidence suggested that women who already had body dissatisfaction are primed by media ideals, particularly in experiments. Effects were smaller in child samples than in adult and college samples, and publication bias may be inflating effect estimates in some areas.

1879.content: In Experiment 1, 68 female US undergraduates (61 analysed) watched a woman do well or badly on a pattern-learning task after being told her score came from prior training or from being misled, so it said nothing about their own ability. Her score did not move the self-rated ability of students left free to think. Students kept busy rehearsing an 8-digit number rated themselves higher when she did badly and lower when she did well. The authors read this as a comparison that is made first and corrected afterwards, which needs free attention.

In Experiment 2, 48 female undergraduates (of 53) reported their mood while believing a machine was reading it. When another woman scored higher or lower than them on an unrelated, easier or harder version of the task, they did not change their self-rated ability, yet their mood still rose when she did badly and fell when she did well, as much as when she had done the same task. The mood shift had faded by the end of the session.

1880.content: A review of amygdala circuit research states that the main amygdala nuclei and their basic circuit connections and functions are conserved across vertebrates: a lizard, the mouse (Mus musculus), the rat (Rattus norvegicus), the cat, a monkey and the human share the basolateral and central nuclei or their analogues, and reptiles, birds and fish have an amygdala-like region with similar circuits and functions, although species differences exist.

The review reports that the amygdala processes rewarding as well as threatening events. In within-subject recordings in rodents and non-human primates, some basolateral amygdala neurons respond to cues for reward and others to cues for threat, and many follow the outcome when the cue-outcome pairing is reversed. Optogenetic studies, mostly in mice (Mus musculus), show that different amygdala output pathways shift behaviour toward approach or toward avoidance. The authors write that the view of the amygdala as specialised only for fear is too narrow.

1881.content: In an experiment, women and men rated their current romantic relationship after seeing opposite-sex people who varied in dominance and physical attractiveness. Men who saw physically attractive women rated their relationship less favourably than men who saw average-looking women, though only when the women were low in dominance; the women's dominance did not move men's ratings directly. Women's ratings were unchanged by men's attractiveness and were lower after seeing highly dominant men.

1882.content: In the 2007 European Quality of Life Survey (over 34,000 adults in 31 European countries), people in more unequal countries more often agreed with the single item 'Some people look down on me because of my job situation or income' (the authors' status anxiety measure) at every point of the income ladder; country inequality (Gini) and mean reported status anxiety correlated at 0.51. Agreement ranged from 5.4% in Norway and 7.4% in Sweden to 24.1% in Romania and 25.1% in Macedonia.

Within countries, the lower a person's income rank, the more often they reported feeling looked down on (the authors' status anxiety item; correlation -0.13 across countries, up to -0.28 in Germany, Ireland and the UK). In multilevel models income rank stayed large and significant once absolute income was added, while absolute income was not significant, so relative position mattered more than the amount of money.

1883.content: In male mice (Mus musculus), 24 hours of social isolation strengthened excitatory inputs onto dopamine neurons of the dorsal raphe nucleus, which a move to a new cage did not do, and in isolated mice these neurons fired more on first contact with a young mouse than in group-housed mice. Switching the neurons on by light in group-housed mice raised their preference for company; with no mouse present, the mice avoided the side of the chamber where the light switched them on and did not work to get it.

When these dorsal raphe dopamine neurons were silenced by light, male mice (Mus musculus) isolated for 24 hours no longer showed the usual rise in time spent near another mouse, while silencing did not change sociability in group-housed mice. Across tests, the more dominant a mouse was in its cage, the larger the change in its behaviour when the neurons were switched on or off (for example r squared 0.62 for the drop in social time under silencing, 11 mice).

1884.content: In wild female chacma baboons (Papio hamadryas ursinus), dominance rank and the quality of close bonds were each related to how long a female lived: high-ranking females lived longer than lower-ranking ones, and, separately, females who formed stronger and more stable bonds with other females lived significantly longer than females with weaker and less stable relationships.

1885.content: Over 27 years of observation of 204 adult female baboons (Papio cynocephalus) in eight wild groups at Amboseli, Kenya (1,968 female-years), females in the top quarter of grooming connectedness to other adult females were 34% less likely to die in a given year than those in the bottom quarter, and those in the top quarter of connectedness to adult males were 45% less likely, with rank, group size and kin in the model. Median adult survival was about 2 years longer for well-connected females (18.4 against 16.4 years) and 3.3 years longer for females well connected to males.

1886.content: A systematic review of nationally representative surveys from 2000 to 2019 found loneliness data for 113 countries or territories (57 studies) and pooled 212 estimates for 106 countries from 24 studies. The pooled share of adolescents aged 12 to 17 who reported loneliness at a problematic level, nearly all from the Global School-Based Student Health Survey, ranged by WHO region from 9.2% in South-East Asia to 14.4% in the Eastern Mediterranean.

For adults, pooled estimates were possible for Europe only, all from single questions or the de Jong Gierveld scale in large multicountry surveys. The share reporting problematic loneliness was lowest in northern Europe (2.9% of young adults, 2.7% of middle-aged adults, 5.2% of adults 60 and over) and highest in eastern Europe (7.5%, 9.6% and 21.3%). Among older adults, middle income European countries had higher pooled figures than high income ones.

1887.content: In two population-based US studies of middle-aged and older adults (a national telephone sample aged 54 and over, and a Cook County, Illinois sample aged 50 to 67 followed for three years), higher loneliness went with more reported depressive symptoms after age, sex, ethnicity, education, income, marital status, social support and perceived stress were counted, and in the Cook County sample hostility as well. In the three-year data, latent growth models showed each rising with the other over time.

1888.content: In a population-based, ethnically diverse sample of 229 adults aged 50 to 68 in Cook County, Illinois, tested yearly from 2002 to 2006, loneliness (UCLA scale) in one year predicted a rise in depressive symptoms (CES-D score without its loneliness item) the next year (B = 0.18, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.30), while depressive symptoms did not predict a rise in loneliness (B = 0.10, CI -0.05 to 0.20). The loneliness path held with social network size, neuroticism, perceived stress, social support, medications and demographics in the models; with stressful life events added, both paths were significant.

1889.content: In Experiment 1, 96 unmarried male introductory psychology students helped an attractive woman on a task and then either did or did not receive a benefit from her in return. When she was described as unmarried (a communal relationship desired), the men liked her less if she repaid them than if she did not; when she was described as married (an exchange relationship preferred), they liked her more if she repaid them.

In Experiment 2, 80 female introductory psychology students were led to expect either a communal relationship (the other woman wanted to meet people and shared their interests) or an exchange relationship (she was busy and had different interests). A request for a favour right after the other had helped them raised liking when an exchange relationship was expected and lowered it when a communal one was expected; a request with no prior help lowered liking when an exchange relationship was expected.

1890.content: In a preregistered field experiment, the seating charts of 182 classrooms (grades 3 to 8) in 40 primary schools in rural central Hungary were randomised for one semester (September 2017 to January 2018), seating students at two-person desks. Among 2,966 students, being seated next to each other raised the chance of a mutual best-friend nomination from 15% to 22% on average, and the push toward friendship was the same whatever the pair's similarity in grades, gender or Roma or non-Roma ethnicity.

1891.content: In a 1977 survey of personal networks in California, people's active relations with relatives outside the household (ties with existing or likely exchanges) tended to be geographically dispersed and focused on immediate kin, especially parents and adult children, while ties to extended kin were largely latent. The more educated had the most dispersed networks and were least dependent on kin.

1892.content: A preregistered meta-analysis of 120 between-subjects Cyberball experiments (N = 11,869), in which people are left out of a virtual ball-toss game by players who are in fact a computer program, found that right after being left out, people scored on average 1.36 standard deviations worse than included people (95% CI -1.54 to -1.18) on the first measure taken. The effect did not differ by age, sex or country of the sample or by the number of players, tosses or game length, and held across measures of belonging, control, self-esteem and meaningful existence, of mood and of behaviour toward others, though behaviour toward others shifted less.

On the last measure taken, on average 4.85 minutes after the game, ostracised people still scored about 0.73 standard deviations lower than included people (95 studies), and the time elapsed within that window did not shrink the effect further.

1893.content: In a nationally representative Dutch survey (2,977 people under 65 from 1,706 households; both partners interviewed separately), the number of best friends people named (up to five, not counting partner or children) fell from about four among single men and women to about three in the empty-nest stage. The largest drops came when people started dating and when they began living together; later declines followed age more than life stage. Among people living with a partner who named friends, the average was 3.3, of whom 20% were relatives.

In the same Dutch survey, the share of friends that partners shared, and the share of friend contacts made together, rose over the life course: a step up when partners began living together, then a steady rise with age, and a further rise in the empty-nest stage. Women had more frequent contact with friends than men, had more contacts without their partner, and less often shared friends with their partner; after a first child, women's joint contacts with friends fell.

1894.content: Among Aka foragers of the Central African Republic (109 people: 41 Bagandou men interviewed in 1977 and 68 randomly sampled N'Dele adolescents and adults in 1980), the chance that a person had ever visited a place fell off exponentially with its straight-line distance from camp. Pooled over everyone, half of the listed places a person had visited lay within 30 km (the half-range; the mean distance is about 1.44 times that, 43 km). Among the less settled N'Dele Aka, men had a mean half-range of 58.3 km and women 32.4 km; Aka who had taken a village Bofi identity had about 22 km, so village life more than halved the range. Because the half-range did not differ between the three adult classes, the authors read most of the range as explored between about 10 and 25 years of age. Bagandou Aka, living at about twice the population density, ranged about half as far as N'Dele Aka, which the authors read as people going farther where people are fewer, to meet the same number of individuals.

Among N'Dele and Bagandou Aka foragers, visiting family was the main reason people gave for travelling to a place, and among the traditional reasons for travel, family visits took them the farthest (on average about 48 km). Hunting and gathering places were visited often and lay well inside the range. Dances, where Aka from many bands gathered, were another main reason; 28 N'Dele Aka gave looking for a man or woman as a secondary reason for a trip, and 18 of these 28 (64%) named a dance as the primary reason, which the authors read as dances being places to find partners.

1895.content: In the same Aka forager sample from the Central African Republic, the average distance between the birthplaces of spouses was very similar to the mean exploration range, the distance over which a person has visited places in a lifetime. Correlations between individual exploration and mating ranges led the authors to suggest that among the Aka it may be the man who chooses the marriage partner.

1896.content: Layton, O'Hara and Bilsborough describe three levels of social organisation among human hunter-gatherers, the domestic unit, the band and the wider community, and show how they are connected. They argue that bands arose within existing communities, out of the passing fission seen in chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) communities, to meet the need for closer cooperation in hunting and division of labour across a thinly spread community, while the wider community stayed useful when disputes broke out or a band's territory ran short.

From four lines of evidence (group sizes estimated from neocortex ratios, the distances raw materials were carried in different periods of hominin evolution, the authors' compilation of forager daily ranges and population densities, and fossil hominin anatomy), Layton and colleagues conclude that the key features of modern hunter-gatherer social organisation, nested bands inside a wider community, probably appeared during the evolution of Homo heidelbergensis.

1897.content: In a computer patch-foraging game, 47 adults (21 in experiment 1, 26 in experiment 2) chose on each step between harvesting apples from a depleting tree and paying a travel delay to reach a fresh one, for money. The marginal value theorem (Charnov 1976) says the rate-maximising rule is to leave when the expected reward of one more harvest falls below the average reward rate of the whole environment. Players moved their leaving point in the direction the theorem predicts when travel time or depletion rate changed (for example travel time F(1,25) = 42.1, depletion F(1,25) = 82, both p < .001), and their trial-by-trial choices were fitted better by a learning rule built on the theorem (a running average of rewards as the threshold) than by temporal-difference learning. They also stayed too long: thresholds sat below the optimum and they earned about 9 to 10% less than the optimal policy (a random policy tuned to each environment lost 25 to 33%).

1898.content: In a commentary on Wiessner's Ju/'hoansi firelight study, Dunbar argues that control of fire extended the human active day into the evening, adding as much as 4 hours, and that this evening time could be used for little but conversation, storytelling, singing and dancing. Using a primate equation that links group size to required social time and group sizes estimated from fossil cranial volumes, he estimates that archaic Homo would have needed 2.3 and anatomically modern humans 3.1 more hours of social time a day than earlier hominins could fit into a 12-hour day, a deficit that extending the day by 2 to 3 hours into the evening would close.

1899.content: In a set of British samples, Dunbar and Spoors counted the adults each person contacts at least once a month; the totals matched the typical size of the human sympathy group. Within this network a small inner clique served as the support group, the people a person is most likely to ask for advice or help in time of need. Men and women had networks of the same total size. Women had more women and more kin in their networks.

In the same British samples, kin made up a larger share of each person's monthly-contact network than chance would give, and people from large families had proportionally fewer non-kin in their networks, which the authors read as a limit of time or of cognition on network size. Kin were no more common in the support clique than in the wider network, and both men and women strongly preferred members of their own sex.

1900.content: Among Hadza hunter-gatherers of northern Tanzania (study 1, August 2017: 96 Hadza from seven camps against 124 Poles; study 2: 145 Hadza against 156 Poles), Hadza rated their happiness clearly higher than Poles. In study 1, on a simplified 3-point item about the past week, the Hadza mean was 2.91 against 2.18 for Poles, and society accounted for 35.7% of the variance. In study 2, on the 4-item Subjective Happiness Scale translated into Swahili (7 points), the Hadza mean was 5.83, and the gap between the societies equalled a Cohen's d of about 1.25; the Hadza mean was also higher than published community-sample means on the same scale from 12 industrialised populations (from Russia at 4.02 to the United States at 5.62), samples the authors note were collected between 1999 and 2018. Sex was unrelated to happiness in both societies.

Happiness fell with age among Poles (r = -0.44, p < 0.001 in study 2, with a curved pattern) but showed no link with age among the Hadza (r = -0.08, p = 0.34); the difference between the two correlations was significant (Fisher's z = 3.37). The authors suggest that older Hadza keep a valued place in camp life, pointing to grandmothers who provision grandchildren, and also name other differences such as living in groups of 20 to 30 people rather than communities of millions.

1901.content: Among 88,905 UK Biobank adults (mean age 62, 57% women) who wore a wrist light sensor for one week between 2013 and 2016 and were followed for about 8 years (3,750 deaths), people in the brightest 10% of night light had a 21 to 34% higher risk of death from any cause than people with dark nights (the darker half), and those in the 70th to 90th percentile a 15 to 18% higher risk. People in the brightest 10% of day light had a 17 to 34% lower risk than those in the dimmer half of day light. The ranges span three models adjusted step by step for age, sex, ethnicity, photoperiod, employment, education, income, deprivation, physical activity, smoking, alcohol, urban living and social activity. Night light was associated more strongly with cardiometabolic deaths (brightest 10%: 33 to 46% higher risk) than with other causes.

In the same cohort, a mathematical model of the human circadian pacemaker, fed with each person's light data, gave each person's circadian amplitude and phase. Lower modelled amplitude went with higher all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.90 to 0.96 per standard deviation of higher amplitude), and both an earlier phase (1.16 to 1.30) and a later phase (1.13 to 1.20) went with higher all-cause mortality.

1902.content: Reviewing their own and others' brain-imaging work, Goldstein and Walker report that after one night without sleep, the amygdala's response to unpleasant pictures (measured by fMRI) was 60% greater than after a normal night (Yoo et al. 2007), and its functional connectivity with medial prefrontal regions that regulate it from above was weaker, while its coupling with the brainstem locus coeruleus, which drives fight-or-flight arousal, was stronger. A similar pattern of greater amygdala reactivity and weaker prefrontal connectivity was reported after 5 nights of 4 hours' sleep (Motomura et al. 2013).

1903.content: Pooling 241 effect sizes from 64 experiments in which healthy people of 2 years and older had their sleep taken away entirely or cut short, Tomaso and colleagues found that sleep loss raised negative mood moderately (Hedges' g = 0.45, larger with total deprivation than with restriction and larger in younger samples) and lowered positive mood strongly (g = -0.94). The effect on rated reactions to emotional pictures and other stimuli was small after correcting for publication bias (g = -0.11). In youth samples, restricted sleep reduced adaptive emotion regulation (g = -0.32).

1904.content: In zebrafish (Danio rerio), the dorsal habenula, which corresponds to the mammalian medial habenula, connects asymmetrically to the interpeduncular nucleus. When the authors genetically silenced the lateral part of the dorsal habenula, the fish responded to a stimulus they had learned to fear by freezing instead of by the normal flight, which the authors read as this habenula to interpeduncular pathway controlling how fear responses are changed by experience.

1905.content: Bandler and Shipley review findings from several laboratories that the midbrain periaqueductal gray is organised in longitudinal columns of inputs, output neurons and interneurons. Its classic functions, defensive reactions, pain suppression and autonomic regulation, are carried by overlapping columns, and different kinds of threatening or painful stimuli switch on specific columns, each of which sets off its own coordinated pattern of skeletal, autonomic and pain-suppressing changes. They conclude that the columns coordinate distinct strategies for coping with different types of stress, threat and pain.

1906.content: In flocks of common redshank (Tringa totanus) attacked by sparrowhawks, birds that had not seen the predator took their cue from a flockmate's departure, which can lead to time-wasting false-alarm flights after mistaken or harmless departures. On sparrowhawk attacks, the delay before the next birds followed got shorter as more birds left at once, controlling for how visible and close the hawk was and for flock size and spacing, which fits a rule of flying at once only after several simultaneous departures. False-alarm flights that followed a harmless bird mistaken for a raptor, or a departure with no predator, did not become rarer in larger flocks, and birds in small flocks lost significantly more feeding time to them.

1907.content: Reviewing clock research across cyanobacteria, fungi, plants, flies, birds and mammals, Bell-Pedersen and colleagues describe the mammalian system as a hierarchy. Destroying the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus abolishes daily rhythms in behaviour, hormones and many biochemical processes, and SCN tissue transplanted into SCN-lesioned laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus) restores behavioural rhythms. The SCN holds the only mammalian clocks known to be set by light, through the retinohypothalamic tract, and tissue clocks elsewhere in the body run 4 to 12 hours behind it, which the authors take as the time the SCN signal needs to reach them. Up to 10% of genes show a daily rhythm in any given tissue, but fewer than 1% cycle in several tissues at once.

In the same review, Bell-Pedersen and colleagues report that offering food only at a restricted time of day resets the circadian clocks in peripheral tissues of laboratory rodents while the SCN master clock appears unaffected, so feeding time can pull tissue clocks out of step with the light-set master clock. They add that under natural conditions the SCN probably sets feeding time itself, through the sleep-wake cycle, which keeps the tissue clocks in their proper phase.

1908.content: A systematic review of repeated cross-sectional surveys of community-dwelling adults (12 studies from 278 reports, covering 15 countries from the 1960s to the 2000s, with comparable sampling and measures over time) found no consistent fall in the sleep adults reported. Average reported sleep rose in 7 countries (Bulgaria, Poland, Canada, France, Britain, Korea and the Netherlands; by 0.1 to 1.7 minutes a night each year), fell in 6 (Japan, Russia, Finland, Germany, Belgium and Austria; by 0.1 to 0.6 minutes a night each year), and was inconsistent in the United States and Sweden. Whether the shares of very short and very long sleepers changed was left open.

1909.content: In a laboratory forced-desynchrony study, 24 healthy young adults (16 men, 8 women) lived on a 30-hour sleep-wake schedule for 19 to 23 days or a 28-hour schedule for 33 to 36 days, so that their sleep-wake cycle drifted apart from their internal circadian clock. Mood, rated on visual analogue scales every 2 hours and every 20 minutes while awake, varied significantly with circadian phase, while time since waking had no reliable effect on its own. The two interacted: at some circadian phases mood improved with time awake, at others it worsened or stayed level. The authors conclude that moderate changes in the timing of the sleep-wake cycle may have profound effects on mood.

1910.content: In a preliminary within-subject study of eight non-dependent, non-treatment-seeking cocaine users who took intranasal cocaine at three doses, acute phenylalanine-tyrosine depletion, which transiently lowers the precursors of dopamine and noradrenaline, lowered craving set off by cocaine cues and by cocaine itself. Euphoria and how much freely available cocaine they took did not change. Depletion followed by L-dopa also lowered craving.

1911.content: Liebenberg, from his 1985 fieldwork on hunting and tracking with two groups of !Xo hunter-gatherers in the Kalahari and from earlier Kalahari ethnography, describes how trackers work when signs are sparse: they build a working hypothesis of what the animal was doing and where it is going, look for signs where the hypothesis says they should be, and revise it when signs confirm or refute it. He writes that predicting an animal's movements is therefore a continuous process of problem-solving, new hypotheses and new information.

1912.content: In a cluster randomised trial in 34 US primary care clinics (166 clinicians, 135 completed; upper Midwest and New York City), intervention clinics got feedback on their own work conditions and chose changes such as workflow redesign, better communication between clinicians and staff, and quality projects aimed at clinicians' concerns; follow-up came after 12 to 18 months. The clinic-level model showed no group treatment effect, but in the per-clinician analysis more intervention clinicians improved on the authors' burnout measure (21.8% vs 7.1% fewer burned out, p = 0.01) and on satisfaction (23.1% vs 10.0%, p = 0.04). Workflow changes went with improved burnout (odds ratio 5.9) and so did targeted quality projects (odds ratio 4.8).

1913.content: MacLean, in a review of brain evolution, argues that three developments marked the transition from reptiles to mammals: nursing with maternal care, sound and voice communication that keeps mother and young in contact, and play. He proposes that the separation call may be the earliest and most basic mammalian vocalization, that play may first have kept harmony in the nest, and that this behavioural triad may have depended on the evolution of the thalamocingulate division of the limbic system, which he says has no distinct counterpart in the reptile brain.

1914.content: In an elementary school study, 135 children in classes that got Energizers (short classroom activity breaks) took more in-school steps than 108 children in control classes (5,587 vs 4,805, effect size 0.49). On-task behaviour during academic instruction, observed in 62 third and fourth graders with a multiple-baseline design across classrooms, rose by 8% from before to after the activity breaks (effect size 0.60), and the least on-task children improved by 20% (effect size 2.20).

1915.content: In a lab experiment with 48 participants (81% German university students, mean age 26) who answered a block of work emails, being interrupted every two minutes by phone or instant message, on the same topic or a different one, did not slow the email work and did not lower its quality: interrupted emails were finished in less time. Participants rated stress (F(2,92) = 12.15, p < .001), frustration, time pressure and effort higher in the interrupted conditions than without interruptions, on a modified NASA workload scale.

1916.content: In a field study at a large US scientific research organisation, 13 information workers (mean age 46) were followed for three days of normal email use and then five workdays with email cut off. Without email they switched between computer windows less often and kept each window active longer (F(1,13) = 44.23, p < .0001). Heart rate variability, taken as the standard deviation of heart rate from chest-strap monitors in the seven people with usable data, tended to be higher without email, which the authors read as less stress (paired t-test, p = .065); mean heart rate was also higher without email, which the authors link to more time out of the office.

1917.content: Maslach and Leiter describe burnout as a prolonged response to chronic interpersonal stressors on the job, with three dimensions: overwhelming exhaustion, cynicism and detachment from the job, and a sense of ineffectiveness. Their Areas of Worklife model places its sources in six person-job mismatches: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values; the greater the mismatch the more likely burnout, the greater the match the more likely engagement. They report initial support from cross-sectional and longitudinal studies.

Maslach and Leiter write that most burnout interventions have targeted the individual, with little attention to social or organisational change, although the research points to situational factors as primary. They add that very little research has evaluated any intervention and that randomised trials are especially rare.

1918.content: Reviewing 25 years of burnout research, Maslach, Schaufeli and Leiter report that experienced workload and time pressure are strongly and consistently related to burnout, especially exhaustion, with both strain as people rated it and more objective demands such as hours worked and number of clients. Lack of social support, especially from supervisors, lack of feedback and little participation in decision making are also consistently linked to burnout.

The same review reports that personal factors (age, education, personality, work attitudes) are related to burnout, but less strongly than features of the work situation, and the authors conclude that burnout is more a social phenomenon than an individual one; they call it paradoxical that most proposed interventions focus on the individual.

1919.content: A systematic review of 39 studies of classroom-based physical activity (active breaks, curriculum-focused active breaks and physically active lessons; most in the USA, the Netherlands and Australia) found that 10 of 12 studies of classroom behaviour showed an immediate improvement in on-task behaviour or a fall in off-task behaviour. A meta-analysis of the 4 controlled studies with usable data gave a standardised mean difference of 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 1.00). In the two studies with longer follow-up, the improvement appeared to fade, with no group difference in reported behaviour incidents.

1920.content: In 29 captive-bred American mink (Neovison vison) on a US research farm, housed for about seven months in either non-enriched cages (16) or larger enriched cages with wading water and objects to handle (13), the non-enriched mink approached all ten test stimuli, whether aversive (such as air puffs), rewarding or ambiguous, faster than enriched mink (P = 0.003), spent longer oriented to or in contact with them (P < 0.0001 with stimulus type pooled) and ate more food rewards (P = 0.037). They showed no sign of apathy or of lost interest in rewards; the authors read the raised interest in any stimulation as boredom, possibly marked by lying still while awake, and conclude that enrichment reduces it.

1921.content: In 1,278 male and female blue-collar workers (study from an occupational health institute in Israel), objective work conditions (work underload, repetitive work, as against varied work) and felt monotony were related to lower job satisfaction, more psychological distress and more sickness absence. The links were partly carried by felt monotony and partly direct from repetitive work and underload; job satisfaction and distress went mainly with felt monotony, sickness absence equally with work conditions and felt monotony, and the strongest links were for short-cycle repetitive work. Sickness absence was related to work conditions in women but not in men.

1922.content: In two cross-lagged longitudinal studies of parents (918 French-speaking, 96.9% from Belgium, with waves 5.5 months apart; and 822 English-speaking employed parents recruited online), each surveyed three times over a year, higher scores on the Parental Burnout Inventory predicted later escape ideation (thoughts of running away or suicide), neglect and violence towards one's children, with aggregated effect sizes of d = 1.31, 1.25 and 1.25. Paths in the reverse direction were smaller. The authors define parental burnout as exhaustion in the parental role, emotional distance from one's children and a sense of parental ineffectiveness, arising from a chronic imbalance of stressors over resources.

1923.content: Nolen-Hoeksema, Wisco and Lyubomirsky review response styles research and report well-supported evidence that rumination worsens depressive symptoms as the studies measured them, enhances negative thinking, impairs problem solving, interferes with instrumental behaviour and erodes social support. They report that rumination more consistently predicts onset of depression, as the studies diagnosed it, than its duration, and that it predicts how long depressive symptoms last when combined with negative cognitive styles. In the authors' account, dozens of experiments show that positive distraction relieves depressed mood, though distraction has not consistently gone with fewer symptoms in correlational studies.

1924.content: Ormel, Hollon, Kessler, Cuijpers and Monroe review why the population prevalence of depression, as diagnosed in population surveys, has not fallen since the 1980s although treatments improved and became far more available. Of seven explanations they find little evidence that diagnosed incidence or prevalence rose, either through misdiagnosis of distress or as a real rise. They find strong evidence that the published literature overestimates short- and long-term treatment efficacy, that treatments are considerably less effective as deployed in real-world settings, and that treatment impact differs substantially for chronic-recurrent cases; they report that little research exists on harmful effects of current treatments.

1925.content: In a pooled database of doubly labelled water measurements from 6,421 people (64% female) aged 8 days to 95 years in 29 countries, fat-free mass explained 83% of the variation in total daily energy expenditure. Adjusted for body size and composition, expenditure rose rapidly in the first year to about 46% above adult values, fell slowly through childhood and adolescence to adult levels at about age 20, stayed stable from 20 to 60, also during pregnancy, and declined after about 60, reaching about 26% below middle-aged adults in people in their nineties.

1926.content: Among 263 students at a North American university (60% female, mean age 20.7), randomly assigned to 66 mixed-sex project groups of 3 to 5 for a 16-week semester, teammates rated each other on prestige, dominance and social rank at weeks 2, 6, 10 and 16. Both prestige and dominance went with higher rank when the groups were new, but in the following weeks dominance had no substantial effect on rank while prestige strongly raised later rank, and rank in turn raised later prestige. Prestige and dominance stayed distinct throughout.

1927.content: In a study of students, people reported greater happiness and greater feelings of belonging on days when they interacted with more classmates than usual. In two further studies that covered all daily interactions, with strong and weak ties, interactions with weak ties (acquaintances) were again related to social and emotional well-being.

1928.content: Among 157 healthy White women, where a woman placed herself on a ladder of social standing (subjective social status) was more consistently and more strongly related to psychological functioning and to health measures (self-rated health, heart rate, sleep latency, body fat distribution, and cortisol habituation to repeated stress) than objective indicators of socioeconomic status were; 59 of the women also took part in a laboratory stress study. Most of these associations held after controlling for objective status and negative affectivity.

1929.content: Akiskal and Akiskal propose evolutionary uses for the affective temperaments, reading the mood diagnoses as the extremes of traits that in milder form give advantages to the person or the group: depressive traits as sensitivity to the suffering of others, which would help the survival of kin and other members of the species; the romantic pursuits and creative bent of the cyclothymic temperament as aids to mating; and hyperthymic traits as advantages in leadership, exploration, territoriality and mating.

In questionnaire data, Akiskal and Akiskal report correlations between the scales of the TEMPS temperament questionnaire and between the TEMPS and the Temperament and Character Inventory, which they read as harm avoidance counterbalancing the risk taking of people scoring high on cyclothymic temperament, in both men and women.

1930.content: A Cochrane review of 35 randomised and controlled trials (4,319 participants, 13 different psychosocial interventions) found that adding a structured psychosocial intervention to methadone or other agonist maintenance gave no added benefit over standard maintenance on retention in treatment (27 studies, 3,124 participants, RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.07), opiate abstinence during treatment (8 studies, RR 1.12, 0.92 to 1.37), compliance, psychiatric symptoms or depression scores.

The authors of the same Cochrane review state that the control arm in the included trials routinely offered counselling sessions with methadone, so the review did not test whether any psychosocial support is needed with methadone, only whether a more structured intervention adds to standard support; study durations were too short to analyse outcomes such as mortality.

1931.content: A systematic review of 176 studies (1980 to 2012) of school outcomes followed for 2 years or more found that, of the reported outcomes comparing people diagnosed with ADHD and left untreated against controls without the diagnosis, 79 percent of achievement test outcomes and 75 percent of academic performance outcomes were worse in the diagnosed group, and 72 and 81 percent when IQ differences were controlled. The percentages count outcomes across studies, not people.

1932.content: A review of hyperfocus found almost no direct research on it: a title search turned up 6 papers and a PubMed title or abstract search 19, of which 7 were empirical studies of hyperfocus. The authors note that hyperfocus is widely reported in people diagnosed with ADHD, is absent from the DSM criteria, and on anecdotal evidence appears to be a core symptom; they write that attentional control may not be as impaired in people diagnosed with ADHD as once thought.

The same review proposes a testable definition of hyperfocus with four parts: the task is engaging (fun, interesting or important), attention is intensely sustained or selective, things not relevant to the task are perceived less, and task performance improves. The authors read the flow state as the same thing, and propose that the hyperfocus reported in the ADHD and autism literature fits this definition while the usage in the schizophrenia literature does not.

1933.content: In full birth cohorts from Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Israel and Western Australia (2,001,631 children born 1998 to 2011, followed to age 16, 22,156 of them diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder in national registers), family-based models put the heritability of the diagnosis at a median of 80.8 percent (95% CI 73.2 to 85.5) across countries, from 50.9 percent in Finland to 86.8 percent in Israel, and 81.2 to 82.7 percent for the Nordic countries combined. Maternal effects were estimated at 0.4 to 1.6 percent.

1934.content: In the E-Risk study of 1,116 pairs of same-sex British twins born 1994 to 1995, mothers' reports of borderline-type traits at age 12 (a scale drawn from the SWAP-200-A) correlated 0.66 between identical twins and 0.29 between fraternal twins; twin modelling put the genetic share of the variance at 66 percent. For the extreme group, concordance was 52 percent in identical and 7 percent in fraternal twins.

In the same twin cohort, children whose mothers reported physical maltreatment before age 10 scored higher on the borderline-type trait scale at 12 (r = .20). Comparing twins within a family, the maltreated twin scored higher than the non-maltreated co-twin, with a small effect (r = .06, p = .023); within identical pairs the effect was similar (r = .07) but not significant, as few pairs differed in maltreatment.
