Maternal negative expressed emotion, rated from the mother's speech, went with higher scores (r = .39), and the link held within twin pairs (r = .31) and within identical pairs (r = .22).

1935.content: Following 3.56 million people born in Denmark 1945 to 1996 through national registers from 1977 to 2010 (78 million person-years; 91,637 with hospital contacts for a mood disorder diagnosis), a prior hospital contact for autoimmune disease went with a 45 percent higher rate of a later first diagnosis of mood disorder by a psychiatrist (IRR 1.45, 95% CI 1.39 to 1.52), and any hospitalisation for infection with a 62 percent higher rate (IRR 1.62, 1.60 to 1.64); both together gave IRR 2.35, with a dose-response for the number of infections and autoimmune diseases. 32 percent of those diagnosed had a previous hospital contact for infection.

1936.content: In a 21-day electronic diary study of community adults, 41 who met interview criteria for borderline personality disorder and 38 healthy controls rated perceived rejection and rage at random prompts (about 77 of 105 entries each). A 1 SD rise in perceived rejection went with a much larger rise in momentary rage in the diagnosed group (B = .29) than in controls (B = .05, p < .06); the group by rejection interaction was significant (F = 38.59, p < .0001).

In the same study, the 45 participants who met interview criteria for borderline personality disorder scored far higher on the Adult Rejection Sensitivity Questionnaire than the 40 healthy controls (mean 14.86 against 6.19), above the 90th percentile of a general sample of 681 adults; in a priming task they also pronounced rage words faster after rejection primes than controls did.

1937.content: In an 8-week randomised double-blind trial, 95 adults diagnosed with DSM-IV borderline personality disorder received extended-release quetiapine 150 mg a day (33), 300 mg a day (33) or placebo (29). The low-dose group improved more than placebo on the clinician-rated Zanarini scale; time to a 50 percent score drop was shorter on both doses (HR 2.54 and 2.37). Among completers, 82, 74 and 48 percent were rated responders. Only 67 percent completed (58 percent on 300 mg, 79 percent on placebo); sedation, appetite change and dry mouth were common, and those sedated were more likely to drop out.

1938.content: In the SMILE trial, 202 adults diagnosed with major depression by structured interview were randomised to 16 weeks of supervised group aerobic exercise, home-based exercise, sertraline (50 to 200 mg a day) or a placebo pill. Remission (no longer meeting the criteria and a HAM-D score below 8) was 45 percent with supervised exercise, 40 percent with home exercise, 47 percent with sertraline and 31 percent with placebo (p = .057); HAM-D scores fell in all groups and the active groups did not differ significantly from placebo (p = .23).

In the same trial, remission did not differ between patients who exercised in a supervised group and those who exercised alone at home; the supervised group reached higher aerobic fitness. The authors read this as social support in the group not being necessary for the benefit of exercise.

1939.content: In the Dutch DRD trial, 289 adults with at least two previous episodes that met the trial's criteria for depression, in remission on antidepressants for at least 6 months, were randomised to preventive cognitive therapy while tapering off the antidepressant (85), the antidepressant alone (100), or both (104), and followed for 24 months with masked assessors. The authors report that staying on the antidepressant alone was not superior to preventive cognitive therapy while tapering for relapse or recurrence (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.32, p = 0.502); adding the therapy to the antidepressant lowered relative risk by 41 percent against the antidepressant alone (HR 0.59, 0.38 to 0.94).

1940.content: A meta-analysis of 21 population-based incidence studies (published 1977 to 2008) found that, against non-migrants in the same host country, first-generation immigrants had a mean weighted incidence rate ratio of 2.3 (95% CI 2.0 to 2.7; 61 effect sizes) for a diagnosis of schizophrenia or a related psychotic disorder, and their children born in the host country 2.1 (1.8 to 2.5; 28 effect sizes). The two generations did not differ significantly; the rate varied with ethnic group and host country.

1941.content: An individual participant data meta-analysis by the authors of 4 randomised trials (714 adults in full or partial remission, 73 percent women, mean age 49) compared preventive cognitive therapy or mindfulness-based cognitive therapy during or after tapering off antidepressants with staying on antidepressants alone. Time to relapse, assessed by blinded diagnostic interview over 15 months, did not differ significantly (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.23); 325 of 712 participants relapsed. Younger age at onset, shorter remission and more residual symptoms at baseline went with more relapse in both arms, and no factor singled out who did better on either strategy.

1942.content: In Belgium, 142 parents who reported parental burnout symptoms on a screening subscale of the Parental Burnout Assessment took one of two 8-week programmes of weekly two-hour group sessions, allocated by enrolling in a location and date without knowing which programme it offered (14 groups in 10 cities; the letter calls this random assignment): a directive programme on stressors and resources (77) or a non-directive group led by psychologists trained in active listening, where parents shared their difficulties (65). In a subgroup of 40 who waited two months or more first, scores did not fall while they waited. After both programmes self-reported burnout fell 37 percent, negative emotions 29 percent, reported neglect 35 percent and reported violence 32 percent, partners reported similar changes, and the effects held at 3 months, with no difference between programmes.

In the same trial, hair cortisol, a measure of cortisol deposited over about the previous 3 months, fell after both group programmes: the time effect on log-transformed values was significant (F(1,86) = 37.09, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.60) and the mean raw concentration fell by 52 percent. Burnout scores and hair cortisol were not correlated at baseline.

1943.content: In drug-safety surveillance data from psychiatric hospitals in the AMSP project (2001 to 2011), 2,195 inpatients diagnosed with borderline personality disorder were prescribed psychotropic drugs at high rates: 70 percent antipsychotics and/or antidepressants, 33 percent anticonvulsants, 30 percent benzodiazepines and 4 percent lithium; 90 percent received at least one psychotropic drug, 80 percent two or more and 54 percent three or more at once (mean 2.8). Quetiapine was the single most used drug (22 percent) and its use rose over the period, although, as the authors report, no drug is approved or recommended in the guidelines for this label.

1944.content: Case vignettes were sent to 1,000 child psychologists, psychiatrists and social workers, who were asked for a diagnostic label. One vignette met all DSM-IV and ICD-10 criteria for ADHD; three others described several ADHD symptoms but stated that other required criteria were not met, so the diagnosis could not be given. For those three, 16.7 percent of the therapists diagnosed ADHD, and they gave it about twice as often when the case was a boy than when it was a girl. The authors had hypothesised that therapists judge by resemblance to a prototypical ADHD child (the representativeness heuristic).

1945.content: In kittens (domestic cat, Felis catus) whose right eyelids were sutured shut for various periods at different ages, with recordings made later from the striate (primary visual) cortex, susceptibility to the effects of closing one eye began suddenly near the start of the fourth week of life, stayed high until some time between the sixth and eighth weeks, then declined and disappeared around the end of the third month. Closing one eye for over a year in an adult cat had no detectable effect.

In the same kitten experiments, closing one eye for only 3 to 4 days in the fourth and fifth weeks sharply cut the number of visual cortex cells that both eyes could drive and shifted influence away from the closed eye; a 6-day closure cut the cells the closed eye could drive to a fraction of normal. This matched the picture after 3 months of closure from birth, in which the share of cells the deprived eye could influence fell from 85 percent to about 7 percent.

After 3 months of closing one eye, opening it again for up to 5 years gave only a very limited recovery in the visual cortex and no obvious recovery of the shrunken cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus, although the cats regained some vision in that eye in behaviour. Closing the good eye, needed for the behavioural recovery, had no detectable effect on the cortex. After a 5-week closure recovery was clearly better, though far from complete.

1946.content: Kirschbaum and colleagues describe the Trier Social Stress Test: a 10-minute anticipation period followed by a 10-minute test in which the person gives a free speech and does mental arithmetic in front of an audience. In six independent studies the protocol produced considerable changes in ACTH, cortisol (serum and saliva), growth hormone and prolactin and significant rises in heart rate; salivary cortisol rose 2 to 4 times above baseline, with similar peak levels across studies.

Across the summarised studies, sex, genetics and nicotine use went with differences in how strongly cortisol rose during the Trier test, while personality traits showed no correlation with the cortisol response.

1947.content: In a review, Knudsen defines a sensitive period as a limited time in development when experience shapes the brain particularly strongly, and a critical period as a sensitive period in which experience supplies information essential for normal development and changes performance permanently. He states that sensitive periods show in behaviour but are a property of neural circuits.

Knudsen proposes that experience during a sensitive period changes the architecture of a circuit in fundamental ways, so that some patterns of connectivity become highly stable. Plasticity after the period ends is substantial in many circuits, but in his reading it works inside the architectural limits laid down during the sensitive period.

1948.content: In a review of archaeological human remains worldwide, Larsen reports that the move from foraging to farming went with an overall decline in oral and general health. Prehistoric farmers, compared with foragers, show skeletal and dental pathological conditions more often and altered skeletal and dental growth. He states that the older picture, in which health and nutrition improved, longevity rose and workload fell with farming, is incorrect.

Larsen also reports that changes in food and food preparation went with changes in the skull, face and teeth of early farmers, and that lower activity levels and less mobility went with a general decrease in skeletal robusticity.

1949.content: In 4 adult rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) with neural tracers injected into the amygdala, prefrontal areas differed vastly in how strongly they were connected with the amygdala: most densely in posterior orbitofrontal and posterior medial cortex, most sparsely in anterior lateral prefrontal cortex, especially area 10. Comparing each area's share of input from the amygdala with its share of output to it, anterior cingulate areas 25 and 24 sent comparatively more projections to the amygdala than they received, while caudal orbitofrontal areas received more than they sent (that difference was not significant), and caudal medial area MPAll received significantly more than it sent.

In rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) with tracers injected in the amygdala, prefrontal neurons projecting to the amygdala sat mainly in cortical layer 5, with significant numbers also in layers 2 and 3 of posterior medial and orbitofrontal cortex. Axons from the amygdala ended in prefrontal cortex mostly in two bands, one in the superficial and one in the deep layers, or in columns through the whole cortical depth, and less often in small patches; the heavy endings in layers 1 and 2 overlapped with calbindin-positive inhibitory neurons. The authors read this as the same laminar pattern as connections between cortical areas, with widespread 'feedback' from the amygdala.

1950.content: Injecting a tracer carried forward along axons into each major division of the amygdala in crab-eating macaques (Macaca fascicularis), Amaral and Price found amygdala projections to widespread regions of frontal, insular, temporal and occipital cortex: heaviest to medial and orbital frontal areas (24, 25, 32, 14, 13a, 12), the temporal pole and perirhinal cortex, along the whole inferotemporal cortex, a surprisingly strong projection to prestriate visual areas and, in at least one case, clear labelling in primary visual cortex (area 17).

1951.content: In three experiments, participants held a painful isometric wall-sit ski exercise as long as they could, each 20 seconds earning money for a named recipient: themselves (r = 1), a parent or sibling (r = 0.5), a grandparent, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew (r = 0.25), a cousin (r = 0.125), and in some trials a same-sex best friend or a children's charity. Among Oxford students (11 men, 13 women), London students (20 men, 20 women) and London male students (22), the time held fell in a reliable linear trend with the recipient's relatedness; differences between the most distant kin categories were mostly not significant.

The same task with Zulu men in two poor rural communities in South Africa (31 at Emmaus in the Drakensberg, 20 at Hluhluwe), with payment as food hampers for the recipient, gave the same reliable linear trend with relatedness. Unlike the London men, the Zulu men did not distinguish between kin of r = 0.5 and r = 0.25, and they did distinguish cousins from a local school; the authors suggest living in extended families may act as a cue of relatedness.

Among 40 London students, a same-sex best friend received as much effort as relatives of r = 0.25 but less than the closest kin, and about 15 percent more than a children's charity; women held the position longer for a best friend than for relatives of r = 0.25. Asked whether a recipient had helped them before or would help them later, participants' answers did not predict how long they held the position, with one exception in the London sample.

1952.content: Mark, Marion and Hoffman formalise the claim that natural selection favours perceptions that depict the world accurately, and test it in "interface games", evolutionary games in which perceptual strategies compete, using closed-form solutions and Monte Carlo simulations of simple games with frequency-dependent selection and complete mixing in infinite populations. In these games, accurate (veridical) perceptual strategies could go extinct in competition with strategies tuned to utility rather than to objective reality.

1953.content: In a review, Nestler states that drugs of abuse have very different immediate mechanisms of action but converge on the brain's reward pathways, producing a series of common functional effects after both single and repeated use, and that some similar actions occur for natural rewards as well.

1954.content: In the 2011 National Mental Health Literacy and Stigma Survey, a nationally representative sample of Australian adults read a vignette of a person described with depression symptoms (893 people) or with depression symptoms and suicidal thoughts (903 people). Over 80 percent named each of these as a cause of what the person in the vignette had: day-to-day problems, the death of a close friend or relative, a recent traumatic event, childhood problems, and a chemical imbalance in the brain. The authors conclude that most of the Australian public believe both psychosocial and biological factors cause the condition the vignette labels depression.

Compared with national surveys in 1995 and 2003/4, the 2011 respondents more often endorsed psychosocial and genetic causes for the vignette, and less often infection, allergy and weakness of character. Respondents who correctly gave the vignette the depression label were more likely to name psychosocial causes and less likely to name an allergic reaction, a virus or an infection.

1955.content: Forty children (mean age 9 years 3 months; 23 physically abused, with abuse verified from clinical and legal records, and 17 non-abused children matched on age and IQ) sorted and told apart faces morphed in 10 percent steps between happiness, anger, fear and sadness. The abused children placed the category boundary differently only on the two continua that involved anger: they saw anger in more of the blended faces, a broader category for anger against fear and against sadness. On happiness blended into fear or sadness the two groups did not differ.

Pollak and Kistler read the broader anger category as an adaptive process that lets maltreated children track signs of anger in their surroundings better, at the possible cost of reading signals as threatening too often and misjudging other facial expressions.

1956.content: Comparing doubly labelled water measurements of total daily energy expenditure in 17 primate species (19 populations, among them chimpanzees Pan troglodytes, bonobos Pan paniscus, gorillas Gorilla gorilla, orangutans Pongo pygmaeus, Hadza foragers and Western humans) with 67 other placental mammal species, primates spent on average 50.4 percent (SD 17.8) of the energy expected for a placental mammal of their body mass. Basal metabolic rate in primates was similar to that of other placental mammals.

The authors judge the gap too large to come from differences in physical activity: to match other mammals, Hadza foragers in Tanzania would need about 45 km of extra running each day and the chimpanzees in the sample about 48 km of extra travel. Captive and wild primates did not differ in daily energy expenditure (captive lemurs spent about 20 percent more than wild ones), consistent with earlier findings of similar expenditure in Hadza and Western humans. The authors read this as a systemic reduction in cellular metabolism in primates.
Across species, the authors' comparisons of growth, reproduction and maximum life span indicate that the low metabolic rates of primates contribute to their slow life histories.

1957.content: Pool and colleagues note that animal research has shown a reward can be wanted without being liked once obtained, but that experiments in humans have given contradictory results, raising doubts about whether wanting and liking act as separate influences in human reward processing. They attribute much of the contradiction to inconsistent ways of measuring the two.

Searching ProQuest and PubMed for human studies from January 1990 to April 2015 that measured wanting or liking with explicit reference to the incentive salience framework, the authors kept 84 articles. Most measured wanting after a reward-associated cue and liking during or just after the reward, as the animal model defines them, and half of the procedures used food rewards. A far from negligible number used measures that do not match the animal definitions, some measuring wanting in the same way others measured liking. The authors name expected pleasantness, a cognitive desire distinct from both animal wanting and animal liking, as the main confound.

1958.content: In a review of evolutionary traps, Robertson, Rehage and Sih attribute species declines worldwide to human-induced rapid environmental change, such as climate change or introduced species, and state that although flexible behaviour has buffered some species, maladaptive behaviour patterns called evolutionary traps are increasingly common and threaten the survival of the species affected.

To explain why some animals fall into traps, the authors combine the cost-benefit approach of behavioural ecology with an evolutionary approach to cue-response systems (reaction norms and signal detection), and argue that wildlife conservation and management need a significant change in thinking to remove and mitigate traps.

1959.content: Schlaepfer, Runge and Sherman state that organisms often rely on environmental cues to make behavioural and life-history decisions, and that in environments suddenly altered by humans, formerly reliable cues may no longer go with adaptive outcomes, so organisms can become trapped by their evolved responses and suffer lower survival or reproduction. An ecological trap is a poor habitat choice made on cues that once went with habitat quality; it is one kind of evolutionary trap, in which the cues an organism uses for any decision have come apart from the outcomes that normally followed.

The authors add that a trap can end in extinction if a population falls below a critical size before it adapts to the new environment, and that conservation must be designed in light of the behavioural mechanisms and evolutionary history of species to avoid trapping them.

1960.content: A meta-analysis of 54 studies (63 effect sizes) of zoo mammals of many species found that 57 of 63 effect sizes (90 percent) went in the predicted direction, with animals showing less stereotypic behaviour during enrichment than at baseline. The mean effect size was r = 0.46, and 1,726 unpublished null studies would be needed to cancel the result.

1961.content: A review and meta-analysis of published zoo research found enrichment a successful technique for reducing stereotypic behaviour: enrichment went with a significant reduction in stereotypic behaviour in about 53 percent of cases. The authors add that problems with scientific methods and data presentation severely limit the conclusions, and that most studies cover large, charismatic and often endangered species.

1962.content: In the US National Human Activity Pattern Survey, a probability telephone survey of 9,386 people of all ages run almost daily from September 1992 to September 1994 with 24-hour recall diaries, respondents reported spending on average 87% of their time in enclosed buildings and about 6% in enclosed vehicles. About 7 to 8% of the day was spent outdoors, and 69% was spent in a residence. The authors report the indoor share as fairly constant across US regions, Canada and California.

1963.content: On one free US online dating site in a mid-sized southwestern city (6 months of 2011; 8,259 heterosexual men and 6,274 heterosexual women), users sent 177,404 first contacts, 142,444 of them by men, a four-to-one ratio. Nearly all women (98%) received at least one message from a man, while about 18% of men received no message from a woman. The average man received 4.5 times fewer messages than the average woman.

On the same site, both men and women sent their first messages mostly to the daters other users rated most desirable, whatever their own rating. Seventy-nine percent of men's first messages and 58% of women's went unanswered, and only 3% of men's and 7% of women's messages were followed by more than five exchanges. Women who wrote first reached more desirable men than women who waited, yet women were four times less likely than men to send a message.

1964.content: In the All Our Families cohort in Calgary, Canada (2,441 mothers and children, data 2011 to 2016), mothers reported their child's screen time and filled in the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3), a developmental screening questionnaire, at 24, 36 and 60 months. In a random-intercepts cross-lagged panel model that separates within-child change from stable differences between children, more screen time at 24 months predicted lower screening scores at 36 months (beta -0.06) and more screen time at 36 months predicted lower scores at 60 months (beta -0.08); lower scores did not predict later screen time. Children watched on average about 17, 25 and 11 hours a week at 24, 36 and 60 months.

1965.content: Marwick and boyd asked Twitter users directly who they imagine reading their tweets, what makes someone seem authentic and what they will not tweet about, and received 226 responses from 181 users, from people with few followers to the most-followed accounts. They report that Twitter flattens many audiences into one (context collapse): even with private accounts, users face friends, family, co-workers and acquaintances at once. Users handled this by concealing information, targeting tweets to different audiences, and trying to show both an authentic self and an interesting personality; some users with 100,000 or more followers described their audience as a fan base or community to connect with or manage, which the authors link to micro-celebrity and personal branding.

1966.content: Newman linked every known validated supercentenarian (110 or older) and semi-supercentenarian (105 or older) in the Gerontology Research Group and International Database on Longevity tables, and centenarian counts from the USA, France, Japan, England and Italy, to registration and socioeconomic data by region of birth. In the United States, supercentenarian status was associated with the absence of vital registration, and the state-by-state introduction of birth certificates went with a 69 to 82% fall in supercentenarian records. In Italy, England and France, reaching a remarkable age was associated with poverty, low incomes, shorter life expectancy, higher crime, worse health and fewer people over 90. Only 18% of validated supercentenarians had a birth certificate (none in the USA), and their birthdates cluster on days divisible by five.

Newman reports that the designated longevity regions of Sardinia, Okinawa and Ikaria are regions with low incomes, low literacy, high crime and life expectancy below their national average. He cites a US federal estimate placing Loma Linda's average lifespan in the unremarkable 27th to 75th percentile range, EU data ranking the Sardinian and Ikarian regions 36th to 44th and 56th to 65th in the EU for survival past 85, and past error findings in each region, among them that 42% of Costa Rican people aged 99 and over misstated their age in the 2000 census.

1967.content: In Sardinia, validated centenarians are frequent and the share of men among them is unusually high. Using an extreme longevity index (the percentage of people born in Sardinia in 1880 to 1900 who reached 100) and spatial smoothing, the AKEA study located a 'Blue Zone' of concentrated longevity in the mountainous central-eastern part of the island. Life expectancy there was longer than in the rest of the island, especially for men, and the sex ratio among centenarians born there was 1.35 against 2.43 in the rest of Sardinia (given in the abstract as the male to female ratio). The authors say the mechanism is unknown and propose environment, genes from inbreeding and low immigration, or both.

1968.content: Using the Costa Rican voter registry linked to birth-registration dates (24,400 nonagenarians born 1878 to 1913, followed 1983 to 2004), Rosero-Bixby estimated that mortality at age 90 in Costa Rica was at least 14% lower than the average of 13 high-income countries, an advantage growing about 1% per year of age, with a further 12% advantage for men. Life expectancy at 90 for Costa Rican men was 4.4 years, half a year more than any other country. Ages were computed from birth-register dates, not from reported ages, and the advantage held when the analysis was restricted to timely registered births in the Central region. The more remote non-Central regions showed 15% lower mortality by 1995, which the author flags as possibly reflecting data errors and which disappeared at older ages and in later years.

1969.content: In a survival follow-up of 16,300 elderly Costa Ricans (1990 to 2011), men living in the Nicoya region had a death rate ratio of 0.80 against other Costa Rican men. A 60-year-old Nicoyan man had seven times the chance of a Japanese man of reaching 100 and 2.2 more years of life expectancy. The advantage was absent in women, held after adjusting for socioeconomic conditions, was absent in people who had moved out of Nicoya, and came from lower cardiovascular mortality (death rate ratio 0.65). In the CRELES sample (about 3,000 people, 350 from Nicoya), Nicoyans were leaner and taller, had lower cardiovascular risk markers and fewer disabilities, and ate a plain traditional diet (rice, beans, animal protein) with a lower glycemic index and more fibre.

1970.content: Using a new nationwide survival database of 550,000 adult Costa Ricans alive at any point in 1990 to 2020 (electoral and birth registry records, Gompertz regression), Rosero-Bixby found that the longevity advantage of Nicoyan men is disappearing in a trend that follows birth cohort: Nicoyan men born in 1905 had 33% lower adult mortality than other Costa Ricans, while those born in 1945 had 10% higher mortality. The original hotspot has shrunk to a small area in the south of the peninsula, from Hojancha to Samara. Nicoyans born before 1930 who are still alive continue to show exceptionally high longevity.

1971.content: In a narrative review of loneliness and social internet use, Nowland, Necka and Cacioppo note that the evidence is contradictory and mostly cross-sectional, and propose a two-way relation: social technology used as a way-station to strengthen existing relationships or form new ones goes with less loneliness, while social technology used to escape the social world and withdraw from the pain of interaction goes with more. They report that lonely people prefer communicating online to face to face, feel more in control and more themselves online, lurk passively more often, and tend to keep friends made online as online-only contacts, so that they are more likely than less lonely people to replace offline interaction with online interaction.

1972.content: Przybylski, Rigby and Ryan propose a model, rooted in self-determination theory, in which both the appeal of video games and their effects on well-being rest on how far games satisfy the basic psychological needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness. The article reviews evidence on need satisfaction in games and short-term well-being, the appeal of violent content, aggression after play, problem patterns of play and immersion.

1973.content: In four studies, Ryan, Rigby and Przybylski measured players' sense of autonomy, competence and relatedness during computer game play. In studies 1 to 3, undergraduates played one, two or four games in the laboratory (study 1: 89 students); in-game autonomy and competence were associated with enjoyment, preference for future play and changes in well-being from before to after play. In study 4, an online survey of 730 members of a gaming community with experience of massively multiplayer online games (679 men, mean age 22), autonomy, competence and relatedness were each independently associated with enjoyment and preference for future play.

1974.content: In a critical review of research on social network sites and subjective well-being, Verduyn and colleagues report negative relations between passive use (watching others' posts without interacting) and subjective well-being, and positive relations between active use and well-being, the first more robust than the second. They state that passive use provokes social comparison and envy, which have negative downstream consequences for well-being, while active use relates to well-being through social capital and a feeling of connectedness.

1975.content: Among 148 US college students at a midsouthern university, identification with the school's men's basketball team was correlated with a combined index of social psychological health (low scores on the UCLA Loneliness Scale plus collective self-esteem), r = .24, and so was the number of games attended (r = .19). In regression, only team identification accounted for unique variance in the index, and attendance and identification did not interact. The authors note that the data are correlational.

1976.content: Among 177 US high school students, identification with their school's football team correlated with satisfaction with their social life (r = .19) and with social connections through the team (the share of friends who follow it, and the sense that being a fan helps form and keep friendships). Contrary to the authors' model, these social connections did not mediate the link between team identification and social life satisfaction (Sobel tests not significant).

1977.content: Van Vugt, Hogan and Kaiser argue that leading and following evolved to solve coordination problems (group movement, peacekeeping within the group, competition between groups) in small egalitarian bands where leadership was informal, consensual and situational, and where leaders drew their power from followers. They propose a mismatch with modern organizations: leaders are appointed by and answer to their own superiors, subordinates have little power to sanction their bosses, status and pay gaps are large (US chief executives averaged 179 times worker pay), and units are far larger than a band. They suggest this mismatch may explain the alienation and frustration of many employees and citizens, and cite climate surveys in which most employees name their immediate boss as the most stressful part of their job.

1978.content: In American Time Use Survey diaries, US men aged 21 to 30 increased their recreational computer time (video games and other computer leisure) by 2.7 hours a week between 2004-2007 and 2014-2017, a 60% rise, of which 1.8 hours a week was video gaming; this more than accounted for their 2.3-hour rise in total weekly leisure. Among young men without a job, recreational computing rose from 5.4 to 12.0 hours a week and by 2014-2017 exceeded their time spent socializing (6.8 hours a week). Market work of young men fell more than that of older men or of women over the same years.

Using leisure demand curves estimated from variation in leisure across US states and industries, the authors attribute 38 of the 60 percentage points of the rise in young men's computer leisure to better leisure technology, and estimate that these innovations reduced young men's market work hours by about 2%, much of their decline relative to older men.

1979.content: Al-Shawaf, Conroy-Beam, Asao and Buss argue that emotions are superordinate programs that evolved to coordinate the activity of other programs (attention, perception, memory, learning, energy allocation, physiology and behaviour) in solving adaptive problems. Holding that differential reproductive success is the engine of selection, they expect emotions for a wide range of problems tied to reproduction: mate competition, mate retention, status gains and losses, punishing free riders, kin protection and investment, food acquisition and others. They expect many evolved emotions to have no outward signal and to be unique to humans, and they derive new hypotheses for disgust and sexual arousal.

1980.content: Andreassen and colleagues built the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale from 18 items, three for each of six elements taken from addiction models (salience, mood modification, tolerance, withdrawal, conflict and relapse), and gave it with other self-report scales to 423 students. The best item per element was kept, giving a six-item scale with good factor structure, alpha .83 and three-week test-retest reliability .82. Scores converged with other measures of Facebook activity, were positively related to Neuroticism and Extraversion and negatively to Conscientiousness, and high scores were associated with later bedtimes and rising times.

1981.content: Arnaboldi and colleagues built ego networks from contact frequency in a regional Facebook data set (more than 3 million users and 23 million friendship links) and in 2,463,692 Twitter accounts downloaded between November 2012 and March 2013. Online ego networks showed the same layered structure found offline, with layers of compatible size and composition, and a ratio between the sizes of adjacent layers close to 3 on both platforms, as found in offline networks. In Twitter, how often a user was in direct contact with a friend correlated highly with how often the user retweeted that friend.

1982.content: Extending an earlier review, the authors found 13 studies on how grandparents bear on grandchildren's psychological, social and emotional adjustment in post-demographic-transition (low-fertility, industrialised) societies. Most of them (77%) found a beneficial association, which looked stronger where parental resources were fewer, as in step and single-parent families. The studies are correlational, and none of the three that linked grandparental childcare to weakly worse outcomes could weigh the quality of that childcare.

Across 39 populations (historical and contemporary, high and low fertility) in which the presence of a woman's parents or parents-in-law was tested against her fertility (age at first birth, birth intervals, number of children), only 5 (13%) showed no kin effect. Parents-in-law almost always went with higher fertility; a woman's own parents more often went with lower fertility, much of it in low-fertility societies, where living with both parents went with fewer teenage births.

1983.content: In five studies, telling others about one's own thoughts and feelings went with stronger activation in the mesolimbic dopamine system, including the nucleus accumbens and ventral tegmental area, and participants gave up money to disclose about themselves. Two further studies separated the value of thinking about oneself from the value of sharing information with others; both carried value on their own.

1984.content: Across samples from 123 countries, the fulfilment of needs went with subjective well-being in every world region. Life evaluation went most with basic needs being met; positive feelings went most with social and respect needs; negative feelings went most with unmet basic, respect and autonomy needs. The link between each specific need and well-being was largely independent of whether the other needs were met, and the pattern held when household income was taken into account.

In the same 123-country analysis, how far a whole society met people's needs went with an individual's well-being beyond whether that individual's own needs were met, most clearly for life evaluation.

1985.content: In eight studies with 2,836 participants, shared painful or frightening experiences went with identity fusion (a felt oneness with the group) and stated willingness to sacrifice for it. Among 380 US Vietnam combat veterans, more exposure to shared combat ordeals such as losing a close comrade went with stronger fusion (r = 0.203) and more willingness to support veterans in need (r = 0.184). Among 146 fraternity and sorority members, how self-defining their initiation had been went with fusion (r = 0.43) and willingness to sacrifice for the group (r = 0.43). Among 564 Brazilian Jiu Jitsu practitioners, harsher belt promotions went with stronger fusion (rho = 0.135), and fusion went with willingness to risk one's life for the club (rho = 0.542).

In a twin sample (260 identical and 246 non-identical twins), both being an identical twin and the amount of experience shared with the twin went with identity fusion, and shared experience still went with fusion after shared genes were controlled. In a vignette experiment (198 participants), imagined shared experience raised fusion with a person more than an imagined shared biology, matched it on trust, but shared genes drew more economic sacrifice.

1986.content: The authors classified 168 analyses in 155 papers on income distribution and population health. Of the analyses that were either wholly supportive or unsupportive, 70 percent found health less good in societies with bigger income differences. Support was more common when inequality was measured across large areas, which the authors read as income inequality standing for how hierarchical a society is.

1987.content: The authors propose fitness interdependence, the degree to which individuals depend on each other for survival or reproduction, as a unifying framework for cooperation that kinship and reciprocity models do not easily explain, as among mates, risk-pooling partners and brothers-in-arms.

1988.content: Larval zebrafish (Danio rerio), 10 to 15 days old, given repeated mild shocks (1 Hz for 30 minutes) first swam more, then switched to a passive state of reduced movement. Brainwide imaging showed neurons of the ventral (lateral) habenula being recruited progressively as the fish turned passive, while serotonergic raphe neurons were suppressed. Optogenetically activating the ventral habenula, or silencing serotonergic raphe neurons, made fish passive; silencing the ventral habenula after the shocks restored movement.

After the shock protocol, zebrafish larvae did not recover normal swimming within the first 5 minutes even in a new tank. Over 30 minutes, fish moved to a neutral tank of a different colour with fresh water recovered more than fish kept in the same tank with fresh water or in the same tank and water, and came back to the movement rate of unshocked fish.

1989.content: In a public goods experiment with 200 University of Wisconsin students playing 40 rounds in groups of five, showing group members only the amounts given, or only each other's photographs, had no significant effect against an anonymous baseline. Showing both photographs and each person's contribution raised giving to the public good by 59 percent. Some players consistently gave large amounts first and raised others' giving; low givers appeared mainly when actions and actors were hard to identify.

In the same study, when players could choose whether their contribution was reported to their group, virtually none chose to stay anonymous, yet this treatment raised contributions to their highest level and produced the most leaders who gave large amounts early. Reporting gifts in categories shifted gifts up to the lower bound of the next category.

1990.content: The review concludes that indirect, relational and social aggression (gossiping, spreading rumours, excluding) are essentially the same form of aggression, and that analogous forms are not found in other species. The authors' functional account: it is an alternative to direct aggression, used when direct aggression is costly, and it aims to socially exclude a victim or harm the victim's social status.

1991.content: De Waal reviews primate research that recasts aggression as a tool of competition and negotiation that is held in check where survival depends on mutual help. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) kiss and embrace after fights, and other nonhuman primates show similar reconciliations. He argues that human aggression, from families to high schools, is subject to the same constraints, and that natural checks work fully only where relationships are valued.

1992.content: In chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), consolation (friendly contact from a bystander toward the victim of an attack) reduced behavioural measures of stress in the victims. Consolation was more likely when the former opponents had not reconciled, and more likely between individuals with more valuable relationships.

1993.content: Reviewing studies across animal phyla, the authors find that dopamine is involved in reward learning and responses to food rewards in nematodes (for example Caenorhabditis elegans), flatworms (Platyhelminthes), molluscs and vertebrates. Arthropods are the exception: in insects such as the honey bee (Apis mellifera) and the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), and in crabs, the related amine octopamine has the larger role in reward learning, while dopamine is needed for aversive learning in flies.

The authors note that, as far as they know, dopamine modulates motor circuits in every animal phylum in which it has been investigated, including Cnidaria such as Hydra, where it affects mouth opening in response to food. They propose that reward functions grew out of this ancestral role of modulating movement in response to salient stimuli, and that, since the vertebrate cortex and the insect mushroom bodies evolved independently, brain reward systems almost certainly evolved independently in these groups from a shared molecular toolkit.

1994.content: In three studies with student samples, the authors built the Motives to Gossip Questionnaire and separated four motives for gossip: negative influence, information gathering and validation, social enjoyment, and group protection. The informational motive was the most common reported reason to start gossip. Group protection mattered most when the chance to gossip about another member's norm-violating behaviour was salient, and participants who ascribed gossip about a norm violation to group protection rated it as social and did not disapprove of it.

1995.content: Reviewing published estimates, the authors found that the rate of paternal discrepancy (a child fathered by someone other than the man who believes he is the father) ranged from 0.8% to 30% across 17 studies, with a median of 3.7%. From genetic and behavioural studies they identify higher risk among those who conceive younger, live in deprivation, are in long-term relationships rather than marriages, or belong to certain cultural groups.

1996.content: In recorded gossip on Nukulaelae, a Polynesian atoll of the Central Pacific, speakers often withhold a piece of information so that a listener asks for it and the speaker then supplies it. Besnier reads this three-turn sequence as drawing the audience in as co-producers of the gossip while securing the teller's control of the floor, so that gossip works at once as group-binding and self-serving behaviour.

1997.content: Pooling the 2013 and 2014 Health Survey for England (16,872 individuals) and Living Costs and Food Survey (9,975 households), the authors estimate that people drinking above government low-risk guidelines accounted for 68% of alcohol sales revenue in 2013/14 (81% of off-trade and 60% of on-trade revenue). The heaviest-drinking 4% of the population accounted for 30% of all consumption and 23% of all industry revenue. If everyone drank within the guidelines, sales revenue could fall by 38% (13 billion pounds).

1998.content: In a secondary analysis of two English case-control studies (400 SIDS infants and 1,386 controls with sleep-environment data; south-west England and four other former health regions 1993 to 1996, south-west England 2003 to 2006), co-sleeping on a sofa or chair, or next to an adult who had drunk more than two units of alcohol, went with about 18 times the risk of SIDS against not co-sleeping, and sleeping next to a parent who smoked with about four times the risk. Bed-sharing without these hazards showed no significant risk (multivariable odds ratio 1.1). In infants over 3 months it went with lower risk: one SIDS case (0.6%) against 8.5% of controls.

1999.content: Combining individual records from five case-control studies (Europe, Scotland, New Zealand, Ireland, Germany; 1,472 SIDS cases and 4,679 controls), 22.2% of cases and 9.6% of controls had been bed-sharing (adjusted odds ratio 2.7 for all ages). When neither parent smoked, the mother had taken no alcohol or drugs and the baby was breastfed and under 3 months with no other risk factors, bed-sharing against room-sharing had an adjusted odds ratio of 5.1. The odds ratio fell as infants got older.

2000.content: A review of research on embarrassment reports that the human embarrassment display unfolds as gaze aversion, a controlled smile, head movements down and, in about a quarter of cases, face touching, and that the appeasement displays recorded in other species, seen when one animal tries to reduce another's aggression, share gaze aversion, smiling, head movements down that expose the neck, reduced body size and self-touching or grooming. The authors propose that embarrassment has its origin in the appeasement system of other species.

The same review reports that human embarrassment draws amusement, laughter, mild sympathy and forgiveness from others, and leads them to infer that the embarrassed person respects the broken norm, in parallel with the embracing, grooming and reconciliation that appeasement displays draw from other primates.

2001.content: In 5 studies, the nonverbal behaviour that followed reports of embarrassment was distinct from that of amusement, followed the time course of other facial expressions of emotion, went with participants' own accounts of feeling embarrassed and not with accounts of amusement, and was identified accurately by observers who judged spontaneous displays of several emotions. In Study 1, 35 displays of embarrassment and 28 of amusement were coded with the Facial Action Coding System. Observers were more accurate, and attributed more emotion, when the embarrassment display came from female and African American targets than from male and Caucasian targets, which the author reads as the appeasement prediction that displays from lower-status groups are more readily perceived.

In Study 5, 183 University of Wisconsin students judged 3-second silent clips of spontaneous displays by 24 boys aged 12 to 13 from the Pittsburgh Youth Study, filmed while an adult gave them an intelligence test: four boys each for amusement, enjoyment, anger, disgust, embarrassment and shame. Overall accuracy was .53 against .167 expected by chance; embarrassment and shame displays were the most accurately judged of the six, and observers seldom confused the two. Shame displays were head and gaze movements down; embarrassment displays were gaze down, a controlled smile, head turned away and face touching. Observers judged African-American boys' embarrassment and shame displays more accurately than Caucasian boys'.

2002.content: A meta-analysis of human neuroimaging studies published from 1990 to 2007 on the experience and perception of anger, disgust, fear, happiness and sadness found little evidence that any of these categories is consistently and specifically localized to a distinct brain region. Where a region activated consistently for one category, for example the amygdala when people perceived fear, it also activated for other categories. The authors read the data as support for a psychological constructionist account in which networks for core affect, conceptualization, language and executive attention take part in every emotion category.

In the same meta-analysis, amygdala voxels activated more consistently when people perceived fear than other emotions, but they were equally likely to activate for other emotion categories. When people experienced fear, neither amygdala showed a consistent increase in activation compared with the chance level for other brain regions.

2003.content: Nesse proposes that emotions are specialized states shaped by natural selection that raise fitness in specific situations, so that the physiological, psychological and behavioural features of each emotion can be analysed as design features for coping with the threats and opportunities of its situation. He illustrates the approach with the match between subtypes of fear and kinds of threat, between happiness and sadness and favourable and unfavourable situations, and between the social emotions and the problems of reciprocity relationships.

2004.content: In laboratory rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) studied between 18 and 64 days of age, social isolation markedly increased play measured as pinning. Play rose from 18 to 28 days of age, peaked between 32 and 40 days and then slowly declined. Pairs developed stable dominance relations in which one rat pinned the other about 70% of the time, and the author suggests that one function of play may be to establish stable social relationships.

2005.content: In juvenile laboratory rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) whose whole neocortex was removed shortly after birth, pinning fell by about 50% and pins were shorter when two decorticate rats played together, yet their play looked essentially normal, overall play vigour on an activity platform did not differ from controls, pin frequency did not differ when a decorticate rat played with an intact one, and play solicitation did not differ, which the authors read as play motivation left essentially intact. Removing parietal cortex alone cut pinning by 65%. The authors conclude that the neocortex takes little part in starting rough-and-tumble play and attribute the numerical changes to motor changes and reduced touch sensitivity.

2006.content: In a representative sample of men from an industrial society, social status did not correlate with reproductive success measured as actual fertility, but it was highly correlated with potential fertility estimated from copulation frequency, accounting for as much as 62% of its variance. The author argues that the pattern is similar to that of many traditional societies and would yield a substantial positive relationship between status and reproductive success in industrial populations were it not for contraception and monogamy.

2007.content: A systematic review of 75 studies (66 quantitative, 9 qualitative) published from 1995 to 2015 found that adolescents use pornography at rates that differ widely between studies: lifetime exposure ranged from 25% of Taiwanese adolescents (internet pornography) to 98% of German boys and 81% of German girls (a pornographic film), and unintentional exposure to internet pornography from 19% of US 10 to 12 year olds to 84% of Australian boys aged 16 to 17. Adolescents who used pornography more often were more often male, further along in puberty, sensation seekers, and had weak or troubled family relations.

In the same review, adolescents' pornography use was associated with more permissive sexual attitudes, tended to be linked with stronger gender-stereotyped sexual beliefs, and seemed related to having had sexual intercourse, more casual sex and more sexual aggression, both as perpetrator and as victim. The authors state that methodological and theoretical shortcomings and biases in the literature preclude internally valid causal conclusions about effects of pornography on adolescents.

2008.content: In the English and Romanian Adoptees study, children reared in profoundly depriving Romanian institutions and then adopted into UK families were compared at age 11 with children adopted within the UK before 6 months of age who had never been in an institution, using parent reports, a Strange Situation procedure adapted for the home, and standardised investigator ratings. Disinhibited attachment as reported by parents showed a high degree of persistence from age 6 to 11, with some fall in frequency that investigator ratings suggested was partly an artefact of the parent measure. It was strongly associated with institutional rearing, with no significant further increase for institutional deprivation lasting beyond 6 months of age. In the institution-reared children it went with a marked increase in service use and with other forms of what the authors call psychopathology.

2009.content: Sandseter and Kennair argue, in a theoretical paper, that children develop fears of stimuli such as heights and strangers through normal maturation, without a frightening experience (the non-associative account of fear), and that risky play, which is thrilling and exposes the child to those stimuli as coping skills grow, lets the child master them so they are no longer feared. They propose that risky play evolved for this anti-phobic effect and suggest that society may see more neuroticism or psychopathology if children are kept from age-adequate risky play.

2010.content: Sear reviews data showing that across subsistence societies women typically contribute a substantial share of the calories in the diet, on average slightly below half, with some societies where women produce few calories and some where they produce most. Both sexes tend to remain net producers, producing more calories than they consume, until late in life, and the surplus supports their children and grandchildren.

Sear concludes from anthropological and historical evidence that isolated nuclear families, raising children with no help beyond the two parents, barely exist even in 20th and 21st century Western societies, and that male breadwinning is both rare and recent in human history, spreading with industrialization in Western Europe. In most subsistence economies the economic contributions of women and children are vital to the family.
Sear cites a UK study in which 38% of new mothers spent more than 8 hours a day alone with their infant and 34% spent 4 to 8 hours alone.

2011.content: Miller and Raison review the evidence and argue that crosstalk between inflammation and the brain gave ancestral humans an advantage against pathogens, predators and rivals: an inflammatory bias that saved energy for fighting infection and healing wounds while keeping vigilance against attack. They propose that this bias was held in check by steady exposure to minimally pathogenic organisms in traditional rural environments. They propose that in sanitized modern cities, short of those organisms and full of psychological challenges, psychosocial stressors set off the same immune and behavioural repertoire, and they tie this to the high rates of depression diagnosed today.

Miller and Raison report that raised inflammatory markers are found in only a subgroup of patients diagnosed with depression, and also in patients diagnosed with anxiety disorders and schizophrenia; they argue the markers track symptom dimensions across diagnoses (anhedonia, fatigue, slowed movement, threat sensitivity). In one study they cite, 45% of patients whose depression scores did not respond to standard antidepressants had CRP above 3 mg/L. In the one trial of a cytokine blocker in medically healthy adults diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression, a post hoc analysis found that infliximab did better than placebo only at higher baseline CRP (at 5 mg/L or more, with an effect size like that of standard antidepressants), and in patients with low inflammation it impaired the placebo response, as the authors report.

2012.content: Noguchi and Moore stained brain tissue from 70 patients who had died with general paralysis (paresis, the authors' and their era's label) at Central Islip State Hospital, New York, with a modified Levaditi silver stain, and found the syphilis organism Treponema pallidum in the brain tissue of 12 of them. The 12 (10 men, 2 women, aged 33 to 60) all showed the classical physical signs and the post-mortem brain findings of general paralysis, and the organisms lay within the cortex itself. Before this report the organism had not been found in the nervous tissue of paresis, and leading writers still disputed whether syphilis was essential to it.

2013.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (searched to June 2020, NOVA classification of ultra-processed food) pooled five cross-sectional studies with 73,169 people: those in the highest category of ultra-processed food intake had 39% higher odds of overweight or obesity (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.29 to 1.50, no heterogeneity), 39% higher odds of a high waist circumference, and higher odds of low HDL cholesterol (OR 2.02) and the metabolic syndrome (OR 1.79, two studies). No association was found with high blood pressure, high blood sugar or high triglycerides.

Pooling the prospective cohort studies (183,491 people followed 3.5 to 19 years in Spain, France, Brazil, Italy and the USA), the highest category of ultra-processed food intake was associated with 25% higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.37, five studies, 4,687 deaths), 29% higher cardiovascular disease (three studies), 34% higher cerebrovascular disease (two studies), 23% higher incident overweight or obesity (two studies) and 20% higher incident depression as defined in the two cohort studies (RR 1.20).

2014.content: Pooling participant-level data from 15 cohorts (eight in the USA, four in Europe, one each in Japan and Australia, one spanning 40 countries; 47,471 adults, mean age 65, who wore a step counter for a week; 3,013 deaths over a median 7.1 years), adults in the second, third and fourth quarters of daily steps (medians 5,801, 7,842 and 10,901 steps) had hazard ratios for death of 0.60, 0.55 and 0.47 against the lowest quarter (median 3,553 steps), after adjustment for age, sex, education or income, body mass index and health status.

In the same analysis the fall in death risk levelled off: at about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults aged 60 and over and about 8,000 to 10,000 steps a day for adults under 60; the lowest risk overall was at about 7,000 to 9,000 steps, and high step counts were not associated with higher risk. Evidence that walking pace mattered once total steps were accounted for was inconsistent across the pace measures.

2015.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 experiments that changed how fast people ate found that a slower eating rate went with lower energy intake at the meal than a faster rate (standardised mean difference 0.45, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.65), whatever method was used to change eating speed, with large heterogeneity between studies. Eating rate showed no relation to hunger at the end of the meal or up to 3.5 hours later. The authors conclude that eating rate affects energy intake.

2016.content: Stool samples from 27 Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania (two camps, aged 8 to 70, eating wild meat, honey, baobab, berries and tubers with under 5% of calories from farm foods) and 16 urban adults from Bologna, Italy, sequenced for bacterial 16S rDNA, showed much higher gut microbial richness and diversity in the Hadza on every measure used (P < 0.001). The Hadza gut was enriched, compared with the Italians, in Treponema, Prevotella and other fibre-digesting groups and lacked Bifidobacterium, and Hadza men and women differed in gut composition, which the authors tie to the sexual division of foraging labour.

2017.content: In 4,799 adults in the USA and Europe whose total daily energy expenditure was measured with doubly labelled water between 1981 and 2017 (IAEA database), expenditure adjusted for body composition and age fell over 30 years by 7.7% in men and 5.6% in women, while adjusted activity expenditure rose in both sexes. Adjusted basal expenditure fell by 14.7% in men (2%, not significant, in women), and a larger set of 9,912 basal metabolic rate measurements from 163 studies over 100 years showed the same fall in both sexes. The authors conclude that rising obesity in the USA and Europe has probably not been fuelled by less physical activity lowering total expenditure.

2018.content: Using daily energy expenditure measured with doubly labelled water in adults in Maastricht, the Netherlands, and North America back to the 1980s, the authors found that physical activity expenditure had not declined: in Europe it rose slightly but significantly, with no trend in physical activity level, and in North America it also rose. Daily expenditure in Europe and North America did not differ significantly from that measured in people in developing countries, and the 9.2 MJ a day predicted for a 78 kg wild terrestrial mammal at 20 degrees C did not differ significantly from that of modern humans (about 10.2 to 12.6 MJ a day). The authors conclude it is unlikely that falling expenditure fuelled the rise in obesity.

2019.content: Using six decades of archived population data on older Okinawans (aged 65 and over), the cohort said to have eaten a calorically restricted traditional diet, the authors report low caloric intake and negative energy balance at younger ages, little weight gain with age, low body mass index throughout life, relatively high plasma DHEA in old age, low mortality from age-related diseases, and survival patterns consistent with a longer mean and maximum life span. They read this as epidemiological support, in humans, for the health benefits of caloric restriction seen in animals.

2020.content: In a counterbalanced crossover experiment, 10 untrained to recreationally active adults (5 men, 5 women) spent 4 days sitting about 13.5 hours a day at about 3,500 to 4,000 steps a day, once without exercise and once with a 1 hour treadmill bout (about 63% of maximal oxygen uptake) on the evening of day 4. In a high-fat glucose tolerance test the next morning, plasma triglyceride, glucose and insulin responses did not differ between the two trials. The authors call this exercise resistance: after days of inactivity, one bout of exercise no longer gave the usual next-day metabolic gains.

2021.content: In survey data from 136 countries, prosocial spending (using one's money to help others) went with greater happiness, in poor and rich countries alike. In experiments in Canada, Uganda and India, recalling a past purchase for someone else raised reported happiness. In Canada and South Africa, participants randomly assigned to buy items for charity reported more positive feeling than those assigned to buy the same items for themselves, even though the giving built no social tie.

2022.content: In a laboratory study in Vancouver, Canada, 20 toddlers just under two years old were given treats and then asked to give one to a puppet; coders blind to the hypotheses rated their facial happiness on a 7-point scale. The toddlers looked happier when giving a treat to the puppet than when receiving treats themselves (effect size d 0.88 for giving a found treat, d 1.35 for giving one of their own), and happier when giving away their own treat than when giving a treat that cost them nothing.

2023.content: Reviewing their own laboratory's experiments, the authors report that laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus) kept for three weeks or more on a schedule of 12 hours without food followed by 12 hours of access to a 10% sugar solution and chow came to drink sugar in large bouts at the start of each access period, and took as much sugar in 12 hours as rats with round-the-clock access took in 24. Each bout released dopamine in the nucleus accumbens, as drugs of abuse do. When the opioid blocker naloxone was given, or food was removed for 24 hours, the rats showed signs like opiate withdrawal (teeth chattering, forepaw tremor, head shakes, anxiety on an elevated plus-maze, and more immobility in a forced-swim test, which the authors label behavioural depression); after abstinence they worked harder for sugar.

2024.content: Among the Aka forest foragers of the Central African Republic, who live in camps of about 30 people (six to eight households), each woman cooks what she has gathered or received in one pot and, when there is enough, serves it out in plates to every household in the camp, visitors included. Bahuchet reports that 60% of the dishes cooked in a camp each day are handed round to other residents in this way.

In an Aka population of 72, the 31 adults did 73% of all food-getting work, 9 adolescents 19%, 5 old people 8% and 27 children none. Only about half of hunts succeeded, and hunting took 56% of yearly work time, so of every two hunters who left camp only one was likely to bring back game. Bahuchet concludes that adults supply most of the food of children and old people, and that handing plates to other households makes sure even the families of unlucky hunters eat.

2025.content: In representative samples of 49,493 adults aged 18 to 65 from 20 countries (2002 to 2004), asked about usual weekday hours spent sitting (IPAQ question), the median reported sitting time was 300 minutes a day (interquartile range 180 to 480). Medians were 180 minutes or less in Portugal, Brazil and Colombia and 360 minutes or more in Taiwan, Norway, Hong Kong, Saudi Arabia and Japan. People with post-school education reported more sitting (OR 1.35), adults aged 40 to 65 less than those aged 18 to 39, and people reporting low physical activity were three times as likely to be in the highest sitting fifth.

2026.content: In the French NutriNet-Sante cohort, 110,260 adults (mean age 43, 78% women) recorded their diet in repeated 24-hour records classed by NOVA processing level and were followed 2009 to 2019. A 10-point higher share of ultra-processed food in the diet went with greater gain in body mass index, an 11% higher risk of becoming overweight (7,063 cases among 55,037 people not overweight at the start, median 4.1 years) and a 9% higher risk of obesity (3,066 cases). Those in the top quarter of intake had a 26% higher risk of becoming overweight than those in the bottom quarter (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.35). The links held after adjustment for diet quality and energy intake.

2027.content: Twenty healthy medical students were tested with fMRI on an attention-shifting task after 4 weeks of preparing for a major examination and compared with 20 controls matched for age, sex and occupation. The stressed students scored higher on the 10-item Cohen Perceived Stress Scale and paid a larger time cost when shifting attention between colour and motion (t = 2.10, P = 0.04); across both groups the stress score correlated with the shift cost (r = 0.51), while plain speed and response reversals did not differ. The stressed students showed weaker functional coupling of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with premotor, ventral prefrontal and posterior parietal areas.

Fifteen of the stressed students were scanned again about 4 weeks after the examination, with an equal number of retested controls. After this month of reduced stress they no longer differed from controls on the perceived stress score or on attention shifting, and the disrupted prefrontal coupling had returned in all areas tested except the ventral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann area 13/47), which stayed decoupled. Stressed students whose stress score stayed one standard deviation above the population mean were excluded from the second session.

2028.content: In the Bucharest Early Intervention Project, a randomised trial, children raised from infancy in Romanian institutions were assigned to high-quality foster care or to remain in institutional care; at a mean age of 12.9 years they did a social stress test (speech and mental arithmetic), a peer evaluation task and a frustration task. The 43 children who stayed in institutional care showed blunted sympathetic (blood pressure, pre-ejection period) and cortisol responses compared with the 48 children randomised to foster care, whose responses were close to those of 47 never-institutionalised Romanian children. Some blunting persisted in the foster care group: blood pressure and pre-ejection period reactivity during the stress test and cortisol over the session stayed lower than in never-institutionalised children.

Within the foster care group, earlier placement went with a larger cortisol response and more vagal engagement during the social stress test. Children placed in foster care before 24 months had a significantly greater cortisol response than those placed after 24 months (t = 3.22, P = 0.002), and placement before 18 months went with vagal (respiratory sinus arrhythmia) enhancement during each part of the stress test; in both cases the earlier-placed children resembled never-institutionalised children.

2029.content: A meta-analysis of human studies on chronic stress and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis found that the contradictory results in the field (some studies raised activity, others lowered) are largely explained by features of the stressor and the person. Timing matters most: hormone activity is raised at the onset of a stressor and falls as time passes. Stressors that threaten physical integrity, involve trauma and cannot be controlled go with a high, flat daily cortisol profile.

In the same meta-analysis, HPA activity also depended on the person's response to the situation: it was higher with more subjective distress and lower in persons diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder.

2030.content: Ten healthy right-handed men were scanned with PET while angry faces were flashed for 30 ms and masked by a neutral face; one angry face had earlier been paired with a 100 dB noise burst. None of the masked target faces were detected, yet skin conductance was higher to the masked noise-paired face. When this face was unseen, the right amygdala showed increased covariation with the superior colliculus and the pulvinar, and decreased covariation with fusiform and orbitofrontal cortex; the left amygdala, which responded to the seen face, showed no such change.

2031.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 studies (20 at moderate risk of bias in the main analyses) found that in the period after the media reported a celebrity's death by suicide, suicides in the general population rose by 13 percent (rate ratio 1.13, 95 percent CI 1.08 to 1.18; 14 studies; median follow-up 28 days). When the celebrity's method was reported, deaths by the same method rose by 30 percent (rate ratio 1.30; 11 studies). The rise was larger after suicides of entertainers (1.17, six studies) than of other celebrities (1.08, eight studies).

In the same meta-analysis, general reporting of suicide (any coverage, not tied to a celebrity) was not associated with later suicides: the rate ratio was 1.002 (0.997 to 1.008; five studies; median follow-up 1 day) for each extra article.

2032.content: A meta-analysis of 60 independent studies of deindividuation, which classically manipulate anonymity, self-awareness and group size, found little support for the claim that these conditions produce antinormative behaviour or a deindividuated state. Instead, groups and individuals who were made anonymous or deindividuated conformed more to the norms specific to the situation; the authors read this as support for a social identity model of deindividuation effects.
In the same meta-analysis, groups and individuals conformed more to the norms of the specific situation when they were deindividuated (anonymous, low in self-awareness or in a larger group).

2033.content: In the Changing Lives of Older Couples study, 846 married adults in the Detroit area (mean age 71) reported in 1987 to 1988 their stressful life events of the past year and whether they had given unpaid practical help (errands, housework, child care, other tasks) to friends, neighbours or relatives outside the home; 134 died over five years. With adjustment for age, baseline health and functioning, and psychosocial variables, helping and stress interacted (hazard ratio 0.58). Among those who had not helped, each additional stressful event went with a 30 percent higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.30, 95 percent CI 1.05 to 1.62); among those who had helped, stress was not associated with death (hazard ratio 0.96, 0.79 to 1.18).

2034.content: Across six studies, 3,377 participants saw racist, sexist or unpatriotic posts followed by expressions of outrage and formed impressions of one commenter. The same commenter was judged more negatively when many others had posted similar outrage (viral) than when few had (nonviral), and this was explained by greater sympathy for the original offender when the outrage was viral. The authors argue that outrage which would be praised alone comes to look like bullying when echoed by a multitude.

2035.content: In two adult Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) reared in a walled-off enclosure where, the authors believe, they had no chance to meet snakes, 745 neurons in the medial and dorsolateral pulvinar were recorded; 91 visually responsive neurons were tested with photos of snakes, monkey faces, monkey hands and simple shapes. Snake-best neurons were the most common (37 of 91, 40.6 percent), mean responses were largest to snakes, and in the short-latency group the response to snakes came first (55.4 ms on average), significantly earlier than to angry faces, neutral faces, hands or shapes. Responses held up when the images were low-pass filtered (coarse outline only) and fell when they were high-pass filtered.

2036.content: Seventy-nine people approached on the University of British Columbia campus were randomly assigned to recall the last time they spent about 20 dollars on someone they were very close to or on someone they were not very close to, then rated their feelings. Those who recalled spending on a close tie reported more positive affect (mean 2.76 against 2.37 on a 1 to 5 scale, t(76) = 2.09, p < .05), also when controlling for how recently the spending took place. Closeness predicted the difference; whether the person was family or a friend did not.

2037.content: Acoustic analysis with the modulation power spectrum showed that human screams cluster in a restricted part of acoustic space, modulation rates of about 30 to 150 Hz, perceived as roughness, a region separate from other vocal signals including speech. Roughness is present in natural alarm signals and in artificial alarms, boosted the detection of sounds in several psychophysical tasks, and in fMRI engaged subcortical structures that the authors call critical to rapidly appraise danger.

2038.content: In a longitudinal study, 132 students were assessed repeatedly over 18 months after entering university on the Big Five personality factors, the subfactors sociability and shyness, and all their significant social relationships; a subsample kept diaries of their social interactions. With the initial correlation between personality and relationships controlled, extraversion and its subfactors, agreeableness and conscientiousness predicted aspects of relationships such as the number of peer relationships, conflict with peers and falling in love, while relationship qualities did not predict later personality.

2039.content: A meta-analysis of 14 studies (17 effect estimates) on road traffic noise and coronary heart disease found a pooled relative risk of 1.08 (95 percent CI 1.04 to 1.13) for each 10 dB(A) increase in the weighted day-night noise level, within a range of about 52 to 77 dB(A). There was no significant heterogeneity between studies, although the handling of sex, the youngest age studied and the lowest noise cut-off changed the estimates. The result matches an earlier meta-analysis on road traffic noise and high blood pressure.

2040.content: A meta-analysis of 21 longitudinal epidemiological studies (searched 1980 to 2010) related insomnia complaints at baseline to depression at follow-up as measured in each study. The random-effects model gave an overall odds ratio of 2.60 (95 percent CI 1.98 to 3.42); after adjusting for outliers the studies were no longer heterogeneous and the fixed-effects odds ratio was 2.10 (1.86 to 2.38). The authors conclude that non-depressed people who report insomnia have a twofold risk of later meeting the studies' criteria for depression, compared with people without sleep difficulties.

2041.content: A meta-analysis of 172 studies (2,263 participants classed by the authors as anxious, 1,768 as nonanxious) found that a bias of attention toward threat is reliably shown across experimental paradigms and conditions, with an effect size of d = 0.45. The bias was also found with threat stimuli presented outside awareness, was of comparable size across groups diagnosed with different anxiety disorders, high-anxious nonclinical people, and anxious children and adults, and was not found in nonanxious people.
