In the same meta-analysis, processes that need conscious perception of threat contributed to the attention bias, but a significant bias was also found when the threat stimuli were presented outside awareness.

2042.content: Bar-Yosef dates the Natufian culture of the Levant to about 15,000/14,500 to 11,500 calibrated years before present. Early Natufian sites in the central Levant (larger sites over about 1,000 square metres) are read as hamlets or villages from pit-houses, burials, grinding stones and rich tool industries, and are defined as sedentary by the presence of commensal animals (such as house mice). The cause of this sedentism is debated. It lasted only about two and a half thousand years, and site layers show intervals of abandonment of unknown length.

Bar-Yosef reports that most authorities agree Late Natufian society was more mobile than the Early Natufian, probably because of the harsher, less stable conditions of the Younger Dryas; many but not all hamlets dispersed, and burial practices shifted from a non-egalitarian society back to a more egalitarian one. He also writes that most, but not all, of the first Neolithic villages that followed were three to eight times larger than the largest Natufian sites, reflecting rapid population growth.

2043.content: Toates proposes a theoretical framework for sexual motivation, arousal and behaviour that combines incentive motivation theory with the hierarchical control of behaviour. In the model both excitation and inhibition act at several levels of a hierarchy. The author applies the framework to attachment, aggression, drug taking, gender differences, and what he calls sexual deviancy and sexual addiction.

2044.content: In four studies of US participants (160 and 300 undergraduates rating 48 items, 1,118 adults from all 50 states rating 27 items online, and 507 undergraduates), ratings of how disgusting acts and objects are fell into three separate factors: pathogens, sexual acts and partners, and moral violations. A single-factor model fit poorly in the adult sample and a three-factor model fit much better. The three factors related differently to other measures: in Study 2 primary psychopathy scores went with lower moral and sexual disgust and not with pathogen disgust, while perceived vulnerability to disease went with pathogen and sexual disgust.

Women rated items as more disgusting than men did, and the gap was by far the largest for sexual items. Among 160 US undergraduates the sex difference was Cohen's d 0.32 for pathogen, 1.07 for sexual and 0.32 for moral disgust. Among 1,118 US adults it was d 0.17 for pathogen and 1.24 for sexual disgust, and the sexes did not differ on moral disgust (d 0.04). Watching pornography was among the sexual items with a large sex difference (d 0.60 in Study 1).

2045.content: Across three British national probability surveys (Natsal-1 1991, Natsal-2 2001, Natsal-3 2012; ages 16 to 44 compared), the share reporting no sex in the past month fell from 28.5% to 23.0% in women and from 30.9% to 26.0% in men between 1991 and 2001, then rose to 29.3% in women and 29.2% in men by 2012. The share reporting sex 10 or more times in the past month fell between 2001 and 2012 from 20.6% to 13.2% in women and from 20.2% to 14.4% in men. The steepest falls were among people aged 25 and over and among the married or cohabiting.

In the same British surveys, the share of sexually active 16 to 44 year olds who said they would prefer to have sex more often rose between 2001 and 2012 from 39.1% to 50.6% of women and from 51.2% to 64.3% of men. The rise was seen in every age group and in both marital-status groups, and was steeper among the married or cohabiting. So reported sex became less frequent while the share wanting more grew.

2046.content: Young and Wang review laboratory work on the prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster), a monogamous rodent that forms lasting pair bonds. Infusing oxytocin into the brain of females or vasopressin into the brain of males lets a partner preference form after brief cohabitation without mating, and blocking oxytocin receptors (females) or vasopressin V1a receptors (males) stops a bond from forming. Dopamine D2 receptors in the nucleus accumbens are also needed: a D2 blocker stops the mating-induced preference, a D2 stimulant induces a preference after 6 hours of cohabitation without mating, and that effect is blocked by an oxytocin receptor blocker. The authors' model: the bond forms when neuropeptide and dopamine receptors in reward areas are active together during mating, a conditioned preference for the partner.

In the meadow vole (Microtus pennsylvanicus), a species that does not form pair bonds, the authors' group used a viral vector to add the vasopressin V1a receptor gene to the ventral pallidum of males. After cohabiting and mating with a female, these males showed a stronger preference for that partner than control males, and a dopamine D2 blocker given beforehand stopped the preference. The authors read this as showing that a change in where a single gene is expressed can change a complex social behaviour; differences in receptor distribution, partly tied to a repeat sequence near the receptor gene, are their proposed reason some vole species bond and others do not.

2047.content: Acevedo and Aron review taxonomies, theory and research on love in long relationships and conclude that romantic love, meaning intensity, engagement and sexual interest without the obsession typical of early love, can and does exist in long-term marriages and goes with marital satisfaction, well-being and high self-esteem. In a moderately large data set of community couples, romantic love and obsession came out as separate factors, and a subsample reported very high romantic love without obsession after controlling for social desirability. A meta-analysis of 25 studies found romantic love strongly associated with relationship satisfaction in both long and short relationships, while obsession was negatively correlated with satisfaction in long relationships and positively in short ones.

2048.content: Cronk interviewed 10 Maasai men aged 25 to 73 (mean 45) in Maa, in Mukogodo Division, Laikipia District, Kenya, about osotua, their word for umbilical cord used for gift partnerships. The men agreed closely on its rules: a partnership usually starts with a request for a gift or favour that arises from real need and is limited to what is needed; gifts are given freely and also limited to the need; once set up, osotua is held to last forever and to pass to the partners' children; partners must help when asked, but gifts need not be reciprocal or roughly equal over long periods, and the flow may run mostly one way if that is where the need is. Osotua gifts are not debts and are never called payments; debt (sile) is a separate kind of relationship.

In 50 trust games played by Maasai men at the same Kenyan site, 25 were played without framing and 25 were introduced with the words 'This is an osotua game'. Under the osotua frame both players gave less: across all transfers as a share of what each player had, 28.2% framed against 35.3% unframed (one-tailed p .024). In unframed games, the more the first player gave, the more he expected back; under the osotua frame that link disappeared, and the more the first player gave, the smaller the share the second player returned.

2049.content: Al-Shawaf, Lewis and Buss report that women have consistently higher levels of disgust than men, a sex difference that is substantial, highly replicable, found with diverse assessment methods and tied to outcomes such as job selection, mate choice and food aversions. They argue that theory has lagged behind these findings, and set out four evolutionary-functional hypotheses for the sex difference in sexual disgust and six for pathogen disgust, with testable predictions.

2050.content: From 930 national survey observations in 194 countries or areas, modelled with a Bayesian hierarchical model, the share of married or in-union women aged 15 to 49 worldwide who used contraception rose from 54.8% in 1990 to 63.3% in 2010. Unmet need for family planning fell from 15.4% to 12.3% over the same years, and in 2010 about 146 million such women had an unmet need. The number of married women either using contraception or with an unmet need was projected to grow from 900 million in 2010 to 962 million in 2015.

2051.content: In a 2004 survey in Western Chitwan Valley, Nepal, 329 currently married people answered 74 items on their marriage, which factor analysis grouped into satisfaction, communication, togetherness, problems and disagreements. Spouses had been chosen by the family alone for about 40%, by family and respondent together for 32%, and by the respondent for the rest. Compared with those whose families chose, respondents who chose their own spouse scored over a third of a standard deviation higher on satisfaction and togetherness and over a third lower on disagreements; spouse choice was not associated with communication or problems. The association did not change with how long the couple had been married. Women scored lower than men, and more schooling went with higher scores. Together all measured factors accounted for 14 to 17% of the variation.

2052.content: Bancroft and Janssen propose a dual control model of male sexual response: response depends on a balance between central excitation and central inhibition, and men differ in their propensity for each. A self-report questionnaire (SIS/SES) yields one excitation factor (SES) and two inhibition factors. The first inhibition factor (SIS1) is linked to fear of performance failure; the second (SIS2) is proposed to relate to external threats, for example from within the sexual relationship. The authors expect that men high on SIS2 will respond to psychological treatment and men high on SIS1 to drug treatment.

2053.content: Basson presents a model of women's sexual response during long-term relationships that she argues depicts more accurately the responsive component of women's desire and the motivational forces that trigger it, and that acknowledges a variety of arousal and orgasm responses. Her stated purpose is to avoid labelling a response as a dysfunction when it simply differs from the traditional human sex-response cycle, and to define subgroups of difficulty more clearly.

2054.content: Bengtson argues, against the 'family decline' view built on a two-parent nuclear model, that relations across several generations are becoming more important in American families for three reasons: population aging gives generations longer years of shared lives, grandparents and other kin increasingly fulfil family functions, and intergenerational solidarity is strong and resilient over time. He adds that these relations are becoming more diverse through divorce and stepfamilies, longer-lived kin and different types of intergenerational relationship, and presents results from the Longitudinal Study of Generations on the strength of multigenerational ties over time.

2055.content: From 100 personal letters written by female romantic partners of heavy pornography users, Bergner and Bridges build a composite portrait of these women. The portrait centres on an often traumatic discovery of the partner's use and on the meaning the women gave it for their relationship, for their own worth and desirability, and for the character of their partner. The paper ends with recommendations for therapists.

2056.content: In two experiments with American 9-month-old infants, 12 sessions of 25 minutes over 4 weeks in which native Mandarin speakers read and played with them (10 infants completed) reversed the usual decline in telling apart a Mandarin speech contrast, measured against 11 infants given the same sessions in English. Infants given the same speakers and material from studio-quality DVD with picture and sound (15 completed) or sound only (13 completed) showed no learning: their scores did not differ from the English controls, and they paid less attention than the infants with a live speaker.

2057.content: A meta-analysis of 122 independent effect sizes from 59 reports on children aged 0 to 6 years found that children learned less from video than from the same material presented face to face, by about half a standard deviation on average. The gap shrank with age, was larger in object-retrieval studies than in other domains, and did not differ between studies using live and prerecorded video. The authors flag quality and publication-bias issues that may have inflated the estimate.

2058.content: From the 100 most informative surviving listings of inhabitants of English communities, set beside the British census from 1801, Laslett reports that mean household size in England and Wales stayed at about 4.75 or a little below from the sixteenth century until 1911 and fell by about a third only from 1921. He reports that the English household was not extended on any definition since at least the sixteenth century: a majority of people lived in households of six or more, and the large households held many live-in servants, while resident kin were rare.

2059.content: Comparing Highland Maya families with middle-class US families over the child's first 2 years, all 14 Mayan children slept in their mothers' beds into toddlerhood. None of the 18 US infants slept in bed with their mothers on a regular basis as newborns; 15 slept near their mothers until 3 to 6 months of age, when most were moved to a separate room. Mayan parents explained their practice by the value of closeness with infants, US parents by the value of independence for infants.
The US families, and none of the Mayan families, used bedtime routines and objects to help the child make the transition to sleep.

2060.content: In the NICHD Study of Early Child Care (1,153 infants and their mothers at 10 sites, Strange Situation at 15 months), infants with extensive child-care experience in the first year did not differ from infants without it in distress at separation from the mother, and the quality, amount, age of entry, stability and type of child care showed no main association with attachment security or avoidance. Maternal sensitivity and responsiveness did go with attachment security.

In the same cohort, infants were less likely to be securely attached when low maternal sensitivity and responsiveness was combined with poor-quality child care, with more than minimal hours of care, or with more than one care arrangement.

2061.content: Combining trait data for 230 primate species with Bayesian phylogenetic models of correlated evolution, the authors found that the presence of male infanticide was the one trait that reliably raised the probability of a shift to social monogamy, while paternal care and discrete female ranges followed monogamy rather than preceding it. They read the origin of primate monogamy as a defence against infanticidal males, made necessary by long lactation in slow-developing infants, and report that biparental care shortens relative lactation length.

2062.content: A systematic review of antenatal risk factors for postpartum depression, as measured in the pooled studies, drew on two meta-analyses of over 14,000 subjects and later studies of nearly 10,000 more. The authors report that the strongest predictors of the scored or diagnosed outcome were depression and anxiety during pregnancy, stressful life events during pregnancy or the early puerperium, low levels of social support, and a previous history of depression.

2063.content: In 48 Israeli kibbutz infants aged 14 to 22 months, 80% of the 25 infants whose kibbutz let them sleep at their parents' home were securely attached to their mothers in the Strange Situation, against 48% of the 23 infants who slept at night in communal infants' houses away from their parents. The two groups did not differ in temperament, early life events, mother-infant play, quality of daytime care or several maternal measures. Counting the disorganized classification (44% communal, 32% home-based) did not change the result, and no avoidant relationships were found.

2064.content: Adults who had been classified in the second year of life as inhibited (children who avoid unfamiliar people, objects and situations) showed a greater functional MRI signal response in the amygdala to novel faces than to familiar ones, compared with adults who had been classified as uninhibited.

2065.content: Among Efe foragers of Zaire, infants' and toddlers' social contacts with mother, father, other adults and children were observed in daily life at 5 and 8 months and at 1, 2 and 3 years. The authors report that the Efe infant has many relationships at the same time from early on, in place of a pattern that starts with one person, usually the mother, and widens later; they tie the pattern to physical and social ecology and to cultural practice.

2066.content: Resequencing 600 DRD4 alleles from a worldwide population sample, the authors found that the 2R to 6R repeat variants differ from the common 4R allele by single steps, while the 7R allele differs by more than six recombination or mutation events and sits in strong linkage disequilibrium with the surrounding markers. Allele ages from intra-allele variability put 7R at about 30,000 to 50,000 years, 5 to 10 times younger than 4R, while its worldwide frequency would suggest more than 300,000 years. From that gap, a bias toward amino-acid-changing variants and the unusual sequence, they propose that 7R arose as a rare mutation and rose to high frequency through positive selection.

2067.content: In 723 residents of 7 Dutch nursing homes (19 psychogeriatric and 11 somatic wards), 3,282 observations at 5 random times between 7 am and 11 pm found residents mostly sleeping, doing nothing or watching TV (45% to 77% across the observation times). They were engaged in activities of daily living 15% to 38% of the time, mainly moving about and eating or drinking, were rarely seen in instrumental activities such as household tasks (up to 3%), and were lying or sitting 89% to 92% of the time.

2068.content: Reviewing research on wild animals, Hart groups vertebrate behaviour against viral, bacterial, protozoan and metazoan parasites into five strategies: avoiding parasites; controlled exposure to parasites that primes the immune system; the behaviour of sick animals, including not eating, that helps them overcome febrile infections; helping sick animals; and choosing mates with the genetic endowment to resist parasites. He sets a test for calling any behaviour a parasite defence: the parasite must be shown to harm fitness, and the behaviour must be shown to reduce exposure or vulnerability.

2069.content: Presenting a new dataset of battle deaths in armed conflicts from 1946 to 2002, the authors report that global battle deaths decreased over most of that period, mainly through a decline in interstate and internationalised civil armed conflict. They separate combatant deaths, battle deaths and war deaths, and write that war deaths, which include deaths from displacement and disease, are far harder to assess.

2070.content: In the Kuopio Ischemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, 2,315 men aged 42 to 60 from Eastern Finland were followed for a median of 20.7 years. After adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors, men taking 4 to 7 sauna sessions a week had a hazard ratio of 0.37 for sudden cardiac death against men taking one a week, with similar associations for fatal coronary heart disease, fatal cardiovascular disease and all-cause death. All-cause deaths were 49.1%, 37.8% and 30.8% in the once-a-week, 2-to-3 and 4-to-7 groups. Sessions longer than 19 minutes went with lower sudden cardiac death than sessions under 11 minutes, with no such association for all-cause death.

2071.content: In four experiments, participants imagined receiving one of several positive or negative reactions from another person (Experiments 1 to 3) or actually received evaluations from another person (Experiment 4), then completed measures of state self-esteem. In all four, how participants felt about themselves was a curvilinear, S-shaped (ogival) function of the other person's appraisal. Trait self-esteem went with state self-esteem as a main effect but did not change how strongly participants reacted to the feedback.

2072.content: Using data on body size, resting metabolism and activity budgets for selected anthropoid primate species and for human hunter-gatherers to estimate total energy expenditure, the authors found that relative energy expenditure and day range rise with diet quality across primates, and that human foragers sit at the high end of all three: high expenditure, large ranges and very high-quality diets.

Assuming the same activity budgets for all early hominids, the authors estimate that total daily energy expenditure of Homo erectus was 40 to 45 percent greater than that of the australopithecines; assuming that early Homo also shifted to a more human-like foraging strategy, the estimate is 80 to 85 percent greater. They link the rise partly to larger body size and partly to likely increases in day range and activity.

2073.content: Maner and Case review their laboratory's experiments in which participants were made leaders of small groups whose rank was either unstable (roles could be reassigned) or stable, or were placed in an egalitarian control condition; participants rated their own dominance motivation and prestige motivation, and both were entered together. In two studies (Maner and Mead 2010), leaders high in dominance motivation whose rank was unstable assigned a highly skilled group member to a role with almost no influence, and when given the chance chose to exclude the skilled member and keep an inept one. The pattern did not appear under stable leadership or in the control condition, and leaders high in prestige motivation gave the skilled member an influential role.

In four further experiments by the same laboratory (Case and Maner 2014), leaders high in dominance motivation whose rank was unstable kept a skilled subordinate from forming ties: they placed the skilled member alone in a separate room although told that working together face to face would help the group, chose a task-only working style that left no room for personal talk, and paired the skilled member with a partner of a clashing personality type. When their rank was secure, even highly dominant leaders paired members with similar partners, and leaders high in prestige motivation encouraged face-to-face contact and bonding.

2074.content: Marteau, Hollands and Fletcher review behaviour-change efforts against overeating, smoking, excessive alcohol use and physical inactivity. They write that most interventions so far have asked people to reflect on their behaviour, that these are often ineffectual, and that this fits the observation that much human behaviour is automatic, cued by things in the surroundings and largely not accompanied by conscious reflection. They propose that interventions targeting these automatic processes may work better.

2075.content: Reviewing neurochemical, tract-tracing, developmental-gene and lesion or stimulation studies across the five major vertebrate lineages (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and teleost fish), O'Connell and Hofmann find putative homologues for most nodes of the mesolimbic reward system and of the social behaviour network, and conclude that both circuits were already present in early vertebrates. They propose that the two circuits together form one social decision-making network. Homologies for a few nodes remain uncertain, among them the ventral pallidum and extended amygdala in teleost fish.

2076.content: In male adult vervet monkeys (Chlorocebus aethiops, then named Cercopithecus aethiops), dominant males had whole-blood serotonin concentrations about twice those of subordinate adult males. Examining spontaneous and experimentally induced changes in social status, temporary isolation from the social group and living in single-male groups, the authors found that the raised serotonin is a state-dependent consequence of actively occupying the dominant position.

2077.content: In an anonymous online survey, 100 Tinder users (31 men, 69 women) were compared with 1,047 non-users (203 men, 844 women), adjusting for BMI and age. Tinder users of both sexes reported lower satisfaction with their face and body and higher internalisation of appearance ideals, more appearance comparison, and more body shame and body surveillance than non-users. On self-esteem, male Tinder users scored lower than both male and female non-users.

2078.content: Sixteen men viewed the same erotic film segment on many occasions, or repeated the same erotic fantasy many times. Penile tumescence and self-rated sexual arousal fell over the trials, and the men reported feeling less absorbed in the film or fantasy (and, for fantasy, less vivid images). When a new erotic stimulus was introduced after habituation, sexual arousal rose again, and arousal also recovered when the original stimulus was brought back; both changes went with shifts in absorption and vividness of imagery.

2079.content: Reviewing the network literature, McPherson, Smith-Lovin and Cook find that similarity structures ties of every type, including marriage, friendship, work, advice, support and information exchange, so that personal networks are homogeneous on many social, behavioural and personal characteristics. In the US studies they review, race and ethnicity create the strongest divides, followed in roughly this order by age, religion, education, occupation and gender.

The same review finds that geographic nearness, families, organisations and similar positions in social systems create the settings in which ties between similar people form, with space the most basic of these; and that ties between dissimilar people dissolve at a higher rate, which sorts people into niches of similar others.

2080.content: In the US National Survey of Families and Households, 2,737 adults who were single and under 50 at the first wave were followed to the second wave about six years later. Using fixed-effects models that compare each person with themselves, entering cohabitation, direct marriage or marriage after cohabitation all reduced contact with parents and social evenings with neighbours, coworkers and friends, relative to staying single, and to a similar extent. The quality of the relationship with parents did not change, and contact did not rebound with longer unions. Entering a union raised happiness and lowered scores on a 12-item CES-D depressive symptoms scale, gains that tended to fade over time.

2081.content: A systematic review of 51 general-population studies (28 cross-sectional, 23 prospective; 12 rated high quality, all prospective) of social support, social networks or social connectedness and depression as the included studies measured it (symptom scales or diagnostic interviews). Perceived emotional support went with fewer depressive symptoms or less onset in 32 of the 35 studies that measured it, perceived instrumental (practical) support in 11 of 12, and a larger social network in 9 of 13; the authors call these the strongest and most consistent protective findings. In 5 of 7 studies, support from friends mattered as much as support from family. Little evidence was found on social connectedness or negative interactions.

2082.content: Reviewing long-term field studies, Seyfarth and Cheney report that some individuals form friendships lasting years in horses (Equus caballus), elephants (Loxodonta africana), spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta), bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops aduncus), monkeys such as baboons (Papio) and rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), and chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes). Bonds between elephant mothers and daughters and between sisters can last over 20 years, and bonds between allied male dolphins up to 20 years. Kinship shapes who befriends whom, yet many friendships are between unrelated individuals, and female baboons and male chimpanzees consistently formed at least one enduring bond, even with no close kin in the group.

The same review reports that these bonds pay off: allied males have greater competitive ability and reproductive success, and females with the strongest, most enduring friendships have lower stress, higher infant survival and longer lives (baboons and feral horses among the cases). In the female primates studied, the benefits appear not to include better defence against predators, more food or higher rank. When a baboon female loses a close companion to predation, she grooms more and with more partners, which the authors read as forming a new bond.

2083.content: In the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, 6,500 men and women aged 52 and over were assessed in 2004-05 and followed for all-cause death to March 2012 (mean 7.25 years; 918 died). Social isolation was scored from not being married or cohabiting, less than monthly contact with children, other family and friends, and no membership of organisations; the top fifth counted as isolated. Isolated people died at a higher rate (21.9 against 12.3 percent). The hazard ratio was 1.50 after adjusting for age and sex and 1.26 after also adjusting for wealth, education, marital status, ethnicity and baseline illness, mobility and mood (including CES-D scores and diagnosed depression); adding loneliness did not change it.

In the same cohort, loneliness measured with the three-item short form of the Revised UCLA loneliness scale also went with higher death rates (19.2 against 13.0 percent; hazard ratio 1.26 after adjusting for age and sex), but the link fell to nonsignificance after adjusting for demographic factors and was 0.92 (95 percent CI 0.78 to 1.09) after adjusting also for baseline health and mobility. The authors conclude that the mortality link of isolation does not run through the feeling of loneliness.

2084.content: Reviewing the literature on loneliness and alcohol abuse, Akerlind and Hornquist find that systematic studies are sparse and mostly from the 1980s. Concordant reports show that people labelled alcoholics feel lonelier than members of most other groups, and the review suggests loneliness may matter at all stages, contributing to and maintaining the growth of abuse and hindering attempts to stop. In advanced abusers loneliness is linked to a poor prognosis. Loneliness showed no obvious relation to the external social network or to the amount of drinking, and was connected instead with a negative view of oneself and one's relations to other people.

2085.content: During a four-day gift-giving week at the University of Virginia, 78 new sorority members recorded 496 benefits received from an anonymous older member. How thoughtful the giver seemed (the authors' measure of perceived responsiveness) went with more gratitude (B = .46, d = 0.79). The money spent and the effort seen also went with more gratitude, but once thoughtfulness was taken into account, cost no longer did: thoughtfulness fully carried the effect of cost and largely carried the effect of effort.

The average gratitude a new member felt during the gift week went with how she rated her interactions with the giver and how integrated she felt in the sorority at the reveal, and with her rating of the relationship one month later. It also went with the givers' own ratings of the relationship and of time spent with the new member one month later (marginally significant, d = 0.64 to 0.85). Gratitude did not go with how much time the new members said they had spent with the giver.

2086.content: A preregistered umbrella review of 14 meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials of mobile phone-based interventions for mental health, covering 145 trials and 47,940 participants, graded 34 representative effect sizes. None met the authors' criteria for convincing evidence (n above 1000, p below 10 to the minus 6, low heterogeneity, no publication bias), and publication bias was rarely assessed. Smartphone interventions beat inactive controls such as waitlists on reported symptoms of anxiety, depression and stress and on quality of life by small margins (d 0.32 to 0.47). The margins shrank and the evidence weakened as the comparison grew stricter: against active controls, smartphone apps were ahead on depression scores by d 0.22, and against specific active controls (other interventions meant to help) every comparison but one failed to show the phone intervention ahead, the exception being meditation apps on depression scores (d 0.28, weak evidence). No moderators were found, and adverse effects were not reported.

2087.content: In 63 heterosexual dating couples (24 Asian American, 25 Caucasian and 14 Latino, mean age about 21, together 17.6 months on average) filmed in a 3-minute conversation, romantic love as the partners reported it correlated with affiliation cues (Duchenne smiles, affirmative head nods, positive hand gestures, leaning toward the partner; r .28) and reported sexual desire correlated with sexual cues (lip licks, lip bites, lip touches, tongue protrusions; r .34), and each set of cues did not track the other state. Love correlated with relationship commitment (r .60) and was higher in couples who had discussed marriage; desire correlated negatively with commitment (r minus .30) and positively with sexual satisfaction (r .34), and was higher in couples who were having intercourse. The pattern held across the three ethnic groups, attachment styles and lengths of relationship.

In a second study, 26 nulliparous women aged 23 to 35 recalled and relived an experience of love or infatuation while blood was drawn through a catheter. Their display of affiliation cues correlated with the rise in plasma oxytocin (partial r .50), while their display of sexual cues did not; the difference between the two correlations was not significant, and the love the women reported did not correlate with the oxytocin rise. The authors did not measure any hormone linked to sexual desire and note the small sample.

2088.content: Among 1,300 Tsimane forager-horticulturalist adults aged 20 to 90 in the Bolivian Amazon, resting metabolic rate measured by indirect calorimetry in mobile village clinics was 18 to 47 percent higher in women and 22 to 40 percent higher in men than six standard prediction equations expected, and higher than in 90 to 96 percent of high Human Development Index samples measured the same way. Raised white blood cell counts and intestinal helminth infection were associated with the excess; together they accounted for an expected excess of 10 to 15 percent. Field conditions (no guaranteed overnight fast, no temperature control) explain part of the excess, by the authors' estimate at most 26 to 46 percent of it in women and 54 to 85 percent in men.

In a subsample of 40 Tsimane adults, total daily energy expenditure measured with doubly labelled water was 3,065 kcal in men and 2,186 kcal in women. Against other populations it was 284 kcal a day higher after controlling for weight, age and sex (p 0.10), 177 kcal higher once physical activity level was added, and no different once resting metabolic rate was controlled for (p 0.88). The authors read this as consistent with total energy expenditure held within a relatively narrow range: for people as physically active as the Tsimane, an additive, unconstrained model would expect a higher total than they measured.

2089.content: In the WHO Collaborative Study on determinants of outcome of severe mental disorders, 12 research centres in 10 countries monitored defined populations for 2 years and examined 1,379 people making a first-in-lifetime contact with any helping agency for psychotic symptoms who met the study's criteria for schizophrenia and related non-affective conditions, with standardized instruments at entry and at two annual follow-ups. The two-year course was considerably more favourable in patients in developing countries than in developed countries, and the difference could not be fully explained by the higher frequency of acute onsets in the developing countries. The authors read this as support for earlier findings that prognosis is better in less industrialized societies.

In the same WHO study, patients meeting the ICD and CATEGO criteria for schizophrenia were remarkably similar in their symptom profiles across cultures, and 49 percent presented the central conditions the CATEGO program classes as S+. Age- and sex-specific incidence rates for a broad diagnostic group differed significantly between centres, while the rates for the narrowly defined S+ cases differed non-significantly or marginally; the authors conclude that schizophrenic illnesses occur with comparable frequency in different populations.

2090.content: Among 150 adults from three lowland Bolivian horticulturalist populations (Tsimane, Mosetén and a multicultural community), each given 21 bolivianos (a third of a day's wage) to share among themselves and photographs of three strangers from their own group and three from an out-group in a non-anonymous game, participants gave away 74 percent on average: 14 percent of the stakes to each in-group stranger and 10 percent to each out-group stranger. Those who rated their own access to money and market goods lower than others in their community gave more to out-group strangers and not more to in-group strangers; those who had lived in more places gave more to out-group strangers (0.21 bolivianos per extra place), and those with partners for traditional cooperative labour gave more to out-group strangers, while a recent illness went with giving less to them. Household income and market asset value were largely unrelated to giving.

2091.content: Twenty-three experiments in six cultures (the US, Australia, Turkey, Romania, India and Shuar hunter-horticulturalists in five villages of the Ecuadorian Amazon) tested predictions of the recalibrational theory of anger with vignettes. People judged that anger would be stronger when the cost imposed was large, when the offender gained little from imposing it, and when the offender knew the victim was the person to be harmed; and offenders preferred arguments saying the cost was small or their benefit large. Among 90 Shuar adults the preference for 'I imposed only a small cost' was large (d 2.3) and for 'I benefited greatly' moderate (d 1.0). Among 63 Shuar adults, women's anger dropped when the offender had a large benefit and men's did not differ significantly between conditions; the targeting prediction was not run among the Shuar. The authors report the results replicated across all six cultures and read them as against equity theory and social constructivist accounts of anger.

2092.content: Using historical data on the constraints and ritual requirements that 83 nineteenth-century US communes imposed on their members, the authors tested whether communes that imposed costlier requirements survived longer than less demanding ones, and whether costly requirements and religiosity interact to promote cooperation. They report that the results support aspects of the costly signaling theory of religion, which holds that ritual and taboo promote cooperation within a group.

2093.content: In the database of nineteenth-century US utopian communes, religious communes survived on average 35.6 years against 7.7 years for secular ones. Survival peaked for communes founded with about 64 members (secular) and about 171 members (religious). Among 97 fission events in two Hutterite lineages from 1880 to 1970, colonies split at a mean size of 166.5, and survival time adjusted for size was highest for colonies founded near 50 and near 150. Among 240 Israeli kibbutzim, religious kibbutzim grew faster than secular ones. The authors note that these sizes match the band (about 50) and clan (about 150) layers of hunter-gatherer societies.

2094.content: In tissue explants from PER2::LUCIFERASE reporter house mice (Mus musculus), pulses from 36 to 38.5 degrees C, the range of the daily body temperature rhythm, strongly reset the circadian clocks of all peripheral tissues tested (lung and pituitary among them) to a common new phase, and 12-hour temperature cycles entrained lung and pituitary within 3 days. The adult suprachiasmatic nucleus (the master clock) resisted the same pulses at most times of the circadian cycle; it became sensitive when communication between its neurons was blocked with tetrodotoxin or an L-type calcium channel blocker, or when its regions were cut apart. Blocking the heat shock pathway (HSF1) with KNK437 blocked temperature resetting and lengthened the circadian period. The authors propose that the master clock drives the body temperature rhythm, which then acts as a universal cue that synchronizes the clocks throughout the body.

2095.content: Adults aged 18 to 65 wore a clip-on spectrophotometer near eye level at home for up to 4 evenings (163 evenings from 59 participants). Melatonin-relevant (melanopic) light in the 3 hours before bed averaged 17.9 mlux and ranged twentyfold between homes (3.9 to 77.4 mlux); at 8 pm and 10 pm the medians (13.4 and 11.0 mlux) sat near the light level that halves melatonin in the average person. Applying laboratory dose-response curves from 56 young adults, whose sensitivity varied more than fiftyfold, the authors' model put 48 percent of homes at 50 percent or more melatonin suppression, 73 percent at 20 percent or more and 15 percent at 80 percent or more, averaging across individual sensitivity levels. A recorded natural sunset fell through the same range in 22 minutes, while home light held it all evening. Evenings lit mainly by LED or fluorescent lights had about twice the melanopic light of incandescent evenings (19.7 against 10.3 mlux).

In the same 59 adults, on evenings when melanopic light in the 3 hours before bed was higher than that person's own average, actigraphy showed more wakefulness in the first 90 minutes after going to bed (beta 0.89, p below 0.00001), adjusting for age, sex, bedtime, chronotype, insomnia, sleepiness and sleep quality scores. A person's average evening light level across evenings was not associated with their wakefulness (p 0.59), which the authors attribute to the large differences in individual light sensitivity.

2096.content: Wrist actimetry in 98 Toba/Qom people (aged 12 to 75) in three communities of Formosa province, Argentina, one rural without electricity, one rural with limited electricity and one at the edge of a town with full electric light, showed sleep onset at its latest and sleep at its shortest 3 to 5 days before the full moon, when moonlight is available in the hours after dusk. Compared with nights with no early moonlight, sleep on moonlit nights was 25, 19 and 11 minutes shorter and started 22, 22 and 9 minutes later in the no-electricity, limited-electricity and urban communities respectively; sleep offset did not shift consistently. Across communities, more access to electric light went with later sleep onset and shorter sleep. 464 Seattle university students showed a similar lunar pattern.

2097.content: A review of 85 articles on human exposure to artificial light at night (databases searched to August 2014) reports that bright artificial light at night suppresses melatonin secretion, lengthens the time taken to fall asleep and increases alertness; that the circadian phase disruption it produces grows with longer exposure and with exposure later in the evening; and that shorter wavelengths of light disturb melatonin secretion and shift circadian phase preferentially, even when the light is not bright. Observational studies in the review linked outdoor light at night, indoor light intensity and lighting habits with breast cancer.

2098.content: De Backer argues that people more readily believe what they see, so pictures and screen images of stars feel like a personal eye-witness view of a real person, and so engage psychological mechanisms that evolved for dealing with people in one's own world. She calls this a mismatch outcome of evolved psychological mechanisms, comparable to a fear reaction to a water hose that looks like a snake, and proposes that mainly visual stimuli build the one-way (parasocial) bonds audiences form with stars whom they are very unlikely ever to meet.

2099.content: House mice (Mus musculus), which normally eat about 80 percent of their food at night, were fed only during the light phase. Restricting feeding to the daytime, under a light-dark cycle or in constant darkness, shifted the phase of circadian clock gene expression in peripheral tissues by up to 12 hours (a full inversion in the liver), while the phase of clock gene expression in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the master clock, did not change. The shift built up gradually over several days, faster in the liver than in the kidney, heart or pancreas, and after one week of daytime feeding all peripheral tissues examined were in the same new phase.

2100.content: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in the Detroit area, 12 healthy normal sleepers aged 19 to 48 took 400 mg of caffeine at bedtime, 3 hours before or 6 hours before their usual bedtime, or placebo, sleeping at home with a single-channel EEG headband. Measured total sleep time fell by 1.1 to 1.2 hours relative to placebo at each of the three times, with no significant difference between them; wake time during the night rose by 27.6 minutes at 3 hours and 8 minutes at 6 hours, and sleep efficiency fell in every caffeine condition. In the sleepers' own diaries the 0 and 3 hour doses reduced sleep significantly, while the 6 hour dose reduced it by 41 minutes, short of significance (p 0.08).

2101.content: Twelve young heterosexual couples (24 adults aged 18 to 29 in Kiel, Germany) who usually slept together spent four nights in a sleep laboratory under polysomnography: one weekend sleeping in separate rooms and one weekend in adjacent beds, in counterbalanced order. Sleeping beside the partner went with a higher share of REM sleep (23.0 against 21.0 percent, about 10 percent more), fewer REM interruptions (5.4 against 8.5) and longer unbroken REM stretches (22.0 against 13.4 minutes), and with more leg movements; no other sleep stage changed significantly. The partners' sleep stages were more synchronized when they slept together, and more so in couples who rated their relationship as deeper; individuals who rated their partner's support as less than optimal showed the largest REM difference between the two arrangements.

2102.content: In two longitudinal samples, children's attachment security to mother, father and professional caregiver was assessed in the Strange Situation at 11 to 14 months and scored as a family network (mother and father) and an extended network (mother, father and professional caregiver). In the Israeli kibbutz sample (86 infants from 15 kibbutzim, 59 retested about three and a half years later), a secure extended network went with higher IQ, with more empathy on a test, and with more independent, more resilient and more goal-directed behaviour as rated by kindergarten teachers and caregivers: eight outcomes for the extended network, five for the family network, and none for the infant-mother attachment on its own.

In the Dutch sample (80 dual-earner, middle-class families with infants of 12 months, 68 retested about two years later), a secure extended network (mother, father and professional caregiver) went with a higher developmental quotient and more autonomous preschool behaviour, while the infant-mother attachment went only with autonomous preschool behaviour. The authors conclude that children appear to do best with three secure relationships, and that an insecure attachment to the mother is partly made up for by secure attachments to father and professional caregiver.

2103.content: Abstract only. Overnight video and physiological recordings in the infants' own homes in Dunedin, New Zealand, compared 40 infants aged 5 to 27 weeks who routinely shared their parents' bed with 40 routinely cot-sleeping infants matched for age and season. Total sleep time was similar (medians 8.6 and 8.2 hours). Bed-sharing parents looked at or touched their infant more often (median 11 against 4 times a night), not always fully waking to do so, and bed-sharing infants fed 3.7 times as often. The authors conclude that bed-sharing infants without known risk factors for sudden infant death get more maternal touching and looking, more breastfeeding and faster, more frequent maternal responses.

Abstract only. In the same home recordings of 40 bed-sharing and 40 cot-sleeping infants in New Zealand, bed-sharing infants spent most of their sleep on their side (median 5.7 hours, 66 percent of sleep time) while cot infants slept on their back (median 7.5 hours, 100 percent). Head covering above the eyes occurred in 22 bed-sharing infants and 1 cot-sleeping infant, and 5 of the bed-sharing infants were head covered at final waking. Prone sleep was uncommon in both groups. The authors say whether side sleeping and head covering raise sudden infant death risk during bed-sharing, as they do in cot sleeping, needs further study.

2104.content: In a randomised trial on the postnatal wards of the Royal Victoria Infirmary, Newcastle, UK, 64 newly delivered mother-infant pairs (vaginal births, no opiate analgesia in the previous 24 hours, mothers intending to breastfeed) were allocated to the baby sleeping in the mother's bed with a cot-side, in a side-car crib attached to the bed, or in a stand-alone cot beside the bed, and filmed at night. Over standardised 4-hour observations, babies in the bed and in the side-car crib made more feeding attempts (successful plus unsuccessful) than babies in the stand-alone cot: mean differences 2.56 and 2.52 per hour, with no difference between bed and side-car crib. Maternal and infant sleep duration, staff assistance and maternal satisfaction did not differ.

In the same trial, none of the 61 observed infants experienced an adverse event. Potential breathing risk (airway covered), coded from video, occurred more often and for longer in the mother's-bed condition than in the side-car crib or stand-alone cot; the infant with the most potential breathing risks had crossed over from the bed to the stand-alone cot, and all of that infant's airway covering happened in the cot during swaddling. The authors say coding from a fixed camera may overstate risk and conclude that the side-car crib combined frequent feeding with low potential risk.

2105.content: Abstract only. In 193 infants whose sleeping and feeding were logged in daily and weekly diaries over the first six months, more weeks of co-sleeping (sleeping in the parents' bed or in the parents' room) went with lower salivary cortisol reactivity to the Strange Situation at 12 months, after maternal sensitivity, attachment status, feeding and sleeping arrangements at 12 months and other confounders were controlled. More weeks of breastfeeding went with quicker cortisol recovery.

2106.content: Abstract only. In extensive data from pre-industrial humans, the presence of a maternal grandmother aged 50 to 75 went with higher grandchild survival after weaning, while living with a paternal grandmother aged 75 or more went with lower grandchild survival, most of all when that grandmother was close to death. Both the opportunity and the ability to help grandchildren declined with grandmother age, and women's hazard of death rose steeply in their late 60s and 70s. The authors conclude that grandmothering can select for post-reproductive longevity only up to a certain age.

2107.content: Abstract only. A randomised trial in Colombia (1993 to 1996) compared kangaroo mother care (a package of skin-to-skin carrying, breastfeeding and early discharge for preterm and low birthweight infants) with traditional incubator care. From 2012 to 2014, 441 of the 716 participants known to be alive were re-enrolled and the 264 born at 1,800 g or less were analysed. The gains in IQ and home environment seen at one year were still present 20 years later in the most fragile individuals; kangaroo-care parents were more protective and nurturing, and the young adults had less school absenteeism and scored lower for hyperactivity, aggressiveness, externalising and socially deviant conduct. Neuroimaging showed a larger left caudate nucleus in the kangaroo-care group.

2108.content: In the UK Millennium Cohort Study (16,701 mothers of children born 2000 to 2002, data collected at about 9 months, breastfeeding recalled by the mother), more frequent face-to-face contact with maternal or paternal grandmothers went with fewer mothers starting breastfeeding and earlier stopping. Compared with daily contact, mothers who saw the maternal grandmother once every few months had about 2.6 times the odds of starting breastfeeding (95% CI 2.15 to 3.20) and a 25 percent lower hazard of stopping (HR 0.749). The exception: mothers living with a paternal grandmother breastfed longer (HR for stopping 0.700). Financial help from grandparents was unrelated to breastfeeding.

In the same cohort, mothers in father-present households had 33.6 percent higher odds of starting breastfeeding than single mothers (95% CI 1.15 to 1.55), with no link to duration. Among father-present households, each 1 SD more paternal involvement in childcare went with 12.3 percent higher odds of stopping breastfeeding (95% CI 1.08 to 1.17), with no link to starting. The authors read father presence as a cue that supports maternal investment, and hands-on help as a route to shared formula feeding.

2109.content: Abstract only. In detailed records of pre-industrial French settlers in the St Lawrence Valley (Quebec) in the 17th and 18th centuries, daughters whose mothers were alive had 2.1 more children born and 1.1 more surviving to age 15 than when the grandmother was dead, accounting for family genetic and environmental effects. Age at first birth did not differ with the grandmother alive or dead. With the grandmother alive, the further away she lived (0 to 325 km), the fewer children the daughter had, the lower her lifetime reproductive success and the later her first birth.

2110.content: Twelve healthy infants aged 1 to 6 months were recorded with audio-video and electrocardiogram while lying in a crib, held by the mother sitting on a chair, or carried by the mother walking, each for about 30 seconds in random order. When the mother stood up and began walking, the infants quickly stopped voluntary movement and crying, and the interval between heartbeats lengthened by about 7 percent within about 3 seconds (heart rate slowed). The heart-rate change also appeared in infants who were not crying while held, so it was partly independent of crying stopping. All measures generally rose in the crib and fell during carrying.

Animal evidence. In house mice (Mus musculus, strain C57BL/6), pups carried by the mother or picked up at the nape by an experimenter went still in a compact posture, emitted fewer ultrasonic distress calls and their heart rate slowed (interbeat interval up about 5 percent); the slowing did not occur when pups were held without being lifted or lifted on a platform. Touch at the grasp and proprioception were both needed. Pups whose calming was blocked (proprioception impaired with pyridoxine) or whose posture was lost (limp under anaesthesia) took their mothers significantly longer to carry out of a cup.

2111.content: Abstract only. In an exploratory within-subjects study, 10 retired volunteers (8 women, mean age 70) spent 3 weeks receiving Swedish massage three times a week and 3 weeks giving massage to infants at a nursery school three times a week, in counterbalanced order. Right after the first and last sessions of giving massage, the volunteers reported less anxiety and less depression on self-report measures and had lower salivary cortisol. Over the 3 weeks of giving massage, reported depression and catecholamines (norepinephrine and epinephrine) fell and lifestyle and health improved. These effects were weaker for the 3 weeks of being massaged.

2112.content: Abstract only. Three nights of polysomnography were recorded in 35 breastfeeding mother-infant pairs with infants aged 11 to 15 weeks: an adaptation night, one bed-sharing night and one solitary night; 20 infants were routine bed-sharers and 15 routine solitary sleepers. Infants rarely woke or aroused in stage 3-4 (deep) sleep, and bed sharing raised awakenings and transient arousals selectively in that stage: awakenings from stage 3-4 were more frequent on the bed-sharing night in both groups, and routine bed-sharers had more transient arousals in stage 3-4 on both nights. In both groups the number of infant arousals overlapping the mother's doubled during bed sharing, with the infant's arousal usually coming first.

Abstract only. In the same 35 mother-infant pairs, the number of infant arousals (awakenings plus transient arousals) that overlapped one of the mother's doubled on the bed-sharing night compared with the solitary night, in both routine bed-sharing and routine solitary-sleeping infants, and in most overlapping pairs the infant aroused first.

2113.content: Abstract only. Using comprehensive records of the early French Canadian population of Quebec, motherless children had a higher risk of dying that stayed significant across all of childhood and long after the mother's death. Comparing each child's mortality before and after the mother's death, to control for differences between families, the authors found no difference between boys and girls before age 3, while older girls were three times as susceptible to the mother's death as boys. The authors suggest that older girls who took over the missing mother's work had a lower chance of survival.

2114.content: Abstract only. Animal evidence. Reviewing the literature and their own laboratories' data, Schanberg and Field report that in rat pups (laboratory rat, Rattus norvegicus) separated from the mother, growth hormone release and protein synthesis are suppressed, and that only brush stroking of the deprived pups returned these growth measures to normal; kinesthetic and vestibular stimulation did not.

Abstract only. In the same review, the authors present data showing that very small preterm infants given tactile-kinesthetic stimulation gained more weight per day, spent more time awake and active, and showed more mature habituation, orientation, motor and state behaviour on the Brazelton neonatal assessment than preterm infants without it.

2115.content: In two Mandinka farming villages in rural Gambia (Keneba and Manduar), with demographic and anthropometric records from 1950 to 1974 (natural fertility and mortality: about 7 births per woman, over 40 percent of children dying before age 5), the only kin besides mothers to improve children's nutritional status were maternal grandmothers: children with a living maternal grandmother were taller at every age after the first year and heavier in the first two years (1,998 children measured). Children whose maternal grandmother was no longer reproducing were taller than those whose grandmother was still having children. Paternal grandmothers made children taller and heavier only in the first year; fathers and grandfathers had no consistent effect.

In the mortality analysis of 1,691 children (622 deaths) from the same Gambian villages, children whose mother had died had 11 to 13 times the odds of dying in infancy and the second year, with no significant difference after age two. A living maternal grandmother significantly raised survival in the second year of life (12 to 23 months), the age of weaning; the trend was the same in infancy and later childhood without reaching significance. Fathers, paternal grandmothers and both grandfathers had no significant effect on survival.

2116.content: In 61 girls aged 7 to 12 in a US laboratory, a social stressor (Trier Social Stress Test for Children) raised salivary cortisol in all. The girls were then randomly assigned to 15 minutes of comfort from their mother in person including touch (19), a telephone call with her mother with no visual or physical contact (20), or no contact while watching a neutral film (22). Urinary oxytocin rose within 15 minutes in both the in-person and the phone groups and stayed raised at one hour, while it did not change in the no-contact group. Cortisol fell fastest with in-person contact; by one hour the phone and in-person groups were indistinguishable and near baseline, while the no-contact group still had higher cortisol.

2117.content: In the Wirral Child Health and Development Study (UK), 271 infants from a stratified random sample of 316 first-time mothers were followed from pregnancy. Mothers reported how often they stroked their babies at 5 and 9 weeks; mothers' symptoms of depression were scored on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at 32 weeks of pregnancy. At 29 weeks, a higher prenatal depression score went with less vagal withdrawal to a stressor (less physiological adaptability) and with more anger proneness and fear as rated by the mothers, but only among infants whose mothers reported stroking them less than the median. Among infants stroked more often, prenatal depression scores showed no link to anger proneness or fear, and the vagal link reversed direction. Breastfeeding, which also involves skin contact, did not show this pattern.

2118.content: Abstract only. Adolescents who had been cared for by multiple changing caregivers in residential nurseries until at least age 2, then adopted or returned to a biological parent, were followed into mid-adolescence. The early lack of a stable caregiver did not prevent strong and lasting attachments to parents once the children were placed in families, but whether such attachments formed depended on the family: they were much more common in adopted children than in children restored to a biological parent. Both groups alike sought adult attention more, had more difficulties with peers and had fewer close relationships than matched comparison adolescents.

2119.content: In the same cohort, how much infants slept in the parents' room over their first 7 weeks showed no link with the cortisol response to routine vaccinations at 8 weeks of age; cortisol levels did not differ between the three groups at any sampling time.

2120.content: Modelling the energy needs of Homo erectus females (estimated over 50 percent heavier than australopithecine females) from living-primate data on activity, body mass and life history, the authors find that daily energy needs in pregnancy and lactation would have been much higher, as would the total cost per offspring under an ape-like reproductive schedule. Shortening the interbirth interval would cut the cost per offspring and raise reproductive output, but adds the daily cost of caring for dependent young; the authors argue this required a change in how females obtained energy, through a cooperative economic division of labour and other energy-saving changes.

2121.content: Comparing infant-to-mother body mass ratios, human newborns weigh about 6 percent of the mother's mass against about 3 percent for chimpanzees (3.3 percent in 47 captive chimpanzee dyads), although adult female body mass is similar in the two species. In 2,607 mother-infant pairs from the Cebu cohort (Philippines) the ratio was 6.1 percent, and across 18 human populations (11,317 people) it was 5.7 percent, ranging from 4.8 to 6.5 percent, with no overlap with any great ape.

Estimating newborn mass for extinct hominins from adult brain size and comparing it with fossil female body size, the study finds that 4.4-million-year-old Ardipithecus had an ape-like infant-to-mother ratio, while Australopithecus females are estimated to have given birth to infants more than 5 percent of their body mass. The author argues that carrying such large, immobile infants may have limited tree climbing and selected for help with infant care from others earlier than the genus Homo; he also notes that the link between relatively large newborns and shared care in primates is not supported once phylogeny is controlled for.

2122.content: Using a survival analysis built for censored, small-sample birth-interval data, the authors estimate the median birth interval (when the child opening the interval survives it) at 43.3 months among the Gainj of highland Papua New Guinea, 45.5 months for wild mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei, Virunga), 66.6 months for wild chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes, Gombe) and 92.6 months for wild orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus, Tanjung Puting).

2123.content: Among the Hadza foragers of Tanzania, who sleep in grass huts with no electric light or climate control, interviews found that most people share their sleeping place with at least one other person, and most married couples sleep on the same surface as their spouse and their children.

In actigraphy of 33 Hadza adults (1-minute epochs), breastfeeding mothers rose earlier and were less active by day. The total number of people sharing the sleeping place, and not breastfeeding, was associated with shorter and poorer sleep; the authors read their preliminary data as showing that breastfeeding does not lower mothers' sleep quality.

2124.content: Among the Beng, a small minority group in the rain forest of Cote d'Ivoire, the ethnographer reports that relatives teach infants to be at ease with strangers: a visitor is linked to a host before arriving and is introduced as 'my stranger' with handshakes, a chair and water, and a newborn is introduced to each visitor. Beng mothers say that fearful wariness of strangers is rare in their infants, and most Beng infants seemed as comfortable with a range of other people, strangers included, as with their mothers; being handed to others is a routine part of the day.

In 875 hours of documented daytime naps of Beng infants, about two-thirds of nap time was spent asleep joined to another person (on a back or in a lap), and almost 90 percent of napping babies slept outside amid village life; at night babies sleep against the mother and often an older sibling.

2125.content: Reviewing her group's and others' cross-cultural studies, Keller describes infant care in Western middle-class families as mainly by the mother, with some help from the father and occasionally a grandmother or babysitter, built on one-to-one face-to-face exchanges. In rural subsistence farming villages (for example the Nso of Cameroon) infants have many social partners in large multigenerational households, are in near-constant body contact, and are often cared for most by other children; in South Madagascan villages children up to 5 years old did almost all the social interacting with infants.

Keller reports that most Nso children in Cameroonian farming villages were not afraid when an unfamiliar woman approached, picked them up and moved away from the mother with them: they kept neutral faces, and their salivary cortisol fell from the stranger's visual approach to the physical pick-up. She reads this as the result of socialising children to emotional neutrality within a network of many caregivers.

2126.content: Reviewing the anthropological literature on childbirth, the authors report that it gives little evidence of the state labelled post-partum depression, and they identify six common elements in how other cultures structure the weeks after a birth: a distinct post-partum period, measures to shield the vulnerable new mother, social seclusion, mandated rest, help with tasks from relatives or a midwife, and public recognition of her new status through rituals or gifts.

The authors propose that post-partum social organisation and the post-partum depression label are linked, and that the U.S. experience labelled post-partum depression may be a culture-bound syndrome arising from the lack of a structured post-partum period, of social recognition of the new mother's role change, and of practical help for her.

2127.content: A qualitative systematic review of 51 studies of traditional post-partum practices in more than 20 countries found common themes across cultures: organised support for the mother, periods of rest, prescribed or forbidden foods, hygiene practices and practices around infant care and breastfeeding. The authors describe these rituals as letting the mother be 'mothered' for a time after the birth, and note that migration and modern life can leave women unable to carry them out.

2128.content: Among 70 lactating Toba women of Namqom, Formosa, Argentina (formerly foragers, now settled, well nourished, breastfeeding for 2 to 3 years with solid foods added around 6 months), lactational amenorrhoea lasted 10.2 months on average (SD 4.3). The return of menses showed no association with nursing behaviour or with body mass index. It was associated with month-to-month gain in body mass index: women were in a sustained positive energy balance by the time menses returned.

In the same women, urinary C-peptide (a marker of insulin production) was low in early lactation and rose steadily after birth; aligned to the month of first menses, it showed a short, sharp peak of insulin production in the months just before menses returned, then fell back. The authors read this as the body timing the return of ovarian function to the falling energy cost of milk production.

2129.content: In 2,213 children from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, parents' 24-hour time-use diaries (one weekend day and one weekday) recorded unstructured quiet and active play at ages 2 to 3 and 4 to 5. More time in unstructured quiet play in the toddler and preschool years went with better self-regulation, rated by parents, teachers and observers, at ages 4 to 5 and 6 to 7, after controlling for earlier self-regulation and other known predictors; between 1 and 5 hours of unstructured active play at preschool age also predicted self-regulation 2 years later.

2130.content: In a cluster randomised trial in 12 primary schools in Guangzhou, China (2010 to 2013), 6 schools added one 40-minute class of outdoor activity to each school day and encouraged outdoor time after school (952 first-graders, mean age 6.6), while 6 control schools (951 children) carried on as usual. Over 3 years, new myopia developed in 30.4 percent of eligible children in the outdoor schools (259 of 853) against 39.5 percent in the control schools (287 of 726), a difference of 9.1 percentage points; refraction shifted slightly less toward myopia (-1.42 against -1.59 dioptres), while eyeball elongation did not differ significantly.

2131.content: In a randomised trial in Illinois, 221 children aged 7 to 9 were assigned to a 9-month after-school physical activity programme (2 hours each school day, at least 70 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity) or a wait-list control. The programme group gained more in aerobic fitness (d 0.34), in inhibition (3.2 percent, d 0.27) and in cognitive flexibility (4.8 percent, d 0.35), and only the programme group showed larger P3 brain responses on the harder tasks. Gains in brain response and flexibility rose with attendance (r 0.22 and 0.24).

2132.content: The authors coded touch between National Basketball Association players during the 2008-2009 regular season. More touch early in the season went with better individual and team performance later in the season, also after allowing for player status, preseason expectations and early season performance, and coded cooperative behaviour between teammates explained the link between touch and team performance.

2133.content: In a within-subjects field experiment, 23 nine-year-old children were observed for 14 weeks while the time they spent in class before playtime was set shorter or longer. Children were less attentive to seat work the longer they had been in class, longer confinement went with more exercise play for boys and more social sedentary behaviour for girls at playtime, and social behaviour at playtime was related to attention to seat work afterwards.

2134.content: A meta-analysis of 17 studies in patrilineal populations, using two methods, found that the survival of the maternal grandmother and the maternal grandfather was associated with lower grandchild mortality, and the survival of the paternal grandmother and paternal grandfather was not. The authors read the pattern as most in line with local resource competition: in patrilineal and mostly patrilocal societies, the grandparents most likely to live with the grandchildren have a less beneficial association than those who do not.

2135.content: In two neighbouring elementary schools in suburban southern Taiwan, children aged 7 to 11 at one school (333) took part in a programme that sent them outside during class recess, and children at the other school (238) were the controls. The schools did not differ at the start (myopia in 47.75 and 49.16 percent). After one year, new onset of myopia was 8.41 percent in the recess-outdoors school against 17.65 percent in the control school, and the yearly myopic shift was smaller (0.25 against 0.38 diopter).

2136.content: A meta-analysis of 25 studies (23 in children) found that more time outdoors protected against new myopia: risk ratio 0.536 in the three clinical trials and 0.574 in cohort studies comparing high with low outdoor time. A dose-response analysis estimated that about 76 more minutes outdoors a day would halve incident myopia. In the trials, outdoor time reduced the myopic shift by about 0.30 diopter over 3 years, but in children who were already myopic no link between time outdoors and progression was found.

2137.content: Reviewing 543 ethnographies in the Human Relations Area Files, the authors assessed how often parents and offspring agreed or disagreed over the choice of a partner in arranged marriages. In all world areas, parents and offspring overwhelmingly chose different partners, they disagreed over traits of the potential spouse that bear on fitness, and both sides sometimes used extreme methods to influence the outcome.

2138.content: In live-birth records from four lowland South American peoples with partible paternity beliefs (Bari of Venezuela, Ache of Paraguay, Surui of Brazil, Ese Eja of Bolivia; 1,918 births pooled), births attributed to one father had a sex ratio of 109 males to 100 females, births attributed to two fathers 143 to 100 (364 births) and births attributed to three or more fathers 75 to 100 (93 births). The two-father against three-or-more difference was significant (chi-square 7.47, p 0.006). The authors suggest a Trivers-Willard effect: a woman with a husband and one lover may be in better condition in pregnancy.

Restating their own Bari data and Hill and Hurtado's Ache data, the authors report that children with a husband and a single secondary father had higher survival than children with only one father or with two or more secondary fathers, and they think better health the most likely reason. From their 2002 Bari analysis (reproductive histories of 114 post-reproductive women) they quote that the odds of dying before 15 for a child with two or more secondary fathers were 5.188 times those of a child with one secondary father (p 0.0001), and 0.632 times those of a child with none (not significant).

2139.content: From 23 years of fieldwork among the Yanomamo of Amazonas (Venezuela), Chagnon reports that 44 percent of men estimated to be 25 or older had taken part in killing someone, about 30 percent of adult male deaths were due to violence, and nearly 70 percent of adults over about 40 had lost a close genetic relative to violence. His demographic data indicate that men who had killed had more wives and more offspring than men who had not.

2140.content: In hourly scan observations (about 15,000, over 165 days in six Hadza bush camps in northern Tanzania, 2005) of 76 children aged 2 to 16, about 50 to 60 percent of in-camp time was spent resting or eating at every age and for both sexes, and walking, running and playing (recorded together) took 23 to 43 percent, less in adolescence than in early or middle childhood. Older children did more economic work; girls did more work in camp (childcare, food processing) and boys more economic activity out of camp and toolmaking.

In 13 out-of-camp focal follows of 9 Hadza children, each observed over 60 days, children left camp to forage on 8 to 32 days (13 to 53 percent of days), boys and girls alike (32 and 33 percent of days on average), and foraging trips almost always brought back more calories than they cost: boys returned a mean of 2,874 kcal and girls 964 kcal per trip.

2141.content: Reviewing the forager evidence against the view that men hunt mainly to signal their quality and gain mates, Gurven and Hill find little support for signaling as the sole reason: hunting returns are variable but buffered by sharing, meat sharing is often contingent on return (among the Hiwi the meat one family gave another was the strongest predictor of what came back), and the children of good Ache hunters survived better. They propose that hunting pays through provisioning and through signaling benefits for mating and alliances together.
Gurven and Hill restate, from Kaplan and colleagues (2000) and Marlowe (2001), that men contribute on average about 65 percent of the calories and 85 percent of the protein in forager diets.

2142.content: In 456 high-coverage Y chromosome sequences from around the world (299 new), compared with mitochondrial DNA from the same people, the authors find a second strong bottleneck in male lineages within the last 10,000 years: around 8,000 to 4,000 years ago the female effective population size was up to 17 times the male. The drop came earlier where farming spread earlier (Near East, East Asia, South Asia) than in Europe, and the authors propose that cultural changes that increased variance in men's reproductive success explain it, since selection on the Y chromosome is unlikely.

2143.content: In complete multi-generational church and parish records of pre-modern farming populations in Finland (about 500 women) and Canada (about 2,300 women) in the 18th and 19th centuries, women who lived longer after age 50 had more grandchildren. In both countries the gain was about two extra grandchildren for every ten years a woman survived beyond 50, with socio-economic status, period, place and her own number of children controlled.

In the Finnish records, sons and daughters whose post-reproductive mother was alive when they began having children had more children in their lifetime and raised more to age 15, and the longer she survived the more grandchildren were raised. Offspring living in the same village as their mother had more children than those living more than 20 km away. The authors report that a living grandmother let her children start breeding earlier, breed more often and raise more children to adulthood.

2144.content: Sequencing about 500 kb of the Y chromosome and the whole mitochondrial genome in 623 men from 51 populations of the Human Genome Diversity Panel, and modelling the history by simulation, the authors estimate that the female effective population size has been larger than the male one throughout the history of modern humans: about 60 females and 30 males in the founding African population and about 25 females and 15 males at the out-of-Africa bottleneck. The female to male ratio rose further in recent times.
