They read this as a sign that processes that cut the number of men who pass on genes, such as polygyny or sex-specific migration, marked most of human prehistory.

2145.content: Among Palanan Agta fisher-foragers of Luzon, Philippines (fieldwork 2013 and 2014), the total fertility rate from 41 live births was 7.7, and the 117 women interviewed (aged 16 to 75) reported a mean of 4.4 live births. Of 520 live births reported by 124 mothers, 19% of children died before age 1, 13.9% between ages 1 and 5, and 6% between ages 5 and 15. The infant death figure is lower than the 28 to 29% earlier reported for neighbouring Agta.

Across Agta camps that differed in how settled they were, settled mothers had higher fertility than mothers who moved camp (total fertility 7.7 against 6.6), and mothers in camps with permanent housing lost more children, as did people in settled camps carry more viral and worm infections in blood tests of 345 Agta. Settled mothers still had more children alive at 16 (4.4 against 3.8). Mothers who spent more than 75% of their work time foraging had lower fertility. The authors read this as a trade of child survival for more births when people settle and farm.

2146.content: In reproductive histories of 110 Himba women, semi-nomadic pastoralists of northwest Namibia, 31.8% of women attributed at least one birth within marriage to an affair, and these extra-pair births made up 17.6% of all 329 marital births. The author calls this a conservative estimate, since children who died were not recorded and memory loss would lower the count.

Among the same Himba women, no extra-pair births were reported within love matches (0 of 79 births), against 23.2% of births in arranged marriages. Post-menopausal women who had at least one extra-pair birth had more children surviving to age five than women with none (Poisson coefficient 0.562, p = 0.002; 33 women).

Scelza reports that the only earlier genetic paternity study in a small-scale natural fertility population, research among the Yanomamo in the 1960s, found a non-paternity rate of 9.1%, at the high end of reported rates worldwide, against worldwide rates of 1 to 10% mostly from Western industrialised populations.

2147.content: Among the Dogon of Mali, a natural-fertility farming population without contraception, Y chromosome testing of about 1,700 father and son pairs from 29 patrilineages in 10 villages found a mismatch, read as non-paternity, in only 1.8% of pairs (31 cases). The authors note this is similar to rates in modern populations and contradicts the view that traditional populations have high rates of non-paternity.

In the same Dogon sample, the non-paternity rate was 1.3% when the mother used the menstrual hut required by the indigenous religion and 2.9% when she did not (p = 0.019). Among men born from 1930 on, the odds of non-paternity were about five times higher in Christian families than in families of the indigenous religion; wealth, polygyny and year of birth did not explain the difference.

2148.content: In a survey of Canadian Inuit, the share of people with myopia among those under 30 was far higher than among their elders, especially in females. The authors find little if any genetic contribution, read the age and sex pattern as pointing to an environmental, probably cultural, factor, and report other data implicating school attendance.

2149.content: Reviewing published 20th-century data on myopia in circumpolar Inuit populations, the authors report that the share of people with myopia rose from under 3% to over 50% in the new generations of young adults after the Second World War. They judge the most likely reasons to be the rise in near work (from almost no reading to daily reading) and the move from a mostly outdoor to a mostly indoor life, made worse by fewer hours of sunshine during waking hours, low Arctic light levels and the stress of the residential schools.

2150.content: In two longitudinal intervention studies in Australia, 52 adults at risk of depression joined a community recreation group and 92 adults diagnosed with depression joined a clinical psychotherapy group. In both, how strongly a person came to identify with the group predicted recovery in depression symptom scores, with initial symptom level, frequency of attendance and type of group controlled. In the clinical sample the link was larger for depression symptoms than for anxiety symptoms or quality of life.

2151.content: A psychiatrist examined 14 prison inmates in the United States exposed to periods of increased social isolation and sensory restriction in solitary confinement, described the psychiatric symptoms that appeared in them, and asserts that these symptoms form a major, clinically distinguishable syndrome.

2152.content: In a randomised trial in two small US cities, 202 children in kindergarten to second grade (mean age 6.8), 94 rated at risk for ADHD on a parent and teacher rating scale and 108 not, did either 31 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity games or 31 minutes of sedentary classroom art before school each school day for 12 weeks. Both groups improved. Parents rated the physical activity group as improving more on inattention and moodiness; teacher ratings of symptoms and moodiness did not differ between the two programmes.

2153.content: In Illinois, 150 people leaving inpatient treatment for alcohol or drug use were randomly assigned to an Oxford House (a house run democratically by its own residents, with no professional staff, where residents vote new members in, elect officers, pay rent, share chores and are evicted for drug or alcohol use) or to usual aftercare such as outpatient treatment or self-help groups. At 24 months, 31.3% of the Oxford House group reported substance use against 64.8% of the usual-care group, monthly income was $989 against $440, and 3% against 9% were incarcerated.

2154.content: In the full report of the same Illinois trial (150 people; 62% women, 77% African American), Oxford House residents who stayed 6 months or more reported substance use at 24 months in 15.6% of cases, against 45.7% for those who stayed under 6 months and 64.8% in usual aftercare. Younger residents who stayed at least 6 months had the lowest rate (6.7%). On average Oxford House participants spent 256 days in a house.

2155.content: In a 6-week randomised double-blind trial, 46 adults diagnosed with bipolar I or II disorder who scored as moderately depressed and stayed on stable antimanic medication received either 7,000 lux bright white light or 50 lux dim red placebo light at midday (23 per group). With bright light, 68.2% met the remission cutoff on the SIGH-ADS depression scale at weeks 4 to 6 against 22.2% with placebo light (adjusted odds ratio 12.6), and endpoint scores were lower (9.2 against 14.9). The authors report no mood polarity switches. Sleep quality improved in both groups.

2156.content: In a Dutch trial with a partially randomised patient preference design, 141 patients diagnosed with depression or anxiety disorders (mean age 38, 58% women) received 16 weeks of either an antidepressant (escitalopram or sertraline; 45 people) or group running therapy at least twice a week (96 people). By intention-to-treat analysis, the authors report remission at week 16 of 44.8% with antidepressants and 43.3% with running (p = .881).

In the same trial, the authors report that the running group and the antidepressant group differed on changes in body measures over 16 weeks: weight (d = 0.57), waist circumference (d = 0.44), systolic (d = 0.45) and diastolic (d = 0.53) blood pressure, heart rate (d = 0.36) and heart rate variability (d = 0.48). The authors report both larger improvements with running and larger deterioration with antidepressants.

2157.content: In US time-diary data, the time women spent preparing food and cleaning up after meals fell by about 50 percent between 1965 and 1995, for women with and without paid work. Over a similar span, reported food intake in national food surveys rose by 268 kcal a day for men and 143 for women between the mid-1970s and mid-1990s, most of it from snacks, while dinner calories fell slightly; the US food supply rose from 3,200 to 3,900 kcal per person per day from 1978 to 1999 (418 kcal after a wastage adjustment). The authors read the rise in eating as the result of mass food preparation lowering the time cost of food.

Across eight US demographic groups, groups that had spent more time preparing food in 1965 had larger rises in body mass index afterwards: each half hour of daily food preparation time in 1965 went with a rise in BMI of nearly 0.5, and groups whose preparation time fell most had the largest BMI rises. Women, who had spent most time on preparation, now spend less time on it and are much more obese than they used to be.

2158.content: In a randomised crossover trial, 18 healthy young adults who exercised less than an hour a week (mostly women students in Maastricht) each followed three 4-day regimes: sitting 14 hours a day; the same with 1 hour of sitting replaced by vigorous cycling; or 6 hours of sitting replaced by 4 hours of leisurely walking and 2 hours of standing, with the same extra energy use (about 450 kcal) as the cycling day. Measured by ActivPAL monitors, the walking regime averaged 27,590 steps a day against 4,324 when sitting. After the walking and standing regime the insulin response to an oral glucose load was lower than after both the sitting and the exercise regime, and triglycerides, non-HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B were lower than after sitting. One hour of cycling a day did not lower these values significantly against the sitting regime.

Replacing about 6 hours of daily sitting with walking and standing for 4 days lowered insulin levels during the glucose test by 15 percent and C-peptide by a non-significant 11 percent in 18 young sedentary adults, at the same energy use as one hour of vigorous cycling.

2159.content: A harmonised meta-analysis of individual data from eight prospective cohorts in the US and western Europe (36,383 adults, mean age 62.6, 72.8 percent women, median follow-up 5.8 years, 2,149 deaths) with activity measured by hip-worn accelerometers found that any activity, at any intensity, went with lower mortality. Against the least active quarter, hazard ratios for total activity were 0.48, 0.34 and 0.27 for the second to fourth quarters; for light-intensity activity 0.60, 0.44 and 0.38; for moderate-to-vigorous activity 0.64, 0.55 and 0.52. The largest risk reduction for light activity was seen at about 375 minutes a day.

In the same harmonised meta-analysis (36,383 adults, eight cohorts), device-measured sedentary time went with higher mortality: hazard ratios of 1.28, 1.71 and 2.63 for the second to fourth quarters against the least sedentary quarter. Risk rose gradually from about 7.5 to 9 hours a day and more steeply above 9.5 hours; 10 and 12 hours of sedentary time a day went with hazard ratios of 1.48 and 2.92.

2160.content: In a single-blind randomised trial, 120 older adults without dementia in Illinois were assigned to supervised walking (building up to 40 minutes, 3 days a week) or to a stretching and toning control for one year. On MRI the walking group's left and right hippocampus grew by 2.12 and 1.97 percent while the control group's shrank by 1.40 and 1.43 percent; the gain was in the anterior hippocampus and went with higher serum BDNF. Caudate and thalamus volumes did not differ. Spatial memory improved in both groups and the walking group did not improve more than the control group, though within the walking group a larger hippocampal gain went with a larger memory gain.

2161.content: Across 2,733 meals eaten ad libitum on four dietary patterns, meal energy intake rose with the meal's energy density, with eating rate and with the share of hyper-palatable foods, consistently on all four diets. Protein content went with higher intake on the ultra-processed and unprocessed diets but not on the minimally processed low-fat or low-carbohydrate diets.

2162.content: A meta-analysis of 83 randomised and non-randomised controlled trials (143 effects, 3,769 people) of exercise training lasting at least 2 weeks found a decrease in C-reactive protein after training (effect size 0.26, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.34). The decrease was larger when body mass index fell (effect size 0.38) and still present without weight loss (effect size 0.19). The authors report the decrease regardless of age or sex.

2163.content: Twenty preterm infants (mean gestational age 31 weeks, mean birth weight 1,280 g, after a mean 20 days in neonatal intensive care) were given body stroking and passive movements of the limbs for three 15-minute periods a day over 10 days in a transitional nursery and compared with 20 control infants. The stroked infants gained 47 percent more weight per day (mean 25 g against 17 g), were more active and alert in sleep-wake observations, scored as more mature on several Brazelton scale clusters, and left hospital 6 days earlier.

2164.content: A Cochrane review of randomised trials of systematic tactile stimulation by human hands in preterm or low birth-weight infants found that massage raised daily weight gain by 5.1 g (95% CI 3.5 to 6.7) and shortened hospital stay by 4.5 days (95% CI 2.4 to 6.5), while gentle still touch without stroking gave no weight benefit (0.2 g a day). The reviewers judged the trials' quality seriously flawed, especially selective reporting, and called the evidence for developmental benefit weak.

2165.content: Ten healthy people ate test meals of apples, apple puree or apple juice, each with 60 g of available carbohydrate. Juice could be consumed eleven times faster than whole apples and four times faster than puree. With eating speed made equal, juice was rated less filling than puree and puree less filling than whole apples. Blood glucose rose to similar levels after all three, but showed a striking rebound fall after juice, and less so after puree, which did not happen after whole apples; insulin rose higher after juice and puree than after apples.

2166.content: In a cross-sectional analysis of 4,757 US adults from NHANES 2003-06 wearing hip accelerometers (average 8.44 hours a day sedentary), more sedentary time went with larger waist, lower HDL cholesterol, and higher C-reactive protein, triglycerides and insulin, after adjusting for moderate-to-vigorous exercise and other factors. Adjusted mean CRP rose from 0.17 mg/dL in the least sedentary quarter to 0.19 mg/dL in the most sedentary (P for trend 0.032). Independently of total sedentary time, more breaks in sitting went with lower CRP and a smaller waist (4.1 cm smaller in the top quarter of breaks).

2167.content: A Cochrane review pooled randomised trials that changed how far food was placed from people. Across 15 comparisons from 12 studies (1,098 participants), food placed farther away was eaten less: standardised mean difference -0.60 (95% CI -0.84 to -0.36), low-certainty evidence. The effect was larger the farther away the food was placed. Most trials were short laboratory studies of snack foods in high-income countries, and 20 of the 24 included studies raised concerns about risk of bias.

In the same Cochrane review, three randomised comparisons (154 participants) that cut the number of food options on offer found people selected far less of the targeted foods (standardised mean difference -1.13, 95% CI -1.90 to -0.37); for consumption, three comparisons (150 participants) gave -0.55 (95% CI -1.27 to 0.18), not statistically clear. Both were rated low certainty.

2168.content: In a cross-sectional study of 1,856 community-dwelling older adults in Kashiwa, Japan, depressive symptoms were scored on the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale. Social engagement measures, including eating alone, were associated with higher scores. People who lived with their families yet ate alone had the highest odds of a high score: odds ratio 5.02 (95% CI 2.5 to 9.9) among the young-old and 2.41 (95% CI 1.2 to 4.8) among the old-old. The associations were stronger in younger and less mentally frail people.

2169.content: In two experiments (77 and 54 participants), a bowl of snacks was placed at random 20, 70 or 140 cm away. In Study 1 fewer people ate any snacks, and less was eaten, when the bowl was at 70 or 140 cm than at 20 cm, with no rise in food craving. Study 2 repeated the result and found that distance changed how much effort people felt it took to get a snack, while it did not change how noticeable the snacks were.

2170.content: A meta-analysis of four randomised trials (159 participants with at least one component of the metabolic syndrome) compared a Paleolithic diet (unprocessed meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit and nuts, no grains, dairy or industrial products) with diets based on national guidelines over up to 6 months. The Paleolithic diet gave larger short-term improvements in waist circumference (-2.38 cm), triglycerides (-0.40 mmol/L), systolic (-3.64 mm Hg) and diastolic (-2.48 mm Hg) blood pressure, HDL cholesterol (+0.12 mmol/L) and fasting blood sugar (-0.16 mmol/L), statistically clear for waist and triglycerides, and 2.69 kg more weight loss. The evidence was rated moderate quality.

2171.content: In the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study, 240,819 US adults aged 50 to 71 without cancer or heart disease reported their television viewing, total sitting and exercise and were followed 8.5 years. Those watching 7 or more hours of television a day had higher all-cause (HR 1.61), cardiovascular (HR 1.85) and cancer (HR 1.22) mortality than those watching under 1 hour, after adjusting for moderate-to-vigorous activity. Among people reporting more than 7 hours a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity, 7 or more hours of television a day still went with higher all-cause (HR 1.47) and cardiovascular (HR 2.00) mortality.

In the same cohort of 240,819 US adults, total sitting time as the participants reported it showed the same pattern as television viewing but more weakly: it was associated with all-cause mortality after adjusting for exercise, while its associations with cardiovascular and cancer mortality were no longer significant once exercise was taken into account.

2172.content: In an Australian randomised trial, 152 adults aged 18 to 65 who reported depression were assigned either to fortnightly food hampers and Mediterranean-diet cooking workshops for 3 months plus fish oil capsules for 6 months, or to fortnightly social groups for 3 months. Only 95 completed the 3-month and 85 the 6-month assessment. At 3 months the diet group scored higher on a Mediterranean diet score, ate more vegetables, fruit, nuts, legumes and wholegrains and fewer unhealthy snacks, and had a greater fall in their depression score (t = -2.24, P = 0.03) and better mental-health quality-of-life scores; the authors report both held at 6 months. A larger rise in diet score, nuts and vegetable diversity went with a larger fall in depression score.

2173.content: A meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (2,300 adults, at least 12 weeks) found that Mediterranean diets lowered high-sensitivity C-reactive protein by 0.98 mg/l (95% CI 0.49 to 1.48), interleukin-6 by 0.42 pg/ml and ICAM-1 by 23.73 ng/ml more than control diets, and raised flow-mediated dilatation by 1.86 percent and adiponectin by 1.69 ug/ml. Heterogeneity for CRP was very high (I squared 91 percent).

2174.content: In the French NutriNet-Sante web cohort, 105,159 adults (79% women, mean age 43) recorded their diet in on average 5.7 repeated 24-hour records, classed by NOVA processing level, and were followed for a median 5.2 years. A 10-point higher share of ultra-processed food in the diet went with a 12% higher rate of cardiovascular disease (1,409 cases; HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.20), 13% for coronary heart disease and 11% for cerebrovascular disease. The links held after adjustment for saturated fat, sodium, sugar, fibre and a healthy dietary pattern.

In the same cohort, a 10-point higher share of unprocessed or minimally processed food in the diet went with a 9% lower rate of overall cardiovascular disease (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.97), and 9% lower rates of coronary and of cerebrovascular disease.

2175.content: In 25,241 UK Biobank adults who reported no leisure-time exercise (mean age 61.8, 56% women), wrist accelerometers worn for a week picked up brief bursts of vigorous movement inside daily life (up to 1 or 2 minutes, such as very fast walking or stair climbing). Over a mean 6.9 years (852 deaths), more such bursts went with lower all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality in a near-linear way. About three bursts a day, the sample median, went with roughly 38 to 40% lower all-cause and cancer mortality and 48 to 49% lower cardiovascular mortality than none; the median of 4.4 minutes a day went with 26 to 30% lower all-cause mortality.

Vigorous activity of any kind among 62,344 UK Biobank participants who did exercise showed an almost identical dose-response with all-cause mortality to the short daily-life bursts among non-exercisers, with a modest difference in the minimum dose (4.8 against 3.4 minutes a day).

2176.content: A meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials (1,847 overweight or obese adults) of aerobic exercise programmes alone, without diet change, mostly 120 to 240 minutes a week at moderate intensity, found a mean weight loss against controls of 1.6 kg at 6 months and 1.7 kg at 12 months, with waist reductions of about 2 cm. The authors conclude that aerobic exercise alone is not an effective weight-loss therapy in these patients.

2177.content: A narrative review found few human studies of ultra-processed food and markers of low-grade inflammation: seven observational studies, all cross-sectional analyses (from 391 to 21,315 people in Brazil, Australia, Portugal, Norway and Italy), and one clinical trial. Most found higher C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, interleukin-8 or a composite inflammation score with more ultra-processed food, but several links held only in women or only in men, or faded after adjusting for body mass index. The authors call the evidence still limited and in some cases discordant.

2178.content: In the Thai Cohort Study, 39,820 adult distance-learning students across Thailand answered a mailed survey in 2013: about 11% ate main meals alone four or more times a week. Those who reported being happy only a little or none of the time in the past four weeks were more likely to eat alone often (adjusted odds ratio 1.54, 95% CI 1.30 to 1.83), most of all women (1.90). Unhappiness in 2009 and 2013 went with eating alone in 2013 in a dose-response pattern (odds ratios 1.29, 1.31 and 1.72). Men, older, unmarried, lower-income, urban people and those in small households ate alone more often.

2179.content: A prevalence survey on an isolated, urbanized Central Pacific island found that 34.4% of people aged 15 and over met the authors' criteria for diabetes: 10.4% had known diabetes and the rest were diagnosed by a plasma glucose of at least 160 mg/100 ml two hours after a 75 g oral glucose load. A further 11.3% had borderline values (140 to 159 mg/100 ml). The authors relate the high prevalence to a diabetic genotype, urbanization and obesity.

2180.content: Diet records from 77 adult Nauruans taken during a diabetes survey showed that nearly all food eaten on the island was imported from Australia, and that calorie intake of men and women was at least twice the amount recommended for Western or developing Pacific populations. The authors describe the way of life as almost completely Westernized, obesity as pronounced, and suggest that high calorie intake with reduced physical activity is a major factor, and that a genetic susceptibility to diabetes may have been unmasked by the change from a traditional to a Western way of life.

2181.content: Among 6,338 Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of lowland Bolivia aged 0 to 90, blood samples from 2004 to 2014 showed most of 22 immune measures raised against US and European reference values, above all immunoglobulins, eosinophils, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, B cells and natural killer cells, while monocytes and basophils were lower and naive CD4 T cells were depleted in older age groups. The authors link the pattern to heavy exposure to helminths, protozoa and other infections from early childhood.

C-reactive protein, the usual marker of low-grade inflammation, was raised in Tsimane children (median 1.21 mg/L against 0.40 mg/L in US NHANES; 94% above the US median) but in adults it was not: median 1.74 mg/L at ages 18 to 50 and 2.30 mg/L at 50 and over, not significantly different from the US medians of 1.80 and 2.50 mg/L. Unlike in the US, Tsimane CRP stayed about level across age groups.

2182.content: In a food exchange, 20 healthy middle-aged African Americans were fed a high-fibre, low-fat African-style diet and 20 rural South Africans a high-fat, low-fibre Western-style diet for two weeks under supervision, each compared with two weeks on their own usual food. At home the Americans ate 2 to 3 times as much animal protein and fat and the Africans more fibre, mostly resistant starch; polyps were found in nine Americans and no Africans. After the swap, colonic proliferation fell in the Americans below the Africans' baseline and rose in the Africans above the Americans' baseline, and mucosal inflammation markers (intraepithelial lymphocytes, lamina propria macrophages) rose in the Africans and fell in the Americans, along with reciprocal shifts in butyrate production and secondary bile acids.

2183.content: Fecal, oral and skin samples from 34 members (aged about 4 to 50) of a Yanomami village in the Venezuelan Amazon with no documented earlier contact with Western people held the highest bacterial diversity and diversity of genetic functions recorded in any human group. Fecal and skin diversity was significantly higher than in US subjects, and fecal diversity higher than in partly westernized Guahibo Amerindians and in Malawians. The villagers ate wild bananas, fruits, plantain, palm hearts and cassava and hunted small game. Even with no known antibiotic exposure their bacteria carried functional antibiotic resistance genes.

2184.content: Dietler's review of two decades of anthropological and archaeological work describes alcohol as the most widely used psychoactive agent in the world and as an important social, economic, political and religious artifact for millennia. He reports that the field has moved away from the earlier functionalist emphasis on drinking as socially integrative, and now studies drinking through practice, politics and gender, and alcohol as a commodity in colonial and postcolonial struggles over state power and household authority.

2185.content: Eaton estimates that ancestral humans ate perhaps 100 g of fibre a day or more. Wild plant foods eaten by recent hunter-gatherers contain about 133 g of dietary fibre per kg against 42 g per kg for commercial produce, and a calculation on a 50:50 animal to plant subsistence ratio (revised from the 35:65 ratio used in 1985) gives an average total fibre intake of over 100 g a day, against US recommended intakes of 25 to 38 g a day, which are about twice the current median American intake. Phytate content was minimal, and the fibre was more fermentable than cereal fibre.

2186.content: Comparing C-reactive protein in the Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of Bolivia with people in the United States, Gurven and colleagues found high CRP significantly more common among the Tsimane up to middle age; by age 35 Tsimane had spent more years with high CRP than Americans had by age 55. They read the strong acute-phase response as needed for survival under high infection, and propose that reduced lifetime infection and inflammation partly explain longer modern lifespans.

2187.content: Using a phylogenetic model of 69 primate species, Jaeggi and colleagues estimated that humans should spend about 4% of daytime grooming (95% credible interval 0.07% to 14%). Daytime behavioural scans (mean 23,514 per society) among the Maya, Pume, Sanoma, Tsimane, Yanomamo and Ye'kwana found allo-grooming (removing parasites, dirt or dead skin from another person) took only 0.8% of time, lower than 89% of the expected values. Time on any hygiene (3.0%) and on conversation (7.3%) fell within the range expected for a primate.

2188.content: Over a year, Koster recorded every gift of meat between the 25 households (about 200 people) of Arang Dak, a Mayangna and Miskito horticulturalist community in lowland Nicaragua, about 5.5 gifts a year per pair of households. Pairs of households that gave each other more than their general giving and receiving tendencies would suggest almost always had it returned (dyadic reciprocity correlation 0.95), and reciprocal sharing stayed considerable after adjusting for other factors. At the same time some households were net givers and others net receivers (generalized reciprocity -0.48): those who harvested more game and owned more pigs gave more, wealthier households received less, and the two pastors' households received more.

In the same community, meat went more to close kin (most of all between mother and offspring households, then full siblings and father-offspring) but the kin effect faded by the level of cousins. Households living farther apart gave each other less (10% more distance, about 6.3% fewer gifts), and households that spent more time together exchanged more meat even after adjusting for kinship and distance.

2189.content: Analysing which Yanomamo men killed together (co-unokais), Macfarlan and colleagues found that lethal coalitions were usually made of men from the same population but from different villages and patrilines, close in age and often maternal half-first cousins. Men who had killed together more often, and who were more closely related, were more likely to live in the same village later in life, and joint killers were more likely to engage in marriage exchange. The authors read this as support for a strategic alliance model over the fraternal interest group model in which coalitions are kin groups of co-resident men, as in chimpanzee border patrols.

2190.content: In 52 adults in the southeastern Ecuadorian Amazon, where infectious disease remains common, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein was measured four times at weekly intervals. Median CRP was 0.52 mg/L. About 34.6% had CRP above 3 mg/L at one sampling, but nobody had it above 3 mg/L at two or more, and CRP showed little stable difference between individuals. Applying current guidelines for chronic inflammation, the authors found not a single case of 'high risk' CRP, a pattern unlike that in post-transition populations, where differences in CRP between people are stable over time.

2191.content: Among 72 Yanomami (hunter-gatherer-gardeners with almost no Western contact) and 83 neighbouring Yekwana (reached by missions and an airstrip that bring medicine, some processed food and salt), aged 1 to 60 and measured once in 2015 to 2016 in the Venezuelan rainforest, systolic blood pressure did not rise with age among the Yanomami (slope 0.00 mm Hg per year, SE 0.07) and rose 0.25 mm Hg per year among the Yekwana. Mean systolic pressure was 95.4 against 104.0 mm Hg. The gap between the groups was 5.8 mm Hg at age 10 and 15.9 mm Hg at age 50, and the steeper slope among the Yekwana was already present between ages 1 and 20. For comparison the authors give US slopes of about 1.5 to 1.9 mm Hg per year in children and 0.6 in adults.

2192.content: Among the Yanomamo of the rainforest of northern Brazil and southern Venezuela, who use no salt in their diet, blood pressure rose from the first to the second decade of life and then did not rise systematically with age, unlike in Western populations. In 24-hour urine collections from adult men, sodium excretion averaged 1 mEq (SD 1.5). Plasma renin activity and aldosterone excretion were high, at the levels Western subjects reach when put briefly on a 10 mEq sodium diet; the authors read these levels as probably the human norm for much of evolution.

2193.content: 44 Hadza adults (20 men, 24 women) from two camps in northern Tanzania wore GPS units from dawn to dusk over four two-week periods in 2009 to 2011, in rainy and dry seasons. Of 342 foraging bouts (the longest of each person-day), 46.3% fit a truncated power law and 1.6% a power law, the step-length pattern called a Levy walk, in which many short moves are broken by rare long ones; nearly all the rest fit composite Brownian walks, and 0.6% simple Brownian walks. Women's bouts were Levy walks more often than men's (56.7% against 36.6%), and the pattern held across camps and across foods sought, from game and honey to tubers and berries.

2194.content: Adults of the Sierra Madre in Mexico were examined with oral glucose tolerance tests. After adjusting for age and sex, 6.9% of Pima Indians there had type 2 diabetes, against 38% of Pima Indians in Arizona and 2.6% of non-Pima Mexicans living nearby. Obesity was much less common among the Mexican Pima (7% of men, 20% of women) than among the Arizona Pima, and physical activity was much higher in both Mexican groups. DNA typing showed the two Pima groups to be genetically close relative to other Native Americans.

2195.content: Using plant-to-animal subsistence ratios, the authors calculated the carbohydrate share of 229 hunter-gatherer diets worldwide: about 3% to 50% of total energy, with median and mode at 16% to 22%. Between 11 and 40 degrees of latitude the share was 30% to 35%; from 41 degrees to beyond 60 degrees it fell from about 20% to 9% or less. Foragers of deserts and tropical grasslands ate the most carbohydrate (about 29% to 34%), and those of tundra and northern coniferous forest 15% or less.
The authors report that whatever the local environment, the carbohydrate share of most of the 229 hunter-gatherer diets was markedly lower than the amounts currently recommended for healthy humans.

2196.content: Testart argues that where hunter-gatherers store food on a large scale, reserves become insurance for the future and lower the advantages of sharing: to meet a shortage people rely more on their food stocks than on the help of others, and he expects food sharing to fall into disuse as intensive storage develops. Among nomadic non-storing foragers such as the San, he writes, a universal rule requires that the products of hunting, and to a lesser extent of gathering, be shared by all, and storage carries the immoral connotation of hoarding.

From the ethnographic record, Testart identifies the hunter-gatherers that practised intensive seasonal storage, chiefly the Northwest Coast Indians, peoples of south-eastern Siberia and northern Japan (Ainu, Gilyaks, Itelmens) and the California Indians, living on stored salmon or acorns. All of them lived in permanent villages for most of the year, at population densities far above those usual for hunter-gatherers, and all showed socioeconomic inequalities; storing hunter-gatherers were absent, with one possible exception, from deserts and tropical lands.

2197.content: Reviewing traumatic injuries in ancient human skeletons, Walker reports that interpersonal violence, especially among men, has been common throughout the history of the species: cannibalism seems to have been widespread, mass killings, homicides and assault injuries are well documented in both the Old and New Worlds, and no form of social organisation, mode of production or environmental setting appears to have stayed free of interpersonal violence for long.

2198.content: Among the Ache of eastern Paraguay, the authors split hunting ability into finding prey and the probability of a kill once prey is met, for the main prey species. Hunting outcomes reached their peaks surprisingly late in life, significantly after the peak in strength, which the authors read as evidence that skill learning is central to the human foraging niche.

2199.content: In a food-sharing network of households in a predominantly Dolgan hunting community in the Taimyr Autonomous Okrug of northern Russia, a kinship link between nuclear families was the variable most strongly associated with which households shared meals with which, and the summed number of hunters in a pair of households also accounted for much of the variation. Reciprocal meal sharing took place in 26 of 84 host-guest household pairs, and within these pairs its frequency rose with average household relatedness.

2200.content: In the Whitehall II prospective cohort of British civil servants (6,895 men and 3,413 women aged 35 to 55, mean follow-up 5.3 years), an imbalance between personal efforts (competitiveness, work-related overcommitment, hostility) and rewards (poor promotion prospects, a blocked career) went with a 2.15-fold higher risk of newly reported coronary heart disease. Low job control was strongly associated with new disease, with odds ratios of 2.38 for control as rated by the workers themselves and 1.56 for control as assessed from outside, while job strain and high job demands were not related to it. The work measures were adjusted for each other, employment grade, negative affectivity and coronary risk factors.

2201.content: Among Chicago neighbourhoods in 1988 to 1993, homicide rates varied more than 100-fold and male life expectancy at birth, with homicide deaths removed, ranged from 54 to 77 years. This life expectancy was highly correlated with homicide rates; a measure of economic inequality added significant further prediction of the homicide rate, while median household income did not. Where life expectancy was lower, women had their children earlier, though by age 30 the neighbourhood no longer made a difference to age-specific fertility.

2202.content: In an experiment with 96 five-year-old children (24 per condition), each child played a sticker game either alone or watched by an unfamiliar same-sex child from another group of the same day-care centre, and could take a sticker meant for an absent, anonymous next child or leave one for that child. Watched children stole in 4% of trials against 24% when alone (p = .02, one-tailed), and helped in 28% of trials against 11% (a trend, p = .07).

In the same paper, 14 captive chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) at a research centre in Leipzig could pull a rope that took food away from, or brought food to, a low-ranking female groupmate, either alone or watched by a high-ranking adult male. Being watched made no difference: they stole in 20% of trials watched against 23% alone, and helped in 34% against 36%.

2203.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of Bolivia (871 households in 40 communities, community wealth Gini 0.15 to 0.53), lower household wealth and greater community inequality were both associated with higher blood pressure, and inequality with more respiratory illness (odds ratio 1.36). The authors' model gives systolic pressure 4.0 mm Hg and diastolic 3.7 mm Hg higher in the most unequal than in the most equal communities, mainly in men, which they equate to as much as 40 years of age-related blood pressure rise among the Tsimane.

In the same Tsimane study, greater community inequality was, against the authors' prediction, largely associated with fewer stressors and fewer psychological or social problems, most clearly fewer non-social problems such as food insecurity, illness or debt, and with lower odds of what the authors call other infections (odds ratio 0.54). Depressive symptom scores on an adapted 18-item interview and the other psychosocial measures did not carry the links between wealth and health.

2204.content: In a cross-sectional ecological study of 39 US states, income inequality was strongly correlated with lower per capita membership in voluntary groups (r = -0.46) and with lack of social trust (r = 0.76), both measured from General Social Survey items. Both social trust and group membership were associated with 1990 age-standardised total mortality and with death rates from coronary heart disease and cancer and with infant mortality.

2205.content: A random-effects meta-analysis of multilevel studies that adjusted for age, sex and individual socioeconomic status (nine cohort studies with 59,509,857 people; 19 cross-sectional studies with 1,280,211 people) found a relative risk of death of 1.08 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.10) and an odds ratio of poor self-rated health of 1.04 (1.02 to 1.06) for each 0.05 rise in the Gini coefficient of income in the area where people lived.

In meta-regressions of the same studies, the association between income inequality and mortality was stronger in cohort studies where the Gini was 0.3 or above (relative risk 1.09, 1.07 to 1.12, five studies) than below 0.3 (1.02, 0.97 to 1.07, four studies), and associations were also stronger with data after 1990, longer follow-up and time lags between inequality and outcome. Analyses that adjusted for unmeasured regional characteristics showed a weaker association.

2206.content: A systematic review of 26 studies of income inequality and depression, mostly from high-income countries, found that 16 studies (61.5 percent) reported a significant positive relationship between income inequality and depression as each study measured it, six reported none and one a negative relationship; five of the six longitudinal studies reported a positive relationship. In a meta-analysis of 12 studies with populations split into higher and lower inequality, the pooled risk ratio for depression, scored or diagnosed on each study's own instrument, was 1.19 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.31), with very high heterogeneity (I2 98 percent).

Of the seven studies in the review that split their analysis by absolute income, two found a significant link between income inequality and depression as measured only among low-income participants, and two found the effect strongest among low-income individuals. Of five studies that split by gender, three found the association in women only.

2207.content: In three online experiments with US Amazon Mechanical Turk workers (n = 811 in all), participants shown a more unequal spread of earlier players' winnings in a gambling game made riskier gambles. In study 1 (n = 221) the high-inequality group stated a higher minimum win they needed to feel satisfied ($0.76 against $0.61) and chose gambles with a higher probability of losing (0.51 against 0.44). In study 3, participants who chose to look mostly at the top earners gambled far more riskily on high-inequality trials (mean 81.7 against 58.9), while those who looked mostly at the bottom took less risk.

Across the 50 US states, an index of Google searches for risky ways to get money (payday loans, lottery, win money, no down payment) was higher where the income Gini coefficient was higher (r = 0.57), and the link held when median income, population and population density were controlled (beta 0.40). Inequality at the top of the distribution (the 90/50 income ratio) went with these searches more than inequality at the bottom, and the association ran partly through searches for status goods.

2208.content: A systematic review of 27 studies and a random-effects meta-analysis of nine, which required mental health problems scored on standardised instruments for individuals and income inequality measured for their area, found small pooled associations between greater income inequality and any mental health problem as measured (Cohen's d 0.06, 95% CI 0.015 to 0.10) and depressive disorders as diagnosed or scored (d 0.12, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.20). Common mental disorders as scored showed no association (d -0.04, not significant), and when inequality was entered as a continuous predictor the pooled effect was not significant (d 0.07, p 0.09). About 89 percent of the variation was heterogeneity between studies, and Egger's test indicated small-study bias.

2209.content: In a giving game set up to rule out direct reciprocity, Wedekind and Milinski found that donations were more frequent to receivers who had been generous to others in earlier rounds; the authors conclude that image scoring, a record of how a person is viewed by the group, promotes cooperation where direct return is unlikely.

2210.content: A close replication of Wedekind and Milinski (2000), with six groups of ten participants playing a donation game in which partners were anonymous and each player saw the other's past generosity, found that participants gave significantly more money to partners with higher image scores than to partners with lower ones.

2211.content: In a field experiment with 1,408 customers of a California electric utility living in homeowners associations, residents signed up for a blackout-prevention programme on sheets posted near their mailboxes. Where the sheet showed each signer's name and unit to neighbours, 8.8 percent joined against 3.0 percent where sign-up was anonymous, nearly three times as many; the observability effect was larger than that of the $25 payment the utility had used before.

In the same experiment the effect of being seen held where neighbours meet and stay. In apartment buildings, where residents share public spaces, 11.4 percent joined with named sign-up against 4.8 percent anonymously (n = 582), while in row houses and single homes the difference was small and not significant (3.8 against 2.4 percent, n = 826). Among owners 9.9 against 2.4 percent joined (n = 1,015), among renters, who move more, 5.9 against 4.5 percent (not significant, n = 393). When the materials dropped the framing of the programme as a public good (1,005 more customers), the effect of being seen was much smaller.

2212.content: Among Martu hunters, cooperative hunting gave higher returns only to poorer hunters and left better hunters worse off, yet better hunters cooperated as often as poorer ones. Better hunters did not pair up more with kin and gained no extra consumption from acquiring more: they shared a larger share of their harvest, so that better and worse hunters, cooperators and solitary hunters all ate the same amount in the end. The authors propose that cooperation by better hunters is a costly signal of commitment to the public interest that builds trust and strong social networks, particularly among women, who cooperate more than men.

2213.content: Reviewing studies that tested whether striving for cultural goals is a proximate means to high reproductive success, Borgerhoff Mulder reports data from the Kipsigis of Kenya that she calls a robust demonstration that wealth enhances a man's reproductive success. She also discusses the problem of interpreting such studies in rapidly changing modern environments.

2214.content: Bowles, Smith and Borgerhoff Mulder write that sustained economic inequality generally leaves archaeological signatures (grave goods, storage, dwellings, ceremonial objects, signs of nutrition), and that the absence of these suggests that before about 24,000 years ago, and possibly much more recently, most humans lived in foraging bands with little economic difference between families. Substantial inequality became common in many, far from all, populations only after plants and animals were domesticated, except among groups at especially rich fishing and hunting sites. They propose that the degree to which wealth passes from parents to children is the key to how far wealth differences between families build up over time.

2215.content: Using more than 40 measures of embodied, material and relational wealth from 21 small-scale societies, the authors estimated how closely children's wealth tracks their parents' (the transmission coefficient b). Weighted by how much each kind of wealth matters in each way of life, transmission was modest among hunter-gatherers (b 0.19) and horticulturalists (0.18) and about twice as high among farmers (0.36) and herders (0.43). Material wealth (land, livestock) was passed on most strongly (average b 0.37, against 0.12 for embodied wealth such as strength and skill), and in herding and farming societies material wealth mattered most and passed on at b 0.61, against 0.13 among hunter-gatherers and horticulturalists. The degree of transmission correlated with wealth inequality.

2216.content: Falk and Hildebolt related war deaths to actual population size in 11 chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) communities, 24 human non-state societies, and the 19 and 22 countries that fought in World War I and World War II. Mean yearly battle deaths as a percentage of the population fell as population size rose, in chimpanzees and in humans, which the authors read as greater vulnerability of small populations rather than greater violence. The absolute number of mean yearly war deaths rose superlinearly, and almost identically, with population size across human groups, though not in chimpanzees. They conclude that people from non-states are neither more nor less violent than people from states, and that humans evolved to be more violent than chimpanzees.

2217.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of the Bolivian Amazon, interviewed on daily production and food sharing from 2005 to 2009 (1,245 individuals in 11 villages; wealth and income for 119 households in nine villages), household wealth and income were not associated with how much of a household's food came from others or with reciprocal sharing. Wealthier households gave a larger percentage of the food they produced to other households and had more food and labour sharing partners. Households shared food with 2.5 other households on average and received from 2.3.

Across the nine Tsimane villages, the average income Gini coefficient was 0.42, lower than the 0.59 reported for Bolivia in 2001. Villages with higher mean income showed less reciprocal (contingent) food sharing, while income inequality was greater in villages with broader sharing, more households and greater distance from the market town, and wealth inequality was greater in villages with higher giving intensity and in larger villages.

2218.content: Haas and Piscitelli argue that researchers who found the archaeological record lacking on the origins of war turned to historical ethnographies of hunter-gatherers, which show groups already living inside a dense, colonial world of nation states. They state that there is extremely limited empirical evidence of any warfare among past hunters and gatherers, and that the claim of warfare being rampant among almost all hunter-gatherers rests on those ethnographies.

2219.content: In a standardised study of 10,079 men and women aged 20 to 59 from 52 centres around the world, 24-hour urinary sodium excretion ranged from 0.2 mmol a day among Yanomamo Indians in Brazil to 242 mmol a day in north China. Within centres, sodium excretion was significantly related to blood pressure in individuals. Four centres had very low sodium excretion, low blood pressure, and little or no rise of blood pressure with age.

Across the other 48 Intersalt centres, population sodium excretion was significantly related to how steeply blood pressure rose with age, though not to median blood pressure or to the share of people with high blood pressure. Potassium excretion went with lower blood pressure in individuals after adjustment, with no consistent association across centres; body mass index and heavy alcohol intake had strong independent relations with blood pressure.

2220.content: In a Quechua agropastoral community of 24 households in highland Peru (about 4,400 m, eight months of fieldwork in 2010 and 2011), households that gave more time to collective work on communal herds, fields and buildings had heads whom fellow villagers named more often as reliable and hardworking in that work, and also as generally generous, influential and respected, controlling for age, health and other factors. Generosity was the reputation most strongly tied to contributions.

In the same village, household heads with higher total reputation scores received agricultural help from more households (network indegree), controlling for distance, dependency, herd size and years in the community; the model explained 80 percent of the variance. In a mediation analysis, contributions to collective work went with larger support networks only through reputation. Households with more helpers had fewer illness symptoms on average, in a model that was only marginally significant (P < 0.1). Kinship was not correlated with the key variables.

2221.content: Among the Turkana, nomadic herders of northern Kenya with no chiefs or formal courts, a representative sample of 88 recent raids (interviews with participants) showed raiding parties of several hundred warriors drawn from many settlements, age groups and territorial sections, who were not kin or day-to-day companions. Desertion was known of in at least 43% of force raids and cowardice in combat in 45%. In 47% of force raids with a reported desertion and 67% with reported cowardice, at least one offender was sanctioned: first by criticism from age-mates, women and seniors, and, where the community agreed it was deserved, by being tied and beaten by his age-mates and fined an animal. Members of the offender's age group carried out the punishment even when they had not been on the raid.

In the same Turkana sample, killing inside the group was rare: homicide or other internal violence accounted for about 1% of adult male deaths within nomadic settlements, against about 50% of adult male deaths from warfare with other ethnic groups. Twenty percent of all male deaths, infants and children included, came from warfare (survivorship of siblings and offspring of 107 men and 121 women). In a vignette study, 24 men of one territorial section approved of raiding another ethnic group and wanted warriors who raided a different Turkana section criticised and punished, even though their own section gained the cattle.

2222.content: Comparing standardised linear selection gradients (b, the change in relative reproductive success per standard deviation of the trait) across 11 human samples, the authors found the gradient on male wealth weakest in three contemporary industrial samples (US, Sweden, Britain; b 0.10 to 0.17, mean 0.13), higher in three historical European and European-descended farming samples (mean 0.24), and highest among Kipsigis farmers and Mukogodo herders of Kenya, both polygynous (mean 0.63). For three hunter-gatherer samples, among them the Ache and the Hadza, where little wealth is stored, gradients on hunting ability ranged from 0.22 to 0.36 (mean 0.30). Even the industrial gradients sat near the middle of the gradients reported from field studies of other species.

In the British National Child Development Study (people born in 1958, followed to age 46 in 2004; analysis of several thousand men and women), men with higher income had more children, and this came from low-income men being more often childless; among men who had children, income made no difference to how many. For women the association went the other way: higher personal income went with fewer children and more childlessness.

2223.content: Across 295 societies with known population (P) and war group size (W) and 430 conflicts with known war group size and casualties (C), war group size rose with population along a sublinear power law, so the share of a population that fights falls as populations grow. Casualties rose faster than war group size. After allowing for scale, the scaling exponent for conflict investment was the same for small-scale societies and states (X = 0.96 for both), and comparing 18 small-scale societies in conflict with 133 twentieth and twenty-first century states in conflict or with conscription found no significant difference in conflict investment (t test, P = 0.14) or in conflict lethality.

2224.content: Abstract only. In two behavioural allocation games played by 591 people (35,400 observations) in eight communities (inland and coastal Tanna, Vanuatu; Yasawa and Lovu, Fiji; Pesqueiro, Brazil; Pointe aux Piments, Mauritius; the Tyva Republic, Siberia; and Hadzaland, Tanzania), the more punitive and knowing participants rated their moralistic gods, the more coins they allocated to geographically distant strangers of their own religion, relative to themselves and to local co-religionists, holding a range of other variables constant.

2225.content: Abstract only. Among BaYaka foragers of Congo (219 people in four camps, reported uses of 33 plants), the authors measured which pairs of people reported the same plant uses. Medicinal plant knowledge was shared mainly between spouses and between biological and affinal kin. Knowledge of plant uses for foraging and for social norms and beliefs was shared more widely among campmates whether related or not, and the authors link it to camp-wide cooperative activities. Most medicinal plants named have known bioactive properties, and some were positively associated with children's body mass index.

2226.content: Among Agta hunter-gatherers of the Philippines, 290 adults in 18 camps played a sharing game (dividing rice tokens between themselves and photographed campmates) and a taking game. In the 11 camps with repeated residence counts over at least two months, camp stability (1 = no change in who lived there, 0 = complete change) ranged from 0.12 to 0.79 (mean 0.51). Adults in more stable camps kept less rice for themselves and took less from others: a camp with no change in composition was estimated to give 67.7 percentage points more than one that changed completely, while involvement in rice harvesting added 20.1 points.

In observed food sharing (daily household interviews over 103 days in six Agta camps), three camps showed significant reciprocity between households and three did not. The reciprocal camps were more stable (mean stability 0.57 against 0.28) and larger (mean 16.7 against 8.3 families). Kin effects were also stronger in the reciprocal camps. People from the reciprocal camps kept less rice in the sharing game (68.2% against 90.5%) and took less in the taking game (66.5% against 87.9%).

2227.content: In the same sharing game among Agta hunter-gatherers (290 players, 18 camps, 1,312 possible recipient pairs, 492 of whom received rice), players gave more often to primary kin (odds ratio 4.01) and distant kin (1.78), and to campmates who had given to them (1.68). They gave more often to less cooperative campmates: a 2 standard deviation drop in the recipient's own giving went with about 50% higher odds of receiving (odds ratio 1.58), and there was no sign of cooperators preferring cooperators. A composite measure of need (dependent children, no stored rice, age over a threshold) went with about twice the odds of receiving per unit (odds ratio 2.08), mostly through giving to older people.

Asked why they chose each recipient (1,001 answers), Agta players most often named kinship (over 40% of reasons, about a quarter genetic kin and a sixth in-laws). About 25% of reasons were need: old age, pregnancy, many children, weakness, inability to work, having no food, or simply to help. About one in ten referred to reciprocity between giver and receiver.

2228.content: Strontium isotope ratios of 27 ostrich eggshell beads from two rock shelters in highland Lesotho (Melikane and Sehonghong), spanning about 33,000 years to the recent past, show that the beads were made from eggs laid outside the highlands, where ostriches do not live. 78% (21 beads) came from at least 109 km away, 22% (6) from at least 164 km, and 11% (3) from at least 326 km; these are minimum distances, and most beads match rock units up to more than 1,000 km away. The authors read the beads as gifts in long-distance exchange networks like Ju/'hoansi hxaro, present since about 33,000 years ago.

2229.content: Abstract only. In a driving simulator experiment, drivers high and low in trait driving anger were randomly assigned to drive as anonymous or identifiable drivers and to see aggressive or neutral stimuli. Participants drove more aggressively when anonymous (d = 0.28) and when shown aggressive stimuli (d = 0.05); men drove more aggressively than women (d = 0.06). Trait driving anger showed no main or interaction effect.

2230.content: Searching the Human Relations Area Files Probability Sample (one randomly chosen well-documented culture from each of 60 world culture areas) for paragraphs on suicide, the authors found suicidal behaviour, as cases or as a cultural model, in 53 of the 60 cultures, from 213 documents (1704 to 2000, median 1963), yielding 474 coded accounts. Hunter-gatherers, horticulturalists, pastoralists and intensive farmers were all represented, and six of seven inhabited continental regions (all but Australia). Most accounts were completed suicides (84.6%), almost all by one person acting alone.

Coding the 474 accounts against two evolutionary models, the authors found little support for the inclusive fitness model (suicide by people who are a burden on kin): 22.8% of records had any supporting evidence, and only 5.7% of cultures had evidence that a completed suicide improved outcomes for others. They found wide support for the bargaining model (suicidal behaviour as a costly signal of need in a conflict with others): 80.6% of records had evidence for at least one of its variables, and a threat to the person's fitness, powerlessness and conflict with social partners were present in 88.7%, 84.9% and 77.4% of cultures. Of 84 accounts of non-lethal attempts, 30 reported a gain for the person, often in disputes over marriage, punishment or abuse.

In the same 474 ethnographic accounts of suicide, the authors coded evidence of mental illness in only about 10% of records, and about 3% appeared to involve what they classified as affective disorders (depression and anxiety); close to half of those reported were of unknown kind. They report little evidence either for or against mental illness as a factor.

2231.content: Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania (51 adults in 2013, 66 in 2014) heard picture stories in which an item fell into a pot of honey or broth and was taken out again. After hyena meat, a cough or poison, only 4 to 10% said they would still eat the honey and 6 to 12% the broth; after a harmless bead, 36 to 44% would. Most gave sickness as the reason after the cough (94% for honey). Among Tannese subsistence farmers of Vanuatu (20 children aged 6 to 11, 21 adolescents, 22 adults), yams touched by faeces, blood, a fly or a cough were rejected far more than yams touched by a leaf, stone, bead or sea water, with no difference by age group.

2232.content: In a subsample of social network site users drawn from representative survey data in South Korea, the authors classed ties on the sites as social (reciprocal, between a user and friends) or parasocial (following a celebrity who is not aware of the user). Relying more on parasocial ties went with more loneliness and less interpersonal distrust; relying more on reciprocal ties went with less loneliness and more trust. Relying more on either kind went with more reported social network site addiction.

2233.content: In the UK Biobank cohort (466,901 adults aged 40 to 69 at baseline in 2007 to 2010, mean follow-up 6.5 years, 11,593 deaths), people scored as socially isolated (at least two of: living alone, friends or family visiting less than once a month, no weekly leisure or social activity) had a hazard ratio for death from any cause of 1.73 after adjustment for age, sex, ethnic origin and chronic disease, and 1.26 after further adjustment for socioeconomic factors, health behaviours, depressive symptoms, biological factors, cognitive performance and self-rated health. The added factors accounted for 64% of the excess risk, and over a third remained. Isolated people also died more often of cancers (sub-hazard ratio 2.06) and circulatory disease (1.68).

In the same cohort, people classed as lonely (often feeling lonely and never or almost never able to confide in someone close) had a hazard ratio for death of 1.38 after minimal adjustment, which fell to 0.99 after full adjustment; depressive symptoms and self-rated health carried most of it. With isolation and loneliness in one model, only isolation went with death (hazard ratio 1.27).

2234.content: In a randomised field experiment in Boston suburbs that were almost wholly Anglo-white, pairs of Spanish-speaking confederates waited on commuter rail platforms at the same time every weekday for up to 10 working days; one train time of each matched pair at nine stations was randomly treated and the other left alone. Among 109 commuters surveyed before and after, those exposed moved toward more exclusionary answers than controls on admitting fewer immigrants from Mexico (0.33 SD) and on not letting undocumented immigrants stay (0.20 SD); the shift on making English the official language (0.08 SD) was not significant.

In the same experiment, commuters randomly surveyed after 3 days of exposure had shifted further toward exclusion than those surveyed after 10 days (55 and 54 people; differences not significant, P 0.09 to 0.31), and in the last days the confederates reported that commuters had begun to recognise them, smile and greet them.

2235.content: In a laboratory experiment, 53 three-person groups made up either of friends or of acquaintances each did a decision-making task and a motor task. Friendship groups performed significantly better than acquaintance groups on both tasks; in the authors' mediation analysis the advantage ran through greater group commitment and cooperation, and on the motor task through positive communication.

2236.content: In 59 premenopausal women studied before and after a session of warm contact with their husband or partner ending in hugs, higher plasma oxytocin before the contact went with lower blood pressure and heart rate, and oxytocin met the authors' criteria for a partial mediator of the lower resting blood pressure in women who reported more frequent partner hugs. Oxytocin during a later stress task was unrelated to hugs or blood pressure, and menstrual cycle phase did not affect oxytocin.

2237.content: A registered systematic review (CRD42014010225) found 23 papers from 16 longitudinal cohorts in high-income countries (181,006 adults, 4,628 coronary heart disease and 3,002 stroke events, follow-up 3 to 21 years). Pooling 11 coronary heart disease studies and 9 stroke samples, poor social relationships (loneliness, social isolation or both) went with a 29% higher risk of new coronary heart disease (pooled relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.59) and a 32% higher risk of stroke (1.32, 1.04 to 1.68). Estimates did not differ between loneliness and isolation or by gender.

2238.content: Using four nationally representative US longitudinal samples (Add Health, ages 12 to 32; MIDUS, 25 to 64; HRS, 50 to 98; NSHAP, 57 to 91), the authors related earlier social integration, support and strain to later C-reactive protein, blood pressure, waist circumference and body mass index. More social integration went with lower odds of high inflammation in adolescence (odds ratio 0.74, adjusted for age, sex and race) and late adulthood (HRS 0.86, NSHAP 0.59). In Add Health, social isolation went with high inflammation about as strongly as physical inactivity did (odds ratios 1.27 and 1.21).

In the NSHAP sample of US adults aged 57 to 91, followed over about 6 years with blood pressure measured at both waves, social isolation at baseline went with higher odds of developing hypertension (odds ratio 2.42), larger than the odds ratio for diabetes in the same model (1.49).

2239.content: Daily diaries and salivary cortisol were collected from 42 couples over 21 days timed around a naturally occurring separation of 4 to 7 days, such as work travel. From before the separation to the separation, and from the separation to the reunion, the authors found significant changes in the quality of the partners' interactions, positive and negative affect, sleeping problems, subjective stress, physical symptoms and cortisol. The changes were generally larger in the partner who stayed home, in partners scoring high on attachment anxiety and in partners who had less contact during the separation, and did not depend on relationship length, satisfaction, how often the couple separated or children at home.

2240.content: In the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study, 17,612 men and 19,581 women aged 65 or over who scored below 5 on the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale in 2010 were followed to 2013. After adjustment for income, education, health, nutrition, social support, social participation, meeting friends, work and marital status, men living alone who usually ate alone had 2.36 times the rate of a new score of 5 or more compared with men living alone who ate with others; among men living with others, eating alone made no difference (1.03). Women who ate alone had rate ratios of 1.31 if living alone and 1.21 if living with others.

2241.content: Students on three dormitory floors were surveyed and their social behaviour and use of space observed over 3 months: a long-corridor floor where 40 residents shared space, a short-corridor floor where 20 did, and a long-corridor floor altered by an architectural intervention so that 20 residents shared space. The three groups were comparable at the start. Over time the 40-resident floor reported more crowding and more social problems in the residence, while the short-corridor floor and the altered long-corridor floor reported fewer of these problems.

2242.content: A registered dose-response meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42018095507) of 15 prospective cohort studies (191,130 adults, 2,110,588 person-years; each with at least 3,000 people and 3 years of follow-up) related self-reported physical activity to later depression as defined by the studies: a reported physician diagnosis, a registry or interview diagnosis, or a score above a validated cutoff on a screening scale. Against adults reporting no activity, those at half the recommended volume (4.4 marginal MET-hours a week) had 18% lower risk and those at the recommended volume (8.8, equal to 2.5 hours a week of brisk walking) had 25% lower risk, with little further difference and more uncertainty above that. Heterogeneity was large (I2 74%).

2243.content: A systematic search of PubMed (1975 to July 2003) for randomised controlled trials of light therapy in people diagnosed with mood disorders found that only 13 percent of studies met the inclusion criteria. In the meta-analyses, depression symptom scores fell with bright light treatment in seasonal affective disorder as the trials defined it (8 studies, effect size 0.84, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.08), with dawn simulation in seasonal affective disorder (5 studies, effect size 0.73, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.08) and with bright light in patients diagnosed with nonseasonal depression (3 studies, effect size 0.53, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.89). Bright light added to antidepressant drugs in nonseasonal depression showed no effect on symptom scores (5 studies, effect size -0.01, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.34). The authors state the effect sizes equal those in most antidepressant drug trials.

2244.content: In a laboratory study at Northwestern University, 20 healthy young adults (mean age about 27) were randomised to two nights of sleep in dim light (under 3 lux) or to one dim night followed by one night with overhead room light at 100 lux. After the lit night, heart rate during sleep was higher and heart rate variability shifted toward sympathetic balance, sleep held more stage N2 and less slow wave and REM sleep, and next-morning insulin resistance rose: HOMA-IR went up about 15 percent against a fall of about 4 percent in the dim group (P = 0.018), and the early insulin response in a glucose test was higher. Melatonin levels did not differ between the groups.

2245.content: Linking over 7 million nighttime sleep records from wristband devices in 68 countries (2015 to 2017) to local weather, and comparing each person with themselves across nights, the authors found that warmer nights shortened measured sleep, mainly by delaying sleep onset. Nights with a minimum above 25 degrees C cut sleep by just over 7 minutes against nights of 5 to 10 degrees C, delayed sleep onset by about 6 minutes, advanced waking by about 2.5 minutes, and raised the chance of sleeping under 7 hours by 3.5 percentage points. Daytime naps did not make up the loss, and the authors found no sign of short-term acclimatisation.

In the same wearable-device data, the sleep lost per 1 degree C of warmer night was nearly twice as large for older adults as for middle-aged adults, larger for women than for men and larger for residents of lower-middle income countries. The authors also report a consistent temperature effect among people in high-income countries where air conditioning is plausibly available.

2246.content: Among 765,000 US respondents to the CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Survey (2002 to 2011), each month that nights ran 1 degree C warmer than the local 1981 to 2010 normal went with about three more self-reported nights of insufficient rest or sleep per 100 people per month (beta 0.028, P = 0.014, n = 766,761), in models with city-by-season and calendar-day controls.

In the same US survey data, the effect of warmer-than-normal nights on reported insufficient sleep was more than twice as large in summer, over three times as large for people earning under 50,000 dollars a year as for those above, and nearly twice as large for people over 65. Among older, lower-income respondents in summer (n = 30,532) it was about 10 times the effect in the rest of the sample.

2247.content: In the US Sister Study, 43,722 women aged 35 to 74 (mean 55) without shift work or daytime sleep reported the light in their bedroom while sleeping and were followed for about 5.7 years. Against women who slept with no light, those who slept with a television or a light on in the room were more likely to gain 5 kg or more (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.27), to show a 10 percent rise in BMI (RR 1.13), to become overweight (RR 1.22) and to become obese (RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.57). The associations held after adjustment for sleep duration and quality, diet and physical activity.

2248.content: In 145 apparently healthy adults (67 men, 78 women, aged 18 to 55, BMI 18 to 35), social jetlag was measured as the difference in the midpoint of sleep between work days and free days. Participants with 2 hours or more of social jetlag had higher cortisol over 5 hours, slept less during the week, were more often physically inactive and had a higher resting heart rate than participants with 1 hour or less.

2249.content: In a photoperiod experiment at the NIMH, healthy people moved from a conventional 16-hour light period to a 10-hour light period (14 hours of darkness) had longer sleep episodes that usually split into two bouts of several hours each, with 1 to 3 hours awake between them. The nightly span of melatonin secretion and of rising sleepiness also lengthened.

2250.content: In the MacArthur Study of Successful Aging, 1,030 relatively high-functioning US adults aged 70 to 79 rated at baseline (1988 to 1989) how often they felt useful to family and friends (60 never or rarely, 349 sometimes, 621 frequently) and were followed for 7 years. Against those who frequently felt useful, those who never or rarely did had about three times the odds of a rise in mobility disability (OR 3.61) or onset of difficulty with daily activities (OR 3.22) and over four times the odds of dying (OR 4.11). After adjustment for age, education, health behaviours, social integration, mood and self-efficacy, the odds ratios stayed near three (3.08, 2.65 and 3.13 for death, 95% CI 1.43 to 6.84). Those who felt useful only sometimes showed small, non-significant rises.

2251.content: In 276 healthy volunteers who completed a life stressor interview and were then given common cold viruses and monitored, severe acute stressful life events lasting under a month were not associated with developing a cold, while severe chronic stressors lasting a month or longer went with a substantial increase in the chance of disease. The chronic stressors were mainly under- or unemployment and lasting difficulties with family or friends. Differences in social networks, personality, health habits and endocrine or immune measures before the virus did not fully account for the link.

2252.content: Among 208 men and women who commuted by suburban rail to Manhattan, New York, a longer commute went with larger rises in salivary cortisol above resting baseline, less persistence on a task at the end of the commute and higher perceived stress. Gender did not change these links.

2253.content: Using individual-level panel data, the author found that people with problems repaying their debts had much worse psychological health on subjective and objective measures, and that selection into problem debt by people already in poor psychological health accounted for much of the difference; the link may run both ways.

Using local house price movements that no single household controls as a natural experiment, the author reports a sizeable causal link from problem mortgage debt to worse psychological health. Local rates of bankruptcy and repossession were used to test whether the stigma of debt depends on how common it is among one's reference group.

2254.content: In the 2007 national survey of England that its authors call a survey of psychiatric morbidity (random probability sample of 7,461 adults, each given the CIS-R interview and scored on it), 8.5 percent of adults were in arrears. Adults in debt were three times as likely as others to meet the survey's criteria for a common mental disorder, whatever the source of the debt (housing, utilities or credit purchases). The rate was higher still among those reported as dependent on alcohol or drugs or as problem gamblers, and reached about 50 percent among people with several sources of debt who had borrowed from pawnbrokers or moneylenders.

2255.content: In a field experiment, residents of a home for the aged were randomly assigned to four conditions: visits by college undergraduates whose frequency and length the resident decided (control), visits announced in advance that the resident could not change (predict), visits on a random schedule, or no visits. Predictable and controllable visits had a strong positive effect on the residents' physical and psychological well-being.

2256.content: In a meta-analysis of studies of job insecurity, the authors found that job insecurity went with worse job attitudes, worse attitudes to the organisation and worse health among employees, and to some extent with their behaviour toward the organisation. Links were stronger in studies with multi-item measures of insecurity, and the behavioural links were stronger among manual than non-manual workers.

2257.content: In 22 volunteers tested in 215 night-time light exposures (30 minutes of monochromatic light at 424, 456, 472, 496, 520 or 548 nm in the biological night), melatonin suppression rose with light intensity at every wavelength and was strongest for short-wavelength light. The action spectrum did not fit the rods or any of the three cones (r below 0.1); a rhodopsin-type pigment peaking at 459 nm fitted best (r squared = 0.74). The authors read this as the first direct evidence of a non-rod, non-cone light receptor in humans.
