2258.content: Among 447 healthy US adults aged 30 to 54 who worked day shifts (53% women, 83% white), social jetlag was measured with wrist actigraphy as the difference in minutes between the midpoint of sleep before work days and on free days. Greater social jetlag went with lower HDL cholesterol, higher triglycerides, higher fasting insulin, more insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), larger waist and higher BMI, after adjustment for sleep duration, sleep efficiency, subjective sleep quality, demographics, physical activity, calories, alcohol, smoking and depressive symptoms scored on a questionnaire. 84.8% slept later on free days than on work days.

2259.content: A meta-analysis of 12 observational studies (28 independent reports, 226,652 participants, 14,595 with diabetes) found that ever having worked shifts went with higher odds of diabetes than normal daytime schedules: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.09 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.12). The association was stronger in men (OR 1.37) than in women (OR 1.09). All shift schedules except mixed and evening shifts were associated with higher odds, and rotating shifts showed the largest increase.

2260.content: A meta-analysis of 7 longitudinal studies (28,431 participants) found that shift work went with higher later odds of poor mental health symptoms as the studies measured them, anxiety, depressive and general symptoms combined (pooled effect 1.28, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.62), and of depressive symptoms specifically (1.33, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.74). Sex explained over 90% of the heterogeneity: women working shifts had 1.73 times the odds of reporting depressive symptoms of women not working shifts.

2261.content: In the Nurses' Health Studies (189,158 initially healthy US women: 73,623 in NHS from 1988 and 115,535 in NHS2 from 1989), followed for 24 years with 10,822 incident coronary heart disease cases, rotating night shift work (3 or more night shifts a month) was associated with higher risk after adjustment for diet, activity, smoking, BMI and other risk factors: in NHS, hazard ratio 1.12 for 5 to 9 years and 1.18 for 10 or more years; in NHS2, 1.12 and 1.15. Fewer than 5 years showed no significant increase in the baseline analysis.

In the younger cohort (NHS2), coronary heart disease risk was lower the longer it had been since a woman stopped working rotating night shifts (trend p below 0.001), and in NHS the association with night shift work was stronger in the first half of follow-up than in the second (27% versus 13% higher risk for 10 or more years). The authors read this as recent shift work being most relevant and call it a new finding that needs replication.

2262.content: In the Sydney Myopia Study (2003 to 2005; 1,765 six-year-olds and 2,367 twelve-year-olds from 51 randomly selected schools, cycloplegic refraction, activity reported by parents and children), 12-year-olds with more total time outdoors had less myopia and more hyperopic refraction after adjusting for near work, parental myopia and ethnicity. Those combining low near work with high outdoor time had the most hyperopic mean refraction (+0.56 D) and those combining high near work with low outdoor time the least (+0.27 D). Indoor sport showed no association, and the 6-year-olds showed no consistent association.

2263.content: Amabile and Kramer studied more than 12,000 daily diary entries written by knowledge workers over three years. Comparing each participant's best days with their worst days, they found that the single most important difference was the sense of being able to make progress in the work. Praise without real progress did little for the day and could arouse cynicism; progress met with criticism of trivial issues could bring anger and sadness. People performed better on days with more positive emotion and stronger intrinsic motivation.

2264.content: In a longitudinal quasi-experiment, a participative action research intervention had employees reorganise their own work to raise the discretion and choice they had in it. At one-year follow-up the intervention had significantly improved mental health, sickness absence and self-rated performance, and the increase in job control mediated these improvements.

2265.content: A two-year follow-up of a job enlargement intervention in a financial services company (445 clerical employees and 70 managers; pretest-posttest and posttest-only quasi-experiments) found that the results depended on the kind of enlargement. Task enlargement, adding more tasks to a job, had mostly long-term costs: less satisfaction, efficiency and customer service, and more mental overload and errors. Knowledge enlargement, jobs requiring more understanding of procedures and products, had mostly benefits: more satisfaction and customer service, and less overload and fewer errors.

2266.content: A meta-analysis of 133 studies with 172 independent samples on job insecurity and its job-related and health-related outcomes found that the negative association of job insecurity with health outcomes was more severe among employees with longer tenure and among older employees, and similar for men and women. Job insecurity was also significantly and negatively associated with job performance. The abstract reports no effect sizes.

2267.content: In the Whitehall II cohort of British civil servants, 931 women and 2,429 men answered a question on job insecurity in 1995/96 and again in 1997/99. Compared with those whose jobs stayed secure, those who lost job security reported more ill health and more minor psychiatric morbidity on the study's screening measures, those who regained security still showed residual worse scores, mainly psychological, and those reporting chronic insecurity had the highest self-reported morbidity. Physiological changes were limited to higher blood pressure in women who lost security and lower body mass index in women reporting chronic insecurity; smoking and drinking did not differ.

2268.content: Using the US National Survey of Families and Households and the US Census public use files, Compton and Pollak found that married women with young children who lived within 25 miles of their mother or mother-in-law had a 4 to 10 percentage point higher predicted probability of employment and labour force participation than those living further away. Within 25 miles, 24 to 27 percent of these women received work-related childcare from their own mother in the past month, against 4.2 percent of those living far from both mothers. The authors argue that available grandmother childcare, including help with irregular and unexpected needs, is the link.

Using the US National Survey of Families and Households, Compton and Pollak report that the median distance between married women and their mothers was 20 miles, with a quarter living within 5 miles; for unmarried women the median was 8 miles counting those living with their mother, 15 miles without them. Living within 25 miles of both mothers was strongly linked to education: 46 percent of couples where neither spouse had a college degree lived that close, against 17 percent of couples where both had one.

2269.content: In 183 healthy adults living with a partner (66 African American, 117 white; 74 women, 109 men), the warm contact group spent 10 minutes holding hands with their partner while watching a romantic video, followed by a 20-second hug; the no contact group rested quietly for the same time. In a public speaking task afterwards, the warm contact group showed smaller increases in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and heart rate. The difference was similar for men and women and larger for African American than white participants.

2270.content: In a group-randomised trial at a US information technology company, 56 study groups were randomly assigned to STAR, an initiative that trained supervisors to support employees' personal and family lives and had employees rework when and where they worked, or to business as usual. Among 694 employees with baseline and six-month data, STAR produced statistically significant but modest falls in work-family conflict and rises in time adequacy for family, and larger increases in employees' schedule control and supervisor support for family and personal life. Work hours and perceived job demands did not rise. Employees more exposed to work-family conflict gained more.

2271.content: In three laboratory experiments on food choice, people chose between foods or between food and money earned by repeated responses on concurrent schedules. When a better-liked food cost more and more responses (from one response per unit up to an average of 32) while a less-liked food stayed at one response, participants first worked for the better-liked food and then switched to the less-liked one as its cost rose. When food-deprived, they preferred a liked breakfast to its money value only when both cost one response each; when not deprived, they worked almost entirely for money.

2272.content: Using life tables built from published data on wild populations of 52 mammal species and a population measure of post-reproductive life (the share of adult female years lived by females past their last reproduction), the authors found a post-reproductive stage significantly greater than chance in only three species: humans (data from Hadza hunter-gatherers, Tanzania; 0.43 of adult female years), killer whales (orca, Orcinus orca; 0.34) and short-finned pilot whales (Globicephala macrorhynchus; 0.26). In the other 49 species, including chimpanzees, African elephants and several other primates, females did not live past their last reproduction longer than chance and senescence predict.

In the three species with a post-reproductive stage, the chance that a female lived to the probable age of her last reproduction was similar (humans, from Hadza data, 0.59; killer whales 0.73; short-finned pilot whales 0.61), and a female who reached that age could then expect to live about 26 more years among the Hadza, 29 years in killer whales and 13 years in short-finned pilot whales.

2273.content: Reviewing primate and human social systems, Grueter, Chapais and Zinner report that nested (multilevel) societies occur in three primate groups: papionins (hamadryas baboons, Papio hamadryas, and geladas, Theropithecus gelada), Asian colobine monkeys (snub-nosed monkeys, Rhinopithecus, and proboscis monkeys, Nasalis) and hominins. Among human hunter-gatherers, citing ethnographic studies, they report that families form bands of 35 to 80 people who cooperate in getting food, and that bands combine into regional communities of 250 to 500 people who share a dialect and meet from time to time for ritual, trade, exchange of mates and other purposes.

The same review contrasts humans with other multilevel primates: in hamadryas baboons and geladas the units of a band have weak ties to other bands, while in humans the bonds and alliances between family groups are strong. The authors trace this to people keeping lifelong bonds with their kin of birth after moving to another group to breed, which creates ties of kinship and of marriage between groups.

2274.content: In rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) living in social groups, the mother was removed for a few days while the infant stayed in its familiar surroundings. The infant at first called a great deal and then showed less movement and less play, and these changes could last for a month after the mother came back. Simple tests 6 months and 2 years later suggested that infants who had been separated still differed from infants who had not. The effects varied with the length of the separation and the infant's sex, and the nature of the mother-infant relationship appeared to matter.

2275.content: Hofer reviews his laboratory's work on why infant rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) call (ultrasonic vocalisation) when abruptly isolated from nest, littermates and mother. Contact with specific parts of the pup's living and non-living surroundings holds the calling system down; in isolation the loss of these regulators produces an outburst of calling. The author reports that drugs acting on receptors change the calling rate in the same direction as they change measures of anxiety in adult animals and in human clinical groups. Cues of a predator stop isolation calling, and a brief exposure to the mother makes the calling stronger afterwards.

2276.content: Infant rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) separated from their mothers called far more and showed activation of the autonomic and pituitary-adrenal stress systems. In a series of drug experiments, a low dose of morphine (0.1 mg/kg) significantly cut separation calls without changing how active the infants were; naloxone at 1.0 mg/kg, which blocks opioid receptors, increased distress calls, while lower doses had no effect; and naloxone at 0.1 mg/kg blocked the morphine effect. Opioid drugs also changed the rise in pituitary-adrenal hormones during separation.

2277.content: Reviewing the sound structure and function of infant distress calls in a wide range of mammals and other vertebrates, given when infants were isolated from the mother or captured by humans, the authors report that in both settings the calls tend to be tonal with a simple rising-falling, flat or falling pitch. Every report found that both kinds of call draw caregivers, and the fundamental frequency of the call is often what matters for that response. They read the differences between isolation and capture calls as differences in how aroused the infant is, with one shared function.

2278.content: In playback experiments, mother mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) and white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) approached a speaker playing the distress calls of infants of other species, among them yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris), fur seals and sea lions, domestic cats (Felis catus), bats and humans (Homo sapiens), when the call's fundamental frequency fell, or was shifted to fall, within the range to which deer respond for their own young. They did not approach predator sounds or control sounds with the same fundamental frequency and a different structure.

2279.content: In a survey of 362 individually housed rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) at a US primate research centre, combined with colony records, 321 showed at least one abnormal behaviour (mean 2.3, range 1 to 8), pacing most often; males showed more than females, and self-injury went with self-directed stereotypies. Individual housing at an early age, longer time housed alone, more blood draws and nursery rearing (raised apart from the mother) were risk factors for abnormal behaviour.

2280.content: Twelve infant rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), raised with surrogates and peers, got food treats in the home cage for 12 weeks from their second month, either when they pressed a lever (master) or at the same times regardless of what they did (yoked). Masters pressed the lever more and did not differ in baseline cortisol. At five months, in a novel environment, masters were significantly more active and had a significantly smaller cortisol response, but only when tested alone and not when tested in their social group. Across infants, more lever pressing went with more activity and a smaller cortisol response to the novel place.

2281.content: Two socially housed groups of rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) were raised in their first year with or without control (mastery) over food, water and treats. At 18 to 24 months both groups were given beta-CCE, a benzodiazepine receptor inverse agonist that the authors call a putative anxiogenic drug. Both groups became more active, with more aggression than fear; the rise in aggression was seen mainly in the monkeys reared with control. Plasma cortisol rose in both groups and rose more in the yoked monkeys, who had been reared without control.

2282.content: House mouse (Mus musculus) pups lacking the mu-opioid receptor gene emitted fewer ultrasonic calls than normal pups when removed from their mothers, but not when exposed to cold or to the odour of male mice. The knockout pups showed no preference for their mother's cues and their calls did not grow stronger after a brief exposure to the mother, as normal pups' calls do.

2283.content: Testing whether play is more common in species that do more of their growing after birth, Pellis and Iwaniuk compared species within two mammal orders, primates and muroid rodents (mice, rats and their relatives), with independent contrasts to allow for relatedness. Species born less developed played more and played more complex play fighting: how developed the body is at birth (newborn weight over adult weight) accounted for 30 percent of the variance in play among the rodents, and how developed the brain is at birth (newborn brain weight over adult brain weight) for 60 percent of the variance in play among the primates.

2284.content: From 16 years of behavioural data on a well-studied population of wild baboons (Papio; the abstract names no species or site), the authors report that adult females who were more social had higher infant survival, independent of dominance rank, group membership and environmental conditions.

2285.content: In the Amboseli baboons of Kenya (an admixed population of yellow baboons, Papio cynocephalus, and anubis baboons, Papio anubis), studied with infants born from 1983 to 2020, a mother's grooming contact with other females peaked in the first six months after a birth and dropped if the infant died, and her contact with males changed with her reproductive state. Measured over different windows, the link between a mother's sociality and her infant's survival changed direction. Repeating the 2003 analysis on the larger dataset gave a smaller positive link (B = 0.095, P = 0.027, against 0.321 in 2003); measuring sociality only outside the infant's first year, or only during pregnancy, gave no significant link (n = 256 and n = 268). The authors conclude that the earlier result is mainly explained by the infant's presence and the mother's reproductive state.

2286.content: Suomi, reviewing rearing studies in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta), reports dramatic short- and long-term effects of differing early social experience on behaviour and physiology, with early relationships with mothers or other caregivers the strongest influence on behaviour across the lifespan. He also writes that clear evidence for the general idea that early experience shapes adult behaviour is surprisingly sparse in humans, while animal evidence is plentiful.

2287.content: In a laboratory group of 8 squirrel monkeys (Saimiri), making food moderately and then extremely hard to obtain cut social play sharply within 4 to 6 days; the stronger condition reduced play to 1 percent of baseline (P < .001). Neither condition removed play completely, as the authors had seen in a field study in south-western Panama, which they take to have involved more severe or longer food shortage. No harmful or dysfunctional effects were seen where play fell to zero or near zero. After each experiment play rebounded to about 50 percent above baseline, peaking 5 to 6 days after food became easy again, then fell back.

2288.content: In free-living yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, Colorado, followed from 2002 to 2011 (27,493 social interactions among 803 marmots), an animal's rank from who won its play bouts as a pup or yearling went with its later rank from fights (estimate 0.136, P = 0.005; 152 males and 127 females), after allowing for sex, body mass, rate of play and individual identity. Rank in pup play predicted rank in fights as a yearling (P = 0.0009). The link weakened with time: rank in early play did not significantly predict rank as an adult (P = 0.351), where age was the main predictor. How much an animal played did not predict its later rank.

2289.content: A review of animal play and welfare states that play has long been named as a possible welfare indicator because it often disappears when animals are under fitness challenge and is thought to go with a pleasurable emotional experience. The authors review four aspects: play indicates the absence of fitness threats, play acts as a reward and flags opioid-mediated pleasure, play brings immediate psychological and long-term fitness and health benefits, and play is socially contagious. They conclude that play holds promise as a welfare indicator and as a tool to improve welfare. The abstract names no species and gives no numbers.

The same review states that play does not always mark good conditions: it can also increase in stressful situations, in response to reduced parental care, or as a rebound after a period of deprivation. The authors call for better knowledge of the functions and mechanisms of play, and of the species-specific play of captive animals, before play is read as a welfare signal.

2290.content: In two aviary experiments, the authors recorded the vocal and nonvocal alarm displays of captive flocks of tufted titmice (Baeolophus bicolor) presented with live predators and with controls (no animal, and a quail), then played the recorded titmouse calls to captive Carolina chickadees (Poecile carolinensis). The titmouse calls fully distinguished the different predation threats, and the chickadees' vocal and nonvocal responses also distinguished the threats encoded in the calls they heard, in parallel with the titmice and appropriate to the threat. The authors propose that titmice act as community informants for other species. The abstract gives no sample sizes.

2291.content: Juvenile laboratory rats (Norway rat, Rattus norvegicus) were housed either with three same-sex peers (play condition) or with one adult (no play condition). As young adults, half of each group received repeated nicotine injections and half saline, and the length and branching of dendrites of medial prefrontal cortex neurons were measured. Play and nicotine each changed the neurons as earlier studies had found, and the neurons responded more to nicotine in rats that had first had play experience. The abstract gives no numbers.

2292.content: A phylogenetic comparative analysis across nonhuman primate species found that the relative volume of the amygdala and of the hypothalamus correlated with the frequency of social play, and not with nonsocial play, after controlling for the size of other brain structures. The authors propose that skills mediated by the amygdala, such as social assessment and responding to facial expression, are developed through social play, and that the hypothalamus may regulate the motivation to play. The abstract gives no number of species.

2293.content: A phylogenetic comparative analysis of nonhuman primates found that the frequency of social play is positively correlated with relative cerebellum size, a structure implicated in motor development and possibly in cognitive skills. The authors frame this against the challenge that play is not simply more common in larger-brained animals, and read it as a link between the evolution of social play and the cerebellum. The abstract gives no number of species or effect size.

2294.content: A review of eavesdropping on the alarm calls of other species reports that it has been shown experimentally in about 70 vertebrate species, between closely or distantly related species. Its benefits include immediate anti-predator responses, indirect gains in foraging or habitat use, and learning about predators; it can add eyes looking for danger and information that complements what the listener gets from its own species. Responses to another species' calls can be unlearned, where the calls share acoustic features with the listener's own calls or are harsh, or learned. Some species are 'keystone' producers of information while others mostly seek it.

2295.content: Using a comparative data set of the frequency of social and nonsocial play across primate species, Montgomery tested two predictions of the idea that play supports complex cognition and behavioural flexibility: that play frequency goes with the amount of brain growth after birth, and that it goes with measures of behavioural flexibility. Both predictions were supported, and the results suggest that social and nonsocial play may contribute to different aspects of behavioural flexibility. The abstract gives no number of species or effect sizes.

2296.content: A review of field studies of juvenile play in Belding's ground squirrels (Urocitellus beldingi) reports that play improves general motor skill, and that social play goes with refinement of temperament toward less docile and more cautious behaviour and with more exploration and adaptable responses in novel situations. The timing of natal dispersal and defence of maternal territories can be influenced by juvenile play. The authors state that social play in this species appears not to bring the range of social benefits seen in species with more complex social organization.

2297.content: In free-living juvenile Belding's ground squirrels (then Spermophilus beldingi), the authors gave some litters extra food and left others unprovisioned, and treated some females with testosterone at birth. Play was most frequent near weaning and declined afterwards in all groups. Food provisioning raised rates of play in males and females of both treated and control litters, which the authors read as energy availability limiting play. Perinatal testosterone raised the sexual play started by young females to near male rates and did not change play fighting. The abstract gives no numbers.

2298.content: In a wild population of meerkats (Suricata suricatta) in the southern Kalahari, followed from 1996 to 2002 (76 individuals from 14 groups; 18 pairs of same-sex littermates known to have fought each other for dominance of a group), Sharpe tested whether play fighting improves later fighting. Play fighting experience did not improve later fighting skill, and the individuals that won the dominant breeding position through serious fighting had played no more often, and no more successfully, as youngsters than the littermates they defeated.

Across the thesis, which tested several proposed functions of play in the same wild meerkat population, play carried an energetic cost and meerkats adjusted how often they played to their energy intake, yet none of the functions tested could be shown: play did not reduce aggression between playmates, did not strengthen bonds to the group so that individuals stayed longer or helped more, and was not used to build alliances or to contest or set dominance, and there was little evidence that it served self-assessment. Sharpe concludes that the most likely function of play is to promote growth of the cerebral cortex.

2299.content: In free-ranging meerkats (Suricata suricatta), pups' long-term nutritional status (weight gain over 6 weeks) correlated positively with their rate of play. Provisioning experiments of 4 to 8 weeks that raised the nutritional status of pups, subadults and adults more than doubled the experimental animals' rate of play compared with unprovisioned controls. Short-term changes in food intake (daily weight gain) did not predict play, and the authors established that the extra energy, and not extra free time from foraging less, raised play. They conclude that play in meerkats was energetically costly.

2300.content: In captive male red-necked wallabies (Macropus rufogriseus banksianus), a marsupial, the way a male play fought depended on his partner's age. With a younger partner he took a defensive strategy and handicapped himself: he stood flat-footed, pawed instead of sparring, did not use his full strength, tolerated the younger one's tactics and did more to keep the bout going. With an older partner he sparred vigorously, spent more time in the high stance and had more high-intensity bouts. Play between same-aged partners tended to be more stable and more competitive. The abstract gives no sample size.

2301.content: Reconciliation, a friendly reunion of former opponents soon after a fight, is common in stumptail macaques (Macaca arctoides) and rare in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta). Juvenile rhesus were housed with stumptail juveniles for 5 months and then observed with their own species only; control rhesus matched in age and sex went through the same steps without the other species. The proportion of reconciled fights rose threefold in the rhesus subjects. The difference grew gradually while they lived with the stumptails and stayed after the stumptails were removed. Grooming and aggression fell over time.

2302.content: In two large outdoor-living groups of chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) at the Yerkes field station, 3,003 aggressive conflicts and the periods after them were recorded. Consolation (the first friendly contact a bystander makes with the recent victim of aggression) went more often to kin and to unrelated individuals with whom the consoler had a strong affiliative tie, and occurred more often when the opponents had not reconciled. Females consoled more than males, except that the highest-ranking males often consoled. Consolation was reciprocated: individuals consoled those from whom they received consolation.

2303.content: The mothers of 4 group-living pigtail macaque infants (Macaca nemestrina) were removed. All 4 infants showed distress, and 3 went on to a state of deep withdrawal that the authors label 'depression' and liken to the anaclitic depression Spitz described in human infants separated from their mothers. The one infant that did not reach that state was the offspring of the dominant female. The authors read the stages of the reaction as successive efforts at adaptation with survival value, partly through what they communicate, and note that the infants' ability to move about appeared to start recovery.

2304.content: The mothers of four pigtail macaque infants (Macaca nemestrina) living in a group were removed for 4 weeks. All four infants first reacted with agitation; three then became what the authors label severely depressed, a state lasting about a week that they liken to the 'anaclitic depression' of human infants who lost their mothers. When mothers and infants were reunited, all four pairs showed a marked and prolonged intensification of the mother-infant relationship.

2305.content: Desert iguanas (Dipsosaurus dorsalis) injected with the bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila develop a fever of about 2 degrees C. Infected lizards were kept at a neutral (38 degrees C), low (34 or 36 degrees C) or high (40 or 42 degrees C) ambient temperature. Raising body temperature after the infection significantly raised the lizards' survival. The abstract gives no survival figures.

2306.content: Desert iguanas (Dipsosaurus dorsalis) infected with live Aeromonas hydrophila were given varying doses of sodium salicylate, a fever-lowering drug. Of 12 lizards given the same bacterial injection and a nontoxic dose of the drug, the 5 that still raised their mean body temperature by at least 0.6 degrees C survived the week, and the 7 that did not develop a fever died within 3 days. The authors conclude that preventing fever with the drug increases death from the infection.

2307.content: Inbred laboratory mice (house mouse, Mus musculus) subjected to repeated social defeat split into susceptible and unsusceptible subpopulations that differed across several behavioural and physiological measures. The authors identify adaptations in the mesolimbic dopamine circuit tied to each outcome, and show that reproducing three adaptations of the unsusceptible animals at the molecular level was each enough to make mice resist. The abstract does not name the behaviours measured and gives no numbers.

2308.content: In female Ldlr-knockout house mice (Mus musculus), an atherosclerosis-prone strain, 4 weeks of a Western-type diet raised blood cholesterol, circulating cytokines, chemokines and acute phase proteins and expanded the myeloid blood cells. After a further 4 weeks back on standard chow, cholesterol and the circulating cytokines were back at baseline, while the responses of myeloid cells to innate immune stimuli stayed enhanced and their bone-marrow precursors (granulocyte-monocyte progenitors) stayed transcriptionally and epigenetically reprogrammed. Mice that also lacked the NLRP3 inflammasome showed neither the systemic inflammation nor the reprogramming. Groups were 3 to 10 mice; experiments were run twice.

2309.content: Abstract only. Laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus) lived in a foraging simulation in which they earned all their daily food: one bar press started a procurement interval, after which a large cup of food was presented and they could eat a meal of any size. As the interval was lengthened from 1 second to 46 hours, meal frequency fell steadily, meal size rose to compensate, and total daily intake was held constant up to an interval of 23 hours. Raising the bar-press requirement to 10 also lowered meal frequency.

2310.content: Abstract only. A review: an adaptive immune system in which each lymphocyte carries its own antigen receptor evolved in the vertebrate ancestors and was added to an existing innate immune system. All jawed vertebrates build these receptors by recombining immunoglobulin or T cell receptor gene segments; the surviving jawless vertebrates, lampreys and hagfish, instead assemble variable lymphocyte receptors from leucine-rich-repeat modules. The authors read the two as convergent systems, each made by modifying components of the innate immune system.

2311.content: Crespi and Denver cloned leptin in the South African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis) and its receptor in Xenopus frogs (the full-length receptor from Xenopus tropicalis). Frog leptin is only about 35% similar in amino acid sequence to mammalian leptins but has a nearly identical predicted structure and activates frog and mouse leptin receptors. Injected into the brain ventricles, recombinant frog leptin cut food intake in juvenile frogs, with maximal inhibition at 0.02 ng per g body weight (n = 4). In tadpoles of the Western spadefoot toad (Spea hammondii) it had no effect on foraging at early prometamorphosis and inhibited feeding dose-dependently at midprometamorphosis (5 to 6 tadpoles per dose).

2312.content: Abstract only. Using a larger primate sample than earlier studies, more recent phylogenies and updated statistical methods, DeCasien, Williams and Higham found that primate brain size, after controlling for body size and phylogeny, is predicted by diet and not by several measures of sociality: frugivores have larger brains than folivores. The authors say this calls into question the emphasis on social over ecological explanations for large primate brains.

2313.content: Abstract only. Across 44 species of free-living primates, how often animals groomed each other correlated with group size and not with body size. Dunbar reads this as evidence for a social function of grooming over a purely hygienic one; among New World monkeys (platyrrhines) body size may matter more.

2314.content: In 3,000 hours of all-day focal follows (2003 to 2006) of 14 adults (9 females, 5 males) of the Tai South group of wild West African chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) in Cote d'Ivoire, grooming given and received was more symmetrical when measured over long periods than within a single bout or day; only 32% of 1,236 bouts were bidirectional. Random giving, uniform allocation, similarity between individuals and kinship did not explain the balance. Earlier consecutive follows showed that a pair groomed on average once every 7 days (range 2 to 18 days).

Gomes, Mundry and Boesch estimated the symmetry of grooming between pairs of Tai chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) over growing spans of data: the estimate rose from 0.53 over 7 months to 0.78 over 15 months and then levelled off (0.83 at 19 months, 0.79 at 22 months), so the balance between partners showed up most clearly over a year or more of exchanges.

2315.content: Abstract only. A review: pathogen recognition, signalling pathways and effector mechanisms of innate immunity are similar in the fruit fly (Drosophila) and in mammals, which the authors read as a common ancestry of these defences. In mammals innate immunity, the first-line defence of the first hours after exposure, also appears to stimulate the later clonal response of adaptive immunity.

2316.content: Abstract only. Eight laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus) were reared for 39 days after weaning in either an enriched or an impoverished environment and then lived for 25 or 30 days in operant chambers where they could take food pellets freely or earn them by lever pressing. The rats reared in the impoverished environment learned to lever press quickly and kept preferring to earn their food by pressing; the rats reared in the enriched environment did not learn to lever press and did not press even when the free food was removed. The authors attribute the difference to higher activity levels after restricted rearing.

2317.content: Compiling published grooming-time data for Old World primate species and populations, Lehmann, Korstjens and Dunbar found that time spent grooming rose with group size, and was also affected by dispersal pattern and sex ratio, but levelled off once groups exceeded about 40 individuals; the same ceiling appeared within apes, papionins (baboons and gelada) and red colobus. In apes a logarithmic relation of grooming time to group size explained 72% of the variance. The authors read the ceiling as time constraints from ecology forcing individuals to compromise on grooming, which lowers group cohesion.

2318.content: In adult fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster), the genes of the embryonic dorsoventral patterning pathway (the Toll ligand spatzle, Toll, cactus and others, except dorsal) control induction of the antifungal peptide gene drosomycin, while antibacterial genes depend on a separate pathway (imd). After pricking with spores of the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus, about one third of wild-type flies died over 6 days, while all Toll-deficient flies died within 2 to 3 days, covered with fungal hyphae. The authors note that this cascade parallels the mammalian Toll/IL-1 and NF-kB cytokine cascade.

2319.content: Abstract only. Using a genetically encoded tracer in mice (Mus musculus), Liu and colleagues found that the receptor MrgprB4 marks a rare group of unmyelinated, nonpeptidergic sensory fibres that innervate only hairy skin and end in large branching terminals similar in size and distribution to the receptive fields of C-fibre tactile afferents. The authors suggest MrgprB4 may give genetic access to these touch fibres in mice.

2320.content: Abstract only. Reviewing enrichment for nonhuman primates kept in research settings, Lutz and Novak test four hypotheses: that enrichment is used, that it normalises the behavioural repertoire, that it lowers abnormal behaviour and that it prevents it. Applied to toys, foraging devices and social interaction, most devices were used, but they differed in how far they normalised behaviour and removed abnormal behaviour; only social contact both promoted a wide range of species-typical activities and reduced or prevented abnormal behaviour.

2321.content: In the genome of the purple sea urchin (Strongylocentrotus purpuratus), an invertebrate deuterostome, Rast and colleagues found 222 Toll-like receptor genes (211 in one greatly expanded family plus 11 divergent ones), 203 NACHT-LRR genes resembling the vertebrate NOD and NALP receptors, and 218 gene models for scavenger receptor cysteine-rich proteins. The authors write that the more than 200 sea urchin NLR genes contrast with about 20 NLR proteins in vertebrates, and that for some receptor classes the sea urchin numbers exceed those of other sequenced animals by more than an order of magnitude.

2322.content: In 16 adult Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata) of a free-ranging, provisioned group on Koshima islet, Japan, studied January to April 2014, an index of hygienic tendencies built from three measures (avoiding wheat placed on fresh faeces, handling sand-covered sweet potatoes before eating, rubbing acorns before eating) went with lower faecal egg counts of two soil-transmitted gut worms, Oesophagostomum aculeatum and Trichuris sp. Females scored higher on the hygiene index than males.

In a field experiment with the same Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata, 151 trials), 37.5% of animals ate a grain of wheat placed on fresh macaque faeces and 56% ate it from a plastic replica of faeces, against 100% from a plastic control. When the reward was half a peanut, about 16 times the calories of a wheat grain, all animals ate it from every substrate.

2323.content: In 42 adult chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes troglodytes) housed at a research centre in Gabon, food placed on a hidden soft, moist substrate (dough, used in human studies as a stand-in for contaminated material) was eaten in 54% of trials, against 91% for food placed on hidden rope. Of the three senses tested, touch gave the strongest avoidance.

In the same chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes troglodytes), sight and smell gave weak results: 20 animals ate bananas from a brown faeces replica about as often as from control foam (89% against 91%), though when three items were offered they tended to take the one on the faeces replica last; with the smell of conspecific faeces bananas were eaten in 83% of trials against 93% with water (p = 0.055), and the smells of blood and semen gave only weak tendencies to move away.

2324.content: Male Wistar rats (Rattus norvegicus, 8 to 9 per group) given standard chow plus a daily assortment of three human snack foods (a cafeteria diet) ate about 30% more calories over 10 weeks than rats on chow, a low-fat diet or a lard-based 45% fat diet, which all ate about 100 kcal a day. Rats on the lard diet cut the grams they ate to hold calories level by week 2; rats on the cafeteria diet did not, ate only about 15% as much chow as chow-only rats, and gained almost twice the weight of chow controls.

After 15 weeks, Wistar rats (Rattus norvegicus) on the cafeteria diet stayed heavier than rats on every other diet and showed greater raised insulin, raised glucose and glucose intolerance than controls and lard-diet rats, with marked inflammation in white fat, brown fat and liver, far beyond that of the lard-diet rats.

2325.content: Germ-free Swiss Webster mice (Mus musculus) given the gut microbiota of one healthy American man were fed a diet high or low in fibre carbohydrates the gut microbes can use. Within one generation, the change was largely reversible: of the 124 of 208 taxa that fell at least two-fold on the low-fibre diet, 58 came back when fibre returned. Over four generations on the low-fibre diet, diversity fell further with each generation and 141 of 208 closely tracked taxa were undetectable by generation four; giving fibre again did not bring them back.

In fourth-generation low-fibre mice (Mus musculus, 3 per group), a faecal transplant from high-fibre control mice together with a high-fibre diet made the microbiota indistinguishable from controls within ten days and restored 110 taxa, mostly of the fibre-eating order Bacteroidales; mice given the high-fibre diet without the transplant regained none.

2326.content: Brown capuchin monkeys (Cebus apella) exchanging with a human experimenter refused to take part when they saw a group mate get a more attractive reward for the same effort, and refused more when the group mate got the better reward for no effort at all. The authors read this as an early evolutionary origin of aversion to unequal outcomes.

2327.content: In a captive colony of common vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus) of mixed relatedness that had lived together for over two years, 20 bats were fasted one at a time on 48 days and food sharing by regurgitation was recorded. Across 312 possible pairs, food a bat had received from a partner was the strongest predictor of food it gave that partner, 8.5 times more important than relatedness, and 64% of sharing pairs were unrelated, close to the 67% expected if kinship played no part.

In the same vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus), donors started 62% of the sharing bouts that were not between mother and young, which counts against sharing extracted by begging; pairs that shared food also groomed each other more on other days, and who fed whom was stable when compared 8 days and 6 months apart. A bat that had just been fed by others did not give more afterwards to others in general.

2328.content: Wild-type zebrafish (Danio rerio) learned to prefer the side of a tank where they had been exposed to cocaine in the water (conditioned place preference). The effect depended on dose and was largest at 10 mg per litre, where 85% of fish shifted their preference; lidocaine, a local anaesthetic like cocaine that is not rewarding, gave no more shift than untreated controls. In a pilot screen of 18 mutagenized families, three had many low responders, and the low response was passed on to the next generation.

2329.content: Daily cycles of about 24 hours in the oxidation of peroxiredoxin proteins were found under constant conditions, with no outside time cues, in mouse liver and the master clock of the hypothalamus, fruit fly heads (Drosophila melanogaster), seedlings of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana, the fungus Neurospora crassa, the alga Ostreococcus tauri, the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus and the archaeon Halobacterium salinarum, that is, in all three domains of life.

In mutants whose transcription-based clocks were broken (fruit flies lacking per or Clk, Neurospora lacking frq, plants and algae overexpressing TOC1, a cyanobacterium lacking KaiA), peroxiredoxin oxidation still cycled at about 24 hours, with a shifted phase. The authors read these rhythms in cell metabolism as at least as old as the separate clock genes of each lineage, which differ from one group of organisms to the next.

2330.content: In singing zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), the authors played a short burst of sound over a chosen syllable of the bird's own song on some renditions. Of 125 neurons recorded in the ventral tegmental area of 26 birds, 17 were briefly suppressed (on average a 75% drop in firing) after a distorted syllable and briefly activated at the moment an expected distortion did not come; 13 of the 14 neurons identified as projecting to the song-learning nucleus Area X of the basal ganglia carried this signal. The neurons did not respond this way when the bird heard the same distorted song played back while not singing.

2331.content: In two studies, captive chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) did not pay a cost to knock food away from a group mate when the outcome alone left them worse off, but did knock the food away when that group mate had actually stolen it from them. The authors conclude that chimpanzees retaliate against harmful acts but are indifferent to outcomes that are merely disadvantageous to them.

2332.content: In a comparative analysis across mammals, cooperative breeding (helpers other than the parents raising young) evolved only in socially monogamous species, which make up about 5% of mammal species. With extra-pair paternity uncommon in these species, the authors read this as support for high kinship among group members as a condition for cooperative breeding in non-human mammals, as in birds and insects.

2333.content: Reviewing comparative anatomy, Preuss argues that the rat medial frontal cortex, usually taken as the equivalent of primate dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, corresponds to primate premotor and anterior cingulate cortex, and that the lateral frontal cortex of rats resembles parts of primate orbital cortex. Rats thus have prefrontal cortex if orbital and cingulate cortex are counted, but no equivalent of the granular dorsolateral prefrontal areas of primates.

2334.content: A review of basal ganglia anatomy across vertebrates reports that in mammals, birds and reptiles the striatum and pallidum are rich in neurons, are made of the same basic neuron populations, and the striatum gets abundant dopamine input from the midbrain tegmentum and input from the cortex. In amphibians and other anamniotes the basal ganglia are present but cell-sparse, with modest dopamine input and little or no cortical input; the authors place a major elaboration at the transition from amphibians to reptiles.

2335.content: Female wild-type Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) were trained to pull a stick that moved food to a partner and not to themselves. After being helped by three different unfamiliar rats in turn, a rat pulled for a new unfamiliar partner on average 21% more often than after three unfamiliar rats had not helped it (median 0.86 against 0.71 pulls per minute, 19 rats), and pulled sooner; how often rats pulled when alone did not differ between the two treatments.

2336.content: In wild bonobos (Pan paniscus) at Kokolopori, Democratic Republic of the Congo, the authors examined grooming, coalitions and food sharing within and between groups. Individuals who cooperated more with members of their own group also formed cooperative relationships with members of other groups, in particular with out-group individuals who were themselves highly cooperative. The authors conclude that cooperation between unrelated individuals across groups, without immediate payoff, is not exclusive to humans and can arise without social norms.

2337.content: Over three years (2017 to 2019; 1,000, 1,075 and 257 observation days on three groups) at Kokolopori, wild bonobos (Pan paniscus) formed stable, separate groups with their own ranges: no pair of adults from different groups associated more than chance, while nearly all pairs within a group did. Even so, the groups met often and peacefully: two groups spent about 35% of observation days together, meetings lasted 1 to 13 consecutive days, and over 68% of between-group pairs of adults associated at least once each year, within a network of 59 potential adult partners. The Ngogo chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) compared in the same analysis showed no such stable separate clusters.

2338.content: Writing in 2006, Sapolsky reports that the low-aggression, high-affiliation culture of Forest Troop, a troop of savanna baboons (Papio anubis) in Kenya that lost its most aggressive males to tuberculosis in the early 1980s, still persisted about 20 years after the die-off, although by the early 1990s every adult male in the troop had immigrated after the epidemic. Males arriving in the troop behaved like newcomers elsewhere at first and later adopted the residents' style.

In Forest Troop, resident female baboons first presented sexually to newly arrived males an average of 18 days after arrival and first groomed them after 20 days, against 63 and 78 days in typical savanna baboon troops, and males in Forest Troop received four times as much grooming from females as elsewhere. Sapolsky offers this welcome as the most likely route by which the troop's culture passes to newcomers.

2339.content: Using immunohistochemistry, tract tracing and whole-cell recordings in the lamprey, a jawless vertebrate of the oldest living vertebrate group (cyclostomes), the authors found all parts of the mammalian basal ganglia: striatum, the internal and external globus pallidus and the subthalamic nucleus, with the same circuit features, molecular markers and activity patterns, including direct and indirect striatal pathways. They conclude that this circuit has been conserved as an action-selection mechanism in all vertebrates for over 560 million years.

2340.content: Among wild common vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus), food sharing by regurgitating blood depended equally and independently on how closely related two bats were and on an index of their opportunity to reciprocate. Data on how often sharing occasions arise, on the economics of sharing blood, and captive experiments in which unrelated bats exchanged blood reciprocally support reciprocity within groups that contain both kin and non-kin.

2341.content: In a captive group of 11 chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) at Walter Zoo, Gossau, Switzerland, unsettled by three newly introduced females and a rank reversal between two males, observers recorded 438 conflicts from 2007 to 2008. Bystanders broke up 69 of them (15.75%) impartially, without siding with either party, and only the alpha and beta males did so; 60 of the 69 interventions (87%) ended the conflict at once, and policing was most likely when a conflict involved several combatants. In three other zoo groups policing was rarer, came more often in times of social instability, and was done by high-ranking males and females.
In the Gossau chimpanzee group, 60 of 69 impartial interventions (86.96%) immediately ended the conflict, and the two policing males received aggression in response only once.

2342.content: A full re-examination of the 61 people buried in the Jebel Sahaba cemetery (Sudan, Nile valley; radiocarbon dated 13.4 to 18.2 thousand years ago; Qadan hunter-fisher-gatherers) found 106 previously undocumented lesions. Forty-one of the 61 (67.2%) had at least one healed or unhealed lesion, most from projectile weapons, in both sexes and including children. Because many skeletons carry both healed and unhealed injuries, the authors reject the reading of a single battle and conclude that violence came in repeated, sporadic episodes, probably driven by climatic and environmental change.

At Jebel Sahaba, 41 of 61 individuals (67.2%) showed at least one healed or unhealed lesion, including three quarters of adults and half of the non-adults with remains; 92.7% of those with lesions had traumatic injuries and 61.0% had projectile impact marks.

2343.content: Eaton and colleagues compare the reproductive lives of women in affluent Western nations with those of women in hunter-gatherer societies and note that the differences match the accepted reproductive risk factors for cancers of the breast, endometrium and ovary; diet, exercise and body composition would add further risk for women in industrialised countries. From a theoretical model they calculate that, to age 60, modern Western women may have a breast cancer risk as much as 100 times that of preagricultural women.

2344.content: Among 919 Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of the Bolivian Amazon aged 8 to 88 (49.9% female), eight cognitive tasks showed the same age pattern seen in industrialised populations: performance on effortful tasks (attention, processing speed, verbal declarative memory) peaked early, on average at 16.2 years, and was substantially lower from early adulthood, while semantic fluency peaked later, at 30.6 years on average, and was only slightly lower in later adulthood. Schooling went with higher scores at all ages but did not slow the age-related decline.

2345.content: In naturalistic behavioural observations of 212 infants and their mothers in three sub-Saharan small-scale populations (one hunter-gatherer, one horticultural, one agropastoral), infant age, maternal age and parity, and the infant's cooperative childcare network were each significantly associated with how much the mother invested, controlling for population. Care by others than the mother came from a wide range of caregivers of different relationships, sexes and ages, and was widely distributed among them.

2346.content: In an ethnographic study of grief and mourning among the Toraja of South Sulawesi, Indonesia, Wellenkamp describes local beliefs that expressing grief releases it, an implicit cathartic theory tied to ideas of 'heat' and 'coolness', and concludes that these local notions correspond closely to what many grieving individuals experience.

2347.content: From retrospective and cross-sectional reproductive histories of 83 females over age 10 among the Pume, South American foragers in Venezuela, girls reached menarche at 12.9 years on average and gave birth to a first child at 15.3 to 15.5. First-time mothers younger than 14 were four times more likely to lose their firstborn than first-time mothers aged 17 or older, but the author finds that starting childbearing in the mid-teens minimised infant mortality and maximised reproductive span, and that waiting until the late teens gave no gain in surviving children.

2348.content: In a bioenergetics model built from data on body size, resting metabolism, brain size, activity budgets and foraging in humans and other anthropoid primates, anthropoid primates spend about 8% of resting metabolism on the brain, other mammals 3 to 4%, and humans 20 to 25%. Total energy expenditure across anthropoids rises with day range and diet quality, and human foragers fit this pattern with high expenditure, large foraging ranges and a high-quality diet.

2349.content: Actical accelerometers worn by 49 Shuar adults (23 men, 26 women, aged 14 to 66) in a rural forager-horticulturalist community of the Ecuadorian Amazon undergoing market integration gave physical activity levels (total energy expenditure over basal metabolic rate) of about 1.54 for men and 1.42 for women, in the light to moderate range, and activity energy expenditure of 762 against 573 kcal a day. The authors describe Shuar activity as relatively low compared with other non-Western populations.

Among the Shuar sample, men whose partner was pregnant or breastfeeding had significantly higher activity energy expenditure and activity levels than other men, while pregnant and breastfeeding women had the lowest energetic output; in households without a pregnant or breastfeeding woman, men and women did not differ. The authors read this as a cooperative household effort to cover the mother's high energy needs, as reported in other subsistence populations.

2350.content: At Nataruk, west of Lake Turkana in Kenya, a lagoon-edge site the authors date to the late Pleistocene or early Holocene, 10 of the 12 articulated skeletons of hunter-gatherers show evidence of violent death, with no evidence of deliberate burial. The authors read the site as evidence that warfare was part of the repertoire of relations between groups of prehistoric hunter-gatherers.

2351.content: Answering Stojanowski and colleagues, who argued that the Nataruk skull fractures came from soil compression and that the site was a cemetery, Mirazon Lahr and colleagues state that most remains were disarticulated and scattered over 20,000 square metres, with no burial pits, that skull 71264 carries two separate impact lesions with in-bent bone and radiating fractures, and that the traumas include embedded projectiles. They hold that conflict between groups remains the best explanation of the site.

2352.content: Among 27 Hadza forager men of northern Tanzania (saliva sampled in 2004), the 10 fathers who were nurturing young children and sharing a hearth with them had 30% lower morning and 47% lower evening salivary testosterone than the 15 men not caring for children (morning 124 against 176 pmol per litre, p=0.03; evening 83 against 157, p=0.007). Among 80 neighbouring Datoga pastoralist men, whose fathers give little direct infant care and sleep apart from wives and children, fathers and non-fathers did not differ. Hadza fathers of younger children showed a larger fall in testosterone from morning to evening (Spearman rho -0.659, n=10).

2353.content: Among one group of Aka forest foragers of the Central African Republic, women net-hunted more often than men. Most of the conditions that theory expects for women's hunting were present: game was relatively abundant, women got relatively high caloric returns from hunting, animals were caught at the same moment, hunting took place with other adults, women had access to the nets, men had little ideological or political control over women, and cultural precedent let women learn hunting.

2354.content: Among 474 adults in three Indigenous societies that mix foraging with farming (137 Tsimane' of lowland Bolivia, 225 Baka of Cameroon, 112 Punan of Indonesian Borneo), asked every three months in 2012 to 2013 to rate their life from very bad (0) to very good (4), the average across 1,180 ratings was 2.54, between fair and good, and 'good' was the most common answer (51.2%, 59.0% and 46.6% of ratings). People gave no reason for 41.4% of ratings, and far more often for positive than for negative ones (Tsimane' 37.3% against 5%, Baka 56.2% against 26.9%, Punan 63.1% against 7.4%). Averages lay within about one point of World Values Survey national averages on a 0 to 10 scale: the Baka above Cameroon (5.46 against 4.24), the Tsimane' and Punan below Bolivia and Indonesia.

Among the Baka of southeastern Cameroon, average life satisfaction was highest (2.9 on a 0 to 4 scale) in the quarter when they go to forest camps to hunt and collect honey and other forest products, and almost one point lower (2.06) in the quarter of opening farm plots, when workload peaks and food is scarce. The Tsimane' and Punan showed less seasonal change.

2355.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists of Bolivia (a skills survey of 421 adults aged 15 to 86 in 2006), 5% of adults aged 15 to 29 and 44% of those aged 60 and over said they told stories. Of the 54 adults who knew at least one of 120 traditional stories, older adults knew more stories and were more likely to tell the stories they knew; 96.7% of the stories held information relevant to food production or social life.

Of 128 story-source nominations made by 54 story-knowledgeable Tsimane adults, 89% named kin and 84% named same-sex older relatives. Grandparents were the most named source (38%), ahead of parents (30%) and aunts or uncles (14%); in the regression, older and closer kin of the same sex were more likely to be named, while being a parent added nothing.

2356.content: In a symposium paper using the !Kung (San) of the Dobe area, Botswana, as the example, Truswell reports that they showed no qualitative deficiency of specific nutrients, though they were thin and may be undernourished by Western standards in some seasons; they showed little or no obesity, dental caries, high blood pressure or coronary heart disease, their blood lipid concentrations were very low, and they could live to a good old age if they survived infections or accidents.

2357.content: Among San of the northwestern Kalahari, whose diets ranged from almost all wild bush food to large amounts of domestic food (mainly milk and maize meal), food intake and production were recorded for more than a year: mean weight and serum lipids were higher in San who ate substantial amounts of domestic food than in those who ate bush food, and body weight rose and fell with the seasons of food production.

2358.content: At Dmanisi, Georgia, a skull and jaw of early Homo from about 1.77 million years ago belonged to an individual who had lost all but one tooth several years before death. The authors call it the earliest case of severe chewing impairment so far found in the hominin fossil record and say it raises questions about other ways of getting food in early Homo.

2359.content: In prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster), a rodent that forms lasting pair bonds, three lines of CRISPR mutants with no functional oxytocin receptor (Oxtr; no receptor binding found in the brain) were housed for 7 days with an opposite-sex wild-type partner. Males and females of every line then spent more time huddling with their partner than with a stranger and, except Oxtr1 males, attacked the stranger more, like wild-type voles, in two different test set-ups (for one line, 21 mutant males and 21 mutant females against 25 and 19 wild-type).

Prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster) mothers with no functional oxytocin receptor gave birth to live pups, and mutant mothers and fathers spent as much time in the nest, in contact with their pups and (mothers) nursing as wild-type parents. Mutant mothers weaned fewer pups per litter, and their pups weighed less at weaning, which the authors read as a milk let-down deficit. In mice lacking the receptor, by contrast, all pups die shortly after birth because milk let-down fails.

2360.content: In a review in Science, Donaldson and Young state that oxytocin and vasopressin are ancient neuropeptides whose gene structure and expression are markedly conserved across species, and that differences in the genetic regulation of their receptors appear to underlie natural variation in social behaviour, both between species and between individuals of one species. They add that human studies were beginning to link variation in the receptor genes to variation in human social behaviour.

2361.content: In wild eastern chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) of Gombe National Park, Tanzania, with genetic paternity for 56 infants born between 1980 and 2014, males with more strong association ties (other males they spent more than the community average time with in small parties) were more likely to sire a given infant: one standard deviation more strong ties went with a 63% higher probability of siring (odds ratio 1.63), after accounting for male age, dominance rank and relatedness to the mother. The link held when the total time a male spent with others was added (odds ratio 1.52). Grooming measures did not improve the model.

In the same Gombe chimpanzee community (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii), subordinate males that had a strong relationship with the alpha male, and subordinate males with many strong association ties to other non-alpha males, were more likely to sire offspring than other subordinate males. Strong bonds with the beta male did not go with more siring. Males with stronger association ties were also more likely to form fighting coalitions together. Among non-alpha males, rank itself did not go with siring once the alpha was excluded; alpha males sired 20% of offspring and males of ranks two to ten roughly 7 to 10% each.

2362.content: Reviewing comparative anatomy across vertebrates, Knobloch and Grinevich state that oxytocin-family peptides (isotocin in fish, mesotocin in amphibians and birds, oxytocin in mammals) are released into the blood in all vertebrates, while release by axons reaching forebrain regions appears only in advanced vertebrates, especially mammals. In basal vertebrates (jawless fish, fish, amphibians) the peptides act mainly through the cerebrospinal fluid and go with simple, stereotyped reproductive behaviour. They review effects on social behaviour in each class: social vocalisation in the plainfin midshipman fish (Porichthys notatus), time spent in groups and with familiar birds in zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), nesting in turtles, and pair bonding in voles. They speculate that the spread of oxytocin axons into the forebrain and the appearance of complex reproductive and social behaviour are causally linked.

2363.content: In wild Assamese macaques (Macaca assamensis), a species in which males disperse, a study of social bonds among males in multimale groups, with genetic paternity, found that males formed differentiated bonds. Stronger bonds went with forming more coalitions, coalitions went with higher dominance later, and later dominance went with paternity. The strength of a male's bonds was also directly linked to the number of offspring he sired. The authors conclude that close relationships matter for breeding success in both sexes, beyond relatedness.

2364.content: In ovariectomised female prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster), a monogamous rodent, oxytocin infused into the brain ventricles at 10 or 100 ng per hour during 6 hours of cohabitation with a male was followed by a significant preference for that partner over an unfamiliar male in a choice test. Females given artificial cerebrospinal fluid showed no such preference, oxytocin given under the skin had no effect, and a selective oxytocin receptor blocker given into the brain prevented the effect.

2365.content: At the Sibilo School Road Site in the Kapthurin Formation, Baringo, Kenya, a Middle Stone Age site with a minimum age of about 200,000 years from the tuffs that encase it, 43% of the stone tool assemblage is obsidian. Geochemistry traces the obsidian to three sources 25 km, 140 km and 166 km away, and most of it comes from the farthest source, 166 km to the south. The author reads this as evidence that long-distance transport of raw material, and the wider contact between groups it implies, was part of hominin behaviour around the time Homo sapiens first appears, about 150,000 years earlier than such behaviour was previously documented in the region.

2366.content: Among the Palanan Agta, hunter-gatherers of the northern Philippines, genealogies collected from all adults in 2013 and 2014 covered 80 marriages. In 78 the spouses had no known shared ancestry, one couple were second cousins and one first cousins. The authors note that in principle the Agta forbid marriage between people who can call each other by a kinship term, with exceptions sometimes made. In 67 of 78 couples with ages known (86%) the husband was older; the mean gap was 4.3 years (SD 5.3), ranging from the wife 7.1 years older to the husband 32.7 years older, the second largest gap being 13.1 years. Together with residence near the kin of both spouses, this gives each household kin in many camps: on average a household could live in 6.7 of the 15 camps.

2367.content: Using United Nations Demographic Yearbook divorce data for 58 peoples, for all available years from 1947 to 1981, Fisher found a consistent pattern: divorces peak early in marriage, on or around the fourth year, and then decline slowly. Divorce risk peaks at ages 25 to 29 for men and 20 to 29 for women, and divorces peak among couples with two or fewer children. The pattern appears in societies with high and with low divorce rates. Data on horticultural and gathering-hunting societies also show divorce peaking among young couples early in marriage, and remarriage of the divorced and widowed of reproductive age is common across cultures.

Fisher proposes that the roughly four-year modal duration of marriages that end in divorce reflects a hominid reproductive strategy that evolved some time after the appearance of Homo, in response to the increased burden on females of raising a dependent infant, and that functioned to keep the infant alive through weaning; serial pairbonding through a woman's reproductive years would have had adaptive advantages.

2368.content: Interviewing 35 Aka foragers and 21 Ngandu farmers of the Central African Republic who were or had been married, the Hewletts found that adults aged 18 to 45 reported sex (coitus) with their spouse about 3.0 times per night among the Aka and 2.2 among the Ngandu, with about 2.1 and 2.7 days of rest between nights with sex; men and women of each group gave similar figures, and age did not change the frequency per night significantly. Both groups explained frequent sex as work to conceive and to help the fetus grow: 'I had sex with him to get infants, not for pleasure, and to show that I loved him' (an Aka woman). Pleasure was named, and placed second.

Among the Aka foragers, the Hewletts found no word for masturbation or for same-sex relations, and Aka men and women had difficulty understanding either when it was described. Men asked about masturbating before marriage or during the post-partum sex taboo all said it did not occur. All Aka and Ngandu interviewed said same-sex relations were unknown or rare. The authors add a personal report from a researcher among Lese men of the Ituri forest that explaining self-stimulation to collect semen samples was very difficult. Aka men either did not hold the post-partum taboo or did not seek other women during it, while almost all Ngandu men said they held the taboo, did not keep it, and sought other women.

2369.content: In a cross-cultural study of responses to a spouse's extramarital affair, Jankowiak and colleagues found that in every culture they examined both men and women actively used mate-guarding tactics to control their partner's extramarital behaviour. How much interest and involvement a person showed did not change with the culture's descent system, its level of social complexity, or whether its norms on sex were permissive or restrictive. The authors read this as support for the sexual jealousy and pair-bond hypotheses: every marriage or love relationship assumes sexual exclusivity, for both sexes.

2370.content: Lovejoy argues that Ardipithecus ramidus shows that living African apes are highly derived and poor models for the last common ancestor, and that the uniquely hominid traits of upright walking and a reduced canine appear to have emerged shortly after the split from the chimpanzee line. He proposes an adaptive suite for the emergence of Ardipithecus that accounts for the main differences between apes and humans.

2371.content: From over 145 teeth of Ardipithecus ramidus from the Middle Awash, Suwa and colleagues report that the species was nearly monomorphic in canine size and shape: males and females had canines of similar size. The canine and lower third premolar complex shows that canine size and its honing function were reduced early in hominid evolution, possibly through selection on the male upper canine.

2372.content: Using the ratio of the second to the fourth proximal finger bone (a proposed marker of prenatal androgen exposure that is lower in polygynous than in pair-bonded living primates), Nelson and colleagues compared fossil hand bones with living apes and 320 contemporary humans. The single Ardipithecus ramidus hand (found associated in situ) and two Miocene apes (Pierolapithecus catalaunicus, Hispanopithecus laietanus) had ratios like those of polygynous great apes and were classed as non-pair-bonded; the Australopithecus afarensis hand fell within the human range and was classed as pair-bonded or intermediate. The authors state that the Ardipithecus result conflicts with Lovejoy's claim, from canine and body size, that Ardipithecus was pair-bonded.

In the same study, five Neanderthal hands (Kebara 2, Shanidar 4, La Ferrassie I, Le Regourdou, Spy II) had a mean second-to-fourth finger-bone ratio of 0.928, against 0.957 in 320 contemporary humans; only 19 of 10,000 resampled sets of five modern humans had a mean as low (about 0.2%). The early modern human Qafzeh 9 (about 90,000 years ago) fell at the low end of the modern range, close to a polygynous Zulu sample. The authors read this as more androgen exposure and possibly more polygyny and male competition in Neanderthals and early modern humans than in most living human populations, with variation between individuals suggesting flexible mating systems.

2373.content: From 19th-century ethnohistorical records of south-eastern Australia, McBryde finds that goods moved between Aboriginal groups mostly at inter-group meetings and ceremonies, and through gifts tied to social and ceremonial obligations, among them initiation ceremonies and marriage arrangements. Greenstone from the Mt William quarry, owned by Kulin people, was a valued gift item: the densest areas of distribution of Mt William greenstone artefacts coincide with the territories of groups who intermarried with the Kulin. She notes that some groups travelled to Mt William for stone although their own territory held greenstone and basalt, and reads this as social and symbolic value beyond need.

McBryde reports that at the Mt William stone quarry outsiders were not allowed to quarry the stone themselves and had to negotiate with the people who held the right to do so; reed spears from the Goulburn reed beds and possum-skin rugs are recorded in exchange, one rug being worth three pieces of stone at the quarry. Messengers were sometimes sent to tell the owners of a need so that a meeting could be arranged. Further inland the Dieri and Yantruwunta of eastern Central Australia travelled hundreds of miles beyond their own country to collect red ochre, sandstone slabs and the narcotic pituri.

2374.content: Summarising Isabel McBryde's petrological and ethnohistorical work on greenstone axes in central Victoria, Brumm states that axes from the Mt William quarry were distributed further than axes from equivalent sources, which he reads as a sign of symbolic value that a purely economic account cannot explain; he places the quarry within Aboriginal beliefs about landscape and the cosmos.

2375.content: Among 100 Himba of the Omuhonga Basin, Namibia (a natural fertility pastoralist population; 49 men and 51 women aged 15 or over), a face-to-face forced-choice vignette asked which was more distressing when a partner both had sex with and fell in love with someone else. 96% of men (47 of 49) and 66% of women chose the sexual infidelity; both sexes chose it above chance, and men chose it more often than women (chi squared 13.89, p below 0.001). With the same vignette, American, Korean and Japanese students gave 33% to 61% of men and 13% to 27% of women choosing the sexual infidelity.

Among the 51 Himba women, the only variable associated with which infidelity upset them more was whether their current or most recent marriage was a love match: women in love matches more often chose the emotional infidelity (chi squared 4.45, p 0.035). Women's own comments tied a husband's sex with another woman to the risk that he would leave them, earlier life-history interviews record lovers giving goods and cows for children of affairs, and men's comments tied it to raising and paying for another man's child ('he eats your cattle').

2376.content: The review reports that virgin male and female laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus) usually avoid contact with foreign pups, yet after continuous exposure to pups they approach them and eventually care for them, a process called sensitization. The model the authors describe has two competing circuits: in virgin males and most virgin females an aversive circuit fed by the vomeronasal (smell) pathway and the medial amygdala dominates and suppresses care, while in females after birth and in sensitized females hormonal, neuromodulatory and experience-dependent factors switch on the caring circuit and silence the avoidance circuit.

The review reports a recent study in house mice (Mus musculus): galanin-expressing neurons of the medial preoptic area are active during parenting by both sexes. Killing these cells impaired parental responses in virgin females, mothers and fathers and brought out attacks on pups in virgin females, while switching them on with light (optogenetics) in virgin males suppressed attacks on pups and brought out pup grooming. The review also reports that laboratory male mice commonly kill pups while virgin and become paternal for a period after mating that starts around the time their own pups are born.

2377.content: Laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus) that had not given birth were exposed to young pups continuously for 10 to 15 days: intact, ovary-removed and pituitary-removed females, and intact and castrated males. Nearly all of them showed the four main items of maternal behaviour, with only minor differences between groups in how long it took to start. The author concludes that all rats have a basic level of maternal responsiveness that does not depend on hormones.

2378.content: In a free-ranging population of mandrills (Mandrillus sphinx) in Lekedi Park, southern Gabon, 25 individuals of known parasite status were watched for 2.5 years. Animals carrying more kinds of gut protozoa (transmitted by the orofecal route) received less grooming from group mates, and fewer grooming bouts on the perianal area, while the grooming they gave did not differ.
