After 16 animals were treated against protozoa, the grooming they received rose (Wilcoxon test, P below 0.01); 9 captured but untreated animals showed no rise. Close spatial association, logged for 13 animals over a year, did not depend on parasite status.

Gut protozoa changed the chemical make-up of mandrill faeces (gas chromatography and mass spectrometry on 59 samples from 30 animals). In 30 choice tests with 16 semi-free-ranging mandrills at a research centre in Franceville, Gabon, given two faecal samples from the same individual on bamboo, one carrying at least two more kinds of protozoa, the animals spent less time within 1 metre of the more parasitized sample (Wilcoxon test, P 0.014).

2379.content: Reviewing comparative work on topology, developmental gene expression, connections and neurochemistry, the authors conclude that the circuits for avoiding risk (defence) are similar in all vertebrates studied and include amygdala homologues in the back half of the cerebral hemispheres, closely tied to smell. With the reward circuits of the ventral striatum, this configuration was present at least in the common ancestor of amniotes (reptiles, birds and mammals), and likely also in amphibians and fish.

Frogs and other amphibians have a simpler amygdala with three parts: a lateral amygdala taking smell and other senses, a central amygdala and a medial amygdala, the last two probably matching the mammalian central and medial nuclei. Reptiles and birds have the fuller pattern seen in mammals. The authors read this as a challenge to the triune brain idea: reptiles and amphibians already have a 'limbic' system for emotional expression.

2380.content: Re-analysing Australopithecus afarensis fossils (the small skeletons Lucy and A.L. 128/129, the A.L. 333 assemblage and the large partial skeleton KSD-VP-1/1, 'Kadanuumuu'), with 1,000 simulated samples each from modern humans, chimpanzees and gorillas, the authors find that the Geometric Mean Method gives gorilla-like dimorphism (ratio 1.299) when Lucy and A.L. 128/129 supply most of the female measurements, and lower values when they do not (1.179 with Lucy scaled to 130% of her size). When each specimen contributes once, both the Template Method and the Geometric Mean Method place A. afarensis skeletal dimorphism within the modern human range.

2381.content: Yellen and Harpending argue that hunter-gatherers, given the kind of resources they use, spread their social relationships diffusely over large areas instead of clustering them in semi-discrete local groups. They read this in low genetic differentiation between local groups (low inbreeding) and in uniform artefact styles over large areas.

2382.content: Doubly labelled water measurements in four orangutans (Pongo spp.; three adults, one juvenile) living in a large indoor and outdoor habitat at the Great Ape Trust in Iowa showed daily energy expenditure for the adults nearly three standard deviations below the mammalian trend for body mass (mean z-score -2.81), in the lowest 1% of mammals and the lowest of any eutherian mammal measured except sloths, and below both sedentary industrial and active subsistence humans. Their activity level (estimated physical activity level 1.7) was similar to or above that of wild orangutans.

The authors read the very low energy use of orangutans (Pongo spp.) as an evolved, risk-averse strategy against starvation: the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra often go through crashes in the ripe fruit orangutans depend on, and the slow growth and reproduction of orangutans would follow from lower energy throughput rather than from a different allocation of energy. They add that in captivity this low requirement likely makes orangutans prone to overfeeding and obesity.

2383.content: In experiments with semi-free-ranging bonobos (Pan paniscus) at the Lola ya Bonobo sanctuary in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 56 bonobos offered three apple slices ate the clean slice in 86% of trials, a soil-covered slice in 21% and a slice smeared with faeces of other bonobos in 11%. When 52 bonobos were offered a chain of six banana slices with the first on top of fresh faeces, they ate the slice on the faeces significantly less often than any of the others, and 23% took none of the slices at all.

In the same series, bonobos (Pan paniscus) trying to reach food in a challenging foraging set-up touched and used tools less often when the odour of faeces, rotten chicken or spoiled banana was present than with a water control, and tasted less often with faeces odour, while a detergent odour did not reduce these behaviours. The authors write that the results fit the parasite avoidance theory of disgust but did not test it directly, and cannot conclude that the bonobos showed disgust.

2384.content: Reviewing work on bony fish, Volkoff reports that, as in mammals, feeding in fish is run by feeding centres in the brain that take in hormone signals from the brain and the gut. Orexins injected into the brain of goldfish (Carassius auratus) increased feeding, and as in mammals orexins raise appetite, locomotor activity and foraging in fish. Ghrelin raised food intake in goldfish and several other species, but in salmonids the evidence is contradictory: in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) ghrelin lowered food intake.

Volkoff stresses that fish differ from mammals in ways that change how energy balance is regulated: they are ectotherms with lower metabolic rates, store fat in the liver rather than under the skin, and keep growing after sexual maturity. In mammals leptin acts as a fat-store signal proportional to body fat, but the review finds little evidence for that role in fish, and the function of leptin in fish feeding varies a lot between species.

2385.content: Among 75 Shuar forager-horticulturalists (ages 5 to 59, 28 households, three communities in Amazonian Ecuador with a high pathogen burden), people who scored higher on a 19-item pathogen disgust questionnaire adapted for the Shuar had lower levels of inflammation markers of current infection (C-reactive protein and interleukin-6). Links between disgust scores and measures of intestinal worm infection (egg counts, IgE) were weaker and ran mostly through differences between households and communities.

Among the same Shuar communities, the most market-integrated community (more purchased goods and modern housing, less hunting and fishing) had the highest disgust scores and the lowest inflammation and worm infection, while the least market-integrated community had the lowest disgust scores and the highest infection. The authors read this as disgust being calibrated to the local costs of avoidance: where clean water, wood floors and other barriers make avoidance cheap, people are more easily disgusted.

2386.content: Measuring trabecular (spongy) bone density at the joint ends of limb bones by CT, the authors found that only recent (Holocene) modern humans, here a nonforaging sample from Puye and the industrial-era Terry collection, have low trabecular density throughout the limb joints. Australopithecus africanus, Paranthropus or early Homo from Swartkrans, Neanderthals and Pleistocene Homo sapiens all kept the high density seen in chimpanzees and other nonhuman primates; the drop was larger in the lower limb than in the upper limb.

2387.content: MicroCT of the top of the thigh bone (proximal femur) in 59 people from four archaeological North American populations and 229 individuals of 31 primate species showed that the two mobile forager populations had significantly higher trabecular bone volume fraction and thicker trabeculae, for body mass, than the two sedentary agriculturalist populations. The foragers' hip bone structure was close to what wild nonhuman primates of the same body mass have.

2388.content: In 1,842 skeletons from across Europe, from the Upper Paleolithic (11,000 to 33,000 years ago) to the 20th century, front-to-back bending strength of the thigh and shin bones relative to body size fell by 20 to 30% between the Upper Paleolithic and the Iron Age and Roman period, in both sexes. The decline began in the Neolithic (about 7,000 to 4,000 years ago), with the start of food production, continued gradually through the Bronze and Iron Ages, and showed no further directional change over the last 2,000 years. Upper limb bones changed much less, which the authors read as a decline in mobility.

2389.content: The authors report a new eutherian mammal (the clade that includes all living placentals) from the Jurassic of China, about 160 million years old. It pushes the first appearance of the eutherian-placental line back by about 35 million years from the earlier fossil record, which narrows the gap between the fossil record and molecular estimates of when placentals and marsupials split. The animal had forelimb features for climbing.

2390.content: In playback experiments on wild African elephants (Loxodonta africana), the authors found that the oldest female in a family group, with better discrimination of other elephants' calls, shaped the social knowledge of the group as a whole, and that this may give higher reproductive success per female in groups led by older individuals. They warn that removing older elephants, often targeted by hunters for their size, could seriously harm endangered populations of social mammals such as elephants and whales.

2391.content: In Amboseli National Park, Kenya, 72 playbacks of lion roars to 39 wild African elephant (Loxodonta africana) family groups showed that all groups reacted more defensively to three roaring lions than to one, but families with younger matriarchs typically under-reacted to roars of male lions, which are the more dangerous predators of elephant calves. Sensitivity to the male lion threat rose with matriarch age and was greatest in families led by the oldest matriarchs.

2392.content: Using wildlife cameras at raccoon (Procyon lotor) latrines, sites that concentrate both seeds and the eggs of a dangerous parasite, the authors recorded over 40 vertebrate species. Raccoons and rats, which tolerate the parasite, were drawn to the latrines, while susceptible birds and small mammals avoided them. The authors read this as parasites, like predators, creating a landscape of fear for vulnerable hosts.

2393.content: Reviewing fossil, archaeological and environmental evidence, the authors conclude that the traits once thought to have arisen together at the origin of Homo (large linear bodies, long legs, large brains, reduced difference in size between the sexes, more meat eating and the human life history) did not arise as one package: some arose earlier and some later. From about 2.5 to 1.5 million years ago three lineages of early Homo evolved amid unstable and fragmented habitats, on seasonal, generational and evolutionary time scales, which favoured traits such as dietary flexibility and larger body size that helped survival in shifting environments.

2394.content: Compiling published mean or median ages at first menstruation for 67 countries, the authors found that mean age at menarche was strongly linked to mean female life expectancy. Among the variables describing living conditions, adult illiteracy rate and vegetable calorie consumption explained the variation best, which the authors read as menarche tracking a girl's energy balance (including energy spent in physical work) more than nutrition alone. Age at menopause, available for 26 countries, was best explained by mean fertility.

2395.content: Examining 543 shin bones (tibiae) and ankle bones (tali) from French and American archaeological series dated from the 1st to the 20th century AD, the author used two skeletal markers formed by pressure and traction when knees and ankles are deeply bent: backward tilt of the top of the tibia and lateral squatting facets on the talus. The markers show that squatting was a regular posture until the end of the Middle Ages, and that it then declined progressively, which the author ties to different ways of life in different periods.

2396.content: In adult male skeletons from a late Byzantine (13th century AD) population in Turkey, lateral squatting facets on the neck of the talus, a bone change linked to habitual squatting, occurred in 37.7%. The authors report this as more frequent than in modern Europeans and similar to some modern Indian populations.

2397.content: In satellite-tracked female polar bears (Ursus maritimus) from Arctic Canada and Greenland, mean home range size was 125,100 square km (plus or minus 11,800; 93 bears), against a predicted 514 square km for a land carnivore of similar weight. Home range size was related to the ratio of land to sea inside the range (42 percent of explained variance) and to seasonal variation in ice cover (24 percent): bears that used land in the ice-free season, and bears living where ice cover varied most across the seasons, had larger ranges. The authors read large ranges as a trade-off: variable ice goes with more seals, but with seals that are harder to predict.

2398.content: A review of what makes fish (and squid) take hooks frames each fish's vulnerability as a state it switches in and out of, set by three linked processes: its internal state (above all hunger, and also aggression that does not depend on hunger, which together motivate it to take a bait or strike a lure), its encounter with the gear, and the traits of the gear, such as hook size and lure colour or type. The authors review evidence that fish learn to avoid gear (carp avoided recapture for up to a year, the crimson spotted rainbowfish (Melanotaenia duboulayi) avoided a trawl for up to 11 months) and argue that gear that mimics normal food items, particularly live bait, will be the hardest to learn to avoid.

2399.content: A review of abnormal repetitive behaviour (stereotypic pacing, over-grooming, self-biting, rocking and similar) in zoo animals argues that environmental enrichment is the preferred remedy, ahead of breeding, drugs, rewarding other behaviour or punishment, because it is the method most likely to tackle the problem behind the behaviour. From earlier zoo reviews it reports that only about 50 percent of enrichment attempts reduce the behaviour, that the mean reduction is about 50 percent, and that no study abolished it in all its subjects; pacing has been seen to persist after animals were moved from small, barren enclosures to large, enriched ones. The authors offer two readings: the enrichments used are never quite optimal, or by the time they are tried the behaviour has become resistant to change.

The same review collects surveys of how many zoo animals show abnormal repetitive behaviour: 76 percent of 55 felids scan-sampled across eight zoos; 13.2 percent of 440 prosimians in 48 accredited US institutions; and in a survey of over 3000 zoo primates, 7 percent of prosimians, 7 percent of New World monkeys, 13.8 percent of Old World monkeys and 39.6 percent of apes. Adding zoo census figures, the authors estimate that over 10,000 zoo animals worldwide are affected, which they call probably an under-estimate.

2400.content: Mason's review of stereotypies (repetitive, invariant behaviour with no obvious goal) reports that they are seen in captive animals, in institutionalized humans and in subjects given stimulant drugs, and that they are often linked in place and time to sub-optimal features of the environment: barren and restrictive housing, frustration, fear and the expected arrival of food. The closer the confinement, the more stereotypy developed in sows, rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) and bank voles (Clethrionomys glareolus), and bank voles performed less stereotypy when moved from a small cage to a bigger, more enriched enclosure. Mason concludes that the acquisition of stereotypies indicates an environment that is probably inadequate, while whether current performance means current suffering cannot be inferred without knowing what performing it does for the animal.

The review contrasts two kinds of stereotypy. 'Deprivation' stereotypies appear in animals isolated or deprived of sensory input since birth or infancy; they are very hard to disrupt and may persist when the animal is put into a normal environment, though deprived rhesus monkeys have been cured with infant 'therapist' monkeys. 'Cage' stereotypies tend to be locomotory, are typical of small or barren cages and can be altered by changes in the environment; Ridley and Baker (1982) proposed that they are the response of a normal central nervous system to a sub-optimal environment.

2401.content: Mason's review of how species differ in their response to captivity lists species that fare worse in zoos than benchmark protected populations: forest duikers (Cephalophus spp.) with infant mortality of 30 to 40 percent; giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis) with shorter lives than protected wild giraffes, at least 75 percent of the North American population showing oral stereotypic behaviour such as wall licking; African elephants (Loxodonta africana) with shorter lives than protected wild elephants and zoo-born Asian elephants (Elephas maximus) with shorter lives than those born in Burmese timber camps, at least half of zoo elephants showing stereotypic behaviour; cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus) with raised cortisol output and enlarged adrenal glands; Humboldt penguins (Spheniscus humboldti) in UK zoos with about half the chick output of undisturbed wild colonies. Close relatives of these species fare well in similar conditions, which she reads as a sign that the poorly faring species have needs that are hard to meet in captivity or not yet understood.

2402.content: Recording stereotyped calls from groups of travelling killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) that swam steadily toward or away from a towed hydrophone array, Miller compared energy above 5 kHz with energy at 1 to 5 kHz. In call types with a separately modulated high-frequency component, high-frequency energy was significantly greater when the whales swam toward the array, by more than 10 dB at the fundamental of that component in the two most common call types. Miller proposes that the change in a call's spectrum with the caller's orientation gives listeners a built-in cue to the caller's direction of movement, which could help the whales coordinate behaviour and keep spacing.

2403.content: In male C57BL/6 laboratory mice (Mus musculus) given running wheels, total energy expenditure rose by about 4 percent in the first three days of wheel use in calorimetry chambers (the 10 of 15 mice that used the wheels), and by about 30 percent from baseline to the first week in home cages (7 mice, 8.5 to 11.0 kcal per day), but did not rise further in weeks two and three although wheel running kept increasing (by 52,000 and then 44,000 wheel turns). In a third group (8 mice) wheel running went with less walking off the wheel throughout the wheel phase, and across 41 mice the amount of daily wheel running did not correlate with total energy expenditure (R squared 0.08, p = 0.08) or food intake. The authors conclude that going from sedentary to light activity raises daily energy expenditure, while further activity adds diminishingly small increments, held down by compensation such as less off-wheel movement.

2404.content: A review of the behavioural needs and priorities of laying hens (Gallus gallus domesticus) concludes that hens appear to have an instinctive need for pre-laying nest-building behaviour and a strong preference for a separate, enclosed nest site, which they will work hard to reach as laying approaches; at that time access to a nest is a high-ranking priority, preferred over food. Foraging is also a behavioural need: hens forage as much when food is freely available and when a cost is imposed. The authors read apparently purposeless behaviour, high aggression and redirected behaviour such as feather pecking and cannibalism as signs that a housing system is not meeting the hens' behavioural needs.

2405.content: Dissection of 13 adult bonobos (Pan paniscus; 6 females, 7 males) that died in captivity found that the fat which could be dissected from trunk and limbs ranged from under 1 to 8.6 percent of body mass in females, while all males had negligible amounts (under 0.01 percent). For comparison the authors list human body fat of 19.0 percent in Hadza women and 10.6 percent in Hadza men of Tanzania, and 28.8 and 19.7 percent in urban Geneva women and men. Among the bonobo females, the one with most fat was lactating at death and one with remarkably little fat (1.2 percent) had never been pregnant. The authors conclude that the ability to store and mobilise body fat must have played a growing role in successful reproduction in human evolution, alongside buffering seasonal and unpredictable food supply.

2406.content: Laboratory mice (Mus musculus) were randomly split at postnatal day 10: one group was exposed for 6 hours every night for 42 days to audio from a cartoon channel at 70 dB and coloured lights changing with the sound on all four cage walls, the other was reared normally. Ten days after exposure ended, overstimulated mice spent more time in the open arms of an elevated plus maze (31.0 against 9.9 seconds; 61 and 48 mice) and in the lit chamber of a light-dark box (82.4 against 53.8 seconds), did worse on novel object recognition, and took longer to find the target hole on the last training day of a Barnes maze. The authors read this as more activity and risk taking, poorer short-term memory and poorer cognitive function after excessive stimulation that no mouse would meet in a natural setting.

2407.content: Reviewing their mouse model of excessive sensory stimulation (6 hours a night of cartoon-channel audio and synchronised coloured lights from postnatal day 10 for 42 days), the authors report that exposed mice travelled further in an open field (72 mice per group), spent more time in open and lit spaces, and learned and remembered worse, and that they also found changes in glutamate transmission in the nucleus accumbens and amygdala. A different group in Israel exposed juvenile rats (Rattus norvegicus) to 1 hour a day of strong, frequently changed odours, and those rats did worse on a five-choice serial reaction time task when sound distractors were present. The authors found no difference in cortisol or body weight between exposed and control mice, and read the results as effects of the intensity of stimulation, independent of content.

2408.content: In 34 patients diagnosed with major depression and 33 matched healthy controls, the patients' gut microbiota showed lower richness and diversity (16S rRNA sequencing of stool). Faecal microbiota from a subgroup of patients and controls was given by oral gavage to rats (Rattus norvegicus) whose own gut microbiota had been depleted. Rats that received the patients' microbiota showed behaviour the authors call characteristic of depression, less interest in reward (anhedonia) and more anxiety-like behaviour, along with changes in tryptophan metabolism. The authors suggest the gut microbiota may play a causal role in features of depression.

2409.content: Reviewing genome and functional data across animals, the authors report a Toll-like receptor (TLR) gene in the starlet sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis), TLR-related genes without the receptor's outer leucine-rich repeats in Hydra, a coral and a demosponge (Suberites domuncula), and TLRs in most animal groups from cnidarians to vertebrates, apparently absent in flatworms and not found outside animals. They place the origin of TLRs in the common ancestor of cnidarians and bilaterians more than 600 million years ago, and of TLR-related genes in the ancestor of all animals more than 700 million years ago. Functional studies existed for only five species, and the authors suggest that different TLRs may have been recruited independently to similar immune roles in insects and vertebrates.

2410.content: In three experiments with adult male rats (Rattus norvegicus; Sprague-Dawley in the first two, Lewis in the third; groups of 8), a light was paired with sucrose for 15 daily sessions with a reward probability of 0, 25, 50, 75 or 100 percent. After a two-week rest the rats were given amphetamine. In all three experiments the group trained on the 50 percent schedule, the one closest to the payout rate of a commercial slot machine (about 46 percent of spins), moved more in response to both challenge doses than the other groups. The authors call the effects modest but consistent and read them as sensitisation of the dopamine system by a gambling-like schedule, much like exposure to amphetamine itself.

2411.content: Adult house mice (Mus musculus) living in an enriched environment had significantly more new neurons in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus than littermates housed in standard cages. Counted by unbiased stereology, the enriched mice also had a larger hippocampal granule cell layer and 15 percent more granule cell neurons in the dentate gyrus.

2412.content: Twenty-two pregnant late-lactation Holstein dairy cows (Bos taurus) in Canada were trained to push a weighted gate, made 7 kg heavier each day, to reach either fresh feed after milking or an outdoor pasture; when tested for pasture they had fresh feed inside the barn all the time. Most cows (59 percent) pushed as hard or harder for pasture as for fresh feed; the mean maximum weight pushed was 31.2 kg for pasture and 36.9 kg for feed, a difference the tests did not detect. Cows pushed harder for pasture after the evening milking (29.3 kg) than in the morning (23.6 kg).

2413.content: In Fondwa, a rural mountain community in Haiti with no electricity for the general population, 58 adults aged 18 to 88 wore wrist actigraphs for 3 nights in February 2003, when sunset fell between 17:24 and 17:55 and sunrise between 6:09 and 6:25. Mean sleep onset was 20:57, sleep end 4:54, time in bed 9.3 hours and actual sleep 7.0 hours, with 54 minutes awake after sleep onset. Nobody slept in a room alone; on average 3.5 people slept in the participant's room. Men and women did not differ.

In the same Fondwa sample, sleep duration, timing, time awake after sleep onset and sleep maintenance did not differ between age groups from 18 to 35 up to 65 and over. Only sleep fragmentation differed, and it was higher in the youngest group than in all older groups. The author contrasts this with the decline in sleep duration and quality with age reported from industrialised countries.

2414.content: In laboratory house mice (Mus musculus), every mouse's running-wheel rhythm was entrained by a light-dark cycle, but only 60 to 80 percent were entrained by daily cycles of ambient temperature (24 to 32 degrees C or 24 to 12 degrees C), and stable entrainment seemed to take longer. With 24-hour temperature cycles 80 percent entrained, with 23-hour cycles 60 percent, and with 25-hour cycles none. The author concludes that temperature cycles are weaker time cues than light-dark cycles, in line with the few earlier studies of mammals.

2415.content: Witherington and Martin report that hatchling sea turtles led off course by artificial light on Florida beaches are taken by beach crabs or shorebirds or die of exhaustion and dehydration in the dunes, and that only the most conspicuous cases are ever seen. As one example they cite the discovery of hundreds of dead loggerhead (Caretta caretta) hatchlings beneath a mercury-vapor light at Melbourne Beach, Florida, a light that had been left on and had drawn hatchlings over many nights.

Witherington and Martin explain why artificial light misleads hatchlings more than the moon does: a celestial light field is lit from many directions, while near a beach lamp the light field is dominated by the one source, which acts as a supernormal stimulus that overrides the hatchlings' other visual cues. In Florida in 1992, 201 cases of hatchling disorientation were reported, most of them on nights on or near the new moon, when no moonlight competed with the artificial lights (data from Salmon and Witherington 1995).

2416.content: Fochesato, Bogaard and Bowles built 150 adjusted wealth Gini coefficients for archaeological site-phases in Eurasia and North and Central America, from 23,000-year-old Ohalo II to 18th-century Pacific Northwest communities, correcting raw Ginis for small samples (which bias them upward), for households without property that leave no trace, and for the use of grave goods instead of house sizes. The average adjustment was 15 percent of the raw Gini, so they judge unadjusted archaeological Ginis to be in general quite unreliable; the adjusted values ranged from about 0.1 to almost 0.8.

In the same study, small samples drawn from much larger populations gave fairly accurate and precise Gini estimates once corrected, and the authors found no plausible adjustment that would change the pattern that Neolithic populations of western Eurasia had considerably less wealth inequality than many later societies. They state that their corrected measures reinforce the main finding of Kohler and colleagues (2017), that post-Neolithic wealth disparities were greater in Eurasia than in North America and Mesoamerica.

2417.content: Garfield, Syme and Hagen coded 109 dimensions of leadership in 1,212 ethnographic texts on 59 mostly nonindustrial societies in the Human Relations Area Files. Candidate universals were that leaders were intelligent and knowledgeable, resolved conflicts and received material and social benefits. Other features varied with subsistence and group context: hunter-gatherers tended to lack leaders with coercive authority, and leaders of kin groups were older and gave counsel and direction. Material, social and mating benefits stood out for leaders.

2418.content: Among Baka foragers living in three roadside settlements in southeastern Cameroon (near Lotong quarter, Moloundou subdivision, studied October 1993 to January 1994; settlements of 24, 63 and 61 people), meat owners generally sold about half of the meat they trapped to passing truck drivers for cash and shared the rest within the settlement, and the other residents accepted this. Cooked meat was never sold, to drivers or to other Baka, although the neighbouring farmers sold cooked meat, which brought them more income than raw meat. Kitanishi reads this as cooked food becoming a resource of the hut-group alone.

In the Baka settlements, a cook almost always gave portions of a meal only within her own hut-group, and sharing between hut-groups was nearly absent: in one settlement 128 and 171 meal shares went within the two hut-groups against 2 and 4 between them, and in another 152 and 189 within against 2 and 5 between. Among the Aka, by contrast, a large stew was shared beyond the cook's hut-group. Kitanishi links the fixed Baka meal partners to settled life, with residential groups that changed little.

2419.content: Wrangham, Wilson and Muller assembled data on lethal aggression from long-term studies of nine communities of chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) in five populations. Average rates of death from aggression in chimpanzees were similar to average rates in subsistence societies of hunter-gatherers and farmers, with high variation between communities. For non-lethal physical aggression, compared in two chimpanzee populations and one population of recently settled hunter-gatherers, chimpanzees had rates two to three orders of magnitude higher than the humans.

2420.content: Animal evidence. Reviewing studies of insects, Adamo reports that turning on the immune response produces the same set of behavioural changes seen in vertebrates across a broad range of insect species: illness-induced loss of appetite, behavioural fever (moving to warmer places), changes in reproductive behaviour and poorer learning. Fight-or-flight behaviour goes with lower disease resistance, which she reads as physiological conflict between the immune response and other body processes.

2421.content: Animal evidence. Heart rate was recorded by telemetry in two middle-ranking adult female rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) living in a large group, while their behaviour was observed, controlling for posture and activity. Heart rate slowed faster while a female was being groomed than in matched control periods.

Animal evidence. In the same two rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) females, heart rate rose after a dominant individual approached them, a risk of aggression the authors expected to be tense for the approached female, and did not rise when the approacher was kin or a subordinate.

2422.content: Animal evidence. Male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) gave up fluid reward for the chance to view pictures of female perinea and of the faces of high-status monkeys, and had to be overpaid in fluid to view the faces of low-status monkeys. The value was highly consistent across subjects and did not depend on the particular images shown.

2423.content: Animal evidence. Eisenstein and Carlson review the behaviour called learned helplessness across the animal kingdom and report that its basic characteristics are similar in intact mammals, lower vertebrates and invertebrates, and are seen even in an isolated thoracic ganglion of an insect, so that a brain is not needed to show it in mammals or in invertebrates.
Eisenstein and Carlson argue that the presence of the behaviour in so many phyla suggests it may be adaptive in a natural ecological setting even though it looks maladaptive in the laboratory.

2424.content: Animal evidence. Reviewing behavioural, connectional and hormone-receptor data, Goodson reports that birds and teleost (bony) fish have a core social behaviour network in the basal forebrain and midbrain homologous to the one described for mammals (medial amygdala and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, lateral septum, preoptic area, anterior hypothalamus, ventromedial hypothalamus and midbrain). The nodes are reciprocally connected, carry sex steroid receptors and take part in several kinds of social behaviour, including aggression, sexual behaviour, communication, bonding, parental care and responses to social stress.

Animal evidence. Goodson reports that in the lateral septum, one node of this network, responses to aggressive encounters are greater in subordinate male Syrian hamsters (Mesocricetus auratus) than in dominant ones, and that in his own work immediate-early-gene responses of the lateral septum fell as aggression rose in wild-caught territorial male song sparrows (Melospiza melodia).

2425.content: Kah and colleagues review GnRH and its receptors across animals. GnRH is the hormone that starts and maintains the vertebrate reproductive axis through the pituitary, and they report that recent data suggest it arose in animals that have no pituitary, controlling simple basic functions in early animals before it came to control the gonads indirectly in vertebrates.

2426.content: Levitis, Burger and Lackey argue that two traits have been lumped together as post-reproductive lifespan: post-fertile viability, surviving past the end of fertility, which is widespread across animal species, and a post-fertile life stage, which they describe as derived in hominins. Comparative gerontologists treat human post-fertile life as one case of a cross-species pattern, quantitatively greater though not qualitatively different; anthropologists treat it as derived; the authors hold that both views contain valid points.

2427.content: Among 90 natives of Easter Island (Rapa Nui) over 45 years old, given full clinical and hearing tests, those who had lived in industrialized societies heard worse than those who had always lived on the island, and the loss grew with the years spent away. The median hearing thresholds of natives who had always lived on the island were similar to those of US women, with no significant difference between island men and women.

2428.content: Salivary cortisol was collected on waking and before bed for three days from 303 Tsimane foragers of the Bolivian Amazon aged 1.6 to 82 (1,564 samples). Their mean cortisol levels and their day slopes were the lowest reported in any population-based study of the stress-hormone axis, dramatically lower than in industrialized populations. Within the Tsimane, cortisol rose with age into adulthood, was higher in adult women than men, and the day slope flattened sharply after age 60.

2429.content: Among the Martu of Australia's Western Desert, where women hunt extensively, women hunt mainly small, predictable game (lizards) to feed small kin networks and children and to keep up cooperative ties with other women, trading large harvests for certainty. Men hunt as a political strategy, using what the authors call competitive magnanimity to rise in the ritual hierarchy, which favours kangaroo, the prey that feeds the most people with the most meat, at the cost of reliable food for the hunter's own family.

2430.content: Using spot-check time allocation data from the UCLA Time Allocation Project (45,019 observations of 863 adults in 8 small-scale populations studied between 1972 and 1987: Kipsigis of Kenya, Mekranoti of Brazil, Madurese of Indonesia, two Machiguenga communities of Peru, Efe of the Ituri Forest, Ye'kwana and Yukpa of Venezuela), men whose work was entirely non-commercial worked about 45 to 47 hours a week, and a shift to fully commercial work went with about 10 to 15 more hours. Women worked about 53 to 55 hours a week whatever the commercial share. Work counted food production, food preparation, housework, manufacture, commercial work, childcare and gathering information; time at night was not observed. Adding 14 OECD countries gave the same pattern across societies.

The authors conclude that market participation does not come with less work time in their data, and that even the least commercial people generally work harder than Sahlins claimed for the 'original affluent society', with wide variation between societies.

2431.content: Applying costly signaling theory to ethnographic data on turtle hunting and public feasts among the Meriam of the Torres Strait, Australia, Smith and Bliege Bird report that turtle hunting meets its key conditions: it is an honest signal of strength, risk-taking, skill and leadership; it is costly in ways that are not paid back; it reaches many people, as the feast draws a large audience; and it seems to benefit the hunters as well as the feast-goers.

2432.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 diary studies (33 samples, 8,690 infants) found mean total fussing and crying over 24 hours stable at 117 to 133 minutes (SD 66 to 70) in the first 6 weeks of life, falling to a mean of 68 minutes (SD 46.2) by 10 to 12 weeks. Across studies the authors found no statistical evidence for a universal crying peak at 6 weeks.

In the same meta-analysis, colic by modified Wessel criteria was found in 17 to 25 percent of infants in the first 6 weeks, 11 percent at 8 to 9 weeks and 0.6 percent at 10 to 12 weeks, and was least frequent in Denmark and Japan.

2433.content: A meta-analysis of 32 samples from eight countries (Germany, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Sweden, Israel, Japan and the United States, with a Chinese sample of US residents counted as the eighth; 1,990 infant-mother Strange Situation classifications) found the secure (B) classification the most common in every country. Across all samples 21 percent were classified avoidant (A), 65 percent secure (B) and 14 percent resistant (C) (Table 1).

In the same meta-analysis, avoidant (A) classifications were relatively more common in Western European samples and resistant (C) classifications in Israel and Japan, but the variation between samples within a country was nearly 1.5 times the variation between countries. Samples from one country often resembled samples from other countries more than each other, and the authors point to low income and family stress in the US samples with many insecure classifications.

2434.content: In California hospital discharge data from October 1996 to December 2000, 273 hospitalisations of children under 18 months were coded as Shaken Baby Syndrome. By age, the cases started at 2 to 3 weeks, peaked at 10 to 13 weeks and fell to baseline by about 36 weeks: the same start and shape as the normal infant crying curve, with the peak about 4 to 6 weeks later than the crying peak of 5 to 6 weeks. The authors read early crying as the only likely predisposing factor that fits this pattern.

2435.content: A meta-analysis of 66 studies (4,176 participants) on parenting and infant attachment security found that in the 21 studies (1,099 participants) of nonclinical samples that used the Strange Situation with observed maternal sensitivity, the combined association was r = .24 after correction for attenuation, moderately strong by Cohen's criteria. The authors conclude that sensitivity is an important but not exclusive condition of attachment security and that several other dimensions of parenting play an equally important role.

2436.content: Among 58 healthy premenopausal US mothers (39 caring for a chronically ill child, 19 with a healthy child), caregiving mothers had shorter telomeres in blood immune cells the more years they had been caring (1 to 12 years; r = -0.40 adjusted for age), with lower telomerase activity and higher oxidative stress. As a group, caregivers did not differ from controls in telomere length; the link was with the number of years of caring.

Across all 58 women, higher perceived stress scores (a 10-item questionnaire on the past month) went with shorter telomeres (r = -0.31; -0.27 after adjusting for age, BMI, smoking and vitamin use), in both caregivers and controls. Women in the highest quarter of perceived stress (n = 14) had telomeres of about 3,110 base pairs against 3,660 in the lowest quarter (n = 14), which the authors equate with at least a decade of additional ageing, and 48 percent lower telomerase activity.

2437.content: In a cross-sectional internet survey and a longitudinal study of adults in romantic relationships, attachment features appeared in a fixed order: seeking closeness first, then turning to the partner for comfort (safe haven), and last using the partner as a secure base. People in longer relationships used their partners more for attachment functions, yet in the longitudinal study, after controlling for relationship length and age, these features changed little over time, and the authors conclude adult attachment bonds may form faster than previously assumed.

2438.content: Among 237 young adults at a US university, 60 percent still used their parents as primary attachment figures but were moving attachment functions to best friends and romantic partners. How far the functions had moved went with how long the peer relationship had lasted, and caregiving, trust and intimate contact in the relationship went with attachment to that peer.

2439.content: 530 participants read 6 vignettes in which they met a person who either cried or did not. They said they would give more emotional support to a crying person and express less negative feeling toward them; regression analyses also showed they judged the crying person less positively and felt more negative feelings in that person's presence. The valence of the situation strongly moderated these reactions.

2440.content: In a longitudinal study of 27 breastfeeding mothers followed from delivery to first ovulation, suckling reached 6.1 feeds and 122 minutes a day by 4 weeks after birth and stayed there until supplementary food was introduced, at a mean of 16 weeks. Suckling frequency and duration then fell sharply, in step with basal prolactin. None of the 27 ovulated during unsupplemented breastfeeding; within 16 weeks of supplements, follicular development had returned in 20 and ovulation in 14.

2441.content: In the same 27 breastfeeding mothers, 14 did not ovulate at any time while breastfeeding and 13 ovulated while still breastfeeding. All 13 had introduced two or more supplementary feeds a day and had cut suckling to fewer than six times and under 60 minutes a day by first ovulation. The mothers who held off ovulation beyond 40 weeks breastfed longest, suckled most intensively, kept night feeds longest and introduced other food most gradually.

2442.content: 13 women caring for a relative with dementia (mean age 62.3) and 13 controls matched for age and family income each received a 3.5 mm punch biopsy wound. Healing, judged by photographs and by the wound no longer foaming with hydrogen peroxide, took 48.7 days on average in the carers against 39.3 days in controls (p < 0.05). The carers' blood leucocytes also produced less interleukin-1 beta mRNA when stimulated.

2443.content: In a 6-year longitudinal community study of 119 older adults caring for a spouse with dementia and 106 noncaregivers (mean age 70.6 at entry, IL-6 measured repeatedly), caregivers' average yearly rise in the inflammatory signal IL-6 was about four times that of noncaregivers (modelled slopes 0.017 against 0.004; the controls' slope did not differ from zero). No systematic group differences in chronic health problems, medications or health behaviours accounted for the steeper slope. Applying an outside cut-off for high IL-6 linked to doubled risk of death, the authors estimate that caregivers would reach it around age 75 and controls after age 90.

In the same cohort, 78 of the 119 caregivers' spouses had died before or during the study. The yearly rise in IL-6 among former caregivers did not differ from that of current caregivers, even several years after the spouse's death; the authors found no notable improvement after caregiving ended.

2444.content: In the Yale Bereavement Study, 233 bereaved people in Connecticut were rated from 1 to 24 months after a family member's death from natural causes on five items. Acceptance was the item most often endorsed, and yearning was the strongest negative response throughout. In models of rise and fall, disbelief was highest at 1 month, yearning peaked at 4 months, anger at 5 months and the rater-scored depressed-mood item at 6 months, while acceptance rose throughout.

In the same study all the negative grief responses (disbelief, yearning, anger and the rater-scored depressed-mood item) reached their highest point within about 6 months of the death. The authors suggest that people who still score high on them beyond 6 months might benefit from further evaluation.

2445.content: In a nationally representative sample of American adults, self-rated adult attachment styles were 59 percent secure, 25 percent avoidant and 11 percent anxious, similar to earlier studies. Childhood adversities of an interpersonal nature were strongly related to insecure adult attachment, and attachment style was also associated with income, age and race.

2446.content: A review and meta-analysis of 16 studies (1,521 father-child pairs, 35 percent boys) found weak to moderate population effects in the links between father-child physical play, such as rough-and-tumble play, and child aggression, social competence, emotional skills and self-regulation. The authors note that rough-and-tumble play is a favoured type of father-child play in Western societies and that studies differed in how they defined, set up and measured the play.

2447.content: 221 healthy women planning a pregnancy stopped birth control, collected daily urine and recorded intercourse each day. In 625 cycles with an estimated ovulation day, 192 pregnancies began and two thirds (129) ended in live births. Conception occurred only when intercourse took place in a six-day window ending on the estimated day of ovulation; the chance of conception ran from 0.10 for intercourse five days before ovulation to 0.33 on the day of ovulation.

2448.content: In a preregistered registered report run by labs in 41 countries on all populated continents (7,007 participants, 24,886 ratings), people saw photographs of faces with or without digitally added tears. Tears raised the intention to support the person, d = 0.49 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.55). The effect appeared in every country sample and never fell below the smallest effect of interest set in advance (d = 0.20).

In the same study, the tear effect ran through seeing the crier as warmer and more helpless, feeling more connected and feeling more empathic concern, and not through the observer's personal distress. The effect was larger in a neutral situation, in observers high in trait empathic concern and for criers the observer did not identify as part of their group. Between countries the effect was larger where GDP per capita and subjective well-being were higher.

2449.content: In a longitudinal study of adolescent girls with 4 waves of data over about 19 months, girls with higher depressive symptom scores at baseline gained more capacity to disengage from goals over time (with no gain in capacity to take up new goals). Gains in goal disengagement capacity then predicted fewer depressive symptoms later. The authors read low mood as serving an adaptive function by helping adolescents let go of goals they cannot reach.

2450.content: In a four-wave prospective study of 565 Dutch children aged 7 to 11 at the start (waves 6 months apart, from 17 elementary schools), parents' overvaluation of their child (rating the child as more special and more entitled than other children) predicted the child's narcissism score six months later, for mothers and for fathers (standardised paths about 0.06 to 0.07), and narcissism did not predict later overvaluation. Lack of parental warmth did not predict narcissism in either direction, and overvaluation did not predict the children's scores on the study's self-esteem scale.

In the same cohort, the warmth children reported getting from father and from mother predicted their score on the study's self-esteem scale six months later (father path about 0.10, mother about 0.05), and that score in turn predicted later child-reported warmth. Warmth as rated by the parents themselves did not predict the score. The authors read this as consistent with sociometer theory: the child's perception of being accepted shapes how the child rates itself.

2451.content: The review reports Chudek and colleagues' 2012 experiments with 3- and 4-year-old children: two adult models differed only in how much attention bystanders paid them, and children were then more likely to share the food, drink, artefact or label preferences of the model the bystanders had watched. In a second study the children followed the watched model only within the domain in which they had seen that model show preferences.

The same review reports a later study by Chudek, Baron and Birch (2016): children aged 2 to 7 watched videos of two adult models, one watched by bystanders and one ignored, or one who said she had won five stickers and one who said she had won none. Copying of the models' unnecessary actions rose with age, and at no age did children copy the watched or the successful model more.

2452.content: Abstract only. Using deep neural networks on about 6 million videos from 144 countries, the authors examined how often 16 types of facial expression occurred in thousands of social contexts (for example weddings or sporting competitions). Each kind of expression had a distinct set of associated contexts, and these associations were 70% preserved across 12 world regions.

2453.content: Abstract only. A review of sleep and wake patterns across adolescence reports that sleep and wake timing shifts later during the second decade of life, and describes environmental, psychosocial and biological factors behind the shift, with a two-process model (circadian timing and the homeostatic build-up of sleep pressure).

Abstract only. The authors propose that delayed sleep phase syndrome, which typically begins in the second decade of life, may be an extreme form of the ordinary circadian and homeostatic changes of adolescence.

2454.content: Abstract only. In two experiments, participants read a vignette about a transgression (Experiment 1, 66 participants) or a mishap (Experiment 2, 62 participants) and then rated photographs of the actor with or without an added blush on sympathy, trustworthiness and other dimensions. In most comparisons the blushing actors were rated more favourably than the same actors without a blush, including when the face showed shame or embarrassment.

2455.content: In three experiments with 140 children, mostly 5-year-olds recruited mainly from a Harvard lab database (mostly European-American), children were assigned to a red or blue group by a coin draw and given a T-shirt of that colour. With no information about status or competition, they liked unfamiliar children in their own colour group more, gave them more coins, preferred them on an implicit association test, attributed more positive actions to them and expected more reciprocity from them. In Experiment 3 they remembered positive actions of their own group's members better.

In Experiment 1, which measured both, preferences for the randomly assigned colour group were about half the size of preferences for the child's own gender (effect sizes for gender about twice as large, driven mostly by girls). The authors call it striking that a group assigned a minute earlier produced preferences about half as strong as those built by a lifetime in a gender role.

2456.content: Abstract only. Children aged 9 to 11 were measured before and after a major new international airport opened, in communities that came under the new aircraft noise and in comparison communities. Over two years the noise-exposed children's resting blood pressure and overnight adrenaline and noradrenaline rose and their quality-of-life indicators fell, at noise levels far below those that damage hearing.

2457.content: Three children of Pakistani origin living in the United Kingdom, born with no working leptin (homozygous for the same frameshift mutation) and severely obese with constant overeating, were given daily leptin injections for 10 to 50 months. Within two months each child ate 45 to 84 percent less at a large test meal offered after an overnight fast, parents reported eating close to normal at home, and fat mass fell while lean mass and growth stayed normal.

During treatment each child had spells when the overeating came back, reported by parents 2 to 4 weeks before fat was regained and confirmed at the test meal; in some spells the children had made antibodies that blocked the injected leptin. Each time, a higher leptin dose brought food intake back down and fat mass fell after about 4 weeks. Leptin had no clear effect on resting metabolic rate or daily energy expenditure.

2458.content: In 85 father and child pairs in Quebec (children aged 2 to 6), fathers reported how often they played rough-and-tumble with the child over the past year and rated the child's physical aggression; observers rated how far the father dominated a videotaped free-play session at home. More frequent rough-and-tumble play went with more physical aggression in children whose fathers were less dominant in play; among more dominant fathers there was no such link. The result held after controlling for the child's sex and age, time the father spent with the child and play in general.

2459.content: Y-chromosome testing of living men in 23 Afrikaner families in South Africa, set against genealogies running back to 1674, covered 1,273 father-to-son conceptions over about 330 years, 93% of them before 1960. Eleven sons were excluded as their recorded father's genetic son, a non-paternity rate of 0.86% (95% confidence interval 0.43 to 1.54%; about 0.9% after correction).

2460.content: Reviewing their own experiments, the authors report that preschool children do not trust every adult equally. Faced with conflicting claims, they side with the person who has given them reliable care or reliable information before, and with the person who belongs to a consensus and keeps to the group's norms. In one study, 3- to 5-year-olds at two preschools each trusted their own familiar caregiver over the other preschool's caregiver when the two gave conflicting names for new objects.

The review reports a longitudinal study: children classed at 15 months as securely, avoidantly or ambivalently attached to their mother were tested at 5 years with pictures of animal hybrids that the mother and an unfamiliar adult named differently. Secure and ambivalent children sided with their mother; avoidant children treated the mother's claims no differently from the stranger's.

2461.content: In experiments with 5-year-old monolingual English-speaking children from mostly White Boston-area schools (16 per condition), children chose to be friends with children who spoke with a native accent (about 80% of choices) over foreign-accented or foreign-language speakers. With silent photographs, White children chose White children (77%); when the photographs were paired with voices, they chose Black children with a native accent over White children with a foreign accent (71%). Children understood the accented speech, so intelligibility did not explain the choice.

2462.content: Abstract only. 1,013 participants from first grade through the last year of college (ages 6 to 22) were given social dilemmas in which gaining popularity was set against friendship, personal achievement, following rules, prosocial behaviour or romantic interests. The priority given to popularity followed a curve that peaked in early adolescence, when participants most often put status first. Across ages, males and majority-group students cared more about reputational status than females and minority students.

2463.content: In Flanders (Belgium), the authors compared Y-chromosome types of living men with genealogies: in 60 pairs of men whose records gave them a shared paternal ancestor within the last few centuries, 8 pairs did not share his Y chromosome. This gives an extra-pair paternity rate of 0.91% per generation (95% confidence interval 0.41 to 1.75%). A second method, based on a sixteenth-century immigration, gave about 2%. Both are far below the 8 to 30% per generation that earlier behavioural studies had suggested, and match genetic studies of living Western Europeans.

2464.content: In the US NHANES III survey, women and girls with lower waist-hip ratios scored higher on cognitive tests: waist-hip ratio alone accounted for 3.6% of the variance in four test scores in girls aged 14 to 16, and for 6% of the variance in two test scores in women aged 18 to 49, and stayed significant after controlling for age, race or ethnicity, income, parity and parental education. Body mass index added nothing once waist-hip ratio was in the model.

2465.content: In four experiments, actors, scientists who study the face and non-actors were coached muscle by muscle to make the facial configurations of anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise, while heart rate, skin conductance, finger temperature and muscle activity were recorded. Making the faces produced reports of the matching emotion and distinct autonomic patterns, between negative and positive emotions and among negative emotions, in men and women and in both trained and untrained people, stronger when the face most resembled a real expression. It did not require seeing a face, and was not explained by how hard the faces were to make.

2466.content: A multilevel meta-analysis of 202 lab studies measuring autonomic changes (heart, breathing, sweat glands) during induced emotions in non-clinical adults found increases from baseline for 59.4% of the autonomic variables, but the pattern of effect sizes did not clearly separate one emotion category from another. Variation within each category was large: heterogeneity was moderate to substantial (I squared of 30% or more) for 54% of effect sizes, and induction method did not explain a large portion of it.

2467.content: Abstract only. In 122 preschool children (57 boys, 65 girls; mostly European American) followed over two years, the share of observed peer play time spent in sociodramatic (pretend) play in Year 1 predicted the children's emotional expressiveness, emotion knowledge and mother-rated emotion regulation in Year 2, after controlling for Year 1 skills. Rough-and-tumble play predicted later emotional expressiveness and emotion regulation, and exercise play predicted only emotion regulation. Some links differed by gender.

2468.content: Abstract only. Three samples (229 adolescents, 183 undergraduates and 289 adults) completed scales of celebrity attitude and of attention to and concern with body shape. Scores on celebrity attitudes went with body image scores only among female adolescents, where the intense-personal kind of celebrity worship explained unique variance in body image. The authors report tentative evidence that the link is found at ages 14 to 16 and disappears by 17 to 20.

2469.content: In three studies of children aged 3 to 5, children as young as 3 preferred the testimony of a communicator described as benevolent over one described as malevolent, while understanding that a lie told by a communicator described as a liar is false appeared only at about 4, and recognising a lie when the communicator was described as intending to deceive emerged around 4 and improved through the fifth and sixth year. The authors read these as three developmentally distinct parts of epistemic vigilance.

2470.content: In a game in which children could accept or reject (punish) proposed splits of resources between two absent, anonymous children, 6-year-olds rejected unfair proposals more than fair ones, while 5-year-olds did not. Children punished less when punishing cost them their own resources, yet still gave up resources to stop unfair splits. In a second experiment, by the abstract, 6-year-olds were less sensitive to unequal splits that came from selfishness than to those that came from generosity.

2471.content: Among 535 children aged 5 to 15 in Canada, India, Peru, Uganda, the USA and Vanuatu, children in every one of the six societies rejected (punished) selfish splits between two absent peers more often than equal splits, in a version where punishing was free and in one where it cost the child one of their own rewards. Older children punished selfishness more in Canada, India, Peru and the USA; children in Canada and the USA punished more when it was free, while children in Uganda punished selfishness more when it was costly.

2472.content: In five online experiments (701 participants in all, most of them Finnish speakers), people coloured on body silhouettes where they felt activity rise or fall for emotion words, stories, film clips and faces. Each emotion had a statistically separable bodily map, and the maps for the six basic emotions were similar between Finnish speakers and a Taiwanese Hokkien-speaking sample of 36 (mean correlation 0.70 for matching emotions against 0.40 for mismatched ones) and between Finnish and Swedish speakers (0.75 against 0.36).

2473.content: In an online sample of 3,954 adults from 101 countries (aged 18 to 90) who coloured body silhouettes for 13 emotion words, the bodily sensation maps were concordant across cultures (correlations above 0.82) and across the sexes (above 0.80); bodily sensations weakened with age.

2474.content: In three experiments with Japanese undergraduates, an apology that cost the apologiser something (a gift, voluntary inconvenience, or a fee to send the apology) was rated more sincere than an apology without cost: in two vignette studies (60 and 77 students) and in a dictator game with a fictitious unfair partner (42 students). In the game, 7 of 21 students who received a no-cost apology sent a complaint to the partner, against 1 of 21 who received a costly one.

2475.content: In three fMRI experiments, six basic emotions (disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, anger and surprise) induced with short films or with mental imagery could be told apart from brain activity patterns by multivariate pattern classification. Classification carried over from one way of inducing the emotion to the other and from one person to another, and emotions that felt more alike gave more alike brain patterns.

2476.content: In questionnaire studies in 37 countries on five continents, reported responses in episodes of joy, fear, anger, sadness, disgust, shame and guilt differed strongly between emotions, with cross-culturally stable profiles of subjective feeling, physiological symptoms and expressive behaviour. The authors also report important cultural differences in what elicits emotions, how they are regulated, represented and shared.

2477.content: In a study reported within a review, female adolescents and adult women played Cyberball, a ball-tossing game in which the other players stop passing to the participant. Being left out produced significantly greater affective consequences in the adolescents than in the adults, which the authors read as the regulation of distress from ostracism still developing between adolescence and adulthood.

2478.content: Four children aged 5 to 17, born with total or near-total absence of the cerebral cortex, showed discriminative awareness: they told familiar from unfamiliar people and places, interacted socially, had functional vision, oriented, showed musical preferences, gave fitting emotional responses and learned by association. The authors attribute this to plasticity of brainstem and diencephalic structures.

2479.content: An activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies of fear, anger, disgust, sadness and happiness found that each emotion had consistent regional brain activations across studies, and that each emotion's pattern could be told apart from every other in pairwise contrasts. The authors read this as support for discrete basic emotions with consistent and discriminable neural correlates.

2480.content: In a preregistered diffusion-chain study in Edinburgh with 72 adults (24 diagnosed or self-identified autistic, 24 non-autistic, 24 in mixed chains; matched on age, education and IQ), a story was passed along chains of eight people. Chains of participants diagnosed or self-identified as autistic kept as many story details as chains of non-autistic people (12.96 against 12.40 of 30), while mixed chains kept fewer and rated their rapport with each other lower.

2481.content: In a Registered Report replicating the 2020 diffusion-chain study at three sites (Dallas, Edinburgh, Nottingham; N = 311), chains of autistic people passed on information as well as chains of non-autistic people, and mixed chains did no worse than either. Reported rapport was highest in non-autistic chains, participants diagnosed or self-identified as autistic particularly enjoyed talking to each other, and telling participants each other's diagnostic status raised rapport.

2482.content: In 5,496 adult twins aged 18 to 86 from 3,644 families in the Netherlands (3,918), Belgium (904) and Australia (674) who filled in a mailed self-report questionnaire of borderline personality disorder features, additive genetic influences explained 42% of the variation in scores in men and women alike, with a similar estimate in all three countries; non-shared environment explained the remaining 58%. Women scored higher than men and younger adults higher than older adults.

2483.content: In a Swedish population-based sample (466 people diagnosed with strict autism and 2,580 others, genotyped at 531,906 markers), common genetic variants explained 49.4% of the liability to the diagnosis, and total narrow-sense heritability came out at 52.4%. Applying the same model to new (de novo) mutations in the Simons Simplex Collection, such mutations explained 2.6% of the variance in liability, although about 14% of those diagnosed carried one and they shifted those carriers' liability a great deal.

2484.content: In a genome-wide meta-analysis of 18,381 people diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and 27,969 controls (the Danish iPSYCH register cohort plus family samples), the common variants linked to the diagnosis were genetically correlated with educational attainment (rG = 0.199). Polygenic scores for more education were raised in people diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome and childhood autism, and were not raised in those with atypical autism or other or unspecified pervasive developmental disorder.

2485.content: 81 participants were randomly assigned to give a speech and do mental arithmetic either in front of evaluators (41) or without evaluation (40). Those who were evaluated showed greater rises in shame and greater falls in social self-esteem, and only they showed rises in salivary cortisol; other states and performance self-esteem did not differ between conditions. Cortisol rose more in those whose shame rose more and whose social self-esteem fell more.

2486.content: 44 children aged 10 to 17 (26 diagnosed with ADHD, 18 typically developing) wore an ankle actometer during a flanker task of cognitive control. In the diagnosed group, movement was more intense on correct trials than on error trials, and more intense than the typically developing group's on correct trials; in typically developing children movement did not differ between correct and error trials. The authors read the extra movement as a possible effort to regulate attention and alertness.

2487.content: In the ENIGMA-ADHD consortium (36 centres; 2,246 people diagnosed with ADHD and 1,934 controls), children diagnosed with ADHD had slightly lower cortical surface area, mainly in frontal, cingulate and temporal regions (largest effect total surface area, Cohen's d = -0.21), and lower thickness in the fusiform gyrus and temporal pole. Adolescents and adults diagnosed with ADHD showed no differences in surface area or thickness. In a population sample of 2,707 children, surface area in overlapping regions went with parent-scored attention problems along a continuum.

2488.content: In two samples of adults with and without an ADHD diagnosis (a pilot sample of 251 and a replication sample of 372), people who scored higher on ADHD symptom scales, including the Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scale, reported more hyperfocus (long spells of intensely focused attention) on a new Adult Hyperfocus Questionnaire: higher total and dispositional scores, more frequent hyperfocus at school, in hobbies and on screens, and more on a subscale of real-world hyperfocus scenarios. The hypothesis was preregistered.

2489.content: In a Swedish total-population nested case-control study, 54,042 people diagnosed in hospital with schizophrenia, 29,644 with a bipolar disorder diagnosis and 217,771 with a unipolar depression diagnosis (1973 to 2003), and their undiagnosed relatives, were compared with controls on holding a creative (artistic or scientific) occupation in the censuses. People diagnosed with bipolar disorder were more often in creative occupations (odds ratio 1.35, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.48), and so were their undiagnosed parents (1.44) and siblings (1.33). Undiagnosed parents (1.55) and siblings (1.36) of people diagnosed with schizophrenia were also over-represented. People diagnosed with unipolar depression and their siblings were not.

The likelihood of a creative occupation was highest in the undiagnosed first-degree relatives of people diagnosed with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder and fell with more distant relation, and maternal and paternal half-siblings did not differ. The authors read this as pointing to a genetic rather than an environmental basis for the family link, and note that the half-sibling comparison had low power. They discuss balancing selection: in relatives without the debilitating condition, the same inheritance might bring creativity and so fitness.

2490.content: A reanalysis of a Swedish population cohort born 1982 to 2006 (37,570 twin pairs, 2,642,064 full sibling pairs, 432,281 maternal and 445,531 paternal half-sibling pairs; 14,516 children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder by 2009) put the heritability of the diagnosis at 0.83 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.87) under the best-fitting model, with non-shared environment at 0.17. Shared family environment contributed little (0.04 in the full model), and twins alone gave 0.87. The authors' earlier analysis of the same data, with a different way of counting sibling pairs, had given 0.50.

2491.content: In 29 boys aged 8 to 12 diagnosed with ADHD and 23 typically developing boys, each given four phonological working-memory tasks in separate sessions while observers coded gross motor activity, the diagnosed boys did better on the working-memory tasks during the stretches when they moved more, though not up to the level of the typically developing boys. In typically developing boys, more movement went with somewhat lower scores. Movement did not change attention in either group. Comparing each boy at his highest and lowest activity, the diagnosed boys were more often classed as reliably improved and the typically developing boys as reliably worse.

2492.content: An exome sequencing study of 35,584 samples, 11,986 of them from people diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, identified 102 genes in which rare damaging variants, new (de novo) in the child or inherited, raise the chance of the diagnosis. Of these, 49 genes were hit more often in children ascertained for severe neurodevelopmental delay and 53 more often in children ascertained for autism; diagnosed children with damaging variants in the delay-linked genes walked 2.6 months later and scored 11.9 IQ points lower on average than those with variants in the autism-predominant genes.

Splitting the diagnosed people with IQ data into those with IQ of 70 or above (69.4 percent) and below 70 (30.6 percent), the higher-IQ group still carried more new damaging variants than expected, and so did those above the cohort mean IQ of 82. The authors conclude that the excess of such variants is not limited to people with low IQ.

2493.content: In 1,402 people aged 6 to 68 with a genetically confirmed 22q11.2 deletion, assessed at 15 sites in North America, Europe, Australia and the Middle East with structured diagnostic interviews against DSM-IV-TR criteria, the rate of a schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis rose with age: 23.5 percent in those aged 18 to 25 and about 41 percent in the two groups over 25. Children were most often diagnosed with ADHD (37.1 percent), and anxiety disorders were diagnosed more often than mood disorders at all ages.

2494.content: Children diagnosed with autism scored better on the Children's Embedded Figures Test (finding a simple shape hidden in a larger drawing) than normal children matched on mental age and than non-autistic children with learning disability matched on mental and chronological age, and used different strategies. Their scores were above what their mental age would lead one to expect and in line with their actual age, which the authors call an islet of ability.

2495.content: Variations of the block design task were given to 20 participants diagnosed with autism, 33 normal and 12 mildly learning-disabled participants. The participants diagnosed with autism, of every age and ability level, scored better than controls when the design was shown whole (unsegmented); when designs were pre-segmented the difference was smaller, and rotating the design or adding oblique lines made no group difference. The authors read this as autistic people needing less effort to break a whole pattern into its parts.

2496.content: In 30,111 complete adult twin pairs from eight countries (Australia, Denmark, Finland, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom), the heritability of body height in men ranged from 0.87 to 0.93 across countries. In women it ranged from 0.68 to 0.84 under a model with shared environment, and from 0.89 to 0.93 in the four populations where a model without shared environment fitted as well. Mean height varied across countries (men 177 cm in Italy to 184 cm in the Netherlands) while heritability in men did not.

2497.content: In 5,486 middle-aged British civil servants in the Whitehall II study, social standing was measured both objectively (employment grade, education, income) and subjectively (where people placed themselves on a social ladder) in 1997 to 1999, and health was measured then and in 2000 to 2001 (SF-36 physical and mental scores, the General Health Questionnaire, self-rated health). Both measures went with health and with decline in health. When both were in the same model, only subjective standing remained significantly associated with health and its change.

2498.content: A meta-analysis of 11 longitudinal studies (chosen from 38 that met quality criteria, out of 24,939 citations from 1994 to 2005) found that job strain (high demands with low decision latitude) and effort-reward imbalance were the two work conditions most strongly linked to later common mental disorders, with pooled odds ratios of 1.82 (95% CI 1.06 to 3.10) and 1.84 (1.45 to 2.35). Low decision authority (1.21), low decision latitude (1.23) and high psychological demands (1.39) carried smaller risks.

Seven research groups studied relationships at work (social support from colleagues or supervisors, or interpersonal conflict); five of the seven found poor work relationships linked to later mental ill health, and the pooled odds ratio was 1.32 (95% CI 1.21 to 1.44), higher in men (1.38) than in women (1.20).

2499.content: Among 258 consecutively seen, unrelated children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada (2008 to 2013), chromosomal microarray gave a molecular diagnosis in 24 (9.3 percent), and whole-exome sequencing in 8 of 95 (8.4 percent). In the 95 children who had both tests, 15 (15.8 percent, 95% CI 9.1 to 24.7) had an identifiable genetic etiology. The yield was higher in children with more physical anomalies (the complex group) than in those with none (the essential group).

2500.content: A meta-analysis of the twin studies of the autism spectrum disorder diagnosis (13 found, 7 meeting the criterion of systematic recruitment) put heritability at 64 to 91 percent, depending on the prevalence of the diagnosis the authors assumed. In liability to being diagnosed, identical twins correlated 0.98, non-identical twins 0.53 at an assumed 5 percent prevalence and 0.67 at 1 percent. Shared environment became significant (7 to 35 percent) only as the authors lowered the assumed prevalence of the diagnosis.

In 6,413 twin pairs from a population sample scored on the Childhood Autism Spectrum Test at age 8, heritability did not change much along the score range, and the high end was not more heritable than the rest. The authors read this as suggesting that the autism diagnosis can be seen as the extreme end of a continuum of autistic traits, rather than a distinct disorder, and ask for replication.

2501.content: In close to 2,800 Norwegian twins from the Norwegian Institute of Public Health Twin Panel, assessed by self-report questionnaire and a few years later by the Structured Interview for DSM-IV Personality, the heritability of the four Cluster B personality disorder scores was around .30 by interview and around .40 to .50 by questionnaire. A latent factor combining both measures gave heritabilities of .67 for the borderline score, .69 for antisocial, .71 for narcissistic and .63 for histrionic personality disorder as scored. Shared family environment was zero.
