2502.content: PET scans of 53 never-medicated adults diagnosed with ADHD and 44 controls (2001 to 2009) found lower dopamine transporter and D2/D3 receptor availability, on average, in regions of the left-sided dopamine reward pathway (nucleus accumbens, midbrain, caudate). For example, transporter availability in the accumbens averaged 0.63 in the diagnosed adults against 0.71 in controls. Lower receptor availability in these regions went with more inattention on the SWAN rating scale; no correlation with hyperactivity-impulsivity was significant.

The authors propose that, as the lower receptor measures went with inattention, the reward pathway may account for why attention problems in ADHD are most evident in tasks that are boring, repetitive and uninteresting, that is, tasks that are not rewarding in themselves.

2503.content: A systematic review of 21 experimental and observational studies of sleep deprivation in healthy people (760 participants in total, sleep loss from 24 hours to 11 nights, on average 72 to 92 hours) found perceptual changes in all studies but one. Symptoms began after one night without sleep and progressed in a near-fixed order: perceptual distortions, anxiety, irritability and depersonalization within 24 to 48 hours, complex hallucinations and disordered thinking after 48 to 90 hours, and delusions after 72 hours, after which the picture resembled acute psychosis or toxic delirium. A period of normal sleep resolved the psychotic symptoms in many cases.

2504.content: In the first genome-wide association study of the borderline personality disorder diagnosis (998 diagnosed patients and 1,545 controls, Germany), no single genetic variant was significantly associated after correction for multiple testing. Gene-based tests found two genes (DPYD and PKP4) and one gene set (exocytosis). The common-variant signal overlapped with that reported for the bipolar disorder (genetic correlation 0.28), schizophrenia (0.34) and major depression (0.57) diagnoses.

2505.content: In a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover PET study (18F-fallypride) in Cambridge, 16 adults diagnosed with ADHD and 16 matched controls showed equivalent striatal and midbrain dopamine D2/D3 receptor availability on placebo, and equivalent rises in endogenous dopamine after a single oral dose of methylphenidate (0.5 mg/kg). The diagnosed group did score worse on a sustained attention task and showed lower grey matter volume in fronto-striato-cerebellar and limbic networks. The authors conclude that dopamine dysregulation by itself is unlikely to be the primary basis of the adult ADHD diagnosis.

In the same study, a single oral dose of methylphenidate raised dopamine in all nigro-striatal regions in diagnosed adults and controls alike. It improved sustained attention according to how poorly a person performed on placebo, whether or not the person had been diagnosed with ADHD. Poor performers from both groups had lower D2/D3 receptor availability in the left caudate on placebo, and smaller drug-induced dopamine release in the midbrain.

2506.content: In a prospective study from the Institute for Aerobics Research in Dallas, 10,224 men and 3,120 women given a preventive medical examination had fitness measured by a maximal treadmill test and were followed for a little over 8 years on average (110,482 person-years; 240 deaths in men, 43 in women). Age-adjusted all-cause death rates fell across fitness fifths from 64.0 to 18.6 per 10,000 person-years in men and from 39.5 to 8.5 in women, from least to most fit. The gradient held after adjustment for age, smoking, cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, fasting glucose, parental history of coronary heart disease and follow-up interval, and was seen for cardiovascular disease and cancer deaths.

2507.content: In the DREW randomised trial, 411 sedentary overweight or obese postmenopausal women (analysed of 464 randomised) did 6 months of supervised exercise burning 4, 8 or 12 kcal per kg per week, or no exercise. At 4 and 8 kcal/kg/week actual weight loss matched the loss predicted from the energy spent in exercise. At the highest dose (about 194 minutes a week) women lost 1.5 kg against 2.7 kg predicted, about half, a shortfall of 1.2 kg that the authors call compensation; 72.6 percent of women in that group compensated against about 53 percent at the lower doses.

In the same trial, all three exercise groups lost waist circumference against the non-exercise control, and the loss held after adjustment for change in weight, also among women who compensated and did not lose weight.

2508.content: In 13 obese adults studied before and after a six-month weight-loss diet, plasma ghrelin rose sharply before and fell after every meal over 24 hours. A diet-induced loss of 17 percent of body weight went with a 24 percent rise in the 24-hour ghrelin profile (area under the curve). In 5 people who had lost 36 percent of their weight after gastric bypass, ghrelin was 77 percent lower than in 10 normal-weight controls and its meal-related swings were absent.

2509.content: In the Midwest Exercise Trial 2 (Kansas), 141 overweight or obese adults aged 18 to 30 were randomised to supervised exercise burning 400 or 600 kcal per session, 5 days a week for 10 months, or to no exercise, all eating as they liked. Among the 92 who completed at least 90 percent of sessions and all assessments, the 400 kcal group lost 3.9 kg (4.3 percent) and the 600 kcal group 5.2 kg (5.7 percent), while controls gained 0.5 kg; men and women did not differ.

In the same trial, the 600 kcal group did not lose significantly more weight than the 400 kcal group, and measured energy intake did not differ between groups over the 10 months. The authors read the missing dose difference and the wide individual variation as signs of compensation in energy balance, whose source (eating, other movement, resting metabolism, appetite hormones) the trial did not identify.

2510.content: Pooling eating-rate measurements from 5 published studies (327 foods from the UK, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Singapore), the authors computed each food's energy intake rate (eating rate in g/min times energy density). Mean energy intake rate rose from 35.5 kcal/min for unprocessed foods to 53.7 for processed and 69.4 for ultra-processed foods (NOVA classes). The spread within each class was wide: some unprocessed foods such as full-fat milk and orange juice reached 230 to 240 kcal/min.

2511.content: Fourteen of 16 contestants of the US television competition The Biggest Loser were measured again 6 years after it. They had lost 58.3 kg on average in the 30-week competition, and their resting metabolic rate had fallen by 610 kcal/d. Six years later they had regained 41.0 kg, yet resting metabolic rate was still 704 kcal/d below baseline, and about 499 kcal/d lower than predicted from their body composition and age (metabolic adaptation), up from 275 kcal/d at the end of the competition.

In the same 14 people, metabolic adaptation at the end of the competition did not go with how much weight they regained (r = -0.1). At 6 years, those who had kept off more weight showed more slowing at that time (r = 0.59), which the authors read as a proportional but incomplete response to ongoing efforts to hold weight down.

2512.content: Goldberger, of the US Public Health Service, collected reports and his own inquiries from asylums and a pellagra hospital in the US and Italy where pellagra arose among inmates after years of residence, while nurses and attendants who lived and worked beside them stayed free of it. At the state hospital for the insane at Jackson, Mississippi, 98 inmates died of pellagra between October 1909 and July 1913, and none of 126 nurses and attendants employed since 1909 developed it. He argues that a communicable disease cannot explain this, and proposes a difference in diet: staff picked the best and most varied food and could add to it.

2513.content: From September 1914 the US Public Health Service changed the diet at two orphanages in Jackson, Mississippi, where pellagra had come back every spring: more milk, eggs, fresh meat, beans and peas, oatmeal in place of grits, little syrup, with hygiene and sanitation left as they were. Of 67 children at one orphanage who had had pellagra in 1914 and were followed past its anniversary, none had a recurrence in 1915, and none of 99 other residents developed it; at the second orphanage 1 of 105 former cases recurred and none of 69 others developed it. The authors expected about half to recur, from recurrence rates of 58 to 76 percent recorded at another orphanage.

In two wards of the Georgia State Sanitarium, an asylum for the insane, 72 women (36 Black, 36 white) who had had pellagra in 1914 were given the same kind of diet and followed for about a year: none had a recurrence. Among comparison patients on the asylum's ordinary wards, 9 of 17 and 6 of 15 had recurrences (47 percent combined), and the authors would have expected 20 to 34 recurrences in their group. They report that in several patients the mental condition improved so much that they were discharged on request before the year was over.

2514.content: In 4,289 British civil servants of the Whitehall II cohort (mean age 49, 3,092 men and 1,197 women) with physical activity as the participants reported it and blood CRP and IL-6 measured in 1991 and 2002, people active at baseline had lower CRP and IL-6, and the gap stayed stable over the 10 years. Those who met the guideline of 2.5 hours a week of moderate to vigorous activity at every assessment had lower log CRP and log IL-6 at follow-up than those who rarely met it (beta -0.07 for each), after adjustment for a range of covariates.

In the same cohort, people who raised their activity by at least 2.5 hours a week between phase 5 (1997 to 1999) and phase 7 (2002 to 2004) had lower log CRP and log IL-6 at follow-up than those whose activity stayed stable (beta -0.05 and -0.06); people whose activity fell did not differ significantly from the stable group.

2515.content: Animal evidence. In adipose tissue from four different rodent models of obesity and diabetes, messenger RNA for the inflammatory cytokine TNF-alpha was induced, and TNF-alpha protein was raised both in the tissue and in the blood. In obese fa/fa (Zucker) rats (Rattus norvegicus), neutralising TNF-alpha significantly increased glucose uptake in response to insulin.

2516.content: A meta-analysis of 108 independent samples from 85 studies found a correlation of 0.43 between successful goal pursuit and subjective well-being.

In the same meta-analysis the link was larger when success was measured as progress toward a goal than as attainment of it, when well-being was measured by positive indicators than by ill-being, when the well-being measure matched the goal content, and in samples from individualistic than from collectivistic cultures.

2517.content: In 18 obese and 23 never-obese adults studied at their usual weight and again after losing 10 to 20 percent of body weight by underfeeding, holding a weight 10 percent or more below the starting weight went with lower 24-hour energy expenditure: 6 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day less in the never-obese and 8 less in the obese. Resting and non-resting expenditure each fell 3 to 4 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day.

In the same study, holding a weight 10 percent above usual weight by overfeeding went with higher 24-hour energy expenditure: 9 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day more in the never-obese and 8 more in the obese, mostly in non-resting expenditure (8 to 9 kcal). The changes did not depend on degree of fatness or sex; the authors conclude that these compensatory changes oppose holding a weight different from the usual one.

2518.content: Sixteen non-obese volunteers were fed 1,000 kcal a day above their weight-maintenance needs for 8 weeks. Two-thirds of their rise in daily energy expenditure came from non-exercise activity thermogenesis (fidgeting, posture and other daily movement). Changes in this everyday movement accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat stored and went with resistance to fat gain (correlation 0.77).

2519.content: In a genome-wide association meta-analysis of body mass index in up to 339,224 people (GIANT consortium), genes near the 97 associated loci were most highly expressed in brain tissue: 27 of the 31 tissues significantly enriched (out of 209 tested) were in the central nervous system, including the hypothalamus. Enriched gene sets included synaptic function and glutamate signalling.
In the same analysis the 97 loci accounted for about 2.7 percent of the variation in body mass index, and common genetic variation as a whole for an estimated more than 20 percent.

2520.content: A preregistered systematic review of 38 prospective studies (58,256 participants, mostly community samples; up to 27 in meta-analysis) found that higher CRP and IL-6 at baseline went with higher depressive symptom scores later, and higher symptom scores at baseline went with higher CRP and IL-6 later. After adjustment for covariates the associations were small (pooled Fisher r of about 0.01 to 0.09); the adjusted link of symptoms with later CRP and of CRP with later symptoms was substantially attenuated. TNF-alpha showed no association in either direction.

In the same review, the six studies that followed people to a later depression diagnosis by clinical interview gave no conclusive result: CRP went with first onset of a diagnosis in one sample of middle-aged women and not in others, and IL-6 and TNF-alpha did not go with later diagnosis. In meta-regression, the link between baseline CRP and later depressive symptom scores was larger in older samples and in studies that did not exclude people with possible infection (extreme CRP values).

2521.content: Twelve healthy young men in Turku, Finland, were scanned twice with PET and the mu-opioid receptor ligand [11C]carfentanil: once after watching comedy clips for 30 minutes with two close friends, and once after 30 minutes alone (order counterbalanced). Social laughter raised pleasurable feelings and released endogenous opioids in the thalamus, caudate nucleus and anterior insula, and men with more opioid receptors in the cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex at baseline laughed more often. In a behavioural control study (43 men and women), pain threshold, a proxy for opioid release, rose more after comedy than after drama watched in groups.

2522.content: In 177 adults (131 Southwestern American Indians and 46 Caucasians, at the NIH in Phoenix) who each spent 24 hours in a respiratory chamber, fat-free mass explained 81 percent of the differences in 24-hour energy expenditure. In the 118 whose movement was tracked by radar, they moved for 3.9 to 16.6 percent of the day, although exercise was not allowed; this spontaneous activity (strolling about the chamber and moving the limbs, such as fidgeting, which the radar could not tell apart) cost on average 348 kcal a day, from 138 to 685, and the abstract puts its range at 100 to 800 kcal a day. The authors suggest the activity may reflect an unconscious need to be active.

2523.content: In an experiment with 28 participants in Vancouver, people who looked at photographs of others showing symptoms of infectious disease, compared with people who looked at photographs of guns, had white blood cells that produced more of the inflammatory cytokine IL-6 when the cells were later incubated with a model bacterial stimulus.

2524.content: Facial reactions to taste were filmed in eight newborn human infants and in 27 infant or adult non-human primates of 11 species (among them chimpanzee Pan troglodytes, orangutan, gorilla, rhesus monkey Macaca mulatta, tamarins, marmosets and a lemur). Sucrose drew the same kind of positive facial reaction in humans and in the other primates, and quinine drew the same kind of aversive reaction. The closer the species to humans, the more alike the reaction patterns: human newborns resembled great apes more than monkeys.

2525.content: Twelve newborns were given sucrose, salt, citric acid and quinine solutions at 2 hours of age and filmed; their faces were coded with an infant version of the Facial Action Coding System. Sucrose drew facial relaxation and sucking. Sour and bitter drew the same negative upper-face actions with different mouth actions (lip pursing for sour, mouth gaping for bitter). Untrained adults watching the films identified the sucrose responses accurately.

2526.content: Online, 255 Japanese and 386 British adults rated their emotional bond with each member of their social network and coloured a body map of where each person would be allowed to touch them. In both countries the partner could touch almost anywhere, close relatives and friends the head and upper torso, and strangers only the hands. Bond strength and how pleasant the touch would be together explained about 20% of the variance in the touchable area (11.3% pleasantness, 8.6% bond), and country only 0.4%. British participants rated touch as more pleasant than Japanese participants did.

2527.content: A systematic review of 15 supervised aerobic exercise trials in sedentary healthy adults computed the energy deficit from measured changes in body fat and lean mass. In 13 of the 15 trials the achieved deficit was below 500 kcal a day, and in most trials it was smaller than the energy the prescribed exercise burned. Where intake was held at baseline (a confined study) or supervised daily, the deficit matched the prescribed exercise. The authors conclude that the small weight loss comes mostly from low prescribed exercise doses together with eating more.

In the one trial that held energy intake at baseline in confined subjects (Bouchard and colleagues, twins exercising for 93 days), resting metabolic rate fell about 7% (81 kcal a day) more than the weight lost would account for, most in the leanest people. In trials where people ate freely, resting metabolic rate hardly changed. The authors propose that eating more after exercise may serve to keep resting metabolic rate from falling.

2528.content: Recording single nerve fibres in the forearm skin of human volunteers by microneurography, the authors found 38 unmyelinated fibres that responded to gentle skin deformation; 27 were low-threshold touch units with properties like the low-threshold C-mechanoreceptors known in other mammals. The authors conclude that human hairy skin has a second, slow touch system of unmyelinated fibres, possibly missing at the far ends of the limbs, and speculate that it relates more to limbic (emotional) functions than to cognitive and motor ones.

2529.content: Ninety-nine fit adults (51 aged 59 to 75, 48 aged 18 to 30) lived for up to 5.5 days in a laboratory on a 90-minute sleep-wake cycle in dim light (under 50 lux awake) and did 1 hour of moderate treadmill exercise on three days at one of eight clock times. The timing of urinary melatonin metabolite showed that exercise at 7 am or from 1 pm to 4 pm moved the clock earlier and exercise from 7 pm to 10 pm moved it later. The size of the shifts was comparable to what bright light of the same duration is expected to do. Age and sex made no difference.

2530.content: In three studies the authors found that people expect to feel better after punishing someone who wronged them, yet in at least some cases revenge leaves them feeling the opposite of what they expected. One reason they report: those who punished kept thinking about the offender, while those who did not punish moved on and thought about the offender less. People also misjudged how differently it feels to watch punishment happen and to carry it out oneself.

2531.content: Measuring facial muscle activity, the authors compared three states: distaste from unpleasant tastes, disgust at photographs of contaminants, and reactions to unfair treatment in an economic game. All three activated the levator labii region, the muscle that raises the upper lip in an oral and nasal rejection response. The authors read this as moral offence calling on the same disgust as bad tastes and disease carriers.

2532.content: In PET scans of 41 healthy adults who recalled and re-lived personal episodes of sadness, happiness, anger or fear, regions that map and regulate the body's internal state were engaged, among them the somatosensory cortices and nuclei of the upper brainstem. The authors read this as the feeling of an emotion resting partly on the brain's moment-to-moment maps of the body.

2533.content: A meta-analysis of 128 experiments found that rewards given for doing, finishing or doing well at a task reduced how much people later chose to do it in free time (effect sizes d -0.40, -0.36 and -0.28), as did tangible and expected rewards overall. Tangible and expected rewards also lowered the interest people rated. Positive feedback raised both free-choice behaviour (d 0.33) and interest (d 0.31). Tangible rewards harmed children more than college students.

2534.content: In six memory-confusion experiments with US undergraduates (59 to 74 per study), participants read about men gathering food for a stranded group. They mentally grouped together men who took the benefit without trying to contribute, and kept them apart from men who contributed just as little by accident; the free riders also drew less trust and more wish to punish. When intent was held equal, how much a man produced did not make him a free rider, although some sorting by competence occurred. Thieves and batterers were sorted apart from free riders.

2535.content: Following 149 US veterans of World War II and the Korean war from the Berkeley longitudinal samples, plus records of a Marine unit that served on Iwo Jima, the authors found that men in heavy combat more often kept lasting ties from the service. Combat alone did not account for the ties: war trauma, and above all losing comrades and friends in the war, went with stronger and longer-kept bonds. Painful memories and later stress symptoms tended to weaken among men with a supportive community of service mates and wives.

2536.content: In an experiment, 5-year-old children spontaneously told a peer which of two absent partners was cooperative and which was not, guiding the peer towards the cooperative one. Three-year-olds rarely gave such evaluative information, though they were willing to inform in a non-evaluative way. A follow-up study linked the age difference partly to the older children's developing ability to give reasons.

2537.content: In experiments with Zurich university students, a third party who lost nothing from the norm violation could spend own money to punish. In a third-party dictator game (66 subjects) almost two-thirds of third parties punished dictators who gave the recipient less than half of 100 points, and punished harder the less was given (dictators who gave nothing lost 42 points on average). In a third-party prisoner's dilemma up to about 60% punished defectors. Second parties, whose own payoff was cut by the violation, punished much more strongly than third parties.

2538.content: In a laboratory experiment at the University of Exeter, 288 participants played repeated one-shot trust games in anonymous networks of 12, in four conditions: no messages, true information, free gossip, and gossip where messages were randomly made wrong half the time. Gossipers sometimes lied, mostly to punish untrustworthy players, and this did not lower trust. Imposed high inaccuracy did lower trust and trustworthiness, yet both stayed higher than when no communication was possible.

2539.content: The authors built a rating scale of anticipated pleasure with items for natural rewards and for supernormal products (snack foods, alcohol, pornography and similar), tested on 5,391 members of an Australian online survey panel. The two kinds of items formed separate factors. People who expected more pleasure from supernormal items reported more daily use of 21 products with supernormal features, while anticipated pleasure from natural rewards went with lower or unchanged use.

2540.content: In two experiments with social bargaining games (a prisoner's dilemma in Study 1, an ultimatum game in Study 2), people who had played non-cooperatively in the first round and then felt guilt cooperated more in the next round than people who felt no guilt, an effect still seen one week later. Guilt was induced by the experimenters in Study 1 and rated by the participants themselves in Study 2. The abstract does not give sample sizes or effect sizes.

2541.content: Kniffin and Wilson recorded the content of talk among members of one competitive sports team over 18 months, combining ethnographic observation with quantitative sampling. The authors report that their results support a multilevel selection model in which gossip serves group-beneficial rules when rewards are shared at the level of the group and the group is small enough for members to monitor each other.

2542.content: In an event-related fMRI study of eight healthy volunteers playing a monetary incentive task, cues announcing larger possible money rewards raised both the happiness participants rated and activation in the nucleus accumbens, while cues announcing larger possible losses raised neither. A different striatal region, the medial caudate, responded to the anticipation of both gains and losses. At the highest reward level ($5.00), accumbens activation tracked how happy each person said the reward cue made them.

2543.content: Nine healthy volunteers did a monetary incentive delay task in the fMRI scanner, responding to cued targets for a money reward, for no reward, or not responding. Anticipating a reward (against no reward) activated foci in the ventral striatum, while reward outcomes (against no reward) activated foci in the ventromedial frontal cortex. The authors read this as anticipation and outcome recruiting distinct regions along the ascending dopamine projections.

2544.content: In a community sample of 998 people whose depression-related cognitions and self-esteem were measured and who were then followed for one year, 63 were classified by the authors as depressed at the first assessment and 85 became depressed during follow-up. People who were later classified as depressed did not differ from people who stayed well on the cognitive measures taken before, and the negative cognitions did not persist after an episode. The authors conclude that depression-related cognitions arise together with the episode.

In the same cohort the negative cognitions measured at the start did not predict who would later be classified as depressed. Among those classified as depressed at the start, those with more negative cognitions were significantly less likely to have improved during the follow-up year.

2545.content: Across four questionnaire studies Litman and Pezzo built a 12-item Attitudes Towards Gossip scale with two factors: the social value and the moral value people place on gossip. People who scored higher on the social value factor reported more interest in gossip and more intent to pass it on; scores went with a separate tendency-to-gossip questionnaire and went against measures of the need for social approval.

2546.content: In three randomised crossover studies at the University of Alabama (226 adults analysed in all, mostly women and college students), blood pressure was taken before and after people watched a recorded hearth or campfire with sound, the same fire muted, and a control screen (a blank screen, then an upside-down still of the fire). In Study 3, with 15-minute conditions (60 analysed), blood pressure fell with fire-with-sound (mean systolic fall 5.9 mmHg, diastolic 3.0) and rose with the muted fire and the control. The muted fire gave inconsistent effects, and the author concludes that fire with sound lowers blood pressure, more so with longer exposure.

2547.content: In transmission-chain experiments, where a story is passed from one participant to the next, information about intense third-party social relationships (gossip) was passed on more accurately and in greater quantity than equivalent non-social information about individual behaviour or the physical environment.

In a second experiment that controlled for how coherent each story was, the advantage for social information held, and information about everyday social interactions that were not gossip was passed on just as well as the intense gossip. The authors conclude that the bias is for social information in general.

2548.content: Nine right-handed women whose romantic relationship had ended within the previous four months were scanned with fMRI while they alternated between a sad, ruminative thought about the ex-partner and a neutral thought about another person known as long. Acute grief went with more activity in posterior regions (cerebellum, posterior brainstem, posterior temporoparietal and occipital cortex) and less activity, mostly anterior and on the left, in the anterior brainstem, thalamus, striatum, temporal cortex, insula and anterior cingulate and prefrontal cortex. Women who reported more grief over the past two weeks showed larger decreases in nearly all of these regions.

2549.content: A nationally representative online panel of Americans was asked to estimate the current distribution of wealth in the United States and to build their ideal one. Respondents greatly underestimated current wealth inequality, and the distributions they built as ideal were far more equal than even their own low estimates. All demographic groups, Republicans and the wealthy included, chose a more equal distribution than the actual one.

2550.content: In a large ultimatum-game experiment, responders rejected small offers most often when they could judge how fair the offer was and could hold the proposer responsible. Anger explained the rejections better than the perception that the offer was unfair, which the authors read as a wounded pride and spite response.

2551.content: Proffitt reviews his laboratory's experiments and argues that explicit perception of spatial layout varies with the cost of the intended action: when walking costs more energy, for example while wearing a heavy backpack, hills are reported as steeper and distances as longer, while visually guided actions are not affected. People standing on a high balcony report a distance to the ground that goes with their fear of falling.

2552.content: Forty-five Swarthmore College undergraduates judged the slope of a 14.5 degree ramp with no backpack (12), with an unexplained 11.3 kg backpack (13), or with the same backpack said to hold muscle-recording equipment (20). The 15 who believed the equipment story gave slope judgments essentially identical to those without a backpack. In the unexplained-backpack group, 12 of 13 guessed the backpack was meant to change their slope judgments, and the 5 who said it had affected them gave higher judgments when standing on the ramp (51 against 27 degrees).

2553.content: In two studies, 2- and 3-year-old children were shown a simple rule game and played it with an experimenter; then a puppet joined and made a move that broke the game's rule. Children protested, criticised or taught the puppet more when the act was a mistake in the game than when the same act was made in a context where it was no mistake. Both ages did this, the 3-year-olds more explicitly.

2554.content: Among 49 forest user groups in Ethiopia, the authors combined experimental measures of conditional cooperation with survey measures of costly monitoring and with measures of forest outcomes. Groups differed in their share of conditional cooperators; groups with a larger share managed their forest commons more successfully, and costly monitoring was a key way conditional cooperators enforced cooperation.

2555.content: Players responding to fair and unfair splits of money in the Ultimatum Game were scanned with fMRI. Unfair offers activated the anterior insula, a region linked to emotion, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Anterior insula activity was significantly higher for unfair offers that players went on to reject.

2556.content: A meta-analysis of 11 fMRI studies of the Ultimatum Game (282 participants) found consistent activation of the anterior insula, anterior cingulate cortex, supplementary motor area and cerebellum in response to unfair offers, and of the anterior cingulate, supplementary motor area and putamen when people decided to reject rather than accept an offer.

2557.content: Snyder and Fromkin introduce need for uniqueness as a positive striving to be different from other people and present a self-report Uniqueness Scale, with reliability, factor-analytic and validity data that they say meet the usual standards for an individual-differences measure, and eight validation studies.

2558.content: In five studies, people responded to taboo trade-offs that put a money price on sacred values with moral outrage and with moral cleansing. Racial egalitarians were least likely to use race-tainted base rates and angriest at those who did, and Christian fundamentalists most often rejected counterfactuals that applied everyday causal thinking to Biblical narratives, cleansing themselves after merely thinking about them.

2559.content: In male Long-Evans rats (Rattus norvegicus) swimming in an inescapable tank, recordings from 160 medial prefrontal neurons in 11 rats showed that 44 percent fired differently during swimming than during floating, most of them firing more while the animal swam. Driving the excitatory neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex as a whole changed nothing (p = 0.23), while driving only those medial prefrontal axons that end in the brainstem dorsal raphe nucleus raised kick frequency at once and reversibly (p = 1.04e-11 across the opsin-expressing rats, p = 0.39 in control rats), with no change in open-field movement.

In a separate group of rats (Rattus norvegicus) in the same study, driving the medial prefrontal axons that end in the lateral habenula had the opposite effect: the animals became less mobile, quickly and reversibly, while control animals did not change. Blocking glutamate receptors in the dorsal raphe abolished the activation produced by the raphe-targeted stimulation, and inhibiting those same axons lowered steady-state mobility.

2560.content: Using positron emission tomography while people decided how to respond to a partner who had abused their trust in an economic exchange, the authors found that punishment that actually cut the defector's payoff activated the dorsal striatum more than punishment that was only symbolic, and that people with stronger activation there were willing to pay more of their own money to punish.

2561.content: The authors proposed and tested a model in which people drink to regulate both good and bad feeling, with coping motives and enhancement motives treated as distinct behaviours with their own antecedents and consequences. They tested it in two random samples, one of adults and one of adolescents, using moderated regression and path analysis corrected for measurement error, and report strong support for the model in both samples.

2562.content: From the answers of more than 1500 college students to 53 driving situations, a cluster analysis produced a 33-item driving anger scale with six subscales: hostile gestures, illegal driving, police presence, slow driving, discourtesy and traffic obstructions. All subscales correlated positively with each other. Men reported more anger at police presence and slow driving, women more at illegal behaviour and traffic obstructions, and total scores did not differ between the sexes.

2563.content: A review of serotonin in the gut. Serotonin is a paracrine messenger released by enterochromaffin cells, which work as sensory transducers; it acts on nerve endings inside the gut wall and on nerves running to the central nervous system, starting movement and secretion reflexes and carrying information to the brain. It is made by two different tryptophan hydroxylases, one in enterochromaffin cells and one in neurons, and is cleared by the serotonin reuptake transporter into gut lining cells or neurons.

2564.content: Eight overweight men with type 2 diabetes, average age 59.3 years, sat in a room at 14 to 15 degrees Celsius for ten days running, 2 hours on day 1, 4 hours on day 2 and 6 hours on days 3 to 10. Measured with a hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp before and after, the glucose infusion rate rose by 43 percent on average, mostly through insulin-stimulated glucose disposal. Glucose uptake into brown fat rose but stayed very low, muscle mitochondrial respiration did not change, and GLUT4 in the muscle cell membrane was about 60 percent higher after acclimation.

2565.content: Six runners crossing the United States on foot, about 250 km a week for 14 to 20 weeks, had their total energy expenditure measured by doubly labelled water before the race, in week 1 and in the final week. For the three with measured resting metabolic rate, the ratio of total expenditure to resting rate went from 1.76 before the race to 3.76 in week 1 and 2.81 by week 20, as expenditure fell by about 1224 kcal a day while resting rate did not change. Pooled with published measurements from events lasting half a day to 95 days and from pregnancy, the highest sustained ratio fell logarithmically with the length of the event (r squared 0.98, n = 11 events in all, P below 0.001) and flattened below 3 times resting rate.

Comparing endurance studies with food freely available (n = 23) against overfeeding studies (n = 6), where people eat far more than they spend, the authors found that sustained energy intake was similar across both kinds of study, 2.36 times resting rate plus or minus 0.59, and unrelated to how long the event lasted. Weight change ran against the ratio of expenditure to resting rate, with the balance point between 2.20 and 2.35 times resting rate, so expenditure above about 2.5 times resting rate is met by drawing on the body's own stores. Pregnancy and lactation peak at about 2.2 times resting rate, and habitual values for 130 population groups sit below 2.5.

2566.content: In laboratory mice (Mus musculus), animals raised without any microbes had less serotonin in the blood, the colon and the faeces than normally colonised mice, and the shortfall sat in the chromogranin A positive enterochromaffin cells of the colon rather than in a smaller number of those cells. Giving germ-free mice a normal microbiota at birth, at weaning or in early adulthood restored blood and colon serotonin and colonic TPH1 expression, and wiping out the microbiota of normally colonised mice with antibiotics reproduced the shortfall. Colonising germ-free mice with spore-forming bacteria alone, dominated by Clostridial species, fully restored blood and colon serotonin, and the change in colonic serotonin altered gut transit and platelet function.
In the introduction the authors state, citing Gershon and Tack 2007, that more than 90 percent of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, where it acts on as many as 14 receptor subtypes.

2567.content: Twenty-four healthy men, 10 lean and 14 overweight or obese, were scanned with combined positron emission tomography and computed tomography at 22 degrees Celsius and again after two hours at 16 degrees Celsius. Brown adipose tissue activity appeared in 23 of the 24 men during mild cold and in none of them at the warmer temperature. Activity was lower in the overweight or obese men than in the lean men (P = 0.007); body mass index and body fat percentage correlated negatively with it and resting metabolic rate positively.

2568.content: Across four studies, the authors measured how strongly people endorse 43 rules of friendship in British, Italian, Hong Kong and Japanese samples, compared reported rule-keeping in friendships that had lasted against friendships that had lapsed, and asked people what ended a friendship. Six rules stood out as very important and also separated behaviour in lapsed from current friendships; they concerned mainly the exchange of rewards and intimacy, and the breakdown of friendships was attributed to failing to keep them.

2569.content: Among 100 psychology freshmen at the University of Konstanz, 82 percent had attended a two-day introductory event before term started and 18 percent had not. Friendship nominations were collected at the start, middle and end of the first semester and modelled with stochastic actor-oriented models. Students who had been at the early event were more likely to form new friendships across the semester, and less likely to keep the ones they had, with time spent with peers, age, gender and personality in the model.

2570.content: Using six waves of the British Household Panel Survey, which records where a person's three closest friends live and how often they meet, the authors modelled friendship formation and residential moves of 20 miles or more together. An additional close friend living within five miles went with a lower chance of moving by about two percentage points, which is 40 percent of the average rate of long moves in the sample, and where the friends lived mattered more than how often people met them. Allowing for the fact that sociable people both keep more friends nearby and move less reduced the size of the association.

Comparing people who did not move during the panel with people who moved once, the authors found that a move of more than five miles broke up part of the person's set of three closest local friends, and that movers then rebuilt local friendships over the following waves.

2571.content: In a counterbalanced within-person study, 18 healthy adults were tested after a night of sleep and after a night without sleep. After the sleepless night they held people at a greater distance in both a real approach task and a computerised version (mean change 4.7 plus or minus 2.1 and 5.76 plus or minus 2.8, differences of 13.2 and 17.7 percent, P at or below 0.05), and the authors report that the change held when their scores on mood and anxiety scales were taken into account. In a separate online study of 138 people over two nights, a fall in sleep efficiency from one night to the next went with more reported loneliness the next day, and a rise with less.

In the same study, 1033 online judges who knew nothing of the experiment watched filmed interviews of the same participants when rested and when sleep-deprived. They rated the sleep-deprived versions as lonelier and as less desirable to interact with, they were less likely to pick them as a collaborator, and they reported feeling lonelier themselves after watching, the more so the lonelier they had rated the person (R = 0.66, P below 0.005).

2572.content: A meta-analysis of how repeated exposure changes liking, familiarity and recognition, fitting 268 curve estimates from 81 articles. The authors report that the relation between repeated exposure and liking has a positive slope with a negative quadratic term, that is, liking rises with exposure and then falls again. The inverted-U shape held for visual but not auditory material, for exposures shorter than 10 seconds and longer than 1 minute, for both homogeneous and heterogeneous presentation, and for ratings taken after all items had been shown. The authors conclude that the existing models of the effect do not account for the findings.

2573.content: In two experiments, pairs of people of the same sex who had not met before interacted with each other for differing lengths of time. The more they interacted, the more attracted to each other they were. The authors identify three processes carrying the result: feeling that the other responded to them, more comfort and satisfaction during the interaction, and feeling that they knew the other person.

2574.content: Three small experiments tested whether people keep track of who put in what. Participants worked on a number-finding task with a partner and could pick a pen of the same colour as their partner, which hides individual contributions, or a different colour, which keeps them separate. In the first study, with 33 male undergraduates working with a female confederate, 88.2 percent of those led to expect an exchange relationship chose a different colour against 12.5 percent of those led to expect a communal relationship (z = 9.42, p below .01). In the second study, with 18 pairs, 94.4 percent of exchange participants against 42 percent of communal participants chose a different colour; in the third, with 20 pairs working face to face, 90 percent of stranger pairs against 30 percent of friend pairs did.

2575.content: Blood leukocytes from 14 adults in the population-based Chicago Health, Aging and Social Relations Study, picked from the top and the bottom 15 percent of the UCLA Loneliness Scale and matched on age, gender and race, were profiled on microarrays covering 22,283 transcripts. Two hundred and nine transcripts, 144 named genes, differed by more than 30 percent between the groups, with 78 higher and 131 lower in the high-scoring group. Scores on the scale had been stable over the three preceding years.

In the same 14 people, promoter analysis showed that genes carrying anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid response elements were expressed less in the high-scoring group (p = 0.032) and genes carrying pro-inflammatory NF-kappaB response elements more (p = 0.011). The authors report that this difference did not track circulating cortisol levels, nor the other measures they held constant, and that the ratio stayed raised when the measured size of a person's social network was held constant; the scale score and network size correlated only weakly.

2576.content: In 141 older adults of the Chicago Health, Aging, and Social Relations Study, sampled up to five times over years 5 to 10 (412 blood transcriptome surveys), those classed as chronically lonely (UCLA Loneliness Scale 41 or more in at least 60% of years 1 to 5; 26% of the sample) showed white blood cell gene expression shifted toward inflammation and away from antiviral and antibody genes (the conserved transcriptional response to adversity), on average 6.5% higher after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, body mass, smoking, alcohol and income, and 12.2% higher after also adjusting for stress, depressive symptoms and social support, none of which went with higher expression of the profile (stress went with lower expression). They also had more circulating monocytes, and in years when people felt lonelier their urinary norepinephrine was higher. Loneliness scores were in turn higher in proportion to the gene profile measured at the same time and one year earlier.

In archival data from 21 individually housed adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) assigned at random to meet for 100 minutes a day, 3 to 5 days a week, either a constantly changing set of unfamiliar partners or the same stable group of partners, the animals that kept meeting strangers had, after 5 weeks, a larger share of circulating monocytes, in particular the immature CD14++/CD16- classical monocytes, than the animals that kept meeting familiar partners.

In a rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) model in which animals were classed by observed behaviour as high in perceived social isolation (little social interaction and wariness of risky social partners) or as controls, the high-isolation animals had more circulating classical monocytes, white-cell interferon gene expression lowered by 82%, 48% and 92% (IFNA, IFNB, IFNG) before infection, reduced sensitivity of immune cells to glucocorticoids, and, after infection with simian immunodeficiency virus, poorer suppression of viral gene expression from the 2-week peak to the 10-week set point.

2577.content: In a narrative review of studies of adolescents and young adults, Creswell reports that most who drink do so only with others and mainly to have a good time with friends, while about 14% of adolescents and 15 to 24% of young adults also drink alone. Solitary drinkers report more negative affect, depressive symptoms and social discomfort (social anxiety, loneliness), and their drinking alone goes with drinking to cope with negative feelings over and above social or enhancement motives. Longitudinal studies she cites found that any drinking alone in adolescence was followed by more alcohol problems in early adulthood, over and above earlier alcohol use.

2578.content: In the US Monitoring the Future study, 4,464 drinkers surveyed at age 18 (classes of 1976 to 2002) and 4,561 at age 23 or 24 were followed to age 35. Those who reported any drinking alone in the past year had higher odds of reporting alcohol use disorder symptoms at 35 (two or more of 8 self-report items that address DSM-5 alcohol use disorder criteria): 1.35 times for drinking alone at 18 and 1.60 times at 23 or 24, after adjusting for how often they drank, how often they binge drank and sociodemographic factors. The link for adolescent solitary drinking held mainly for women (adjusted odds ratio 1.86; men 1.08, not significant). About a quarter of adolescent drinkers and 40% of young adult drinkers reported drinking alone.

2579.content: Using the 'Top Friends' ranking feature of the MySpace social network, the authors collected over 10 million people's friendship rankings. A person's choice of best friend was strongly predicted by how the candidate friends ranked that person, the pattern the alliance hypothesis predicts (people prefer partners who rank them above their other friends).

2580.content: In an experiment with 383 participants who watched a brief video of a woman who either bodily addressed the viewer or did not, the authors compared two questionnaires. The newer Experience of Parasocial Interaction Scale (EPSI) was the better measure of parasocial interaction, the sense during viewing that the figure on screen and the viewer are mutually aware of each other, while the widely used Parasocial Interaction Scale (PSI-Scale) may measure short- or long-term liking of the figure, or something else.

2581.content: A meta-analysis pooled 88 studies (40,068 people) selected from 531 found in a literature search, using a random-effects model. Loneliness scores showed a moderate association with depression scores, which the authors call a moderately significant effect; sample group, type of publication and publication year did not moderate it.

2582.content: In two experiments, participants had a brief experience of acceptance or rejection in a simulated computer chat room and then read a diary containing both social and individual events. In both experiments, those who had been rejected selectively remembered more of the explicitly social events, as the authors predicted from the parallel of physical hunger and selective memory for food.

2583.content: In two studies of social monitoring, people who reported more loneliness remembered more incidental social information (Study 1), and people who reported fewer friends decoded social cues in faces and voices better (Study 2). The authors read this as the attentional and perceptual building blocks of social skill being intact, and perhaps enhanced, in lonely people.

2584.content: In a hypothetical social discounting task (how much of a $75 reward a person would forgo for a named partner) with 63 participants in India and 284 in the US, emotional closeness largely, and often fully, mediated the higher giving to close friends. For mates and genetic kin, people forwent an extra $8.3 (95% CI 4.5 to 12.1) and $9.7 (95% CI 6.5 to 12.8) beyond what their closeness predicted, and these premiums did not differ between the US and India.

2585.content: In three experiments, the authors tested a proposal built on Fiske's relational theory that effort is governed by two kinds of market: in a money market effort tracks the size of the payment, in a social market it does not. Their experiments supported the observation that people sometimes put in more effort for no payment than for a low payment, and showed that mixed markets, with features of both, behaved more like money markets.

2586.content: Forty-two healthy married couples (aged 22 to 77, married 12.6 years on average) were admitted twice for 24 hours to a hospital research unit and given small blister wounds. In the first admission they held a structured social support conversation, in the second they discussed a marital disagreement. After the conflict, the wounds healed more slowly and local cytokine production (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta) at the wound sites was lower than after the support conversation.

In the same study, couples who were consistently more hostile in both conversations healed at 60% of the rate of low-hostile couples, and showed larger rises in plasma IL-6 and TNF-alpha the morning after a conflict than after a support conversation, compared with low-hostile couples.

2587.content: Across 11 studies with 2,918 participants, using hypothetical scenarios, recalled real events and an online manipulation, friendship jealousy was evoked by a third party threatening a friendship and not by the prospect of losing the friend alone (for example a friend moving away), was stronger for more valued friendships (best friends over close friends and acquaintances), tracked cues of being replaced more than cues of lost time, and went with 'friend guarding', behaviour aimed at countering the third party. These effects were specific to jealousy relative to sadness or anger felt at the same time.

In Study 7, 428 US adults recruited online each imagined one of six scenarios that crossed time threat (the best friend spends much or little time with a new friend) with replacement threat (the new friend is likely to take one's place, no information, or unlikely to). Replacement threat moved reported friendship jealousy strongly (means 4.38 high, 2.40 control, 1.52 low; partial eta squared 0.35), while time threat had only a marginal effect (means 2.91 against 2.62, p = .071, partial eta squared 0.008).

2588.content: In four studies (644 participants), sense of belonging went with how meaningful people found life: a strong correlation in Study 1 (126 people); belonging predicted rated meaningfulness 3 weeks later in Study 2 (248), and also independent ratings of participants' essays on meaning; in Studies 3 (105) and 4 (165), participants primed with belongingness, or who rose in belongingness, reported the most meaning, more than those primed with social support or social value, and in Study 4 belonging mediated the effect of condition on meaning.

2589.content: In the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, 4,211 adults aged 50 and over with complete data were followed every 2 years from 2004 to 2017. Each 1-point higher loneliness score at baseline (3-item UCLA scale, range 3 to 9) went with a 0.16 point higher depressive symptom score (CES-D with its loneliness item removed) averaged over six follow-ups, after adjusting for social network size, contact frequency, group participation, social support, polygenic scores for loneliness and depression, baseline depressive symptoms and many health and social factors. The link held across 12 years but grew smaller with longer follow-up. The authors estimated that 18% of cases scoring above the CES-D cutoff at 1 year, and 11% at 12 years, were attributable to loneliness.

2590.content: In a two-wave panel of US respondents from the National Survey of Families and Households who moved between waves, longer time in the new place went with more involvement in social exchanges. Emotional and financial support did not change with the distance moved; tangible favours and companionship fell with it. Exchanges with kin fell after distant and recent moves, while exchanges with non-kin were more extensive for people whose kin lived further away, which the authors read as non-kin replacing kin in the network.

2591.content: A systematic review of 32 longitudinal studies of adults in the general population found that most reported baseline loneliness associated with later onset of depression by each study's criteria. Seven studies with adjusted estimates were pooled (six in older adults, one in new mothers; follow-up 6 months to 17 years; five excluded anyone with current or past depression at baseline): people who were often lonely had 2.33 times the odds (95% CI 1.62 to 3.34) of newly meeting the studies' depression criteria compared with those who were not often lonely, with moderate heterogeneity (I squared 64%). All seven studies with more than 10,000 participants reported the link, and the few studies on anxiety and self-harm also reported positive links.

2592.content: In four experiments, participants who had just been socially excluded, compared with controls, were more likely to buy a product symbolic of group membership (but not practical or self-gift items), to tailor their spending to an interaction partner's preferences, to spend money on an unappealing food a peer favoured, and to say they were willing to try an illegal drug, but only when doing so raised their chances of starting a social connection. The authors conclude that excluded people trade personal and financial well-being for social well-being.

2593.content: In a questionnaire study of 319 people (163 men, 156 women) about help given to a sibling, a friend or a mate, participants overall gave friends and mates as much help as siblings or more. As the cost of help rose, siblings received a progressively larger share and friends and mates a smaller one, although participants felt emotionally closer to their friends and mates than to their siblings.

2594.content: In two laboratory experiments with undergraduates, being excluded lowered how meaningful participants rated their life. In Study 1 (108 students), those told that a partner had refused to meet them after seeing their video rated life as less meaningful (mean 6.26 on a 7-point scale) than accepted (6.54, d = 0.43) or control participants (6.62, d = 0.60). In Study 2 (121 students), those left out of a computer ball-tossing game (Cyberball) rated life as more meaningless than control (d = 0.33) or highly included participants (d = 0.39). Being accepted or highly included did not raise meaning above control in either study. In Study 1 the effect fell below significance when mood was held constant, though mood did not mediate it in a formal test; in Study 2 the effect held with mood held constant.

In Study 3, among 202 undergraduates, loneliness (the authors' measure of chronic exclusion) went with less presence of meaning in life (r = -0.35) and was the strongest single predictor of meaning in a regression that also held depressive symptoms scored on the CES-D, mood, happiness and optimism (beta -0.34). Depressive symptoms and optimism added nothing once the other variables were in the model. In Study 4 (212 undergraduates), the link between loneliness and lower meaning ran through lower sense of purpose, value and self-worth, and marginally through efficacy.

2595.content: Abstract only. In a longitudinal study of 60 recently widowed and 60 matched married men and women, the authors tested whether support from friends and family buffers the loss of a spouse (stress theory) or cannot make up for the loss of an attachment figure (attachment theory). The results supported attachment theory: marital status and social support each related to well-being on their own, the effect of losing the spouse ran through emotional loneliness, and the effect of social support ran through social loneliness.

2596.content: Abstract only. A systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 34 studies of people diagnosed with social anxiety disorder found 20 formal instruments and four other measures of social isolation; most instruments were used in one study only, and simple structural measures such as living alone were used most often. Pooled scores were 38.1 on the Loneliness and Social Dissatisfaction Questionnaire, 33.1 on the avoidance subscale of the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale and 21.1 on the Social Avoidance and Distress Scale. The authors conclude that social isolation is common among people with this diagnosis but is measured in many different ways.

2597.content: Abstract only. Using quantitative and qualitative data from the second East York study (Toronto), Wellman and Wortley found that most relationships give specialised support, and that the kind of support depends more on the relationship than on the people in it. Strong ties gave emotional aid, small services and companionship; parents and adult children exchanged financial aid, emotional aid and large and small services; ties that were physically close gave services; women gave emotional aid. Friends, neighbours and siblings made up about half of all supportive relationships.

2598.content: Abstract only. In parallel behavioural economic experiments in three urban settings (USA, Japan and China), people monitored their friends less carefully than they monitored strangers, were more generous to friends than to strangers, and friends tolerated imbalances in payoffs more than strangers did. Tracking did still occur among friends, to a lesser degree.

2599.content: Abstract only. Zajonc proposed that mere repeated exposure of a person to a stimulus, meaning only that the stimulus is made accessible to perception, enhances the person's attitude toward it. He reviewed four kinds of support: the correlation between how often words occur and how positive they feel; experiments in which more frequent exposure to nonsense words and symbols made them feel more positive; the correlation between word frequency and attitudes to what the words name; and experiments in which more frequent exposure improved attitudes.

2600.content: Abstract only. In the McLean Study of Adult Development, 290 inpatients who met Revised Diagnostic Interview for Borderlines and DSM-III-R criteria for borderline personality disorder were reassessed every two years for ten years. 88 percent reached remission as the authors defined it (no longer meeting the criteria); of the 242 who remitted, 39.3 percent first did so by year 2, a further 22.3 percent by year 4, 21.9 percent by year 6, 12.8 percent by year 8 and 3.7 percent by year 10. Seven baseline variables went with earlier remission in multivariate analysis: younger age, no reported childhood sexual abuse, no family history of substance use disorder, a good work record, no anxious cluster personality disorder diagnosis, low neuroticism and high agreeableness.

2601.content: Buss built a taxonomy of 19 mate retention tactics and 104 acts from acts nominated by 105 US undergraduates, then had 102 undergraduates report how often they performed each act. Men reported more resource display than women; women reported more appearance enhancement and more threats of infidelity than men; the prediction that women would use sexual inducements more was falsified, with men reporting more. Many tactics were used more the more serious the relationship. In a further sample of 46, male resource display and female infidelity threats were judged the more effective.

The most striking result, in Buss's own words, was how alike the sexes were: across the 104 acts of mate guarding and retention, the mean reported frequencies of US undergraduate men and women correlated at +0.91, and a summary score of all 104 acts showed no overall sex difference.

2602.content: In 214 people (107 men, 107 women) married less than a year, contacted through the public records of marriage licences in a large Midwestern US county, husbands who thought it more likely that their wife would be unfaithful in the next year reported more concealment of their wife, more punishment of her threatened infidelity and more derogation of rival men, also after controlling for both spouses' ages, relationship length and his rating of her attractiveness. For wives, none of 38 standard or partial correlations between perceived infidelity threat and mate retention reached significance.

In the same newlywed sample, men married to younger women reported more mate retention effort than men married to older women, from resource display to threats against rivals and violence, also after controlling for the husband's age and relationship length; men's effort also rose with how attractive they judged their wife. Women's effort was only weakly linked with the husband's age, and the link disappeared after controls. Women married to men with higher incomes reported more vigilance and more punishment of the husband's infidelity threats; men's effort was unrelated to the wife's income.

2603.content: Abstract only. Among 2,079 students in seven industrialised nations (Hungary, Ireland, Mexico, the Netherlands, the Soviet Union, the United States and Yugoslavia), a partner kissing, flirting or having sex with someone else set off jealousy in nearly all nations, while dancing, hugging and sexual fantasies about someone else drew on average a neutral reaction everywhere. Nations differed strikingly in how much weight they gave to particular behaviours. In all seven nations women were more upset than men when their partner kissed someone else, and men reacted relatively more negatively than women to a partner's sexual fantasies about another person.

2604.content: A multilevel kernel density meta-analysis of 20 fMRI studies (8 to 53 participants each, 309 in all) of sexual desire and of love found that both recruit a common set of areas, among them the insula, striatum, thalamus, hippocampus and anterior cingulate. They also differed: the posterior insula was active with sexual desire and the anterior insula with love; compared with desire, love showed less activity in the ventral striatum, hypothalamus, amygdala, somatosensory cortex and inferior parietal lobule, and more in the ventral tegmental area and dorsal right striatum.

In the same meta-analysis, love compared with sexual desire went with stronger activation of the ventral tegmental area and more activity in dorsal regions of the right striatum, dopamine-rich regions tied to motivation, reward expectancy and habit formation, while desire went with more activity in the ventral striatum, hypothalamus and amygdala.

2605.content: Conroy-Beam and Buss compared agent-based simulations in which mate preferences either did or did not drive choice with three studies of real couples (214 newlyweds from a Midwestern US county, and 259 and 294 people in relationships recruited on Mechanical Turk). Real couples matched the preference-driven simulations and not the random ones. Preference-driven models reproduced what real couples showed: low correlations between stated preferences and the traits of the chosen partner, people of high mate value securing partners with more desirable traits, and couples matched on overall mate value. The authors present evidence that the effects come from stated preferences guiding choice, and are not better explained by people updating their preferences to match their partner.

2606.content: In a speed-dating study with one month of follow-up, 163 US undergraduates (81 women) stated the usual sex differences in how much they valued physical attractiveness and earning prospects in an ideal partner. In their romantic interest in partners they actually met, during and after the events, there was no sex difference in how much attractiveness and earning prospects mattered. Ideal preferences stated before the event did not predict what drew participants to partners at the event.

2607.content: Abstract only. In a direct replication of Eastwick and Finkel 2008, 307 participants took part in speed dating with follow-up surveys over 30 days. Participants were more romantically interested in partners they saw as attractive and as good potential earners, and these associations did not differ by gender.

2608.content: In one-shot ultimatum games for real money with partners shown only as face photographs of real students, 88 US undergraduate men were more generous toward partners who were physically stronger and who looked more attractive, prosocial, productive, healthy and high in status; the effect of strength ran through how productive the partner looked, not how dangerous. Men gave up earnings by cooperating selectively with partners who looked valuable as long-term partners. Among 67 women playing with female partners, women also treated valuable-looking partners better, but gave partner choice less priority than men did.

2609.content: Abstract only. Ten healthy men were measured twice during sexual arousal and masturbation to orgasm, before and after three weeks of sexual abstinence, with continuous blood sampling and cardiovascular monitoring. Orgasm raised blood pressure, heart rate, plasma adrenaline and noradrenaline and prolactin on both occasions; abstinence did not change this response. Orgasm left testosterone unchanged. Testosterone concentrations were higher after the three weeks of abstinence.

2610.content: Fisher and colleagues propose that mammals and birds have three distinct, interrelated systems for mating, reproduction and parenting, each with its own brain correlates and behaviour: lust (the sex drive) evolved to start mating with any appropriate partner; attraction (romantic love) evolved to let individuals choose and prefer a specific partner, saving mating time and energy; and attachment evolved to keep a pair cooperating until the species' parental duties are done. The paper reports no brain results of its own: the authors' fMRI study was still being analysed, and they cite Bartels and Zeki 2000 (17 people in love) as consistent with the model.

2611.content: Slovic reviews a study by Fetherstonhaugh, Slovic, Johnson and Friedrich (1997) in which respondents stated how many lives a medical research institute would have to save to merit a 10 million dollar grant. Nearly two-thirds raised the number of lives required when the population at risk was larger: the median was 9,000 lives saved when 15,000 were at risk and 100,000 lives saved when 290,000 were at risk, so saving 9,000 in the smaller population was valued above saving ten times as many in the largest. He names this psychophysical numbing and reports that other studies of lifesaving choices found the same pattern.

Slovic argues, from decision research, that most people will make great efforts to rescue a single victim whose plight comes to their attention, yet become numbly indifferent to individuals who are one of many in a larger problem. He proposes that feeling for victims is greatest for one person, begins to fall at two, and collapses at some larger number that becomes a statistic, and that this leaves mass killing without a response.

2612.content: In a field experiment with 121 people approached in a university student centre in Pennsylvania, each paid 5 dollars for an unrelated survey and then given a real Save the Children request letter, those who read about one identified girl (a photograph and a short description) gave a mean 2.12 dollars, against 1.21 dollars from those who read statistics about starvation in Africa. Where no lesson about this bias came first, the identified girl drew a mean 2.83 dollars, against 1.26 dollars across the other three conditions. Reading a short lesson about the bias cut giving to the identified girl and did not raise giving to the statistical victims.

In Study 4, 165 students and others on a Pennsylvania campus were first primed to calculate (maths questions) or to feel (questions about their feelings), then asked to give part of 5 dollars to an identified child or to statistical victims. Those primed to calculate gave less to the identified child than those primed to feel; the primes made no difference to giving to statistical victims. The authors read this as deliberation cutting sympathy for a single victim without creating sympathy for victims shown as numbers.

2613.content: In two between-subjects studies with Swedish university students, people offered to help one identified starving child (a photograph, name and age) or two such children. With hypothetical donations (208 students), the mean offered was 37.7 Swedish crowns for one child and 26.3 for two; with real donations from money just earned (168 students), 24.5 against 21.5 crowns. Self-rated positive feeling was also higher for one child (3.7 against 3.3, and 3.5 against 3.0), and in both studies the drop in feeling accounted statistically for the drop in giving.

Across four studies, positive feeling about helping was strongest for one endangered child and fell as the number grew. In Study 2 (107 Swedish students, within-subject, one, two or eight identified children), facial EMG over the smiling muscle (zygomaticus major) was highest for one child and fell for two and eight, and donations fell from one to two to eight. In Study 3 (131 students), presenting two or eight children as one family raised donations compared with the same number of unrelated children.

2614.content: In 179 male Libyan revolutionaries from four battalions in Misrata, surveyed in 2011 with a pictorial scale of identity fusion (a felt oneness with a group), 99 percent were fused with their own family, 97 percent with their own battalion and 96 percent with other revolutionary battalions, while 1 percent were fused with ordinary Libyans who supported the revolution but did not join a battalion. The authors note that in peacetime samples in more than 10 countries fusion with one's nation ranges from 6 to 41 percent. Fighters described the battalions as microgroups of three to five who ate, prayed, slept and fought together.

Asked which group they felt most fused with, 68 percent of the 179 Libyan revolutionaries named their family and 32 percent their own battalion; none named other battalions or ordinary Libyans. Among the 42 frontline fighters almost half (45 percent) named their battalion, against 28 percent of the 137 logistical supporters. The authors give two readings: that the most fused volunteered for the front, or that shared fighting built the fusion, and do not decide between them.

2615.content: Abstract only. Women answered written items on their sexual interests and their partners' behaviour twice, once within 5 days before a luteinising hormone surge (near ovulation) and once in the luteal phase. Near ovulation they reported more sexual interest in, and fantasy about, men other than their primary partner, and no significant rise in interest in their primary partner. They also reported that their primary partners were both more attentive and more proprietary near ovulation than in the luteal phase. The authors read this as a conflict of interest between the sexes that shifts across the cycle.

2616.content: Among 126 men aged 21 to 38 at a Beijing university (66 unmarried, 30 married without children, 30 fathers, each with one child), the 30 fathers had significantly lower salivary testosterone than both other groups, morning and afternoon: in the morning 33 percent lower than married non-fathers and 44 percent lower than unmarried men, in the afternoon 32 and 44 percent lower. Unmarried men were slightly but not significantly higher than married non-fathers, and fathers of children under 4 were no lower than fathers of older children. The authors note that the design is cross-sectional and cannot say whether fatherhood lowers testosterone or lower-testosterone men become fathers.

2617.content: Abstract only. A meta-analysis of 114 effects from 66 published and unpublished studies tested four predictions of the Challenge Hypothesis in men. Pair-bonded men had lower testosterone than single men, fathers had lower testosterone than childless men, and men more oriented toward pair-bonding or toward investing in their children had lower testosterone. The authors discuss how large these differences are next to known influences such as age and geographic population.

2618.content: Reviewing their own brain-imaging studies of modern people making Lower Palaeolithic stone tools, Stout and Chaminade report that Oldowan flaking (the earliest known technology, about 2.6 million years old) draws mainly on a parietal and ventral premotor circuit for visually guided grasping, while Late Acheulean handaxe making (from about 700,000 years ago) uses the same regions plus right ventral premotor cortex and the dorsal part of right inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis, a region tied to hierarchical action and to parts of language. They argue that this overlap fits hypotheses in which toolmaking and language evolved together, and state that it cannot demonstrate an evolutionary connection.

2619.content: Animal evidence, reviewed. Leptin genes have been cloned from all major vertebrate classes (birds possibly excepted), and leptin given by injection reduces food intake in mammals, birds, amphibians, lizards and fishes. The authors call this appetite-suppressing action perhaps the only leptin function shared across vertebrates without qualification, and read its presence in every group tested as strong support for an ancient origin.

Animal and human evidence, reviewed. Leptin is no faithful report of fat stores outside mammals: in most fish studies leptin rises with fasting and falls quickly on refeeding, and medaka (Oryzias latipes) lacking the leptin receptor eat more and grow faster without more fat in liver or muscle. In hibernating woodchucks (Marmota monax) leptin and body mass are out of phase, and in humans people of the same body mass index can differ tenfold in leptin.

2620.content: Abstract only. Animal evidence. GnRH-like peptides of 10 to 12 amino acids and GnRH receptors are found in invertebrates from annelid worms to tunicates, and a large maximum-likelihood phylogeny groups the GnRH, adipokinetic hormone and corazonin receptors in one superfamily, close to the vasopressin and oxytocin receptors. The authors conclude that GnRH and its receptor go back to the origin of bilaterian animals, that the invertebrate peptides do not always serve reproduction, and that a working pituitary came from genome duplications in early vertebrates.

2621.content: Abstract only. Animal evidence. Adult female monkeys (cynomolgus macaques, Macaca fascicularis, in the PubMed index) were fed a diet that promotes atherosclerosis and housed in small social groups, and the social status of half was reversed: subordinates were made dominant and dominants subordinate. Status change had little effect on risk factors but changed coronary artery atherosclerosis: every animal that changed position had worse atherosclerosis, whichever way it moved. Subordinates made dominant had 44 percent more, and dominants made subordinate 500 percent more, than animals of the same original rank whose status did not change. The authors note that earlier experiments had found subordinate females to have poor ovarian function and worse atherosclerosis.

2622.content: Abstract only. Animal evidence. In the sea lamprey (Petromyzon marinus), a jawless vertebrate, two GnRHs act through the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis to control reproduction, the earliest vertebrate in which such roles are shown. From the lamprey genome the authors identified a new GnRH (lamprey GnRH-II), which they propose is ancestral to the vertebrate GnRHs, and a second glycoprotein hormone receptor. They describe a primitive, overlapping gonadal and thyroid axis in the lamprey, with one or two pituitary glycoprotein hormones and two receptors, against three or four hormones and three receptors in jawed vertebrates.

2623.content: Abstract only. Animal evidence.
