In the same study, email's material properties combined with social norms and interpretations so that informants singled out email as a cultural symbol of the overload in their lives, and by serving as that symbol email drew their attention away from other sources of overload in their work.

2979.content: From the 2017 round of strategic noise mapping reported by the 33 EEA member countries (excluding Turkey), with gaps filled for the more than 30% of required data not reported, an estimated 113 million people were exposed to long-term road traffic noise of at least 55 dB(A) (day-evening-night level), plus 22 million to railway noise, 4 million to aircraft noise and under 1 million to industrial noise at high levels. Road traffic alone puts at least 20% of Europeans above 55 dB(A) over day, evening and night and more than 15% at night, and the agency states the numbers are likely underestimates, as the mapping does not cover all urban areas, roads, railways and airports.

2980.content: The authors estimated that about 104 million people in the United States had annual 24-hour average noise exposure above 70 dBA in 2013, the US EPA limit for preventing noise-induced hearing loss, by applying the EPA's 1981 estimate (33% of the population above that level) to the 2013 population and assuming noise levels had not changed. Applying the 1981 estimate for 55 to 60 dBA day-night levels in the same way gave at least 145.5 million people at potential risk of raised blood pressure from noise.

2981.content: The Population Reference Bureau estimates that about 117 billion members of Homo sapiens have ever been born (117,020,448,575 by 2022), so that the 8 billion alive in 2022 are about 6.8% of all ever born. The estimate starts from two people in 190,000 BCE, assumes constant growth between benchmark years and birth rates of 80 per 1,000 to 1 CE, 60 per 1,000 from 2 CE to 1750 and lower after; the authors call it semi-scientific and say it may underestimate early births.

In the same estimate (Table 1), the world population is put at about 5 million in 8000 BCE, and the cumulative number ever born reaches about 9.0 billion (8,993,889,771) by 8000 BCE, 55.0 billion by 1 CE and 117.0 billion by 2022. By this estimate most of the people ever born were born after 8000 BCE.

2982.content: In an in situ study of 40 volunteers (20 women, 20 men) in a research division of a large corporation, email use was logged by computer and stress was measured by heart rate variability (RMSSD) from chest monitors over about 12 workdays. In mixed models controlling for job demands, decision latitude and baseline stress scores, the longer a person spent on email in an hour, the higher their measured stress in that hour, and longer daily email time went with lower rated productivity. Checking email by habit or by notification made no difference to stress, and batching email did not lower stress.

2983.content: In an online survey by YouGov in January and February 2023 (about 2,000 respondents per market, 46 markets), among people who used a news gateway in the last week, 30% said social media was their main way of coming across news online, 22% said direct access to a news website or app (down from 32% in 2018), 25% search, 9% mobile alerts, 8% aggregators and 5% email. Younger groups everywhere preferred side-door routes such as social media, search and aggregators.

In the Reuters Institute's 2023 online survey of news users in 46 markets (about 2,000 respondents per market), people who used TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat for news said they paid more attention there to celebrities, influencers and social media personalities than to journalists; on Facebook and Twitter, news media and journalists were still central.

2984.content: A meta-analysis of resilience-building programmes run in workplaces (42 independent samples across 37 studies) found a small overall effect (d = 0.21). The effect shrank from about d = 0.26 at one month or less after the programme to about d = 0.07 later. Among people the authors judged to be at greater risk of stress or lacking protective resources, the pattern ran the other way: weak early effects grew stronger at later measurement. One-on-one delivery such as coaching did best and computer-based and train-the-trainer formats did worst.

2985.content: A systematic review of controlled studies of interventions for workers with burnout found 14 studies of 18 interventions; 14 were aimed at the individual and 4 combined individual and occupational approaches. Results were mixed. A meta-analysis of four individually focused randomised trials showed no effect on exhaustion or cynicism, and there were too few studies to pool the effect of combined interventions or the effect on return to work.

2986.content: Using state laws that let unmarried women under 21 consent to medical care (and so obtain the pill without a parent) as a natural experiment, Bailey compared US women born 1940 to 1955. Legal access to the pill before age 21 lowered the likelihood of a first birth before age 22 by 14 to 18 percent, raised labour-force participation among women aged 26 to 30 by about 8 percent, and added at least 68 hours of paid work a year at ages 26 to 30. The author reads this as the pill working through the timing of first births.

2987.content: Canadian provinces introduced public salary disclosure laws at different times. Using administrative data on most Canadian university faculty and an event-study design, the authors find the laws lowered the gender salary gap by 1.2 to 2 percentage points, about 20 to 30 percent of the roughly 6 percent gap of the mid-1990s; disclosure accounts for about 25 to 40 percent of the fall in the gap from then to 2018. With individual fixed effects, slower relative growth of men's salaries contributed to the narrowing, and the effect was larger in unionised workplaces.

2988.content: In a large private organisation, 21 employees moved from traditional offices to open offices were surveyed before the move, 4 weeks after and 6 months after. Satisfaction with the physical environment, physical stress, coworker relations and perceived job performance all worsened after the move, and the dissatisfaction did not ease after the adjustment period.

2989.content: In a field experiment with 2,060 employees of a large corporation in Southeast Asia, employees were given true information about the average salaries of their managers or their peers. Learning that managers earned more than they had thought raised effort: a 10 percent rise in perceived manager salary raised hours worked over the next 90 days by 1.5 percent (elasticity 0.150) and emails sent (elasticity 0.130). Learning that peers earned more lowered effort, with an elasticity of about -0.94 for hours, -0.431 for emails and -0.731 for sales.

2990.content: A systematic review of controlled trials of programmes meant to raise individual resilience found 17 studies; 11 randomised trials entered the meta-analysis. The pooled effect on resilience scale scores was moderate (standardised mean difference 0.44, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.64); only 4 of the 11 trials were significant alone. Combined CBT and mindfulness programmes gave 0.51, CBT-based 0.27, mindfulness 0.46. In the five studies with a 6-month follow-up the effect held for mindfulness programmes (0.58). Every outcome was a self-report resilience scale; no study tested how people fared in a later adversity.

2991.content: In an experiment, people who reported a past or current depressive episode were given the result of a bogus but credible biological test saying their depressive symptoms were, or were not, caused by a chemical imbalance in the brain. Being told it was a chemical imbalance did not lower self-blame, made them more pessimistic about their prognosis, lowered their expectations that they could regulate their negative mood, and made them rate pharmacotherapy as more credible and effective than psychotherapy.

2992.content: A large community survey in which people were followed through job loss and re-employment found substantial rises in distress with unemployment and positive emotional effects of re-employment, with the raised distress gone after re-employment. Baseline emotional functioning was unrelated to the chance of being re-employed, so the authors read the pattern as running from job status to distress.

2993.content: Among 764 municipal employees in Raisio, Finland, who kept their jobs through the 1991 to 1993 downsizing, certified sickness absence was 2.17 times higher (95% CI 1.54 to 3.07) after major downsizing than after minor downsizing, over a mean follow-up of 4.9 years. Downsizing went with more physical demands, more job insecurity, less job control and less support from spouses. Adjusting for the changes in work (physical demands, job control, job insecurity) cut the link between downsizing and sickness absence by 49%; adjusting for lost support or more smoking did not change it.

2994.content: A meta-analysis of feedback interventions (607 effect sizes, 23,663 observations) found that feedback improved performance on average (d = .41) but that more than a third of the interventions lowered performance, which sampling error, the sign of the feedback or existing theories did not explain.
Testing their feedback intervention theory with moderator analyses, the authors found that feedback works less well the more it turns attention away from the task and toward the self.

2995.content: In three experiments with US mental health clinicians (n = 132, 105 and 106; psychiatrists, psychologists and social workers), clinicians read vignettes of patients whose symptoms met the criteria the authors used for schizophrenia, social phobia, major depression or OCD, each paired with a biological (genes, brain) or a psychosocial (life history) explanation. Biological explanations produced significantly less empathy in study 1 (F = 32.66, P < 0.001) and study 2 (F = 18.16, P < 0.001), among medical doctors and others alike, and also when biological information only predominated (study 3).

In the same experiments, clinicians rated psychotherapy as less effective when the vignette patients' symptoms were explained biologically, and for all labels except schizophrenia they rated medication as more effective.

2996.content: A meta-analysis of 104 studies (437 effect sizes) found that unemployed people had lower psychological and physical well-being than employed people. The size of the mental health gap depended on how long people had been unemployed and on sample type, but not on the local unemployment rate or the amount of unemployment benefit. Among the unemployed, how central work was to the person and their coping resources (personal, social, financial and time structure), appraisals and coping strategies related more strongly to mental health than human capital or demographics did.

2997.content: In a randomised trial of 4,834 employees of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (3,300 offered the iThrive programme, 1,534 controls), a two-year workplace wellness programme of paid on-site biometric screening, online health risk assessment and a choice of wellness activities, with cash rewards and paid time off, had no significant effect after 12 or 24 months on 16 clinician-measured biometrics, on claims-based diagnoses of diabetes, hypertension or hyperlipidaemia, or on medical use. More treated employees reported having a primary care physician (92.2% vs 86.1%), and their beliefs about their own health improved slightly. The share who reported never feeling anxious or depressed did not differ between groups (32.6% vs 31.5% in 2018).

2998.content: In a field experiment, 30 allotment gardeners did a stressful Stroop task and were then randomly assigned to 30 minutes of outdoor gardening or indoor reading on their own allotment plot. Salivary cortisol fell in both groups during recovery but fell significantly more after gardening, and positive mood was fully restored after gardening while it worsened further during reading.

2999.content: A survey found that people often use positive self-statements and believe they work. In two experiments, participants with low self-esteem who repeated 'I'm a lovable person' or focused on how it was true felt worse than those who did not, while participants with high self-esteem felt better, to a limited degree.

3000.content: In a preregistered vignette experiment with 1,240 adults recruited online (937 in the US, 303 in India), participants read about a person claiming serious need where helping was costly to them and her true need was private. When the vignette had her show costlier signals, labelled depression or a suicide attempt, participants believed her need more, judged her less manipulative and said they were more likely to help than when she made a plain verbal request or cried. The effect on helping ran largely through belief in her need. The authors read depression and suicidality as credible signals of need in conflicts of interest.

3001.content: Short argues that mammals hold their numbers in balance with the environment through female reproductive variables such as age at puberty, embryonic and neonatal loss and the length of lactational amenorrhoea, and that humans have removed these checks. As natural selection always maximised reproductive potential, he argues, women are physiologically ill-adapted to spending the greater part of their reproductive lives not pregnant, and the choice of contraceptives will affect general health.

3002.content: Greenough, Black and Wallace propose two kinds of information storage in the developing brain. Experience-expectant storage takes in information that is present in every environment and common to all members of the species, such as the basic elements of pattern vision: synapses are overproduced and experience selects which connections remain. Experience-dependent storage takes in information unique to the individual, such as one's own surroundings or vocabulary, by forming new synapses. They offer the scheme in place of the terms critical or sensitive period.

3003.content: From a PubMed literature search, El-Mallakh and colleagues report that patients diagnosed with depression who end up labelled treatment resistant have often responded to antidepressants at first and have taken them for long periods at high doses. They draw a parallel with tardive dyskinesia, propose that changes in the branching of nerve-cell dendrites may underlie the lasting low mood that comes with chronic antidepressant use, name it tardive dysphoria, and say it should be tested in blinded, randomised antidepressant discontinuation trials.

3004.content: Hoffman proposes the social deafferentation hypothesis: just as loss of sensory input produces phantom limbs or visual hallucinations, heavy social withdrawal or isolation in vulnerable people prompts the brain's social cognition systems to produce spurious social meaning, in the form of emotionally compelling hallucinated voices and delusions about other people or agents, which the author says may stand in for impoverished social experience. He builds it on reviewed findings that isolation often precedes the first episode of what is diagnosed as schizophrenia (for example 24% against 1% of students later diagnosed in the schizophrenia spectrum in Kwapil's 10-year follow-up of high against low scorers on a social anhedonia scale).

In the author's own research with patients diagnosed with schizophrenia who hear voices, most could recall their first experience of voices, and among those who could, 73% reported increasing social isolation before the voices began (examples given: moving to a new neighbourhood and losing friends, isolating to write a dissertation, driving alone across the country).

3005.content: Milton, an autistic sociologist, argues that what is labelled a social deficit in autistic people is a 'double empathy problem': a breakdown in reciprocity between two differently disposed people, felt by both, that grows with the gap between how they perceive the world. He argues that non-autistic people's attempts at empathy toward people labelled autistic are often wildly inaccurate, and that they lack insight into the minds of people so labelled as much as those people lack insight into theirs. Differences in neurology, he argues, may produce differences in sociality, and he rejects the 'social deficit' reading measured against an idealised normal.

3006.content: The authors, Moncrieff and Cohen, contrast two models of how antidepressants act. The disease-centred model holds that they correct the biological abnormality behind depression, as insulin does in diabetes; the authors find little evidence for it. Their drug-centred model holds that psychotropic drugs create abnormal states of their own (sedation, cognitive impairment, mild stimulation, sometimes agitation, varying by chemical class) which may coincidentally relieve symptoms, and that trial results can be explained by these drug effects plus amplified placebo responses.

Reviewing the evidence, the authors conclude that there are no specific antidepressant drugs, that most of their short-term effects are shared by many other drugs, and that no drug has been shown to raise mood in the long term. They report that in recent meta-analyses the advantage of antidepressants over placebo in trials was small, about two points on the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression, where items on sleep, anxiety and agitation can score up to 16 points and any sedative drug would be likely to beat placebo.

3007.content: Spikins, Wright and Hodgson argue that once collaborative morality arose in human groups, being valued and prosocially motivated mattered more than being socially clever, citing forager cases: among the Martu of Australia the most generous are favoured as hunting partners, and among the Ache of Paraguay past generosity brings more support when ill or old. In such bands, they argue, a positive reputation for contributing to the group buffered individual weaknesses and opened niches for different social strategies, including people with less complex social cognition.

The authors argue that in small collaborative hunter-gatherer bands a low share of people with autistic traits (they write AS for autism without intellectual impairment) would have been shielded from exploitation and could have been at an advantage where their logic- and detail-based perception gave valued technical and social skills, for example in making complex, standardised tools in variable high-latitude environments.

3008.content: The review describes sickness as a normal response to infection, as fear is to a predator: pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha, IL-6) made at the site of infection act on the brain and produce withdrawal, pain, malaise and loss of interest in reward. The authors describe sickness behaviour as a motivational state that reorganises perception and action so the ill individual copes better with infection.

The authors report from the clinical literature that roughly a third of patients treated with the cytokines IL-2 or interferon-alpha (for cancer or hepatitis C) develop symptoms that meet criteria for major depressive disorder. In these patients fatigue, poor appetite, pain and poor sleep appear early in all of them, while low mood and mild cognitive changes come later in up to half; pretreatment with paroxetine reduced the later psychological symptoms and did little for the early ones, and those who developed them had scored higher on a depression scale before treatment.

The authors state that the likeness between sickness and depression is only partial: sickness is an adaptive response to infection and fully reversible once the pathogen is cleared, while depression is not. They suggest that what is labelled depression may be a maladaptive form of cytokine-induced sickness that appears when the immune response is raised for too long or too strongly, or in people with greater vulnerability.

3009.content: Simpson and Raubenheimer propose the protein leverage hypothesis: protein makes up only about 15% of dietary energy and protein intake has stayed nearly constant within and across populations during the rise of obesity, and these two facts are exactly what give protein appetite leverage over total food intake. If people eat to a protein target, a diet in which protein is diluted by fat and carbohydrate leads them to eat more energy. They formalise this in a mathematical model and present some epidemiological, experimental and animal data in support.

3010.content: In a randomised crossover feeding study in Sydney, 22 lean adults lived in for three 4-day periods with fixed menus of 28 foods matched for taste, variety and availability, disguised so they gave 10%, 15% or 25% of energy as protein. On the 10% protein diet they ate 12% more total energy than on the 15% diet (4.34 MJ more over 4 days), mostly from savoury foods eaten between meals, yet still ate less protein, so the leverage was incomplete. Raising protein from 15% to 25% did not lower energy intake.

3011.content: Pooling 38 published experimental trials that measured how much people ate when confined to menus of differing composition (protein 8 to 54% of energy, carbohydrate 1.6 to 72%, fat 11 to 66%), the authors found that percent dietary protein was negatively associated with total energy intake, whether carbohydrate or fat diluted the protein. They state that the analysis supports protein leverage in lean, overweight and obese people.

3012.content: Boyd, Gintis, Bowles and Richerson modelled 128 groups in which contributors, defectors and altruistic punishers spread by payoff-biased imitation, with occasional group extinction in conflict. Without punishment, group selection kept cooperation only in very small groups. With punishment, cooperation held in much larger groups, since a punisher's cost falls toward zero as defectors become rare. With parameters chosen to represent cultural evolution in small-scale societies, cooperation was sustained in groups of about 100 individuals, and about 600 people if the individuals in the model stand for family groups.

3013.content: Reviewing research with animals and humans, Eisenberger states that rewarded effort contributes to lasting individual differences in industriousness. He proposes that when greater physical or cognitive performance, or tolerance of something unpleasant, is rewarded, the sensation of high effort itself acquires secondary reward value and becomes less aversive, and that this generalises reinforced high effort across different behaviours. He applies the idea to self-control, moral development and education.

3014.content: Fehr and Schmidt start from three sets of experimental results: people exploit bargaining power in competitive markets but not in one-to-one bargaining; they free ride in voluntary cooperation games; yet when they can punish free riders, cooperation holds even though punishing is costly to the punisher. They show that one principle explains all three if some people care about equity, and that the economic setting decides whether the fair or the selfish types set the outcome.

3015.content: Haidt argues, in a theory paper, that moral judgment is generally the result of quick, automatic evaluations (intuitions), and that moral reasoning is usually a post hoc construction made after the judgment is reached. He gives four reasons for this view and presents the social intuitionist model, which places weight on social and cultural influence over private reasoning, as more consistent with findings from social, cultural, evolutionary and biological psychology, anthropology and primatology.

3016.content: Haig argues that pregnancy is not purely cooperative: natural selection on genes expressed in the fetus favours drawing more nutrients from the mother, while selection on genes expressed in the mother favours limiting transfers beyond the mother's own optimum, so an escalation of fetal actions and maternal countermeasures is predicted. Genomic imprinting sets up a similar conflict inside fetal cells between genes expressed when inherited from the mother and genes expressed when inherited from the father.

Haig proposes that trophoblast invasion of the maternal spiral arteries gives the fetus direct access to the mother's arterial blood and lets the placenta release hormones into her circulation. He reads human placental lactogen as acting to raise the mother's insulin resistance and keep her blood glucose higher after meals, countered by more maternal insulin; in his reading gestational diabetes develops when the mother cannot mount an adequate response, and preeclampsia can be interpreted as a poorly nourished fetus raising the mother's blood pressure to increase its supply.

3017.content: Kelly, drawing on his own earlier analysis of colonial records of the Andaman Islanders (about 1858 to 1863), reports that 13 recorded encounters between hunting parties of neighbouring groups produced five serious wounds and six deaths, and that hostile relations between groups amounted to about 0.02 percent mortality per year from lethal clashes over resources, 85 percent of it among men. In the southern Andamans, where hostile relations were endemic, population density was 2.0 persons per square mile, 73 percent of that in North Andaman, where neighbouring bands held peace-making joint gatherings and shared the border zone.

Kelly argues for three eras of lethal violence between groups in human evolution: an era of coalitionary killing like that of chimpanzees, which may have lasted until about 1 million years ago; an era of defensive advantage after the throwing spear, in which ambush hunters made raids costly and selection favoured avoiding conflict and friendly, sharing relations with neighbouring groups; and an era of war, which began only when segmental forms of social organization made raids on settlements possible. He cites the Jebel Sahaba cemetery in Sudan, dated 12,000 to 14,000 years before present, as the earliest conclusive evidence of attacks on settlements, and reports that of the eight unsegmented foraging societies in Ross's cross-cultural sample, attacks on settlements are not reported for six (Mbuti, Semang, Copper Eskimo, !Kung, Yahgan and Slave).

3018.content: Ostrom reports that, after coding many cases of successful and failed systems for governing shared resources (fisheries, irrigation, pastures, forests), no specific rule was linked to success across settings, so she identified broader regularities present in long-surviving systems and absent in failed ones, which she called design principles. The updated list: clear boundaries of users and of the resource; rules that fit local conditions and costs in proportion to benefits; most affected users take part in making the rules; monitors who are the users or are accountable to them; sanctions that start very low and grow for repeat violations; fast, cheap local conflict resolution; government recognition of users' right to make their own rules; and nested layers of governance.

Ostrom reports a study by Gibson, Williams and Ostrom (2005) of 178 forest user groups, which found a strong correlation between how much the users monitored and a forester's rating of forest density, holding constant whether the users were formally organized, how heavily they depended on the forest and the group's social capital. She adds that other studies find users invest more in monitoring when they are given harvesting rights.

3019.content: A review of 91 studies that evaluated Ostrom's eight design principles for managing common-pool resources such as forests and fisheries found the principles well supported. Across the cases that recorded both a principle and the outcome, every principle had at least twice as many supportive as unsupportive cases, and the link between a principle being present and management succeeding was significant (Fisher's exact test) at the 5 percent level for every principle except the eighth (nested enterprises), which was significant at 10 percent. Much of the criticism came from abstract studies without field data.

In the same review, monitoring split into two parts: the presence of monitors (principle 4A) was moderately well supported, while monitors being members of the community or accountable to it (4B) was very strongly supported, with more than ten supportive cases for each unsupportive one. Graduated sanctions, which start low and grow with the seriousness or repetition of a violation, were moderately well supported.

3020.content: In 2002 the authors interviewed 108 fishers from three generations in 11 fishing communities of the central Gulf of California, Mexico (young 15 to 30 years, N 40; middle-aged 31 to 54, N 34; old 55 and over, N 34). Old fishers named a median of 11 species as depleted by fishing, middle-aged fishers 7 and young fishers 2, and old fishers named about four times as many depleted fishing sites as young ones. The number of species named per year of fishing did not differ between generations, so the decline had not slowed. Few young fishers knew that large species had ever been common or that nearshore sites had been productive, although those times were within living memory.

Old fishers in the same survey reported catching up to 25 times as many Gulf grouper (Mycteroperca jordani) on their best ever fishing day as young fishers did. The authors note that in 1995 Pauly described shifting baselines, each generation of scientists viewing as natural the environment of their youth, and that their survey was the first quantitative field test of the idea.

3021.content: Sperber and colleagues argue, in a theory paper drawing on philosophy, linguistics, psychology and the social sciences, that because humans depend so heavily on information from others and others' interests rarely coincide with their own, humans have a suite of cognitive mechanisms for epistemic vigilance aimed at the risk of being misinformed, accidentally or on purpose, and that this vigilance is what keeps communication advantageous.

The authors argue that when a person belongs to a relatively small group in which many people know her qualities and shortcomings directly and can compare opinions freely, for instance by gossip, her actual behaviour can shape her reputation. Many reputations, however, spread on a larger scale through people with no direct knowledge, and a listener judging an unfamiliar source may then have nothing to go on except a reputation she cannot check and accepts for want of better; reputations can become inflated well beyond opinions formed individually.

3022.content: Tooby and Cosmides argue that war, aggression between coalitions, needs cooperation within each coalition, and that cooperation of this kind needs mechanisms to detect and exclude cheaters. They propose that this cognitive demand explains why coalitional aggression is far rarer among animals than the social conditions favouring it would lead one to expect, and why only humans and common chimpanzees (possibly also bonobos and dolphins) are known to wage it with coalitions of more than four individuals. They propose that humans have evolved a specialized coalitional psychology.

The authors argue that if victory is certain, the risk of death is spread at random among participants, the benefits are shared fairly and reproductive resources are reallocated among survivors, selection favours men joining coalitional aggression whatever the level of mortality, within broad limits, because the deaths of some coalition members need not lower the average reproduction of the members. They predict that women, who are rarely limited by access to men, gain less and lose more from coalitional aggression, and that willingness to fight should collapse when death becomes certain for some participants.

The authors argue that a social psychology which evolved in the Pleistocene to judge the odds of success from the behaviour of dozens or, rarely, hundreds of people may draw supernormal confidence from crowds of hundreds or thousands, because in the Pleistocene having so many on one's side would almost always have meant victory, and nothing in that past prepared people to imagine thousands or millions of unseen opponents.

3023.content: Trivers argues that when parent and offspring relations are seen from the offspring's side as well as the parent's, conflict is an expected feature: they are expected to disagree over how long parental investment should last, how much should be given, and how altruistic or selfish the offspring should be toward other relatives, and sometimes over the sex of future offspring. Conflict is expected to rise during the period of care, offspring are expected to use psychological weapons, and in some species, humans included, parents are expected under some conditions to try to mold an offspring against its interests into a permanent nonreproductive role. He reports that detailed data on mother and offspring relations in mammals are consistent with the argument.

3024.content: Grafen builds an evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) model of Zahavi's handicap principle and proves, under fairly general conditions, that if the principle's conditions are met an evolutionarily stable signalling equilibrium exists, and that any signalling equilibrium satisfies those conditions. He concludes that Zahavi's major claims are vindicated, and discusses cheating in view of the honesty that follows from the handicap principle.

3025.content: Watkins summarizes the control theory account of repetitive thought set out by Martin and Tesser (1989, 1996): rumination is triggered by a discrepancy in progress toward a goal, serves to further that goal, and continues until the goal is met or the person disengages from and abandons it. It turns unconstructive when the person can neither make progress nor give up the goal, so that the thought only keeps the gap salient and worsens negative feeling.

Watkins reports studies consistent with the goal-discrepancy account: repetitive thought about people and activities left behind on going to college rose with how far those activities remained interrupted (Millar and colleagues 1988); important abstract goals such as happiness, and concrete goals linked to them such as a romantic relationship, produced more repetitive thought when not attained (McIntosh and colleagues 1992, 1995); and in a diary study negative events tied to personal goals produced more repetitive thought than unrelated negative events (Lavallee and Campbell 1995).

3026.content: The authors argue that early and long dependence on caregivers and limited physical strength put humans at risk when isolated, so an aversive signal that one's social connections are frayed or broken, and that motivates their repair, would have been adaptive. Like hunger, thirst and pain, loneliness in their account evolved to change behaviour in ways that protect the individual and the survival of their genes: as physical pain protects the physical body, loneliness protects the social body.

The authors report twin data from the Netherlands Twin Register (Bartels, Cacioppo, Hudziak and Boomsma 2008): in 7,995 Dutch twin pairs scored on two loneliness items of the Child Behavior Checklist at ages 7, 10 and 12, loneliness averaged over those ages was 46 percent heritable, with 12 percent from shared environment. Heritability was estimated at 60 percent at age 7, 54 percent at age 10 and 17 percent at age 12, while shared family environment rose from 4 percent to 12 percent to 41 percent. In an extended twin-family design of 8,683 twins and their relatives (Distel and colleagues 2010), loneliness was again moderately heritable, with no sign of cultural transmission from parents.

The authors argue that heritable differences in sensitivity to the pain of social disconnection are kept in the population because both kinds of people were useful: those less sensitive may serve as explorers who travel alone and find new territory, threats or opportunities, and those more sensitive stay in or return to the group and help protect and maintain it. A population of only one type would be at risk, from splintering in one case and from slow discovery, starvation or predation in the other.

3027.content: Epley, Waytz and Cacioppo propose a theory of when people anthropomorphize nonhuman agents, built on three determinants: how accessible and applicable knowledge about humans is, the motivation to explain and understand the behavior of other agents (effectance), and the desire for social contact (sociality). The theory predicts more anthropomorphism when human knowledge is accessible, when people are motivated to be effective, and when they lack a sense of social connection to other humans.

3028.content: In three studies, people who were chronically lonely (Study 1) and people induced to feel lonely (Studies 2 and 3) anthropomorphized nonhuman agents such as gadgets and pets more, making them seem more humanlike, and reported more belief in commonly anthropomorphized religious agents such as God. Study 3 suggests the result is not produced by any negative mood. The authors read this as people without social connection to other humans compensating by creating a sense of human connection with nonhuman agents.

3029.content: House, Landis and Umberson review the evidence up to 1988 and report that prospective studies which control for baseline health consistently show a higher risk of death among people with a low quantity, and sometimes low quality, of social relationships, and that experimental and quasi-experimental studies of humans and animals also suggest that social isolation is a major risk factor for death from widely varying causes.

3030.content: Qualter and colleagues set out the reaffiliation motive, part of the evolutionary theory of loneliness: the aversive feeling of loneliness signals that connections are broken or threatened, prompts brief withdrawal and raises vigilance for social threat, and usually leads to reconnection, which is why loneliness is usually transient. They write that from an evolutionary view loneliness itself is no more a problem at any age than hunger, thirst or pain; prolonged loneliness arises when parts of this motive fail, for instance when vigilance for social threat and withdrawal feed each other.

The review reports, from multiwave longitudinal studies by several groups, that between 3 and 22 percent of people follow a path of prolonged loneliness from childhood to early adulthood, and that 15 to 25 percent of older adults report social or emotional isolation lasting months or years; those on high stable or rising loneliness paths showed relatively poor mental and physical health. The share reporting feeling lonely sometimes or often is estimated at under 20 percent of children aged 7 to 12, 20 to 71 percent of late adolescents and young adults, 11 to 30 percent of middle-aged adults and 40 to 50 percent of adults over 80.

3031.content: Rook argues that organisms humans had to tolerate through their evolutionary past (the human microbiota, environmental microbes contaminating food and water, infections picked up at birth that established carrier states, and helminths) took on roles in setting up immune regulation, including regulatory T cells that stop attacks on self, harmless allergens and gut contents and that switch inflammation off when it is not needed. In high-income countries, and above all in cities, many of these Old Friends are almost gone, and he attributes part of the rise in chronic inflammatory conditions and persistently raised C-reactive protein to this failing immunoregulation, which leaves people more dependent on microbes from mothers, other people, animals and the natural environment.

Rook argues that the long-term health benefits linked to living near the natural environment are usually put down to exercise, social contact, sunlight and fast psychological effects, but that there is little evidence those fast, transient effects cause long-term benefit. He proposes that a major part of the benefit is the microbial input from green space that drives immunoregulation, which needs prolonged exposure, especially in childhood, and adds that sunlight (through vitamin D and nitric oxide) and exercise (through regulatory T cell activity) supplement it.

3032.content: Taylor and colleagues propose that, although fight-or-flight may describe the main physiological stress response of both sexes, the behaviour of females under stress is marked more by a pattern they call tend-and-befriend. Tending is nurturing that guards the self and offspring, promotes safety and lowers distress; befriending is making and keeping the social networks that help in this. They propose that the pattern draws on the attachment and caregiving system, with oxytocin, together with female reproductive hormones and endogenous opioids, at its core, and they build it from animal and human studies.

In the same review the authors report that the wish to affiliate with others under stress is much stronger in women than in men, and call it the main gender difference in adult behavioural responses to stress. They cite an analysis of gender differences in coping by Luckow, Reifman and McIntosh (1998): seeking and using social support showed the largest difference, and of 26 studies that tested for it, 25 favoured women, one found no difference and none went the other way.

3033.content: Buss argues that sexual jealousy is a basic emotion that evolved because it solves adaptive problems of mating, though it has no distinctive facial expression and does not solve problems of survival. Some functions are shared by men and women, such as warding off would-be mate poachers and deterring a partner from leaving; others differ by sex, such as raising paternity certainty for men and keeping a mate's economic commitment for women. He reviews dozens of studies of sex-differentiated design features, and notes that jealousy also leads to great destruction, from humiliation to homicide.

Summing up the evolutionary accounts of Symons and of Daly and Wilson, Buss writes that sexual jealousy is read as a functional emotion rather than as a pathology, a character defect, or a product of culture or of capitalism. Its core function is keeping access to a valued mate, and it should be set off by threats to the mateship: signs of the mate's infidelity, would-be mate poachers, and signs that the mate may leave.

3034.content: In an essay review Stearns defines a trade-off as the cost paid in fitness when a change that helps one trait is linked to a change that harms another. He argues that trade-offs must exist: without them selection would push every trait tied to fitness to the limits set by history and design, yet many life-history traits are held well inside those limits. The most prominent life-history trade-off, he writes, is the cost of reproduction, paid in survival and in future reproduction.

Stearns writes that the cost of reproduction has two main components, costs paid in survival and costs paid in future reproduction, and that such costs have been measured through field observation, experimental manipulation in laboratory and field, and phenotypic and genetic correlations. In his conclusion he asks that these correlations be measured across the range of environments organisms naturally meet before costs are claimed to be known.

3035.content: In a critical review Penn and Szamado argue that Zahavi's Handicap Principle, that signals are honest because they are wasteful and costly, is wrong, and that Grafen's 1990 models, long taken to vindicate it, support instead Zahavi's second hypothesis: males adjust how much they invest in sexual signals to their condition and their ability to bear the costs and risks. Honest signals then come from efficient investment in signalling, and theory shows that costs paid at equilibrium are neither sufficient nor necessary for honesty. They conclude that there is no theoretical or empirical support for the Handicap Principle.

3036.content: In a field experiment in the Kalahari, wild southern pied babblers (Turdoides bicolor), a cooperatively breeding bird, were handed 1, 2 or 3 mealworms at 0, 50, 100 or 150 m from their nest (1,018 trials on 116 birds from 17 groups). Birds were more likely to carry the food back to the chicks when closer to the nest (82.1 percent at 0 m against 51.3 percent at 150 m) and when given a bigger load (54.0 percent with one mealworm against 78.4 percent with three). The interaction of load and distance was not significant, so the prediction of Orians and Pearson's central place foraging model, that a forager farther from its nest should bring back a bigger load, did not hold here.

The authors state that the main prediction of Orians and Pearson's (1979) central place foraging models, that load size should rise with distance from the central place, has had wide support in studies of nesting birds, while some studies, such as one of female calliope hummingbirds, found no link between load size and distance.

3037.content: Pirolli models how people use the web within information foraging theory. Choosing which link to follow is modelled as a random utility choice guided by information scent, the cues in the browser linked to the user's goal; leaving a website is modelled as a running judgement of the expected benefit of staying against going elsewhere. The models are evaluated against web user behaviour with a computer model (SNIF-ACT) and with the Law of Surfing, the distribution of path lengths of visitors to a site.

3038.content: Stephens reviews how behavioural ecologists study animal foraging, using decisions about when to leave a food patch. He argues that binary choice tests are poor models of foraging, since natural foraging choices are sequential, with one option always in the background; that foraging is a hierarchy of decisions from choosing a habitat to choosing a food; and that data suggest foraging animals weigh several trade-offs, among them competitors, group mates and the risk of predators.

3039.content: Boyce and Ellis argue that high stress reactivity reflects a raised biological sensitivity to context, more than exaggerated arousal or an old and harmful legacy: its effects on health run both ways, with harm under adversity and benefit under support and protection. They state that developmental experience, along with heritable polygenic variation, calibrates the stress response systems, and propose that these systems are conditional adaptations that monitor features of the childhood environment and set their own development to match it.

From this theory Boyce and Ellis derive a new hypothesis: a U-shaped relation between early adversity and stress reactivity, with highly reactive profiles arising more often both in very stressful and in very protected early social environments.

3040.content: Butler and Randall define emotional coregulation as the process by which relationship partners form a two-person emotional system, an oscillating pattern of arousal and dampening that keeps both at an optimal emotional state. They propose an operational definition: a two-way linkage of oscillating emotional channels between partners that adds to emotional stability for both, and they list open questions for its relevance to adult well-being.

3041.content: From years of watching ring doves and other pigeons, Craig describes an appetite as a state of agitation that lasts as long as a certain stimulus is absent. When that stimulus is at last received it releases a consummatory act, after which the searching stops and gives way to relative rest, a state of satisfaction. The searching before it is varied and partly learned by trial and error; the consummatory act at the end is innate. He holds that all human behaviour runs in the same cycles of rising appetite and its ending.

Craig observes that when a bird's appetite fails to reach its normal stimulus it sometimes fades, but some appetites are so persistent that they attach to an abnormal stimulus instead: the consummatory act is performed on it, the tension of the appetite is relieved and the animal shows satisfaction. He likens this to what psychiatry calls compensation.

3042.content: Ellis and colleagues synthesise life-history theory and data into a developmental theory of human life-history strategy. Correlated traits such as the timing of puberty, age at first sex and first birth, and parental investment lie on a slow-to-fast continuum, and the two most fundamental environmental influences on that strategy are harshness (outside causes of illness and death) and unpredictability (variation in harshness across space and time). These influences depend in turn on population density, competition and scarcity, age patterns of death, and on how much an organism's own choices change its risk.

3043.content: Ellis, Boyce, Belsky, Bakermans-Kranenburg and van IJzendoorn join two evolutionary models, biological sensitivity to context and differential susceptibility, which agree that some individuals are more susceptible than others to both harmful and helpful environments. They set this against the dominant diathesis-stress (dual risk) view of personal vulnerability, call for a paradigm shift in how person-by-environment interactions in development are understood, and conclude that development responds, for better and for worse, to the whole range of species-typical environments.

3044.content: Frijda argues that the word emotion covers an assembly of processes through which we relate to the social and physical world, and that one functional basis of them is action readiness, the preparation for movement or action. Preparation for movement is found in all animals, and preparation for directed action in more recently evolved species such as birds and mammals. Action readiness, he writes, is the basis of the states we now call emotions and, beyond them, an elementary part of how living beings regulate their dealings with the world.

3045.content: Hyman, of the Department of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School, argues in a review that the DSM-III introduced operationalized diagnostic criteria tested for agreement between raters at a time when the science could not yet yield valid disease definitions. He argues that refining the criteria or adding new categories will not make them valid, and that DSM criteria still dominate clinical practice, research, treatment development and law, so the system meant to give a shared language also creates epistemic blinders against valid diagnoses.

3046.content: Kleinman, of Harvard University, puts four questions to cross-cultural psychiatric research from an anthropological point of view, among them whether the standard format of cross-cultural studies creates a category fallacy. He argues that cross-cultural validity must get the same attention as reliability, that culture be measured as a research variable, and that cultural analysis be applied to psychiatry's own taxonomies and methods as well as to the illness beliefs of the peoples studied.

3047.content: Richerson and Henrich argue that human hunter-gatherers keep large networks of kin and non-kin even in the smallest societies, and that members of the ethnolinguistic tribe, from a few hundred to a few thousand people, can organize cooperative ventures and sustain peaceful exchange. They add that ties across tribes, with trade, alliance and a fair amount of intermarriage, are not uncommon. They argue these tribal social instincts arose by gene-culture coevolution under cultural group selection and were probably in place by 50,000 years ago.

Richerson and Henrich contrast chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) with humans: the sight of an unknown chimpanzee sparks fear, hostility and aggression, so the usual human experiments with strangers cannot be run on chimpanzees. Humans, they write, treat other humans as potentially cooperative unless known to be a threat or plainly from a group assumed hostile, while chimpanzees treat any individual not known to be an ally as presumably hostile.

3048.content: Salamone and Correa review rodent work on accumbens dopamine. In a task where trained rats (Rattus norvegicus) can press a lever for a preferred food or eat freely available lab chow, low to moderate doses of drugs that block dopamine D1 or D2 receptors cut lever pressing and raise chow intake, at doses that do not change total food intake or preference between the two foods when both are free. In a T-maze with a barrier in the arm holding more food, dopamine depletion or blockade in the accumbens shifts rats to the low-cost, low-food arm; with no barrier their choice is unchanged. The authors conclude that low dopamine leaves appetite, food preference and the hedonic reaction to food intact and makes animals pick lower-cost ways to get it.

3049.content: Treadway and Zald review laboratory measures of pleasure in people diagnosed with major depressive disorder. Across four separate studies using the sweet taste test, people with the diagnosis and matched controls reported the same pleasantness of sugar solutions. The authors read the literature as a whole as showing some reduction in hedonic capacity on questionnaires, with unclear generality, and state that they knew of no laboratory study that had directly measured motivation in people with the diagnosis.

Treadway and Zald propose that anhedonia in people diagnosed with major depressive disorder be split into motivational anhedonia (less drive to pursue rewards, the 'wanting' side tied to dopamine in animal work) and consummatory anhedonia (less pleasure on getting them, the 'liking' side), and add 'decisional anhedonia' for impaired weighing of costs and benefits. They argue that dopamine findings in depression have been contradictory because the label did not separate these parts.

3050.content: Zhi-Xuan and colleagues argue that the dominant practice of AI alignment rests on three commitments: that preferences adequately represent human values, that human rationality is the maximizing of preference satisfaction, and that AI systems should be aligned with the preferences of one or more humans. They call this the preferentist approach and argue against it, proposing that AI systems be aligned with normative standards fitted to their social roles and agreed by those affected.

The same paper explains that rational choice theory, and machine learning methods built on it, derive what a person prefers from what that person chooses (revealed preferences). The authors argue that preferences are constructed from underlying reasons and values, so without those reasons a model is unlikely to capture how a person's preferences would extend to new options in ways the person would endorse.

3051.content: Bernheim and Rangel propose an economic model of addiction on three premises: use among addicts is often a mistake, experience sensitizes a person to cues in the environment that trigger that mistaken use, and addicts understand their susceptibility and manage it. They argue the premises are supported by psychology, neuroscience and clinical practice, and that the model maps behaviour onto features of the user, the substance and the environment and gives a clear welfare standard.

3052.content: Matthews and Tye propose that contact with others is regulated like a homeostatic need such as energy or fluid balance: a detector senses the amount and quality of that contact, a control centre compares it with a set point, and effector systems act to restore contact. From rodent studies of acute isolation they group the responses into three themes, hypervigilance and arousal, social motivation, and passive coping, and they speculate that loneliness leads to long-term disease through sustained recruitment of these circuits.

The review reports rodent evidence of a vigilant response to isolation: adult rats (Rattus norvegicus) show more escape-related behaviour over 1 to 4 days of isolation, less exploration and more self-grooming. In mice (Mus musculus), feeding evoked by stimulating hunger-signalling AgRP neurons in the hypothalamus goes on in isolated mice even when a novel male or female mouse is present, which the authors read as hunger overriding a competing social drive.

3053.content: Carneiro considers and rejects traditional theories of how states began in favour of an ecological hypothesis, the circumscription theory. He argues that it explains why states arose where they did and failed to arise elsewhere, and shows the state as a predictable response to specific cultural, demographic and ecological conditions.

3054.content: Eaton, Konner and Shostak argue that people alive today are, genetically, Stone Age hunter-gatherers living in a world different from the one their genes were selected for. They argue that this discordance does little to reproductive success but promotes chronic illnesses (atherosclerosis, essential hypertension, many cancers, diabetes mellitus and obesity) through nutrition, exercise and exposure to noxious substances, and they state that these 'diseases of civilization' together account for 75 percent of all deaths in Western nations and are rare among people whose ways of life reflect those of preagricultural ancestors.

3055.content: Using one week of smart-card records from Singapore's buses (more than 20 million trips by 2,895,750 anonymous users, about 55 percent of residents), Sun and colleagues built a network of everyone who shared a bus at the same time. Pairs who met more than once (18,724,388 pairs) mostly met again at 24, 48, 72 or 96 hours, about 75 percent of cases, and about 85 percent of repeat encounters happened at about the same time of day: the 'familiar strangers' who are seen again and again and may never be addressed.

In the same Singapore data, the number of different people a regular rider shared a bus with grew in a straight line through the week without levelling off, which the authors read as the people one meets differing from day to day. The time-aggregated network of 783,247 regular riders formed one connected small-world graph across the whole city.

3056.content: Berkowitz's review of the 1939 Dollard frustration-aggression hypothesis finds the evidence mixed: some studies gave negative results, others support the core proposition that interference with an expected attainment of a desired goal produces hostile, emotional aggression. The review concludes that frustrations can create aggressive inclinations even when the frustration is neither arbitrary nor aimed at the person.

Berkowitz proposes a revision of the 1939 model: frustrations produce aggressive inclinations to the degree that they arouse negative affect, and he reviews evidence on the aggressive consequences of aversive events. He sets this inside his cognitive-neoassociationistic model.

3057.content: Nesse argues from signal detection theory that when an all-or-none defence such as flight is cheap compared with the harm it guards against, the best-regulated system will raise many false alarms. Defences with graded responses are best expressed where marginal cost equals marginal benefit, which can sit far from the intuitive optimum. On this reading the over-responsiveness of many defences is only apparent; he adds that in specific instances defences can often be dampened without loss of fitness.

3058.content: Sterling argues that regulation by error-correcting feedback (homeostasis) is too inefficient to be the main way the body is run. In his model, allostasis, the brain anticipates needs and prepares to meet them before they arise: it tracks many variables, sets priorities, mobilises resources from modest stores and shares them between organs.

Sterling argues that the brain pushes an animal toward each need with a lasting unease (his stick) and rewards meeting it with a brief pleasure (his carrot), and that in humans many activities feed this funnel, with reward value depending partly on the effort spent. Modern life, he argues, narrows the variety of small pleasures and reduces effort, lowering their reward value so that larger portions are needed for the same satisfaction, a cycle that produces addictive behaviour. Allostasis points to broader approaches: widening the range of pleasures again and giving people chances to spend effort in pursuing them.

Sterling contrasts how the two models place illness. Homeostasis reads essential hypertension as too much salt water in too small a vascular reservoir and treats it with drugs on those low-level mechanisms. Allostasis reads it as the brain chronically anticipating a need for higher pressure, and would direct therapy upward, to reduce demand and increase the person's sense of control, so that the brain lowers its prediction and relaxes the low-level mechanisms together.

3059.content: From five decades of US time-use surveys (1965 to 2003), Aguiar and Hurst find that leisure per working-age adult rose: by roughly six to nine hours a week for men, through fewer market work hours, and by roughly four to eight hours a week for women, through fewer hours of home production.

The authors document a growing inequality in leisure that mirrors the growing inequality of wages and spending. Their working paper adds that leisure rose across many subgroups and most among less-educated adults, who gained leisure as they fell behind in wages.

3060.content: In seven rounds of Japan's National Fertility Survey (1987 to 2015; 11,553 to 17,850 respondents per round in the 1987 to 2010 rounds), the age-standardised share of adults aged 18 to 39 who reported never having had heterosexual intercourse rose from 20.0 percent in 1992 to 25.8 percent in 2015 among men and from 21.7 to 24.6 percent among women. Around one in ten women and men in their thirties reported no heterosexual experience.

In the 2010 survey, among Japanese men aged 25 to 39, part-time or temporary work (adjusted odds ratio 3.82 against regular employees) and unemployment (adjusted odds ratio 7.87) went with a much higher chance of never having had heterosexual intercourse, and the odds fell with each step up in income. Among women the pattern ran the other way for income and unemployment. About four in five of the inexperienced aged 25 to 39 (78.2 percent of men) said they wished to marry.

3061.content: The WHO and ILO estimate that in 2016, 488 million people, 8.9 percent of the world's population, worked 55 hours a week or more, a share that rose 9.3 percent from 2000. Applying relative risks from their own systematic reviews (ischaemic heart disease 1.17, 22 studies; stroke 1.35, 7 studies; both against 35 to 40 hours a week), they attribute 745,194 deaths and 23.3 million disability-adjusted life years from these two causes to long working hours: 3.7 percent of ischaemic heart disease deaths and 6.9 percent of stroke deaths.

3062.content: From ethnographic fieldwork in Las Vegas among game developers and machine gamblers, Schull links digitally enhanced game features to the gamblers' experience, and reports a close connection between extreme absorption in play and design elements that manipulate space and time to speed up the extraction of money from players.

3063.content: Observing 57 US physicians in family medicine, internal medicine, cardiology and orthopaedics for 430 hours, Sinsky and colleagues found that physicians spent 27.0 percent of the office day in direct face time with patients and 49.2 percent on electronic health record and desk work. Even in the examination room, 37.0 percent of the time went to records and desk work. The 21 physicians who kept diaries reported 1 to 2 more hours of after-hours work each night, mostly on the records.

3064.content: In a survey of 679 remote gig workers in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa who found work through two leading online labour platforms, with 107 interviews, Wood and colleagues found that platform rating systems left workers wide discretion over how they worked: 72 percent felt able to choose and change the order of their tasks and 74 percent their methods of work. The authors contrast this with Taylorist control.

The same remote gig workers reported intense and irregular work: 54 percent had to work at very high speed, 60 percent to tight deadlines, 22 percent had pain from their work, and 80 percent said clients' demands set their pace. Working to clients in US, UK and Australian time zones, 54 percent lost sleep at night, 54 percent said there was not enough work to go round, and interviewees working alone from home described social isolation.

3065.content: Boehm traces conflict from the last common ancestor of humans, chimpanzees and bonobos, which lived in dominance hierarchies with conflict from individual and coalitional competition and had male and female mediators, to living hunter-gatherers, whose coalitions suppress dominance and competition except in competition for mates. He argues that foragers can settle conflicts before they break out, and also use truces and peace pacts to limit conflict when its costs grow too high.

3066.content: Reviewing work mainly in rats (Rattus norvegicus) and other mammals and in the monogamous prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster), Numan and Young find that mother-infant bonding and pair bonding share circuitry: the amygdala and the nucleus accumbens to ventral pallidum circuit take part in both, and dopamine and oxytocin acting in the nucleus accumbens appear to let infant or partner cues keep activating these attraction circuits, giving a lasting bond. The medial preoptic area is essential for maternal behaviour; its role in pair bonding is not yet known.

Numan and Young argue that the maternal neural system may have been the scaffold on which other social bonds in mammals were built: pair bonding, found in about 5 percent of mammal species, and possibly other strong social relationships in mammals, humans included.

3067.content: Szasz argues that disease, by the pathologist's criteria, is a material and verifiable characteristic of the body, a structural or functional alteration of cells, tissues and organs, while a psychiatric diagnosis is a physician's judgement about a person's behaviour. When a person diagnosed with a mental illness turns out to have a brain disease, he holds, the person was misdiagnosed: he had an undiagnosed bodily illness, and the condition then passes from psychiatry to neurology, as with neurosyphilis and beriberi.

Szasz contrasts causes with reasons: diseases of the body have causes, such as infectious agents or nutritional deficiencies, and can often be prevented or cured by dealing with those causes, while persons said to have mental diseases have reasons for their actions that must be understood. In his view such persons are not cured by drugs or other medical interventions, and may be helped by people who respect them, understand their predicament and help them overcome the obstacles they face.

3068.content: In 239 twin pairs from a volunteer community sample, self-reported anxious attachment loaded together with 11 personality problem scales of the Dimensional Assessment of Personality Problems on one factor the authors call emotional dysregulation. Twin models put 40 percent of the variance in anxious attachment down to genes, and 63 percent of its overlap with the matching personality problem scores down to genes shared by both. Avoidant attachment showed shared family environment instead of genes, and its overlap with the matching scores came from experiences unique to each twin.

3069.content: At a hospital in Puerto Ayacucho, Amazonas State, Venezuela, the authors sequenced bacterial 16S rRNA genes from 9 mothers (Mestizo and Amerindian) and their 10 newborns, 4 born vaginally and 6 by Caesarean section. Minutes after birth, the newborns' bacteria were the same across skin, mouth, nasopharynx and first stool, and the main thing that set their makeup was how they were born: vaginally born infants carried communities like their own mother's vaginal bacteria (Lactobacillus, Prevotella or Sneathia), while Caesarean-born infants carried communities like skin bacteria (Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, Propionibacterium) and lacked the vaginal bacteria.

In the same study, in three of four vaginal births the mother's vaginal bacterial community was more like her own baby's bacteria than like those of other vaginally born babies, a sign of direct passing from mother to child. The skin bacteria of mothers who had a Caesarean were no more like their own babies' bacteria than like those of other Caesarean-born babies, and the authors suggest that Caesarean-born babies pick up skin bacteria from the hospital environment.

3070.content: In a cross-sectional survey of 738 mothers of infants aged 6 to 12 months at Maternal and Child Health Centres in three middle-class areas of Melbourne, Australia (94 percent response), 46 percent reported their infant's sleep as a problem, 15 percent scored above 12 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and 18 percent scored 10 to 12. After adjustment for other risk factors, a mother's report of an infant sleep problem went with about twice the odds of scoring above 12 (odds ratio 2.13, 95% CI 1.27 to 3.56) and nearly three times the odds of scoring above 10 (odds ratio 2.88, 1.93 to 4.31).

In the same survey, mothers who reported good sleep quality of their own, despite an infant sleep problem, were not more likely to score high on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Infant patterns that mothers counted as a sleep problem included sleeping in the parent's bed, being nursed to sleep, taking longer to fall asleep, waking more often and for longer at night, and short naps.

3071.content: In 2,794 young adult twins of the Norwegian Institute of Public Health Twin Panel, interviewed with the Structured Interview for DSM-IV Personality, the heritability of the criterion counts for the 10 DSM-IV personality disorders as scored ranged from 20.5 percent (schizotypal) to 40.9 percent (antisocial), with 37.1 percent for the borderline score. The authors found no evidence that shared family environment mattered for any of them.

In the same twins, the genetic factors did not follow the grouping of personality disorders that the DSM-IV labels clusters A, B and C. One broad genetic factor loaded on six criterion counts from all three clusters (paranoid, histrionic, borderline, narcissistic, dependent, obsessive-compulsive), a second only on the borderline and antisocial scores, and a third only on the schizoid and avoidant scores. The factors for experiences unique to each twin did follow the three clusters, and the authors suggest that experiences, more than genes, explain why personality disorders as scored within one cluster tend to occur together.

3072.content: Twelve adults (7 women, 5 men; 9 not parents; mean age 29.5) were scanned with magnetoencephalography while they ignored faces and watched a fixation cross. Unfamiliar infant faces, matched with adult faces for emotional valence, arousal, attractiveness, size and luminosity, drew a brief burst of activity in the medial orbitofrontal cortex, a reward area, at about 130 ms after the face appeared (10 to 15 Hz band, p below 0.001); adult faces did not. Restricting the analysis to the non-parents gave the same result.

3073.content: Torgersen and colleagues (Oslo University) interviewed 92 identical and 129 fraternal twin pairs, found through twin and patient registries, with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R Personality Disorders, and combined the data with prevalence rates from a population study of more than 2,000 people. The best-fitting models gave a heritability of .60 for personality disorders as scored overall and, for single labels, .69 for borderline, .79 for narcissistic, .78 for obsessive-compulsive, .67 for histrionic, .61 for schizotypal, .57 for dependent, .54 for self-defeating and .28 to .29 for schizoid, paranoid and avoidant. The best-fitting models never included shared family environment.

3074.content: Sixty white middle-class infants (authors at the State University of New York at Stony Brook) were seen in the Ainsworth Strange Situation at 12 months, and 50 of them were interviewed 20 years later with the Berkeley Adult Attachment Interview by interviewers blind to the infant classification. 72 percent received the same secure or insecure classification in early adulthood (kappa .44). Of the infants whose mothers reported negative life events (loss of a parent, parental divorce, life-threatening illness of parent or child, a parent's psychiatric disorder, or physical or sexual abuse by a family member), 44 percent (8 of 18) changed classification, against 22 percent (7 of 32) of those whose mothers reported none.

3075.content: In an audit of monthly referral data from 12 breast cancer family history clinics and 9 regional genetics services in the UK, referrals rose from May 2013, when the actress Angelina Jolie made public her BRCA1 test and risk-reducing mastectomy. They were nearly 2.5 times the 2012 figure in June and July (4,847 against 1,981), about twice to October, and 32 percent higher in November and December; over the year they rose from 12,142 to 19,751. Demand for BRCA1/2 testing nearly doubled and enquiries about risk-reducing mastectomy rose. In the Manchester clinic the share of referrals eligible to be seen stayed at 66.5 percent, against 63 and 67 percent in the two years before.

3076.content: A meta-analysis of 291 studies of 296,284 women in 56 countries that scored mothers on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale in the first year after birth gave a pooled share of 17.7 percent (95% CI 16.6 to 18.8) scoring above the cutoff, ranging from 3 percent in Singapore to 38 percent in Chile. Countries with more income inequality (R squared 41 percent), higher maternal mortality (19 percent), higher infant mortality (16 percent) or more women of childbearing age working 40 or more hours a week (31 percent) had higher shares of mothers scoring above the cutoff; together these explained 73 percent of the variation between countries.

In the same meta-regression, the national share of infants born outside marriage, living in single-parent homes or living in cities did not go with the national share of mothers scoring above the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale cutoff, and neither did national paid or unpaid maternity leave.

3077.content: Thirty-five boys aged 5 to 7 whose mothers described them as sugar sensitive were randomly assigned with their mothers to two groups; every boy drank a placebo (aspartame), but half the mothers were told their son had been given a large dose of sugar. Mothers who believed their son had had sugar rated him as significantly more hyperactive, and on video they kept more control by staying physically close and tended to criticise, watch and talk to their sons more than control mothers. The expectancy shift was stronger in cognitively rigid mothers on several measures.

3078.content: Pooling a large number of studies, O'Hara and Swain put the average share of mothers meeting the studies' criteria for non-psychotic postpartum depression at 13 percent, higher in studies using self-report scales and in studies covering a longer period after birth. In a meta-analysis of risk factors measured during pregnancy, the strongest predictors the pooled studies reported were a past history of psychopathology and psychological disturbance during pregnancy, a poor marital relationship and low social support, and stressful life events; indicators of low social status had a small but significant link.

3079.content: Reviewing research on television and children under 2 (the American Academy of Pediatrics then advised no television before 24 months), Anderson and Pempek report that very young children pay substantial attention to programmes and videos made for them, that they usually learn substantially less from a video than from an equivalent live presentation, that one study found positive links between some children's programmes and language while other studies found negative links between viewing and language, cognitive and attentional development, and that background television disrupts.

3080.content: In a meta-analysis of gene by environment studies of children up to 10 years old involving dopamine-related genes (DRD2, DRD4 and the dopamine transporter), children who carried the less efficient variants, usually called risk genes, did worse than non-carriers in negative rearing environments and also gained most from positive rearing environments.

In the new study in the same paper, 91 seven-year-old children were given the chance to donate money to UNICEF. Children with secure attachment representations, assessed with an attachment story completion task, donated more, but only if they carried the DRD4 7-repeat allele.

3081.content: In a study of people playing a computer game, the game's in-game reinforcement characteristics and the player's skill significantly changed several measures of the player's emotional state, most of all excitement and frustration. The abstract gives no sample size, no effect sizes and no measure of the wish to keep playing.

3082.content: A meta-analysis of seven longitudinal studies (343 children classed as behaviourally inhibited and 534 controls, with 4 to 6 years on average between the temperament rating and the anxiety assessment; samples about 91 percent white) found that children classed in early childhood as behaviourally inhibited (wary and avoidant with unfamiliar people, places and objects) had 7.59 times the odds of later meeting the authors' criteria for social anxiety disorder (95% CI 3.03 to 19.00). In the studies that gave counts, 43 percent of inhibited children (107 of 246) met the criteria against 12 percent of non-inhibited children (57 of 446), so 57 percent of the inhibited children did not. The authors describe behavioural inhibition as a heritable trait shown in extreme form by an estimated 15 to 20 percent of young children.

3083.content: In the Dunedin birth cohort (1,037 children born 1972 to 1973 in Dunedin, New Zealand; 972 seen at age 32), children who in their first decade lived in low socioeconomic status, were maltreated or were socially isolated had more age-related disease risks at 32, counting a diagnosis of past-year major depression, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein above 3 mg/L and a cluster of metabolic risk markers: incidence rate ratios 1.89 (95% CI 1.36 to 2.62), 1.81 (1.38 to 2.38) and 1.87 (1.38 to 2.51). Each exposure added its own risk, the count of risks rose with the number of exposures, and the link held after controlling for family history, low birth weight, childhood body mass index and adult smoking, inactivity, poor diet and adult socioeconomic status. Maltreatment was a five-part index: maternal rejection rated by observers at age 3, harsh discipline reported by parents at 7 and 9, two or more changes of primary caregiver, and physical and sexual abuse reported by the study members as adults.

In the same Dunedin cohort, childhood social isolation was scored from two items rated by parents and teachers at ages 5, 7, 9 and 11 (the child tends to do things alone and is rather solitary; is not much liked by other children).
