3198.content: In two preregistered replications, with the original studies' first author (Sznycer) as third author, 81 students at the University of Hawaii rated 25 imagined situations (pride study) and 29 imagined situations (shame study), with pride or shame rated by one half of the sample and audience valuation or devaluation by the other half. Mean anticipated pride tracked how positively others would view a person in each situation (r = 0.90 across 25 situations), and mean anticipated shame tracked how negatively others would view them (r = 0.73 across 29 situations). Both results fell inside the confidence intervals of the original studies and met all three preregistered replication criteria, including a replication Bayes factor above 3.

3199.content: In 10 healthy adults given meals on a fixed schedule, with blood drawn 38 times over 24 hours, plasma ghrelin rose nearly twofold just before each meal and fell to its lowest level within an hour after eating, the mirror image of insulin. Between meals ghrelin followed a daily rhythm in step with leptin, rising through the day to a peak at 1 a.m. and falling overnight to a low at 9 a.m. The authors read the rise before meals as support for a role of ghrelin in starting a meal.

3200.content: In an online survey of 215 students at a large US state university (116 men, 99 women, mean age 18.7), people described up to ten times they had felt envy. Coded by two blind coders, the advantages named most often were a peer having more success attracting romantic partners (13.0% of all responses), a peer being more attractive (13.0%), a peer having more money (10.4%), a peer owning a status item such as an expensive car (8.3%) and a peer doing better at school (8.3%). The authors read this as envy being set off mostly by advantages tied to old adaptive problems such as getting resources and attracting mates.

In a second sample of 203 US undergraduates (101 men) who ranked 19 envy scenarios, the seven sex differences the authors expected from mate-preference research all appeared: women ranked a more attractive peer, a peer whose partner had more money and a peer with no sexual experience as more envy-provoking than men did, and men ranked a peer with more status, more signs of earning power, a more attractive partner, more athletic talent and more sexual success as more envy-provoking than women did. Success at attracting partners, popularity and sense of humour drew equal envy from both sexes, as the authors expected; a kinder peer drew more envy from women, which they had not expected.

3201.content: On the Fundamental Social Motives Inventory, a self-rating of how much each social motive matters, 7,296 people in 27 countries from the United States to Uganda (mean age 24) rated caring for kin and keeping a partner above seeking a new mate, and the same order held within each of the 27 countries. An earlier US online sample (1,560 adults) and a US life-coaching sample (3,214 adults ranking goals) showed the same order. The gap between mate-seeking and kin care was large (d = 1.54 for family, 1.67 for children in the 27-country data).

The order held in the groups expected to care most about finding a mate. Among 497 US undergraduates, mate-seeking was rated higher than in older samples, yet caring for family and keeping a partner were still rated far above it (d = 1.52 and 3.55). People not in a committed relationship rated mate-seeking much higher than those in one (d = 1.21), yet still rated kin care for family above it (d = 1.03). Women rated family motives somewhat higher than men did, but these sex differences were small next to the gap between family motives and mate-seeking.

3202.content: In three experiments, people rating themselves were flashed a comparison person too briefly to be seen consciously (subliminal priming), either a moderate or an extreme standard, high or low. Their self-ratings moved toward a moderate standard and away from an extreme one. The shift appeared only when the people were thinking about themselves while the standard was flashed. The authors read this as social comparison running even on a standard the person never knowingly saw.

3203.content: In Studies 1 to 4 of seven, pride split into two facets, which the authors call authentic and hubristic. The split appeared in how people grouped pride-related words, in how prone they said they were to pride, and in their reports of actual pride episodes. The two facets went with different personality traits and with different explanations people gave for their success, and the split was not a matter of pleasant against unpleasant, high against low arousal, or state against trait. Studies 5 to 7 built two short 7-item scales to measure each facet.

3204.content: In six studies in mainland China (students at Southwest University, samples of 104, 87 and 100), South Korea (one sample of 63 at Korea University, used in two studies) and the United States (203 students using Korean-derived words), pride split into the same two facets found in North America: an achievement-oriented authentic pride and an arrogant hubristic pride. In China, authentic pride went with crediting success to effort and with a pro-social, achievement-oriented personality, and hubristic pride with crediting it to fixed ability and a largely anti-social profile, as in the US.

3205.content: Vallerand and colleagues define passion as a strong liking for an activity that a person finds important and gives time and energy to, and propose two kinds. In harmonious passion the activity is taken into the person's identity freely and they choose to do it; in obsessive passion it is taken in under pressure, so the person feels pushed to do it. The authors report that four studies with more than 900 participants from different populations supported this model, with harmonious passion going with healthy adjustment and obsessive passion with negative feelings and rigid persistence.

3206.content: A random-effects meta-analysis of 94 studies (1,308 effect sizes) on the two kinds of passion found that harmonious passion went with more reported positive affect, life satisfaction, vitality, engagement, concentration, flow and self-esteem, and with less reported burnout, anxiety and conflict with the rest of life. Obsessive passion went with more reported negative affect, burnout, anxiety, rumination and conflict with the rest of life, and its small links with positive outcomes mostly vanished once harmonious passion was held constant. The pattern held across age and sex; some links varied by domain and culture.

3207.content: In two experiments, de Hooge and colleagues induced guilt or shame and measured short-term cooperation, with a two-person social dilemma game in Experiment 1 and an everyday cooperation measure in Experiment 2. Guilt raised cooperation among people who are mainly out for themselves (proselfs), repeating Ketelaar and Au (2003). Shame had no such effect.

3208.content: Mental health staff at the same public health service were surveyed in 2000 and again in 2015 with a short 10-item version of the Attitude to Personality Disorders Questionnaire and the same open questions about patients given the label borderline personality disorder. In 2000 staff more often described these patients in negative words such as 'attention seeking' and 'manipulative'; in 2015 they wrote more about treatment approaches and skills, such as 'management plan' and 'empathy', and their questionnaire scores were more positive.

3209.content: In an experiment, people who looked at their own Facebook profile rated their self-esteem higher afterwards than people in the comparison conditions, the opposite of what objective self-awareness theory predicts from seeing oneself. People who edited their own profile during the session and viewed it also reported higher self-esteem. The authors read this as selective self-presentation online shaping how people see themselves.

3210.content: In a German sleep laboratory, 72 healthy adults (aged 18 to 71) slept 11 consecutive nights, 8 of them with recorded air, road or rail traffic noise played at night (40, 80 or 120 events). Changes in sleep structure were small, which the authors attribute to habituation and rising arousal thresholds within and across nights. Brain (EEG) arousals to noise habituated across nights, but the heart-rate rise after each noise event did not: it habituated within a night but not from one night to the next.

Most noise-induced awakenings (up to 93%) took the place of awakenings that would have happened anyway, which kept the overall sleep structure largely intact, but only 62% to 67% of noise-induced brain arousals replaced spontaneous ones, so the rest added to the night's arousals and sleep was more fragmented at the fine scale. Road traffic noise changed sleep structure most, while people rated nights with air and rail noise as more disturbing; brain arousals and heart-rate responses rose with how fast a noise event rose in loudness and with its high-frequency energy.

3211.content: Participants did a memory task under either low or high social evaluation. Under high social evaluation they reported a stronger spotlight effect, the sense that others notice them, and judged their own performance more negatively; the sense that others could read their feelings (illusion of transparency) did not differ between the conditions. Under low evaluation the illusion of transparency was reported more than the spotlight effect, and under high evaluation the reverse. The authors relate this to the cognitive model of social phobia and read the spotlight effect as tied to being evaluated by others.

3212.content: In the cohort the authors draw on, the Oregon Adolescent Depression Project, 1,709 high-school students from western Oregon were interviewed in 1987 to 1989 (mean age 16.6) and a selected subset of 816 was interviewed again at about age 30. Excluding those who already met criteria at the start, adolescents diagnosed with social anxiety disorder by interview at entry had 6.5 times the odds of later meeting DSM-IV criteria for cannabis dependence (odds ratio 6.58, 95% CI 1.94 to 22.34) and 4.5 times the odds for alcohol dependence (odds ratio 4.47, 1.48 to 13.45), after adjusting for sex, depression, conduct disorder and other anxiety diagnoses; there was no link with the lighter labels cannabis abuse or alcohol abuse. By about age 30, 22% of those with the social anxiety diagnosis had met criteria for cannabis dependence against 5% of the rest. Adolescents diagnosed with other anxiety or mood labels at entry showed no such link after adjustment.

3213.content: In 394 healthy adults who filled in stress questionnaires and were then given nasal drops with one of five respiratory viruses (rhinovirus types 2, 9 or 14, respiratory syncytial virus or coronavirus 229E) and kept in quarantine, rates of infection and of clinical colds rose step by step with the degree of psychological stress reported beforehand. Infection rates ran from about 74 to about 90 percent and clinical colds from about 27 to 47 percent across stress levels. Controls for age, sex, allergy, season, housing, baseline antibodies, smoking, alcohol, exercise, diet, sleep quality and personality did not remove the association, and it held for all five viruses. The extra risk came from more infections, not from more symptoms once infected.

3214.content: In two longitudinal panels with a one-month gap (Study 2, 168 students; Study 3, 442 online respondents, preregistered), a sense of existential mattering, also called significance, at the first time point predicted higher meaning-in-life judgments a month later, while a sense of purpose and a sense of coherence did not. In a first study of 314 social media users the three senses and the meaning judgment were distinct from each other and from sense of control, belonging, self-esteem and mood.

3215.content: In an fMRI study of 19 people who received monetary rewards and, separately, social rewards in the form of a good reputation, acquiring a good reputation strongly activated reward-related areas, notably the striatum, and these areas overlapped with those activated by monetary reward. The authors read this as a common neural currency for rewards.

3216.content: In a prospective study of 91 patients with traumatic brain injury followed at 3, 6 and 12 months, with 27 multiple-trauma patients without brain injury as controls, 30 of the 91 (33 percent) met DSM-IV criteria for major depressive disorder on a structured clinical interview during the first year, significantly more often than the controls. Those diagnosed more often had a personal history of mood and anxiety disorders, showed anxiety (76.7 percent) and aggressive behaviour (56.7 percent), had poorer executive function and social functioning, and had smaller left prefrontal grey matter volumes on MRI at 3 months.

3217.content: Across studies with naturally occurring and experimentally induced emotion, fearful people gave pessimistic risk estimates and made risk-averse choices, while angry people gave optimistic risk estimates and made risk-seeking choices, closer to happy people than to fearful ones. Appraisals of certainty and control moderated these effects, and the sense of control mediated them.

3218.content: In a registered report with 780 US online adults (Amazon Mechanical Turk CloudResearch), a close replication of Experiments 1 to 3 of Lerner and Keltner (2001) supported the appraisal-tendency account for risk optimism in general and for positive and ambiguous events, but not for risk preference (choices) and not for risk optimism about negative events. Adding hope as a low-certainty, low-control positive emotion did not support the framework's assumptions.

3219.content: In 64 community adults aged 21 to 35 randomly given alcohol (target 0.08 percent blood alcohol; mean peak 0.079) or a placebo drink, eyeblink startle was potentiated by cues that predicted shock and by cues during blocks where shock could come at any time, by similar amounts (63.9 and 59.2 microvolts). Alcohol cut startle potentiation to cues in the unpredictable-shock blocks by 25.7 microvolts and left potentiation to predictable shock cues unchanged (a 4.6 microvolt difference, not significant). The alcohol effect did not extend to the intervals between cues in the unpredictable blocks.

3220.content: In a double-blind crossover study of 16 healthy recreational cannabis users (mean age 20.8, using about twice a month), oral THC (7.5 mg) or placebo was given before fMRI while they matched angry, fearful or happy faces. On placebo the right lateral amygdala responded more to threatening (angry, fearful) than to happy faces; on THC this threat response was absent, and THC significantly reduced it (Cohen's d 0.34 in the region-of-interest analysis). THC did not change visual or motor cortex activity or task performance, and the anxiety ratings participants reported did not change, while ratings of feeling high rose.

3221.content: In a 2 by 2 experiment, participants who had either never seen a Pleo toy dinosaur robot or had played with it for 10 minutes watched a video of friendly interaction with the robot and a video of the robot being tortured. During the torture video they showed higher physiological arousal than during the friendly video, and afterwards they reported fewer positive and more negative feelings and expressed empathic concern for the robot. Prior interaction with the robot made no difference.

3222.content: Across four studies, actors who imagined committing a social blunder (Study 1), who failed publicly on an intellectual task (Studies 2 and 3) or who were described in an embarrassing way (Study 4) expected to be judged more harshly by others than they actually were. The authors attribute the overestimate partly to the actors' focus on their own misfortune and their failure to consider the situational factors that soften onlookers' impressions.

3223.content: In 720 social drinkers (360 men, 360 women) placed in groups of three unacquainted people and randomly given a moderate alcoholic drink (mean blood alcohol about 0.06 percent after the interaction), a placebo drink or a plain control drink over 36 minutes, video coding showed that people given alcohol displayed Duchenne smiles for longer and negative facial expressions for shorter times, and alcohol groups spent more time with all three members smiling at once. Self-reported bonding on the Perceived Group Reinforcement Scale was higher with alcohol (mean 7.22) than with placebo (6.74), but did not differ significantly from the control drink (7.07, p = .27).

3224.content: A meta-analysis of 18 twin cohorts with 31,859 people from Europe, the United States and Australia estimated that, for separation anxiety disorder diagnoses and separation anxiety symptom scores, genes explained 43 percent of individual differences, the shared family environment 17 percent, and the rest came from non-shared environment. Heritability was higher in females (0.52) than males (0.26). Shared-environment estimates were higher when parents rated the child (0.23) than with self-report (0.05), which the authors say may reflect an age difference between subsamples.

3225.content: In a blinded field study, 75 healthy volunteers (mean age 26) slept at home for one night each, in random order, with no added noise or with 30 or 60 recorded aircraft noise events played in the bedroom (average maximum about 60 dB(A)). Noise worsened sleep quality. After the 60-event night, flow-mediated dilation of the arm artery was blunted, with a dose-dependent trend across conditions (10.4, 9.7 and 9.5 percent), and the blunting was larger when the 30-event night came first. Morning adrenaline rose from 28.3 to 33.2 and 34.1 ng/L, and pulse transit time shortened. Vitamin C reversed the vessel effect in a subgroup. Morning cortisol, IL-6 and C-reactive protein did not change.

3226.content: In a nationally representative telephone survey of 569 US adults three to five days after the September 11, 2001 attacks, 44 percent reported one or more substantial stress symptoms and 91 percent reported at least one symptom to some degree, with respondents throughout the country reporting them. People coped by talking with others (98 percent), religion (90 percent), group activities (60 percent) and donations (36 percent). Parents reported one or more stress symptoms in 35 percent of children, and 47 percent of children were worried about their own or loved ones' safety.

3227.content: Of 80 healthy students at Ruhr University Bochum, 67 who liked all the foods were assigned to stress (34) or a warm-water control (33), and 60 who learned the task were analysed. The stress was the socially evaluated cold pressor test (hand in ice water for up to 3 minutes while watched and filmed by an unfamiliar person), given before learning two actions that earned chocolate milk or orange juice. After one food was devalued by eating it to satiety, unstressed participants chose the action for the devalued food less, while stressed participants chose it as often as the action for the still-valued food. Stressed participants also knew fewer of the action-outcome links, and fewer known links went with more habitual choice (r = -0.31).

3228.content: In a Danish population cohort of 57,053 people aged 50 to 64 at enrolment (1993 to 1997), 1,600 had a first heart attack by 2006 (mean follow-up 9.8 years). Road traffic noise at the home address, estimated from address histories, was associated with heart attack, with a rate ratio of 1.12 per 10 dB (95 percent CI 1.02 to 1.22 for exposure in the year of the heart attack), after adjustment for air pollution (NOx), age, sex, education, lifestyle, and railway and airport noise, in a linear dose-response pattern.

3229.content: A meta-analysis of 30 laboratory studies in humans found that circulating interleukin-6 rose after acute psychological stress tasks (r = 0.19, p = 0.001), as did interleukin-1 beta (r = 0.58, p < 0.001), with a marginal rise in C-reactive protein (r = 0.12, p = 0.088). Effects on stimulated cytokine production were less consistent, and the size of the response varied with participants' health status and with when the post-stress blood samples were taken.

3230.content: In experiments, people who posed a fear face reported a larger visual field, made faster eye movements when locating targets, and drew in more nasal air volume and air velocity on inhaling; posing a disgust face gave the opposite pattern. A statistical model of how expressions look found that fear and disgust faces have opposite shape and surface features.

3231.content: A literature review on mood symptoms during corticosteroid treatment such as prednisone found that few studies used recognised symptom measures or defined diagnostic criteria. The limited data suggest that symptoms the authors label hypomania, mania, depression and psychosis are common during treatment, appear dose dependent and generally begin within the first few weeks; risk factors were not known.

3232.content: Nursing staff completed questionnaires about patients under three psychiatric labels (borderline personality disorder, schizophrenia and depression), rating dangerousness, social distance, optimism for change and their own experience of working with each group. Registered mental health nurses expressed more social rejection toward, and rated as more dangerous, patients with the borderline personality disorder label than patients with a schizophrenia diagnosis; health care assistants made no such distinction. Staff were least optimistic about patients with the borderline label and were more negative about working with them.

3233.content: A network meta-analysis of 101 randomised trials (13,164 adults who met diagnostic criteria for social anxiety disorder; 41 interventions or control conditions) found that only two classes beat an appropriate placebo on social anxiety scales: SSRIs and SNRIs against pill placebo (standardised mean difference -0.44, 95% credible interval -0.67 to -0.22) and individual cognitive behavioural therapy against psychological placebo (-0.56, -1.00 to -0.11). Against a waitlist, the largest effects were individual CBT (-1.19), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (-1.01) and benzodiazepines (-0.96).

3234.content: A Cochrane review of 66 placebo-controlled randomised trials (11,597 adults diagnosed with social anxiety disorder; trials of 1 to 24 weeks) found more treatment responders on SSRIs than on placebo (24 trials, 4,984 participants, risk ratio 1.65, 95% CI 1.48 to 1.85), and the authors rated that evidence very low quality. MAOIs, RIMAs and benzodiazepines also showed benefit on low-quality evidence, anticonvulsants that are GABA analogues on moderate-quality evidence, and the remaining drugs showed no benefit over placebo. More people withdrew from SSRI treatment than from placebo (risk ratio 2.59, low-quality evidence), though absolute withdrawal rates were low.

The same Cochrane review found the SSRI trials for the social anxiety disorder label carried very low-quality evidence and a high risk of publication bias: funnel plots and Egger tests showed that small trials with non-significant results appeared to be missing, so the size of the response to SSRIs and to drugs overall may be exaggerated.

3235.content: On a task that required keeping one's place in a sequence of steps, interruptions averaging 4.4 seconds tripled the rate of sequence errors on the trials just after the interruption compared with baseline trials, and interruptions averaging 2.8 seconds, about the time one step takes, doubled it. Errors unrelated to the sequence showed no interruption effect, and response times showed smaller effects than sequence errors.

3236.content: In a field survey of 88 office employees at two sites, 99% reported that their concentration was impaired by parts of office noise, above all telephones left ringing at empty desks and people talking in the background. The study found no evidence that longer exposure to these sounds led workers to habituate.

3237.content: In an fMRI experiment with 30 adults from a US university community, participants kept to a chosen goal more often after setbacks they could control than after setbacks they could not, although both came equally often (F(1,29) = 20.69, p < .001). Ventral striatum activity to controllable setbacks went with more persistence, and ventromedial prefrontal activity to uncontrollable setbacks went with both persistence and how negative the setbacks felt.

3238.content: In a network study of 36 employees of a public child care organisation, analysed with exponential random graph models, both positive and negative gossip were about colleagues in the gossiper's own work group. Negative gossip singled out specific individuals, particularly those low in informal status, while positive gossip spread more evenly through the network.

3239.content: In an experiment, 40 female clerical workers were randomly assigned to 3 hours of low-intensity noise made to resemble a typical open office, or to a quiet control condition. The noise raised urinary epinephrine (adrenaline) but not norepinephrine or cortisol, and afterwards the noise group made fewer attempts at unsolvable puzzles, which the authors read as lower motivation; they also made fewer posture adjustments at their workstation. The noise group rated their setting as noisier, yet the two groups did not differ in perceived stress.

3240.content: Gilbert and Allan built new self-report scales of defeat and entrapment and gave them, with other social rank measures, to a student sample and to patients diagnosed with depression. Both scales correlated significantly with depression scores; defeat kept a strong association with depression scores after controlling for hopelessness (r = 0.62), while the link between hopelessness and depression scores shrank substantially once defeat was controlled. Entrapment and defeat added substantially to the explained variance in depression scores beyond the other social rank variables.

3241.content: In a social network study of employees, friendship ties between two employees went with both positive and negative gossip between them, while workflow ties, which the authors describe as less trusting, went only with positive gossip; being embedded in the same friendship network made it more likely that a pair shared negative gossip. Employees who gossiped more were rated lower on performance by their supervisors and higher on informal influence by their peers.

3242.content: In three tasks with 40 heterosexual US university students (20 men, 20 women), the chance to view photos of opposite-sex strangers behaved like other rewards: it lost value with delay, it traded against money, and people pressed keys to see a photo again. Men gave up money to see attractive women (0.45 cents per image) and, less, average-looking women (0.19 cents), while women valued attractive men only slightly (0.05 cents, not significant) and needed payment to view unattractive men (-0.18 cents). Men worked about twice as hard as women to view photos, and both sexes worked harder for more attractive faces.

3243.content: Using project data from an Indian software services firm, the authors found that team familiarity, the average number of times each member had worked with every other member, went with better team performance (the authors report a significant positive effect), while conventional measures of individual experience such as years at the firm were not consistently related to performance. The years individuals had spent in a given role within a team also went with better team performance.

3244.content: In a lab study, 40 inpatients in treatment for depression (the authors' clinical group) and 38 controls without depression worked on anagrams, some unsolvable. The inpatients spent less time on the unsolvable anagrams, while the two groups did not differ in the time they needed to solve the solvable ones. The authors read this as evidence that low mood helps a person let go of goals that cannot be reached.

3245.content: Kurzban reanalysed the raw data of four experiments from Gailliot and colleagues (2007) in which participants who had not been asked to fast had blood glucose measured before and after a self-control task (an attention task in two studies, the Stroop task, emotion regulation; 65 people in all). In none of the four did the reduction in glucose replicate (Study 3 showed a non-significant fall of 4.40 mg/dL): the change across them averaged plus 1.58 mg/dL, and the share of people whose glucose dropped did not differ from chance. Only the original Study 1, whose raw data were reported lost and in which participants had fasted for three hours, showed a fall, which Kurzban reads as possibly regression to the mean.

From published brain metabolism figures, Kurzban argues that the brain as a whole uses about a quarter of a calorie per minute and that local task-related increases are on the order of 1 percent, so a 5-minute self-control task would cost about .0125 extra calories, and well under .2 calories even on extreme assumptions. He also cites a direct measure (Madsen and colleagues 1995) in which the glucose the brain took from the blood did not change during a 10-minute card-sorting task.

3246.content: In two experiments, people who switched from an unfinished task to another kept thinking about the first task (attention residue) and performed worse on the next one. Finishing the first task was not enough by itself to free attention: finishing it under time pressure helped people disengage from it and went with higher performance on the next task.

3247.content: Mael and Ashforth define identification with an organisation as perceived oneness with it and experiencing its successes and failures as one's own. In survey answers from 297 alumni of an all-male religious college, identification with the college went with the college's distinctiveness and prestige and with absence of competition inside it, with satisfaction, years spent as a student and sentimentality, and with giving money, advising one's children and others to attend, and taking part in school functions. It did not go with competition against other schools, time since attending, number of schools attended or having had a mentor.

3248.content: In interviews with 40 employees, most had been in situations where they were concerned about an issue at work and did not raise it with a supervisor; silence covered a wide range of issues, and several said they did not feel comfortable raising any concern with those above them. The reason given most often was fear of being viewed or labelled negatively, and so of damaging valued relationships.

3249.content: In an fMRI experiment with 27 healthy women, moderate acute stress was induced by strongly aversive film clips (against neutral clips) with an instruction to relate them to themselves, checked with autonomic, hormonal and subjective measures. During a numerical N-back working-memory task, stress reduced working-memory activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and was accompanied by less deactivation of the default mode network.

3250.content: In a commentary, Raichle and Gusnard report that the human brain is about 2 percent of body weight but accounts for about 20 percent of the body's oxygen and calorie use, at a rate that stays remarkably constant despite widely varying mental and motor activity. The changes in blood flow and metabolism that go with task activation are very small against this ongoing activity: local blood-flow changes measured with PET during most cognitive tasks are often 5 percent or less, and attempts to measure whole-brain changes during intense mental activity have found none.

3251.content: In a teaching hospital, the authors studied total joint replacement operations, with procedure completion time as the measure of performance. Separating three kinds of experience (each team member's own cumulative experience, the organisation's cumulative experience, and the team members' cumulative experience of working together), they found that each kind made a distinct contribution to team performance.

3252.content: From participant observation as a worker in one piecework machine shop, Roy reports that loafing on the job was more than simple inactivity: the work group restricted its production every day, and keeping to an agreed ceiling (a 'bogey') was only one of several kinds of output restriction the machine operators used.

3253.content: In interviews with 38 people (19 workplace peer friendships), the authors found three transitions: from coworker or acquaintance to friend, from friend to close friend, and from close friend to almost best friend. Participants attributed the first transition mainly to working together in close proximity, sharing common ground and socialising outside work; the second mainly to problems in personal and work life; the third to life events, work problems and the passage of time. Talk became broader, more intimate and less cautious at each step.

3254.content: In the 2011 Dutch wave of an international student survey (GUESSS), 10,104 students at 14 universities and 24 universities of applied sciences in the Netherlands answered the six-item WHO adult ADHD self-report screener (ASRS-6) and said which career they intended to follow after their studies. Students who scored higher on the screener were more likely to intend to start a business than to become employees (odds ratio 1.28 per unit of the average score), and part of the link ran through a higher self-reported propensity to take risks.

3255.content: In a quasi-experimental field study of female healthcare assistants, 13 who reported working under two differently perceived supervisors at the same workplace on different days had ambulatory blood pressure recorded every 30 minutes over 12 hours on three days. Their systolic pressure was 15 mm Hg and diastolic 7 mm Hg higher on days under the less favoured supervisor. The 15 controls, with one supervisor or two similarly perceived ones, showed a 3 mm Hg systolic difference and no significant diastolic one. The larger the gap in how the two supervisors were perceived, the larger the blood pressure difference, and the gap in perceived interpersonal fairness was the strongest predictor.

3256.content: Two groups of participants did either high-demand or low-demand cognitive control tasks through an approximate workday, making economic choices in between, while magnetic resonance spectroscopy followed brain metabolites. Only the high-demand group showed the markers of fatigue in its choices: less pupil dilation while deciding and a shift toward options with short delay and little effort. At the end of the day the high-demand group had higher glutamate concentration and glutamate/glutamine diffusion in the lateral prefrontal cortex, relative to the low-demand group and to the primary visual cortex.

3257.content: Interviewing 14 entrepreneurs who had been diagnosed with ADHD and ran their own firms (recruited through Sweden's largest ADHD support organisation), the authors built a model in which impulsivity is a major spur to entrepreneurial action and hyperfocus a major catalyst for its consequences, good and bad. Respondents with hyperfocus on their business built expertise and acted productively; those without it tended to spread into unrelated areas and reported overload and stress.

All 14 respondents said their energy levels vary a great deal during the day, and the interviews put being able to work in the hours when energy is high, whenever that is, as one of the largest advantages of running one's own business. Several reported higher work capacity, higher energy and less need for sleep than people they know.

3258.content: In a review, Zentall argues against the then-current practice of reducing stimulation for hyperactive children: she proposes that hyperactive behaviour may come from a homeostatic mechanism that raises stimulation for a child who is getting too little sensory input, and cites the effects of drug and behaviour therapies and research on sensory deprivation as support.

3259.content: Using registers of the whole Swedish population, the authors find that parents who lose a child earn less, are more often out of work, divorce more often and are more often admitted to hospital afterwards. The authors' 2012 discussion-paper version gives the sizes: six years after the loss mothers' labour income was about 12 percent lower and fathers' about 10 percent lower; married mothers' risk of divorce was 5.3 percentage points higher six years on; and in the year of the death the probability of a hospital stay with a mental diagnosis rose by 1 percentage point for mothers (almost 150 percent) and 0.84 points for fathers (about 100 percent).

3260.content: In a phase 2 double-blind randomised trial, 59 patients diagnosed with long-standing, moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder got either two doses of 25 mg psilocybin three weeks apart plus six weeks of daily placebo (30 patients) or two doses of 1 mg psilocybin plus six weeks of daily escitalopram (29 patients); all received psychological support. On the primary outcome, the change in the self-rated QIDS-SR-16 depression score at week 6, scores fell by 8.0 points with psilocybin and 6.0 points with escitalopram, a difference of 2.0 points that was not significant (95% CI -5.0 to 0.9). On secondary outcomes, which the authors did not correct for multiple comparisons, 70% against 48% met the response cut-off and 57% against 28% scored in the remission range.

3261.content: In a randomised waiting-list-controlled trial at Johns Hopkins (enrolment 2017 to 2019), 27 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder and not taking antidepressants were assigned to immediate treatment (15) or treatment after an 8-week delay (12); 24 completed. Treatment was two psilocybin sessions (20 and 30 mg per 70 kg) within about 11 hours of supportive psychotherapy. Clinician-rated GRID-HAMD depression scores in the immediate group were 8.0 and 8.5 at weeks 1 and 4 after treatment, against 23.8 and 23.5 in the waiting group at the same time points (Cohen d 2.5 and 2.6). Across the whole sample, 71% met the authors' response cut-off at weeks 1 and 4 and 58% and 54% scored in the remission range.

3262.content: All 24 completers of the Davis 2021 psilocybin trial were followed for 12 months after their second dose. Clinician-rated GRID-HAMD depression scores stayed far below baseline at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months (Cohen d 2.3, 2.0, 2.6 and 2.4), and at 12 months 75% met the authors' response cut-off and 58% scored in the remission range. By 12 months 8 of the 24 (33%) had started or resumed daily antidepressant medication; those 8 had higher baseline scores, and their 12-month scores did not differ significantly from the others'.

3263.content: In a phase 2 double-blind trial funded by COMPASS Pathfinder, 233 adults diagnosed with a treatment-resistant episode of major depression were randomised to a single dose of a proprietary synthetic psilocybin at 25 mg (79), 10 mg (75) or 1 mg as control (79), each with psychological support. On the clinician-rated MADRS depression scale (baseline 32 or 33), scores fell by 12.0 points with 25 mg, 7.9 with 10 mg and 5.4 with 1 mg by week 3; 25 mg beat 1 mg by 6.6 points (95% CI -10.2 to -2.9) and 10 mg did not differ from 1 mg. Response and remission at week 3 in the 25 mg group were in line with this, sustained response to week 12 was not. Adverse events occurred in 77% of participants, and suicidal ideation or behaviour or self-injury occurred in all dose groups.

3264.content: The Collaborative Longitudinal Personality Disorders Study followed treatment-seeking patients aged 18 to 45 from 19 clinical settings in four northeastern US cities for 10 years: 175 diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, 312 with cluster C personality disorders and 95 with major depressive disorder only (63% of the borderline group completed). By 10 years, 85% of the borderline group had remitted by the authors' definition (two or fewer of the nine criteria for 12 months; 91% with a 2-month definition). Of those who remitted, 11% met the criteria again within 10 years (12% in the abstract), against 25% in the other personality disorder group; with the 2-month definition, 21% against 67% in the depression group.

In the same cohort, social functioning improved only modestly: patients diagnosed with borderline personality disorder stayed more impaired than the other two groups throughout, their mean Global Assessment of Functioning score stayed in the mid 50s, and after 10 years only about one third had full-time employment. Fewer borderline criteria in one year went with better functioning scores the next year, while better functioning did not go with fewer criteria the next year.

3265.content: A systematic review of 182 studies of practising doctors (109,628 people in 45 countries, published 1991 to 2018) found reported prevalence of overall burnout from 0% to 80.5%. Studies used at least 142 different definitions of burnout or its parts; 85.7% used a version of the Maslach Burnout Inventory, with at least 47 different definitions of overall burnout among them. The authors judged pooling unreliable given this heterogeneity, and could not reliably link burnout to sex, age, country, year, specialty or reported depressive symptoms.

The authors point out that the most common Maslach cut-offs mark a doctor as emotionally exhausted for feelings a few times a month, and as depersonalised for feelings once a month or less, so the prevalence figures in the literature mostly count reported symptoms of burnout and not a clinical syndrome.

3266.content: A systematic review of 113 studies and a meta-analysis of 61 of them (45,539 nurses in 49 countries, several specialties) put the pooled share of nurses reporting burnout symptoms at 11.23%. Rates differed by region, specialty and burnout measure: highest in Sub-Saharan Africa and lowest in Europe and Central Asia, highest among paediatric nurses and lowest among geriatric care nurses.

3267.content: Fourteen information workers (analysts, software developers and managers) in one team of a US investment-management IT company, most of them in cubicles in an open office, were shadowed and timed to the second for three days each (about 26 hours of formal observation per person). They spent on average about three minutes on an event and a little over two minutes with any one device or paper document before switching. Each person worked on about ten separate projects or areas of work ('working spheres') a day and stayed in one for about 11.5 minutes at a stretch before switching to another.

3268.content: Twenty-four information workers (7 managers, 9 analysts, 8 developers) in two teams of one IT outsourcing company were shadowed for three days each (over 700 hours in all). On average 57.1% of their stretches of work on a project were interrupted by something outside that project. Workers whose desk shared a wall with a teammate's cubicle had more of their stretches interrupted than teammates seated apart (62.9% against 49.3%), though they also stayed a little longer per stretch (11 min 56 s against 9 min 56 s). People overheard neighbours through the cubicle walls and were drawn into their problems.

In the same study, 77.2% of interrupted work was taken up again the same day. When it was, it took on average 25 minutes 26 seconds (SD 54 min 48 s) before the person returned to it, and in between they worked on an average of 2.26 other projects.

3269.content: WHO's guideline development group strongly recommends keeping road traffic noise below 53 dB Lden (a day-evening-night average), as road traffic noise above this level is associated with adverse health effects, and below 45 dB Lnight at night, as above that it is associated with adverse effects on sleep. The 53 dB value comes from the evidence on annoyance (an absolute risk of 10% of being highly annoyed at 53.3 dB Lden, rounded to 53); the group rated the evidence on the adverse effects of road traffic noise as moderate quality.

The guideline group notes that road traffic is the most widespread source of noise pollution, by the number of people affected inside and outside urban areas, and cites the European Environment Agency's estimate (Blanes et al. 2017) that more than 100 million people in Europe are exposed to road traffic noise above 55 dB Lden and over 72 million above 50 dB Lnight. It expects road traffic noise is unlikely to fall much, as transport demand and city populations are expected to grow.

3270.content: In the sixth European Working Conditions Survey (2015; 43,850 workers interviewed face to face in 35 countries), the share of EU28 workers who said they could choose or change the order of their tasks was 68%, the speed or rate of their work 71% and their methods of work 69%, up from 63%, 69% and 67% in 2005. 29% said they had a say in the choice of their colleagues always or most of the time. Discretion was higher among the self-employed and in micro and small firms, and highest among managers, professionals and agricultural workers.

In the same survey, about half of EU28 workers took part in decisions about their own work: 46% were consulted always or most of the time before objectives were set for their work, 49% were involved in improving the work organisation or processes of their department, and 47% said they could influence decisions important for their work always or most of the time. About one third of plant and machine operators and workers in elementary occupations were involved in such decisions, against eight in ten managers.

3271.content: A meta-analysis of 26 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trials (2,160 adults diagnosed with depression or scoring above a cut-off; trials published before 20 December 2017) found omega-3 fatty acid supplements lowered depression scores more than placebo overall (SMD -0.28), with effect sizes the authors call small to modest and high heterogeneity (I squared 75%). Formulas that were all or mostly (60% or more) EPA, at an EPA dose of 1 g a day or less, lowered scores more than placebo (SMD -0.50 and -1.03), while formulas that were all or mostly DHA did not.

3272.content: Pooling 3,663 population-based studies that measured height and weight in 222 million people in 200 countries and territories, the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration estimated that the global age-standardised share of adults with obesity (BMI of 30 or more) rose from 8.8% in 1990 to 18.5% in 2022 among women and from 4.8% to 14.0% among men, so that 504 million women and 374 million men had obesity in 2022. Among school-aged children and adolescents it rose from 1.7% to 6.9% in girls and from 2.1% to 9.3% in boys. In 2022 obesity was more common than underweight in 177 countries for women and 145 for men.
